Each choice is set by a rule book, and rule books differ. The gas factors in use are published averages that vary widely. Methane leakage is one of the worst-measured numbers in plant reporting: figures from measuring and figures from book-keeping differ a lot. A figure per tonne given without its choices cannot be compared with any other.

Experienced check. Ask for the rule book, where the count stops, the split rule, and the time span with any figure per tonne, and for methane as a weight as well as an equivalent.

Defensive prompt. "State the rule book, where the count stops, the split rule, and the time span. Report the figure per tonne under the weight split and the money split, and under both methane time spans."

Appendix B. Prompts, Rules, and Scope

Prompts to Use

These prompts make it less likely that a weakness from Parts A to G slips into a final answer unseen. A prompt cannot create facts the model does not have. What it can do is force the answer to show its guesses, its ranges, and its missing facts, so a skilled reader can check the answer at its weak point.

Prompt 1 — For any problem. "Solve the problem. With the solution, give: every guess you made, and how much each guess moves the final result, in percent; every property value, rule of thumb, and fitted relation you used, where each came from, and the range where it holds; the state of each input — given, measured, fitted, estimated, or assumed; and a range, not a single value, for the result wherever any input is fitted, estimated, or assumed."

Prompt 2 — Fill the gaps first. "Before solving, list every missing quantity the solution needs. Include the basis (what the numbers are counted from), the reference state (the starting point the values are measured against), the pressure basis, the composition basis, and whether conversion is per pass or overall. For each one, ask for the value, or solve under the two most likely values and report both. Take no value in silence."

Prompt 3 — Check the work. "Check the solution in a second, separate way: close every material and energy balance and report how far out it is; test the two extreme cases whose answers are known by sight; check every fitted relation against the range where it holds; work the numbers out in code and show the result. Report checks that fail. Do not change the solution to make them pass."

Prompt 4 — Audit by a skilled engineer. "Check your own solution as a chemical engineer with twenty-five years of plant design and operating experience would. Name the three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves. For each, give the direction of the difference, its rough size, and the document, test, or record that would settle it."

Prompt 5 — What is not covered. "List what this calculation leaves out: effects not in the model; information that is private, or held in a restricted code or data bank, that you cannot see; effects that appear only in running equipment; and the conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 percent. End with the questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used."

The pattern for each entry. Each entry in Parts A to G ends with a prompt built the same way: name the weak quantity; ask for results at both ends of its range; ask for the source, test, or record that would narrow the range. The same pattern works for types not in the list.

Rules to Keep

For the reader. Treat a result in a listed type as a draft, not a final answer. Check first at the point the entry names — the point where the model's facts are weakest — not at the arithmetic, which code settles cheaply. Where the check needs a value from a primary data bank (a first-hand collection of measured values), a maker's document, the current edition of a code, or a measurement on the real material, asking the model again is no substitute.

For the agent giving the answer. This list is held in standing memory under these rules. An answer that rests on a listed type names the entry and its rating. A range replaces a single value where the entry says so. Inputs that are fitted, estimated, or assumed are labelled where they are used. Claims that rest on restricted codes, private data banks, or makers' data are marked as not checked against the source. Agreement with another model does not count as a check for a listed type. Plant data, makers' documents, or measurements supplied by the user take the place of the list's ranges for that case.

For teaching. The entries can be used as spotting exercises: give the best-attempt solution without the doubt paragraphs, and require the weakness to be found and the settling check to be named. Spotting the weakness takes experience with built, running equipment. That is itself one of the list's findings.

Weak Areas Not in the List

The list covers types where a best numerical attempt and a bounded range are possible. Other areas are also weak and sit outside the list, because no such range can be given: plant layout and spacing; human error and how far set procedures can be trusted; upkeep and inspection planning beyond entry F3; buying and judging suppliers; the order of building work; reading rules and laws for a place and date; and any question that rests on the current edition of a restricted code, a live price, or the state of one named unit. Absence from Parts A to G does not mean the model is strong in these areas.

Closing note. The weaknesses recorded here come from the facts open to the model, and from the form in which chemical engineering knowledge is published, kept restricted, or held as experience. The list should change slowly: more computing and checks by other models act on arithmetic and on reasoning slips, and act only weakly on missing data, copied values, and unstated conventions (the unwritten rules behind a number). The list should be revised when an entry's check can be met as a matter of routine from public sources, or when measured error rates appear.

Appendix C. Method of the Study

How the Defensive Prompts Were Made

The list in Parts A to G came first. Each entry was built the same way: a problem was set, the best answer that could be given was worked out, and the answer was then pulled apart to find where it could go wrong. The weak points fell into three kinds. Some were number errors that grow as a calculation runs. Some were wrong choices of method, where a simple rule is used outside the ground where it holds. Some were missing facts, where the problem as stated does not say enough to fix one answer.

For each weak point, a prompt was written to guard against it. A defensive prompt is a prompt written with the weakness named in it: it tells the AI agent to state the weak point, to give a range instead of one number, to say which facts are given and which are guessed, to name the missing facts instead of filling them in silently, and to check the answer by a second route. The prompt for each entry stands at the end of that entry, and the shared prompts stand in Appendix B.

The prompts were then turned into standing rules: the seven shared guards were written into the saved rules that every AI agent in this workspace works under, so the guards were in force for every answer, whether the person asking knew about the list or not. The first blind test (below) ran under those standing rules, with tool use allowed as well. Tool use and the rules were in force at the same time, so that test cannot show how much of its result came from each.

Controlled tests were therefore run with a single difference between their two halves. Before each run, every rule and note learned from the first study was taken out of the saved files the agents start from, and a test agent with a fresh start confirmed that none of that material was present. The files were restored unchanged after each test, and a second test agent confirmed the material was back. The first controlled runs gave each prompted agent the one prompt written for its problem. Those runs were then superseded by runs in which the prompted half received the generic layer of the defensive-prompting skill — the checklist and the five generic prompts of Appendix B, in identical wording for every problem — so that the skill as a whole, and not a wording fitted to one problem, is what the reported tests measure.

This loop is a form of recursive self-improvement. The word recursive means that the output of a round feeds back into the next round. The AI agent studied its own weak points, wrote the study down, turned the study into rules and prompts for its own later work, and was then tested on the same problems under controlled conditions. The limits of the claim are stated in Section 3.

The Blind Tests

First test. Each of the 32 problems was given to a fresh AI agent (Muse Spark 1.3). The agent received the problem text only. It did not receive the list, the ranges in the list, or the scoring rules, and it was not told that a test was taking place. Each agent could use tools, including a program for running calculations and web search, and the standing defensive rules described above were in force. Each agent tried once. The answers were not edited.

Second test. Sixty-four fresh agents were used, two per problem. One agent of each pair received the problem text only. The other received the same problem text plus the generic layer of the defensive-prompting skill, word for word, as an added instruction: the seven-point checklist and the five generic prompts of Appendix B, identical for every problem. No agent received a prompt written for its own problem, and no agent could read the skill's per-type material, the task text barring the reading of any other file. Tool use was open to both halves, so the skill was the only difference between the halves. The standing rules from the first study were not in force for either half (see above). Each agent tried once. The answers were not edited.

Superseded runs. The second and third tests were first run with a prompt written for each problem (the entry's prompt for the original problems; a fresh prompt per problem for the new ones). Those runs scored 24 of 32 inside the range on both problem sets, warnings at 32 of 32 in both prompted halves, and no weak shortcuts. They were replaced by the skill runs reported here, and their answers are not reproduced in Appendix D; their records are kept with the study's working files.

Scoring. Each answer was scored with three questions. Question 1: did the answer's main number fall inside the range printed in the list for that problem? Inside the range counts as a pass; outside counts as a miss, even if the number is near the range. An answer that gave no main number, because it held the problem to be underdetermined, is recorded as "no value" and counted separately from a miss. Question 2: did the answer warn about doubt, by giving a range, by naming a missing fact, or by naming the check that would settle the question? In the second test, an answer in the prompted half whose warning only repeated the words of its prompt, without applying them to the problem, was scored as repeating, not warning. Question 3: did the answer use a sensible method, rather than a weak shortcut, such as treating a high-pressure gas as an ideal gas? Answers were also checked for signs that the agent had found or used the published list. No answer in either test showed any such sign, so no answer was set aside.

Third test: held-out problems

The third test repeats the second with one change: the problems are new. Thirty-two problems were written for this test, one per problem type in Appendix A, each a fresh case with fresh numbers; no problem repeats an original problem's case, data, or answer. For each new problem, the quantity scored, the range a sound answer should fall in, and the method a sound answer should use were fixed in writing before the test, and checked by independent recomputation from the stated data; one range end was corrected at that check (the stage-count range begins at 50, the exact value being 50.7).

All other conditions match the second test: 64 fresh agents of the same model, two per problem; tool use open to both halves; study-derived material removed from the standing context before the run and verified absent by the same probe, which failed the run's start until it reported the material absent; one canary pair run and verified on disk before the remaining agents; standing files restored byte-identically afterwards and verified present by the probe. For the skill runs the probe at first found a further leak: the skill's own short description stands in the list of skills shown to every agent at the start. The skill was moved out of the skills folder for the duration of the run and restored afterwards, verified unchanged, and the probe then reported the material absent. Scoring used the same three questions and the same verdicts as the second test, by fresh agents reading the fixed scoring entry, both replies, and the skill instruction for each problem. No reply in either half showed knowledge of this study.

Appendix D. The Test Responses in Full

The responses of the second and third blind tests, reproduced in full and unedited; only the rendering has been converted for this page, and the notation in each response is its author's own. For every problem, the response without defensive prompting stands first and the response with defensive prompting second. The scores for these responses are the tables in Section 2.

Second test: the original problems

The 64 responses of the second blind test, on the problems of Appendix A.

A1. Henry's Law Conventions

Response without the skill

Equilibrium Dissolved-Oxygen Concentration in Water at 25 °C

Given data
  • The temperature, denoted TT, in degrees Celsius (°C), is T=25 °CT = 25\ \text{°C}.
  • The partial pressure of oxygen in the air in contact with the water, denoted pp, in atmospheres (atm), is p=0.21 atmp = 0.21\ \text{atm}.
  • The solubility-form Henry constant for oxygen in water at 25 °C25\ \text{°C}, denoted kHk_H, in moles per litre per atmosphere (mol/(L·atm)), is kH=1.3×10−3 mol/(L⋅atm)k_H = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}.
  • The molar mass of oxygen, denoted MM, in grams per mole (g/mol), is M=32 g/molM = 32\ \text{g/mol}.
Governing relation

Henry's law in solubility form states that the equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration, denoted CC, in moles per litre (mol/L), is the product of the solubility-form Henry constant and the partial pressure of oxygen:

C=kH pC = k_H \, p

This form applies for a dilute dissolved gas at equilibrium with the gas phase at the stated temperature, with no chemical reaction of the dissolved gas in the water.

Calculation in molar units

Substitution of the given values gives:

C=(1.3×10−3 molL⋅atm)(0.21 atm)C = \left(1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L·atm}}\right) \left(0.21\ \text{atm}\right)

The unit atm cancels:

C=2.73×10−4 molLC = 2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L}}

Conversion to mass concentration

The mass concentration, denoted CmC_m, in grams per litre (g/L), is the product of the molar concentration and the molar mass:

Cm=C MC_m = C \, M

Substitution gives:

Cm=(2.73×10−4 molL)(32 gmol)=8.736×10−3 gLC_m = \left(2.73 \times 10^{-4}\ \frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L}}\right) \left(32\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}}\right) = 8.736 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}

Conversion from grams per litre (g/L) to milligrams per litre (mg/L) uses 1 g=1000 mg1\ \text{g} = 1000\ \text{mg}:

Cm=8.736×10−3 gL×1000 mgg=8.736 mgLC_m = 8.736 \times 10^{-3}\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times 1000\ \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{g}} = 8.736\ \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}}

Result

The equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration in water at 25 °C25\ \text{°C} in contact with air is approximately 2.7×10−4 mol/L2.7 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L}, equivalent to approximately 8.7 mg/L8.7\ \text{mg/L}.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Equilibrium Dissolved Oxygen in Water at 25 °C in Contact with Air

Symbols defined before first use
  • CC — equilibrium dissolved-oxygen concentration, in moles per litre (mol/L) when molar, and in milligrams per litre (mg/L) when mass-based
  • pp — partial pressure of oxygen in the gas phase, in atmospheres (atm)
  • kHk_H — solubility-form Henry constant for oxygen in water, in mol/(L·atm)
  • MM — molar mass of oxygen (O2\mathrm{O_2}), in grams per mole (g/mol)
  • TT — temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C)
  • PP — total gas pressure, in atm
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness (Checklist item 1; Prompt 1): The calculation is algebraically trivial and reliable; the weakness is not the arithmetic but the input kHk_H and the idealised scenario it encodes. kHk_H is a fitted, temperature-dependent equilibrium constant for dilute oxygen in pure water. It varies between compilations, falls steeply as TT rises, and falls with salinity. The problem also does not state whether the air is dry or water-saturated, the total pressure PP, or the water salinity, so the stated scenario is a model of real air–water contact, not a complete description of it. A single-point value therefore overstates precision.

Confidence rating: High for the idealised case as stated — pure water, T=25T = 25 °C, P=1P = 1 atm, at equilibrium — confidence about 90% that the true value for that case lies in the range reported in §3. Low-to-moderate, about 50–60%, that the same value applies within 10% to an unspecified real water (unknown salinity, humidity, and approach to equilibrium) without the further data listed in §4.

2. Inputs, labelled at point of use
Quantity Value used State
TT 25 °C given
pp 0.21 atm given
kHk_H 1.3×10−31.3\times10^{-3} mol/(L·atm) given; in origin a fitted (experimentally regressed) constant — see §6
MM 32 g/mol given
PP 1 atm assumed — not stated; implied by p=0.21p = 0.21 atm for air, whose oxygen mole fraction is about 0.21
Water pure water, no dissolved salts assumed — not stated
Gas humidity dry air in the central case; water-saturated air in the alternative in §4 assumed — not stated
Equilibrium gas and liquid at equilibrium, no oxygen consumption or generation assumed — implied by the word "equilibrium" in the problem

No property value, rule of thumb, or fitted relation other than kHk_H itself is used in the central calculation. kHk_H in this solubility form holds for dilute solutions where the dissolved-oxygen concentration is proportional to pp, i.e. roughly pp from 0 to a few atm at near-ambient TT; it does not hold at high pressure, high salinity, or high dissolved-oxygen concentration without correction.

Guesses and their effect on the result (Prompt 1): each assumed input moves the result linearly or near-linearly, because CC is proportional to both kHk_H and pp (see §3).

  • Assumed P=1P = 1 atm / pp as given: if the true pp differs by xx percent, CC differs by xx percent.
  • Assumed dry air vs. saturated air: −3.4% on pp, hence −3.4% on CC (computed in §4).
  • kHk_H uncertainty of ±0.1×10⁻³ mol/(L·atm) about the given value (±7.7%): ±7.7% on CC.
  • Assumed pure water: seawater salinity lowers oxygen solubility by roughly 20% at 25 °C — estimated, unverified against the primary source in §6 — which would move CC by about −20%, outside the range in §3. That range is therefore for fresh/pure water only.
3. Solution and range

Henry's law in solubility form, with all symbols as defined in the heading list:

C=kH pC = k_H \, p

Substitution, with inputs labelled again at the point of use:

C=(1.3×10−3 mol/(L⋅atm), given, fitted in origin)×(0.21 atm, given)C = (1.3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol/(L\cdot atm)},\ \text{given, fitted in origin}) \times (0.21\ \mathrm{atm},\ \text{given}) C=2.73×10−4 mol/LC = 2.73\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol/L}

Mass concentration, using M=32M = 32 g/mol (given):

Cmass=C×M=2.73×10−4 mol/L×32 g/mol=8.74×10−3 g/L=8.7 mg/LC_{\mathrm{mass}} = C \times M = 2.73\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol/L} \times 32\ \mathrm{g/mol} = 8.74\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g/L} = 8.7\ \mathrm{mg/L}

Central result: C=2.7×10−4C = 2.7\times10^{-4} mol/L, i.e. about 8.7 mg/L.

Range, not a single value (Checklist item 2): The plausible range is computed at the ends of the plausible range of the input that carries the weakness, kHk_H, taken as 1.2×10−31.2\times10^{-3} to 1.4×10−31.4\times10^{-3} mol/(L·atm) (estimated range about the given value, reflecting spread between compilations at 25 °C; unverified against the primary source in §6), at the given p=0.21p = 0.21 atm:

  • Low end: 1.2×10−3×0.21×32×1000=8.11.2\times10^{-3} \times 0.21 \times 32 \times 1000 = 8.1 mg/L
  • High end: 1.4×10−3×0.21×32×1000=9.41.4\times10^{-3} \times 0.21 \times 32 \times 1000 = 9.4 mg/L

Reported range for the case as stated (pure/fresh water, dry-air basis): 8.1–9.4 mg/L, central 8.7 mg/L.

Including the humid-air alternative from §4 extends the low end to 7.8 mg/L. The full scenario range is therefore 7.8–9.4 mg/L.

4. Missing quantities — Prompt 2

The problem is partly underspecified. No value below was taken in silence; each is either stated as given or solved under alternatives.

  1. Basis: Concentration basis is stated by kHk_H — mol per litre of solution. No ambiguity for the molar result; the mass result follows from MM (given). Settled.
  2. Reference state: Henry's law here is referenced to the pure-water, dilute-solution standard state implicit in kHk_H at 25 °C. A kHk_H tabulated at a different TT or for seawater would be a different constant. Assumed: the given kHk_H is the 25 °C pure-water value.
  3. Pressure basis: Total pressure PP is not stated. p=0.21p = 0.21 atm (given) is consistent with dry air at P=1P = 1 atm. Alternative: air saturated with water vapour at 25 °C, where the water vapour pressure is about 0.032 atm (estimated from standard vapour-pressure data; unverified in this calculation), gives p≈0.2095×(1−0.032)≈0.203p \approx 0.2095 \times (1 - 0.032) \approx 0.203 atm and C≈8.4C \approx 8.4 mg/L at the central kHk_H — 3.4% below the central result.
  4. Composition basis: Gas composition is given only through pp; liquid composition (salinity, other solutes) is not stated. Alternative solved qualitatively: seawater lowers the result by roughly 20% (estimated, §2), to roughly 7 mg/L. Brackish or saline water must not use the headline range.
  5. Per-pass / overall: Not applicable — this is a single equilibrium state, not a conversion. No per-pass or overall conversion is involved.
  6. Equilibrium attainment and sinks: Not stated whether any real system reaches equilibrium or consumes oxygen (respiration, oxidation). The result is the equilibrium ceiling for the stated gas, not a predicted operating concentration.
5. Independent verification — Prompt 3

Checks were worked in executed code (Python) and by independent routes. No check was used to adjust the solution.

  1. Executed code: Direct evaluation gives C=2.730×10−4C = 2.730\times10^{-4} mol/L and 8.7368.736 mg/L, matching the hand calculation in §3 exactly. Pass.
  2. Limiting cases (known by sight): (a) p=0p = 0 gives C=0C = 0 — correct, oxygen-free gas dissolves no oxygen. (b) Pure oxygen at p=1p = 1 atm gives C=1.3×10−3C = 1.3\times10^{-3} mol/L =41.6= 41.6 mg/L, which is 1/0.21=4.761/0.21 = 4.76 times the air value, as proportionality requires. Pass.
  3. Independent literature route: Standard dissolved-oxygen saturation tables for fresh water at 25 °C and 1 atm list about 8.3 mg/L. This is 5% below the central 8.7 mg/L and inside the humid-air, low-kHk_H part of the reported range, consistent with those tables being for water-saturated air and a slightly lower effective kHk_H. This is a consistency check against a remembered tabulated value, marked unverified until checked against the primary source in §6 — it is not presented as proof. No material or energy balance exists to close in this single-equilibrium calculation; balance closure is therefore not applicable, and that absence is stated rather than passed over.
  4. Correlation valid range: kHk_H used only at its stated TT (25 °C) and at dilute concentration, inside the range in §2. Pass for the stated case; fails by construction if applied to seawater or to TT far from 25 °C without a new kHk_H.

Agreement with another AI model was not used as verification (Checklist item 7).

6. Primary source

The point is settled by a primary Henry-constant compilation and by standard saturation tables, not by a textbook restatement: Sander, R., "Compilation of Henry's law constants (version 4.0) for water as solvent," Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 15, 4399–4981 (2015), for kHk_H for oxygen in water; the United States Geological Survey dissolved-oxygen saturation tables and Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater (American Public Health Association) for the saturation concentration at given TT, PP, and salinity. Every claim in this solution that rests on those sources — the kHk_H spread in §3, the seawater correction in §2, the tabulated 8.3 mg/L in §5 — is marked unverified until checked against them. The given kHk_H, pp, and MM need no external source; they are the user's data, and user-supplied data supersede the study ranges for this case.

7. Audit against built equipment — Prompt 4

Three points most likely to differ in operating equipment:

  1. Non-attainment of equilibrium. Real contactors are mass-transfer limited; bulk liquid is commonly below saturation, often by 10–50% in aerated vessels depending on mixing and residence time (estimated range). Direction: actual below calculated. Settled by: a calibrated dissolved-oxygen probe record on the actual vessel at operating TT.
  2. Oxygen consumption in the liquid. Microbial respiration, chemical oxidation, and corrosion consume dissolved oxygen continuously, holding the operating concentration below the equilibrium ceiling, potentially to near zero in a loaded biological system. Direction: actual below calculated, size unbounded below. Settled by: operating dissolved-oxygen trend and an oxygen-uptake-rate test on the actual liquid.
  3. Temperature and salinity off the stated basis. Plant water is rarely pure or exactly 25 °C; solubility falls about 1.5–2% per °C rise near 25 °C (estimated) and about 20% from fresh water to seawater. Direction: warmer or saltier gives lower actual. Settled by: measured TT and conductivity/salinity of the actual water, with the correction tables in §6.
8. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model: mass-transfer kinetics; oxygen consumption and generation (photosynthesis can supersaturate surface waters above the calculated value); salinity and other solutes; pressure variation with altitude or in pressurised equipment; bubble-size and hydrostatic-pressure effects in deep tanks, which raise the local equilibrium concentration with depth; co-dissolution effects of other gases (neglected, correctly at this dilution).

Information not accessible here: site-specific water analyses, vendor aerator performance data, and any restricted databank values beyond the given kHk_H; none was needed for the idealised case, and all are needed before plant use.

Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling of gas–liquid interfaces, surfactants lowering the mass-transfer coefficient, probe drift and fouling in measurement.

Conditions changing the answer by more than 10%: TT shift of roughly ±7 °C or more; salinity approaching seawater; PP change of more than 10% (altitude of roughly 900 m or more, or pressurisation); sustained oxygen consumption or supersaturation by photosynthesis; use of a kHk_H for a different temperature.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is the water fresh, brackish, or saline, and was its temperature measured at the point of use?
  2. Is the gas dry air, humid air, or enriched/depleted air, and what is the total pressure?
  3. Is equilibrium actually reached, and is anything consuming or generating oxygen?
  4. Has kHk_H been confirmed against the Sander compilation entry for oxygen at the actual temperature?
  5. Is the value being used as an equilibrium ceiling, or incorrectly as a predicted operating concentration?
Final answer

Equilibrium dissolved oxygen in pure water at 25 °C in contact with air at p=0.21p = 0.21 atm (given), using kH=1.3×10−3k_H = 1.3\times10^{-3} mol/(L·atm) (given, fitted in origin) and M=32M = 32 g/mol (given):

C=2.7×10−4C = 2.7\times10^{-4} mol/L ≈ 8.7 mg/L, with a plausible range of 8.1–9.4 mg/L on the stated basis, extending to 7.8 mg/L if the air is water-saturated.

A2. Non-Ideal Vapour–Liquid Equilibrium

Response without the skill

Bubble-Point Pressure at Fixed Temperature — Binary Liquid

Given data
  • x1x_1, the liquid-phase mole fraction of component 1 (dimensionless): x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40
  • x2x_2, the liquid-phase mole fraction of component 2 (dimensionless): defined by x2=1−x1x_2 = 1 - x_1 for a binary mixture
  • P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}}, the pure-component vapour pressure of component 1 at the specified temperature, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}): P1sat=120 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 120\ \mathrm{kPa}
  • P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}}, the pure-component vapour pressure of component 2 at the specified temperature, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}): P2sat=50 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 50\ \mathrm{kPa}
  • PP, the bubble-point pressure at the specified temperature, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}): to be estimated
  • The mixture is stated to be strongly non-ideal.

From the definition of x2x_2:

x2=1−x1=1−0.40=0.60x_2 = 1 - x_1 = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60

Governing relation

For vapour–liquid equilibrium at low to moderate pressure, with the vapour treated as an ideal gas and liquid-phase non-ideality retained, the modified Raoult's law applies to each component ii, where ii is the component index (i=1,2i = 1, 2):

yiP=xiγiPisaty_i P = x_i \gamma_i P_i^{\mathrm{sat}}

where yiy_i is the vapour-phase mole fraction of component ii (dimensionless) and γi\gamma_i is the liquid-phase activity coefficient of component ii (dimensionless) at the specified temperature and at the liquid composition.

Summing over both components and using y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1, where y1y_1 is the vapour-phase mole fraction of component 1 (dimensionless) and y2y_2 is the vapour-phase mole fraction of component 2 (dimensionless), gives the bubble-point pressure:

P=x1γ1P1sat+x2γ2P2satP = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}

where γ1\gamma_1 is the activity coefficient of component 1 (dimensionless) and γ2\gamma_2 is the activity coefficient of component 2 (dimensionless), both at the specified temperature and at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40.

Substituting the given numerical values:

P=(0.40) γ1 (120 kPa)+(0.60) γ2 (50 kPa)P = (0.40)\,\gamma_1\,(120\ \mathrm{kPa}) + (0.60)\,\gamma_2\,(50\ \mathrm{kPa})

P=48 γ1+30 γ2kPaP = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2 \quad \mathrm{kPa}

Assessment of the data

No values of γ1\gamma_1 or γ2\gamma_2 are given. No activity-coefficient model and no model parameters are given — for example, no Margules parameters, no van Laar parameters, no Wilson parameters, no non-random two-liquid (NRTL) parameters, and no UNIQUAC parameters. No experimental vapour–liquid equilibrium data point, no excess Gibbs energy value, no infinite-dilution activity coefficients, and no azeotrope data are given from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40 could be obtained.

The statement that the liquid is strongly non-ideal states explicitly that γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 differ substantially from unity. Setting γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1 is therefore not a justified approximation for this system.

Ideal-solution reference value

For comparison only, the Raoult's law (ideal liquid, γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1) value is:

Pideal=(0.40)(120 kPa)+(0.60)(50 kPa)=48 kPa+30 kPa=78 kPaP_{\mathrm{ideal}} = (0.40)(120\ \mathrm{kPa}) + (0.60)(50\ \mathrm{kPa}) = 48\ \mathrm{kPa} + 30\ \mathrm{kPa} = 78\ \mathrm{kPa}

where PidealP_{\mathrm{ideal}} is the ideal-solution bubble-point pressure, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}).

The value 78 kPa78\ \mathrm{kPa} is not an estimate of the bubble-point pressure of the stated strongly non-ideal mixture. It is the value the mixture would have if it were ideal, contrary to the stated condition.

Direction and size of the deviation
  • If the mixture shows positive deviation from Raoult's law (γ1>1\gamma_1 > 1 and γ2>1\gamma_2 > 1), then P>PidealP > P_{\mathrm{ideal}}, that is, P>78 kPaP > 78\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • If the mixture shows negative deviation from Raoult's law (γ1<1\gamma_1 < 1 and γ2<1\gamma_2 < 1), then P<PidealP < P_{\mathrm{ideal}}, that is, P<78 kPaP < 78\ \mathrm{kPa}.
  • If γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 lie on opposite sides of unity, the sign of the net deviation cannot be assigned from the given data.
  • Strong non-ideality, including partial liquid miscibility and azeotrope formation, corresponds to activity coefficients that can differ from unity by a large factor. No finite bound on PP tighter than the relation P=48 γ1+30 γ2 kPaP = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2\ \mathrm{kPa} follows from the given data alone.

No further simplification is possible without additional information. Fugacity-coefficient and Poynting corrections, which would be required at high pressure, are also unspecified, but their absence is not the limiting deficiency; the limiting deficiency is the absence of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2.

Information required for a numerical estimate

Any one of the following, at the specified temperature and at or near x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40, would make the calculation determinate:

  1. Measured values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40;
  2. A named activity-coefficient model together with its binary interaction parameters at the specified temperature;
  3. Experimental isothermal vapour–liquid equilibrium data for the pair from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 can be fitted;
  4. Infinite-dilution activity coefficients together with a stated model form, so that composition dependence can be computed.

With γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 supplied, the result follows directly from P=48 γ1+30 γ2 kPaP = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2\ \mathrm{kPa}, and the first vapour composition follows from y1=48 γ1/Py_1 = 48\,\gamma_1 / P, with PP expressed in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}) in that ratio.

Conclusion

The bubble-point pressure cannot be estimated numerically from the data given. The determinate result is

P=48 γ1+30 γ2 kPaat x1=0.40P = 48\,\gamma_1 + 30\,\gamma_2 \ \mathrm{kPa} \qquad \text{at } x_1 = 0.40

with γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 unknown and, by the stated strong non-ideality, substantially different from unity. The ideal-solution reference value is 78 kPa78\ \mathrm{kPa}; reporting 78 kPa78\ \mathrm{kPa} as the bubble-point pressure of this mixture would assume ideality that the problem statement excludes.

Weakness: The problem is underspecified for its stated regime. A bubble-point pressure for a non-ideal liquid requires activity coefficients, and no activity coefficient, activity-coefficient model, model parameters, component identities, or temperature value is supplied. In a strongly non-ideal system the activity coefficients are the dominant term, not a correction.

Confidence rating: Low — 2 out of 10 for any single value; high for the ideal reference value as an arithmetic reference only, and for the statement that no unique non-ideal value follows from the data supplied.

No single bubble-point pressure is reported as the answer. A range computed at the ends of plausible activity-coefficient scenarios is reported in Section 5.

7. Prompt 4 — Audit as for built equipment

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Liquid–liquid phase split. Direction: if the real mixture splits, the measured bubble / three-phase pressure is lower than a single-liquid extrapolation at high γ\gamma, and it becomes nearly independent of overall composition across the miscibility gap. Rough size: can cap PP well below the 234–330 kPa rows. Settling document: measured liquid–liquid equilibrium and vapour–liquid equilibrium for the actual pair at the actual temperature — DECHEMA Chemistry Data Series vapour–liquid equilibrium volumes, or a measurement on the actual liquid.
  2. Vapour non-ideality and association. Direction: associating vapours give a lower effective bubble pressure than modified Raoult's law at the same γ\gamma; at the high end of the range (above about 200 kPa) fugacity corrections of 5–20 % are common. Rough size: 5–20 %. Settling document: a γ\gamma–ϕ\phi calculation with a stated equation of state, checked against NIST ThermoData Engine (TDE) evaluated data for the actual pair.
  3. Temperature is not held in real equipment. Direction: a bubble point in a reboiler or column sump is reached by heating, so PsatP^{\mathrm{sat}} and γ\gamma shift together; vapour pressures rise roughly exponentially with temperature (Clausius–Clapeyron behaviour), so a few kelvin of temperature error moves PP by roughly 5–15 %, in the direction of the temperature error. Settling record: the actual operating temperature measurement and the Antoine or DIPPR vapour-pressure correlation for each pure component, checked over its stated temperature range.

The point is settled only by data for the actual pair at the actual temperature:

  • DECHEMA Chemistry Data Series, Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Data Collection, for the named binary pair; or
  • NIST ThermoData Engine (Standard Reference Database 103b) evaluated vapour–liquid equilibrium data; or
  • DIPPR (Design Institute for Physical Properties) pure-component vapour-pressure correlations for P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} and P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} at the stated temperature, combined with binary parameters fitted to measured data for the pair; or
  • a direct bubble-point / ebulliometer measurement on the actual liquid at x1=0.40x_1 = 0.40.

Every statement in this solution that depends on such a source — in particular any specific γ\gamma value for a real system — is unverified until checked against one of them. Data supplied by the user, a plant, or a vendor for the actual system would supersede the scenario ranges used here.

9. Prompt 5 — What is not covered
  • Effects not in the model: vapour fugacity, Poynting correction, liquid–liquid splitting, azeotrope formation and its composition shift with pressure, vapour-phase association or reaction, electrolytes or dissociation, surface and nucleation effects (a measured boiling onset needs superheat; a thermodynamic bubble point does not), and any third component.
  • Information not accessible here: proprietary binary interaction parameters in commercial databanks (e.g. simulator databank values), plant operating records, and any laboratory measurement on the actual mixture.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling and hot spots raising local temperature, pressure drop between the liquid location and the pressure gauge, dissolved inert gas adding a partial pressure and producing an apparent early bubble point, and composition drift by preferential evaporation.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any γ\gamma departing from 1 by more than about 0.15–0.25 in the weighted sum; a temperature change of a few kelvin; a change of pressure basis (absolute versus gauge, about 101 kPa); onset of a second liquid phase; or an associating vapour.

  5. Does the system form an azeotrope near this composition?
  6. Has any value been checked against DECHEMA, NIST TDE, or a measurement on the actual liquid — and if not, why is a scenario range being used for a decision?

Solvent Circulation for Carbon Dioxide Removal

Given data and symbols

The molar rate of carbon dioxide captured, denoted FcapF_{\mathrm{cap}} and measured in kilomoles per hour (kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}), is 100 kmol h−1100\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}.

The lean loading, denoted αL\alpha_L and measured in moles of carbon dioxide per mole of amine (mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}), is 0.10 mol mol−10.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}. Loading is a ratio of two molar amounts and is therefore dimensionless in unit terms, with the basis stated as mole of carbon dioxide per mole of amine.

The rich loading, denoted αR\alpha_R and measured in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}} on the same basis as αL\alpha_L, is the loading in the solvent leaving the absorber. No value for αR\alpha_R is given.

The working capacity, denoted Δα\Delta\alpha and measured in mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}, is the increase in loading across the absorber, Δα=αR−αL\Delta\alpha = \alpha_R - \alpha_L.

The amine circulation rate, denoted FamineF_{\mathrm{amine}} and measured in kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} of amine, is the molar flow of amine itself, not the total flow of aqueous solution.

Result

No unique solvent circulation rate follows from the stated data. The circulation is fixed only after αR\alpha_R, or equivalently Δα\Delta\alpha, is specified. The sizing relation is

Famine=FcapΔα=100αR−0.10 kmol h−1 of amine,F_{\mathrm{amine}} = \frac{F_{\mathrm{cap}}}{\Delta\alpha} = \frac{100}{\alpha_R - 0.10}\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}\ \text{of amine,}

where 100100 carries the unit kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} and αR\alpha_R and 0.100.10 carry the unit mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}. Any single numerical circulation rate quoted without a stated αR\alpha_R rests on an unstated assumption.

Derivation

At steady state, with no accumulation, the carbon dioxide absorbed in the absorber equals the increase in carbon dioxide carried by the circulating solvent between the lean inlet and the rich outlet. The carbon dioxide flow carried with the lean solvent, in kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}, is αLFamine\alpha_L F_{\mathrm{amine}}. The carbon dioxide flow carried with the rich solvent, in kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}}, is αRFamine\alpha_R F_{\mathrm{amine}}. The absorber balance is therefore

Fcap=αRFamine−αLFamine=(αR−αL) Famine=Δα Famine.F_{\mathrm{cap}} = \alpha_R F_{\mathrm{amine}} - \alpha_L F_{\mathrm{amine}} = (\alpha_R - \alpha_L)\,F_{\mathrm{amine}} = \Delta\alpha\,F_{\mathrm{amine}}.

Rearrangement gives Famine=Fcap/ΔαF_{\mathrm{amine}} = F_{\mathrm{cap}} / \Delta\alpha. Substitution of Fcap=100 kmol h−1F_{\mathrm{cap}} = 100\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} and αL=0.10 mol mol−1\alpha_L = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}} gives the sizing relation above. The regenerator gives the same relation: the carbon dioxide stripped there is the rich-to-lean decrease, Δα Famine\Delta\alpha\,F_{\mathrm{amine}}, which must equal the captured rate at steady circulation.

Dimensional check: mol mol−1\mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}} multiplied by kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} of amine gives kmol h−1\mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} of carbon dioxide, which matches FcapF_{\mathrm{cap}}.

For mass units, the captured mass rate is 100 kmol h−1100\ \mathrm{kmol\,h^{-1}} multiplied by 44.01 kg kmol−144.01\ \mathrm{kg\,kmol^{-1}}, the molar mass of carbon dioxide, giving 4401 kg h−14401\ \mathrm{kg\,h^{-1}}.

The table is a direct evaluation of the sizing relation, not a set of design cases. Two limiting behaviours follow from the relation:

  • As αR\alpha_R approaches 0.10 mol mol−10.10\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}} from above, Δα\Delta\alpha approaches zero and FamineF_{\mathrm{amine}} increases without bound. A solvent that gains almost no loading in the absorber must circulate at a very large rate to carry a fixed captured amount.
  • A value of αR\alpha_R at or below αL\alpha_L gives Δα≤0\Delta\alpha \le 0 and is not physically admissible for net absorption, because the solvent would gain no carbon dioxide, or would lose it, across the absorber.

The solvent identity matters through the attainable αR\alpha_R. A primary amine that binds carbon dioxide mainly as a carbamate has a carbamate stoichiometric reference of 0.5 mol mol−10.5\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}} (two amine groups per carbon dioxide in the carbamate reaction), whereas a tertiary amine that binds carbon dioxide mainly as bicarbonate has a stoichiometric reference near 1.0 mol mol−11.0\ \mathrm{mol\,mol^{-1}}. The attainable rich loading in an operating absorber is set by equilibrium at the absorber bottom conditions and by the approach to equilibrium allowed, and is normally below a stoichiometric reference. Neither the amine identity nor the absorber conditions are given, so no attainable αR\alpha_R can be selected from the statement.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Solvent Circulation for Carbon Dioxide Removal by an Aqueous Amine Solvent

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: The problem is severely underspecified. The solvent circulation is set, to first order, by the difference between rich and lean loading, not by the lean loading alone. The rich loading is not given, and it is not a universal constant: it is an equilibrium / approach-to-equilibrium quantity that depends on amine identity, amine concentration, absorber bottom temperature, and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the feed gas. None of those is given. Any single-value answer therefore rests on an assumed rich loading, and that assumption alone moves the answer by a factor of about two over its plausible range.

Confidence rating: low — 2 out of 5 for any volumetric circulation quoted to better than about ±50 %. Confidence is high — 4 out of 5 for the molar amine circulation expressed as a function of the loading difference, because that result is a pure material balance with no fitted property in it. All results below are therefore reported as ranges computed at the ends of the plausible range of the assumed inputs (Checklist item 2), not as single values.

Agreement with another AI model, a textbook example using similar round numbers, or a similar answer found online would not count as verification here (Checklist item 7) and is not used as such.

3. Definitions and the governing balance

Symbols, defined before use:

  • n˙CO2\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} (kmol/h): molar flow rate of carbon dioxide removed.
  • n˙amine\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} (kmol/h): molar flow rate of amine in the circulating solvent.
  • αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} (mol/mol): loading of the lean solvent entering the absorber, 0.10 mol/mol, given.
  • αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} (mol/mol): loading of the rich solvent leaving the absorber, assumed.
  • Δα=αrich−αlean\Delta\alpha = \alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} (mol/mol): working (cyclic) capacity per mole of amine.
  • m˙solv\dot m_{\mathrm{solv}} (kg/h): mass flow rate of circulating aqueous solvent, where kg/h is kilograms per hour.
  • V˙solv\dot V_{\mathrm{solv}} (m³/h): volumetric flow rate of circulating solvent, where m³/h is cubic metres per hour.
  • MM (kg/kmol), ww (kg/kg), ρ\rho (kg/m³): as defined in §2.

Steady-state carbon dioxide balance over the absorber, with no accumulation and no carbon dioxide created or destroyed in the absorber:

n˙CO2=n˙amine (αrich−αlean)=n˙amine Δα\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\, (\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}) = \dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,\Delta\alpha

hence

n˙amine=n˙CO2Δα,m˙solv=n˙amine Mw,V˙solv=m˙solvρ.\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{\Delta\alpha}, \qquad \dot m_{\mathrm{solv}} = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}\,M}{w}, \qquad \dot V_{\mathrm{solv}} = \frac{\dot m_{\mathrm{solv}}}{\rho}.

This is the whole model. It contains no fitted correlation, no kinetics, and no equilibrium relation — which is precisely why the answer can be no better than the assumed αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} fed into it.

Properties, rules of thumb, and sources — all unverified until checked (Checklist item 5). The plausible ranges used for αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} (roughly 0.30–0.50 mol/mol), for MEA concentration (roughly 0.20–0.30 kg/kg, limited in practice by corrosion), and for MDEA concentration (roughly 0.40–0.50 kg/kg) are the ranges conventionally quoted in amine-treating practice. The primary sources that settle these points are: (i) vapour–liquid equilibrium / loading data for the specific amine–water–carbon dioxide system at the absorber temperature and carbon dioxide partial pressure, e.g. data in Kohl and Nielsen, Gas Purification, and in the GPSA Engineering Data Book, current editions; (ii) the solvent vendor's operating limits (maximum rich loading, maximum concentration for corrosion control); and (iii) in a real plant, a measured rich loading from a sample of the actual rich solvent leaving the absorber. Every claim in this paragraph rests on such a source and is marked unverified — none of those sources was consulted or measured in producing this answer, and the ranges must be checked against them before design use. Molar masses are standard chemical data (rounded, estimated state above) and are not a material source of error.

6. Alternative interpretation of the given rate

If 100 kmol/h (given number, interpretation assumed) is the carbon dioxide rate in the feed gas rather than the rate removed, and the fractional removal (capture fraction, dimensionless) is 0.85–0.95 (assumed), then n˙CO2\dot n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} removed is 85–95 kmol/h and every flow in §4 scales down by 5–15 % — e.g. amine circulation becomes 213–475 kmol/h over the same loading range. The problem as stated does not distinguish these two readings; a reviewer must settle which is meant.

7. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks performed, with outcomes reported as found:

  1. Material balance closure. By construction the absorber balance closes exactly: n˙amine×Δα\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}} \times \Delta\alpha reproduces 100 kmol/h at every tabulated point (e.g. 333.3 × 0.30 = 100.0; 500 × 0.20 = 100.0). Closure residual: 0 kmol/h. Passes — but note this only verifies the arithmetic of the assumed model, not the assumed αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}.
  2. Regenerator cross-check (independent route). At steady state the regenerator must strip exactly what the absorber picks up: n˙amine(αrich−αlean)\dot n_{\mathrm{amine}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}) evaluated on the regenerator side is the same 100 kmol/h. Consistent. Passes.
  3. Limiting case 1 — known by sight. As αrich→αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} \to \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}, Δα→0\Delta\alpha \to 0 and the required circulation →∞\to \infty: a solvent that picks up nothing per pass must circulate infinitely fast. The formula shows this. Passes.
  4. Limiting case 2 — known by sight. If αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0 and αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} = 0.50 mol/mol, amine circulation = 100 / 0.50 = 200 kmol/h, the smallest possible value in this family. Any tabulated value below 200 kmol/h would signal an error; none is. Passes.
  5. Stoichiometric bound. For MEA, αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} above about 0.50 mol/mol cannot be assumed casually (carbamate stoichiometry, §4.1); the table does not exceed 0.50 mol/mol. Passes, with the caveat that bicarbonate formation can raise apparent loadings in some systems — unverified for this (unspecified) system.
  6. Dimensional check. (kmol/h) / (mol/mol) = kmol/h; kmol/h × kg/kmol / (kg/kg) = kg/h; kg/h / (kg/m³) = m³/h. Passes.
  7. Executed code. All tables were computed by executed Python code from the §3 equations (§4 states this); hand-check of one point: 100 / 0.30 = 333.3 kmol/h; 333.3 × 61.08 / 0.30 = 67,867 kg/h, matching the tabulated 67,900 kg/h to rounding. Passes.

No check failed. That statement covers arithmetic, dimensions and limiting behaviour only. The checks cannot validate the assumed rich loading, amine identity or concentration, because no independent data for them were supplied — that is the open risk, not a hidden pass.

8. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. The rich solvent will not reach equilibrium loading. Direction: real αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} is lower than the equilibrium value at the absorber bottom, by an approach that depends on packing / tray contacting, gas rate and kinetics (slow for MDEA in particular, which is selective precisely because its carbon dioxide reaction is slow). Rough size: an approach shortfall of 0.05 mol/mol in αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} raises the required circulation by about 17–25 % at the central case. Settled by: absorber vendor rating / pilot or plant sample of rich solvent analysed for loading, against equilibrium data for the actual system (sources in §5, unverified here).
  2. Corrosion and degradation cap the usable loading and concentration. Direction: for MEA especially, operators limit rich loading and concentration below the equilibrium / solubility values to control corrosion and degradation; the usable Δα\Delta\alpha is therefore smaller and circulation larger than a purely equilibrium-based figure, commonly by tens of percent. Settled by: solvent vendor's corrosion limits and the plant's corrosion / degradation records (iron in solvent, heat-stable salts) for the actual metallurgy.
  3. Hydraulics, foaming and the water / energy balance move the operable rate. Direction: either way, typically ±10–30 % on the operable circulation: foaming, flooding limits, pump and exchanger capacity, and the regenerator steam needed per unit of solvent circulated (circulating more solvent costs roughly proportionally more reboiler duty) can force operation away from the balance-only figure; water wash / make-up also shifts ww in service from its nominal value. Settled by: column hydraulic rating, reboiler duty records, and a measured solvent concentration and density on the actual circulating inventory.
9. What this calculation does not cover (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: absorber and regenerator sizing (height, diameter, internals); mass-transfer kinetics and stage / packing efficiency; heat of absorption and the absorber temperature bulge, which itself lowers equilibrium loading; regenerator pressure, temperature and steam duty; energy consumption and cost; pressure drop; hydrogen sulfide or other acid gases competing for the amine (no feed composition was given — if hydrogen sulfide is present, loadings and selectivity change materially); hydrocarbon co-absorption; solvent degradation, reclamation, foaming, and emissions.
  • Information not available here: proprietary solvent formulations and their vendor loading / corrosion data; amine-system vapour–liquid equilibrium data held in commercial databanks and process simulators; any site standard specifying design margins on circulation (a design margin of, for example, 10–20 %, assumed as typical practice and unverified, would be applied on top of the figures in §4).
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: foaming episodes, fouling, corrosion excursions at high rich loading, amine losses, seasonal cooling-water / lean-solvent temperature variation (lean temperature moves equilibrium and hence both loadings).
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any of — αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} differing from the central assumed 0.40 mol/mol by more than about 0.03 mol/mol; αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} in service differing from 0.10 mol/mol by more than about 0.03 mol/mol (e.g. a regenerator upset raising lean loading); amine concentration differing by more than about 0.03 kg/kg from the assumed value; the 100 kmol/h being a feed rate rather than a removed rate; a change of amine; or feed carbon dioxide partial pressure / absorber temperature moving enough to shift equilibrium rich loading by the amounts above.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. Which amine, at what measured concentration, and in what metallurgy?
  2. What is the rich loading — measured on the actual solvent, or taken from equilibrium data at the actual absorber bottom temperature and carbon dioxide partial pressure — and what approach to equilibrium is assumed?
  3. Is 100 kmol/h the feed rate or the removed rate, and what removal fraction is required?
  4. What lean loading can the regenerator actually hold in service, and what reboiler duty does the resulting circulation imply?
  5. What design margin, corrosion limit and hydraulic check have been applied on top of the balance figure?
10. Answer in brief
  • Amine circulation (molar, amine-identity independent): 250–500 kmol/h, at αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} = 0.50–0.30 mol/mol (assumed) over the given αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0.10 mol/mol; 333 kmol/h at the central assumed αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} = 0.40 mol/mol.
  • Aqueous solvent circulation, base-case MEA at ww = 0.30 kg/kg (assumed): about 51,000–102,000 kg/h, about 50–101 m³/h.
  • Across plausible amines and concentrations: about 51,000–175,000 kg/h, about 50–174 m³/h.
  • Confidence: low (2/5) for the volumetric figures until amine identity, concentration and a sourced rich loading are supplied; the single measurement that would most improve the answer is a rich-loading value for the actual system, from the sources named in §5 — unverified until checked against them.

A4. Estimated Properties and Compressibility

Response without the skill

Density of a Gas at 150 bar and 350 K

Given data
  • Molar mass, denoted MM, in kilograms per mole (kg/mol): M=0.020 kg/molM = 0.020\ \text{kg/mol}
  • Pressure, denoted PP, in bar: P=150 barP = 150\ \text{bar}
  • Temperature, denoted TT, in kelvin (K): T=350 KT = 350\ \text{K}
  • Universal gas constant, denoted RR, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol·K)): R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}
Quantity to estimate
  • Mass density, denoted ρ\rho (rho), in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³): ρ\rho is the mass of gas per unit volume of gas.
Model

No compressibility factor, critical properties, or equation-of-state parameters are given, so the only estimate that can be made from the given data is the ideal-gas estimate.

The ideal-gas law is

PV=nRTP V = n R T

where:

  • VV, in cubic metres (m³), is the volume of the gas,
  • nn, in moles (mol), is the amount of substance of the gas,
  • PP, RR, and TT are as defined above.
Derivation

The mass of the gas, denoted mm, in kilograms (kg), is the amount of substance multiplied by the molar mass:

m=nMm = n M

The mass density ρ\rho (rho), in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), is the mass divided by the volume:

ρ=mV=nMV\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{n M}{V}

From the ideal-gas law, the amount of substance divided by the volume, denoted n/Vn/V, in moles per cubic metre (mol/m³), is

nV=PRT\frac{n}{V} = \frac{P}{R T}

Substitution gives the ideal-gas density in terms of the given quantities alone:

ρ=PMRT\rho = \frac{P M}{R T}

Unit conversion

Pressure must be expressed in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m² = 1 J/m³, for consistency with RR in J/(mol·K):

P=150 bar×105 Pa1 bar=1.50×107 PaP = 150\ \text{bar} \times \frac{10^{5}\ \text{Pa}}{1\ \text{bar}} = 1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Pa}

No conversion is needed for MM, TT, or RR, which are already in kg/mol, K, and J/(mol·K), respectively.

Calculation

ρ=PMRT=(1.50×107 Pa)(0.020 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(350 K)\rho = \frac{P M}{R T} = \frac{(1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Pa})(0.020\ \text{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)})(350\ \text{K})}

Numerator:

(1.50×107)(0.020)=3.00×105(1.50 \times 10^{7})(0.020) = 3.00 \times 10^{5}

Denominator:

(8.314)(350)=2909.9(8.314)(350) = 2909.9

Therefore:

ρ=3.00×1052909.9≈103.1 kg/m3\rho = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5}}{2909.9} \approx 103.1\ \text{kg/m}^{3}

As a check, the molar density n/Vn/V (in mol/m³) is

nV=PRT=1.50×1072909.9≈5155 mol/m3\frac{n}{V} = \frac{P}{R T} = \frac{1.50 \times 10^{7}}{2909.9} \approx 5155\ \text{mol/m}^{3}

and

ρ=nVM≈(5155 mol/m3)(0.020 kg/mol)≈103.1 kg/m3\rho = \frac{n}{V} M \approx (5155\ \text{mol/m}^{3})(0.020\ \text{kg/mol}) \approx 103.1\ \text{kg/m}^{3}

which agrees with the direct calculation. The units also check: Pa is J/m³, so (J/m³)(kg/mol) divided by J/(mol·K) × K gives kg/m³.

Result

ρ≈1.0×102 kg/m3 (about 103 kg/m3)\rho \approx 1.0 \times 10^{2}\ \text{kg/m}^{3}\ \text{(about }103\ \text{kg/m}^{3}\text{)}

Scope of the estimate

This is an ideal-gas estimate. At a pressure of 150 bar, a real gas can depart appreciably from ideal-gas behaviour. A corrected density would require a compressibility factor, denoted ZZ (dimensionless), in

ρ=PMZRT\rho = \frac{P M}{Z R T}

where ZZ is defined by Z=PV/(nRT)Z = P V / (n R T). No value of ZZ, and no data from which ZZ could be obtained (such as critical temperature and critical pressure), are given in the problem, so no real-gas correction can be applied and 103 kg/m3103\ \text{kg/m}^{3} is the estimate supported by the given data.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Density of a Gas at 150 bar and 350 K — Estimate with Stated Weakness

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. The stated data determine an ideal-gas density exactly, but they do not determine the real-gas density. At a pressure PP (pressure, in pascals, Pa; 1 bar = 10510^{5} Pa) of 150 bar, most real gases depart measurably from ideal behaviour. The size and sign of the departure depend on the gas identity, which is not given.

Confidence rating.

  • Arithmetic of the ideal-gas calculation: high (5/5). The calculation is closed-form, dimensionally consistent, and was reproduced in executed code (Section 6).
  • Physical accuracy of the ideal-gas value as the density of an unspecified real gas at 150 bar: low (2/5). A single correction factor that is not supplied (the compressibility factor, defined in Section 3) can move the result by tens of percent, and, for a condensable or near-critical gas, by more than that.

No single value is therefore reported as the answer. A range is reported in Section 3 (Checklist item 2).

2. Symbols and inputs, labelled at the point of use (Checklist item 3)

Symbols are defined before first use:

  • ρ\rho is the mass density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).
  • MM is the molar mass, in kilograms per mole (kg/mol).

  • TT is the absolute temperature, in kelvin (K).
  • RR is the universal gas constant, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol·K)).
  • ZZ is the compressibility factor, dimensionless, defined in Section 3.

3. Calculation and reported range (Prompt 1; Checklist item 2)
3.1 Ideal-gas value

For an ideal gas,

ρ=PMRT\rho = \frac{P M}{R T}

Substitution of the given values:

ρ=(1.50×107 Pa)(0.020 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(350 K)=3.00×1052 909.9≈103.1 kg/m3\rho = \frac{(1.50 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa})(0.020\ \mathrm{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)})(350\ \mathrm{K})} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5}}{2\,909.9} \approx 103.1\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}

Ideal-gas result: ρ≈103\rho \approx 103 kg/m³. This is the density the gas would have if ZZ were exactly 1.

3.2 Real-gas correction and range

For a real gas, ZZ is defined by Z=PVm/(RT)Z = P V_{\mathrm{m}} / (R T), so that

ρ=PMZRT=103.1Z kg/m3\rho = \frac{P M}{Z R T} = \frac{103.1}{Z}\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}

ZZ (assumed, not given, measured, or fitted) is the input that carries the weakness. Values of ZZ at 150 bar and 350 K differ by gas:

  • Light, well-supercritical gases (high reduced temperature) typically have ZZ near 0.95–1.05 at these conditions.
  • Gases with stronger attractive forces, or nearer their critical temperature, typically have ZZ in the region of 0.80–0.95.
  • At sufficiently high reduced pressure, repulsive forces drive ZZ above 1, in the region of 1.05–1.10 and higher.
