If the gas is near-critical or condensable at 350 K (Section 4), ZZ can fall below 0.70 and the density can fall outside even the stress range; if the fluid is in fact a liquid or a two-phase mixture, a gas-density calculation does not apply at all.

3.3 Sensitivity of the result to each guess (Prompt 1)
  • ZZ (assumed, dominant guess): a change of ZZ from 1.00 to 0.90 raises ρ\rho by 11.1 %; to 0.80, by 25.0 %; to 1.10, lowers ρ\rho by 9.1 %. Roughly, a 1 % error in ZZ gives a 1 % error in ρ\rho, of opposite sign.
  • Pressure basis (assumed absolute): if 150 bar is gauge rather than absolute, the absolute pressure is about 151 bar, and ρ\rho rises by about 0.7 %. Small compared with the ZZ effect, but not zero.
  • MM (given): ρ\rho is proportional to MM. If MM = 0.020 kg/mol is a rounded value (for example, a true value in the range 0.019–0.021 kg/mol), ρ\rho moves by −5 % to +5 % (97.9 to 108.3 kg/m³ on the ideal basis).
  • TT (given): ρ\rho is inversely proportional to TT. An error of 1 K in TT moves ρ\rho by about 0.29 %.
  • PP (given): ρ\rho is proportional to PP. An error of 1 bar in PP moves ρ\rho by about 0.67 %.
  • RR (given): stated to four significant figures; its rounding moves ρ\rho by well under 0.1 %.
4. Missing quantities — the problem is underspecified (Prompt 2; Checklist item 4)

The following quantities are needed for a real-gas density and are not supplied. No value has been taken in silence; the alternatives solved are stated.

  1. Gas identity and composition basis. Needed to obtain ZZ or an equation of state. Missing entirely. Solved under the alternatives: (a) ideal gas, Z=1Z = 1, giving 103 kg/m³; (b) ZZ spanning 0.80–1.10, giving 94–129 kg/m³ (Section 3.2).
  2. Compressibility data: ZZ itself, or the critical temperature, the critical pressure, and the acentric factor (for a corresponding-states or cubic equation-of-state calculation), or a measured density. None supplied. - Illustrative scale of the gap, using critical properties of named gases as examples only (estimated context, not data for this gas): at 350 K and 150 bar, methane would be at a reduced temperature of about 1.84 and a reduced pressure of about 3.3; nitrogen at about 2.77 and 4.4; carbon dioxide at about 1.15 and 2.0. The reduced state — and therefore ZZ — is not the same in these cases, so no single ZZ follows from PP and TT alone.
  3. Pressure basis: absolute or gauge. Not stated. Solved as absolute in the main calculation; the gauge alternative moves the result by about +0.7 % (Section 3.3).
  4. Phase / reference condition: confirmation that the fluid is a single-phase gas at 350 K and 150 bar, rather than a supercritical fluid, a liquid, or a two-phase mixture. Not stated. Assumed single-phase gas. If the (unspecified) gas has a critical temperature above 350 K, condensation is possible and the calculation is invalid as a gas density.
  5. Purity / mixture basis: whether MM = 0.020 kg/mol is the molar mass of a pure gas or a mole-fraction-weighted mean for a mixture. Not stated. The calculation uses the stated MM as an effective molar mass, which is correct for an ideal mixture and an approximation otherwise.

Basis and reference state in the strict sense (feed basis, per-pass versus overall conversion) do not arise here, because no reaction, separation, or flow balance is involved; density is a state property and needs no reference state. That absence is stated rather than left implicit.

5. Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5)

The point at issue — the real ZZ (equivalently, the real density) of the actual gas at 350 K and 150 bar — is settled by, in order of authority:

  1. A measurement of density (or of PP, TT, and molar volume) on the actual gas at, or near, the stated conditions.
  2. The NIST REFPROP database (National Institute of Standards and Technology) or the NIST Chemistry WebBook, evaluated for the named gas at 350 K and 150 bar.
  3. A validated databank implementation of a reference equation of state for the named gas, for example the DIPPR (Design Institute for Physical Properties) correlation set, or the equation of state cited in Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook for that gas.

Unverified: every statement in this solution about the size of ZZ for any real gas, and the plausible range ZZ = 0.80–1.10, rests on general corresponding-states behaviour and has not been checked against any of the sources above, because the gas is not named. Those statements are marked unverified until a named gas is checked against REFPROP or a measurement. The ideal-gas arithmetic (Section 3.1) does not rest on those sources and is verified in Section 6.

6. Verification by an independent route (Prompt 3; Checklist item 6)

Checks were carried out separately from the hand calculation. Checks that fail are reported as failures.

  1. Executed code. The calculation was run in Python:

P = 150e5 Pa; M = 0.020 kg/mol; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T = 350 K rho = P*M/(R*T) = 103.0963 kg/m³

Code result 103.10 kg/m³ agrees with the hand result 103.1 kg/m³. The code also returned: molar volume Vm=RT/P=1.94×10−4V_{\mathrm{m}} = R T / P = 1.94 \times 10^{-4} m³/mol (194 cm³/mol), and ρ\rho for ZZ = 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00, 1.10, 1.20 as 147.3, 128.9, 114.6, 103.1, 93.7, 85.9 kg/m³ respectively, matching the table in Section 3.2 (the 0.85, 0.95, and 1.05 rows were evaluated by the same relation). 2. Dimensional check. Pa = J/m³, so PM/(RT)P M / (R T) has units (J/m³)(kg/mol) / (J/mol) = kg/m³. Pass. 3. Limiting case known by sight — low pressure. At 1 bar and 350 K the same relation gives ρ\rho = 0.687 kg/m³. Density at fixed TT is proportional to PP for an ideal gas, so the 150 bar value must be 150 × 0.687 = 103.1 kg/m³. It is. Pass. 4. Limiting case known by sight — magnitude. A molar volume of 194 cm³/mol at 150 bar, against about 24 000 cm³/mol for an ideal gas near ambient conditions, is the correct order for compression by a factor of about 150 with a temperature increase from near 298 K to 350 K (24 000 × (350/298) / 150 ≈ 188 cm³/mol, the residual difference being the ambient reference chosen). Pass, to order of magnitude. 5. Balance closure. No material or energy balance exists in a single state-property calculation, so there is no balance to close. Stated explicitly rather than omitted. 6. Correlation valid-range check — FAILED / not applicable. The only relation used, the ideal-gas law, has no stated valid range in the data supplied, and at 150 bar it is outside the low-pressure range in which it is normally applied without a ZZ correction. This check therefore fails: the ideal-gas value cannot be certified as a real-gas density from the supplied data. The solution was not altered to make this check pass; instead, the result is reported as a range (Section 3.2). 7. Independent-model agreement. No second equation of state could be evaluated, because no gas identity or critical properties were supplied. Agreement with another AI model was not used as verification, and would not count as verification in any case (Checklist item 7).

7. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Real-gas non-ideality (Z≠1Z \neq 1). Direction: unknown without the gas identity; for most gases at 150 bar and 350 K with attractive forces dominant, Z<1Z < 1 and the real density is higher than 103 kg/m³. Rough size: +5 % to +25 % over the plausible range in Section 3.2, larger near the critical point. Settled by: a REFPROP or reference equation-of-state evaluation for the named gas, or a density measurement on the actual gas (Section 5).
  2. State in the equipment is not the stated state. Plant pressure and temperature are measured at a tapping and a thermowell, not throughout the volume; pressure drop, temperature gradients, and Joule–Thomson cooling across a let-down can make the local state differ from 150 bar and 350 K. Direction: either way. Rough size: a 5 K local temperature difference moves density by about 1.4 %; a 5 bar pressure difference by about 3.3 % — smaller than the ZZ effect, but larger than the precision of the arithmetic. Settled by: the instrument datasheets and calibration records for the actual pressure and temperature transmitters, and the piping and instrumentation diagram showing tapping locations.
  3. Composition in the equipment is not the stated molar mass. Trace heavy components, moisture, or a composition swing raise the effective molar mass and, separately, lower ZZ; both raise density. Direction: usually upward for contamination by heavier species. Rough size: 1 mol % of a component of molar mass 0.044 kg/mol in a gas of molar mass 0.020 kg/mol raises the mean molar mass by about 1.2 %, before any ZZ effect. Settled by: a gas chromatograph analysis of the actual stream, against the composition basis assumed for MM.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: real-gas behaviour beyond a single constant ZZ (in reality ZZ varies with PP and TT across any equipment volume); condensation and two-phase flow; adsorption, solubility in any liquid present, and reaction; transient and start-up states; velocity and elevation effects on measured pressure.
  • Information not available here: the gas identity and any proprietary or restricted-databank property data for it (for example, licensed REFPROP/DIPPR evaluations and vendor-supplied fluid data), and any plant measurement records. The range in Section 3.2 is a substitute for that information, not a replacement for it.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling and restriction changing the local pressure; instrument drift; composition swings with feed or recycle; temperature stratification in large vessels.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any of — ZZ below 0.91 or the corresponding attractive-force regime (density more than 10 % above the ideal value); MM in error by more than 10 % (for example, a misidentified gas); TT below about 318 K at the same pressure (ideal density alone rises by more than 10 %); PP above about 165 bar at the same temperature; or the onset of condensation, which changes the density by far more than 10 % and invalidates the gas model.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the gas, and what is its measured or REFPROP density at 350 K and 150 bar?
  2. Is 150 bar absolute or gauge, and where is it measured?
  3. Is the fluid confirmed single-phase gas at these conditions (critical temperature and dew point checked)?
  4. Is MM = 0.020 kg/mol a pure-component value or a mixture mean, and on what composition basis?
  5. What accuracy does the use require — is a range of 94–129 kg/m³ acceptable, or must ZZ be obtained before the number is used for sizing, relief, or inventory?
Answer in brief

Ideal-gas density: 103 kg/m³. Reported as a range for an unspecified real gas at 150 bar, with the compressibility factor ZZ (assumed) spanning 0.80–1.10: 94–129 kg/m³, low confidence (2/5) as a physical density until the gas is named and ZZ is taken from REFPROP or a measurement — a step not yet performed, so the real-gas claim is unverified.

A5. Crystallisation Yield

Response without the skill

Crystal Yield from Cooling a Saturated Solution

Given data
  • Initial temperature, denoted by T1 (temperature in degrees Celsius, °C): T1 = 60 °C
  • Final temperature, denoted by T2 (temperature in degrees Celsius, °C): T2 = 20 °C
  • Solvent mass, denoted by W (mass in grams, g): W = 100 g of solvent
  • Solubility at T1, denoted by S1 (mass of solute in grams per 100 g of solvent, g per 100 g solvent): S1 = 30 g per 100 g solvent
  • Solubility at T2, denoted by S2 (mass of solute in grams per 100 g of solvent, g per 100 g solvent): S2 = 12 g per 100 g solvent

The solution is saturated at T1, and it is cooled to T2. No solvent is lost by evaporation, no solute is lost except as crystals, and the remaining liquid at T2 is saturated.

Principle

For a fixed mass of solvent, the mass of solute that can remain dissolved falls from the solubility value at the initial temperature to the solubility value at the final temperature. The difference precipitates as crystals, provided equilibrium is reached at the final temperature.

The crystal yield, denoted by Y (mass of crystals in grams, g), on the stated solvent basis is therefore the initial dissolved mass minus the final dissolved mass.

Calculation

Initial dissolved solute mass, denoted by M1 (mass in grams, g), on a basis of W = 100 g of solvent:

M1 = S1 = 30 g

Final dissolved solute mass, denoted by M2 (mass in grams, g), remaining in the saturated liquid at T2 on the same basis:

M2 = S2 = 12 g

Crystal yield:

Y = M1 − M2

Y = 30 g − 12 g = 18 g

In general form, for solvent mass W, the yield is scaled in proportion to W:

Y = (S1 − S2) × W / (100 g of solvent)

For W = 100 g of solvent, the numerical result is 18 g, consistent with the direct calculation.

Result

Crystal yield = 18 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent.

This corresponds to 18 / 30 = 0.60, i.e. 60 % of the solute initially dissolved, crystallising on cooling, with 12 g remaining dissolved in the mother liquor per 100 g of solvent.

Assumptions and limits
  • Equilibrium is reached at 20 °C, so the mother liquor is saturated at the final solubility.
  • No evaporation of solvent during cooling; the solvent mass stays at 100 g.
  • Crystals are pure solute and carry no adhering mother liquor in the stated yield; a wet-cake mass in practice would be higher because of retained liquor.
  • No supersaturation persists; if supersaturation persisted, the actual yield at the moment of measurement would be lower.
Response with the skill (generic layer)

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution from 60 °C to 20 °C

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is a simple solubility difference, but the result rests entirely on two solubility values for an unnamed solute in an unnamed solvent, from a single unnamed data set, with no stated uncertainty, crystal form, purity, or equilibrium condition. Solubility is system-specific: hydrate or solvate formation, polymorphism, impurities, pH (the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity, dimensionless), and incomplete attainment of equilibrium can each change the amount that crystallises by more than the rounding in the numbers. A difference of two solubilities is therefore reliable as a textbook equilibrium estimate and unreliable as a plant yield prediction without system-specific data.

Confidence rating. High for the equilibrium arithmetic on the stated basis (the balance closes exactly, Section 5). Low to moderate — estimated 40–60 % — that a real crystalliser, run once under unspecified conditions, would deliver the nominal value within ±10 %. The range in Section 3, not the nominal value, is the defensible result.

2. Symbols, inputs, and their state

Symbols are defined at first use:

  • msolv = mass of solvent, in grams (g), the basis quantity.
  • S(T) = solubility at temperature T, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g solvent), where T is temperature in degrees Celsius (°C).
  • Y = crystal yield, in grams of dry, pure crystals per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g solvent).

Inputs, labelled at the point of use:

Input Value State
S(60 °C) 30 g per 100 g solvent Given — "in one data set"; not measured here, no source named, no uncertainty stated
S(20 °C) 12 g per 100 g solvent Given — same status as above
msolv (basis) 100 g solvent Given — the requested reporting basis
Initial state: saturated at 60 °C — Given
Final state: saturated mother liquor at 20 °C, i.e. equilibrium reached — Assumed — not stated; see Section 4
No solvent evaporates or is entrained during cooling — Assumed
Crystals are pure solute, anhydrous and solvent-free, containing no mother liquor — Assumed
No solute is lost, decomposed, or remains supersaturated — Assumed

No fitted relation, correlation, or rule of thumb is used. The only relation used is a mass balance (Section 3), which holds generally and has no restricted range. No property value other than the two given solubilities is used.

3. Solution and range

On a basis of msolv = 100 g solvent (given):

  • Solute dissolved at 60 °C = S(60 °C) = 30 g (given solubility applied to the given basis).
  • Solute remaining dissolved at 20 °C = S(20 °C) = 12 g (given solubility applied to the same basis), provided the solvent mass is unchanged (assumed, Section 2) and equilibrium is reached (assumed, Section 2).
  • Crystal yield Y = 30 g − 12 g = 18 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent.

Derived quantities, same basis:

  • Fraction of the initially dissolved solute that crystallises = 18 g / 30 g = 0.60, i.e. 60 %.
  • Initial solution mass = 100 g solvent + 30 g solute = 130 g.
  • Final mother-liquor mass = 100 g solvent + 12 g solute = 112 g.
  • Crystals as a fraction of initial solution mass = 18 g / 130 g = 0.138, i.e. 13.8 % by mass.
Range, not a single value

The two solubilities carry the weakness: given, but with no stated uncertainty and no named source. Two plausible uncertainty scenarios are carried through the same balance. These are scenario ranges, not measured confidence intervals.

  1. Rounding / reading uncertainty of ±1 g per 100 g solvent on each solubility (estimated — the smallest plausible error for values quoted to two figures): - Low end: (30 − 1) − (12 + 1) = 16 g per 100 g solvent. - High end: (30 + 1) − (12 − 1) = 20 g per 100 g solvent. - Range: 16–20 g per 100 g solvent, i.e. about ±11 % on the nominal 18 g.

  2. Data-set / system uncertainty of ±10 % relative on each solubility (estimated — a plausible spread between independent solubility data sets for an unnamed system): - Low end: 30 × 0.90 − 12 × 1.10 = 27.0 − 13.2 = 13.8 g per 100 g solvent. - High end: 30 × 1.10 − 12 × 0.90 = 33.0 − 10.8 = 22.2 g per 100 g solvent. - Range: 13.8–22.2 g per 100 g solvent, i.e. about −23 % to +23 % on the nominal 18 g.

Reported result: nominal Y = 18 g per 100 g solvent; defensible range 14–22 g per 100 g solvent (rounded from scenario 2), with 16–20 g per 100 g solvent if the only error is rounding in the quoted values.

Sensitivity of the result to each assumption
  • Each 1 g per 100 g solvent error in S(60 °C) moves Y by 1 g, i.e. 5.6 % of 18 g, in the same direction.
  • Each 1 g per 100 g solvent error in S(20 °C) moves Y by 1 g, i.e. 5.6 %, in the opposite direction.
  • Solvent loss by evaporation (assumed zero): loss of 5 g of the 100 g solvent leaves 95 g solvent holding 12 g per 100 g × 0.95 = 11.4 g solute at 20 °C, so Y = 30 − 11.4 = 18.6 g, a +3.3 % change, before any effect of evaporation on the stated basis itself.
  • Incomplete desupersaturation (residual supersaturation, assumed zero): every 1 g per 100 g solvent of solute that remains supersaturated at 20 °C reduces the recovered crystals by 1 g, i.e. −5.6 %.
  • Hydrate or solvate formation (assumed absent): if the crystal contains solvent, the dry-solute yield falls and the wet-crystal mass rises; the size cannot be computed without the crystal stoichiometry, which is not given. This is the largest unbounded sensitivity in the problem.
4. Missing quantities — Prompt 2

The problem is underspecified. The missing quantities, and how each is handled, are:

  1. Identity of solute and solvent — missing. Needed because solubility, crystal form, and hydrate formation are system-specific. Handled by: reporting the result only for the system behind the given data set, unverified (Section 6).
  2. Basis — given for reporting (per 100 g solvent), but ambiguous in one respect: whether "solvent" means solvent charged or solvent remaining at 20 °C. Solved under the plausible alternative of unchanged solvent mass (main result); the 5 g evaporation alternative is quantified in Section 3 (+3.3 %).
  3. Reference state — missing: whether the 60 °C solution is exactly saturated, or saturated with excess solid present. If excess solid is present at 60 °C, the yield per 100 g solvent is larger by the mass of that excess solid, which is not given. Solved under the stated reading "a saturated solution", i.e. no excess solid.
  4. Pressure basis — missing. Solubility of a solid in a liquid is weakly pressure-dependent at near-ambient pressure, so atmospheric pressure is assumed; at high pressure this assumption would need checking against primary data. The effect at ambient conditions is expected to be well below 1 %, but this is an estimate, unverified.
  5. Composition basis — the solubilities are given on a mass-of-solute per mass-of-solvent basis, which is used throughout. No mole or solution-mass basis conversion is possible or needed without a molar mass, which is not given.
  6. Per-pass or overall — not applicable to a single batch cooling step; the result is a single-pass (single-batch) equilibrium yield. A plant overall yield with mother-liquor recycle would be higher and cannot be computed without a recycle ratio and purge rate, neither given.
  7. Crystal form, purity, and dryness — missing. Solved under pure, anhydrous, dry crystals (assumed); the wet-cake alternative is discussed qualitatively in Sections 3 and 7 because the entrainment fraction is not given.
  8. Cooling path and residence time — missing. Solved at equilibrium; kinetic shortfall is treated in Section 7.

No missing value has been taken in silence: each is either given, assumed and labelled, or solved under a stated alternative.

5. Independent verification — Prompt 3

Checks were executed in code (Python) and are reported as run.

  1. Solute balance closure. In: 30 g. Out: 12 g dissolved + 18 g crystals = 30 g. Closure error = 0 g. Pass.
  2. Solvent balance closure. In: 100 g. Out: 100 g in mother liquor + 0 g in pure crystals (assumed crystal form) = 100 g. Closure error = 0 g. Pass.
  3. Total mass closure. In: 130 g solution. Out: 112 g mother liquor + 18 g crystals = 130 g. Closure error = 0 g. Pass.
  4. Limiting case 1 — no cooling. If the final temperature equals 60 °C, S(20 °C) is replaced by S(60 °C) and Y = 30 − 30 = 0 g, as required by inspection. Pass.
  5. Limiting case 2 — temperature-independent solubility. If S were the same at both temperatures, Y = 0 g by the same balance. Pass.
  6. Limiting case 3 — zero final solubility. If S(20 °C) = 0, Y = 30 g, i.e. all dissolved solute crystallises. Pass.
  7. Code check. The nominal yield, the 60 % crystallised fraction, both uncertainty ranges in Section 3, and the evaporation alternative were recomputed in executed code; the code returns 18.0 g, 0.60, 16–20 g, 13.8–22.2 g, and 18.6 g respectively, matching the hand calculation. Pass.
  8. Correlation valid-range check. Not applicable: no correlation or fitted relation is used, so there is no valid range to exceed. The two solubilities are used only at the temperatures at which they are given; no interpolation or extrapolation is performed.

No check failed. No solution value was altered to make a check pass.

Agreement with another AI model is not used as verification anywhere in this solution (checklist item 7).

6. Primary source that settles the point

The point is settled only by solubility data for the actual solute–solvent system: a primary databank entry or a measurement on the actual material — for example the IUPAC Solubility Data Series volume for the named system, a peer-reviewed solubility measurement for the named solute and solvent, or a laboratory saturation measurement (gravimetric or analytical) on the actual feed, including identification of the equilibrium solid phase.

Unverified claim notice. Because neither the solute, the solvent, nor the data set is named, the values 30 and 12 g per 100 g solvent, and every result derived from them, rest on an unidentified source and are marked unverified until checked against the primary source above. If user-supplied plant, vendor, or measured data for the actual system become available, those data supersede the scenario ranges in Section 3 for that case.

7. Audit against built equipment — Prompt 4

The three points most likely to differ between this equilibrium calculation and built equipment:

  1. Metastable supersaturation and finite residence time. Direction: actual yield lower. Rough size: a crystalliser discharged before desupersaturation is complete can leave several grams per 100 g solvent in solution; 1–5 g per 100 g solvent (−6 % to −28 %) is a plausible operating shortfall (estimated). Settled by: mother-liquor concentration measurement (density, refractometry, or assay) on the discharge, against the equilibrium solubility at the discharge temperature.
  2. Mother-liquor entrainment in the recovered crystals. Direction: wet-cake mass higher than the dry-crystal yield, dry-solute recovery lower after washing, and wash losses unaccounted. Rough size: an unwashed or poorly dewatered cake commonly retains on the order of 5–20 % of its mass as mother liquor (estimated, equipment-dependent); at the final liquor composition of 12 g solute per 112 g liquor, that retained liquor also carries dissolved solute out of the crystal product accounting. Settled by: cake moisture / liquor-retention measurement and the centrifuge or filter vendor's dewatering data for the actual crystal size distribution.
  3. Crystal form different from the assumed pure anhydrous solute — hydrate or solvate formation, or a polymorphic change on cooling. Direction: either; solvent bound in the crystal raises wet-crystal mass and lowers free-solvent mass, which also changes the mother-liquor basis. Rough size: for a hydrate, the bound solvent is commonly several percent to tens of percent of the crystal mass (estimated; system-specific and not computable here). Settled by: solid-phase characterisation of the actual product (X-ray diffraction, thermogravimetric analysis) and the primary solubility record, which states the equilibrium solid phase.

Fines loss in classification, encrustation on cooled surfaces, and feed impurity build-up are additional plant effects in the same direction as point 1 and are not quantified here.

8. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model:

  • Crystallisation kinetics: nucleation, growth rates, metastable zone width, seeding, and residence-time distribution.
  • Particle properties: crystal size distribution, fines, agglomeration, and breakage, all of which affect separation and the saleable yield.
  • Separation and drying: filtration or centrifugation losses, wash losses, and dryer losses.
  • Thermal effects: heat of crystallisation and the cooling duty are not computed; no energy balance is required for the mass yield, but the temperature trajectory in real equipment is not the equilibrium path assumed here.
  • Impurities: co-crystallisation, solubility change caused by impurities, and product purity are excluded.
  • Encrustation and fouling of cooling surfaces, and solvent vaporisation losses beyond the single alternative quantified in Section 3.

Information not accessible here: the identity and provenance of the data set behind the given solubilities; any proprietary or restricted databank values for the actual system; vendor guarantees for any specific crystalliser, filter, or centrifuge.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: residual supersaturation at discharge, cake liquor retention, wash and fines losses, encrustation, and impurity accumulation over recycles (Section 7).

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 % (i.e. by more than about 1.8 g per 100 g solvent):

  • Either solubility in the actual system differing from the given values by more than about 2 g per 100 g solvent in the unfavourable direction, alone or in combination (Section 3, scenario 2 already spans −23 % to +23 %).
  • Residual supersaturation at discharge above about 1.8 g per 100 g solvent.
  • Hydrate or solvate formation, which changes both the crystal mass and the solvent balance.
  • Excess solid present in the 60 °C feed, or mother-liquor recycle, either of which changes the quantity being reported.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Which solute, which solvent, and which primary source do the values 30 and 12 g per 100 g solvent come from, and what solid phase was in equilibrium in that source?
  2. Is the required figure the equilibrium yield, the single-batch recovered dry-crystal yield, or an overall plant yield with recycle?
  3. What are the measured mother-liquor concentration and cake liquor retention at the intended discharge temperature?
  4. Is the product anhydrous or a hydrate/solvate, and is the yield to be reported as dry solute, dry crystal, or wet cake?
  5. What uncertainty on each solubility is acceptable, and does the 14–22 g per 100 g solvent range remain acceptable for the intended use?
Final answer

Crystal yield (equilibrium, dry pure crystals, unchanged solvent mass): nominal 18 g per 100 g of solvent, reported as a range of 14–22 g per 100 g of solvent given the unidentified source and unstated uncertainty of the two given solubilities (16–20 g per 100 g of solvent if rounding of the quoted values is the only error). The solubilities and the derived yield are unverified until checked against primary solubility data for the named solute–solvent system.

A6. Polymer Viscosity

Response without the skill

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Definitions and given data

The intrinsic viscosity is denoted by [η][\eta], with unit decilitres per gram (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}).

The Mark–Houwink constant is denoted by KK, with unit dL/g\mathrm{dL/g} as stated in the problem.

The viscosity-average molar mass is denoted by MM, with unit grams per mole (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}).

The Mark–Houwink exponent is denoted by aa, dimensionless.

Given values:

  • K=3×10−4 dL/gK = 3 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}
  • M=100,000 g/mol=1.0×105 g/molM = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol} = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{g/mol}

No numerical value for aa is given in the problem statement.

Relation

The Mark–Houwink relation stated in the problem is

[η]=KMa[\eta] = K M^{a}

where [η][\eta], KK, MM, and aa are as defined above.

Substitution

Substitution of the given values for KK and MM gives

[η]=(3×10−4 dL/g)(1.0×105 g/mol)a[\eta] = \left(3 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}\right) \left(1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{g/mol}\right)^{a}

in the unit convention stated in the problem. Simplification of the power of ten gives

[η]=3×10−4×105a dL/g=3×10 5a−4 dL/g.[\eta] = 3 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{5a}\ \mathrm{dL/g} = 3 \times 10^{\,5a-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}.

Result

A single numerical value for [η][\eta] cannot be determined from the data given, because the result depends on the unspecified exponent aa. The determinate result from the stated data is the parametric expression

[η]=3×10 5a−4 dL/g.[\eta] = 3 \times 10^{\,5a-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}.

6. Audit points: where built-equipment / real-material behaviour is most likely to differ (Prompt 4)
  1. Polydispersity. Real samples have a distribution of molar masses. [η][\eta] responds to the viscosity-average, which lies between the number- and weight-averages and depends on aa itself. If the supplied 100,000 g/mol100{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol} is in fact a weight- or number-average, the computed [η][\eta] is biased, typically by tens of percent for broad distributions, direction depending on which average was supplied. Settled by: a molar-mass distribution measurement on the actual material (e.g. size-exclusion chromatography with absolute detection).
  2. Chain architecture. Branching compacts the coil and lowers [η][\eta] at a given molar mass (equivalently, lowers the effective aa); stiffness raises it. A branched or stiff real polymer can fall outside the 0.0950.095–3.0 dL/g3.0\ \mathrm{dL/g} range entirely, by factors, not percent. Settled by: the (KK, aa) table entry for the actual polymer architecture, or direct viscometry.
  3. Solvent quality and temperature drift. A solvent nearer theta conditions than assumed moves aa toward 0.50.5 and [η][\eta] toward the low end (a factor of up to about 3030 across the full range in this problem); temperature changes act through the same route. Settled by: the solvent and temperature recorded with the fitted parameters in the primary databank, matched to the conditions of use.

B1. Reaction Rate at a Higher Temperature

Response without the skill

Rate Constant at 400 K from Arrhenius Extrapolation

Given
  • k1k_1, the rate constant at the reference temperature, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}): k1=0.010 s−1k_1 = 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}
  • T1T_1, the reference temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}): T1=315 KT_1 = 315\ \mathrm{K}
  • T2T_2, the target temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}): T2=400 KT_2 = 400\ \mathrm{K}
  • EaE_a, the activation energy, in joules per mole (J mol−1\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}): Ea=80 kJ mol−1=80,000 J mol−1E_a = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} = 80{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}
  • RR, the gas constant, in joules per mole per kelvin (J mol−1 K−1\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}): R=8.314 J mol−1 K−1R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}
  • k2k_2, the rate constant at T2T_2, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}): to be estimated

The kinetics were measured between 300 K300\ \mathrm{K} and 330 K330\ \mathrm{K}, so 400 K400\ \mathrm{K} lies outside the measured range.

Method

The Arrhenius equation relates a rate constant to temperature:

k=Aexp⁡(−EaRT)k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)

where kk is the rate constant at absolute temperature TT, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}), and AA is the pre-exponential factor, in the same units as kk, here reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}).

Writing the equation at T1T_1 and at T2T_2 and dividing eliminates AA:

ln⁡(k2k1)=−EaR(1T2−1T1)=EaR(1T1−1T2)\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)

where ln⁡\ln is the natural logarithm. This form assumes EaE_a and AA are constant over the temperature interval from T1T_1 to T2T_2.

Calculation

First, the ratio of activation energy to gas constant:

EaR=80,000 J mol−18.314 J mol−1 K−1=9,622 K\frac{E_a}{R} = \frac{80{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}} = 9{,}622\ \mathrm{K}

Next, the difference of reciprocal temperatures:

1T1−1T2=1315 K−1400 K=3.1746×10−3 K−1−2.5000×10−3 K−1=6.746×10−4 K−1\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{315\ \mathrm{K}} - \frac{1}{400\ \mathrm{K}} = 3.1746\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} - 2.5000\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} = 6.746\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}

Then:

ln⁡(k2k1)=(9,622 K)(6.746×10−4 K−1)=6.49\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = (9{,}622\ \mathrm{K})(6.746\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}) = 6.49

k2k1=exp⁡(6.49)=659\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp(6.49) = 659

k2=k1exp⁡(6.49)=(0.010 s−1)(659)=6.6 s−1k_2 = k_1 \exp(6.49) = (0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})(659) = 6.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

As a check, the pre-exponential factor implied by the reference point is A=k1exp⁡(Ea/(RT1))=1.8×1011 s−1A = k_1 \exp(E_a/(R T_1)) = 1.8\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, and Aexp⁡(−Ea/(RT2))A \exp(-E_a/(R T_2)) returns the same value, 6.6 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.

Result

k2≈6.6 s−1 at 400 Kk_2 \approx 6.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \text{ at } 400\ \mathrm{K}

The rate constant increases by a factor of about 660660 between 315 K315\ \mathrm{K} and 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}.

Scope and limitation

This value is an extrapolation, not an interpolation. The target temperature, 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}, is 70 K70\ \mathrm{K} above the highest measured temperature (330 K330\ \mathrm{K}), while the entire measured range spans only 30 K30\ \mathrm{K} (300 K300\ \mathrm{K} to 330 K330\ \mathrm{K}). The calculation is valid only if the reaction mechanism, the reaction order, EaE_a, and AA remain unchanged up to 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}. A change of mechanism, a competing reaction, catalyst deactivation, a phase change, or mass-transfer limitation at the higher temperature would invalidate the extrapolation, and none of these can be ruled out from data at 300 K300\ \mathrm{K} to 330 K330\ \mathrm{K} alone.

The result is also sensitive to EaE_a because EaE_a appears in an exponent multiplied by a large reciprocal-temperature difference. A 10%10\% error in EaE_a changes the estimate to 3.4 s−13.4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} (for 72 kJ mol−172\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) or 13 s−113\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} (for 88 kJ mol−188\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}), a factor of about two in either direction. The value 6.6 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} should therefore be reported as an order-of-magnitude Arrhenius estimate pending measurement at or near 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}, not as a measured rate constant.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Rate Constant at 400 K by Arrhenius Extrapolation

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. The target temperature, 400 K, lies 70 K above the top of the measured range, 300–330 K. The extrapolation distance (70 K) is more than twice the whole measured span (30 K). An Arrhenius extrapolation assumes that the same reaction mechanism, the same rate-limiting step, and a temperature-independent activation energy hold from 315 K to 400 K. None of these is established by data in the measured range alone. Small errors in the activation energy are also amplified exponentially over this distance (Section 5).

Confidence rating. Low for the value as a physical prediction at 400 K. High for the arithmetic, conditional on the Arrhenius model and on the inputs as stated: the calculation is a closed-form evaluation, checked by an independent route in Section 7. The low overall rating is set by model risk (mechanism change outside the fitted range), not by arithmetic risk.

Headline result. Central value 6.6 1/s; defensible reporting range 3 to 15 1/s from activation-energy uncertainty alone, and 2.6 to 16 1/s when plausible measurement uncertainty in the reference rate constant is added (Section 4). A single value should not be used for design.

2. Symbols and model

Symbols are defined at first use:

  • kk — first-order rate constant, in reciprocal seconds (1/s).
  • k1k_1 — value of kk at the reference temperature, in 1/s.
  • k2k_2 — value of kk at the target temperature, in 1/s.
  • TT — absolute temperature, in kelvin (K).
  • T1T_1 — reference temperature, 315 K.
  • T2T_2 — target temperature, 400 K.
  • EaE_a — activation energy, in joules per mole (J/mol) in the equation, reported in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol).
  • RR — gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K).
  • AA — pre-exponential factor, in 1/s, used only in the independent check in Section 7.

Model used — the two-temperature Arrhenius relation, the standard relation for a temperature-independent EaE_a:

k2=k1exp⁡[−EaR(1T2−1T1)]k_2 = k_1 \exp\left[ -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) \right]

Source of the relation: the Arrhenius equation, as given in standard kinetics references (e.g. Fogler, Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering; Laidler, Chemical Kinetics). Range of validity: a single elementary or effectively single-step mechanism with constant EaE_a, no change of rate-limiting step, no onset of mass- or heat-transfer limitation, and no phase or catalyst-state change over the temperature interval. That range is demonstrated only over 300–330 K here; its extension to 400 K is assumed, not demonstrated (see Sections 3 and 8). This claim about validity rests on the original kinetic study behind the reported EaE_a, which has not been seen; it is unverified until checked against that primary source (Section 6).

Adding the assumed ± 10 % uncertainty in k1k_1 (which scales k2k_2 in direct proportion) widens the ± 10 kJ/mol band to 2.6 to 16 1/s. This is the range to report: kk at 400 K ≈ 6.6 1/s, plausible range about 3–15 1/s (2.6–16 1/s including reference-value scatter). The band is asymmetric because the dependence on EaE_a is exponential.

6. Primary source that settles the point

The point — whether Arrhenius behaviour with Ea≈80E_a \approx 80 kJ/mol extends to 400 K — is settled only by the original kinetic dataset and its fit (the study from which k1k_1 and EaE_a were reported: raw rate measurements, their temperatures, replicates, and the reported confidence interval on EaE_a), or, better, by a direct measurement of kk on the actual material and medium at, or near, 400 K. Secondary databanks (e.g. the NIST Chemical Kinetics Database) can corroborate EaE_a for a named reaction, but the reaction is not named here, so no databank check is possible. Every claim in this solution that rests on the reported EaE_a or on Arrhenius behaviour above 330 K is unverified until checked against that primary dataset or a high-temperature measurement.

7. Verification by an independent route (Prompt 3)

Checks performed by executed code (Python, direct evaluation of the expressions above); no check was adjusted to pass, and agreement with any other AI model is not used as verification.

  1. Independent route via the pre-exponential factor. A=k1exp⁡(Ea/(RT1))=1.85×1011A = k_1 \exp(E_a / (R T_1)) = 1.85 \times 10^{11} 1/s (computed). Then k2=Aexp⁡(−Ea/(RT2))=6.593k_2 = A \exp(-E_a / (R T_2)) = 6.593 1/s. Agreement with the direct two-temperature result, 6.593 1/s: exact to the digits shown. Pass.
  2. Limiting case, T2=T1T_2 = T_1. The relation returns k2=k1=0.010k_2 = k_1 = 0.010 1/s exactly. Pass.
  3. Limiting case, sign and direction. For Ea>0E_a > 0 and T2>T1T_2 > T_1, k2>k1k_2 > k_1 is required; obtained factor 659 > 1. At the top of the measured range the same relation gives k(330 K)=0.040k(330\ \text{K}) = 0.040 1/s, a factor of 4 over 15 K, consistent in size with an 80 kJ/mol activation energy (roughly a quadrupling per 15 K near 320 K). Pass.
  4. Dimensional check. The exponent (Ea/R)(1/T)(E_a/R)(1/T) is K × K⁻¹, dimensionless; k2k_2 carries the units of k1k_1, 1/s. Pass.
  5. Balance closure. Not applicable: no material or energy balance exists in a single rate-constant evaluation. Stated explicitly rather than omitted.
  6. Correlation valid-range check. Fails, by construction, and this failure is the central caveat: the Arrhenius fit is demonstrated only over 300–330 K and is used at 400 K, outside its demonstrated range. The numerical result stands as a model-conditional estimate; the valid-range check does not pass and has not been made to pass.
8. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this estimate and behaviour in built equipment:

  1. Change of mechanism or rate-limiting step above 330 K. Direction: either way. If a lower-activation-energy path (or diffusion control, effective EaE_a of order 10–20 kJ/mol) takes over, the true kk falls far below the extrapolation; if a higher-EaE_a path opens, it rises above it. Rough size: illustrative two-segment calculations, using the central fit to 330 K (k=0.040k = 0.040 1/s) and a different EaE_a thereafter, give k(400 K)=0.51k(400\ \text{K}) = 0.51 1/s for a drop to Ea=40E_a = 40 kJ/mol above 330 K (−92 %) and 85 1/s for a rise to 120 kJ/mol. These are scenarios showing the size of model risk, not predictions. Settled by: kinetic measurements between 330 K and 400 K on the actual system (the primary dataset of Section 6, extended).
  2. Mass- and heat-transfer limitation at the much higher rate. At k≈6.6k \approx 6.6 1/s the characteristic reaction time is about 0.15 s. In a real vessel, pore diffusion, film transfer, or heat removal at that rate commonly limits the observed rate below the intrinsic kk. Direction: observed rate lower than predicted, potentially by a factor of several. Settled by: effectiveness-factor or transfer-coefficient calculations for the actual geometry, and by a test varying agitation, particle size, or flow at temperature.
  3. State of the medium and catalyst at 400 K. Solvent boiling or a phase change, catalyst sintering or fouling, and thermal side reactions or decomposition all become more likely 70 K above the studied range, and an exothermic first-order reaction with a 660-fold rate increase carries a thermal-runaway hazard that a rate constant alone does not flag. Direction: rate and selectivity both depart from the single-reaction model; deactivation lowers the rate with time on stream. Settled by: the vendor or literature data sheet for the catalyst/medium (temperature limits), thermal-stability screening (e.g. DSC or accelerating-rate calorimetry) on the actual mixture, and plant or pilot operating records at comparable temperature.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: temperature dependence of EaE_a itself; non-Arrhenius behaviour; reversible reaction and equilibrium shift; parallel and consecutive reactions; diffusion and heat-transfer effects; catalyst ageing; wall effects; pressure effects on any gas-phase concentration basis; mixing and residence-time distribution in any real reactor.
  • Information not available here: the identity of the reaction, the raw kinetic data and their scatter, the confidence interval on EaE_a, and any restricted databank or vendor record for the specific system. Without the reaction identity, no external databank value can be checked.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: hot spots and thermal runaway, fouling, deactivation over time on stream, start-up transients, and control-loop response at a reaction time of about 0.15 s.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: an EaE_a error larger than about 1.2 kJ/mol; a temperature error larger than about 2 K at 400 K; a k1k_1 error larger than 10 %; any mechanism, phase, or rate-limiting-step change between 330 K and 400 K (changes of a factor of 2 to 10 or more, per Section 8).

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the reported uncertainty (confidence interval) on EaE_a, and over exactly what data was it fitted?
  2. Has kk been measured anywhere above 330 K for this system, and does a plot of ln⁡k\ln k against 1/T1/T remain linear there?
  3. What are the reaction, medium, phase, pressure, and catalyst at 400 K, and are all of them within their rated temperature limits?
  4. Is the reaction reversible or exothermic enough at a 660-fold rate increase to raise equilibrium or thermal-runaway concerns?
  5. In the intended equipment, is the observed rate kinetically controlled, or limited by mass or heat transfer at a reaction time near 0.15 s?
  6. Is a design being based on the central value, 6.6 1/s, rather than on the reported range, 3–15 1/s — and if so, why?
10. Result

Conditional on the Arrhenius model with constant EaE_a and unchanged first-order mechanism, the rate constant at 400 K is

k(400 K)≈6.6k(400\ \text{K}) \approx 6.6 1/s, reported as a range of about 3–15 1/s (2.6–16 1/s including assumed reference-value scatter), with low confidence as a physical prediction because 400 K lies far outside the 300–330 K measured range.

The primary source that would raise the confidence is a direct measurement of kk near 400 K, or the original kinetic dataset with its uncertainty on EaE_a; until one of those is checked, the extrapolated value is unverified.

B2. Catalyst Losing Strength

Response without the skill

Conversion after 180 days on stream

Definitions
  • XX is the fractional conversion of the reactant, dimensionless.
  • kk is the fresh first-order rate constant, in reciprocal time (1/time).
  • τ\tau is the residence time, in time.
  • kτk\tau is the product of the fresh rate constant and the residence time, dimensionless. The given value is kτ=2.0k\tau = 2.0.
  • aa is the catalyst activity, dimensionless, with initial value a=1a = 1 for fresh catalyst.
  • kdk_{\mathrm{d}} is the deactivation constant, in reciprocal days (1/day). The given value is kd=0.004 day−1k_{\mathrm{d}} = 0.004\ \mathrm{day^{-1}}.
  • tt is the time on stream, in days (day). The time of interest is t=180 dayt = 180\ \mathrm{day}.

The reactor is treated with the first-order plug-flow (packed-bed) design relation, for which conversion depends on the effective product of rate constant, activity, and residence time, akτa k \tau, dimensionless.

Catalyst activity at 180 days

Exponential activity decay is

a(t)=exp⁡(−kdt)a(t) = \exp(-k_{\mathrm{d}} t)

where a(t)a(t) is the activity at time tt, dimensionless, and exp⁡\exp is the exponential function.

Substitution gives

kdt=(0.004 day−1)(180 day)=0.72k_{\mathrm{d}} t = (0.004\ \mathrm{day^{-1}})(180\ \mathrm{day}) = 0.72

a(180 day)=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a(180\ \mathrm{day}) = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487

The catalyst retains about 48.7% of its fresh activity.

Effective rate group at 180 days

akτ=(0.487)(2.0)=0.974a k \tau = (0.487)(2.0) = 0.974

For a first-order plug-flow reactor,

X=1−exp⁡(−akτ)X = 1 - \exp(-a k \tau)

where the symbols are as defined above.

For fresh catalyst, as a check, a=1a = 1 gives

Xfresh=1−exp⁡(−2.0)=1−0.135=0.865X_{\mathrm{fresh}} = 1 - \exp(-2.0) = 1 - 0.135 = 0.865

At t=180 dayt = 180\ \mathrm{day},

X=1−exp⁡(−0.974)=1−0.378=0.622X = 1 - \exp(-0.974) = 1 - 0.378 = 0.622

The conversion after 180 days on stream is approximately 0.62, i.e. about 62%, down from about 86% for fresh catalyst.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Conversion after 180 days on stream — first-order catalytic reactor with exponential deactivation

Symbols, defined before first use
  • XX — conversion of the limiting reactant, dimensionless (fraction reacted). The value sought is the instantaneous value at the stated time on stream unless otherwise noted.
  • XfreshX_{\mathrm{fresh}} — conversion with fresh catalyst, dimensionless.
  • kk — fresh first-order rate constant, in reciprocal time (1/time), on the same time basis as the residence time below.
  • τ\tau (tau) — mean residence time, in time, on the same basis as kk.
  • kτk\tau — product of kk and τ\tau, dimensionless. Given as 2.0 for fresh catalyst.
  • aa — catalyst activity, dimensionless, defined as the ratio of the current effective rate constant to the fresh rate constant. Initial value 1.
  • kdk_d — deactivation constant, in reciprocal days (1/day).
  • tt — time on stream, in days (d).
  • keffk_{\mathrm{eff}} — effective rate constant at time tt, in reciprocal time, taken here as keff=a kk_{\mathrm{eff}} = a\,k.
1. Weakness and confidence rating (Prompt 1, Checklist 1)

Weakness. The arithmetic of first-order conversion with exponential deactivation is well established. The weakness is not the arithmetic. It is that the problem does not state the reactor flow model, and the deactivation law is stated without its range, source, or mechanism. Conversion for a first-order reaction depends strongly on the flow model at kτ=2.0k\tau = 2.0: plug flow and a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) differ by about 0.13 in absolute conversion at day 180. A single exponential deactivation law also rarely holds unchanged over 180 days in built equipment, where poisoning, sintering, and fouling usually act at different rates and in different parts of the bed.

Confidence rating.

  • In the conditional arithmetic, given a stated flow model and the stated kdk_d: high, about 90% — the calculation is closed-form and was verified in code (Section 6).
  • In either single value as a prediction for built equipment: low to moderate, about 40–50%. The flow model is missing, kdk_d is not sourced, and no temperature, pressure, feed-composition, or catalyst-lot information is given.

No claim in this solution has been verified against a primary plant or vendor source (Section 5). Agreement with another AI model is not used as verification anywhere in this solution (Checklist 7).

The first-order PFR and CSTR conversion relations are textbook design equations (any standard reaction-engineering text, e.g. the PFR and CSTR design equations for a first-order irreversible reaction at constant density); their valid range here is: first order, irreversible, constant density, constant τ\tau, uniform activity throughout the reactor at the instant considered. Outside that range (reversibility, volume change, non-uniform activity) the relations do not hold.

4.1 Activity at 180 days

a(180)=exp⁡(−kdt)=exp⁡[−(0.004 1/day)(180 d)]=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a(180) = \exp(-k_d t) = \exp[-(0.004\ \mathrm{1/day})(180\ \mathrm{d})] = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487

Effective dimensionless rate at day 180:

keffτ=a kτ=(0.487)(2.0)=0.974k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau = a\,k\tau = (0.487)(2.0) = 0.974

4.2 Plug-flow (or batch) case

For a first-order irreversible reaction at constant density in plug flow:

X=1−exp⁡(−keffτ)X = 1 - \exp(-k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau)

  • Fresh: Xfresh=1−exp⁡(−2.0)=0.865X_{\mathrm{fresh}} = 1 - \exp(-2.0) = 0.865
  • At 180 days: X=1−exp⁡(−0.974)=0.622X = 1 - \exp(-0.974) = 0.622

That is a fall of 0.243 absolute, or 28.0% relative to fresh.

4.3 CSTR case (fluid back-mixed, catalyst uniformly aged)

For a first-order irreversible reaction at constant density in a CSTR:

X=keffτ1+keffτX = \frac{k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau}{1 + k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau}

  • Fresh: Xfresh=2.0/(1+2.0)=0.667X_{\mathrm{fresh}} = 2.0/(1+2.0) = 0.667

That is a fall of 0.173 absolute, or 26.0% relative to fresh.

Relative to the nominal PFR value X=0.622X = 0.622:

  • kdk_d guess, ±25%\pm 25\% (assumed range): kd=0.003k_d = 0.003 1/day gives PFR X=0.688X = 0.688 (+10.6%); kd=0.005k_d = 0.005 1/day gives 0.557 (−10.6%). For the CSTR the corresponding moves are +9.1% and −9.1%.

7. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Non-uniform deactivation through the bed. A poison or coke front usually deactivates the inlet of a fixed bed first; the bed-average activity is then not a single exp⁡(−kdt)\exp(-k_d t) applied uniformly, and the effective conversion depends on the front position and shape. Direction: for a sharp inlet front, conversion typically falls faster than the uniform-activity model once the front is established, because the remaining active bed length is what matters in plug flow. Rough size: commonly 0.05–0.15 absolute in XX over a long run — comparable to the whole flow-model spread. Settling document/test: axial temperature-profile records and spent-catalyst activity/carbon assays by bed position at turnaround, held in the plant inspection and laboratory records — unverified.
  2. Temperature drift and compensation. Operators commonly raise inlet temperature to hold conversion as activity falls. If that was done, kk rose while aa fell, kdk_d itself increased with temperature, and the day-180 XX is higher than the isothermal estimate while the catalyst ages faster thereafter. Rough size: holding XX fully would require offsetting a factor of ~2 in keffτk_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau over 180 days; partial compensation of 0.05–0.10 absolute in XX is plausible. Settling document: the historian temperature and conversion record for the run — unverified.
  3. Feed-borne poisons and upsets. A single exponential fitted or quoted for clean feed does not cover poison excursions (sulfur, metals, water, oxygenates, as applicable), start-ups, or flow maldistribution and bypassing that develop with fouling. Direction: excursions make true activity lower than exp⁡(−kdt)\exp(-k_d t) and are often partly irreversible. Rough size: a single severe excursion can remove activity equivalent to tens of days of normal ageing, i.e. several percent relative in XX, and bypassing caps XX regardless of activity. Settling documents: feed assay records, upset/incident reports, and differential-pressure trend records for the run — unverified.
8. What this calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: reversibility and equilibrium limitation; selectivity change with age and any by-product inhibition; internal and external mass-transfer (pore effectiveness changing as pores foul); heat effects and hot spots; volume change on reaction; catalyst particle-size and bed-voidage effects; flow maldistribution, channelling, and bypass; pressure drop growth; regeneration, catalyst replacement, and start-up/shutdown periods within the 180 days; measurement error in any plant conversion used for comparison.
  • Information not available to this calculation: the vendor's proprietary deactivation data and model for the actual catalyst; the plant's design record, historian data, feed assays, and laboratory records named in Sections 5 and 7. These are held by the vendor and the operating site and cannot be seen here.
  • Effects that appear only in running equipment: poison fronts, fouling-driven maldistribution, temperature-compensation practice, excursion damage, and mechanical catalyst loss or attrition (Section 7).
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10% (relative): (i) the reactor is closer to a CSTR than to plug flow, or vice versa (−20.7% between the two ideal limits at day 180); (ii) kdk_d differs from 0.004 1/day by about ±25%\pm 25\% or more (∓\mp~10.6% in PFR XX); (iii) the required figure is the time-averaged rather than instantaneous conversion (+20.4%, PFR); (iv) inlet temperature was raised to compensate for deactivation; (v) a poison excursion or a deactivation law that is not a single exponential (e.g. a fast initial decay followed by a slower tail, which would make a(180)a(180) higher than 0.487 if kdk_d was fitted to early data, or lower if fitted late).

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. What is the reactor's actual flow model and residence-time distribution, per the design record?
  2. What is the source, fitted range, and temperature/feed basis of kd=0.004k_d = 0.004 1/day, and does the vendor's document for this catalyst lot support a single exponential over 180 days?
  3. Is the required conversion per-pass or overall, and instantaneous at day 180 or averaged over the run?
  4. Was inlet temperature, feed rate, or pressure changed during the 180 days?
  5. Were there feed-poison excursions, start-ups, or regenerations in the period?
  6. What does the historian record show for measured conversion near day 180, and does it fall inside the reported 0.45–0.69 range? If it falls outside, which assumption in Section 3 is wrong?
9. Answer in brief

At 180 days, a=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487 (given law, nominal given kdk_d), so keffτ=0.974k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau = 0.974. Instantaneous per-pass conversion is 0.62 for plug flow (fresh 0.865) and 0.49 for a CSTR (fresh 0.667). Reported as a range: X(180 days)≈0.49X(180\ \mathrm{days}) \approx 0.49–0.620.62 at the nominal inputs, widening to ≈0.45\approx 0.45–0.690.69 for kdk_d between 0.003 and 0.005 1/day. Confidence in the conditional arithmetic is high; confidence in any single value as a plant prediction is low to moderate until the flow model and the vendor/plant sources named in Section 5 are checked.

B3. Reactor Cooling

Response without the skill

Cooling Area for a Reactor

Given data
  • QQ is the rate of heat release that must be removed, in kilowatts (kW\mathrm{kW}); Q=500 kWQ = 500\ \mathrm{kW}.
  • ΔT\Delta T is the mean temperature difference between the reaction mass and the coolant, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}); ΔT=25 K\Delta T = 25\ \mathrm{K}. Mean temperature difference means the appropriately averaged driving force over the cooling surface, not necessarily a single inlet or outlet difference.
Missing data

No unique cooling area can be calculated from QQ and ΔT\Delta T alone.

The calculation also requires:

  • UU is the overall heat-transfer coefficient based on the cooling area, in kilowatts per square metre per kelvin (kW m−2 K−1\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}), or equivalently in watts per square metre per kelvin (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}).

The value of UU depends on information not supplied, including the fluids on both sides of the wall, their flow rates and physical properties, the wall material and thickness, the type of cooling surface (jacket, coil, or external exchanger), agitation in the reactor, and fouling. Stating a single area without a stated value of UU would therefore be unjustified.

Sizing equation
  • AA is the required cooling (heat-transfer) area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}).

For steady heat removal with constant UU and the stated mean temperature difference, the heat-transfer rate equation is

Q=UAΔTQ = U A \Delta T

Rearranged for the area:

A=QUΔTA = \frac{Q}{U \Delta T}

Substitution of the given data

A=500 kWU×25 K=20U m2A = \frac{500\ \mathrm{kW}}{U \times 25\ \mathrm{K}} = \frac{20}{U}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

where, in the final form above, UU is inserted numerically in kW m−2 K−1\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}.

In the more common unit for UU:

A=500,000 WU×25 K=20,000U m2A = \frac{500{,}000\ \mathrm{W}}{U \times 25\ \mathrm{K}} = \frac{20{,}000}{U}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

where, in this form, UU is inserted numerically in W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}.

This is the complete result obtainable from the data supplied.

Checks
  • Units: kW/[(kW m−2 K−1)×K]=m2\mathrm{kW} / [(\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}) \times \mathrm{K}] = \mathrm{m^{2}}, as required for an area.

Conclusion

With Q=500 kWQ = 500\ \mathrm{kW} and ΔT=25 K\Delta T = 25\ \mathrm{K}, the required cooling area is A=20/U m2A = 20 / U\ \mathrm{m^{2}} with UU in kW m−2 K−1\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}, equivalently A=20,000/U m2A = 20{,}000 / U\ \mathrm{m^{2}} with UU in W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}. A single numerical area requires a justified value of the overall heat-transfer coefficient UU for the actual reactor, fluids, cooling geometry, and fouling condition, which has not been provided. Once such a value is specified, the area follows directly from the equation above, before any additional design margin is applied.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Cooling Area for a Reactor — 500 kW at a Mean Temperature Difference of 25 K

Weakness and confidence

Weakness: The problem as stated does not contain the quantity that controls the answer. The heat-transfer area is set, in inverse proportion, by the overall heat-transfer coefficient, denoted UU, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}). No value of UU, and none of the information needed to calculate UU (fluid properties, agitation, wall, fouling, jacket or coil type), is supplied. Any single area quoted from the stated data alone would therefore be an assumed UU presented as if it were data.

Confidence rating: Low — 2 out of 5 for the area, High for the arithmetic. The governing relation is exact for a steady duty at a stated mean temperature difference. Confidence is low only, but decisively, because UU must be estimated or assumed, and plausible UU values for jacketed reactors span roughly a factor of 3 within one service type and a factor of 8 across services. The result is therefore reported as a range, with a clearly labelled nominal value for scale only. Agreement with another AI model would not raise this rating and is not used as verification (Checklist item 7).

Symbols
  • Heat release rate, denoted QQ, in kilowatts (kW\mathrm{kW}) or watts (W\mathrm{W}): 1 kW=1000 W1\ \mathrm{kW} = 1000\ \mathrm{W}.
  • Required heat-transfer area, denoted AA, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}).
  • Overall heat-transfer coefficient, denoted UU, in W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}, defined on the same area basis (inside or outside surface) as AA.
  • Mean temperature difference between reaction mass and coolant, denoted ΔT\Delta T, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}).

7. Audit by a skilled engineer (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Fouling and ageing lower the operating UU below the clean value. Direction: area undersized if a clean UU is used. Rough size: 2020–50%50\% more area required in fouling services (see the worked fouling illustration in §4). Settled by: plant fouling records / operating UU trend for the vessel, and the design fouling resistances in the vendor document.
  2. Batch transients and loss of agitation. In a batch reactor the peak heat release can be 1.51.5–3×3\times the average (assumed illustration range), and an agitator trip collapses the inside film coefficient, so the installed area cannot remove even the average duty under the condition that matters most for temperature control. Direction: undersized, at the worst moment. Settled by: reaction calorimetry on the actual recipe (peak rate, not average) and the agitator failure case in the plant safety study / relief design basis.
  3. The stated ΔT\Delta T may not be deliverable over the whole surface. Coolant warming along the jacket, poor jacket circulation or vapour blanketing with a volatile coolant, and dead zones give a local ΔT\Delta T below 25 K25\ \mathrm{K} over part of the area. Direction: effective mean ΔT\Delta T lower, area undersized by roughly the same percentage (a fall to 20 K20\ \mathrm{K} effective requires 25%25\% more area). Settled by: measured coolant inlet and outlet temperatures and flow on the installed jacket, from which the true log-mean ΔT\Delta T is calculated.

  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling growth with time, agitation failures, coolant supply temperature rising in summer (directly cutting ΔT\Delta T), and control-loop response during an exotherm excursion.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%10\%: any error or change greater than about 9%9\% in UU, ΔT\Delta T, or QQ individually — in practice: fouling as in §4; summer coolant warming cutting ΔT\Delta T from 2525 to below about 22.5 K22.5\ \mathrm{K}; peak batch duty above 550 kW550\ \mathrm{kW}; a glass lining or a viscosity rise moving the service from one row of the §3 table to another; loss of agitation.

B4. Mixing in a Larger Vessel

Response without the skill

Stirred-Vessel Scale-Up

Given data and definitions
  • V1V_{1} is the laboratory vessel volume, 0.1 m30.1\ \mathrm{m^{3}}.
  • V2V_{2} is the large-scale vessel volume, 10 m310\ \mathrm{m^{3}}.
  • V2/V1V_{2}/V_{1} is the volume ratio, dimensionless.
  • λ\lambda is the linear scale ratio, i.e. the ratio of any corresponding linear dimension in the large vessel to that in the laboratory vessel, dimensionless.
  • D1D_{1} is the laboratory impeller diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • D2D_{2} is the large-scale impeller diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • N1N_{1} is the laboratory agitator speed, 300 rev min−1300\ \mathrm{rev\ min^{-1}} (rpm\mathrm{rpm}), equal to 5.0 s−15.0\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
  • N2N_{2} is the large-scale agitator speed, in rpm\mathrm{rpm} unless stated otherwise.
  • P1P_{1} is the laboratory power input, 50 W50\ \mathrm{W}.
  • P2P_{2} is the large-scale power input, in W\mathrm{W} unless stated otherwise.
  • P/VP/V is the power input per unit vessel volume, in W m−3\mathrm{W\ m^{-3}}.
  • ρ\rho is the liquid density, in kg m−3\mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}.
  • μ\mu is the liquid dynamic viscosity, in Pa s\mathrm{Pa\ s}.
  • NPN_{P} is the power number, dimensionless.
  • ReRe is the impeller Reynolds number, dimensionless.
  • vtipv_{\mathrm{tip}} is the impeller tip speed, in m s−1\mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}.
  • tmt_{m} is the blend (mixing) time, in s\mathrm{s}.

The same liquid is used at both scales, so ρ\rho and μ\mu are unchanged. The vessels and impellers are geometrically similar, so every linear ratio equals λ\lambda, the impeller type is unchanged, and the vessels are assumed baffled and operated in the turbulent regime, in which NPN_{P} is constant.

1. Geometric scale ratio

Under geometric similarity, volume scales as the cube of a linear dimension:

V2V1=λ3\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \lambda^{3}

V2V1=100.1=100\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \frac{10}{0.1} = 100

λ=1001/3=4.64\lambda = 100^{1/3} = 4.64

Hence:

D2D1=4.64,any large-scale lengthcorresponding laboratory length=4.64\frac{D_{2}}{D_{1}} = 4.64, \qquad \frac{\text{any large-scale length}}{\text{corresponding laboratory length}} = 4.64

The surface-area ratio, relevant to jacket heat transfer area per unit volume, is λ2=21.5\lambda^{2} = 21.5, so area per unit volume falls by a factor of λ=4.64\lambda = 4.64 on scale-up. Heat removal per unit volume at a given temperature difference and heat-transfer coefficient is therefore harder at large scale, independently of the agitation calculation below.

2. Power correlation

For a stirred vessel:

NP=PρN3D5,Re=ρND2μ,vtip=πDNN_{P} = \frac{P}{\rho N^{3} D^{5}}, \qquad Re = \frac{\rho N D^{2}}{\mu}, \qquad v_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N

where, in these expressions, NN is in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}} and DD is in m\mathrm{m}. In the turbulent, baffled regime NPN_{P} is constant for geometrically similar vessels, so, with ρ\rho unchanged,

P∝N3D5P \propto N^{3} D^{5}

and, because V∝D3V \propto D^{3},

PV∝N3D2\frac{P}{V} \propto N^{3} D^{2}

No single choice of N2N_{2} preserves P/VP/V, vtipv_{\mathrm{tip}}, ReRe and tmt_{m} at once, because they depend on different powers of DD. A scale-up criterion must be selected. The criterion most commonly used for scale-up where intensity of agitation, suspension or gas dispersion must be maintained is constant P/VP/V.

3. Primary result: constant power per unit volume

Laboratory value:

(PV)1=50 W0.1 m3=500 W m−3\left(\frac{P}{V}\right)_{1} = \frac{50\ \mathrm{W}}{0.1\ \mathrm{m^{3}}} = 500\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-3}}

Holding P/VP/V constant at large scale:

P2=(PV)1V2=500×10=5 000 W=5.0 kWP_{2} = \left(\frac{P}{V}\right)_{1} V_{2} = 500 \times 10 = 5\,000\ \mathrm{W} = 5.0\ \mathrm{kW}

That is, P2/P1=V2/V1=100P_{2}/P_{1} = V_{2}/V_{1} = 100.

From P/V∝N3D2=constantP/V \propto N^{3}D^{2} = \text{constant}:

N2=N1(D1D2)2/3=N1 λ−2/3=300×4.64−2/3N_{2} = N_{1}\left(\frac{D_{1}}{D_{2}}\right)^{2/3} = N_{1}\,\lambda^{-2/3} = 300 \times 4.64^{-2/3}

N2=300×0.359=108 rpmN_{2} = 300 \times 0.359 = 108\ \mathrm{rpm}

Check with P∝N3D5P \propto N^{3}D^{5}:

P2P1=(N2N1)3(D2D1)5=0.3593×4.645=0.0464×2 154≈100\frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}} = \left(\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{D_{2}}{D_{1}}\right)^{5} = 0.359^{3} \times 4.64^{5} = 0.0464 \times 2\,154 \approx 100

so P2≈100×50 W=5.0 kWP_{2} \approx 100 \times 50\ \mathrm{W} = 5.0\ \mathrm{kW}, as obtained above.

Consequences at this condition:

  • Tip-speed ratio: vtip,2/vtip,1=(N2D2)/(N1D1)=0.359×4.64=1.67v_{\mathrm{tip},2}/v_{\mathrm{tip},1} = (N_{2}D_{2})/(N_{1}D_{1}) = 0.359 \times 4.64 = 1.67. Tip speed rises by 67%67\%, so maximum shear rises.
  • Reynolds-number ratio: Re2/Re1=(N2/N1)(D2/D1)2=0.359×21.5=7.74Re_{2}/Re_{1} = (N_{2}/N_{1})(D_{2}/D_{1})^{2} = 0.359 \times 21.5 = 7.74. The large vessel is more turbulent, consistent with the constant-NPN_{P} assumption if the laboratory vessel was already turbulent.
  • Dimensionless blend time NtmN t_{m} is approximately constant in turbulent geometrically similar vessels, so tm∝1/Nt_{m} \propto 1/N and tm,2/tm,1=N1/N2=2.78t_{m,2}/t_{m,1} = N_{1}/N_{2} = 2.78. Blend time is about 2.82.8 times longer at large scale.

Primary answer: λ=4.64\lambda = 4.64; at constant P/VP/V, N2≈108 rpmN_{2} \approx 108\ \mathrm{rpm} and P2≈5.0 kWP_{2} \approx 5.0\ \mathrm{kW} (500 W m−3500\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-3}}).

5. Interpretation and limits
  1. Constant ReRe and constant blend time are not usable as the sole criteria here: the first reduces P/VP/V by a factor of about 464464, and the second raises it by a factor of about 21.521.5.
  2. Constant tip speed is used where maximum shear must not increase, for example with shear-sensitive material; it accepts a fall in P/VP/V from 500500 to 108 W m−3108\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-3}}, so suspension, blending and gas dispersion must be rechecked.
  3. Constant P/VP/V, giving 108 rpm108\ \mathrm{rpm} and 5.0 kW5.0\ \mathrm{kW}, is the usual starting point when agitation intensity must be maintained. Shaft torque, motor and gearbox rating, tip speed (a factor of 1.671.67 higher) and the longer blend time (a factor of 2.782.78) must still be checked.
  4. The power figures are fluid power inputs on the same basis as the stated laboratory 50 W50\ \mathrm{W}. Motor nameplate power must be larger, allowing for gearbox and seal losses and for any change in NPN_{P} if either vessel is not in the fully turbulent regime.
  5. If the laboratory vessel were in the laminar regime, NP∝Re−1N_{P} \propto Re^{-1} and P∝μN2D3P \propto \mu N^{2}D^{3}, so P/V∝N2P/V \propto N^{2} and constant P/VP/V would instead give N2=N1N_{2} = N_{1}. The regime must therefore be confirmed from ReRe before the turbulent result is applied.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Stirred-Vessel Scale-Up: 0.1 m³ to 10 m³

1. Weakness and Confidence

Weakness (state of each item: stated fact). No single scale-up result exists for this problem as posed. Agitator scale-up requires a chosen criterion — the quantity held constant on scale-up — and no criterion is given. Different standard criteria give answers differing by more than a factor of 20 in speed and a factor of 10,000 in power (Section 4). A second weakness is that the flow regime is unknown: the power relation used below holds only in turbulent flow, and neither fluid property needed to test the regime is given.

Confidence rating. 9/10 for the arithmetic conditional on a stated criterion and on turbulent flow with constant power number; 3/10 (low) for any single unconditional answer, because the criterion and the regime are both unspecified. No unconditional single value is therefore reported; ranges across criteria are reported instead.

2. Symbols and Given Data

Symbols, defined before first use: VV is vessel working volume, in cubic metres (m³); LrL_r is the linear scale ratio, dimensionless; DD is impeller diameter, in metres (m); TT is vessel diameter, in metres (m); NN is agitator rotational speed, in revolutions per minute (rpm) unless stated in revolutions per second (s⁻¹); PP is agitator power input (shaft power), in watts (W); NPN_P is the power number, dimensionless; ρ\rho is liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³); μ\mu is liquid dynamic viscosity, in pascal-seconds (Pa s); ReRe is the impeller Reynolds number, Re=ρND2/μRe = \rho N D^{2}/\mu with NN in s⁻¹, dimensionless; FrFr is the impeller Froude number, Fr=N2D/gFr = N^{2}D/g with gg the acceleration due to gravity, in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), dimensionless; vtipv_{tip} is impeller tip speed, vtip=πDNv_{tip} = \pi D N, in metres per second (m s⁻¹); tmt_m is blend (mixing) time, in seconds (s). Subscript 1 denotes the laboratory vessel and subscript 2 the large vessel.

3. Missing Quantities (Prompt 2 — Fill the Gaps First)

No value below was taken in silence. Each is either solved under alternatives or flagged as a limit on the result.

  1. Scale-up criterion — missing, decisive. Alternatives solved in Section 4: constant P/VP/V, constant vtipv_{tip}, constant NN, constant ReRe, constant FrFr.
  2. Liquid density ρ\rho and viscosity μ\mu — missing. Needed to compute ReRe and hence to confirm turbulent flow and constant NPN_P. They cancel from all ratio calculations only if the same liquid at the same temperature is used at both scales — assumed, not given.
  3. Impeller type, impeller-to-vessel diameter ratio D/TD/T, impeller clearance, and baffling — missing. Needed for NPN_P; they cancel from the ratios only under strict geometric similarity, which is given for the vessel and assumed to extend to impeller, baffles, and clearance.
  4. Power number NPN_P and its regime — missing. No value is needed for ratio calculations if NPN_P is the same at both scales (turbulent, fully baffled). That equality is assumed, not verified.
  5. Basis of P1P_1 — missing. Shaft power, motor output, or electrical input differ by drive and motor efficiency (typically 0.7–0.95, estimated range). Solved as shaft power; if P1P_1 is electrical input, all P2P_2 values scale by the same efficiency ratio at both scales only if efficiencies are equal, which is assumed and unlikely in detail.
  6. Process duty — missing. Blending, solids suspension, gas dispersion, heat transfer, and shear-sensitive duty each select a different criterion (Section 4). No duty is stated.
  7. Gassing, solids content, and non-Newtonian behaviour — missing. Assumed absent: single-phase Newtonian liquid.
  8. Reference and operating state — missing. Temperature and pressure are not stated; they matter only through ρ\rho and μ\mu (item 2). Per-pass versus overall conversion does not arise: no reaction or conversion is specified.

Primary source that settles items 2–4 (unverified): the power-number correlation for the actual impeller — the vendor power curve for the installed impeller, or the Rushton-type NPN_P–ReRe chart as reproduced in the Handbook of Industrial Mixing (Paul, Atiemo-Obeng and Kresta, eds.) — checked against a torque measurement on the actual laboratory vessel. Every claim in this solution that rests on constant NPN_P is unverified until checked against that source and against the actual ReRe.

4. Solution Under Each Plausible Criterion (Prompt 1)
4.1 Linear scale ratio

Under geometric similarity (given), volume scales as the cube of any linear dimension, so

Lr=(V2/V1)1/3=1001/3=4.64L_r = (V_2/V_1)^{1/3} = 100^{1/3} = 4.64

dimensionless. Hence D2/D1=T2/T1=Lr=4.64D_2/D_1 = T_2/T_1 = L_r = 4.64, Lr2=21.54L_r^{2} = 21.54, and Lr5=2154L_r^{5} = 2154.

4.2 Power relation and its range of validity

Relation used (fitted correlation, standard textbook form):

P=NP ρ N3D5(N in s−1)P = N_P \, \rho \, N^{3} D^{5} \qquad (N \text{ in s}^{-1})

Source: the standard power-number definition/correlations for stirred vessels (Rushton and co-workers; Handbook of Industrial Mixing, as cited in Section 3) — unverified against the primary source in this solution. Range of validity: turbulent flow, Re≳104Re \gtrsim 10^{4}, fully baffled vessel, Newtonian liquid, ungassed; there NPN_P is approximately constant for a given impeller geometry (for example NP≈5N_P \approx 5–6 for a Rushton turbine, fitted/estimated literature range). In laminar flow (Re≲10Re \lesssim 10) the relation changes form: NP∝1/ReN_P \propto 1/Re, giving P∝μN2D3P \propto \mu N^{2} D^{3}, and every exponent below changes. In the transitional range (10≲Re≲10410 \lesssim Re \lesssim 10^{4}) NPN_P varies with ReRe and no constant-exponent scaling is reliable.

Because ρ\rho, μ\mu, and the fluid are unchanged (assumed, Section 3) and NPN_P is constant (assumed, turbulent), the ratio form needs no property values:

P2/P1=(N2/N1)3 Lr5P_2/P_1 = (N_2/N_1)^{3} \, L_r^{5}

Each row holds the named quantity constant between scales. Speeds were computed from the ratio relations shown; powers from the ratio relation in Section 4.2. All values were also computed in executed code (Section 5).
