5. Independent Checks (Prompt 3 — Check the Work)

Checks were worked in executed code, by routes independent of the algebra in Section 4. No solution value was altered to make a check pass.

  1. Direct-route check, constant P/VP/V. Holding P/VP/V = 500 W m⁻³ (derived, from given values) at V2V_2 = 10 m³ gives P2P_2 = 500 × 10 = 5,000 W directly, with no use of the power relation. Code result: 5,000.0 W. Agrees with Section 4.3.
  2. Direct-route check, constant tip speed. At constant vtipv_{tip}, P∝N3D5∝D−3D5=D2P \propto N^{3}D^{5} \propto D^{-3}D^{5} = D^{2}, so P2=P1Lr2=50×21.544=1,077P_2 = P_1 L_r^{2} = 50 \times 21.544 = 1,077 W. Code result: 1,077.2 W. Agrees with Section 4.3 (rounding).
  3. Limiting case Lr=1L_r = 1. Every relation in Section 4.3 returns N2=N1N_2 = N_1 = 300 rpm and P2=P1P_2 = P_1 = 50 W. Passes by inspection of the exponents and in the code values (Lr3L_r^{3} = 100.0 recovered exactly from LrL_r = 4.641589).
  4. Limiting case, internal consistency of ratios. For the constant-P/VP/V row, the code gives tip-speed ratio 1.67 and ReRe ratio 7.74: both exceed 1, as expected when speed falls more slowly (Lr−2/3L_r^{-2/3}) than tip speed or ReRe constancy would require (Lr−1L_r^{-1} and Lr−2L_r^{-2}). Directions are correct.
  5. Correlation valid-range check — FAILS to close. The turbulent, constant-NPN_P range (Re≳104Re \gtrsim 10^{4}) cannot be checked because ρ\rho, μ\mu, and DD are all missing. This check is reported as failed / not closable, and it is the reason for the low unconditional confidence in Section 1. Note the direction of the risk: at constant P/VP/V the code-computed ReRe ratio is 7.74, so the large vessel is more turbulent than the laboratory vessel for the same fluid; the laboratory vessel is the one at risk of being transitional, in which case its measured 50 W already contains a non-constant NPN_P and the extrapolation is biased by an amount that cannot be quantified without the missing data.
  6. Balance closure. No material balance arises. The energy balance is the power input itself: all shaft power is ultimately dissipated as heat in the liquid (500 W m⁻³ at constant P/VP/V, i.e. an adiabatic temperature rise of about 0.43 K per hour for a water-like liquid with volumetric heat capacity 4.18 × 10⁶ J m⁻³ K⁻¹, estimated property value, unverified). No independent heat-removal figure is given against which to close it — see Section 7.

Agreement with another AI model was not used as verification anywhere in this solution.

6. Audit as for Built Equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from built-equipment behaviour:

  1. Heat removal does not scale with power. Direction: adverse. Under geometric similarity, jacket area scales as Lr2L_r^{2} while volume and (at constant P/VP/V) heat load scale as Lr3L_r^{3}, so heat-transfer area per unit volume at the large scale is 1/Lr1/L_r = 0.22 of the laboratory value — a factor of about 4.6 less cooling capacity per unit volume at the same temperature difference and heat-transfer coefficient (estimated; coefficient itself also changes with ReRe). A duty that was thermally comfortable at 0.1 m³ can be uncoolable at 10 m³ at constant P/VP/V. Settled by: a heat-transfer calculation for the actual jacket/coil and vendor data for the large vessel, plus the process heat load, none of which is given.
  2. Blend time lengthens at constant P/VP/V. Direction: slower mixing than the laboratory experience suggests. In turbulent flow tm∝1/Nt_m \propto 1/N approximately (fitted relation, estimated), so at 108 rpm the large vessel blends roughly 300/108 ≈ 2.8 times more slowly than the laboratory vessel, and large-scale concentration and temperature gradients (dead zones) appear that a 0.1 m³ vessel does not show. Rough size: factor of about 2.8 on tmt_m; local gradients are not quantified by any correlation used here. Settled by: a tracer blend-time test or vendor mixing guarantee on the actual large vessel.
  3. Installed power exceeds computed shaft power, and NPN_P shifts with real geometry. Direction: installed motor larger than P2P_2; computed P2P_2 uncertain by roughly ±20–30% (estimated). Real vessels depart from geometric similarity (standard D/TD/T, baffle width, clearances, liquid depth-to-diameter ratio), seals and gearboxes add losses, and start-up torque in settled or cold, viscous liquid can govern motor sizing. Settled by: the agitator vendor's selection sheet and torque calculation for the actual vessel, impeller, and fluid.
7. What Is Not Covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: heat-transfer limitation (Section 6, item 1); blend-time increase and spatial gradients; gas dispersion (gassing typically reduces drawn power by roughly 30–70%, estimated literature range, unverified, and changes the correct criterion); solids suspension and drawdown; shear damage at the higher tip speed under constant P/VP/V (tip-speed ratio 1.67); vortexing and FrFr effects if the vessel is unbaffled; non-Newtonian rheology; mechanical design (shaft, gearbox, critical speed, seal).
  • Information not available here: the vendor power and torque curves for the actual impeller; any measured ρ\rho, μ\mu, or laboratory torque record; the process duty specification. These are held by the equipment vendor and the plant, not in any public databank consulted for this solution.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: foaming, fouling of heat- transfer surfaces, viscosity rise at operating temperature extremes, start-up under settled solids, and drive behaviour under load swings.
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10%: choice of scale-up criterion (changes P2P_2 by up to a factor of about 100 across the table); a regime change between scales (changes the scaling exponents themselves); gassing; a temperature change large enough to move μ\mu across a regime boundary; any departure from geometric similarity in D/TD/T or baffling.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the process duty, and which scale-up criterion does that duty require?
  2. What are ρ\rho and μ\mu at operating temperature, and what is ReRe at both scales — is NPN_P in fact constant across them?
  3. Is the given 50 W a shaft power, and what does the vendor torque calculation give for the 10 m³ vessel with its actual impeller?
  4. Can the 10 m³ vessel remove heat at the selected P/VP/V, given the factor of about 4.6 loss of area per unit volume?
  5. Is a blend time about 2.8 times the laboratory value acceptable, and if not, what power increase (toward the constant-NN row, 108 kW) is the process willing to pay for?
8. Summary
  • Linear scale ratio LrL_r = 4.64 (derived from given volumes and given geometric similarity).
  • No unique scale-up exists without a criterion; confidence in any single value is low (3/10).
  • Most likely design range (constant P/VP/V to constant tip speed): N2N_2 = 65–108 rpm, P2P_2 = 1.1–5.0 kW, with the constant-P/VP/V point at N2N_2 = 108 rpm and P2P_2 = 5.0 kW.
  • Full range across standard criteria: N2N_2 = 14–300 rpm, P2P_2 = 0.011–108 kW.
  • The regime check (constant NPN_P) could not be closed for lack of ρ\rho, μ\mu, and DD; all constant-NPN_P claims are unverified until checked against the vendor power curve or a laboratory torque measurement.

B5. Uneven Flow in a Reactor

Response without the skill

Conversion of a First-Order Reaction in a Continuous Reactor

Symbols
  • XAX_A is the fractional conversion of reactant AA, dimensionless.
  • kk is the first-order reaction rate constant, with units of inverse time (time−1\mathrm{time^{-1}}).
  • τ\tau is the nominal residence time, with units of time (time\mathrm{time}).
  • kτk\tau is the product of the rate constant and the nominal residence time, dimensionless. In this problem kτ=2.0k\tau = 2.0.
  • exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function, dimensionless.
  • CAC_A is the concentration of reactant AA, with units of amount per unit volume (mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}).
  • CA0C_{A0} is the inlet concentration of reactant AA, with units of amount per unit volume (mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}).
Given
  • Reaction order: first order in reactant AA.
  • Flow model for the stated ideal case: ideal flow (plug flow) with the full reactor volume active.
  • Dimensionless group: kτ=2.0k\tau = 2.0.
Relation for the Ideal Case

For a first-order reaction under ideal plug flow at steady state, the concentration of reactant AA decreases along the residence time according to

CA=CA0exp⁡(−kτ)C_A = C_{A0} \exp(-k\tau)

where CAC_A is the outlet concentration corresponding to the nominal residence time τ\tau.

The fractional conversion XAX_A is defined by

XA=1−CACA0X_A = 1 - \frac{C_A}{C_{A0}}

Substitution of the concentration relation into the definition of XAX_A gives

XA=1−exp⁡(−kτ)X_A = 1 - \exp(-k\tau)

Calculation

With kτ=2.0k\tau = 2.0:

XA=1−exp⁡(−2.0)X_A = 1 - \exp(-2.0)

exp⁡(−2.0)=0.1353\exp(-2.0) = 0.1353

XA=1−0.1353=0.8647X_A = 1 - 0.1353 = 0.8647

Result

The conversion under ideal flow with the full volume active is

XA≈0.865X_A \approx 0.865

That is, approximately 86.5%86.5\% conversion.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Conversion of a First-Order Reaction in a Continuous Reactor — Estimate with Stated Weakness

Symbols, defined before first use
  • XAX_A = fractional conversion of the limiting reactant A, dimensionless, defined as (molar flow of A in − molar flow of A out) / (molar flow of A in).
  • kk = first-order rate constant, in reciprocal seconds (s−1^{-1}) if time is in seconds.
  • τ\tau = nominal residence time, in seconds (s), defined as reactor volume divided by volumetric feed rate.
  • DaDa = the product kτk\tau, dimensionless, sometimes called a Damköhler number for this purpose. Only the product is supplied, so kk and τ\tau are not known separately.
  • exp⁡\exp = the exponential function.
  • NN = number of equal stirred tanks in series in a tanks-in-series residence-time model, dimensionless, integer.
  • ff = active-volume fraction, dimensionless, defined as actively swept reactor volume divided by nominal reactor volume.
1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1; Prompt 1)

Weakness. The reactor flow pattern is not specified. "Continuous reactor" and "ideal flow" do not say whether the reactor is a plug-flow reactor (no axial mixing) or a continuously stirred tank reactor (complete mixing). For a first-order reaction that choice changes the result materially at the stated DaDa value, because a stirred tank exposes reacting material to the outlet (low) concentration throughout, while plug flow retains the higher inlet concentration along the path. A second weakness of the same kind is that no information is given on dead volume, bypassing, or the actual residence-time distribution.

Confidence rating.

  • Arithmetic, conditional on the plug-flow formula stated in the problem: high.
  • A single conversion value for "a continuous reactor" with no reactor type stated: low. The defensible deliverable is a range bounded by the two ideal limits, not a single value.

Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5), unverified. The reactor design specification, data sheet, or piping and instrumentation diagram identifying the reactor type and its active volume, and, for built equipment, a tracer residence-time-distribution test on the actual unit. No such document was supplied. Every claim below that depends on reactor type is therefore unverified until checked against that source.

  2. Basis — conversion is taken on the limiting reactant A, per the definition of XAX_A above. If a different basis (for example total feed) were intended, the number would differ; no other basis is supplied.

  7. Active volume, bypass fraction, and temperature profile — not supplied; treated as sensitivity cases in Section 5, not as corrections.

7. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from built-equipment behaviour:

  1. Residence-time distribution is neither ideal limit. Real reactors show dispersion, recirculation zones, and short-circuiting. Direction: conversion below the plug-flow value, toward or in adverse cases below the stirred-tank value. Rough size: the full ideal-limit spread is 0.67–0.86, i.e. up to about 23 % below the plug-flow value. Settling document/test: a pulse or step tracer test on the actual unit, analysed for its residence-time distribution.
  2. Dead volume and bypassing. Stagnant zones, fouling, or a partially open bypass reduce the effective DaDa. Direction: lower conversion. Rough size: f=0.80f = 0.80 alone costs about 8 % (plug flow) to 29 % (stirred tank, combined with the mixing penalty); 10 % untreated bypass costs about 10 % on the simple mixing model. Settling document/test: tracer test (as above), internal inspection records, and the vendor data sheet stating the active volume.
  3. Temperature non-uniformity changing kk. The calculation holds kk constant. An exothermic reaction in a real unit develops hot and cold zones; kk varies with temperature by the Arrhenius relation (no activation energy is supplied, so no numerical correction is made). Direction: either way, depending on where the nominal kk was measured. Rough size: a 10 % change in effective DaDa moves plug-flow conversion by about −3.5 % to +2.8 % (Section 5); larger temperature excursions move it more. Settling document/test: kinetic measurement on the actual feed at the operating temperature, and the unit temperature profile from operating records.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: axial and radial dispersion beyond the two ideal limits, temperature gradients and hot spots, pressure drop, density change along the reactor, catalyst deactivation or fouling over time, mass-transfer resistance (internal and external), feed-composition and flow fluctuations, start-up and other transients, and any reaction other than the stated first-order reaction (side reactions, reversibility, inhibition by product).
  • Information not available here: the reactor type, geometry, and active volume (vendor / design records); kinetic data measured on the actual feed; the operating temperature and pressure; and any proprietary databank values. None was supplied, and none has been invented.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: maldistribution that develops with fouling, bypass leakage, instrument drift in flow measurement (which changes the true τ\tau), and control-loop behaviour around the nominal operating point.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: (i) the reactor is well mixed rather than plug flow (−23 %); (ii) about 10 % or more of the feed bypasses untreated (−10 % or more); (iii) effective DaDa falls to about 1.5 or below in plug flow (XA≈0.78X_A \approx 0.78, about −10 %), whether through dead volume, a lower true kk, or a higher true flow rate; (iv) a recycle configuration, if present, changes the meaning of the reported conversion from per-pass to overall.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Which reactor type and flow pattern does the design specification state, and has a tracer test confirmed the residence-time distribution?
  2. Is the reported conversion per pass or overall, and is recycle present?
  3. What is the measured active volume, and is any bypass path present?
  4. At what temperature was kk measured, on what feed, and what is the unit temperature profile?
  5. Is Da=2.0Da = 2.0 a design value, a measured value, or an estimate, and what is its uncertainty?
Bottom line

Conditional on the plug-flow, full-volume-active case stated in the problem, XA=1−exp⁡(−2.0)=0.865X_A = 1 - \exp(-2.0) = 0.865. On the data actually supplied, with reactor type unspecified, the supported result is the range XA=0.67X_A = 0.67 to 0.860.86 (ideal stirred tank to ideal plug flow at Da=2.0Da = 2.0, given), widening to about 0.59 to 0.89 under the assumed dead-volume and DaDa-uncertainty scenarios of Section 5. Confidence in a single value is low until the reactor type is settled against the design specification or a tracer test — unverified.

C1. Relative Volatility Near Unity

Response without the skill

Minimum Number of Theoretical Stages by the Fenske Equation

Symbols
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min} is the minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux, dimensionless. The count includes the reboiler as one theoretical stage.
  • α\alpha is the relative volatility of the more volatile component with respect to the less volatile component, dimensionless. Given: α=1.30\alpha = 1.30.
  • xDx_D is the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the distillate, dimensionless.
  • xBx_B is the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the bottoms, dimensionless.
  • PP is the product of the distillate and bottoms composition ratios appearing in the Fenske equation, dimensionless. Given: P=9,801P = 9{,}801.

PP is defined by

P=(xD1−xD)(1−xBxB)=9,801P = \left(\frac{x_D}{1-x_D}\right)\left(\frac{1-x_B}{x_B}\right) = 9{,}801

Equation

At total reflux, the Fenske equation is

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Pln⁡αN_{\min} = \frac{\ln P}{\ln \alpha}

where ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm. Any logarithm base gives the same result, because the base cancels in the ratio.

Calculation

Substitution of P=9,801P = 9{,}801 and α=1.30\alpha = 1.30 gives

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(9,801)ln⁡(1.30)=9.19020.26236=35.03N_{\min} = \frac{\ln(9{,}801)}{\ln(1.30)} = \frac{9.1902}{0.26236} = 35.03

Check: ln⁡(9,801)=2ln⁡(99)=9.1902\ln(9{,}801) = 2\ln(99) = 9.1902, and 1.3035.03≈9,8011.30^{35.03} \approx 9{,}801, which recovers the stated value of PP.

Result

The minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux is approximately 35.035.0.

As a stage count must be an integer, at least 3636 theoretical stages would be required in practice to meet or exceed the stated separation, with the fractional Fenske value reported as 35.035.0 theoretical stages.

Final answer: 35.0 theoretical stages (35.03 calculated; 36 stages rounded up to a whole number).

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Minimum Theoretical Stages by the Fenske Equation

Symbols defined before use
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min}: minimum number of theoretical stages, a stage count (dimensionless).
  • xDx_D: mole fraction of the more volatile component in the distillate (dimensionless).
  • xBx_B: mole fraction of the more volatile component in the bottoms (dimensionless).
  • SS: the composition-ratio product in the Fenske equation, S=[xD/(1−xD)] [(1−xB)/xB]S = [x_D/(1-x_D)]\,[(1-x_B)/x_B] (dimensionless).
  • α\alpha: relative volatility of the more volatile component to the less volatile component (dimensionless).
Answer

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Sln⁡α=ln⁡9801ln⁡1.30=35.03N_{\min} = \frac{\ln S}{\ln \alpha} = \frac{\ln 9801}{\ln 1.30} = 35.03

  • Continuous Fenske result: 35.03 theoretical stages, reported as a range of 34.52 to 35.55 when the rounding range of α\alpha is carried through (see range calculation below).
  • Whole-stage count that meets or exceeds the stated separation: 36 stages at the nominal α\alpha of 1.30, because 35 stages give α35=9728<9801\alpha^{35} = 9728 < 9801; over the α\alpha rounding range the whole-stage count is 35 to 36.
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: the Fenske result is exact arithmetic only for an idealised model — a binary system, constant α\alpha, equilibrium (theoretical) stages, and total reflux. Its sensitive input is α\alpha, because Nmin⁡N_{\min} varies with 1/ln⁡α1/\ln\alpha and ln⁡1.30\ln 1.30 is small. A change in α\alpha of −2.36%-2.36\% or +2.96%+2.96\% changes Nmin⁡N_{\min} by +10%+10\% or −10%-10\%, respectively (computed in Section 6). The system, its pressure, and the variation of α\alpha with temperature and composition are not identified, so no check of constant α\alpha is possible from the data supplied.

Confidence ratings:

  • Arithmetic, conditional on SS and α\alpha as given: high.
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min} as a description of a real column separating a real mixture: low to moderate, because constant α\alpha, stage efficiency, and the stage-counting convention are untested for any specific system. No numerical confidence percentage is stated for the real-column case; a percentage would itself be an assumed value with no data behind it.

5. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4 — audit by a skilled engineer)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. α\alpha is not constant in a real column. Temperature rises from top to bottom, and α\alpha usually falls as temperature rises. Direction: if the average α\alpha in service is below 1.30, the real minimum stage count is above 35.03. Rough size: an average α\alpha of 1.25 instead of 1.30 raises Nmin⁡N_{\min} to 41.19 (+17.6%+17.6\%). Settling document: measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data for the actual mixture over the column pressure range (NIST ThermoData Engine or DIPPR record, or laboratory measurement on the actual material), marked unverified until consulted.
  2. Real trays or packing sections are not theoretical stages. A theoretical stage assumes equilibrium between leaving streams; built contacting devices have an efficiency below 100% in most services. Direction: the number of real trays, or the packing height, exceeds the theoretical count. Rough size: at an overall efficiency of 0.70 (an assumed illustrative value, not a property of any stated system), 35.03 theoretical stages correspond to about 50 real trays. Settling document: the tray or packing vendor rating for the actual system, or efficiency data from an operating column on the same service.
  3. A working column does not run at total reflux. Nmin⁡N_{\min} is the total-reflux limit; production requires product withdrawal, hence finite reflux and more stages, together with a reboiler and condenser sized for the actual duties. Direction: the installed stage count at any economic reflux ratio is above Nmin⁡N_{\min}, commonly by a factor set by the reflux-ratio choice rather than by the Fenske arithmetic. Rough size: not computable from the data supplied; it requires the feed condition and a reflux policy. Settling document: a rated simulation or design calculation for the actual feed (for example a stage-by-stage calculation at the selected reflux ratio), checked against the column vendor's rating.

Information not available to this calculation: the identity of the mixture and any data held in restricted databanks (NIST, DIPPR) or vendor documents for it; no such source was consulted, and claims depending on them are unverified.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: efficiency loss from maldistribution, fouling, and entrainment; α\alpha drift with operating pressure; composition control error that moves the achieved xDx_D and xBx_B away from design values.

Column Diameter Sizing at the Flooding-Limited Section

Given data
  • QQ is the vapour volumetric flow rate at the flooding-limited section, in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}): Q=3.0 m3/sQ = 3.0\ \mathrm{m^3/s}.
  • uu is the allowable superficial vapour velocity, in metres per second (m/s\mathrm{m/s}): u=1.2 m/su = 1.2\ \mathrm{m/s}. The superficial vapour velocity is the vapour velocity calculated as if the vapour alone occupied the whole cross-section of the empty column. The value of uu is already given at the design fraction of flooding from a generalised capacity correlation, so no further flooding correction is applied in this sizing.
Required
  • DD is the internal column diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
Calculation

AA is the required column cross-sectional area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}).

By definition of the superficial vapour velocity uu:

u=QAu = \frac{Q}{A}

Rearranging for the area AA:

A=Qu=3.0 m3/s1.2 m/s=2.5 m2A = \frac{Q}{u} = \frac{3.0\ \mathrm{m^3/s}}{1.2\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{m^2}

For a circular column, the cross-sectional area AA and the diameter DD are related by:

A=πD24A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4}

where π\pi is the mathematical constant pi, dimensionless.

Rearranging for the diameter DD:

D=4Aπ=4(2.5 m2)π=3.183 m2=1.78 mD = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4(2.5\ \mathrm{m^2})}{\pi}} = \sqrt{3.183\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 1.78\ \mathrm{m}

Result

The required column cross-sectional area is 2.5 m22.5\ \mathrm{m^2}, corresponding to a calculated internal diameter of approximately 1.78 m1.78\ \mathrm{m}.

In practice, a nominal internal diameter of 1.8 m1.8\ \mathrm{m} would be selected, giving a cross-sectional area slightly above the minimum required and therefore a superficial vapour velocity slightly below the allowable value of 1.2 m/s1.2\ \mathrm{m/s} at the stated flow rate.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Column Diameter at the Flooding-Limited Section

Symbols
  • QQ — vapour volumetric flow rate at the flooding-limited section, in cubic metres per second (m³/s)
  • uu — allowable superficial vapour velocity, in metres per second (m/s); superficial means calculated on the empty-column cross-section
  • AA — required column cross-sectional area, in square metres (m²)
  • DD — required column internal diameter, in metres (m)
1. Weakness and Confidence Rating (Prompt 1 — mandatory disclosure)

Weakness. The arithmetic is exact, but the design input is not. The whole result rests on a single value of uu (1.2 m/s) said to come from a generalised capacity correlation (of the Fair / Sherwood–Eckert type) at an unstated design fraction of flooding. Generalised capacity correlations are fitted, system-average relations. Their prediction for a specific system, internal type, liquid load, and foaming tendency routinely differs from measured flood capacity by about ±20 %, and by more for foaming, high-pressure, or high-liquid-load systems. No liquid rate, densities, surface tension, internal type, or foaming factor was supplied to check the correlation's applicability or its valid range.

Confidence ratings (separate, because they are different claims):

  • Arithmetic, given QQ and uu as stated: high, >95 %.
  • DD as a preliminary / study-grade size: moderate, about 60 %.
  • DD as a size that could be issued for construction without further hydraulic rating: low, about 30 %. Unverified — see §5.
2. Inputs, Labelled at the Point of Use
Quantity Value State
QQ 3.0 m³/s given — but see the missing pressure/volume basis in §4; taken here as the actual volumetric flow at the section's temperature and pressure (assumed interpretation of a given value)
uu 1.2 m/s given as an estimate; its origin is a fitted generalised capacity correlation, at a design fraction of flooding that is itself assumed/unstated
Circular cross-section — assumed (standard for a column shell)
uu defined on total cross-section — assumed; if uu is instead on active (bubbling) area, the answer changes — see §3.3

No measured value, vendor value, or property value was supplied or used. No density, viscosity, or surface tension enters the calculation, because QQ was supplied volumetrically and uu was supplied directly — that is itself a limitation: those properties are exactly what would be needed to check uu.

3. Calculation and Result as a Range
3.1 Point calculation

A=Qu=3.0 m3/s1.2 m/s=2.50 m2A = \frac{Q}{u} = \frac{3.0\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}}{1.2\ \text{m/s}} = 2.50\ \text{m}^2

D=4Aπ=4(2.50)π=1.78 mD = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4(2.50)}{\pi}} = 1.78\ \text{m}

Point result: AA = 2.50 m², DD = 1.78 m internal diameter.

3.2 Range from the plausible range of the estimated input

Since D∝u−1/2D \propto u^{-1/2}, a fractional error in uu produces about half that fractional error in DD, of opposite sign. Executed code (§6) gives:

Scenario for uu uu (m/s) AA (m²) DD (m) Change in DD
Correlation 30 % optimistic 0.84 3.57 2.13 +19.5 %
Correlation 20 % optimistic 0.96 3.13 1.99 +11.8 %
Correlation 10 % optimistic 1.08 2.78 1.88 +5.4 %
As stated (central) 1.20 2.50 1.78 0
Correlation 10 % pessimistic 1.32 2.27 1.70 −4.7 %
Correlation 20 % pessimistic 1.44 2.08 1.63 −8.7 %

Reported range (±20 % on the estimated uu, the stated plausible band for a generalised flooding correlation): DD = 1.63–1.99 m, with 1.78 m central. On the wider ±30 % band, DD = 1.57–2.13 m.

Sensitivities of the other guesses, each stated in percent on DD:

  • QQ ±10 % (if the given flow carries that uncertainty): DD changes by −5.1 % / +4.9 % (code-checked at QQ = 2.7 and 3.3 m³/s).
  • Design fraction of flooding: not separable from uu here. If 1.2 m/s corresponds to, e.g., 80 % of flood and a designer required 70 %, uu falls by a factor 0.875 and DD rises by about 6.9 % (by the u−1/2u^{-1/2} scaling). The fraction actually used is unstated — a gap, not a number used in silence.
3.3 Effect of the area basis (an assumed, not given, quantity)

If uu = 1.2 m/s is a velocity on active area rather than on total cross-section, downcomers (tray column) occupy part of the shell:

  • Downcomer area 10 % of total (assumed): total AA = 2.50/0.90 = 2.78 m², DD = 1.88 m (+5.4 %).
  • Downcomer area 15 % of total (assumed): total AA = 2.94 m², DD = 1.94 m (+8.5 %).

For a packed column this correction does not apply in the same form; which case holds cannot be decided from the data supplied.

3.4 Nominal size

Rounding the central value up to a nominal shell size:

  • DD = 1.8 m gives AA = 2.545 m² and an operating superficial velocity of 3.0/2.545 = 1.18 m/s — essentially no margin over the central case, and above the allowable if uu is at the low end of its range.
  • DD = 2.0 m gives AA = 3.142 m² and 0.955 m/s — inside the allowable range even at uu = 0.96 m/s.

A defensible study recommendation, subject to §5 and §7, is therefore DD ≈ 1.9–2.0 m nominal, not 1.78 m built exactly. This is a recommendation under stated assumptions, not a verified design.

4. Missing Quantities — Nothing Taken in Silence (Prompt 2)

The problem as posed is underspecified for a design (though not for the arithmetic above). Missing, with the treatment used here:

  1. Pressure / volume basis of QQ — missing. Is 3.0 m³/s the actual volumetric flow at the section's temperature and pressure, or a standard / normal volumetric flow? Treatment: solved on the actual-flow interpretation (assumed). If it were a standard-condition flow, the actual flow, and hence DD, could differ by a large factor set by the (also missing) operating pressure and temperature; no second number can be computed without those, so this alternative is flagged, not solved.
  2. Design fraction of flooding — missing. The fraction (commonly 0.70–0.85 of flood) behind uu = 1.2 m/s is not stated. Treatment: uu taken as given; sensitivity stated in §3.2.
  3. Internal type — missing. Trayed (and tray type, spacing, downcomer geometry) or packed (and packing type and size). This decides the §3.3 area correction and which capacity correlation is even applicable.
  4. Liquid rate and liquid properties — missing. Flooding is a vapour–liquid interaction; a vapour-only check cannot confirm the section is vapour-flood-limited rather than downcomer- or jet-flood-limited.
  5. Vapour and liquid densities, surface tension, foaming tendency — missing. These are the inputs of the very correlation uu came from; without them its valid range cannot be checked (§6, failed check).
  6. Composition basis — not applicable / not supplied. No composition is needed for A=Q/uA = Q/u, but composition is what would set the densities in item 5.
  7. Per-pass vs overall — not applicable to a single-section sizing; stated explicitly rather than left implicit. Turndown / operating range is likewise missing and is not covered by a single-point sizing.
5. Primary Source That Settles the Point
  • The capacity of the actual internals is settled by the internal vendor's hydraulic rating for the specified tray/packing and, behind it, by Fractionation Research Inc. (FRI) test data or the primary correlation source (Fair, J. R., Petro/Chem Engineer, 1961, for tray capacity) — checked for the actual system properties. Every claim in this solution that rests on uu = 1.2 m/s is unverified until checked against that rating / those data.
  • The actual vapour flow is settled by the design-basis material and energy balance / process simulation at the section conditions, not by the rounded 3.0 m³/s used here. Unverified against it.

No agreement with any other AI model is offered or used as verification.

6. Independent Checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run in executed Python code, not by hand only:

  1. Closure / back-substitution: u×Au \times A = 1.2 × 2.50 = 3.0 m³/s, reproducing QQ exactly (residual 0.0 in code). Pass.
  2. Dimensional check: (m³/s)/(m/s) = m²; m2\sqrt{\text{m}^2} = m. Pass.
  3. Limiting cases: Q→0⇒D→0Q \to 0 \Rightarrow D \to 0; $u \to \infty \Rightarrow D \to 0;doubling; doublingQmultipliesmultipliesDbyby\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41,asthecode′s, as the code'sQ$ = 2.7/3.3 cases confirm in direction and size. Pass.
  4. Code vs hand arithmetic: code gives AA = 2.5000 m², DD = 1.7841 m, and the full sensitivity table of §3.2. Pass — agreement of two routes to the same arithmetic (not independent evidence about uu).
  5. Correlation valid-range check: FAILS — cannot be performed. The densities, surface tension, liquid load, flow parameter, and internal geometry needed to place this system inside the generalised correlation's fitted range were not supplied. This check is reported as failed/open; the solution has not been altered to make it pass.
7. Audit as Built Equipment Behaves (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from real, built equipment:

  1. Real flood capacity vs the generalised correlation. Direction: usually the correlation is optimistic for foaming, viscous, or high-pressure systems, i.e. the real allowable uu is lower and the needed DD larger, by roughly 10–30 % in uu (5–16 % in DD). Settled by: vendor rating and FRI / plant flood data for the actual system.
  2. Downcomer and inactive area (trayed case). A diameter set on total area overstates the area available for vapour–liquid disengaging; the effective capacity is lower. Direction: needed DD larger by about 5–9 % (§3.3). Settled by: the tray vendor's mechanical/hydraulic datasheet for the selected tray.
  3. Operating flow vs design flow, and maldistribution. Fouling, feed-composition drift, and control excursions raise the actual vapour rate above the single design value, while maldistribution wastes part of the cross-section; both act in the same direction — the column floods before the nominal point. Rough size: a 20 % flow excursion alone needs about 9.5 % more DD. Settled by: the design-basis simulation cases (maximum / upset rates) and the plant operating record after start-up.
8. What This Calculation Leaves Out (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: pressure drop; tray efficiency / mass transfer (this sizes diameter only, not height or stage count); weeping and turndown at low rates; entrainment below flood; downcomer backup; foaming; fouling; liquid maldistribution; mechanical design (shell thickness, wind/seismic, nozzles, internals support); control and relief.
  • Restricted information not accessible here: vendor proprietary hydraulic ratings, FRI membership data, and the project's own design basis and simulation files. The value of uu cannot be audited without them.
  • Effects seen only in running equipment: start-up surges, composition transients, foaming episodes triggered by contaminants, and gradual fouling — none is represented by a single steady-state uu.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 % in DD: uu in error by more than about −17 % / +21 % (since D∝u−1/2D \propto u^{-1/2}); QQ in error by more than about ±21 %; QQ turning out to be a standard-condition rather than actual volumetric flow (potentially far more than 10 %); or uu proving to be an active-area velocity with downcomers at the upper end of their usual area fraction, combined with any of the above.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. Actual or standard volumetric flow — and at what pressure and temperature?
  2. What fraction of flooding, what correlation, and what system properties produced uu = 1.2 m/s — and is this system inside that correlation's range?
  3. Trayed or packed, which internal, and has the vendor rated it at this load?
  4. What are the liquid rate, downcomer limit, and foaming factor?
  5. What maximum / upset vapour rate, and what turndown, must the diameter serve?
  6. Why was a nominal 2.0 m (or another size) accepted or rejected against the 1.63–1.99 m range?
Answer

Required area AA = Q/uQ/u = 2.50 m² (central); required internal diameter DD = 1.78 m central, 1.63–1.99 m over the ±20 % plausible range of the estimated allowable velocity uu, rising to about 1.88–1.94 m if uu is an active-area velocity in a trayed column. A nominal 1.9–2.0 m shell is the study-grade recommendation. All values resting on uu = 1.2 m/s are unverified pending the vendor hydraulic rating / primary capacity data and the design-basis flow at section conditions (§5).

C3. Liquid–Liquid Extraction

Response without the skill

Number of Equilibrium Stages for Countercurrent Extraction

Symbols and given data
  • NN is the number of equilibrium stages, dimensionless.
  • ϕ\phi is the fraction of solute remaining in the raffinate, dimensionless, defined as the solute concentration in the raffinate leaving the cascade divided by the solute concentration in the feed entering the cascade.
  • xFx_F is the solute concentration in the feed, in amount per unit volume.
  • xNx_N is the solute concentration in the raffinate leaving stage NN, in the same units as xFx_F, so that ϕ=xN/xF\phi = x_N / x_F.
  • DD is the distribution coefficient, dimensionless, defined as the solute concentration in the extract phase divided by the solute concentration in the raffinate phase at equilibrium.
  • FF is the flow rate of the feed (raffinate) phase, in volume per unit time.
  • SS is the flow rate of the solvent (extract) phase, in volume per unit time, in the same units as FF.
  • S/FS/F is the solvent-to-feed ratio, dimensionless.
  • EE is the extraction factor, dimensionless, defined below.

Given data:

  • ϕ=0.02\phi = 0.02, the target value.
  • S/F=1.0S/F = 1.0
  • D=2.0D = 2.0
Assumptions
  1. The feed and solvent phases are immiscible, so that FF and SS are constant through the cascade.
  2. DD is constant, independent of concentration.
  3. The entering solvent contains no solute.
  4. The stages are equilibrium stages in countercurrent operation.
Extraction factor

EE is defined by

E=DSFE = D \frac{S}{F}

Substitution of the given data gives

E=2.0×1.0=2.0E = 2.0 \times 1.0 = 2.0

Relation for the fraction remaining

For countercurrent equilibrium stages with constant EE, immiscible phases, and solute-free entering solvent, the Kremser relation for extraction, for E≠1E \neq 1, is

ϕ=xNxF=E−1EN+1−1\phi = \frac{x_N}{x_F} = \frac{E - 1}{E^{N+1} - 1}

Here E=2.0≠1E = 2.0 \neq 1, so the relation applies in the stated form.

Calculation

Set ϕ=0.02\phi = 0.02 and E=2.0E = 2.0:

0.02=2.0−12.0 N+1−1=12.0 N+1−10.02 = \frac{2.0 - 1}{2.0^{\,N+1} - 1} = \frac{1}{2.0^{\,N+1} - 1}

Hence

2.0 N+1−1=10.02=502.0^{\,N+1} - 1 = \frac{1}{0.02} = 50

2.0 N+1=512.0^{\,N+1} = 51

Taking logarithms:

N+1=ln⁡51ln⁡2.0=5.67N + 1 = \frac{\ln 51}{\ln 2.0} = 5.67

N=4.67N = 4.67

NN must be a whole number of stages, so NN is rounded up to the next integer.

Check

For N=4N = 4:

ϕ=12.05−1=131=0.032\phi = \frac{1}{2.0^{5} - 1} = \frac{1}{31} = 0.032

The value 0.0320.032 is greater than the target 0.020.02, so four stages are insufficient.

For N=5N = 5:

ϕ=12.06−1=163=0.0159\phi = \frac{1}{2.0^{6} - 1} = \frac{1}{63} = 0.0159

The value 0.01590.0159 is less than the target 0.020.02, so five stages meet the target.

Result

The exact value from the Kremser relation is N=4.67N = 4.67. The number of equilibrium stages required in practice is

N=5N = 5

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Number of equilibrium stages for liquid–liquid extraction

Symbols
  • NN — number of equilibrium (theoretical) stages, dimensionless
  • ϕ\phi — fraction of the feed solute remaining in the raffinate leaving the cascade, dimensionless; ϕ=xN/xfeed\phi = x_N/x_{\mathrm{feed}} in the notation below
  • DD — distribution coefficient, dimensionless; solute concentration in the extract phase divided by solute concentration in the raffinate phase, on a consistent composition basis in both phases
  • FF — feed (raffinate-carrier) flow, in whatever flow units are used for the solvent flow; the units cancel
  • SS — solvent (extract-phase) flow, in the same flow units as FF
  • S/FS/F — solvent-to-feed ratio, dimensionless
  • EE — extraction factor, dimensionless, defined by E=D (S/F)E = D\,(S/F)
  • xx — solute concentration (or solute amount on a carrier basis) in the raffinate phase, in a stated composition unit
  • yy — solute concentration (or solute amount on a carrier basis) in the extract phase, in a composition unit consistent with that used for xx
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. This is a problem type on which AI confidence is low, for a specific reason that is in the problem statement itself: the statement does not identify the contacting configuration, the flow or composition basis, or whether DD is constant. The arithmetic under one standard model is exact and reproducible, but the mapping of that model onto a real extraction is not settled by the data supplied. As Section 4 shows, one plausible alternative configuration (cross-current contacting with the same total solvent) cannot reach the target at any number of stages, and an inverted definition of DD also makes the target unreachable — so the result is configuration-dependent, not merely parameter-dependent.

Confidence rating.

  • Conditional on the counter-current, immiscible, constant-DD model of Section 3: high — the result is closed-form arithmetic, verified by an independent stage-by-stage calculation in executed code (Section 6).
  • As a statement about an unnamed real system: low to moderate — the system identity, temperature, composition range, mutual solubility, solvent inlet purity, and stage efficiency are all absent, and any of them can move the required stage count by more than 10 % (Section 8).

No claim in this solution rests on agreement with another AI model; that is not used as verification anywhere below.

2. Inputs, labelled at the point of use
Quantity Value State
Target raffinate fraction, ϕ\phi 0.02 given
Solvent-to-feed ratio, S/FS/F 1.0 given (basis not given — see Section 4)
Distribution coefficient, DD 2.0 given (composition basis, temperature, and concentration dependence not given — see Section 4)
Contacting configuration Counter-current cascade assumed — the conventional reading of "number of equilibrium stages" for a cascade; alternatives solved in Section 4
Solvent entering solute-free Yes assumed
Phases mutually immiscible; FF, SS constant through the cascade Yes assumed
DD constant over the concentration range traversed Yes assumed
Stages are equilibrium stages (100 % stage efficiency) Yes, by the wording "equilibrium stages" given by the wording; real-stage correction in Section 7
Plausible tolerance on DD for the range calculation ±10 %\pm 10\,\%, i.e. 1.8–2.2 assumed for sensitivity only; no tolerance was supplied
Plausible tolerance on S/FS/F for the range calculation ±10 %\pm 10\,\%, i.e. 0.9–1.1 assumed for sensitivity only; no tolerance was supplied
Stage efficiency for the real-equipment range in Section 7 0.5–0.8 estimated (typical published range for extraction contacting; unverified for any specific device — Section 5)

Relations used, with source and range of validity:

  • Equilibrium relation y=D xy = D\,x: a fitted / definition-level relation here, since DD is supplied as a single number. It holds only where DD is in fact constant — dilute systems with no association, dissociation, or strong composition dependence. Range for the actual system: unknown, unverified.
  • Kremser equation for extraction (Section 3): an exact algebraic consequence of stage-by-stage material balances plus y=D xy = D\,x, constant FF and SS, and solute-free entering solvent. It is exact within those assumptions; it is not a correlation with an empirical range. Standard textbook source: the Kremser–Souders–Brown group of equations as presented for extraction in e.g. Treybal, Liquid Extraction, and in Seader, Henley and Roper, Separation Process Principles. Unverified against the edition in hand in this solution — the equation was instead re-derived and checked numerically (Section 6), which settles the algebra but not the modelling assumptions.
3. Solution under the standard (assumed) model

Model: counter-current cascade of equilibrium stages; immiscible phases; constant FF, SS, and DD; solute-free solvent entering the last stage.

Extraction factor, from the given (labelled above) DD and S/FS/F:

E=D (S/F)=2.0×1.0=2.0(dimensionless)E = D\,(S/F) = 2.0 \times 1.0 = 2.0 \quad\text{(dimensionless)}

Kremser equation for the fraction of solute remaining in the raffinate, for E≠1E \ne 1:

ϕ=E−1E N+1−1\phi = \frac{E - 1}{E^{\,N+1} - 1}

Setting ϕ=0.02\phi = 0.02 (given) and E=2.0E = 2.0:

0.02=12 N+1−1    ⟹    2 N+1=51    ⟹    N=ln⁡51ln⁡2−1=4.670.02 = \frac{1}{2^{\,N+1} - 1} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; 2^{\,N+1} = 51 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; N = \frac{\ln 51}{\ln 2} - 1 = 4.67

Result (single-value form): N=4.67N = 4.67 equilibrium stages, i.e. 5 whole equilibrium stages. At 5 stages the model gives ϕ=1/(26−1)=0.0159\phi = 1/(2^{6}-1) = 0.0159 (1.59 %, meets the target); at 4 stages ϕ=1/(25−1)=0.0323\phi = 1/(2^{5}-1) = 0.0323 (3.23 %, does not meet the target).

Result (range form, as required wherever an input is assumed or estimated). EE enters only as the product D (S/F)D\,(S/F), so a ±10 %\pm10\,\% error in either DD or S/FS/F alone gives the same range:

Case EE NN (exact) NN (whole stages) Change in NN vs. 4.67
DD or S/FS/F 10 % low (assumed tolerance) 1.8 5.32 6 +13.8 %+13.8\,\%
Nominal (given values) 2.0 4.67 5 —
DD or S/FS/F 10 % high (assumed tolerance) 2.2 4.21 5 −9.8 %-9.8\,\%
Both 10 % low 1.62 6.18 7 +32 %+32\,\%
Both 10 % high 2.42 3.84 4 −17.8 %-17.8\,\%

Reported range: N=3.8N = 3.8–6.26.2 exact (4–7 whole equilibrium stages) over the combined ±10 %\pm10\,\% assumed tolerance on DD and S/FS/F; N=4.2N = 4.2–5.35.3 exact (5–6 whole stages) for a ±10 %\pm10\,\% error in one of them alone. The nominal answer, 5 whole stages, sits inside both ranges and is not robust to the combined low case.

Sensitivity to each guess, in percent on NN:

  • Configuration guess (counter-current vs. cross-current, total solvent split): unbounded effect — target becomes unreachable (Section 4). This guess dominates all others.
  • Constant-DD guess: covered only indirectly by the ±10 %\pm10\,\% band above; a systematic fall of DD as xx falls (common when DD is measured at feed concentration) acts like a lower effective EE in the dilute end stages and moves NN upward, by an amount that cannot be quantified without D(x)D(x) data.
  • Solute-free solvent guess: entering solute raises the attainable floor of ϕ\phi; even a small entering yy comparable to D×0.02 xfeedD \times 0.02\,x_{\mathrm{feed}} makes ϕ=0.02\phi = 0.02 unreachable regardless of NN.
  • Immiscibility / constant-flow guess: carrier dissolving in the extract changes FF and SS along the cascade and changes EE stage by stage; direction and size are system-specific and unquantifiable from the data supplied.
4. Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — gaps first)

The following quantities are needed by a complete solution and were not supplied. None was taken in silence; the assumption used is stated with each, and the consequential alternatives are solved.

Target unreachable at any NN. - Single co-current contact: ϕ=1/(1+E)=0.333\phi = 1/(1+E) = 0.333. Target unreachable.
  2. Basis of S/FS/F — missing (mass, molar, or volumetric; total flows or solute-free carrier flows). Assumed: the same basis as the flows entering EE, with constant carrier flows. If S/FS/F is a total-flow ratio while substantial solute or carrier transfers, EE varies by stage.
  3. Composition basis of DD — missing (mass fraction, mole fraction, mass per unit volume, etc.). Assumed: DD as defined in the problem (extract concentration / raffinate concentration) on a basis consistent with S/FS/F, so that E=D (S/F)E = D\,(S/F) is the correct grouping. If the bases are inconsistent, a density or molecular-weight conversion enters EE. If DD were in fact defined inversely (raffinate / extract), then Deffective=0.5D_{\mathrm{effective}} = 0.5, E=0.5<1E = 0.5 < 1, and the minimum attainable ϕ\phi as N→∞N \to \infty is 1−E=0.51 - E = 0.5: target unreachable. The problem's own definition excludes this, and it is listed only because it is the most common transcription error with this quantity.
  4. Solvent inlet composition — missing. Assumed solute-free. See the sensitivity note in Section 3.
  5. Temperature and pressure — missing. Pressure has little effect on liquid–liquid equilibrium in the usual range; temperature sets DD. Assumed: D=2.0D = 2.0 is the value at the operating temperature.
  6. Reference / feed composition — missing in absolute terms. Not needed for ϕ\phi under constant DD, because the model is linear in xx; the feed solute level cancels. It is needed the moment DD depends on concentration.
  7. Per-pass vs. overall — not applicable as stated; there is no recycle in the problem. If the extract or raffinate were recycled in a larger flowsheet, ϕ\phi here is the per-pass (cascade) value.
  8. Stage counting convention — assumed that NN counts equilibrium contacting stages only, with no extra stage credited to a feed mixer, settler, or reboiler-type device (there is none in extraction, but conventions differ in some textbook counts by ±1\pm 1 stage, a ±20 %\pm 20\,\% effect at N≈5N \approx 5).
5. Primary source that would settle the open points
  • Settles DD and its concentration dependence: measured liquid–liquid equilibrium (tie-line) data for the actual ternary system at the operating temperature — e.g. the DECHEMA Chemistry Data Series liquid–liquid equilibrium volumes, the NIST ThermoData Engine, or a measurement on the actual feed and solvent. Every use of D=2.0D = 2.0 beyond the given value's face meaning is unverified until checked against such data.
  • Settles configuration, efficiency, and attainable ϕ\phi in hardware: pilot-column or mixer-settler test records on the actual system, or the equipment vendor's rating for the selected contactor.
  • Settles physical properties if flows must be converted between bases: DIPPR 801 (AIChE) evaluated data for the actual components. Unverified here; no conversion was needed under the stated assumptions.

User-supplied plant, vendor, or measured data, if provided later, supersede the assumed ±10 %\pm10\,\% ranges used in Section 3 for that case.

6. Independent verification (Prompt 3 — check the work)

All checks were run in executed Python code; the Kremser result was not taken on trust.

  1. Independent stage-by-stage route. The counter-current stage balances with y=D xy = D\,x, F=S=1F = S = 1, D=2.0D = 2.0, normalised feed xfeed=1x_{\mathrm{feed}} = 1, and solute-free entering solvent were written as a linear system and solved directly (no Kremser formula used). Results: raffinate fraction 0.032260.03226 at N=4N = 4 and 0.015870.01587 at N=5N = 5, matching the Kremser values 1/311/31 and 1/631/63 to the digits shown. Check passes. Material balance closure is exact in this route by construction (the linear system is the set of stage balances, solved to numerical precision), and the overall balance follows: solute in the extract =1−ϕ= 1 - \phi on the normalised basis.
  2. Limiting case, N=0N = 0: the Kremser formula gives ϕ=(E−1)/(E−1)=1\phi = (E-1)/(E-1) = 1 — no stages, nothing removed. Passes.
  3. Limiting case, N=1N = 1: formula gives ϕ=1/(22−1)=0.333\phi = 1/(2^{2}-1) = 0.333; a single-stage balance with E=2E = 2 gives ϕ=1/(1+E)=0.333\phi = 1/(1+E) = 0.333 by inspection. Passes.
  4. Limiting case, E→1E \to 1: the Kremser form tends to ϕ=1/(N+1)\phi = 1/(N+1), the known result for E=1E = 1 (which would require N=49N = 49 at ϕ=0.02\phi = 0.02). This confirms the steep deterioration as E→1E \to 1 and hence the sensitivity reported in Section 3. Passes.
  5. Limiting behaviour, E<1E < 1: ϕ→1−E\phi \to 1 - E as N→∞N \to \infty; consistent with the unreachable-target conclusions in Section 4. Passes.
  6. Checks that fail: none of the algebraic checks fail. The verification does not cover the modelling assumptions (constant DD, immiscibility, equilibrium stages); no independent check of those is possible from the data supplied, and they are reported as unverified rather than adjusted to pass.
7. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this equilibrium-stage result and built equipment:

  1. Stage efficiency below 100 %. Real trays, mixer-settlers, and column sections do not reach equilibrium; mass-transfer resistance and backmixing intervene. Direction: more real stages than 5. Rough size: at an (estimated) Murphree-type efficiency of 0.5–0.8, about 5/0.8≈75/0.8 \approx 7 to 5/0.5=105/0.5 = 10 real stages — noting that dividing by an efficiency is itself a crude approximation in extraction. Settled by: pilot test records on the actual system, or the contactor vendor's guaranteed efficiency / height-of-transfer-unit data.
  2. DD not constant, and phases not immiscible. In a real ternary, DD varies along the tie-line fan, the raffinate loses carrier to the extract, and the extract gains carrier, so FF, SS, and EE drift stage by stage; the dilute (raffinate-exit) end usually controls. Direction: usually more stages than the constant-DD estimate if DD was quoted at feed conditions, but the sign is system-specific. Rough size: readily 10–30 % on NN for moderately non-ideal systems. Settled by: measured tie-line data for the actual system (Section 5) used in a stage-by-stage calculation with varying DD.
  3. Hydraulics: entrainment, incomplete settling, flooding. Entrained extract in the raffinate sets a floor on ϕ\phi that no number of stages removes; flooding caps the usable S/FS/F. Direction: attainable ϕ\phi higher (worse) than 0.0159 at 5 stages, possibly above the 0.02 target. Rough size: 1 % entrainment of extract phase in the raffinate is by itself of the order of the 2 % target. Settled by: settler / column hydraulic design data and pilot entrainment measurements for the actual dispersion.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • Mass-transfer kinetics and stage efficiency (treated only as the crude range in Section 7); axial backmixing in columns.
  • Variation of DD with concentration and temperature; mutual solubility and the resulting flow variation; volume change on mixing.
  • Entrainment, emulsification, slow coalescence, fouling, and third-phase formation.
  • Solvent recovery duty, solvent losses, and any downstream separation of the extract — the calculation ends at the raffinate specification.
  • Control, start-up, and turndown behaviour.

Information not available to this solution: the identity of the solute, solvent, and carrier; any measured equilibrium or pilot data; any vendor rating; any restricted databank values for the actual system. All such items are marked unverified in Section 5.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %:

  • E=D (S/F)E = D\,(S/F) falling below about 1.8 (a 10 % fall in DD, in S/FS/F, or a smaller fall in both) raises NN by more than 10 %; the rise steepens without bound as E→1E \to 1.
  • Stage efficiency below about 0.9 for real equipment.
  • Solute present in the entering solvent at a level comparable to the raffinate target.
  • Any change of configuration away from counter-current (Section 4), which can make the target unreachable rather than merely more expensive.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What are the solute, solvent, and carrier, and at what temperature was D=2.0D = 2.0 measured — and over what concentration range?
  2. On what bases are DD and S/FS/F stated, and are they mutually consistent?
  3. Is the contacting counter-current, and is the solvent feed solute-free (or what is its recycled-solvent solute content)?
  4. Is 5 the count of equilibrium stages required, or of real stages to be built — and what efficiency or pilot result converts one to the other?
  5. What entrainment and settling performance is expected, and does it set a floor on ϕ\phi above 0.02?
Answer

Under the assumed standard model — counter-current cascade, immiscible phases, constant distribution coefficient D=2.0D = 2.0 (given), solvent-to-feed ratio S/F=1.0S/F = 1.0 (given), solute-free entering solvent (assumed) — the extraction factor is E=2.0E = 2.0, the exact stage requirement is N=4.67N = 4.67, and 5 equilibrium stages are required to bring the raffinate solute fraction to or below 0.02 (the model gives 0.0159 at 5 stages). Reported as a range over the assumed ±10 %\pm10\,\% tolerance on DD and S/FS/F: N=4.2N = 4.2–5.35.3 exact (5–6 whole stages) for one input in error, and N=3.8N = 3.8–6.26.2 exact (4–7 whole stages) if both are in error in the same direction. The result is void if the configuration is not counter-current with the stated total solvent, if the entering solvent carries solute, or if DD in the dilute end is materially below 2.0; measured equilibrium data for the actual system (Section 5) is the source that settles those points, and no such data has been checked in this solution.

C4. Adsorption Breakthrough

Response without the skill

Time to Breakthrough for a Fixed Adsorbent Bed

Problem statement

Estimate the breakthrough time for a fixed bed containing a stated mass of adsorbent, treating a stream that carries solute at a stated mass rate, when the equilibrium adsorbent loading at the feed concentration is known from a fitted isotherm.

Symbols
  • MM is the mass of adsorbent in the bed, in kilograms (kg).
  • qq is the equilibrium capacity at the feed concentration, i.e. the equilibrium mass of solute adsorbed per unit mass of adsorbent, in kilograms of solute per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg).
  • m˙s\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}} is the mass feed rate of solute to the bed, in kilograms per hour (kg/h).
  • WW is the total mass of solute that the bed can hold at equilibrium with the feed concentration, in kilograms (kg).
  • tstt_{\mathrm{st}} is the stoichiometric time, i.e. the time at which the bed would be completely saturated at the loading qq if the adsorption front were infinitely sharp, in hours (h).
  • tbt_{\mathrm{b}} is the breakthrough time, i.e. the time at which solute first appears at the bed outlet at the specified allowable outlet concentration, in hours (h).
  • ϕ\phi is the fractional utilisation of the bed at breakthrough, dimensionless, defined as the fraction of the equilibrium capacity WW that has been used when breakthrough occurs.
Given values
  • M=1,000 kgM = 1{,}000\ \mathrm{kg}
  • q=0.08 kg/kgq = 0.08\ \mathrm{kg/kg}
  • m˙s=0.5 kg/h\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}} = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h}
Assumptions
  1. The solute feed rate m˙s\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}} is constant in time.
  2. Essentially all solute entering the bed is adsorbed until breakthrough; i.e. the outlet solute concentration remains negligible compared with the feed concentration up to breakthrough.
  3. The whole bed can, in the ideal limit, reach the equilibrium loading qq corresponding to the feed concentration. This requires a favourable isotherm and sufficient contact time, so that local equilibrium is approached.
  4. Losses of solute by other routes, adsorbent degradation, and changes in qq with temperature or feed composition during the cycle are neglected.
  5. For the base estimate the adsorption front (mass-transfer zone) is taken as sharp compared with the bed length, so that ϕ\phi is close to 1. The effect of a finite mass-transfer zone is treated separately below.
Calculation

The total equilibrium solute capacity of the bed, WW, is the adsorbent mass multiplied by the equilibrium loading:

W=MqW = M q

Substitution of the given values gives

W=(1,000 kg)(0.08 kg/kg)=80 kgW = (1{,}000\ \mathrm{kg})(0.08\ \mathrm{kg/kg}) = 80\ \mathrm{kg}

of solute.

Under assumptions 1 and 2, solute accumulates in the bed at the rate m˙s\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}}. A solute mass balance over the bed up to time tt, with tt denoting elapsed time in hours (h), therefore gives the mass adsorbed as m˙st\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}} t. Saturation in the ideal, sharp-front limit occurs when m˙stst=W\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}} t_{\mathrm{st}} = W, so

tst=Wm˙s=Mqm˙st_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{W}{\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}}} = \frac{M q}{\dot{m}_{\mathrm{s}}}

Substitution gives

tst=80 kg0.5 kg/h=160 ht_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{80\ \mathrm{kg}}{0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h}} = 160\ \mathrm{h}

The units check: (kg)(kg/kg)/(kg/h)=h(\mathrm{kg})(\mathrm{kg/kg}) / (\mathrm{kg/h}) = \mathrm{h}, as required.

In the sharp-front limit the breakthrough time equals the stoichiometric time:

tb≈tst=160 ht_{\mathrm{b}} \approx t_{\mathrm{st}} = 160\ \mathrm{h}

i.e. approximately 160 h160\ \mathrm{h}, or about 6.76.7 days of continuous operation.

Effect of a finite mass-transfer zone

In a real bed the adsorption front has a finite width. Breakthrough at the outlet occurs while the leading part of that zone is still unsaturated, so only a fraction ϕ\phi of the equilibrium capacity has been used at breakthrough, with ϕ<1\phi < 1. The breakthrough time is then

tb=ϕ tst=ϕ(160 h)t_{\mathrm{b}} = \phi \, t_{\mathrm{st}} = \phi (160\ \mathrm{h})

No bed length, superficial velocity, mass-transfer coefficient, mass-transfer-zone length, or allowable breakthrough concentration is supplied, so ϕ\phi cannot be calculated from the data given and 160 h160\ \mathrm{h} is strictly an upper bound on, and the standard first estimate of, the breakthrough time. For illustration only: a utilisation of ϕ=0.75\phi = 0.75 would give tb=120 ht_{\mathrm{b}} = 120\ \mathrm{h}, a utilisation of ϕ=0.90\phi = 0.90 would give tb=144 ht_{\mathrm{b}} = 144\ \mathrm{h}, and a utilisation of ϕ=0.95\phi = 0.95 would give tb=152 ht_{\mathrm{b}} = 152\ \mathrm{h}. Operation should be scheduled with a safety margin below 160 h160\ \mathrm{h}, and the bed should be taken off line for regeneration or replacement at or before the measured breakthrough, whichever occurs first.

Result

The equilibrium capacity of the bed is 80 kg80\ \mathrm{kg} of solute. At a solute feed rate of 0.5 kg/h0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h} the stoichiometric (ideal, sharp-front) time, and hence the estimated time to breakthrough, is

tb≈160 ht_{\mathrm{b}} \approx 160\ \mathrm{h}

with the actual breakthrough occurring somewhat earlier, by the factor ϕ\phi defined above, because of the finite width of the mass-transfer zone.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Time to Breakthrough — Fixed Adsorbent Bed

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. Only the equilibrium (stoichiometric) capacity can be calculated from the data supplied. Actual breakthrough occurs before the bed is saturated, because a mass-transfer zone (the partially saturated length of bed over which the solute concentration falls from feed value to near zero) reaches the outlet while part of the bed is still unused. No quantity that fixes the length of that zone, or the fraction of the bed used at breakthrough, is supplied. A single breakthrough time stated without that information would be false precision.

Confidence rating: low for an actual breakthrough time; high for the stoichiometric (ideal, sharp-front) time, which is a direct mass balance on the stated numbers.

No agreement with another AI model is used as verification (Checklist item 7).

2. Inputs, labelled at the point of use
Symbol Definition Value Unit State
MM mass of adsorbent in the bed 1,000 kg given
FF mass flow rate of solute in the feed 0.5 kg/h given
qq equilibrium solute capacity at the feed concentration, mass of solute per mass of adsorbent 0.08 kg/kg fitted (from a fitted isotherm; fit error not supplied)
UU bed utilisation at breakthrough: fraction of the equilibrium capacity used when the outlet reaches the breakthrough concentration 0.5–0.9 dimensionless assumed (see §4)
tstt_{st} stoichiometric time: time to saturate the whole bed at equilibrium if the front were sharp calculated h calculated
tbt_b time to breakthrough at the (unspecified) breakthrough concentration calculated h calculated

No other property value, rule of thumb, or fitted relation is used. The only relation used is the definition of equilibrium capacity itself, qq in kg solute per kg adsorbent at the feed concentration; it holds only at that concentration, at the temperature and in the feed matrix of the isotherm fit — all unverified here (§5).

3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — fill the gaps first)

The solution needs the following, none of which is supplied. No value is taken in silence; the two quantities that move the answer are carried as ranges in §4, and the rest are flagged as conditions on the result.

  1. Breakthrough definition — the outlet concentration at which the bed is counted as broken through, as a fraction of the feed concentration (common choices 0.01, 0.05, or 0.10 of feed). Not given. A stricter limit gives an earlier breakthrough.
  2. Feed concentration and total feed flow rate — only the solute rate FF (given, 0.5 kg/h) is supplied. FF alone fixes the stoichiometric time, but the mass-transfer rate, and therefore UU, depends on total flow and concentration separately.
  3. Bed geometry — bed length, diameter, and hence superficial velocity (total volumetric flow divided by bed cross-sectional area, m/s). Not given; needed for any mass-transfer or length-of-unused-bed calculation.
  4. Adsorbent and mass-transfer data — particle size, particle and bed (bulk) density, bed void fraction, effective diffusivity, and any measured mass-transfer coefficient or mass-transfer-zone length for this solute–adsorbent pair. Not given.
  5. Isotherm shape — only the single point qq (fitted) at the feed concentration is given. Whether the isotherm is favourable (concave, self-sharpening front) or not changes the front shape and UU.
  6. Operating basis — temperature, pressure basis (absolute or gauge, if the feed is a gas), composition basis (mass or molar), competing components (for example water), and whether the adsorbent is fresh or regenerated and partly aged. None given.
  7. Feed stability — whether FF (given) is constant, an average, or a peak. Breakthrough is set by cumulative solute loaded, so a varying feed changes clock time at fixed cumulative load.

Primary source that settles the point (unverified until checked against it): a measured breakthrough curve on the actual adsorbent, at the actual feed concentration, temperature, and superficial velocity — or the adsorbent vendor's guaranteed breakthrough capacity / mass-transfer-zone data for this duty, in the vendor document for the actual grade supplied. Every statement below about UU and about the fitted value of qq rests on such a source and is unverified until checked against it.

4. Calculation
4.1 Stoichiometric (ideal) time

Total equilibrium solute capacity of the bed:

M×q=1,000 kg×0.08 kg/kg=80 kg soluteM \times q = 1{,}000\ \text{kg} \times 0.08\ \text{kg/kg} = 80\ \text{kg solute}

where MM is given, qq is fitted.

tst=MqF=80 kg0.5 kg/h=160 h≈6.7 dayst_{st} = \frac{M q}{F} = \frac{80\ \text{kg}}{0.5\ \text{kg/h}} = 160\ \text{h} \approx 6.7\ \text{days}

where FF is given. This is the time to complete saturation with a sharp front and 100 % utilisation. It is an upper bound on breakthrough time, not the breakthrough time itself.

4.2 Breakthrough time — range, not a single value

tb=U×tstt_b = U \times t_{st}

where UU is assumed. UU is taken as 0.5–0.9 as an assumed screening range for a fixed bed with a finite mass-transfer zone; it is not measured, not fitted, and not taken from a named source for this system. It is the largest single source of uncertainty in the result.

At the fitted qq (0.08 kg/kg, fitted):

UU (assumed) tbt_b (h)
0.5 80
0.7 112
0.9 144
1.0 (sharp front, limiting case) 160
4.3 Sensitivity — every guess and how much it moves the result
Guess / uncertain input Plausible range used Effect on tbt_b
qq (fitted; no fit error supplied, so ±\pm25 % is an assumed scenario, not a measured error) 0.06–0.10 kg/kg tstt_{st} = 120–200 h; i.e. −25-25 % / +25+25 % on any time, because tbt_b is directly proportional to qq
UU (assumed) 0.5–0.9 −50-50 % / −10-10 % relative to the stoichiometric time at fixed qq
FF (given, treated as exact and constant) if the true mean rate differed by ±\pm10 %, the time moves by ∓\mp9–11 % tbt_b is inversely proportional to FF; not included in the combined range because FF is stated as given
Breakthrough definition (missing) stricter limit lowers effective UU contained qualitatively in the low end of UU; not separately quantified — a stated limit is required to quantify it

Combined range (ends of the qq range combined with ends of the UU range, computed in §6):

tb≈60 to 180 ht_b \approx 60\ \text{to}\ 180\ \text{h}

with a central screening estimate of about 80–144 h at the fitted qq, against a stoichiometric upper bound of 160 h at that qq.

For planning before any test data exist, the conservative end (about 60–80 h) is the defensible basis for scheduling change-out or switchover; the 160 h figure must not be used as a breakthrough time.

5. Check of the work (Prompt 3)

Checks were worked in executed code (Python), not by hand arithmetic alone. Results: total capacity 80.0 kg; tstt_{st} 160.0 h (6.67 days); tstt_{st} at qq = 0.06 and 0.10 kg/kg = 120 h and 200 h; tbt_b at UU = 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0 = 80, 112, 144, 160 h; combined low 1000×0.06/0.5×0.5=601000 \times 0.06 / 0.5 \times 0.5 = 60 h; combined high 1000×0.10/0.5×0.9=1801000 \times 0.10 / 0.5 \times 0.9 = 180 h.

  1. Balance closure. Over tstt_{st} = 160 h the feed supplies 0.5 kg/h×160 h=800.5\ \text{kg/h} \times 160\ \text{h} = 80 kg of solute, equal to the bed equilibrium capacity MqM q = 80 kg. Closure error: 0 kg (exact, by construction of the stoichiometric definition). This closes the solute balance only under the sharp-front assumption; it does not verify UU.
  2. Limiting cases. (a) q→0q \to 0 gives tb→0t_b \to 0 — correct by sight. (b) U=1U = 1 recovers tb=tstt_b = t_{st} = 160 h — the known sharp-front limit. (c) Doubling FF halves every time — correct for a capacity-limited bed at fixed cumulative load.
  3. Units. kg ×\times (kg/kg) / (kg/h) = h. Consistent.
  4. Fitted relation against its valid range. The isotherm value qq (fitted) is used only at the feed concentration at which it is stated — no extrapolation in concentration is made. Its valid temperature range and fit error are not supplied, so validity outside the (unknown) fit conditions fails to be established; this check is reported as open, not passed, and is the reason the ±\pm25 % scenario range on qq is carried.
  5. Checks that fail or cannot be run. No check against a measured breakthrough curve, a mass-transfer correlation, or a length-of-unused-bed calculation can be run: the data listed in §3 are missing. The solution was not altered to make any check pass.
6. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from how a built bed behaves, each with direction, rough size, and the record that settles it:

  1. Channelling and maldistribution. Flow bypassing part of the bed, or wall flow in a small-diameter bed, lowers effective utilisation below the assumed range. Direction: earlier breakthrough. Rough size: 10–30 % earlier in a poorly distributed bed (assumed magnitude, unverified). Settled by: a measured breakthrough curve on the installed bed, and the vessel distributor design record.
  2. Competing adsorption, fouling, and ageing. Water or other feed components occupying capacity, and capacity loss over regeneration cycles, lower the working qq below the fitted fresh-adsorbent value. Direction: earlier breakthrough. Rough size: 10–40 % loss of working capacity is the scale to test for, not a value asserted for this system (unverified). Settled by: the isotherm measured in the actual feed matrix on used adsorbent from the unit, and the unit's cycle history.
  3. Feed excursions. Concentration or flow peaks load the bed faster than the mean rate FF (given) implies, and temperature rise from the heat of adsorption lowers qq during loading. Direction: earlier breakthrough in clock time. Rough size: proportional to the cumulative-load excess; a sustained 20 % high feed gives about 17 % earlier breakthrough. Settled by: feed flow and composition records (plant historian) over a full cycle, and bed temperature profiles if fitted.
7. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: mass-transfer kinetics and axial dispersion (represented only by the assumed UU); heat of adsorption and temperature fronts; pressure drop and its change with fouling or attrition; adsorbent attrition and fines; regeneration efficiency and heel build-up; desorption or roll-up of previously adsorbed species.
  • Information not accessible here: the vendor's proprietary breakthrough / mass-transfer-zone data for the actual adsorbent grade; the original isotherm data and fit residuals behind qq (fitted); any pilot or plant breakthrough records for this duty. Claims resting on these are marked unverified in §3–§4.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: channelling after bed settling, distributor fouling, feed contaminants not in the design feed, and operator switchover practice.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any change of more than 10 % in qq (temperature, feed matrix, ageing), in mean FF, or in UU (velocity change, stricter breakthrough limit, maldistribution) changes tbt_b by more than 10 %, because tbt_b is proportional to qq and UU and inversely proportional to FF.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What outlet concentration defines breakthrough for this duty, and what limit (product specification or emission limit) sets it?
  2. What are the measured breakthrough curve, mass-transfer-zone length, or vendor-guaranteed working capacity for this adsorbent grade at the actual velocity, concentration, and temperature?
  3. What are the isotherm fit error and fit conditions behind qq = 0.08 kg/kg (fitted), and was the isotherm measured in the actual feed matrix?
  4. Is FF = 0.5 kg/h (given) a mean, a design value, or a peak, and what do feed records show over a full cycle?
  5. Is the adsorbent fresh or regenerated, and what working capacity has the installed bed actually delivered in previous cycles?
8. Result
  • Stoichiometric (complete saturation, sharp front) time: 160 h — from MM (given), qq (fitted), and FF (given); an upper bound only.
  • Time to breakthrough: about 60–180 h as a combined range; 80–144 h at the fitted qq, the spread being set by the assumed utilisation UU = 0.5–0.9 and an assumed ±\pm25 % scenario range on the fitted qq.
  • Confidence: low, pending a measured breakthrough curve or vendor working-capacity data for the actual bed (§3), against which all fitted and assumed values above are unverified.

C5. Membrane Ageing and Fouling

Response without the skill

Membrane Area Sizing

Given data

The permeate volumetric flow rate, denoted QpQ_{\mathrm{p}} and expressed in cubic metres per hour (m3/h\mathrm{m^{3}/h}), is:

Qp=100 m3/hQ_{\mathrm{p}} = 100\ \mathrm{m^{3}/h}

The design flux, denoted JJ and expressed in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^{2}\cdot h)}), is:

J=20 L/(m2⋅h)J = 20\ \mathrm{L/(m^{2}\cdot h)}

Flux is defined as the permeate volumetric flow rate per unit membrane area.

Required

The membrane area, denoted AA and expressed in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}).

Relation

By the definition of flux, where QpQ_{\mathrm{p}} is expressed in litres per hour (L/h\mathrm{L/h}) when JJ is expressed in L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^{2}\cdot h)}:

J=Qp/AJ = Q_{\mathrm{p}} / A

Rearrangement gives:

A=Qp/JA = Q_{\mathrm{p}} / J

Unit conversion

The conversion factor from cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^{3}}) to litres (L\mathrm{L}) is 1 m3=1000 L1\ \mathrm{m^{3}} = 1000\ \mathrm{L}. Therefore:

Qp=100 m3/h×1000 L/m3=100,000 L/hQ_{\mathrm{p}} = 100\ \mathrm{m^{3}/h} \times 1000\ \mathrm{L/m^{3}} = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{L/h}

Calculation

A=Qp/J=100,000 L/h / 20 L/(m2⋅h)=5000 m2A = Q_{\mathrm{p}} / J = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{L/h} \ / \ 20\ \mathrm{L/(m^{2}\cdot h)} = 5000\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

The units check: (L/h)/(L/(m2⋅h))=m2(\mathrm{L/h}) / (\mathrm{L/(m^{2}\cdot h)}) = \mathrm{m^{2}}, as required for an area.

Result

The required membrane area is 5000 m25000\ \mathrm{m^{2}}.

This is the active area corresponding to the stated design flux. No safety factor, fouling allowance, downtime allowance, or module rounding has been applied, because none was specified.

Membrane Area Sizing

Symbols
  • A: membrane area, in square metres (m²)
  • J: permeate flux (permeate volume per unit membrane area per unit time), in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m²·h))
  • Q_p: permeate volumetric production rate, in cubic metres per hour (m³/h), converted below to litres per hour (L/h)
Result

Nominal area, with no allowance, fouling factor, or downtime correction:

A = Q_p / J = 100,000 L/h / 20 L/(m²·h) = 5,000 m²

Reportable range, not a single value: 4,000–6,667 m² for a realised flux of 25–15 L/(m²·h) respectively (assumed range, see "Weakness and confidence"), and 5,500–6,536 m² under the net-production alternatives in "Missing quantities". A procurement figure cannot be selected from the stated data alone; 5,000 m² is the clean arithmetic value only.

Weakness and confidence

Weakness: J is a single lumped design value. In operating equipment J is not a material constant. It depends on transmembrane pressure, feed composition and concentration, recovery, concentration polarisation, temperature (through viscosity), fouling, membrane ageing, and cleaning state. None of those quantities is supplied, so the value of J that built equipment will sustain over a cleaning cycle is the dominant uncertainty, and it enters A inversely: a 25% shortfall in J produces a 33% increase in A.

Confidence rating:

  • Arithmetic, given the two stated inputs: high (effectively 100%; verified in code below).
  • Statement that 5,000 m² will deliver 100 m³/h in built equipment: low to moderate, estimated at 50–60%. The calculation is exact; the applicability of the single flux value to a real feed, a real module train, and time-averaged operation is unverified.

No membrane type, vendor, transmembrane pressure, temperature, feed, or recovery is attached to it, so no validity range can be certified from the statement. Design fluxes of this order are common for reverse osmosis and tight nanofiltration on low-fouling water; microfiltration and ultrafiltration design fluxes are commonly several times higher, and high-fouling feeds lower. Any claim resting on J = 20 L/(m²·h) is unverified until checked against that source. No such source was supplied or consulted for this calculation; agreement with another AI model would not constitute verification and is not claimed.
