Missing quantities (Prompt 2)

The problem is underspecified. No value below was taken in silence; each is either left open or carried as a stated alternative.

  1. Basis of Q_p: gross permeate produced while running, or net permeate delivered averaged over cleaning, backwash, and downtime? Not stated. Solved both ways below.
  2. Reference state and operating point for J: transmembrane pressure, temperature, and feed pressure at which J = 20 L/(m²·h) applies. Not stated. J cannot be corrected to another temperature or pressure without them; viscosity alone changes flux by roughly 2–3% per degree Celsius near ambient conditions (rule of thumb, estimated, unverified for this feed).
  3. Pressure basis: not applicable to the area arithmetic itself, but transmembrane pressure in bar gauge versus bar absolute, and its variation along the train, determine whether the stated J is attainable at all. Not stated.
  4. Composition basis: feed composition, osmotic pressure (for reverse osmosis and nanofiltration), suspended solids, and fouling propensity. Not stated. These set the sustainable J.
  5. Per-pass versus overall: recovery (permeate divided by feed, dimensionless) per pass and overall, and the number of stages or passes. Not stated. Flux declines as concentration rises along a train, so a single J is at best a train average.
  6. Membrane and module identity: type (microfiltration, ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, reverse osmosis), element size, and area per element. Not stated; therefore the result cannot be converted to an element or vessel count, and round-up to whole elements is not included.
  7. Allowances: fouling factor, ageing allowance, design margin, and spare trains. Not stated; nominal case uses 0%, alternatives are tabulated.
  8. Operating schedule: hours per day at 100 m³/h, and whether 100 m³/h is an instantaneous rate or a daily volume divided by 24 h. Not stated; the calculation treats it as an instantaneous rate while running (assumed).

Verification (Prompt 3)

Independent checks, reported as performed:

  1. Executed code: A = 100 × 1,000 / 20 = 5,000 m². Reverse substitution: 100,000 L/h / 5,000 m² = 20 L/(m²·h), recovering J exactly. Pass.
  2. Dimensional check: (L/h) / (L/(m²·h)) = m². Pass.
  3. Limiting cases, known by sight: as J doubles, A halves (J = 40 L/(m²·h) would give 2,500 m²); as J tends to infinity, A tends to zero; as J tends to zero, A tends to infinity. The relation behaves correctly in all three. Pass.
  4. Material balance closure: fails as a check, and is reported as failing. Only the permeate stream is specified. Feed flow and retentate (concentrate) flow are not given, and recovery is not given, so feed = permeate + retentate cannot be closed and no independent balance route to A exists. This is a data gap, not an arithmetic error, and the solution has not been altered to make it pass.
  5. Energy balance: not applicable to area sizing from a stated flux; no check performed. Transmembrane pressure and pump energy would be required for any energy statement.
  6. Correlation valid range: no fitted correlation was used. The one relation used is the definition of flux, valid for a uniform average flux. Whether the stated J lies inside the vendor's valid range for a specific element cannot be checked, because no element is identified: check not possible, flagged as unverified.
Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ in built equipment, as a design and operating audit would raise them:

  1. Fouling and flux decline over a cleaning cycle. Direction: sustained average J below the clean or initial design value, so required A is larger. Rough size: 10–50% more area for fouling feeds; a few percent for clean, pre-treated water (estimated ranges). Settled by: pilot flux-decline data on the actual feed, or the plant cleaning and permeate-flow records for an existing identical train.
  2. Non-uniform flux along the train. Front elements operate at higher net driving pressure and higher flux; tail elements at higher concentration, higher osmotic pressure, and lower flux, with scaling and fouling risk concentrated at the tail. Direction: a train sized on a single average J can meet total flow while over-fluxing the front elements (accelerated fouling) and under-using the tail. Rough size: element-to-element flux variation of a factor of about 2 within a vessel is common in reverse osmosis design (estimated). Settled by: the manufacturer's stage-by-stage projection for the selected element and array.
  3. Temperature and viscosity, and net versus gross production. Cold feed raises viscosity and lowers J at fixed pressure; backwash, cleaning, and downtime reduce net output. Direction: both effects increase the area needed for a stated net 100 m³/h. Rough size: about 2–3% change in J per degree Celsius near ambient (rule of thumb, estimated); 8–31% more area under the net-production alternatives tabulated above. Settled by: feed temperature records for the design minimum case, and the vendor's stated backwash and cleaning regime for the selected system.
What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • Transmembrane pressure, pump sizing, and energy consumption.
  • Recovery, staging, element count, vessel count, and array configuration, including round-up to whole elements.
  • Concentration polarisation, osmotic pressure, scaling, and rejection or permeate quality. Area alone does not establish that the permeate meets any quality specification.
  • Flux decline, cleaning frequency and effectiveness, membrane life, and replacement rate.
  • Pretreatment requirements, which in practice determine the sustainable J.
  • Cost, footprint, piping, instrumentation, and turndown or operation away from 100 m³/h.

Information not available to this calculation: the vendor's proprietary element performance and projection software, any pilot data on the actual feed, and the applicable design code or client specification, none of which was supplied. Any of these can supersede the assumed ranges used here; data supplied by the user, the plant, or the vendor supersedes the study ranges in this answer for the case in question.

Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling under real feed variability, cleaning recovery that is incomplete and declines over membrane life, element telescoping or damage at excessive front-element flux, and seasonal temperature swings.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%:

  • Realised time-averaged J below 18.2 L/(m²·h) or above 22.2 L/(m²·h).
  • Any design, fouling, or ageing allowance above 10%.
  • Net-production duty with availability below 0.95 combined with backwash loss, per the alternatives table.
  • Design minimum feed temperature materially below the temperature at which J was stated, via the viscosity effect.
  • A recovery or feed-composition change that lowers the train-average flux by more than about 9%.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What membrane type and element is J = 20 L/(m²·h) taken from, and at what transmembrane pressure, temperature, feed composition, and recovery was it measured or projected?
  2. Is 100 m³/h a gross instantaneous rate or a net rate averaged over backwash, cleaning, and downtime, and over what operating schedule?
  3. Is J a clean-membrane value, or a time-averaged value over a cleaning cycle on this feed, supported by pilot or operating data?
  4. What fouling, ageing, and design allowances, and what spare capacity, does the governing specification require?
  5. What recovery and staging are intended, and does a stage-by-stage vendor projection confirm the train-average flux and the front-element flux limit?
  6. What permeate quality is required, and is it met at this flux and recovery?

C6. Column Efficiency

Response without the skill

Actual Tray Count from Theoretical Stages and Overall Column Efficiency

Given data
  • NtheoreticalN_{\mathrm{theoretical}} is the number of theoretical stages required, dimensionless: Ntheoretical=20N_{\mathrm{theoretical}} = 20.
  • EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is the overall column efficiency, dimensionless: Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65.
Definition

NactualN_{\mathrm{actual}} is the number of actual trays required, dimensionless.

The overall column efficiency EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is defined as the ratio of the number of theoretical stages required to the number of actual trays required:

Eo=NtheoreticalNactualE_{\mathrm{o}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{theoretical}}}{N_{\mathrm{actual}}}

Calculation

Rearrangement of the definition for NactualN_{\mathrm{actual}} gives:

Nactual=NtheoreticalEoN_{\mathrm{actual}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{theoretical}}}{E_{\mathrm{o}}}

Substitution of the given values gives:

Nactual=200.65=30.77N_{\mathrm{actual}} = \frac{20}{0.65} = 30.77

NactualN_{\mathrm{actual}} must be a whole number of trays, and a fractional tray cannot be installed. The result is therefore rounded up to the next whole number, because rounding down to 30 trays would provide fewer trays than the calculated requirement.

Nactual=31N_{\mathrm{actual}} = 31

Result

31 actual trays are required.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Actual Tray Count from Theoretical Stages and Overall Column Efficiency

Symbols and definitions
  • NthN_{\mathrm{th}} — number of theoretical stages required, dimensionless; a theoretical stage is a stage that leaves in equilibrium.
  • EoE_{\mathrm{o}} — overall column efficiency, dimensionless; defined here as Eo=Nth/NactE_{\mathrm{o}} = N_{\mathrm{th}} / N_{\mathrm{act}}.
  • NactN_{\mathrm{act}} — number of actual trays required, dimensionless (a count); obtained by rounding the exact quotient up to the next whole tray.

No other symbol is used before it is defined in the text where it appears.

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The relation Eo=Nth/NactE_{\mathrm{o}} = N_{\mathrm{th}} / N_{\mathrm{act}} is a single lumped ratio. It assigns the same efficiency to every tray, in both the rectifying and the stripping sections, at all compositions, liquid and vapour rates, and degrees of fouling, weeping, entrainment, and maldistribution. In built equipment efficiency varies tray to tray and with load. The arithmetic is exact; the model that supplies EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is the weak step.

Confidence rating: low for the tray count as a design number, high for the arithmetic. Confidence in the division and rounding is high (verified in code, Section 5). Confidence that 31 trays will deliver the specified separation in built equipment is low, because it rests entirely on a single value of EoE_{\mathrm{o}} whose origin is not stated and on an unstated counting basis for NthN_{\mathrm{th}} (Section 3). Agreement with another AI model would not raise this rating and is not used as verification (Checklist item 7).

2. Inputs, labelled at the point of use
Quantity Value State
NthN_{\mathrm{th}} 20 given
EoE_{\mathrm{o}} 0.65 given — but see note below

Note on the state of EoE_{\mathrm{o}}: the value 0.65 is given in the problem statement. Its provenance is not given. It is not stated whether it was measured on the actual system, fitted to pilot or plant data, estimated from a correlation such as the O'Connell correlation, or assumed as a rule of thumb. Until that provenance is known, it must be treated in use as estimated or assumed, not as measured, and the result must therefore be reported as a range (Section 4).

No property value, fitted relation, or rule of thumb other than the defining relation for EoE_{\mathrm{o}} above is used in the base calculation.

3. Missing quantities — not completed silently

The problem as stated is underspecified. The following quantities are missing, and the solution is given under the plausible alternatives for the most consequential one:

  1. Counting basis for NthN_{\mathrm{th}} (missing). Whether the 20 theoretical stages include (a) a reboiler, which normally counts as one theoretical stage, (b) a partial condenser, which normally counts as one theoretical stage, or (c) neither — a total condenser normally counts as no theoretical stage. This changes the tray count directly (alternatives below).
  2. Basis of EoE_{\mathrm{o}} (missing). Whether EoE_{\mathrm{o}} applies to trays only (reboiler and condenser excluded from the efficiency correction, the usual convention) or to all stages.
  3. System and conditions (missing). Components, composition basis (mole, mass, or volume fraction), pressure basis (absolute or gauge, and the pressure value), temperature, and feed condition — all of which determine whether Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 is plausible for this system at all.
  4. Tray type and hydraulics (missing). Tray type (sieve, valve, bubble-cap, or packing converted to trays), diameter, spacing, and design load as a percentage of flood.
  5. Per-pass or overall (not applicable in form, missing in substance). No conversion is stated, so this item does not arise directly; the analogous ambiguity is item 1 — whether stages are counted per unit (trays only) or overall (trays plus reboiler and condenser).
  6. Rounding and spare-tray policy (missing). Whether the count is the bare minimum or includes spare trays, a feed-tray relocation allowance, or a design margin.
Alternatives for the counting basis (item 1), at Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 (given)
  • Alternative A — 20 theoretical stages are tray stages only (total condenser, reboiler counted separately or not in the 20): Nact=⌈20/0.65⌉=31N_{\mathrm{act}} = \lceil 20 / 0.65 \rceil = 31 trays, where ⌈x⌉\lceil x \rceil denotes the smallest whole number not less than xx (dimensionless).
  • Alternative B — 20 includes a reboiler (1 stage) only: tray theoretical stages =19= 19 (assumed decomposition); Nact=⌈19/0.65⌉=30N_{\mathrm{act}} = \lceil 19 / 0.65 \rceil = 30 trays, plus the reboiler.
  • Alternative C — 20 includes a reboiler (1 stage) and a partial condenser (1 stage): tray theoretical stages =18= 18 (assumed decomposition); Nact=⌈18/0.65⌉=28N_{\mathrm{act}} = \lceil 18 / 0.65 \rceil = 28 trays, plus the reboiler and the partial condenser.

The spread from the counting basis alone is 28–31 trays, i.e. about −10 % to 0 % relative to Alternative A. Alternative A is used as the headline case only because it is the literal reading of the statement; it is not confirmed.

4. Calculation and range
Base calculation (Alternative A)

Nact,exact=NthEo=200.65=30.77N_{\mathrm{act,exact}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{th}}}{E_{\mathrm{o}}} = \frac{20}{0.65} = 30.77

where Nact,exactN_{\mathrm{act,exact}} is the unrounded actual tray count, dimensionless.

Nact=31 traysN_{\mathrm{act}} = 31 \text{ trays}

Range, not a single value

EoE_{\mathrm{o}} carries the weakness. A plausible range for an estimated overall column efficiency, in the absence of system-specific data, is 0.55–0.75 (estimated range, centred on the given 0.65, ±0.10). This range is a judgement range for reporting sensitivity, not a measured interval. Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor supersede it for the case in question.

For context, a wider screening range of EoE_{\mathrm{o}} from 0.50 to 0.80 (estimated) gives 40 to 25 trays. That wider range shows how strongly the answer depends on a quantity that is not settled by the problem statement.

5. Verification by an independent route

Checks performed in executed Python code; all passed unless stated.

  1. Back-substitution (balance-type closure). 31×0.65=20.1531 \times 0.65 = 20.15 theoretical stages, which is not less than the required 20. 30×0.65=19.5030 \times 0.65 = 19.50, which is less than 20. Therefore 31 is the smallest whole tray count that meets the requirement at Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65. Check passes.
  2. Limiting cases, known by sight. At Eo=1.00E_{\mathrm{o}} = 1.00 (dimensionless, perfect stages) the formula gives 20/1.00=2020 / 1.00 = 20 trays, as required. As EoE_{\mathrm{o}} approaches 0, NactN_{\mathrm{act}} increases without bound, as required. Checks pass.
  3. Code result. 20/0.65=30.7692…20 / 0.65 = 30.7692\ldots, ceiling 31; 20/0.55=36.3636…20 / 0.55 = 36.3636\ldots, ceiling 37; 20/0.75=26.6666…20 / 0.75 = 26.6666\ldots, ceiling 27; 19/0.65=29.2307…19 / 0.65 = 29.2307\ldots, ceiling 30; 18/0.65=27.6923…18 / 0.65 = 27.6923\ldots, ceiling 28. All match the hand arithmetic above. Check passes.
  4. Correlation valid range. No correlation was used to obtain EoE_{\mathrm{o}} in the base case, so no valid-range check can be performed on it. This check fails by absence: if Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 came from the O'Connell correlation or a similar fitted relation, its applicable range (in particular the liquid viscosity and relative volatility range of the underlying data) has not been checked, because the system is not identified. That check remains open and unverified.

No material or energy balance arises in this conversion itself; the balance that matters is the stage-requirement closure in check 1, which is the balance analogue for a stage count.

6. Guesses, and how much each moves the result
  • Guess 1 — Counting basis Alternative A (assumed): choosing Alternative C instead moves the central result from 31 to 28 trays, −9.7 %.
  • Guess 2 — Plausible range for EoE_{\mathrm{o}} of ±0.10 (estimated): at 0.55 the result moves +18.2 % in the exact count (30.77 to 36.36), at 0.75 it moves −13.3 % (30.77 to 26.67). This is the largest single source of movement.
  • Guess 3 — EoE_{\mathrm{o}} applies to trays only (assumed, usual convention): if it were instead applied to all stages including the reboiler, the result coincides numerically with Alternative B or C above, i.e. up to about −10 %.
  • Guess 4 — Rounding up with no spare trays or margin (assumed): rounding itself moves the exact count by +0.75 % (30.77 to 31). Any spare-tray or margin policy would move it by the number of trays added; none is included, because none was given.
  • Guess 5 — Constant EoE_{\mathrm{o}} over all trays and loads (assumed, inherent in the given model): unquantifiable from the data given; Section 7 gives the expected direction and rough size from operating experience.

Primary source that settles the point (unverified). The value of EoE_{\mathrm{o}} for this system is settled only by (a) operating data from a column separating the same or a closely similar system on the same tray type, or (b) a vendor hydraulic and efficiency rating for the specified trays and loads, or (c) pilot-plant data on the actual material. A correlation databank value (e.g. the O'Connell correlation as reproduced in a current separations text or databank) is a secondary estimate. Every claim in this solution that Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 is appropriate for any real system is unverified until checked against one of those primary sources. No such source was supplied or consulted for a specific system, because no system was identified.

7. Audit as a skilled engineer would — three points most likely to differ in built equipment
  1. Section-to-section efficiency difference. Rectifying and stripping sections commonly differ in efficiency because liquid viscosity, surface tension, and traffic differ. Direction: one section is likely to be under-trayed if a single EoE_{\mathrm{o}} is split uniformly. Rough size: a section efficiency differing by 0.10–0.15 from the column average changes that section's tray need by roughly 15–25 %. Settled by: section-wise efficiency or operating composition profiles from a comparable running column, or a rate-based (non-equilibrium stage) simulation validated against such data.
  2. Load dependence — weeping at low load and entrainment or flooding at high load. Efficiency falls outside the design load window. Direction: at turndown or at rates above design, effective efficiency is lower than 0.65, so more trays (or more reflux) are needed. Rough size: efficiency losses of 0.05–0.15 in EoE_{\mathrm{o}} are plausible off-design, i.e. roughly +8 % to +30 % in tray count at fixed separation. Settled by: the tray vendor's hydraulic rating sheet (weep point, entrainment, and flood curves for the actual tray, diameter, and spacing) and the column's operating record.
  3. Fouling, corrosion products, and maldistribution over run length. Efficiency at start of run is not efficiency at end of run. Direction: effective efficiency decreases with time on stream, so a column sized exactly at 31 trays has no allowance for degradation. Rough size: system-dependent, from negligible for clean services to the dominant effect for fouling services; a 0.05 fall in EoE_{\mathrm{o}} alone raises the exact count from 30.77 to 33.33 (+8.3 %). Settled by: inspection and performance records from the previous run of the same or a similar service, and the maintenance history.
8. What this calculation does not cover
  • Effects not in the model: variation of efficiency with composition, temperature, and load; tray hydraulics (weeping, dumping, entrainment, flooding, pressure drop); foaming; fouling; liquid and vapour maldistribution; back-mixing; heat effects on a tray; the effect of feed-tray location and of relocating the feed; interaction with reflux ratio — the 20 theoretical stages themselves depend on the reflux chosen, which is not stated.
  • Information not available here: any proprietary tray-vendor efficiency and hydraulic data, restricted databank values, and the design basis (system, pressure, compositions, specifications for distillate and bottoms) from which the 20 theoretical stages were obtained. Without that basis, neither Nth=20N_{\mathrm{th}} = 20 nor Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 can be independently confirmed.
  • Effects that appear only in running equipment: turndown performance, start-up, control stability, foaming excursions, fouling rate, and tray damage or displacement found at inspection.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: (i) EoE_{\mathrm{o}} at or below about 0.59 or at or above about 0.72 in place of 0.65; (ii) counting basis C instead of A (−9.7 %, at the threshold, and more once combined with any efficiency shortfall); (iii) any off-design or fouled operation that lowers effective EoE_{\mathrm{o}} by 0.05 or more; (iv) a change in the underlying separation requirement (reflux, specifications, feed condition) that changes NthN_{\mathrm{th}} by 2 stages or more (±10 % directly).
9. Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used
  1. What system, pressure, and product specifications produced the requirement of 20 theoretical stages, and at what reflux ratio?
  2. Do the 20 stages include the reboiler and a partial condenser, and does the efficiency correction apply to trays only?
  3. Where did Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 come from — measurement on this system, vendor rating, correlation, or assumption — and what range did its source report?
  4. What tray type, diameter, spacing, and percentage of flood does the count assume, and has a vendor rated them?
  5. Are spare trays, a feed-location allowance, or a fouling margin required by the project design practice, and if so, how many?
  6. Is a rate-based check planned before the tray count is frozen for fabrication?
Answer in brief

31 trays at the given Eo=0.65E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.65 on the literal counting basis, reported as a range of 27–37 trays over the plausible efficiency range 0.55–0.75, and 28–31 trays over the plausible counting bases at the given efficiency. The efficiency value and the counting basis, both unsettled by the statement, control the result; the arithmetic does not.

D1. Exchanger Fouling

Response without the skill

Heat Exchanger Sizing

Given data
  • The heat duty, denoted QQ, in megawatts (MW), is Q=2 MWQ = 2\ \text{MW}.
  • The logarithmic mean temperature difference, denoted ΔTlm\Delta T_{\text{lm}}, in kelvin (K), is ΔTlm=20 K\Delta T_{\text{lm}} = 20\ \text{K}.
  • The clean overall heat transfer coefficient, denoted UU, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W/(m2⋅K)\text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K})), is U=1,000 W/(m2⋅K)U = 1{,}000\ \text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K}).
Required quantity
  • The required heat transfer area, denoted AA, in square metres (m2\text{m}^{2}).
Governing equation

For a heat exchanger, the heat duty QQ, in watts (W), is related to the overall heat transfer coefficient UU, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W/(m2⋅K)\text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K})), the heat transfer area AA, in square metres (m2\text{m}^{2}), and the logarithmic mean temperature difference ΔTlm\Delta T_{\text{lm}}, in kelvin (K), by

Q=UAΔTlmQ = U A \Delta T_{\text{lm}}

Rearrangement for the area AA, in square metres (m2\text{m}^{2}), gives

A=QUΔTlmA = \frac{Q}{U \Delta T_{\text{lm}}}

Unit conversion

The duty QQ, in watts (W), is obtained from the value in megawatts (MW) using 1 MW=106 W1\ \text{MW} = 10^{6}\ \text{W}:

Q=2 MW×106 WMW=2,000,000 WQ = 2\ \text{MW} \times 10^{6}\ \frac{\text{W}}{\text{MW}} = 2{,}000{,}000\ \text{W}

Calculation

Substitution of Q=2,000,000 WQ = 2{,}000{,}000\ \text{W}, U=1,000 W/(m2⋅K)U = 1{,}000\ \text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K}), and ΔTlm=20 K\Delta T_{\text{lm}} = 20\ \text{K} into the rearranged equation gives

A=2,000,000 W1,000 W/(m2⋅K)×20 KA = \frac{2{,}000{,}000\ \text{W}}{1{,}000\ \text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K}) \times 20\ \text{K}}

The denominator is

1,000 W/(m2⋅K)×20 K=20,000 W/m21{,}000\ \text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K}) \times 20\ \text{K} = 20{,}000\ \text{W}/\text{m}^{2}

Therefore

A=2,000,000 W20,000 W/m2=100 m2A = \frac{2{,}000{,}000\ \text{W}}{20{,}000\ \text{W}/\text{m}^{2}} = 100\ \text{m}^{2}

Unit check

W(W/(m2⋅K))×K=WW/m2=m2\frac{\text{W}}{(\text{W}/(\text{m}^{2}\cdot\text{K})) \times \text{K}} = \frac{\text{W}}{\text{W}/\text{m}^{2}} = \text{m}^{2}

The resulting unit is square metres (m2\text{m}^{2}), as required for an area.

Result

The required clean heat transfer area is A=100 m2A = 100\ \text{m}^{2}.

This area is the clean, theoretical area from Q=UAΔTlmQ = U A \Delta T_{\text{lm}} with the stated values. A practical installed area would normally be larger after allowance for fouling, design margin, and selection of a standard exchanger size; no such allowance was specified in the given data.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Heat Exchanger Sizing — Duty 2 MW, Logarithmic Mean Temperature Difference 20 K, Clean Overall Coefficient 1,000 W/(m²·K)

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. The arithmetic is exact, but the problem as stated specifies a clean overall heat transfer coefficient, not a service (fouled, in-operation) coefficient, and it specifies no flow arrangement. A clean-coefficient area is therefore a lower bound on the area of equipment that will deliver the duty in service, not a purchasable size. How far above the lower bound the built exchanger must lie depends on quantities not supplied: fouling resistance, the logarithmic mean temperature difference correction factor, and any design margin. Presenting the clean area alone as "the size" is the specific failure this calculation is prone to.

Confidence ratings.

  • Clean area, given the three stated inputs taken at face value: high — a single algebraic relation, verified by executed code and by balance closure in Section 6.
  • Area of an exchanger that will deliver 2 MW in sustained service: low — it rests on estimated fouling resistances and an assumed correction factor, neither supplied. The range in Section 3, not the single clean value, is the defensible statement for that question.
  • No claim in this solution rests on agreement with another AI model (Checklist item 7). Verification is by dimensional check, balance closure, limiting cases, and executed code only.
2. Symbols, inputs, and their state (Prompt 1; Checklist item 3)

Symbols are defined at first use, with SI units.

  • Heat duty, denoted QQ, in watts (W), here in megawatts (MW): given, Q=2 MW=2,000,000 WQ = 2\ \mathrm{MW} = 2{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{W}.
  • Clean overall heat transfer coefficient, denoted UcleanU_{\mathrm{clean}}, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W/(m²·K)): given, Uclean=1,000 W/(m2⋅K)U_{\mathrm{clean}} = 1{,}000\ \mathrm{W/(m^2\cdot K)}. The qualifier "clean" is part of the given: it is the coefficient with no fouling layer present.
  • Logarithmic mean temperature difference, denoted ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}, in kelvin (K): given, ΔTlm=20 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}} = 20\ \mathrm{K}. Whether this value is the true countercurrent logarithmic mean or an already-corrected value is not stated — see Section 4.
  • Heat transfer area, denoted AA, in square metres (m²): the quantity to be found.
  • Logarithmic mean temperature difference correction factor, denoted FF, dimensionless, 0<F≤10 < F \le 1: assumed per scenario in Section 3. F=1F = 1 for true countercurrent flow, for a condensing or boiling stream at constant temperature, and is <1<1 for multipass or crossflow arrangements.
  • Total fouling resistance (both sides combined), denoted RfR_{\mathrm{f}}, in square metres kelvin per watt (m²·K/W): estimated per scenario in Section 3. No value was supplied.
  • Service (dirty) overall coefficient, denoted UdirtyU_{\mathrm{dirty}}, in W/(m²·K): derived from UcleanU_{\mathrm{clean}} and RfR_{\mathrm{f}} by 1/Udirty=1/Uclean+Rf1/U_{\mathrm{dirty}} = 1/U_{\mathrm{clean}} + R_{\mathrm{f}}.

No property value, correlation, or fitted relation is used. The only relation used is the defining design equation in Section 3, which holds for a constant overall coefficient and a constant-temperature-difference driving force characterised by ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}; it does not hold where the coefficient varies strongly along the exchanger (large viscosity change, phase change over a temperature glide) without a zoned calculation.

so

A=QUclean ΔTlm=2,000,000 W1,000 W/(m2⋅K)×20 K=100 m2.A = \frac{Q}{U_{\mathrm{clean}}\, \Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}} = \frac{2{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{W}}{1{,}000\ \mathrm{W/(m^2\cdot K)} \times 20\ \mathrm{K}} = 100\ \mathrm{m^2}.

  • RfR_{\mathrm{f}}: the dominant guess.   • FF: AA scales as 1/F1/F. F=0.90F = 0.90 instead of 1.00 moves AA by +11%; F=0.80F = 0.80 by +25%.
  • ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}} (given, but shown for scale): AA scales as 1/ΔTlm1/\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}. The following quantities are needed to select a single service area and none was supplied. For each, the solution above either states the assumption used or solves under the plausible alternatives.

  6. Allowable pressure drops, geometry, and construction — tube diameter, length, pitch, shell diameter, materials of construction, design pressure and temperature: none given. Area alone does not specify buildable equipment; the same 100–235 m² can be met by many geometries with very different pressure drops and velocities.

Reference state / pressure basis / composition basis / per-pass versus overall — not applicable to the area arithmetic itself (no enthalpy, equilibrium, or conversion quantity is computed), but each becomes required the moment QQ or ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}} is to be re-derived rather than taken as given: an enthalpy balance needs a reference state and composition basis, a condensing pressure needs its pressure basis (absolute or gauge), and a multipass unit needs FF stated per shell pass and overall for shells in series. They are listed here so the gap is on record rather than silent.
5. Primary sources that settle the open points (Checklist item 5)

All claims resting on the following sources are unverified until checked against them; none was consulted for this calculation, and no value above is attributed to them beyond the general ranges noted.

  • Fouling resistance for the actual fluids: the fouling-resistance tables of the current edition of the TEMA Standards, selected for the named fluids and velocities; better, the plant's own fouling history or a measured dirty coefficient on the existing or a comparable exchanger on the same streams.
  • Correction factor FF: computed from the four terminal temperatures by the standard FF-factor relations (Bowman, Mueller and Nagle, as reproduced in TEMA and in Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook, current edition) once the pass arrangement is fixed.
  • Rating of a specific geometry (pressure drop, vibration, zoned coefficient): a vendor rating or a rating run in a recognised program (e.g. HTRI Xchanger Suite) on a completed process data sheet — the data sheet, with fluids, flows, temperatures, and allowable pressure drops, is the document of record that supersedes every estimated value in this solution. Per the task instruction, data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor supersede the ranges used here for the case in question.
  • Design margin and mechanical design: the project specification and the applicable pressure-equipment code edition (e.g. ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section VIII) via the vendor's mechanical design.

7. Audit as built equipment behaves (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Fouling in service. Direction: the built, operating coefficient will be below the clean value, so a 100 m² unit will fall short of 2 MW as fouling builds, or will meet duty only when newly cleaned. Rough size: −17% to −50% on the coefficient for RfR_{\mathrm{f}} of 0.0002–0.001 m²·K/W (Section 3.2), i.e. the largest single effect in the problem. Settled by: the TEMA fouling entry for the actual fluids, plant fouling history, or a measured in-service coefficient (flows and all four temperatures logged on the operating unit).
  2. Correction factor and temperature cross. Direction: if the arrangement is multipass and the programme approaches a temperature cross, the effective driving force is below the stated ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}, FF falls steeply with small temperature changes, and the unit can become inoperable rather than merely undersized. Rough size: +5% to +25% on area for FF of 0.95–0.80; unbounded (no area suffices) at a true cross in a single shell pass. Settled by: the four terminal temperatures and pass arrangement on the process data sheet, with FF computed from them, and shells in series specified if FF falls below about 0.75–0.80.
  3. Coefficient not constant, and pressure-drop constraint. Direction: the calculation treats the overall coefficient (in W/(m²·K)) as one constant along the unit; in built equipment it varies with local temperature, viscosity (notably a cold-wall viscosity correction for viscous liquids), fouling distribution, flow maldistribution and bypass streams in the shell, generally downward from the nominal value, and the geometry that delivers the computed area may exceed the allowable pressure drop, forcing fewer, longer, or larger passages and a different coefficient. Rough size: commonly 5–20% on effective coefficient for maldistribution and viscosity effects; pressure drop can rule a geometry out entirely rather than shift it by a percentage. Settled by: a vendor or HTRI rating of a specified geometry (tube size, pitch, baffles, passes) against the allowable pressure drops on the data sheet, plus bundle bypass provisions per TEMA.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: fouling growth with time and cleaning interval; start-up, turndown, and off-design operation; phase change over a temperature glide and the zoned coefficient it requires; flow-induced vibration; thermal expansion and mechanical design; pressure drop on both sides; control and operability at low flow; heat loss to surroundings.
  • Information not accessible here: proprietary rating correlations (e.g. inside HTRI/HTFS software); the current-edition TEMA fouling table entries for the unnamed fluids; project specifications, vendor data, and plant operating records. The estimated RfR_{\mathrm{f}} and assumed FF values stand in for these and are marked as such wherever used.
  • Effects that appear only in running equipment: actual fouling rate on these streams, maldistribution and bypass leakage as built, gasket and pass-partition leakage, and the measured clean coefficient of the fabricated bundle, which differs from a nominal catalogue value.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%: any one of — total fouling resistance above 0.0001 m²·K/W; FF below 0.90; true ΔTlm\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}} below 18 K or duty above 2.2 MW; a temperature cross in a single shell pass (change is qualitative, not only numerical); a gas or viscous-liquid service for which the given clean coefficient does not apply.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is 100 m² being quoted as a clean area or as a purchase size — and who has recorded that distinction?
  2. What are the two fluids, their flow rates, and all four terminal temperatures, and do they close an enthalpy balance at 2 MW with a 20 K logarithmic mean temperature difference?
  3. Is the 20 K already corrected by FF, or is FF still to be applied?
  4. What fouling resistances were specified, from which TEMA edition or plant record, and what cleaning philosophy follows from them?
  5. What are the allowable pressure drops, and has a specified geometry been rated against them?
  6. What design margin does the project specification require, and is it inside or outside the 125–235 m² service range reported here?

D2. Multiphase Pressure Drop

Response without the skill

Pressure Drop of a Gas–Liquid Mixture in 1 km of Horizontal Line

Result in brief

No unique numerical pressure drop can be estimated from the data given. The only quantity supplied, a liquid-only pressure drop of 0.4 bar km−10.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}, fixes one reference value. The two-phase pressure drop is that reference value multiplied by a two-phase multiplier that is greater than or equal to 11 and that depends on properties and flow rates that are not supplied. The defensible result is therefore parametric,

Δptp=ϕLO2 ΔpLO=ϕLO2 (0.4 bar),\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}} = \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}\,\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}} = \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}\,(0.4\ \mathrm{bar}),

with ϕLO2≥1\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} \ge 1, i.e. $\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}} \ge 0.4\ \mathrm{bar}$ over the kilometre, and with no finite upper bound until the gas fraction and the phase properties are specified. Any single number larger than 0.4 bar0.4\ \mathrm{bar} quoted without those data would be an invented value, not an estimate derived from the statement.

Symbols

Each symbol is defined here and at its first use in the text.

  • LL, the pipe length, in metres (m\mathrm{m}); here L=1000 mL = 1000\ \mathrm{m}.
  • Δptp\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}}, the two-phase (gas–liquid) pressure drop over the length LL, in bar.
  • ΔpLO\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}}, the liquid-only pressure drop over the length LL, computed as if the total (gas plus liquid) mass flow flowed as liquid alone, in bar; here ΔpLO=0.4 bar\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{bar}.
  • (dp/dz)LO(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}}, the liquid-only pressure gradient, in bar km−1\mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}; here (dp/dz)LO=0.4 bar km−1(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}, where zz is the axial distance along the pipe, in metres (m\mathrm{m}), and pp is pressure, in bar.
  • ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}, the dimensionless two-phase friction multiplier referred to the liquid-only basis, defined in Eq. (1).
  • GG, the total mass flux (total mass flow rate divided by pipe cross-sectional area), in kg m−2 s−1\mathrm{kg\ m^{-2}\ s^{-1}}.
  • xx, the quality, the mass fraction of the total flow that is gas, dimensionless, 0≤x≤10 \le x \le 1.
  • ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}}, the liquid density, in kg m−3\mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}.
  • ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, the gas density at line conditions, in kg m−3\mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}.
  • ρm\rho_{\mathrm{m}}, the homogeneous mixture density, in kg m−3\mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}, defined in Eq. (4).
  • μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}}, the liquid dynamic viscosity, in Pa s\mathrm{Pa\ s}.
  • μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}, the gas dynamic viscosity, in Pa s\mathrm{Pa\ s}.
  • DD, the pipe inside diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • fLOf_{\mathrm{LO}}, the dimensionless (Darcy) friction factor for the total flow treated as liquid.
  • fmf_{\mathrm{m}}, the dimensionless (Darcy) friction factor for the homogeneous mixture.
  • (dp/dz)L(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}}, the pressure gradient of the liquid phase flowing alone in the pipe at its own (liquid-only share of the) flow rate, in bar km−1\mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}.
  • (dp/dz)G(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{G}}, the pressure gradient of the gas phase flowing alone in the pipe at its own flow rate, in bar km−1\mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}.
  • XX, the dimensionless Lockhart–Martinelli parameter, defined in Eq. (2).
  • ϕL2\phi_{\mathrm{L}}^{2}, the dimensionless two-phase multiplier referred to the liquid-alone basis (dp/dz)L(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}}.
  • CC, the dimensionless Chisholm constant in Eq. (3), which depends on whether each phase, flowing alone, is laminar or turbulent.
  • Δpacc\Delta p_{\mathrm{acc}}, the acceleration (momentum-change) part of the pressure drop, in bar, arising if the mixture density changes along the pipe.
1. What is given
  • LL, the pipe length, is L=1 km=1000 mL = 1\ \mathrm{km} = 1000\ \mathrm{m}.
  • The line is horizontal, so there is no hydrostatic (elevation) term: the pressure drop is friction plus, in general, the acceleration term Δpacc\Delta p_{\mathrm{acc}}.
  • (dp/dz)LO(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}}, the liquid-only pressure gradient, is 0.4 bar km−10.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}, hence ΔpLO\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}}, the liquid-only drop over this length, is

ΔpLO=(dp/dz)LO L=(0.4 bar km−1)(1 km)=0.4 bar.\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}} = (dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}}\,L = \left(0.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}\right)(1\ \mathrm{km}) = 0.4\ \mathrm{bar}.

Nothing else is given: no value of xx, the quality; no value of GG, the total mass flux, beyond what is already implicit in ΔpLO\Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}}; no ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}} or ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, the phase densities; no μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}} or μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}, the phase viscosities; no DD, the pipe diameter; no inlet pressure or temperature, which would be needed to obtain ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}} for a real gas and to evaluate Δpacc\Delta p_{\mathrm{acc}}; and no flow-regime information (bubbly, slug, annular, etc.).

2. Why the liquid-only value does not determine the two-phase value

ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}, the two-phase multiplier on the liquid-only basis, is defined by

ϕLO2≡(dp/dz)tp(dp/dz)LO,(1)\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} \equiv \frac{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{tp}}}{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}}}, \tag{1}

where (dp/dz)tp(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{tp}} is the two-phase frictional pressure gradient, in bar km−1\mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}. Equation (1) is a definition, not a correlation. A correlation is required to supply ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}, and every standard correlation requires data that are absent here.

2.1 Lockhart–Martinelli / Chisholm form

XX, the Lockhart–Martinelli parameter, is

X2=(dp/dz)L(dp/dz)G,(2)X^{2} = \frac{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}}}{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{G}}}, \tag{2}

where (dp/dz)L(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}} and (dp/dz)G(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{G}} are the gradients for the liquid and the gas flowing alone at their own respective flow rates. The Chisholm form of the multiplier on the liquid-alone basis is

ϕL2=1+CX+1X2,(3)\phi_{\mathrm{L}}^{2} = 1 + \frac{C}{X} + \frac{1}{X^{2}}, \tag{3}

where CC, the Chisholm constant, is 55, 1010, 1212, or 2020 according to whether the liquid-alone and gas-alone flows are laminar or turbulent (C=20C = 20 for both turbulent, the commonest engineering case). Evaluating Eq. (2) requires xx, ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}}, ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}}, μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}, GG and DD: (dp/dz)L(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}} scales with the liquid share (1−x)(1-x) of GG and with ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}} and μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}}, and (dp/dz)G(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{G}} scales with the gas share xx of GG and with ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}} and μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}. Note also that Eq. (3) is on the liquid-alone basis, not on the liquid-only basis of the given 0.4 bar km−10.4\ \mathrm{bar\ km^{-1}}; converting between the two bases itself requires xx and the friction-factor ratio, i.e. the same missing data. None of xx, the densities, the viscosities, GG or DD is supplied, so XX, and therefore ϕL2\phi_{\mathrm{L}}^{2}, cannot be evaluated.

2.2 Homogeneous-model form

ρm\rho_{\mathrm{m}}, the homogeneous mixture density, for a mixture treated as a single pseudo-fluid, is

1ρm=xρG+1−xρL.(4)\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{m}}} = \frac{x}{\rho_{\mathrm{G}}} + \frac{1-x}{\rho_{\mathrm{L}}}. \tag{4}

In the homogeneous model the frictional gradient ratio to the liquid-only gradient is, to leading order,

(dp/dz)tp(dp/dz)LO≈fmfLO ρLρm,\frac{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{tp}}}{(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{LO}}} \approx \frac{f_{\mathrm{m}}}{f_{\mathrm{LO}}}\, \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{L}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{m}}},

where fmf_{\mathrm{m}} and fLOf_{\mathrm{LO}} are the mixture and liquid-only Darcy friction factors. By Eq. (4), ρL/ρm=(1−x)+x ρL/ρG\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = (1-x) + x\,\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, which is 11 at x=0x = 0 and rises without bound as xx increases whenever ρL/ρG\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{G}} is large — for a typical liquid–gas pair ρL/ρG\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{G}} is of order 10210^{2} to 10310^{3} at low pressure. The homogeneous model reaches exactly the same conclusion as §2.1: the multiplier is controlled mainly by xx and by ρL/ρG\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, neither of which is given.

3. Range consistent with the given data

Because ϕLO2≥1\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} \ge 1, with equality only in the limit x→0x \to 0 in which there is no gas at all, and because ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} grows without bound as xx and ρL/ρG\rho_{\mathrm{L}}/\rho_{\mathrm{G}} increase, the given data are consistent with all of the following, among infinitely many others:

ϕLO2\phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} (dimensionless) Δptp=ϕLO2 (0.4 bar)\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}} = \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}\,(0.4\ \mathrm{bar})
1 0.4 bar0.4\ \mathrm{bar}
2 0.8 bar0.8\ \mathrm{bar}
5 2.0 bar2.0\ \mathrm{bar}
10 4.0 bar4.0\ \mathrm{bar}
25 10 bar10\ \mathrm{bar}
100 40 bar40\ \mathrm{bar}

The rows are illustrations of Eq. (1), not predictions: each row corresponds to a different (unspecified) combination of quality, density ratio, viscosity ratio and flow regime, and the statement of the problem does not distinguish between them. Multipliers of order 55–2525 are common in gas–liquid service, which is why a two-phase drop is normally several times the liquid-only drop, but selecting any one row as "the" answer would require data that are not present.

Two further terms cannot be assessed at all from the statement:

  1. Δpacc\Delta p_{\mathrm{acc}}, the acceleration pressure drop, is non-zero if the gas expands as pressure falls along the 1 km1\ \mathrm{km} line. It requires the inlet pressure, the temperature, and the variation of ρm\rho_{\mathrm{m}} along the line. For a drop that is a substantial fraction of the inlet pressure it is not negligible.
  2. If the flow is intermittent (slug or plug flow) or if the line has fittings, valves or a non-uniform diameter, additional losses arise that no multiplier on a straight-pipe liquid-only value captures.
4. Data required for a numerical estimate, and the calculation that would then be performed

A numerical estimate requires, as a minimum:

  1. xx, the quality (or, equivalently, the separate gas and liquid mass or volumetric flow rates, from which xx and GG follow);
  2. ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}} and ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, the phase densities at line pressure and temperature (ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}} requires the inlet pressure, the temperature, and the gas composition or compressibility);
  3. μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}} and μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}, the phase viscosities;
  4. DD, the pipe inside diameter (and, for fLOf_{\mathrm{LO}} and fmf_{\mathrm{m}}, the pipe roughness);
  5. The flow regime, or enough of the above to determine it from a flow-pattern map.

With those data the standard calculation is:

  • Step 1: compute (dp/dz)L(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}} and (dp/dz)G(dp/dz)_{\mathrm{G}} from the single-phase Darcy–Weisbach relation at the liquid-alone and gas-alone flow rates, respectively — verify: each gradient reduces to a standard single-phase value.
  • Step 2: form XX from Eq. (2) — verify: X→∞X \to \infty as x→0x \to 0 and X→0X \to 0 as x→1x \to 1.
  • Step 3: select CC in Eq. (3) from the laminar/turbulent state of each phase alone and obtain ϕL2\phi_{\mathrm{L}}^{2} — verify: ϕL2→1\phi_{\mathrm{L}}^{2} \to 1 as X→∞X \to \infty.
  • Step 4: obtain $(dp/dz){\mathrm{tp}} = \phi{\mathrm{L}}^{2}\, (dp/dz)_{\mathrm{L}}$, cross-check with a second correlation (for example the Friedel correlation, which uses the same input set plus surface tension and DD), and multiply by L=1 kmL = 1\ \mathrm{km} — verify: the result is ≥ΔpLO=0.4 bar\ge \Delta p_{\mathrm{LO}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{bar}, and the two correlations agree to within their usual scatter (typically ±30%\pm 30\%).
  • Step 5: add Δpacc\Delta p_{\mathrm{acc}} if the estimated drop is a non-negligible fraction of the inlet pressure, iterating because ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}} then varies along the line.
5. Answer

Over L=1 kmL = 1\ \mathrm{km} of horizontal line,

Δptp=ϕLO2 (0.4 bar),ϕLO2≥1,\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}} = \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2}\,(0.4\ \mathrm{bar}), \qquad \phi_{\mathrm{LO}}^{2} \ge 1,

so Δptp≥0.4 bar\Delta p_{\mathrm{tp}} \ge 0.4\ \mathrm{bar}, the gas–liquid drop exceeds the liquid-only drop, and in typical gas–liquid service it is expected to be several times larger — of order 22–10 bar10\ \mathrm{bar} for multipliers of 55–2525. No single value within, or outside, that illustrative range can be selected from the information provided. The quality xx, the phase densities ρL\rho_{\mathrm{L}} and ρG\rho_{\mathrm{G}}, the phase viscosities μL\mu_{\mathrm{L}} and μG\mu_{\mathrm{G}}, and the pipe diameter DD (§4) are required before a defensible numerical estimate can be reported.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Pressure Drop in a Horizontal Gas–Liquid Line — Estimate

Symbols
  • Δp\Delta p — pressure drop, in bar per kilometre (bar/km)
  • ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO} — pressure drop computed as if the total mass flow flowed as liquid alone, in bar/km
  • ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} — two-phase (gas–liquid) pressure drop, in bar/km
  • ΔpL\Delta p_L — pressure drop if the liquid flowed alone at its own flow rate, in bar/km
  • LL — line length, in kilometres (km)
  • xx — gas mass quality, the gas mass flow divided by the total mass flow, dimensionless
  • ρL\rho_L — liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³)
  • ρG\rho_G — gas density at line pressure and temperature, in kg/m³
  • ρh\rho_h — homogeneous mixture density, in kg/m³
  • XX — Lockhart–Martinelli parameter, dimensionless
  • CC — Lockhart–Martinelli regime constant, dimensionless
  • ϕL2\phi_L^2 — two-phase multiplier on the liquid-alone basis, dimensionless
  • ϕLO2\phi_{LO}^2 — two-phase multiplier on the total-flow-as-liquid basis, ϕLO2=ΔpTP/ΔpLO\phi_{LO}^2 = \Delta p_{TP}/\Delta p_{LO}, dimensionless
1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. The problem is severely underspecified for the quantity that controls the answer. Two-phase friction is not a fixed multiple of ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO}. It is set mainly by xx and by ρG/ρL\rho_G/\rho_L, neither of which is supplied, and secondarily by the flow regime, the mass flux, the pipe diameter, and the phase viscosities, none of which is supplied. The supplied value ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO} fixes only the no-gas limit.

Confidence rating: very low for any single value; low for any range narrower than an order of magnitude. Conditional ranges for stated, assumed scenarios (Section 4) carry moderate confidence as arithmetic from the named correlations, and no confidence that the assumed scenarios describe the actual line. No single-value estimate is defensible from the data supplied.

No input other than LL, orientation, and ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO} is given, measured, or fitted to the actual line. Every other number in this solution is assumed or is a fitted literature constant, and is labelled as such where used.

3. Missing quantities (Checklist item 4; Prompt 2)

The solution needs, and the statement does not supply:

  1. Composition / flow basis: xx on a mass basis. A gas fraction quoted by volume, by moles, or at standard conditions is a different number and converts to a mass xx only with the phase densities and the reference state. Basis: missing.
  2. Reference state: the pressure and temperature at which any quoted gas volume or gas fraction is measured — line conditions or standard conditions. Missing.
  3. Pressure basis: the absolute operating pressure. The stated 0.4 bar/km is a differential, so its basis does not matter; ρG\rho_G, and hence the answer, depends on the absolute pressure, which is missing. Whether any pressures elsewhere in the source calculation were gauge or absolute is also unstated.
  4. Phase properties at line conditions: ρL\rho_L, ρG\rho_G, both viscosities, surface tension — requiring composition, pressure, and temperature. Missing.
  5. Line and flow quantities: pipe internal diameter, roughness, total mass flux or velocity, and the fitting/valve count. Partly embedded in ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO}, but needed separately for regime determination and for any correlation using the Froude or Weber number (for example Friedel). Missing.
  6. Flow regime: stratified, slug, annular, dispersed, or other. Missing, and not determinable without items 4 and 5.
  7. Per-pass or overall: not applicable to a single line with no reaction or recycle, but the analogous ambiguity does apply: whether xx is an inlet value, an outlet value, or a line average is missing. xx can change along the line by flashing, condensation, or gas expansion (Section 8).
  8. Scope of ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO}: friction only, or friction plus fittings and entrance/exit losses. Missing.

Per Prompt 2, no missing value is taken in silence. Section 4 solves under the plausible alternatives for the two controlling missing quantities, xx and ρG\rho_G.

5. Properties, rules, and relations used, with provenance and range (Prompt 1)
  • Lockhart–Martinelli correlation, ϕL2=1+C/X+1/X2\phi_L^2 = 1 + C/X + 1/X^{2}: fitted empirical relation, Lockhart and Martinelli (1949). Developed largely on small-diameter, near-atmospheric air–water and air–oil data; extrapolation to large lines, high pressure, and other fluid pairs is outside the fitted base. CC values 5, 10, 12, 20 correspond to laminar/turbulent pairings of the two phases. Status: unverified against the primary source in this solution (Section 7).
  • Homogeneous model: assumes no slip between phases and a single mixture density ρh\rho_h. Known to underpredict friction where slip is large (stratified and slug flow) and to be more reasonable for dispersed flow. Used here only as an independent bracket, not as a preferred model.
  • Turbulent scaling Δp∝(mass flow)2/ρ\Delta p \propto (\text{mass flow})^{2}/\rho: approximation; with a Reynolds-number-dependent friction factor the exponent is nearer 1.75. This approximation contributes part of the Route A / Route B discrepancy at high xx.
  • No rule of thumb of the form "two-phase drop equals a fixed multiple of the liquid-only drop" is used, because no such multiple exists independently of xx and ρG/ρL\rho_G/\rho_L; any source quoting one without those two quantities is quoting a case-specific result.
6. Verification by an independent route (Checklist item 6; Prompt 3)

All numbers in Section 4 were computed by executed code (Python, both routes evaluated over the tabulated xx and ρG\rho_G grid), not by hand arithmetic.

Checks performed:

  1. Limiting case, x→0x \to 0: both routes return ΔpTP→ΔpLO=0.4\Delta p_{TP} \to \Delta p_{LO} = 0.4 bar/km. Passes. A gas-free line must recover the given liquid-only value.
  2. Limiting case, horizontal line: no static (elevation) head term appears, consistent with the given horizontal orientation for a perfectly level line. Passes for the stated geometry; see Section 8 for built-line departures.
  3. Independent-route comparison: Route B (homogeneous) lies below Route A (Lockhart–Martinelli) at every tabulated point, by 37 % at x=0.01x = 0.01 and by 61 % at x=0.10x = 0.10. This check fails as a confirmation: the two routes do not agree within any design tolerance. The disagreement is reported, not reconciled, and is the reason the result is stated as a bracket rather than a value. The homogeneous model neglects slip; Lockhart–Martinelli at high xx with the squared scaling of Section 5 overstates ΔpL\Delta p_L's share. The true value for a real regime is expected between the routes for dispersed flow and can lie above Route A in slug flow.
  4. Limiting case, x→1x \to 1: Route A does not recover a finite gas-only pressure drop; ϕLO2\phi_{LO}^2 grows without bound as xx increases at low ρG\rho_G. Fails. Route A is therefore not used to extrapolate beyond x=0.20x = 0.20, and values at x=0.20x = 0.20 are flagged as upper, model-limited figures.
  5. Correlation valid range: the Lockhart–Martinelli fitted base (small diameter, near-atmospheric, Section 5) cannot be checked against the actual line because diameter, pressure, and fluids are missing. Check cannot be completed — reported as failed/open, not as passed.
  6. Balance closure: no material or energy balance can be closed; no flow rates, compositions, or temperatures are supplied. Check cannot be performed. No balance has been silently assumed closed.
  7. Agreement with any other AI model has not been used as verification, and none is claimed (Checklist item 7).
7. Primary sources that settle the point (Checklist item 5)

Every claim resting on the following is unverified until checked against them:

  • The point is settled for the actual line only by measurement on that line: differential-pressure tappings over a known straight length of the actual line at metered gas and liquid rates. No correlation supersedes this.
  • Phase properties: NIST REFPROP or the DIPPR databank, evaluated at the actual composition, pressure, and temperature — not generic densities of the kind assumed in Section 4.
  • Correlation and regime: Lockhart and Martinelli (1949), Chemical Engineering Progress 45(1), for the multiplier and its fitted base; Friedel (1979) for a multiplier on the ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO} basis that uses mass flux, diameter, and surface tension; Taitel and Dukler (1976) for the flow-regime determination. Bibliographic details here are from memory and are unverified against the publisher records.
  • Design practice: the current edition of the applicable piping design code and the line's own design basis document, for allowable velocity, erosion, and slug-load criteria.

Data supplied by the user, the plant, or a vendor for the actual line supersede every assumed range in this solution.

8. Audit by a skilled engineer (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from built-equipment behaviour:

  1. The built line is not level. As-built lines have undulations; liquid accumulates in low points and is periodically swept out as slugs. Direction: actual Δp\Delta p is higher than the level-line friction value and is unsteady; transient slug peaks can exceed the steady value severalfold. Rough size: static head of one liquid-filled riser leg of a few metres is of the order of 0.1–0.3 bar per leg, comparable to the entire given friction term. Settled by: the as-built isometric/elevation profile and a differential-pressure trend record on the operating line.
  2. Fittings, valves, and entrance/exit losses are treated differently in two-phase flow. If the given ΔpLO\Delta p_{LO} is straight-pipe friction only (scope missing, Section 3), local losses — which carry their own, usually larger, two-phase multipliers — are absent from every figure in Section 4. Direction: actual Δp\Delta p higher. Rough size: tens of percent on a fitted line, more on a short, heavily fitted run. Settled by: the line's fitting count from the isometric and the source calculation for the given 0.4 bar/km.
  3. xx and ρG\rho_G change along the kilometre. Gas expands as pressure falls, and flashing or condensation can change xx itself; if ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} is several bar and the absolute pressure is low (pressure missing, Section 3), the accelerational pressure drop and the density change along the line are first-order, and a per-kilometre constant multiplier is the wrong model. Direction: actual Δp\Delta p higher than an inlet-conditions estimate. Rough size: exceeds 10 % whenever ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} exceeds roughly 10 % of the absolute line pressure. Settled by: the operating pressure and temperature, a flash calculation at inlet and outlet conditions, and outlet pressure measurement.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: accelerational pressure drop from gas expansion; flow-regime transitions along the line; slugging and all transients; entrance, fitting, and valve losses (see Section 8); fouling, corrosion, wax, hydrate, or scale changing roughness and bore; heat transfer with the surroundings changing xx; non-Newtonian liquid behaviour; solids.
  • Information not accessible here: the actual fluids, composition, rates, pressure, temperature, and pipe data (plant-held); proprietary databank values and vendor two-phase sizing methods held in restricted databanks or software; the provenance of the given 0.4 bar/km.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: slug-induced vibration and loads, erosion at bends at high gas velocity, liquid hold-up dynamics on rate changes, and control-valve behaviour under two-phase flow.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: essentially all plausible ones. A change in xx from 0.01 to 0.05, a halving of the absolute pressure (through ρG\rho_G), a regime change altering CC from 20 to 5, or model choice alone each move the result by 30–215 % (Section 4.4). The 10 % threshold is crossed by any single missing quantity being resolved differently from the assumed scenario values.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What are xx (on what basis, at what reference state), the absolute pressure, and the temperature?
  2. What are ρL\rho_L and ρG\rho_G from REFPROP/DIPPR at line conditions, not assumed values?
  3. What is the flow regime, from a regime map at the actual mass flux and diameter — and is slug flow possible?
  4. Does the given 0.4 bar/km include fittings, and what friction factor and roughness produced it?
  5. Is ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} small compared with the absolute pressure, so that constant-property, per-kilometre treatment is valid at all?
  6. Has any measured differential pressure on this or a comparable operating line been compared with the estimate?
10. Conclusion

ΔpLO=0.4\Delta p_{LO} = 0.4 bar/km (given) is the no-gas limit, not an estimate of the two-phase drop. From the data supplied, ΔpTP\Delta p_{TP} over 1 km can only be bounded as 0.4 bar/km to more than 30 bar/km. For the assumed low-quality, mid-pressure scenario of Section 4.3 (xx between 0.01 and 0.10, ρG≈20\rho_G \approx 20 kg/m³, both assumed), the two independent routes bracket approximately 0.6 to 5.0 bar/km. A design value requires, at minimum, xx, the absolute pressure, and the phase densities at line conditions (Section 7); a measured differential pressure on the actual line supersedes all of these figures.

D3. Net Positive Suction Head

Response without the skill

Available Net Positive Suction Head

Given data
  • ρ\rho is the liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}): ρ=650 kg/m3\rho = 650\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}
  • gg is the acceleration due to gravity, in metres per second squared (m/s2\mathrm{m/s^2}): g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}
  • PsP_{\mathrm{s}} is the pressure at the liquid surface in the vessel, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}): Ps=101 kPaP_{\mathrm{s}} = 101\ \mathrm{kPa}, atmospheric pressure
  • PvP_{\mathrm{v}} is the liquid vapour pressure at the liquid temperature, in kilopascals (kPa\mathrm{kPa}): Pv=80 kPaP_{\mathrm{v}} = 80\ \mathrm{kPa} at 60 ∘C60\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, where ∘C^{\circ}\mathrm{C} denotes degrees Celsius
  • zz is the static elevation of the liquid level above the pump centreline, in metres (m\mathrm{m}): z=3 mz = 3\ \mathrm{m}
  • hfh_{\mathrm{f}} is the total head loss in the suction line, in metres (m\mathrm{m}) of liquid: hf=1 mh_{\mathrm{f}} = 1\ \mathrm{m}
Definition

NPSHA\mathrm{NPSH_A} is the available net positive suction head, in metres (m\mathrm{m}) of liquid. It is the total suction head at the pump inlet, measured above the vapour-pressure head, referred to the pump centreline:

NPSHA=Ps−Pvρg+z−hf\mathrm{NPSH_A} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{s}} - P_{\mathrm{v}}}{\rho g} + z - h_{\mathrm{f}}

where ρg\rho g is the specific weight of the liquid, in pascals per metre (Pa/m\mathrm{Pa/m}), and (Ps−Pv)/(ρg)(P_{\mathrm{s}} - P_{\mathrm{v}})/(\rho g) is the pressure head available above vapour pressure, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).

Velocity head at the vessel surface is negligible for a large vessel, and no separate velocity-head term is added at the pump inlet in this standard form, because NPSHA\mathrm{NPSH_A} as defined above is already the total head above vapour pressure at the inlet when hfh_{\mathrm{f}} includes the suction-line losses to the inlet.

Calculation

Pressure difference above vapour pressure:

Ps−Pv=101 kPa−80 kPa=21 kPa=21,000 PaP_{\mathrm{s}} - P_{\mathrm{v}} = 101\ \mathrm{kPa} - 80\ \mathrm{kPa} = 21\ \mathrm{kPa} = 21{,}000\ \mathrm{Pa}

where Pa\mathrm{Pa} denotes the pascal, the SI unit of pressure.

Specific weight:

ρg=(650 kg/m3)(9.81 m/s2)=6,377 Pa/m\rho g = (650\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 6{,}377\ \mathrm{Pa/m}

Pressure head:

Ps−Pvρg=21,000 Pa6,377 Pa/m=3.29 m\frac{P_{\mathrm{s}} - P_{\mathrm{v}}}{\rho g} = \frac{21{,}000\ \mathrm{Pa}}{6{,}377\ \mathrm{Pa/m}} = 3.29\ \mathrm{m}

Available net positive suction head:

NPSHA=3.29 m+3 m−1 m=5.29 m\mathrm{NPSH_A} = 3.29\ \mathrm{m} + 3\ \mathrm{m} - 1\ \mathrm{m} = 5.29\ \mathrm{m}

Result

NPSHA≈5.3 m of liquid\mathrm{NPSH_A} \approx 5.3\ \mathrm{m\ of\ liquid}

The pump's required net positive suction head, NPSHR\mathrm{NPSH_R}, in metres (m\mathrm{m}), must be less than 5.3 m5.3\ \mathrm{m}, with an adequate operating margin, for cavitation-free operation at the stated conditions. The margin is small in pressure terms because the liquid at 60 ∘C60\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} is close to boiling at atmospheric pressure: only 21 kPa21\ \mathrm{kPa} separates the surface pressure from the vapour pressure.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Available Net Positive Suction Head — Light Hydrocarbon Pump

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The defining equation for available net positive suction head (NPSHa, in metres of liquid, m) is exact for steady, single-phase flow, and the arithmetic is not the weakness. The weakness is the inputs: NPSHa depends on the small difference between two large pressures, vessel pressure minus vapour pressure, so a modest error in vapour pressure, temperature, composition, or operating liquid level moves the result by metres. Vapour pressure of a light hydrocarbon is also strongly temperature- and composition-dependent, and neither the composition nor a vapour-pressure–temperature relation is supplied. Suction-line loss varies with flow rate squared, and no flow rate is supplied.

Confidence rating: Low to moderate — 5/10 for the central value as a design value, 8/10 for the arithmetic on the stated inputs. The central value below is correct for the inputs exactly as stated. Confidence that built, operating equipment will show that value at all times is low, because level, temperature, composition, and flow all move in operation. No judgement about cavitation is possible at all from NPSHa alone, because the pump required net positive suction head (NPSHr, in m) is not supplied (see §3).

2. Symbols and definitions

Every symbol is defined at first use, with SI units.

  • NPSHa — available net positive suction head, in metres of pumped liquid (m): the pressure at the pump suction, expressed as head of liquid, minus the liquid vapour pressure expressed as head of liquid, both referred to the pump centreline (impeller eye datum).
  • p0p_0 — absolute pressure at the liquid surface in the vessel, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • pvp_{\mathrm{v}} — absolute vapour pressure of the liquid at its pumping temperature, in kPa.
  • ρ\rho — liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).
  • gg — acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 metres per second squared (m/s²); standard value, assumed.
  • z0−zpz_0 - z_{\mathrm{p}} — static elevation of the liquid surface z0z_0 (in m) above the pump centreline elevation zpz_{\mathrm{p}} (in m).
  • hLh_L — total head loss in the suction line between the vessel surface and the pump suction flange, in metres of liquid (m), including friction and fittings, on the convention stated in §3.
  • pinp_{\mathrm{in}} — absolute static pressure at the pump suction (inlet), in kPa, used only in the independent check in §6.

No value below was taken in silence. Each gap is listed with the treatment used.

Missing quantity Why it is needed Treatment in this solution

A gauge/absolute mix-up shifts the pressure difference by about 101 kPa, i.e. about 15.9 m of head — larger than the whole answer. Assumed: both absolute. This is the only physically consistent reading of "vessel at atmospheric pressure, 101 kPa" with "vapour pressure 80 kPa". Alternative solved in §5.
Pump NPSHr, and its basis (NPSH3, the head at 3 % head drop, per Hydraulic Institute / ISO 9906 convention) NPSHa alone cannot show whether the pump cavitates. Adequacy requires NPSHa − NPSHr and a margin policy. Not solvable from supplied data. Stated as an open item; no adequacy claim is made.
Reference elevation for NPSHa (pump centreline, impeller eye, or suction flange centreline) Datums differ by typically 0.1–0.5 m on a real pump. Assumed: pump centreline as stated, consistent with the given 3 m level. Alternative effect quantified in §5.
Whether the stated 3 m level is normal level, minimum (low-low) operating level, or a single snapshot Design NPSHa is normally calculated at the lowest operating level. Assumed: 3 m is the operating level to be used. Sensitivity to ±0.5 m reported in §5; design should be re-run at low-low level.
Scope of the stated 1 m suction-line loss: friction only, or friction plus entrance loss, strainer, fittings, and the velocity head at the suction flange NPSHa definitions differ on whether velocity head is included in the suction total head. Assumed: 1 m is the total loss between the vessel surface and the pump inlet, and NPSHa is stated on the static-pressure basis used in §4 (the standard textbook form). If a velocity head, v2/(2g)v^2/(2g) where vv is suction-line velocity in m/s, must additionally be deducted, the deduction is typically 0.05–0.3 m for suction velocities of 1–2.5 m/s.
Flow rate at which the 1 m loss applies Suction loss varies approximately with flow rate squared. Assumed: loss applies at the duty flow. At 120 % of duty flow the loss would be about 1.22×1 m=1.441.2^2 \times 1\ \text{m} = 1.44 m, reducing NPSHa by 0.44 m.
Composition of the "light hydrocarbon" and a vapour-pressure–temperature relation Needed to correct pvp_{\mathrm{v}} for any temperature other than 60 °C, and for composition drift (light ends). Not supplied. Temperature/composition effect is carried as a range on pvp_{\mathrm{v}} (§5), not as a corrected value.
Density at 60 °C specifically Density falls with temperature; a density quoted at 15 °C would be higher. Assumed: 650 kg/m³ is the density at the pumping temperature of 60 °C, as the problem presents it with the duty. Sensitivity in §5.
Vessel pressure control / altitude / weather variation An atmospheric (vented) vessel follows local atmospheric pressure, which varies. Range on p0p_0 carried in §5.

Basis statements: pressures are counted on an absolute basis; head is counted in metres of the pumped liquid at 650 kg/m³ (not metres of water); the calculation is a steady-state, single operating point calculation — per-pass/overall conversion language does not apply to a suction-head calculation, and no conversion is involved.

4. Solution
4.1 Inputs, labelled at the point of use
  • p0=101p_0 = 101 kPa — given; interpreted as absolute (assumed basis, §3).
  • pv=80p_{\mathrm{v}} = 80 kPa at 60 °C — given; interpreted as absolute (assumed basis, §3). This is the single most sensitive input (§5).
  • ρ=650\rho = 650 kg/m³ — given; assumed to be at 60 °C.
  • z0−zp=3z_0 - z_{\mathrm{p}} = 3 m — given.
  • hL=1h_L = 1 m — given as a single figure; its scope and flow basis are assumed (§3). In practice a single round figure of this kind is an estimate, and it is treated as one in the range calculation.
  • Liquid temperature 60 °C — given; it enters only through pvp_{\mathrm{v}} and ρ\rho, both already stated at that temperature, so it is not used separately.
  • g=9.81g = 9.81 m/s² — standard constant, assumed; its uncertainty is negligible here (well under 0.1 %).

No property value, rule of thumb, or fitted relation other than the defining equation below and the constant gg is used. The defining equation is the standard NPSHa definition found in pump textbooks and in Hydraulic Institute standard ANSI/HI 9.6.1 (Rotodynamic Pumps — Guideline for NPSH Margin); that source is named here as the primary source for the definition and for margin practice, and any claim resting on its specific margin recommendations is unverified until checked against the current edition (see §7).

4.2 Calculation

NPSHa=p0−pvρg+(z0−zp)−hL\mathrm{NPSHa} = \frac{p_0 - p_{\mathrm{v}}}{\rho g} + (z_0 - z_{\mathrm{p}}) - h_L

Specific weight term (pressure corresponding to 1 m of this liquid):

ρg=650 kg/m3×9.81 m/s2=6376.5 Pa/m=6.377 kPa per m of liquid\rho g = 650\ \text{kg/m}^3 \times 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 6376.5\ \text{Pa/m} = 6.377\ \text{kPa per m of liquid}

Pressure-difference head:

p0−pvρg=101−80 kPa6.377 kPa/m=216.377=3.29 m\frac{p_0 - p_{\mathrm{v}}}{\rho g} = \frac{101 - 80\ \text{kPa}}{6.377\ \text{kPa/m}} = \frac{21}{6.377} = 3.29\ \text{m}

Total:

NPSHa=3.29 m+3 m−1 m=5.29 m≈5.3 m\mathrm{NPSHa} = 3.29\ \text{m} + 3\ \text{m} - 1\ \text{m} = 5.29\ \text{m} \approx 5.3\ \text{m}

Central result: NPSHa ≈ 5.3 m of liquid, on the stated inputs, absolute-pressure basis, pump-centreline datum.

Note the structure of the result: the pressure-difference term (3.29 m) is the difference of two large terms — the surface-pressure head is 101/6.377=15.84101/6.377 = 15.84 m and the vapour-pressure head is 80/6.377=12.5580/6.377 = 12.55 m. NPSHa is therefore a small remainder, and percentage errors in pvp_{\mathrm{v}} are amplified roughly sixfold in the pressure-difference term.

5. Range, not a single value (Prompt 1)
5.1 Sensitivity of the result to each guess and input

All figures computed with the equation in §4.2 (executed code, §6). Percentage changes are relative to the central value 5.29 m.
