Useful conversion for review: 1 kPa of pressure error = 0.157 m of NPSHa for this liquid (1/6.3771/6.377 m/kPa). Hence a vapour-pressure error of only 6.4 kPa moves NPSHa by a full metre.

The dominant guess is therefore the vapour pressure (equivalently, temperature and composition). A ±10 kPa band on pvp_{\mathrm{v}} is a plausible band for a light hydrocarbon whose exact composition and temperature control band are unspecified — for many light hydrocarbons vapour pressure changes by roughly 2–4 kPa per °C near 60 °C, so a ±3–5 °C temperature excursion alone produces a band of this size. That per-degree figure is a rule of thumb, estimated for light hydrocarbons in this range, unverified for this specific fluid; the primary source that settles it is a vapour-pressure measurement or a validated property databank entry (e.g. DIPPR / NIST ThermoData Engine) for the actual composition — see §7.

5.2 Reported range
  • Plausible operating range (one input varied at a time, bands in §5.1): approximately 3.7 m to 6.9 m, set by the vapour-pressure band.
  • Combined adverse case (p0=98p_0 = 98 kPa, estimated low-normal atmospheric; pv=90p_{\mathrm{v}} = 90 kPa; level 2.5 m; hL=1.5h_L = 1.5 m): NPSHa ≈ 2.25 m.
  • Combined favourable case (p0=102p_0 = 102 kPa; pv=70p_{\mathrm{v}} = 70 kPa; level 3.5 m; hL=0.5h_L = 0.5 m): NPSHa ≈ 8.02 m.

Result as reported: NPSHa = 5.3 m central; plausible range about 2.3 m to 8.0 m with combined extremes, and about 3.7 m to 6.9 m for single-input variation. For any design or adequacy decision the low end, not the central value, is the relevant figure, and it must be re-evaluated at low-low level, maximum temperature, and maximum flow together.

5.3 Alternative solved for the pressure-basis ambiguity (§3)

If — contrary to the assumption in §3 — the vessel pressure of 101 kPa were a mis-stated value and the vessel in fact sat at a lower absolute pressure, NPSHa falls by 0.157 m per kPa of shortfall (e.g. a vessel at 90 kPa absolute, as at altitude, gives 3.29−11×0.157+2=3.573.29 - 11 \times 0.157 + 2 = 3.57 m). If both pressures were (incorrectly) read as gauge, the difference is unchanged and the numerical answer is the same 5.29 m, because NPSHa depends only on p0−pvp_0 - p_{\mathrm{v}}; the basis matters only if the two pressures are on different bases, which would be an error of about ±15.9 m and would be visible at once as a non-physical result (negative or implausibly large NPSHa).

6. Independent verification (Prompt 3)

The solution was checked by routes independent of the main calculation. No check was used to adjust the solution; results are reported as found.

  1. Executed code. All numbers in §4, §5, and this section were computed in Python (not by hand arithmetic alone). Code result: ρg=6.3765\rho g = 6.3765 kPa/m; pressure-difference head 3.293 m; NPSHa = 5.293 m; combined adverse 2.255 m; combined favourable 8.018 m. Check passes — code and the hand calculation in §4.2 agree to the figures quoted.
  2. Independent route — inlet pressure. Compute the suction inlet pressure first, then the margin over vapour pressure. Static plus net elevation head: pin=p0+ρg [(z0−zp)−hL]=101+6.3765×(3−1)=113.75p_{\mathrm{in}} = p_0 + \rho g\,[(z_0-z_{\mathrm{p}}) - h_L] = 101 + 6.3765 \times (3-1) = 113.75 kPa absolute (computed). Margin over vapour pressure: 113.75−80=33.75113.75 - 80 = 33.75 kPa, i.e. 33.75/6.3765=5.2933.75/6.3765 = 5.29 m. Check passes — identical result by a separate algebraic route.
  3. Limiting case 1 — boiling at the surface. If pv=p0p_{\mathrm{v}} = p_0 (liquid at its boiling point in the vessel), NPSHa must reduce to static head minus loss =3−1=2.00= 3 - 1 = 2.00 m. Code gives 2.00 m. Check passes.
  4. Limiting case 2 — no static head, no loss. If z0−zp=0z_0 - z_{\mathrm{p}} = 0 and hL=0h_L = 0, NPSHa must equal the pressure-difference head alone, 3.29 m. Code gives 3.293 m. Check passes.
  5. Dimensional check. kPa divided by (kg/m³ × m/s²) gives (kN/m²)/(kN/m³) = m. All head terms are in m of the same liquid. Check passes.
  6. Balance closure. This is a mechanical-energy (head) balance, not a material or energy balance over a process; the head balance closes exactly by construction (terms sum: 15.84 m surface head + 3 m static − 1 m loss − 12.55 m vapour head = 5.29 m; residual 0.00 m). There is no material balance to close in a single-point suction calculation; stating otherwise would be a false check.
  7. Correlation / valid-range check. No fitted correlation is used, so there is no correlation range to violate. The one rule of thumb used (vapour-pressure temperature sensitivity, §5.1) is flagged estimated and unverified there.

Failed checks: none. The checks verify the arithmetic and the equation, not the inputs — the input risk in §5 stands regardless of these passes. Agreement with any other AI model was not used as verification and is not claimed.

7. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

Review as a plant design and operating engineer would. The three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. Vapour pressure in the actual liquid is higher than the stated value at times. Direction: NPSHa lower than calculated. Rough size: −0.157 m per +1 kPa; a temperature excursion of +5 °C, solar heating of an uninsulated suction line, or a lighter composition (more light ends after a feed change) can each add of the order of 10 kPa, i.e. about −1.6 m. A flashing-prone suction line with heat in-leak can lose more locally. Settling source: a vapour-pressure measurement on a sample of the actual liquid (e.g. Reid / true vapour pressure test, ASTM D6377 or equivalent) at the maximum operating temperature, or a validated DIPPR/NIST property calculation for the assayed composition — unverified for this fluid until obtained.
  2. Suction-line loss in the built line exceeds the stated 1 m at duty, and grows in service. Direction: NPSHa lower. Rough size: a fouled or partially blocked suction strainer alone commonly adds 0.5–2 m of loss; an undersized or extra-fitting line adds a similar order; loss rises with flow squared (+20 % flow → +44 % loss). Settling source: the as-built isometric with a line-loss calculation, plus a measured suction-pressure reading at duty flow on the installed pump (suction gauge reading versus level gives the true loss directly).
  3. The level used is not the level the pump will see. Direction: NPSHa lower at low level. Rough size: 1 m of NPSHa per 1 m of level, exactly; a normal-to-low-low level span of 1–2 m is common on a vessel, and vortexing / gas entrainment at low level can effectively remove more. Datum mismatch between vessel level tapping and pump impeller eye adds a further fixed error, typically 0.1–0.5 m. Settling source: the vessel drawing and level-instrument range (low-low trip level), and the pump vendor general-arrangement drawing showing the NPSH datum.

Primary sources that settle the open points, all unverified until checked: pump vendor NPSHr curve and datum drawing for the actual pump (vendor document); ANSI/HI 9.6.1 current edition for NPSH margin practice; a measured vapour pressure or DIPPR/NIST databank entry for the actual composition; as-built suction-line isometric and a field suction-pressure measurement.

8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • NPSHr and margin. Whether 5.3 m (or 2.3 m at the adverse end) is enough is not addressed and cannot be without the vendor NPSHr curve at the duty and runout flows, and a margin policy. Many light-hydrocarbon pumps have NPSHr of 2–5 m, so the adverse end of the range could be at or below NPSHr — this is a statement of typical magnitudes (estimated, unverified for any specific pump), not a finding about this pump.
  • Transient and two-phase effects: start-up, level sloshing, vortexing and entrained gas at low level, flashing in a sun-heated or long suction line, dissolved gas coming out of solution, and pressure surge — none is in a steady-state head balance.
  • Incipient cavitation versus NPSH3: damage and noise can begin at heads above the NPSH3 (3 % head-drop) value, particularly on continuous duty; a single NPSHa number does not address this.
  • Fluid change over time: composition drift, weathering, water content, and temperature excursions beyond 60 °C.
  • Mechanical state: strainer fouling, partially closed suction valve, impeller wear — all move the installed result away from the calculated one.

Information not accessible here: the vendor NPSHr curve and test record for the actual pump; the plant's level, temperature, and pressure operating records; the as-built piping isometric; any site margin standard held in a restricted company standard or code subscription.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 % (i.e. by more than about 0.53 m): vapour pressure up by more than 3.4 kPa (roughly a 1–2 °C temperature rise for a typical light hydrocarbon — estimated, unverified); level down by more than 0.53 m; suction loss up by more than 0.53 m (about +15 % in flow, or moderate strainer fouling); vessel pressure down by more than 3.4 kPa; or any combination of smaller changes in the same direction.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. What is the vendor NPSHr at duty and at runout flow, on what datum, and what margin policy applies to this service?
  2. Is the 3 m level the low-low operating level? If not, what is NPSHa at low-low level?
  3. Was the vapour pressure measured on the actual liquid, and at what maximum credible temperature and lightest credible composition?
  4. Does the 1 m loss come from an as-built calculation at maximum flow, and does it include the strainer (clean and fouled), entrance, and fittings?
  5. Are both pressures confirmed on an absolute basis, and is the vessel truly vented to atmosphere at all times (no vacuum/pressure control, no blanketing)?
  6. What does the installed suction gauge read at duty flow, and does it reproduce the calculated 113.8 kPa inlet pressure?
9. Result

NPSHa ≈ 5.3 m of liquid on the stated inputs (central value); plausible range about 3.7–6.9 m for single-input variation and about 2.3–8.0 m at combined extremes. Confidence: low to moderate (5/10) as a design value, limited by vapour pressure, level, and loss — not by the arithmetic, which was verified by executed code, an independent inlet-pressure route, and two limiting cases, with no failed checks. No adequacy judgement against cavitation is made, because pump NPSHr was not supplied.

D4. Compressor Work

Response without the skill

Shaft Work for Compression of Air from 1 bar to 10 bar

Given data and symbols
  • cpc_p = specific heat capacity at constant pressure, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)): cp=1.005 kJ/(kg⋅K)c_p = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}
  • kk = heat-capacity ratio, dimensionless: k=1.4k = 1.4
  • P1P_1 = inlet pressure, in bar: P1=1 barP_1 = 1\ \text{bar}
  • P2P_2 = outlet pressure, in bar: P2=10 barP_2 = 10\ \text{bar}
  • T1T_1 = inlet (absolute) temperature, in kelvin (K): T1=300 KT_1 = 300\ \text{K}
  • T2T_2 = outlet (absolute) temperature after compression, in kelvin (K), to be found
  • wsw_s = specific shaft work input, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg), to be found

The gas is treated as air, as an ideal gas with constant cpc_p and constant kk.

Assumptions
  1. Steady-flow, single-stage compression.
  2. The compression is adiabatic and reversible, i.e. isentropic. No efficiency is given, so the isentropic work is the standard estimate; a real machine would require more work.
  3. Changes in kinetic energy and potential energy are negligible.
  4. cpc_p and kk are constant over the temperature range.
Theory

For a steady-flow adiabatic compressor with negligible kinetic-energy and potential-energy changes, the steady-flow energy balance per unit mass gives the shaft work input equal to the enthalpy rise:

ws=h2−h1w_s = h_2 - h_1

where h1h_1 is the specific enthalpy at the inlet, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg), and h2h_2 is the specific enthalpy at the outlet, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).

For an ideal gas with constant cpc_p:

ws=cp (T2−T1)w_s = c_p\,(T_2 - T_1)

For a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) change of an ideal gas with constant kk, temperature and pressure are related by:

T2T1=(P2P1)(k−1)/k\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k}

Combining the two relations:

ws=cp T1[(P2P1)(k−1)/k−1]w_s = c_p\,T_1\left[\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} - 1\right]

Calculation

Pressure ratio, dimensionless:

P2P1=10 bar1 bar=10\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{10\ \text{bar}}{1\ \text{bar}} = 10

Exponent, dimensionless:

k−1k=1.4−11.4=0.41.4=0.2857\frac{k-1}{k} = \frac{1.4-1}{1.4} = \frac{0.4}{1.4} = 0.2857

Temperature factor, dimensionless:

(P2P1)(k−1)/k=100.2857=1.931\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = 10^{0.2857} = 1.931

Outlet temperature:

T2=T1×1.931=300 K×1.931=579 KT_2 = T_1 \times 1.931 = 300\ \text{K} \times 1.931 = 579\ \text{K}

Specific shaft work:

ws=cp T1[1.931−1]w_s = c_p\,T_1\left[1.931 - 1\right] ws=1.005 kJ/(kg⋅K)×300 K×0.931w_s = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)} \times 300\ \text{K} \times 0.931 ws=301.5 kJ/kg×0.931≈281 kJ/kgw_s = 301.5\ \text{kJ/kg} \times 0.931 \approx 281\ \text{kJ/kg}

Numerical check with the enthalpy form gives the same result:

ws=cp (T2−T1)=1.005 kJ/(kg⋅K)×(579−300) K≈1.005×279 kJ/kg≈281 kJ/kgw_s = c_p\,(T_2 - T_1) = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)} \times (579 - 300)\ \text{K} \approx 1.005 \times 279\ \text{kJ/kg} \approx 281\ \text{kJ/kg}

Result

The estimated (isentropic, single-stage) shaft work is approximately 281 kJ/kg, with an isentropic outlet temperature of approximately 579 K.

This is the ideal, reversible adiabatic value. A real compressor with an isentropic efficiency below 1 would require proportionally more work, ws,actual=ws/ηsw_{s,\text{actual}} = w_s / \eta_s, where ηs\eta_s is the isentropic efficiency, dimensionless, and ws,actualw_{s,\text{actual}} is the actual specific shaft work, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg). Intercooling or multistage compression would reduce the work toward the isothermal limit.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Shaft Work to Compress Air from 1 to 10 bar at 300 K

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. The arithmetic for an ideal, reversible, adiabatic (isentropic) compression is exact, but the problem as stated does not say that ideal compression is what is wanted. No compressor efficiency, no number of stages, no intercooling, no pressure basis (absolute or gauge), and no statement of whether the pressures are absolute is supplied. An actual machine needs substantially more work than the isentropic value, and a multi-stage intercooled machine needs substantially less than a single-stage actual machine. The dominant uncertainty is therefore the scenario, not the formula or the arithmetic.

Confidence rating. High for the isentropic value under the stated ideal model (the calculation is closed-form and was checked by an independent route, Section 6): approximately 95%. Low to moderate for the value as an estimate of work in built equipment: approximately 40–50%, because efficiency, staging, and pressure basis are all missing. No single value should be used for equipment sizing.

2. Symbols

Every symbol is defined here and at its first use in the text.

  • cpc_p: specific heat capacity at constant pressure, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)).
  • γ\gamma: heat-capacity ratio, cpc_p divided by the specific heat capacity at constant volume, dimensionless.
  • P1P_1: inlet pressure, in bar.
  • P2P_2: outlet pressure, in bar.
  • rpr_p: pressure ratio, P2P_2 divided by P1P_1, dimensionless.
  • T1T_1: inlet temperature, in kelvin (K).
  • T2,sT_{2,s}: outlet temperature after isentropic compression, in kelvin (K).
  • WsW_s: isentropic (ideal, reversible adiabatic) shaft work per unit mass, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • WW: actual shaft work per unit mass, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
  • ηs\eta_s: isentropic efficiency, WsW_s divided by WW, dimensionless.
  • RR: specific gas constant, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)).
  • hh: specific enthalpy, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).

Isentropic efficiency ηs\eta_s Converts ideal work to actual shaft work ηs\eta_s = 0.70, 0.80, and 0.85 (assumed, Section 4)
Number of stages and intercooling Intercooling lowers work toward the isothermal limit Single-stage (base case); two-, three-, and four-stage with perfect intercooling to T1T_1 for comparison
Pressure basis Gauge pressures change the true pressure ratio rpr_p (a) Both pressures absolute (base case); (b) both pressures gauge
Composition basis The gas is stated only as "treated as air" Dry air treated as an ideal gas with the given cpc_p and γ\gamma (given/assumed); humidity and composition variation not modelled
Reference state Needed only for tabulated enthalpy, not for a work difference Work is a difference of enthalpy, so the reference state cancels; no reference state is needed for WsW_s or WW
Basis of the result Work must be stated per unit of what Per kilogram of gas compressed (given by the requested unit, kJ/kg); no molar or volumetric basis is used
Per-pass or overall Not applicable to a single compression step Single pass assumed (assumed); no recycle is described
Mechanical and motor losses Shaft work at the coupling differs from electrical input Excluded; WW is work delivered to the gas divided by ηs\eta_s only. Electrical input would be higher
Inlet/outlet velocity and elevation Kinetic and potential energy terms in the steady-flow energy balance Assumed negligible (assumed), as is standard for a compressor estimate at this level
4. Inputs, labelled at the point of use (Prompt 1)
  • cpc_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) — given. Held constant in the base model (model assumption; see the check with temperature-dependent properties in Section 6).
  • γ\gamma = 1.4 — given. Held constant in the base model (model assumption; in real air γ\gamma falls as temperature rises).
  • P1P_1 = 1 bar — given; treated as absolute (assumed, see Section 3).
  • P2P_2 = 10 bar — given; treated as absolute (assumed, see Section 3).
  • T1T_1 = 300 K — given.
  • Gas treated as air, ideal gas — given as the treatment, with the ideal-gas model itself assumed.
  • ηs\eta_s = 0.70 to 0.85 — assumed / estimated. No value was given. The range is the range commonly encountered for industrial centrifugal and axial compressors in textbook and vendor practice. This claim rests on vendor performance data and on a compressor test code (Section 7) and is unverified against any specific machine.
  • RR = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) — estimated, derived in Section 6 from the given cpc_p and γ\gamma, and consistent with the standard value for dry air. Used only for the isothermal limiting-case check.
  • Number of stages = 1 — assumed for the base case.

Property values and relations used, with source and valid range:

  • Isentropic temperature relation for an ideal gas with constant cpc_p and γ\gamma: standard ideal-gas thermodynamics, valid where the ideal-gas assumption and constant properties hold — for air at 1–10 bar and 300–580 K the ideal-gas error is small (compressibility factor close to 1), and the constant-property error is quantified in Section 6 (about 0.2%).
  • ηs\eta_s range: rule-of-thumb range, not a fitted relation for any specific machine; it holds only as a screening range and must be replaced by vendor data for design (Section 7).
5. Solution
5.1 Isentropic (ideal) work — base case

Pressure ratio (with P1P_1 and P2P_2 as defined in Section 2):

rp=P2/P1=10/1=10r_p = P_2 / P_1 = 10 / 1 = 10

Isentropic outlet temperature T2,sT_{2,s}:

T2,s=T1 rp(γ−1)/γ=300×10(1.4−1)/1.4=300×100.2857=579.2 KT_{2,s} = T_1 \, r_p^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} = 300 \times 10^{(1.4 - 1)/1.4} = 300 \times 10^{0.2857} = 579.2\ \mathrm{K}

For a steady-flow adiabatic compressor with negligible kinetic and potential energy change, the shaft work per unit mass equals the enthalpy rise, hh being specific enthalpy as defined in Section 2. With constant cpc_p:

Ws=cp (T2,s−T1)=1.005×(579.2−300)=280.6 kJ/kgW_s = c_p \, (T_{2,s} - T_1) = 1.005 \times (579.2 - 300) = 280.6\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}

Isentropic shaft work: WsW_s ≈ 281 kJ/kg.

This is a lower bound for any single-stage adiabatic machine handling the same pressure ratio. It is not, by itself, an estimate of the work of a real compressor.

5.2 Actual single-stage work — range, not a single value

With W=Ws/ηsW = W_s / \eta_s:

ηs\eta_s (assumed) WW (kJ/kg) Increase over WsW_s
0.85 330 +18%
0.80 351 +25%
0.70 401 +43%

Actual single-stage shaft work: approximately 330 to 400 kJ/kg for ηs\eta_s from 0.85 down to 0.70, with 351 kJ/kg at the mid-range assumed value ηs\eta_s = 0.80. The corresponding actual outlet temperature at ηs\eta_s = 0.80 is T1+W/cpT_1 + W/c_p ≈ 300 + 349 = 649 K, which exceeds the discharge-temperature limits of many machines and is one practical reason large ratio duties are staged (Section 8).

5.3 Effect of staging with intercooling

For nn stages (where nn is the number of stages, dimensionless) of equal pressure ratio with perfect intercooling back to T1T_1 = 300 K, isentropic work is:

nn Isentropic WsW_s (kJ/kg) WW at ηs\eta_s = 0.80 (kJ/kg)
1 281 351
2 235 294
3 222 277
4 216 270

Staging and intercooling are therefore not a refinement: they move the result by about −16% (two stages) to −23% (four stages) relative to the single-stage isentropic value, before efficiency is applied.

5.4 Effect of the pressure-basis alternative

If both stated pressures were gauge rather than absolute (alternative (b) in Section 3), the absolute pressures would be approximately 2.013 bar and 11.013 bar (adding atmospheric pressure, approximately 1.013 bar, estimated), giving rpr_p ≈ 5.47 and:

Ws≈1.005×300×(5.470.2857−1)≈188 kJ/kgW_s \approx 1.005 \times 300 \times (5.47^{0.2857} - 1) \approx 188\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}

That is −33% relative to the base case. The pressure basis alone can move the answer by more than 10%; it must be confirmed before the result is used.

6. Verification by an independent route (Prompt 3)

All numbers were worked in executed code (Python), not by hand arithmetic alone. Checks:

  1. Consistency of the given properties. For an ideal gas, R=cp(γ−1)/γ=1.005×0.4/1.4=0.287R = c_p (\gamma - 1)/\gamma = 1.005 \times 0.4/1.4 = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). This matches the standard specific gas constant for dry air. Check passes. A failure here would have shown the given cpc_p and γ\gamma were mutually inconsistent.
  2. Temperature-dependent properties (independent databank route). Repeating the isentropic calculation with temperature-dependent air properties (CoolProp property library, used as a computational databank) gives T2,sT_{2,s} = 574.5 K and WsW_s = 280.2 kJ/kg. This differs from the constant-property value of 280.6 kJ/kg by about 0.2%. Check passes; the constant-cpc_p, constant-γ\gamma simplification is not a significant error source for this duty. The primary source that settles air properties definitively is the NIST reference databank (REFPROP / NIST WebBook); the CoolProp result is unverified against NIST REFPROP in this calculation.
  3. Limiting case — isothermal compression. The reversible isothermal work, $R \, T_1 \ln(r_p) = 0.287 \times 300 \times \ln(10)$ = 198 kJ/kg, is a known lower bound for any compression between the same pressures. The isentropic value (281 kJ/kg) and every staged value in Section 5.3 lie above it and approach it as the number of stages increases (281 → 235 → 222 → 216 kJ/kg). Check passes, in the correct order and direction.
  4. Limiting case — unit pressure ratio. At rpr_p = 1 the formula gives T2,sT_{2,s} = T1T_1 and WsW_s = 0, as required. Check passes.
  5. Energy balance closure. By construction of the steady-flow model, WsW_s equals the enthalpy rise cp(T2,s−T1)c_p (T_{2,s} - T_1) with heat transfer set to zero for the adiabatic ideal case; the balance closes exactly (0% out of balance) because the work was defined as that enthalpy rise. This is a definitional closure, not an independent measurement, and is reported as such.
  6. Failed or inapplicable checks. No check failed. No material balance applies beyond unit mass throughput (1 kg in, 1 kg out), which closes trivially. No fitted correlation was used, so no correlation valid-range check applies; the ηs\eta_s range in Section 5.2 is a screening range, not a correlation, and its limits are stated in Section 4.

No agreement with any other AI model is presented as verification. All checks above are algebraic, limiting-case, or databank checks.

7. Sensitivity: how much each guess moves the result (Prompt 1)

Reference: WsW_s = 281 kJ/kg (base case, Section 5.1).

Guess or assumption Plausible change Effect on result
Machine is ideal (no efficiency applied) vs. actual, ηs\eta_s = 0.85–0.70 Scenario change +18% to +43% (330–401 kJ/kg) — largest effect
Pressures are gauge, not absolute rpr_p 10 → 5.47 −33% (188 kJ/kg)
Single-stage vs. two-stage intercooled Scenario change −16% on isentropic work (235 kJ/kg)
γ\gamma constant at 1.4 vs. effective 1.36 with higher mean cpc_p (1.02 kJ/(kg·K)) over the temperature range Property model About −8% (≈257 kJ/kg) on a crude constant-property recalculation; the databank check (Section 6, item 2) shows the net variable-property effect is in fact only about −0.2%, because the cpc_p rise and γ\gamma fall largely cancel
cpc_p value itself, ±0.01 kJ/(kg·K) around 1.005 Given value, small uncertainty About ±1% (±3 kJ/kg)
T1T_1, ±10 K around 300 K Given value, if inlet condition varies About ±3.3% (±9 kJ/kg); WsW_s is proportional to T1T_1
Ideal-gas model at up to 10 bar Model assumption Small; databank check bounds the combined property-model effect at about 0.2%

Guesses ranked by consequence: (1) efficiency / whether the ideal value is even the quantity wanted; (2) pressure basis; (3) staging and intercooling; (4) inlet temperature if it is not controlled at 300 K. Property-model guesses are minor by comparison.

Primary sources that settle the open points:

  • Compressor efficiency and actual work for a specific duty: the vendor performance curve / vendor selection datasheet for the actual machine, and, for acceptance, a test under ASME PTC 10 (Performance Test Code on Compressors and Exhausters), current edition. Until one of these is consulted, every actual-work figure in Section 5.2 is unverified.
  • Air properties: NIST REFPROP / NIST Chemistry WebBook. The databank check in Section 6 is unverified against NIST.
  • Pressure basis: the plant instrument record or P&ID (piping and instrumentation diagram) notation for the stated pressures. Unverified; the values were taken as absolute by assumption.
8. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Efficiency is not a constant. Real ηs\eta_s varies with flow, inlet conditions, fouling, and operating point relative to the compressor map; off-design operation can fall well below 0.70. Direction: actual work higher than the mid-range estimate. Rough size: +10% to +30% on WW off-design. Settled by: the vendor performance map for the installed machine and plant operating records (measured flow, pressures, temperatures, and driver power).
  2. A single stage at a pressure ratio of 10 is generally not built. Discharge temperature (about 649 K at ηs\eta_s = 0.80, Section 5.2) and rotor-dynamic and pressure-rating limits lead to multi-stage machines with intercoolers, whose pressure drops and imperfect intercooling (approach to cooling-water temperature, not a return to exactly 300 K) add work back. Direction: staged ideal values in Section 5.3 are optimistic; real intercooled work sits between the staged and single-stage figures. Rough size: 5–15% above the perfect-intercooling staged values. Settled by: the vendor datasheet stating stage count, intercooler approach temperature, and intercooler pressure drop.
  3. Shaft work is not electrical input. Seal losses, bearing and gear losses, and motor efficiency intervene between work delivered to the gas and metered power. Direction: metered input higher. Rough size: typically +3% to +10%. Settled by: motor and drive vendor efficiency data and plant power metering.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • Temperature dependence of cpc_p and γ\gamma in the base formula (bounded at about 0.2% net by the check in Section 6).
  • Real-gas departure from ideal behaviour (small at these conditions, included in the databank check).
  • Intercooler pressure drop, imperfect intercooling, seal leakage, internal recirculation, fouling, surge and off-design operation.
  • Humidity in the inlet air and any condensation in intercoolers.
  • Mechanical, gear, and motor losses (Section 8, item 3).
  • Transient behaviour: start-up, surge control, and anti-surge recycle, all of which consume additional power in operation.

Information not accessible here:

  • Vendor-proprietary compressor maps and selection software, which hold the actual efficiency for any real machine.
  • Plant-restricted operating data for any specific installed unit.
  • The current-edition text of ASME PTC 10, which is a paid code.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%:

  • Any application of a realistic efficiency (changes the result by +18% or more, Section 5.2).
  • Pressures being gauge rather than absolute (−33%, Section 5.4).
  • Two or more stages with intercooling (−16% or more, Section 5.3).
  • Inlet temperature above about 330 K or below about 270 K (WsW_s is proportional to T1T_1).
  • Operation far from the design point of a real machine (Section 8).
10. Result and questions for a reviewer

Result, stated as ranges:

  • Isentropic (ideal, reversible adiabatic, single-stage) shaft work, pressures absolute: WsW_s ≈ 281 kJ/kg (280–281 kJ/kg across the constant-property and variable-property calculations). Outlet temperature T2,sT_{2,s} ≈ 575–579 K.
  • Actual single-stage shaft work, at the assumed ηs\eta_s range 0.70–0.85: approximately 330 to 400 kJ/kg (unverified — no vendor or test source consulted).
  • If the duty is staged with intercooling, or if the pressures are gauge, the applicable figure is materially lower (Sections 5.3 and 5.4); those alternatives give isentropic values of about 216–235 kJ/kg (staged, absolute) and about 188 kJ/kg (single-stage, gauge basis), before efficiency.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is the required quantity the ideal isentropic work or the work of a specified real machine?
  2. Are the 1 bar and 10 bar pressures absolute or gauge, and from which instrument or document do they come?
  3. What are the stage count, intercooling arrangement, and intercooler approach temperature?
  4. What efficiency, from which vendor curve or test, applies at the actual operating point — and is shaft work or electrical input required?
  5. Is the inlet temperature controlled at 300 K, and is the inlet air dry?
  6. What discharge-temperature limit applies, and does the selected configuration meet it?

D5. Solids Drying

Response without the skill

Batch Drying Time — Constant-Rate Estimate

Given data
  • msm_s = mass of dry solid, in kilograms (kg) = 100 kg100\ \mathrm{kg}
  • Δmw\Delta m_w = mass of water to be removed, in kilograms (kg) = 25 kg25\ \mathrm{kg}
  • AA = drying area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}) = 10 m210\ \mathrm{m^2}
  • NcN_c = constant-rate drying flux, in kilograms of water per square metre per hour (kg/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{kg/(m^2\cdot h)}) = 1.0 kg/(m2⋅h)1.0\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2\cdot h)}

No critical moisture content, equilibrium moisture content, initial moisture content, final moisture content, or falling-rate curve is given.

Definitions
  • XX = moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg\mathrm{kg/kg} dry solid), defined as the mass of water present divided by msm_s.
  • ΔX\Delta X = decrease in XX during drying, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg\mathrm{kg/kg} dry solid).
  • RcR_c = constant-rate mass drying rate, in kilograms of water per hour (kg/h\mathrm{kg/h}).
  • tct_c = time spent in the constant-rate period, in hours (h\mathrm{h}).
  • tt = total batch drying time, in hours (h\mathrm{h}).

From the definition of XX:

ΔX=Δmwms\Delta X = \frac{\Delta m_w}{m_s}

Calculation

Decrease in moisture content:

ΔX=25 kg100 kg=0.25 kg/kg dry solid\Delta X = \frac{25\ \mathrm{kg}}{100\ \mathrm{kg}} = 0.25\ \mathrm{kg/kg}\ \text{dry solid}

Constant-rate mass drying rate, obtained from the definition of a flux as a mass rate per unit area:

Rc=NcA=(1.0 kgm2⋅h)(10 m2)=10 kg/hR_c = N_c A = \left(1.0\ \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m^2\cdot h}}\right)(10\ \mathrm{m^2}) = 10\ \mathrm{kg/h}

Time to remove Δmw\Delta m_w at the constant rate RcR_c:

tc=ΔmwRc=ΔmwNcA=25 kg10 kg/h=2.5 ht_c = \frac{\Delta m_w}{R_c} = \frac{\Delta m_w}{N_c A} = \frac{25\ \mathrm{kg}}{10\ \mathrm{kg/h}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}

Equivalently, in dry-basis form:

tc=msANc ΔX=10010×1.0×0.25=2.5 ht_c = \frac{m_s}{A N_c}\,\Delta X = \frac{100}{10 \times 1.0} \times 0.25 = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}

Unit check: kg/(kg/h)=h\mathrm{kg} / (\mathrm{kg/h}) = \mathrm{h}, as required for a time.

Result

t≈tc=2.5 ht \approx t_c = 2.5\ \mathrm{h}

under the assumption stated below.

Assumptions and scope
  1. All 25 kg25\ \mathrm{kg} of water is removed in the constant-rate period. The solid surface remains saturated throughout, so the flux remains NcN_c for the whole batch.
  2. Drying conditions, and therefore NcN_c, remain constant, and AA does not change (no shrinkage or change in exposed area).
  3. Heat-up and cool-down times are negligible, and no water is removed in a falling-rate period.

The stated data are sufficient only for the constant-rate calculation. If the final moisture content lies below the critical moisture content, part of the water would be removed in the falling-rate period at a flux below NcN_c, and the actual total time would exceed 2.5 h2.5\ \mathrm{h}. In that case 2.5 h2.5\ \mathrm{h} is a lower bound, and a quantitative correction would require the critical moisture content, the equilibrium moisture content, and the falling-rate curve, none of which is given. Subject to that limitation, the estimated batch drying time is 2.52.5 hours.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Batch drying time — estimate

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is trivial, but the model is not established by the data. The problem supplies only a constant-rate flux. A real batch normally dries at the constant rate only while the surface stays wet, then at a falling rate. Whether any of the 25 kg is removed in the falling-rate period depends on moisture contents that are not supplied. The single value obtained from the supplied flux is therefore a lower bound, not a prediction of elapsed batch time.

Confidence. - In the arithmetic, given the stated inputs and the constant-rate-only assumption: high. - In 2.5 h as the time a real batch will take: low. The missing falling-rate information can change the result by tens of percent, and by more if the final moisture content approaches the equilibrium moisture content.

No agreement with any other model or source is used as verification in this solution.

2. Symbols, defined before first use
  • LSL_S is the mass of dry (bone-dry) solid, in kilograms (kg).
  • ΔW\Delta W is the mass of water to be removed, in kilograms (kg).
  • AA is the exposed drying area, in square metres (m²).
  • NcN_c is the constant-rate drying flux, in kilograms of water per square metre per hour (kg/(m²·h)).
  • tt is the drying time, in hours (h).
  • XX is the moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg).
  • XiX_i is XX at the start, XfX_f is XX at the end, XcX_c is the critical moisture content at which the falling-rate period begins, and XeX_e is the equilibrium moisture content under the drying air conditions, all in kilograms per kilogram (kg/kg).
3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — fill the gaps first)

The solution needs the following, none of which is supplied. No value is taken in silence; the calculation in §4 is solved under the stated alternative in the last column.

Missing quantity Why it is needed Treatment here
Initial moisture content XiX_i and final moisture content XfX_f Only their difference is fixed by the data: Xi−Xf=ΔW/LS=0.25X_i-X_f=\Delta W/L_S=0.25 kg/kg. The position of that interval relative to XcX_c decides how much drying is in the falling-rate period. Solved under four alternatives in §5, from all-constant-rate to mostly falling-rate.
Critical moisture content XcX_c Marks the end of the constant-rate period. Material-specific; depends on solid structure, particle or slab size, and bed depth. Assumed (labelled as such) in the scenarios in §5.
Equilibrium moisture content XeX_e Sets the lower limit of XfX_f and the end of the falling-rate curve. Depends on air humidity and temperature and on the solid's sorption isotherm. Assumed (labelled as such) in the scenarios in §5.
Falling-rate curve (flux as a function of XX below XcX_c) Needed for any time spent below XcX_c. A linear fall from NcN_c at XcX_c to zero at XeX_e is assumed for the illustrative scenarios only; it is a common first approximation, not a property of this solid.
Basis of the stated area AA Whether AA is tray area, exposed surface area, or total particle area changes the meaning of NcN_c; the two must be on the same basis. Assumed: AA and NcN_c are on the same basis, and AA stays constant (no shrinkage).
Air conditions and pressure basis Air temperature, humidity, velocity, and total pressure set NcN_c and XeX_e. No pressure, temperature, or humidity is supplied. Assumed: conditions stay constant through the batch, so a single NcN_c applies throughout the constant-rate period. Pressure basis is not needed for the constant-rate arithmetic, but is needed to reproduce NcN_c or XeX_e from any correlation.
Source and status of NcN_c A flux measured on this solid in this dryer behaves differently from a generic value. Treated as given (see §4); a ±20 % sensitivity is shown in §5 because no measurement basis is stated.
Composition basis The volatile is stated to be water only. If other volatiles are present, ΔW\Delta W and the flux are not water-only quantities. Assumed: water is the only volatile removed.
Per-pass or overall Not applicable to a single batch in the recycle sense; the relevant distinction is batch-total versus constant-rate-period-only removal. ΔW\Delta W is taken as the batch total to be removed.

Primary source that settles the point (unverified until checked against it). A measured drying curve — mass versus time, or flux versus XX — for the actual solid, at the actual bed depth, particle size, and air temperature, humidity, and velocity, in the actual or a pilot dryer of the same type. That measurement gives XcX_c, XeX_e, and the falling-rate curve directly. Textbook treatments (for example the drying chapters in Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook and in Geankopolis, Transport Processes and Separation Process Principles) give the rate-period equations used here, but they do not supply this solid's XcX_c or falling-rate curve. Any claim resting on those texts for material-specific values is unverified until checked against a measurement on the actual material.

4. Constant-rate calculation (Prompt 1)

Inputs at the point of use:

  • LS=100L_S = 100 kg — given. Note: LSL_S is not actually needed for the constant-rate time, only to express ΔW\Delta W on a dry basis (Xi−Xf=0.25X_i-X_f = 0.25 kg/kg); it is needed for the falling-rate scenarios.
  • ΔW=25\Delta W = 25 kg — given.
  • A=10A = 10 m² — given; constancy during drying is assumed.
  • Nc=1.0N_c = 1.0 kg/(m²·h) — given; whether it was measured, fitted, or estimated is not stated, so its uncertainty is not known from the problem.

Water removal rate in the constant-rate period:

NcA=1.0 kg/(m²⋅h)×10 m²=10 kg/hN_c A = 1.0\ \text{kg/(m²·h)} \times 10\ \text{m²} = 10\ \text{kg/h}

Time if all 25 kg is removed at that rate:

t=ΔWNcA=25 kg10 kg/h=2.5 ht = \frac{\Delta W}{N_c A} = \frac{25\ \text{kg}}{10\ \text{kg/h}} = 2.5\ \text{h}

Result, constant-rate only: t=2.5t = 2.5 h. This is a lower bound on batch time, because any falling-rate portion removes water at less than NcN_c and therefore takes longer per kilogram.

5. Range, not a single value (Prompts 1 and 2)
5.1 Sensitivity to the flux

NcN_c is the only rate input. The time varies inversely with it. The ±20 % band below is an assumed sensitivity band (a round allowance for an unstated measurement basis), not a supplied tolerance:

Each guess and its effect: a 10 % error in NcN_c moves tt by about 10 % in the opposite direction; a 10 % error in AA does the same; a 10 % error in ΔW\Delta W moves tt by 10 % in the same direction. These follow from t=ΔW/(NcA)t=\Delta W/(N_cA) and were confirmed in the executed code in §6.

5.2 Falling-rate scenarios

For a linear falling-rate curve, the falling-rate time from XcX_c to XfX_f is

tfall=LSA Xc−XeNc ln⁡ ⁣(Xc−XeXf−Xe)t_{\text{fall}} = \frac{L_S}{A}\,\frac{X_c-X_e}{N_c}\,\ln\!\left(\frac{X_c-X_e}{X_f-X_e}\right)

with all symbols as defined in §2. This relation and the constant-rate relation are the standard rate-period equations; their valid range is Xf≥XcX_f \ge X_c for the constant-rate equation alone, and Xe<Xf<XcX_e < X_f < X_c for the falling-rate equation with a linear falling-rate curve assumed.

Four alternatives, each removing exactly ΔW=25\Delta W = 25 kg (Xi−Xf=0.25X_i-X_f = 0.25 kg/kg). All values of XiX_i, XfX_f, XcX_c, and XeX_e in this table are assumed for illustration; none is given, measured, or fitted:

  • Lower bound (supplied data only, constant-rate throughout): 2.5 h.
  • Plausible range from the scenarios and flux sensitivity above: about 2.1 h to about 4.4 h, the low end requiring a flux 20 % above the stated value with no falling-rate portion, the high end corresponding to scenario D at the stated flux.

Only a measured drying curve for the actual solid closes this range.
6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were worked in executed Python code, separate from the hand arithmetic. Results:

  1. Balance closure. Removal rate × time =10 kg/h×2.5 h=25= 10\ \text{kg/h} \times 2.5\ \text{h} = 25 kg =ΔW= \Delta W. Closure error: 0 kg. In each scenario in §5.2, (Xi−Xf)LS=0.25×100=25(X_i-X_f)L_S = 0.25 \times 100 = 25 kg, checked by assertion in the code. Pass.
  2. Code versus hand calculation. Code gives t=2.500t = 2.500 h for the constant-rate case, scenario totals 3.079 h, 3.291 h, and 4.385 h for scenarios B, C, and D, matching §5.2 to the rounding shown. Pass.
  3. Limiting cases. (a) ΔW→0\Delta W \to 0 gives t→0t \to 0: correct by inspection of t=ΔW/(NcA)t=\Delta W/(N_cA). (b) Nc→∞N_c \to \infty gives t→0t \to 0, and AA doubled halves tt: correct for a surface-evaporation-limited period. (c) Xf→XeX_f \to X_e in the falling-rate equation gives tfall→∞t_{\text{fall}} \to \infty: correct behaviour — equilibrium moisture cannot be removed by that air. Pass.
  4. Correlation / model valid range. The constant-rate equation holds only for X≥XcX \ge X_c. The problem does not state that Xf≥XcX_f \ge X_c, so applying it to the whole 25 kg is outside its established range for this batch — this check fails as a justification for 2.5 h as a prediction, which is why 2.5 h is reported as a lower bound only. The linear falling-rate curve is an assumption, not a fitted relation for this solid; its range cannot be checked without data. Reported as failed / not checkable; the solution was not altered to make it pass.
7. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from how a built dryer behaves:

  1. Falling-rate behaviour and internal moisture transport. Direction: real time is longer than 2.5 h. Rough size: +25 % to +75 % in the scenarios above, more for a thick bed, large particles, or a low final moisture target, where diffusion inside the solid controls. Settled by: a pilot or plant drying test on the actual material recording mass versus time to the target final moisture content.
  2. Effective area and bed uniformity. In a tray or bed dryer, channelling, uneven loading, and shrinkage or crusting reduce the effectively wetted area below the nominal 10 m², and local areas reach XcX_c at different times. Direction: real time is longer. Rough size: a 10–30 % loss of effective area adds about 11–43 % to the constant-rate time alone (from t∝1/At \propto 1/A). Settled by: the dryer's loading and airflow records, tray-by-tray final moisture sampling, and the vendor's rated capacity for the actual duty.
  3. Drift of air conditions and heat supply during the batch. NcN_c holds only if inlet air temperature, humidity, and velocity and the heat input hold. Recirculation raises humidity as the batch proceeds, and a heat-supply limit can make the process heat-transfer-limited rather than at the stated flux. Direction: real time is longer (flux falls); a falling flux of 20 % adds 25 % to the time. Settled by: logged inlet and outlet air temperature and humidity over a batch, and the heater or steam supply rating in the equipment data sheet.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: falling-rate and internal diffusion resistance; shrinkage, cracking, crusting (case hardening), and agglomeration; bed channelling and non-uniform initial moisture; warm-up and cool-down time; loading, unloading, and turnaround time, which are part of plant cycle time but not of drying time; product quality limits (maximum solid temperature, overdrying); dusting and solids losses.
  • Information not available here: the solid's identity, sorption isotherm, and XcX_c; the dryer type and its vendor rating; measured air conditions. These are held in plant records, vendor documents, and databanks that this calculation does not access, and the material-specific values are marked unverified in §3.
  • Effects that appear only in running equipment: fouling of trays and air passages, fan performance drift, seasonal inlet-air humidity, and operator loading practice.
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10 %: any part of the removal occurring below XcX_c (about +23 % already in scenario B); NcN_c or effective AA differing from the stated values by more than about 10 %; a final moisture target within roughly 0.05 kg/kg of XeX_e; inlet-air humidity high enough to raise XeX_e materially during the batch.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What are XiX_i and XfX_f, and what is the measured XcX_c for this solid at this bed depth?
  2. Was Nc=1.0N_c = 1.0 kg/(m²·h) measured on this solid in this dryer, and at what air temperature, humidity, and velocity — and is A=10A = 10 m² on the same basis as NcN_c?
  3. Is there a measured drying curve, and what total batch time does it give to the target XfX_f?
  4. Does the schedule need drying time only, or full cycle time including loading, warm-up, and unloading?
  5. What final-moisture specification and tolerance must the batch meet, and how close is that specification to XeX_e under worst-case (most humid) inlet air?
9. Answer in brief

At the stated constant-rate flux over the stated area, water is removed at 10 kg/h, so the 25 kg takes 2.5 h if the whole removal occurs in the constant-rate period. That figure is a lower bound. With the falling-rate behaviour and flux uncertainty that the supplied data leave open, a plausible range is about 2.1 h to about 4.4 h, unbounded above if the target final moisture content approaches equilibrium. A measured drying curve on the actual solid is the source that settles the value.

D6. Compressible-Cake Filtration

Response without the skill

Filtration Time at Constant Pressure Difference

Problem

Estimate the time required to obtain a specified filtrate volume under a constant pressure difference through a filter of specified area.

Symbols and Given Data

Each symbol is defined at its first appearance, with its value and SI units.

  • VV is the filtrate volume, in cubic metres (m³): V=1 m3V = 1\ \text{m}^{3}
  • tt is the filtration time, in seconds (s): the quantity to be estimated
  • ΔP\Delta P is the constant pressure difference across the filter cake and filter medium, in pascals (Pa): ΔP=200 kPa=200×103 Pa=2.00×105 Pa\Delta P = 200\ \text{kPa} = 200 \times 10^{3}\ \text{Pa} = 2.00 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}
  • AA is the filter area, in square metres (m²): A=2 m2A = 2\ \text{m}^{2}
  • μ\mu is the filtrate viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa·s): μ=0.001 Pa⋅s\mu = 0.001\ \text{Pa·s}
  • cc is the mass of dry cake solids deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³): c=50 kg/m3c = 50\ \text{kg/m}^{3}
  • α\alpha is the specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg): α=3×1011 m/kg\alpha = 3 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m/kg}

No value is given for the filter-medium resistance. The estimate therefore neglects the filter-medium resistance relative to the cake resistance. The cake is also treated as incompressible, so that α\alpha is constant at the stated ΔP\Delta P.

Governing Equation

For filtration at constant ΔP\Delta P, flow through the deposited cake follows Darcy's law applied to a cake whose thickness, and therefore whose resistance, grows in proportion to VV. Integration from zero filtrate volume to VV, with the filter-medium resistance neglected, gives the standard constant-pressure filtration relation:

tV=μαc2A2ΔP V\frac{t}{V} = \frac{\mu \alpha c}{2 A^{2} \Delta P} \, V

where every symbol in the equation has been defined above. Rearranged for tt:

t=μαcV22A2ΔPt = \frac{\mu \alpha c V^{2}}{2 A^{2} \Delta P}

The V2V^{2} dependence is physical: doubling VV doubles the volume that must pass and also doubles the cake thickness through which it must pass.

Calculation

Substitution of the given values:

t=(0.001 Pa⋅s)(3×1011 m/kg)(50 kg/m3)(1 m3)22 (2 m2)2 (2.00×105 Pa)t = \frac{(0.001\ \text{Pa·s})(3 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m/kg})(50\ \text{kg/m}^{3})(1\ \text{m}^{3})^{2}}{2\,(2\ \text{m}^{2})^{2}\,(2.00 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa})}

Numerator:

(0.001)(3×1011)(50)(1)=1.5×1010(0.001)(3 \times 10^{11})(50)(1) = 1.5 \times 10^{10}

Denominator:

2×4×2.00×105=1.6×1062 \times 4 \times 2.00 \times 10^{5} = 1.6 \times 10^{6}

Therefore:

t=1.5×10101.6×106=9375 st = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{10}}{1.6 \times 10^{6}} = 9375\ \text{s}

Unit check: the combination μαcV2/(A2ΔP)\mu \alpha c V^{2} / (A^{2} \Delta P) reduces to (Pa⋅s)(m/kg)(kg/m3)(m6)/[(m4)(Pa)]=s(\text{Pa·s})(\text{m/kg})(\text{kg/m}^{3})(\text{m}^{6}) / [(\text{m}^{4})(\text{Pa})] = \text{s}, as required for a time.

Conversion:

t=9375 s60 s/min=156.25 min≈2.60 ht = \frac{9375\ \text{s}}{60\ \text{s/min}} = 156.25\ \text{min} \approx 2.60\ \text{h}

Result

The estimated time to obtain 1 m31\ \text{m}^{3} of filtrate is approximately 9.4×103 s9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{s}, i.e. about 156 min156\ \text{min} or 2.6 h2.6\ \text{h}.

This is a lower bound if the filter-medium resistance is not in fact negligible: inclusion of a non-zero filter-medium resistance would add a positive term proportional to VV and would increase tt.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Constant-Pressure Cake Filtration — Time for 1 m³ of Filtrate

Symbols

All symbols are defined here, at first use.

  • tt — filtration time, in seconds (s), with hours (h) also reported
  • VV — cumulative filtrate volume, in cubic metres (m³)
  • ΔP\Delta P — pressure difference across cake and filter medium, in pascals (Pa); 1 kPa=1000 Pa1\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1000\ \mathrm{Pa}
  • AA — filtration area, in square metres (m²)
  • μ\mu — filtrate viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa·s)
  • cc — dry cake mass deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³)
  • α\alpha — specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg)
  • RmR_{\mathrm{m}} — filter medium resistance, in reciprocal metres (m⁻¹)
  • mcakem_{\mathrm{cake}} — total dry cake mass deposited, in kilograms (kg)
  • scs_{\mathrm{c}} — cake compressibility exponent, dimensionless
Weakness and Confidence Rating

Weakness: the result is controlled by α\alpha, a fitted cake property, and by RmR_{\mathrm{m}}, which is not supplied at all. α\alpha in practice is obtained from a laboratory filtration test on a particular slurry, at a particular ΔP\Delta P, with a particular medium and slurry preparation. Its transfer to another pressure, medium, or batch is the main source of error. The integrated equation itself is standard and its arithmetic is checkable exactly; the applicability of the supplied α\alpha to the case in question is not checkable from the data given.

Confidence ratings:

  • Arithmetic and integration, given the stated inputs and the stated model: high.
  • Base-case time as a calculation from the stated inputs: high.
  • Time predicted for built equipment: low to moderate. The missing RmR_{\mathrm{m}}, the missing reference pressure for α\alpha, and the missing compressibility behaviour can each move the result by more than 10 percent, as quantified below.

No agreement with any other model or AI system is used as verification in this solution. Verification is by dimensional check, limiting cases, numerical integration in code, and a mass balance, in §6.

Primary source that settles the central point: a constant-pressure laboratory filtration test on the actual slurry, at ΔP=200\Delta P = 200 kPa, with the actual filter medium, recording tt against VV. In such a test a plot of t/Vt/V against VV has a slope that gives α\alpha and an intercept that gives RmR_{\mathrm{m}}. No such test record was supplied. Every claim in this solution that rests on the supplied α\alpha applying at 200 kPa, and on RmR_{\mathrm{m}} being negligible, is therefore unverified until checked against that test record. Vendor data for the medium and the plant filtration record for a comparable batch are the corresponding sources for RmR_{\mathrm{m}} and for cycle behaviour.

Relations used, with source and range of validity:

  • Cake filtration rate equation and its constant-pressure integral, §3: the standard Darcy-law treatment of cake filtration as given in standard chemical engineering texts on filtration (for example the filtration chapters of Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook and of Richardson and Harker, Chemical Engineering, Volume 2). It holds for flow through a growing cake where α\alpha, cc, and μ\mu are constant during the run, the cake is formed uniformly, and no sedimentation, cake cracking, or pore blocking dominates. Those conditions are assumptions here, not verified facts.
  • Compressibility relation α\alpha proportional to ΔP\Delta P raised to the power scs_{\mathrm{c}}: same standard sources; used only as a scenario form in §5 and §7, with no numerical scs_{\mathrm{c}} asserted.
  • No rule of thumb, no empirical constant, and no property correlation is used. Every property value in the calculation is a given input in the table above.
3. Governing Equation

For cake filtration, Darcy's law applied to the cake and the medium in series gives the instantaneous rate:

dVdt=A ΔPμ(αcV/A+Rm)\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{A\,\Delta P}{\mu\left(\alpha c V / A + R_{\mathrm{m}}\right)}

where dV/dtdV/dt is the volumetric filtrate rate in cubic metres per second (m³/s), αcV/A\alpha c V / A is the cake resistance in reciprocal metres (m⁻¹), and all other symbols are as defined above.

At constant ΔP\Delta P, with μ\mu, α\alpha, and cc constant, integration from V=0V = 0 at t=0t = 0 to VV at tt gives:

t=μ α c2A2 ΔP V2+μ RmA ΔP Vt = \frac{\mu\,\alpha\,c}{2 A^{2}\,\Delta P}\,V^{2} + \frac{\mu\,R_{\mathrm{m}}}{A\,\Delta P}\,V

The first term is the cake term, quadratic in VV. The second term is the medium term, linear in VV.

Denominator: 2×4×2.00×105=1.6×1062 \times 4 \times 2.00\times10^{5} = 1.6\times10^{6} Pa.

t=1.5×10101.6×106=9375 s=2.60 ht = \frac{1.5\times10^{10}}{1.6\times10^{6}} = 9375\ \mathrm{s} = 2.60\ \mathrm{h}

Base-case result: t=9375t = 9375 s, i.e. about 2.6 h, for the cake term alone. This is a single value only for the base case with RmR_{\mathrm{m}} assumed zero. The reportable result is the range in §5.

7. Audit Against Built Equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves, in the judgement of plant design and operating experience:

  1. Filter medium resistance and blinding. Direction: actual tt longer than the base case. Rough size: +3 percent at Rm=1×1011R_{\mathrm{m}} = 1\times10^{11} m⁻¹, +27 percent at 1×10121\times10^{12} m⁻¹, and growing over successive cycles as the medium blinds, which the constant-RmR_{\mathrm{m}} model does not represent at all. Settling document or test: the intercept of a constant-pressure test on the actual slurry and medium (named in §1), and the plant record of filtration time against cycle number for the actual filter.
  2. Cake compressibility and pressure dependence of α\alpha. Direction: if the cake is compressible and α\alpha was fitted below 200 kPa, actual α\alpha at 200 kPa is higher, so actual tt is longer; if α\alpha was fitted above 200 kPa, the reverse. Rough size: unbounded from the given data; a factor of 2 in α\alpha is a factor of 2 in tt (§5.4 scenario). Settling document or test: filtration tests on the actual slurry at two or more pressures spanning 200 kPa, from which α\alpha against ΔP\Delta P and hence scs_{\mathrm{c}} are obtained.
  3. Non-uniform cake formation, sedimentation, and start-up. Direction: actual tt longer, because settling of coarse or dense solids, uneven slurry distribution, and the pressure ramp while the filter fills all depart from the uniform-cake, constant-ΔP\Delta P-from-zero model. Rough size: not computable from the given data; the area sensitivity in §5.1 bounds one part of it — maldistribution equivalent to a 10 percent loss of effective area adds 23.5 percent to the cake term. Settling document or record: the operating record of the actual filter (filtrate volume against time for a production batch), which shows the ramp and any departure from the V2V^{2} law directly.
8. What Is Not Covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • Cake washing, air blowing or cake drying, cake discharge, cloth washing, and filter filling: the result is filtration time only, not cycle time. Total cycle time on built equipment exceeds tt, by amounts not supplied.
  • Sedimentation in the feed, particle size distribution effects, flocculation or its breakdown under pumping, and slurry ageing: all act through α\alpha and cc and are invisible in the model once those two values are fixed.
  • Cake cracking, cake slumping, and bypassing, which shorten tt while degrading filtrate clarity; filtrate quality is not modelled at all.
  • Pore blocking of the medium as a mechanism distinct from a constant RmR_{\mathrm{m}}.
  • Temperature drift during the run acting through μ\mu; pump and piping behaviour if the stated constant ΔP\Delta P is not in fact held.

Information not available to this calculation: the laboratory test record behind α\alpha (restricted to whoever ran the test), the medium vendor's resistance data for the actual medium, and any plant operating record for the actual filter. Each is named in §1 and §7 as the source that would settle the corresponding point; none was supplied, and claims depending on them are marked unverified above.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: progressive medium blinding over cycles, cloth wear, maldistribution from worn feed ports, operator variation in cycle start and end points, and slurry variability between batches.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 percent:

  • α\alpha differs from 3×10113\times10^{11} m/kg by more than 10 percent, from any cause in §7.
  • RmR_{\mathrm{m}} exceeds about 3.8×10113.8\times10^{11} m⁻¹ (the value at which the medium term reaches 10 percent of the base cake term, from §5.3).
  • μ\mu or cc differs by more than 10 percent, for example through temperature or feed solids variation.
  • ΔP\Delta P falls by more than about 9 percent from 200 kPa.
  • Effective AA falls by more than about 5 percent (1/0.952=1.1081/0.95^{2} = 1.108).

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. On what slurry, at what ΔP\Delta P, and with what medium was α=3×1011\alpha = 3\times10^{11} m/kg measured, and is there a test record?
  2. What is RmR_{\mathrm{m}} for the actual medium, new and after repeated cycles?
  3. Is the cake compressible, and what are α\alpha against ΔP\Delta P and scs_{\mathrm{c}} for the actual slurry?
  4. Is c=50c = 50 kg/m³ dry cake per filtrate volume, and was it measured on the actual feed?
  5. Is the required time filtration time only, or full cycle time including filling, washing, discharge, and cleaning?
  6. At what temperature is μ=0.001\mu = 0.001 Pa·s, and what temperature will the filter run at?
  7. Is ΔP=200\Delta P = 200 kPa held for the whole run, and what do the pump and control system actually deliver during filling?
Answer

Base case, with Rm=0R_{\mathrm{m}} = 0 m⁻¹ assumed and cake compressibility neglected: t=9375t = 9375 s =2.60= 2.60 h.

Reportable result, allowing for the precision of α\alpha as quoted and a medium term up to Rm=1×1011R_{\mathrm{m}} = 1\times10^{11} m⁻¹: tt from about 7.8×1037.8\times10^{3} s to 1.12×1041.12\times10^{4} s, i.e. about 2.2 h to 3.1 h. Under the wider fitted-α\alpha transfer scenario of §5.4 (factor 0.5 to 2 in α\alpha), the cake term alone spans 1.30 h to 5.21 h. Prediction for built equipment carries low to moderate confidence until the filtration test record named in §1 is checked.

E1. Relief Sizing

Response without the skill

Relief Orifice Sizing

Symbols and given values
  • WW, the required relieving mass flow rate, in kilograms per second (kg/s\mathrm{kg/s}): W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \mathrm{kg/s}.
  • GG, the vapour mass flux through the orifice, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m2⋅s)\mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}): G=1200 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 1200\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}.
  • AA, the required orifice flow area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}).
  • dd, the diameter of a circular orifice of area AA, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • π\pi, the ratio of a circle circumference to its diameter, dimensionless: π≈3.1416\pi \approx 3.1416.

The relieving fluid is treated as vapour only, as stated. The value of GG is the mass flux at the orifice, so the required area follows directly from the mass balance at the orifice. No separate discharge coefficient is applied, because any such effect is contained in the stated value of GG.

Required area

By definition of mass flux, the mass flow rate is the product of the mass flux and the flow area:

W=GAW = G A

Rearrangement for the unknown area AA gives:

A=WGA = \frac{W}{G}

Substitution of the given values gives:

A=2 kg/s1200 kg/(m2⋅s)=1.667×10−3 m2A = \frac{2\ \mathrm{kg/s}}{1200\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}} = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}

Unit check: (kg/s)÷(kg/(m2⋅s))=m2(\mathrm{kg/s}) \div (\mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}) = \mathrm{m^2}, as required for an area.

In other units:

A=1.667×10−3 m2=16.67 cm2=1667 mm2=2.58 in2A = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2} = 16.67\ \mathrm{cm^2} = 1667\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 2.58\ \mathrm{in^2}

Equivalent circular diameter

For a circular orifice, the area AA and the diameter dd are related by:

A=πd24A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}

Rearrangement for dd gives:

d=4Aπd = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}}

Substitution of A=1.667×10−3 m2A = 1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2} gives:

d=4(1.667×10−3 m2)π=0.0461 md = \sqrt{\frac{4(1.667 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2})}{\pi}} = 0.0461\ \mathrm{m}

That is:

d=46.1 mm=1.81 ind = 46.1\ \mathrm{mm} = 1.81\ \mathrm{in}

  • AstdA_{\mathrm{std}}, the flow area of a selected standard orifice, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}).
  • WstdW_{\mathrm{std}}, the relieving capacity of the selected standard orifice at the stated mass flux GG, in kilograms per second (kg/s\mathrm{kg/s}), calculated as Wstd=GAstdW_{\mathrm{std}} = G A_{\mathrm{std}}.

Under the American Petroleum Institute (API) 526 effective-area series, the area immediately below the required area, 1.838 in21.838\ \mathrm{in^2} (the K orifice), gives a capacity of 1.42 kg/s1.42\ \mathrm{kg/s} at G=1200 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 1200\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}, which is below 2 kg/s2\ \mathrm{kg/s} and is therefore insufficient. The next larger area, 2.853 in22.853\ \mathrm{in^2} (the L orifice), gives:

Astd=2.853 in2=1.841×10−3 m2A_{\mathrm{std}} = 2.853\ \mathrm{in^2} = 1.841 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}

Wstd=GAstd=1200 kg/(m2⋅s)×1.841×10−3 m2=2.21 kg/sW_{\mathrm{std}} = G A_{\mathrm{std}} = 1200\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)} \times 1.841 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2} = 2.21\ \mathrm{kg/s}

The capacity Wstd=2.21 kg/sW_{\mathrm{std}} = 2.21\ \mathrm{kg/s} exceeds the required W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \mathrm{kg/s} by 10.4%10.4\%. The equivalent circular diameter of the L orifice is 48.4 mm48.4\ \mathrm{mm}.

  • Equivalent circular diameter: d=46.1 mmd = 46.1\ \mathrm{mm} (1.81 in1.81\ \mathrm{in}).

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Relief Orifice Sizing at a Stated Vapour Mass Flux

1. Weakness and Confidence Rating

Weakness. The arithmetic in this problem is exact, but the physical adequacy of the result rests almost entirely on one quantity whose derivation is not supplied: the orifice mass flux, denoted GG, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m²·s)). A relief-valve mass flux is normally a consequence of relieving pressure, relieving temperature, fluid molecular weight, compressibility, heat-capacity ratio, discharge coefficient, and back-pressure corrections. None of those quantities is given, so GG cannot be checked, the choked-flow (critical-flow) condition cannot be confirmed, and the vapour-only assumption cannot be tested. An orifice selected from an unchecked GG can be undersized for built equipment even though the division that produced its area is correct.

Confidence rating.

  • Arithmetic, conditional on the stated inputs: high, 9/10.
  • Adequacy of the selected device for a real relieving duty: low, 4/10, until the derivation of GG and the relieving scenario are checked against the primary sources named in §6. Those claims are unverified until so checked.
2. Inputs, Labelled at the Point of Use
Symbol Definition Value State

GG Orifice mass flux under a vapour-only assumption, in kg/(m²·s) 1,200 kg/(m²·s) given (derivation not supplied; treat as assumed for device adequacy)
AreqA_{\mathrm{req}} Required orifice flow area, in square metres (m²) unless stated otherwise calculated derived
deqd_{\mathrm{eq}} Diameter of a circular orifice of area AreqA_{\mathrm{req}}, in metres (m) unless stated otherwise calculated derived
KdK_{d} Discharge coefficient, dimensionless not given missing (see §3; used only in the sensitivity cases of §5)

No property value, fitted relation, or rule of thumb is used in the central calculation. The only relation used is the definition of mass flux for flow through an area, G=W/AG = W/A, rearranged in §4. That relation holds by definition for steady flow through a single flow area; it carries no valid-range limit. Standard orifice areas quoted in §4 are from the American Petroleum Institute (API) Standard 526 letter designations, as recalled values; they are unverified until checked against the current edition of API 526 (§6).

3. Prompt 2 — Missing Quantities (Listed Before Solving)

The central division needs only WW and GG. Verifying that GG — and therefore the selected orifice — is correct needs all of the following, none of which was supplied. No value is taken in silence; §5 solves under the plausible alternatives for the items that change the result.

  1. Relieving scenario and basis of WW. Which scenario sets WW (fire, blocked outlet, runaway, utility failure), and whether the value of W=2W = 2 kg/s (given) is the worst-case required rate or one scenario only.
  2. Pressure basis and pressures. Set pressure, permitted overpressure or accumulation, and back pressure (superimposed plus built-up), each stated as absolute or gauge. These decide whether flow is choked and what flux is attainable.
  3. Relieving temperature, in kelvin (K). Required to derive GG from pressure.
  4. Fluid identity and composition basis (mass or mole basis), molecular weight, compressibility factor, and heat-capacity ratio. Required to derive GG and to test the vapour-only assumption.
  5. Phase at relieving conditions. Vapour-only is assumed, as instructed. A liquid-bearing, flashing, or two-phase relief requires a different (two-phase) sizing method and a larger area, by an amount not calculable from the supplied data.
  6. Whether GG is an effective or an ideal flux. Specifically, whether the stated G=1,200G = 1{,}200 kg/(m²·s) (given) already includes the discharge coefficient KdK_{d} (dimensionless), the back-pressure correction, the rupture-disc combination correction, and any viscosity correction, or whether those factors must still be applied to it. This is the single ambiguity with the largest effect on the result (§5).
  7. Installation quantities. Inlet pressure drop to the valve, presence of a rupture disc, and required margin or spare capacity. These affect realised capacity, not the area arithmetic.

E2. Thermal Runaway Time

Response without the skill

Response Time under Adiabatic Conditions

Given data and definitions
  • TT is the absolute temperature of the reacting mass at the start of the estimate (kelvin, K); T=393 KT = 393\ \mathrm{K}, which is 120 ∘C120\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}.
  • RR is the universal gas constant (joules per mole per kelvin, J/(mol·K)); R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}.
  • qq is the specific self-heating power at TT (watts per kilogram, W/kg), that is, the heat released by reaction per unit mass of reacting mass and per unit time at TT; q=5 W/kgq = 5\ \mathrm{W/kg}.
  • cpc_p is the specific heat capacity of the reacting mass (joules per kilogram per kelvin, J/(kg·K)); cp=2,000 J/(kg⋅K)c_p = 2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}.
  • EaE_a is the activation energy (joules per mole, J/mol); Ea=100 kJ/mol=100,000 J/molE_a = 100\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}.

The quantity to be estimated is defined next.

  • tMRt_{\mathrm{MR}} is the time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions (seconds, s), commonly abbreviated TMRad_{\mathrm{ad}}: the time, starting when the mass is at TT, for the self-heating rate to accelerate to its maximum under adiabatic conditions. In practical terms tMRt_{\mathrm{MR}} is the time available for response after the mass reaches TT, before thermal runaway is fully developed.
Assumptions
  1. Adiabatic conditions: no heat is removed to the surroundings and no heat is lost to a vessel or to evaporation.
  2. cpc_p is constant over the temperature interval considered.
  3. Reactant consumption is neglected over the acceleration interval. The reaction is treated as zero order in reactant concentration, so the heat release accelerates only through its temperature dependence.
  4. The temperature dependence of the reaction rate follows the Arrhenius law, with the single activation energy EaE_a.
  5. No phase change, decomposition-path change, or onset of a second reaction occurs in the interval considered.

The result is therefore an estimate, and under assumptions 3–5 it is the standard adiabatic induction-time estimate. Neglect of reactant consumption makes the estimated time short relative to a calculation in which depletion slows the reaction, which is the direction normally accepted for a response-time estimate.

Temperature rise rate at TT

Under adiabatic conditions all heat released raises the temperature of the mass itself. The energy balance per unit mass is

cpdT′dt=q′c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}T'}{\mathrm{d}t} = q'

where T′T' is the instantaneous absolute temperature of the mass (kelvin, K) during the subsequent self-heating, tt is time (seconds, s), and q′q' is the instantaneous specific self-heating power (watts per kilogram, W/kg) at T′T'.

At the starting condition, T′=TT' = T and q′=qq' = q, so the initial temperature rise rate, denoted (dT′/dt)T\left(\mathrm{d}T'/\mathrm{d}t\right)_T (kelvin per second, K/s), is

(dT′dt)T=qcp=5 W/kg2,000 J/(kg⋅K)=0.0025 K/s\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}T'}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_T = \frac{q}{c_p} = \frac{5\ \mathrm{W/kg}}{2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}} = 0.0025\ \mathrm{K/s}

that is, 0.15 K/min0.15\ \mathrm{K/min}. The runaway does not occur at that initial rate; the rate increases sharply as T′T' rises, because of the Arrhenius temperature dependence.

Acceleration of the self-heating rate

By the Arrhenius law, for temperatures close to TT,

q′≈qexp⁡ ⁣[EaRT2(T′−T)]q' \approx q \exp\!\left[\frac{E_a}{R T^{2}}\left(T' - T\right)\right]

where exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function. The approximation replaces 1/T−1/T′1/T - 1/T' by (T′−T)/T2(T' - T)/T^{2}, which is valid when T′−TT' - T is small compared with TT.

The characteristic temperature rise that increases q′q' by a factor of e\mathrm{e} (the base of the natural logarithm, approximately 2.7182.718) is therefore

ΔTchar=RT2Ea\Delta T_{\mathrm{char}} = \frac{R T^{2}}{E_a}

where ΔTchar\Delta T_{\mathrm{char}} is that characteristic temperature rise (kelvin, K). Numerically,

ΔTchar=(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(393 K)2100,000 J/mol=8.314×154,449100,000 K≈12.8 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{char}} = \frac{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)})(393\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}} = \frac{8.314 \times 154{,}449}{100{,}000}\ \mathrm{K} \approx 12.8\ \mathrm{K}

A rise of only about 13 K13\ \mathrm{K} multiplies the heat release rate, and hence the temperature rise rate, by about 2.72.7. Most of the induction time is spent in the first few such increments, close to TT; the later acceleration takes progressively less time. That behaviour is what the integration in the next section evaluates.

Integration to the time to maximum rate

Combining the energy balance with the Arrhenius approximation gives

dT′dt=qcpexp⁡ ⁣[EaRT2(T′−T)]\frac{\mathrm{d}T'}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{q}{c_p} \exp\!\left[\frac{E_a}{R T^{2}}\left(T' - T\right)\right]

Separating the variables and integrating T′T' from TT to infinity, which represents complete acceleration with reactant consumption neglected, gives

tMR=cpq∫T∞exp⁡ ⁣[−EaRT2(T′−T)]dT′=cpq⋅RT2Eat_{\mathrm{MR}} = \frac{c_p}{q} \int_{T}^{\infty} \exp\!\left[-\frac{E_a}{R T^{2}}\left(T' - T\right)\right] \mathrm{d}T' = \frac{c_p}{q}\cdot\frac{R T^{2}}{E_a}

Hence the standard estimate is

tMR=cpRT2qEat_{\mathrm{MR}} = \frac{c_p R T^{2}}{q E_a}

Equivalently, tMR=ΔTchar/(dT′/dt)Tt_{\mathrm{MR}} = \Delta T_{\mathrm{char}} / \left(\mathrm{d}T'/\mathrm{d}t\right)_T, the characteristic temperature rise divided by the initial temperature rise rate.

Numerical evaluation

tMR=(2,000 J/(kg⋅K))(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(393 K)2(5 W/kg)(100,000 J/mol)t_{\mathrm{MR}} = \frac{(2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)})(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)})(393\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{(5\ \mathrm{W/kg})(100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol})}

Using 1 W=1 J/s1\ \mathrm{W} = 1\ \mathrm{J/s} so that the units reduce to seconds:

tMR=2.568×1095.00×105 s≈5.14×103 st_{\mathrm{MR}} = \frac{2.568 \times 10^{9}}{5.00 \times 10^{5}}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 5.14 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}

Conversion to minutes (min) and hours (h):

tMR≈5,136 s60 s/min≈85.6 min≈1.43 ht_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{5{,}136\ \mathrm{s}}{60\ \mathrm{s/min}} \approx 85.6\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.43\ \mathrm{h}

Check by the equivalent form: ΔTchar/(dT′/dt)T=12.84 K/0.0025 K/s≈5,136 s\Delta T_{\mathrm{char}} / \left(\mathrm{d}T'/\mathrm{d}t\right)_T = 12.84\ \mathrm{K} / 0.0025\ \mathrm{K/s} \approx 5{,}136\ \mathrm{s}, in agreement.

Result

The estimated response time after the reacting mass reaches 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} (120 ∘C120\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}) under adiabatic conditions is

tMR≈5.1×103 s≈86 min≈1.4 ht_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx 5.1 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 86\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.4\ \mathrm{h}

After about 1.4 h1.4\ \mathrm{h} at and above 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} with no heat removal, the self-heating is expected to have accelerated to its maximum rate, so corrective action must be completed within that interval. Any heat removal, reactant depletion, or heat loss to the vessel would lengthen the available time; an additional exothermic process or a higher actual self-heating rate at 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} would shorten it.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Response Time at 393 K, Adiabatic

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. The standard time-to-maximum-rate formula used here is a single-step, no-consumption, perfectly adiabatic approximation. It holds the reaction as one Arrhenius step whose rate at the stated temperature is known, ignores reactant depletion, phase change, gas generation, mixing, heat loss and vessel thermal mass, and uses a high-activation-energy expansion. A small error in the heat-release rate at 393 K, or in the activation energy extrapolated to 393 K, propagates directly, or more than directly, into the time. This is the class of estimate for which a screening number is routinely wrong by a factor of two or more when applied to built equipment.

Confidence rating. Low to moderate: 4 out of 10 as a basis for an emergency-response decision on real equipment; 7 out of 10 as an order-of-magnitude screening value if the supplied inputs are exact for the actual material at 393 K. Arithmetic confidence is high (check in §6); model confidence is the limiting factor.
