4. Calculation

Under adiabatic conditions the energy balance on unit mass is: the rate of sensible-heat accumulation, cpc_p multiplied by the temperature rate of change dT/dt\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t (kelvin per second, K s−1\mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}), equals q˙\dot q at the current temperature. With a single Arrhenius step, q˙\dot q grows with temperature with sensitivity set by EaE_a. Integrating that balance with the standard high-activation-energy expansion (Ea/(RT)≫1E_a/(RT) \gg 1) gives the time to maximum rate

tMR  ≈  cp R T2Ea q˙t_{\mathrm{MR}} \;\approx\; \frac{c_p\,R\,T^{2}}{E_a\,\dot q}

evaluated with all quantities at TT. Substitution:

tMR≈(2,000)(8.314)(393)2(100,000)(5)=5,136 s=85.6 min=1.43 ht_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{(2{,}000)(8.314)(393)^{2}}{(100{,}000)(5)} = 5{,}136\ \mathrm{s} = 85.6\ \mathrm{min} = 1.43\ \mathrm{h}

Nominal result: tMR≈86 mint_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx 86\ \mathrm{min} (about 1.4 h1.4\ \mathrm{h}) from reaching 393 K.

Derived check quantity: the initial temperature rate at 393 K is $\dot q / c_p = 5/2{,}000 = 0.0025\ \mathrm{K\,s^{-1}} = 0.15\ \mathrm{K\,min^{-1}} = 9\ \mathrm{K\,h^{-1}}$.

Alternative from §3, item 2: if the effective system carries ϕ=1.5\phi = 1.5 (sample plus container or vessel wall acting as a heat sink with no other change), the elapsed time scales approximately with ϕ\phi, giving about 128 min128\ \mathrm{min}. Conversely, an uncorrected laboratory time measured at ϕ=1.5\phi = 1.5 corresponds to a shorter true adiabatic time, by roughly the same factor. Which direction applies cannot be settled from the data supplied.

5. Primary source that settles the point

The settling sources are: (i) a calorimetric test on the actual material — accelerating rate calorimetry or equivalent adiabatic calorimetry, ϕ\phi-corrected — reported per the methodology in the Center for Chemical Process Safety (CCPS) Guidelines for Chemical Reactivity Evaluation and Application to Process Design and the Design Institute for Emergency Relief Systems (DIERS) literature, including the Townsend and Tou ϕ\phi-correction treatment; and (ii) the fitted-kinetics source for EaE_a, e.g. a test performed to ASTM E698 (kinetic parameters from differential scanning calorimetry) with its stated temperature range. Every claim in this solution that rests on those sources — the formula form, the ϕ\phi scaling, and the applicability of a single Arrhenius step — is unverified until checked against the current edition of the source and against test data on the actual material. No such check was possible from the data supplied. Agreement with any other AI model is not verification and was not used (Checklist item 7).

8. Audit as a plant engineer would (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. Heat loss and vessel thermal mass. A real vessel is not adiabatic: wall mass (ϕ>1\phi > 1 for the inventory) and external loss lengthen the time, typically by tens of percent, and a small vessel with a high surface-to-volume ratio can fail to run away at all from 393 K. Direction: real time longer than 86 min. Settled by: the vessel's mass, material and insulation record, and a ϕ\phi calculation for the actual fill.
  2. q˙\dot q at 393 K is probably extrapolated, and the reaction may not be a single step. Autocatalysis, a second decomposition step, or contamination (rust, acid, a wrong charge) can raise the rate at 393 K by a factor of two to ten. Direction: real time shorter, potentially much shorter. Settled by: the raw adiabatic calorimeter trace on the actual, plant-representative sample (including aged and contaminated samples), not a fitted EaE_a from a screening scan.
  3. Temperature is not uniform and 393 K may be a local, not bulk, value. Poor agitation, a hot spot at a heating surface, or a failed agitator leaves part of the mass hotter and already further along its induction time. Direction: effective available time shorter than the bulk-temperature figure. Settled by: agitator and temperature-instrument records, and the location of the sensor that reads 393 K relative to heating surfaces.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: reactant consumption and the finite adiabatic temperature rise; autocatalysis and multi-step kinetics; gas generation and pressure rise (the response criterion in a closed vessel may be pressure, reached earlier in effect); phase change, boiling and evaporative cooling; viscosity change, fouling and loss of agitation; heat loss; relief venting and its required capacity, which this calculation does not size.
  • Information not visible here: proprietary or databank kinetics for the specific material; the plant's own calorimeter reports, incident history and management-of-change records; the current edition text of the CCPS/DIERS sources named in §5.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: contamination and ageing of the charge, scale effects (laboratory adiabaticity does not transfer directly to plant surface-to-volume ratios), sensor lag and alarm/operator response time, which consume part of the 86 min before any action begins.
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10%10\%: any of — q˙\dot q in error by more than 10%10\%; EaE_a in error by more than 10 kJ mol−110\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}; ϕ\phi above about 1.1; cpc_p varying by more than 10%10\% over the excursion (e.g. through a phase change); the true criterion being a 20 K20\ \mathrm{K} rise (69 min, §6) or pressure rather than maximum rate.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used: (1) Where is the ϕ\phi-corrected calorimeter trace for this exact material and composition, and was 5 W kg−15\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}} read from it at 393 K or extrapolated? (2) Over what temperature range was Ea=100 kJ mol−1E_a = 100\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} fitted, and does a second step appear above 393 K? (3) What is ϕ\phi and the heat-loss figure for the actual vessel at the actual fill? (4) Is the response trigger a temperature, a temperature rate, or a pressure — and how much of the time is consumed by detection and operator action? (5) Has the relief system been sized separately for the resulting maximum rate? Until (1)–(3) are answered from primary records, treat the value as a screening estimate with the wide range of §7.

E3. Gas Dispersion

Response without the skill

Ground-Level Centreline Concentration at 500 m Downwind

Given data and definitions
  • CC is the ground-level centreline concentration, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}).
  • QQ is the continuous release rate, Q=1 kg/sQ = 1\ \mathrm{kg/s}.
  • uu is the wind speed, u=3 m/su = 3\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  • xx is the downwind distance from the source, x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m}.
  • π\pi is the mathematical constant pi, π≈3.1416\pi \approx 3.1416.
  • σy\sigma_y is the lateral (crosswind) dispersion coefficient, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • σz\sigma_z is the vertical dispersion coefficient, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).

The relation to be used, as stated in the problem, is

C=Qπ u σy σzC = \frac{Q}{\pi \, u \, \sigma_y \, \sigma_z}

This relation is the ground-level centreline form of the Gaussian plume equation. It applies for a continuous, steady release, a steady wind, a receptor on the plume centreline at ground level, and total reflection at the ground. It also corresponds to an effective release height, denoted HH and measured in metres (m\mathrm{m}), of H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}, i.e. a ground-level release. For an elevated release (H>0 mH > 0\ \mathrm{m}) the ground-level centreline concentration would be lower than the value from this relation, by an exponential factor in HH and σz\sigma_z.

Information not stated in the problem

Neither σy\sigma_y nor σz\sigma_z is given numerically. Both depend on xx and on atmospheric stability. No stability class, surface roughness, or urban/rural setting is stated. An estimate therefore requires stated assumptions:

  1. Pasquill stability class D (neutral stability) is assumed. Class D is the standard default when no stability information is supplied, and a surface wind speed of 3 m/s3\ \mathrm{m/s} is consistent with neutral conditions occurring under overcast conditions or with moderate wind.
  2. Open-country (rural) dispersion is assumed.
  3. The Briggs formulae for σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z as functions of xx are used. These are standard analytical fits to the Pasquill–Gifford dispersion curves.

The result is therefore an order-of-magnitude screening estimate, not a unique value. The sensitivity to the assumed stability class is quantified at the end.

Dispersion coefficients at x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m}

For stability class D, open country, the Briggs formulae are

σy=0.08 x(1+0.0001 x)1/2\sigma_y = \frac{0.08 \, x}{\left(1 + 0.0001 \, x\right)^{1/2}}

σz=0.06 x(1+0.0015 x)1/2\sigma_z = \frac{0.06 \, x}{\left(1 + 0.0015 \, x\right)^{1/2}}

where xx is in metres (m\mathrm{m}) and σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z are returned in metres (m\mathrm{m}); the numerical coefficients in the formulae are dimensionless fits for this stability class and setting.

Substitution of x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m}:

σy=0.08×500(1+0.0001×500)1/2=40(1.05)1/2=401.025≈39 m\sigma_y = \frac{0.08 \times 500}{\left(1 + 0.0001 \times 500\right)^{1/2}} = \frac{40}{(1.05)^{1/2}} = \frac{40}{1.025} \approx 39\ \mathrm{m}

σz=0.06×500(1+0.0015×500)1/2=30(1.75)1/2=301.323≈23 m\sigma_z = \frac{0.06 \times 500}{\left(1 + 0.0015 \times 500\right)^{1/2}} = \frac{30}{(1.75)^{1/2}} = \frac{30}{1.323} \approx 23\ \mathrm{m}

Reading the Pasquill–Gifford curves directly at x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m} for class D gives values of the same size (approximately σy≈35\sigma_y \approx 35–40 m40\ \mathrm{m} and σz≈18\sigma_z \approx 18–23 m23\ \mathrm{m}), which confirms the fitted values to within the scatter of the curves.

C=1π×3×39×23 kg/s(m/s)(m)(m)C = \frac{1}{\pi \times 3 \times 39 \times 23}\ \frac{\mathrm{kg/s}}{(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})}

Under neutral (class D) stability, open-country dispersion, and a ground-level continuous release, the estimated ground-level centreline concentration at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} downwind is

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Ground-Level Plume Concentration at 500 m

Result

The concentration at ground level on the plume centreline is denoted CC, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}); values are also given in milligrams per cubic metre (mg/m3\mathrm{mg/m^3}, where 1 mg/m3=10−6 kg/m31\ \mathrm{mg/m^3} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}).

  • Central case, neutral stability: C≈1.2×10−4 kg/m3C \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, i.e. about 120 mg/m3120\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.
  • Plausible range over all stability classes: C≈1×10−5C \approx 1 \times 10^{-5} to 8×10−4 kg/m38 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, i.e. about 1010 to 780 mg/m3780\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

No single value is defensible from the data given. The range is a factor of about 79 wide and is set almost entirely by the missing stability class, not by arithmetic.

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. The supplied relation needs the lateral dispersion coefficient, denoted σy\sigma_y, in metres (m\mathrm{m}), and the vertical dispersion coefficient, denoted σz\sigma_z, in metres (m\mathrm{m}). Neither is given, and neither can be derived from the release rate, the wind speed, or the distance. Both depend mainly on atmospheric stability and on the averaging time, and weakly on terrain roughness. At a fixed distance they vary by more than an order of magnitude in product between very unstable and very stable air. The release height, which does not appear in the supplied relation at all, is a second missing quantity of the same size.

Confidence rating: low. Confidence in the arithmetic for a stated pair (σy,σz)(\sigma_y, \sigma_z) is high. Confidence in any single concentration from the inputs as given is low, because the controlling inputs are assumed, not given. This is a screening estimate only. It must not be used for a safety, exposure, or compliance decision without site meteorological data and a validated dispersion model.

4. Relation and fitted dispersion coefficients (Prompt 1)

The supplied Gaussian plume relation for the ground-level centreline is

C=Qπ u σy σzC = \frac{Q}{\pi \, u \, \sigma_y \, \sigma_z}

where every symbol is as defined in §3. The form already contains ground reflection: the standard Gaussian expression carries 2π2\pi in the denominator and a reflection factor of 2 at ground level, which combine to give the π\pi shown. It therefore presumes a ground-level, or fully reflected, plume and no loss at the ground.

The coefficients σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z were obtained from the Briggs open-country interpolation formulas, which are algebraic fits to the Pasquill–Gifford dispersion curves. Provenance and range:

  • Source as recalled: Briggs (1973) fits, reproduced in Turner, Workbook of Atmospheric Dispersion Estimates (2nd ed., 1994), and in standard air-dispersion textbooks. Unverified against the primary source in this calculation — see §8.
  • Valid range: downwind distance xx from about 100 m100\ \mathrm{m} to about 10,000 m10{,}000\ \mathrm{m}, open country, short averaging times. The present x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m} lies inside that range.
  • Form used, with xx in metres (m\mathrm{m}):

That difference alone moves CC by roughly −40 %-40\ \% to +100 %+100\ \%, because CC varies as 1/(σyσz)1/(\sigma_y\sigma_z).

6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run separately from the main calculation. No solution value was altered to make a check pass.

  1. Dimensional check — passes. Q/(u σyσz)Q/(u\,\sigma_y\sigma_z) has units (kg/s)/[(m/s)(m)(m)]=kg/m3(\mathrm{kg/s}) / [(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})] = \mathrm{kg/m^3}, as required for CC.
  2. Mass-flux limiting case — passes in form. Integrating a Gaussian crosswind profile with these coefficients returns a total flux of order QQ through a vertical plane downwind; the supplied relation is the standard reflected ground-level form of that profile. This confirms the relation's internal consistency, not the values of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z.
  3. Limiting behaviour — passes. C→0C \to 0 as u→∞u \to \infty, as σyσz→∞\sigma_y\sigma_z \to \infty, and as x→∞x \to \infty (both coefficients grow with xx); CC increases as stability increases (coefficients shrink), in the expected direction in every row of Table 2, with no non-monotonic rows.
  4. Code re-evaluation — passes. All six rows of Table 2 were computed by direct code evaluation (§5) and the class D row was also computed by hand above; the two agree, 1.2×10−4 kg/m31.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  5. Cross-check against curve magnitudes — passes at order-of-magnitude level. Graphical Pasquill–Gifford values at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} for class D are commonly read as σy\sigma_y about 3535 to 40 m40\ \mathrm{m} and σz\sigma_z about 2020 to 25 m25\ \mathrm{m}, bracketing the 39 m39\ \mathrm{m} and 23 m23\ \mathrm{m} used. This is agreement with a second reading of the same underlying curves, not independent verification of the curves themselves.
  6. Valid-range check — passes. x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m} is inside the stated range of the Briggs fits (§4). The fits are not used outside it.
  7. Check that fails — none in the arithmetic; one in completeness. The calculation cannot be closed against any measurement, because no measured concentration, and no measured stability class, was supplied. That check is open, not passed.

Agreement with another AI model was not used as a check and would not count as verification for this problem type.

7. Audit against built equipment and real releases (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from a real release, in expected size order:

  1. Plume rise and effective height. A real 1 kg/s1\ \mathrm{kg/s} release is usually warm, or has exit momentum, or both. Buoyant or momentum rise can add tens of metres to the effective height HH, and §5 shows H=50 mH = 50\ \mathrm{m} cuts the class D ground-level value by about 91 %91\ \%. Direction: the estimate is high, possibly by an order of magnitude. Settled by: the release temperature, exit velocity, and stack or vent diameter from the vendor or design document for the actual source, with rise computed by the standard Briggs plume-rise formulas. Unverified here — none of those data were supplied.
  2. Building and terrain wake. A release near buildings is drawn down into the wake cavity, which raises near-field ground-level concentrations and invalidates the Gaussian coefficients used. Direction: the estimate can be low within a few building heights downwind, by a factor of about 2 to 5 in reported wake studies. Settled by: a site plot plan with building dimensions, and a wake assessment (for example the building-downwash procedure in the current United States Environmental Protection Agency AERMOD guidance). Unverified here.
  3. Real meteorology is not one steady class. Wind direction veers, speed varies, and stability changes over an hour. A fixed receptor at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} is on the nominal centreline only part of the time; time-averaged centreline values are usually lower than the steady-plume value, while short peaks are higher. Direction: the estimate is high for a long average at a fixed point, low for a short peak. Settled by: at least one year of hourly site meteorological data (wind speed, direction, and a stability indicator) processed through a regulatory model, or tracer-release measurements on the actual site. Unverified here.
8. Primary sources that settle the open points

Every claim below rests on a source not consulted in this calculation and is marked unverified until checked against it:

  • Dispersion coefficients and their stability dependence: Turner, Workbook of Atmospheric Dispersion Estimates, 2nd edition (1994), presenting the Pasquill–Gifford curves and the Briggs fits. Unverified.
  • Regulatory treatment, including building downwash, plume rise, and meteorological data requirements: the current edition of the United States Environmental Protection Agency guidance for AERMOD (40 CFR Part 51, Appendix W). Unverified — the current edition must be confirmed before use.
  • Plume rise: the original Briggs plume-rise formulas as reproduced in that guidance. Unverified.
  • The settling measurement for this specific case: a tracer or concentration measurement at about 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} from the actual release, with simultaneous on-site wind and stability measurement. No such measurement was supplied.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model

  • Plume rise (buoyancy and momentum), release height, and stack-tip downwash.
  • Building wake, terrain channelling and elevation, land–sea or valley flows.
  • Dry and wet deposition, chemical reaction, radioactive or biological decay, aerosol settling, and dense-gas slumping. A release denser than air does not follow a Gaussian plume at all in the near field.
  • Wind shear with height, direction veer, low-wind meander, and calm conditions. The relation fails as u→0u \to 0: it predicts C→∞C \to \infty, which is an artefact, not a result.
  • Short-duration peaks, odour-relevant fluctuations of seconds to minutes, and indoor infiltration at the receptor.
  • Any health, toxicity, flammability, or exposure-limit comparison. No property of the released material was supplied, so no such comparison is made.

Information not available to this calculation

  • Site meteorological records and any regulatory dispersion modelling files for the actual location (held by the operator or the regulator).
  • Vendor data for the source: temperature, exit velocity, diameter, height.
  • Any measured concentration data for this release.

Effects that appear only in running equipment

  • Start-up, shutdown, relief, and upset releases, which are not continuous at 1 kg/s1\ \mathrm{kg/s}.
  • Fouling, partial blockage, or fan degradation changing the exit velocity and hence the rise.
  • Rain, fog, and inversion break-up fumigation, which can raise ground-level concentrations for a period above any steady-class value in Table 2.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %

Almost any realistic change does so: one stability class step (−57 %-57\ \% to +132 %+132\ \%); a release height of 10 m10\ \mathrm{m} in class D or F (in class F, σz=7 m\sigma_z = 7\ \mathrm{m}, H=10 mH = 10\ \mathrm{m} gives a factor of about 0.360.36, i.e. −64 %-64\ \%); urban roughness; a 1-hour instead of a 10-minute average; a wind speed error above about 11 %11\ \%; deposition of a reactive or particulate material over 500 m500\ \mathrm{m}. A result stable to within 10 %10\ \% cannot be obtained from these inputs.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used

  1. What was the stability class, from what measurement, over what averaging period?
  2. What are the release height, temperature, exit velocity, and vent diameter, and what plume rise do they give?
  3. Are there buildings or terrain within about 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} that put the receptor in a wake?
  4. Is the released material a passive gas, a dense gas, a particle stream, or reactive — and does a Gaussian model apply to it at all?
  5. Which averaging time does the decision need, peak or long-term mean, and does Table 2 match it?
  6. Has a validated regulatory model (for example AERMOD) with site meteorological data been run, and how does it compare?
  7. Against which exposure or safety criterion, from which current document, will the concentration be judged?

F1. Control-Loop Tuning

Response without the skill

Proportional–Integral Controller Tuning by Internal Model Control

Symbols

Each symbol is defined at its first appearance here, before use in any equation.

  • KpK_p (dimensionless, process output per unit controller output): steady-state process gain.
  • τ\tau (seconds, s): process time constant.
  • θ\theta (seconds, s): process dead time.
  • θc\theta_c (seconds, s): desired closed-loop time constant.
  • KcK_c (controller output per unit process output, i.e. per unit error): proportional gain of the controller.
  • τI\tau_I (seconds, s): integral time of the controller, also called the reset time.
  • KIK_I (controller output per unit process output per second, s−1^{-1} in the gain ratio): integral gain of the controller, defined by KI=Kc/τIK_I = K_c / \tau_I.
  • ss (per second, s−1^{-1}): Laplace variable.
  • Gp(s)G_p(s) (process output per unit controller output): process transfer function.
  • e(t)e(t) (process output units): control error at time tt (seconds, s), defined as set point minus measured process output.
  • u(t)u(t) (controller output units): controller output at time tt (seconds, s).
Given data
  • Kp=1.5K_p = 1.5
  • τ=60 s\tau = 60\ \text{s}
  • θ=5 s\theta = 5\ \text{s}
  • θc=θ=5 s\theta_c = \theta = 5\ \text{s}, by specification.
Process model

A self-regulating process with one time constant and dead time is represented by the first-order plus dead-time model

Gp(s)=Kp e−θsτs+1G_p(s) = \frac{K_p\, e^{-\theta s}}{\tau s + 1}

Substitution of the given data gives

Gp(s)=1.5 e−5s60s+1G_p(s) = \frac{1.5\, e^{-5s}}{60s + 1}

where the ss in 5s5s and 60s60s in the preceding expression is the Laplace variable defined above, and the numerical coefficients 55 and 6060 carry units of seconds (s).

Controller form

The proportional–integral controller is

u(t)=Kc[e(t)+1τI∫0te(t′) dt′]u(t) = K_c \left[ e(t) + \frac{1}{\tau_I} \int_0^t e(t')\, dt' \right]

where t′t' (seconds, s) is the dummy variable of integration. Two parameters are therefore required: KcK_c and τI\tau_I.

Internal-model-control tuning rules for this model

For the first-order plus dead-time model, the internal-model-control (IMC) design, with the dead time approximated to first order and the IMC filter time constant taken as θc\theta_c, reduces to a proportional–integral controller with

Kc=1Kp τθ+θcK_c = \frac{1}{K_p}\, \frac{\tau}{\theta + \theta_c}

and

τI=τ\tau_I = \tau

The first relation is the gain relation stated in the problem. The second relation states that the controller integral time cancels the process lag in the IMC design.

Calculation of the proportional gain

Kc=1Kp τθ+θc=11.5×60 s5 s+5 sK_c = \frac{1}{K_p}\, \frac{\tau}{\theta + \theta_c} = \frac{1}{1.5} \times \frac{60\ \text{s}}{5\ \text{s} + 5\ \text{s}}

60 s5 s+5 s=6010=6.0\frac{60\ \text{s}}{5\ \text{s} + 5\ \text{s}} = \frac{60}{10} = 6.0

Kc=6.01.5=4.0K_c = \frac{6.0}{1.5} = 4.0

Kc=4.0K_c = 4.0 in units of controller output per unit process output. As a check, KcKp=4.0×1.5=6.0K_c K_p = 4.0 \times 1.5 = 6.0, which is dimensionless, as required for a loop gain formed from KcK_c and KpK_p.

Calculation of the integral time

τI=τ=60 s\tau_I = \tau = 60\ \text{s}

The corresponding integral gain is

KI=KcτI=4.060 s=0.0667 s−1K_I = \frac{K_c}{\tau_I} = \frac{4.0}{60\ \text{s}} = 0.0667\ \text{s}^{-1}

in units of controller output per unit process output per second. The reset rate, 1/τI1/\tau_I, is 1/60 s=0.0167 s−11/60\ \text{s} = 0.0167\ \text{s}^{-1}, equivalent to 1.01.0 repeat per minute.

Result
  • Kc=4.0K_c = 4.0 (controller output per unit process output)
  • τI=60 s\tau_I = 60\ \text{s}
  • KI=Kc/τI=0.0667 s−1K_I = K_c / \tau_I = 0.0667\ \text{s}^{-1} (controller output per unit process output per second)

The tuned controller is therefore

u(t)=4.0[e(t)+160 s∫0te(t′) dt′]u(t) = 4.0 \left[ e(t) + \frac{1}{60\ \text{s}} \int_0^t e(t')\, dt' \right]

with θc=5 s\theta_c = 5\ \text{s}, equal to the dead time θ\theta. This choice of θc\theta_c is the usual lower limit for a robust IMC design for this model: a smaller θc\theta_c would give a larger KcK_c and a faster nominal response with reduced robustness, and a larger θc\theta_c would give a smaller KcK_c and a slower, more robust response.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Proportional–Integral Tuning by the Internal-Model-Control Rule — Solution

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: the arithmetic is exact, but a tuning rule is only as good as the first-order-plus-dead-time model it is applied to and as the particular variant of the rule chosen. The problem statement supplies the gain formula, so the controller gain is pinned; it does not supply the integral-time formula, the controller form, or the sign of action, so the integral part is genuinely underspecified (Section 4).

Confidence ratings:

  • Controller gain from the supplied formula: high, about 95% (residual risk is a transcription or variant error, checked in Section 6).
  • Integral time: low to medium, about 50%, because it depends on which rule variant is adopted (range in Section 4).
  • The closed loop on real equipment actually behaving with the desired closed-loop time constant: low to medium, about 50–60%, because the process gain (defined below), time constant, and dead time are in practice fitted values that drift with operating point.

No agreement with another AI model is used as verification anywhere in this solution (Checklist item 7).

2. Symbols, inputs, and their state

Symbols, defined before first use:

  • KpK_p = steady-state process gain, process output per unit controller output, dimensionless in consistent scaled units: 1.5 — given.
  • τ\tau (tau) = process time constant, in seconds (s): 60 s — given.
  • θ\theta (theta) = process dead time, in s: 5 s — given.
  • θc\theta_c (theta c) = desired closed-loop time constant, in s: set equal to θ\theta, i.e. 5 s — given as a rule, hence its value is derived from a given input, not measured.
  • KcK_c = proportional controller gain, controller output per unit process output (the internal-model-control gain of the statement): to be computed.
  • τI\tau_I (tau I) = integral (reset) time of the proportional–integral controller, in s: to be selected, see Section 4.
  • KIK_I = integral gain, KI=Kc/τIK_I = K_c / \tau_I, in inverse seconds (s−1^{-1}) times KcK_c units: derived.

State of the model itself: the process is stated to be self-regulating and is represented by a first-order-plus-dead-time model. That model form is assumed in the statement; whether KpK_p, τ\tau, and θ\theta were measured, fitted from a step test, or estimated is not stated — see Sections 4 and 5.

Kc=1Kp τθ+θcK_c = \frac{1}{K_p}\,\frac{\tau}{\theta + \theta_c}

7. Independent verification (Prompt 3)

All checks were executed in code (Python) in this session; results quoted from that execution.

  1. Dimensional check — passes. 1/Kp1/K_p carries controller output per process output; τ/(θ+θc)\tau/(\theta+\theta_c) is s/s, dimensionless. KcK_c therefore carries the correct units.
  2. Arithmetic by a second route — passes. 60/(5+5)=660/(5+5) = 6; 6/1.5=4.06/1.5 = 4.0. Code returns 4.0 exactly.
  3. Limiting case, dead time to zero — passes in form, and flags a limit. With θ=θc→0\theta = \theta_c \to 0, Kc→∞K_c \to \infty: the rule demands unbounded gain for a delay-free process asked to respond instantly, which is the expected behaviour of the formula and the reason θc\theta_c must not be set below θ\theta in practice.
  4. Limiting case, large θc\theta_c — passes. θc=10\theta_c = 10 s gives Kc=2.67K_c = 2.67; detuning the desired response detunes the gain monotonically, as required.
  5. Known-case comparison — passes. The supplied gain formula is algebraically identical to the SIMC gain; pairing it with the SIMC reset of Section 4(b) is internally consistent, whereas pairing it with variant (c)'s reset is not (variant (c) carries its own gain, 5.56). This consistency check is what selects the primary τI\tau_I.
  6. Balance closure: no material or energy balance exists in this problem; nothing to close. Stated rather than omitted.
  7. Failed checks: none of 1–5 fail. The open item is not a failed check but an unsettled one: the integral-time variant (Section 4, item 1) cannot be settled by calculation alone.
8. Audit as built equipment will behave (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from the model, with direction, rough size, and the record that settles each:

  1. Process gain varies with operating point (valve characteristic, level/flow nonlinearity). Direction: if the true KpK_p at the working point is higher than 1.5, the loop is more aggressive than designed and can oscillate; lower, and it is sluggish. Rough size: ±25\pm 25–50%50\% in KpK_p across a valve's travel is common, moving effective KcKpK_c K_p by the same fraction. Settled by: step tests at low, normal, and high throughput on the actual loop, and the valve vendor's installed characteristic sheet.
  2. Effective dead time is larger than the fitted 5 s (analyser/sample delay, transmitter damping, scan and sample period, transport lag varying with flow). Direction: always toward less stability margin than designed; at θc=θ\theta_c = \theta there is little margin to spare. Rough size: +1–3 s of effective dead time (20–60% of θ\theta) is enough to make this tuning visibly oscillatory. Settled by: the loop's trend record at the actual scan rate and a re-fit of θ\theta from plant step data.
  3. Actuator saturation and integral windup. The linear design assumes unlimited controller output. Direction: large set-point changes saturate the valve, the integral accumulates, and overshoot appears that no linear calculation predicts. Rough size: overshoot of tens of per cent of the step after a saturating move, absent anti-windup. Settled by: the control block configuration record (limits, anti-windup mode) and operating trends of past large moves.
9. What this calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: higher-order and inverse-response dynamics collapsed into the first-order-plus-dead-time fit; load-disturbance response (the rule as applied is a set-point design; disturbance rejection with τI=40\tau_I = 40 s differs); interaction with neighbouring loops; measurement noise, which a gain of 4.0 passes to the valve and which the (absent) derivative term would have worsened; valve stiction and hysteresis.
  • Information not visible here: the site control standard, the actual block configuration and scaling, and the original step-test data behind KpK_p, τ\tau, θ\theta — all held by the plant.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: gain and dead-time drift with throughput, fouling, and ambient conditions; operator detuning after any oscillatory episode.
  • Conditions changing the answer by more than 10%: any input moving outside the assumed bands of Section 6; θc\theta_c chosen other than θ\theta; series-form implementation without conversion; a scaling change for KpK_p; effective dead time increasing by more than about 0.5 s at fixed settings.
  • Questions a reviewer should ask before use: (i) Which rule variant and site standard govern τI\tau_I, and is 40 s or 60 s entered? (ii) On what scaling was Kp=1.5K_p = 1.5 fitted, at what operating point, and from which step test? (iii) Is the block ideal or series form, reverse acting, with anti-windup enabled and what output limits? (iv) What is the scan period and total measurement delay relative to the 5 s dead time? (v) Has a closed-loop trend at these settings been reviewed after commissioning?

F2. Meter Readings That Do Not Add Up

Response without the skill

Data Reconciliation of a Steady-State Unit

Given Data and Definitions

All flows are in the same flow units.

  • y1=100y_1 = 100: measured value of the first feed flow.
  • y2=50y_2 = 50: measured value of the second feed flow.
  • y3=140y_3 = 140: measured value of the product flow.
  • x1x_1, x2x_2: reconciled (estimated true) values of the two feed flows, in flow units.
  • x3x_3: reconciled (estimated true) value of the product flow, in flow units.
  • σi\sigma_i: standard deviation of meter ii, in flow units, for i=1,2,3i = 1, 2, 3.
  • ai=xi−yia_i = x_i - y_i: adjustment applied to measurement ii by the reconciliation, in flow units.

Each meter standard deviation is 2%2\% of its own reading:

σ1=0.02(100)=2.00,σ2=0.02(50)=1.00,σ3=0.02(140)=2.80.\sigma_1 = 0.02(100) = 2.00, \qquad \sigma_2 = 0.02(50) = 1.00, \qquad \sigma_3 = 0.02(140) = 2.80.

Assumptions used below: the meter errors are independent and approximately normally distributed with the stated standard deviations, and there is no gross (systematic) error. The consequences of the second assumption failing are examined in the final section.

1. The Balance Constraint

At steady state with no inventory change, total feed in equals product out. The reconciled values must therefore satisfy exactly

x1+x2−x3=0.x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 0.

The measured values do not satisfy this relation. The measured imbalance, denoted rr and expressed in flow units, is

r=y1+y2−y3=100+50−140=10.r = y_1 + y_2 - y_3 = 100 + 50 - 140 = 10.

2. Is the Imbalance Consistent with Random Error Alone?

Because the three meter errors are independent, variances add. The variance of the imbalance, denoted σr2\sigma_r^2 and expressed in squared flow units, is

σr2=σ12+σ22+σ32=(2.00)2+(1.00)2+(2.80)2=4.00+1.00+7.84=12.84,\sigma_r^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 = (2.00)^2 + (1.00)^2 + (2.80)^2 = 4.00 + 1.00 + 7.84 = 12.84,

so the standard deviation of the imbalance, σr\sigma_r, is

σr=12.84=3.58 flow units.\sigma_r = \sqrt{12.84} = 3.58 \text{ flow units}.

The standardised imbalance, denoted zz and dimensionless, is

z=rσr=103.58=2.79.z = \frac{r}{\sigma_r} = \frac{10}{3.58} = 2.79.

A 95%95\% random-error band on the imbalance is ±1.96σr=±7.0\pm 1.96\sigma_r = \pm 7.0 flow units. The observed imbalance of 1010 flow units lies outside that band. Random error of the stated size is therefore an unlikely explanation on its own; this is quantified by a formal test in Section 4.

3. Reconciled Values by Weighted Least Squares

The reconciliation chooses x1x_1, x2x_2, and x3x_3 to minimise the variance-weighted sum of squared adjustments, subject to the balance constraint:

minimiseJ=∑i=13(aiσi)2subject tox1+x2−x3=0,\text{minimise} \quad J = \sum_{i=1}^{3} \left(\frac{a_i}{\sigma_i}\right)^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 0,

where JJ is the dimensionless objective function. Weighting by 1/σi21/\sigma_i^2 is the essential point: a meter with a large standard deviation is moved more, in absolute terms, than a precise meter.

Writing the constraint in terms of the adjustments gives a1+a2−a3=−r=−10a_1 + a_2 - a_3 = -r = -10. Minimising JJ subject to this constraint (Lagrange-multiplier result, verifiable by direct substitution) gives each adjustment proportional to the corresponding meter variance:

ai=− rσr2 σi2 ci,a_i = -\,\frac{r}{\sigma_r^2}\, \sigma_i^2\, c_i,

where cic_i is the coefficient of flow ii in the balance x1+x2−x3x_1 + x_2 - x_3, namely c1=1c_1 = 1, c2=1c_2 = 1, and c3=−1c_3 = -1, and where r/σr2=10/12.84=0.7788r/\sigma_r^2 = 10/12.84 = 0.7788 per flow unit. Hence

a1=−0.7788×4.00×1=−3.12,a_1 = -0.7788 \times 4.00 \times 1 = -3.12, a2=−0.7788×1.00×1=−0.78,a_2 = -0.7788 \times 1.00 \times 1 = -0.78, a3=−0.7788×7.84×(−1)=+6.11.a_3 = -0.7788 \times 7.84 \times (-1) = +6.11.

The negative sign for the feeds and the positive sign for the product both act to close the gap: the feeds are adjusted down and the product is adjusted up. The product meter receives the largest absolute adjustment because it has the largest variance, (2.80)2=7.84(2.80)^2 = 7.84, which is 61%61\% of the total variance 12.8412.84.

The reconciled flows, xi=yi+aix_i = y_i + a_i, are:

Stream Measured yiy_i σi\sigma_i Adjustment aia_i Reconciled xix_i
Feed 1 100.00 2.00 −3.12-3.12 96.88
Feed 2 50.00 1.00 −0.78-0.78 49.22
Product 140.00 2.80 +6.11+6.11 146.11

Check: 96.88+49.22=146.1196.88 + 49.22 = 146.11, so the reconciled values satisfy x1+x2−x3=0x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 0 exactly, as required.

4. Global Test on the Reconciliation

The minimised objective value is

Jmin⁡=(−3.122.00)2+(−0.781.00)2+(6.112.80)2=2.43+0.61+4.76=7.79.J_{\min} = \left(\frac{-3.12}{2.00}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{-0.78}{1.00}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{6.11}{2.80}\right)^2 = 2.43 + 0.61 + 4.76 = 7.79.

Equivalently, Jmin⁡=r2/σr2=100/12.84=7.79J_{\min} = r^2/\sigma_r^2 = 100/12.84 = 7.79. Under the hypothesis that only random errors with the stated standard deviations are present, Jmin⁡J_{\min} follows a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom (three measurements, one independent balance constraint used in the fit, leaving one redundant measurement). The critical values are 3.843.84 at the 95%95\% level and 6.636.63 at the 99%99\% level. Since

Jmin⁡=7.79>6.63,J_{\min} = 7.79 > 6.63,

the hypothesis is rejected at both levels; the associated pp-value is approximately 0.0050.005. The standardised adjustments, ai/σia_i/\sigma_i, are −1.56-1.56 for Feed 1, −0.78-0.78 for Feed 2, and +2.18+2.18 for the product. The product meter carries the largest standardised adjustment, but no single standardised adjustment is, by itself, decisive evidence against one particular meter.

5. Conclusion
  1. Formally reconciled flows (weighted least squares, balance imposed exactly): Feed 1 =96.9= 96.9, Feed 2 =49.2= 49.2, Product =146.1= 146.1 flow units, with the balance closing exactly.
  2. The 1010-unit imbalance is 2.792.79 times its own standard deviation of 3.583.58 units, and the global test gives Jmin⁡=7.79J_{\min} = 7.79 on one degree of freedom (p≈0.005p \approx 0.005). The imbalance is therefore not credibly explained by random meter error of the stated 2%2\% size alone.
  3. The reconciled values in item 1 should consequently be reported as the least-squares fit under the stated model, not as established true flows. The significant test result indicates that at least one model assumption is likely wrong: a gross error or bias in one meter (the product meter is the largest contributor to the adjustment, without being proven to be the faulty one), an unmeasured stream or a leak, a true standard deviation larger than 2%2\% of reading, correlated meter errors, or a departure from steady state with an unaccounted inventory change. Those causes should be investigated before the reconciled numbers are used for decisions that depend on their accuracy.

Data reconciliation and gross-error test — two feeds, one product

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. This is a listed weak type for three specific reasons, not as a general disclaimer:

  1. The problem states no explicit question. The calculation below assumes, as an assumed objective, the two questions the data can support: (a) is the imbalance larger than meter noise alone would explain (a gross-error / global test), and (b) if the noise model is nevertheless accepted, what flows close the balance with the smallest weighted corrections (weighted least-squares reconciliation). If the intended question was different (for example, which meter is faulty — see §6, that question is not answerable from one balance), the numerical answer changes in kind, not only in size.
  2. The result rests entirely on the meaning of "2 %". Whether 2 % of reading is one standard deviation, a 95 % limit, or a maximum error changes the significance verdict quantitatively (§5).
  3. A single overall balance carries no information that separates a faulty meter from an unmetered stream, a leak, or a hold-up change. Reconciliation spreads an error it cannot locate.

Confidence rating. Arithmetic, conditional on the stated noise model: high, about 90 % (the algebra is closed-form and was reproduced in code, §7). Inference about the plant — that a gross error exists and where it is: low, about 40 %, because it depends on the unverified meanings and independence in items 2 and 3 above (unverified — see §8).

The only relations used are the total material balance F1+F2−P=0F_1+F_2-P=0 (a conservation law, exact for total mass/moles at steady state with no accumulation) and the weighted least-squares / Gaussian test machinery (exact for the assumed linear-Gaussian model, with no restricted valid range beyond that assumption).
4. Raw imbalance and global (gross-error) test

Raw residual (measured inputs only):

r=m1+m2−m3=100+50−140=10 flow units, as given in the problem.r=m_1+m_2-m_3=100+50-140=10\ \text{flow units, as given in the problem.}

This is a statement about the model-plus-data, unverified against any plant record (§8).

A faulty meter cannot be identified from these data. With a single balance, the measurement test gives the same magnitude, ∣z∣=2.79|z|=2.79, for all three meters (a known algebraic property of one-constraint reconciliation, reproduced in the code in §7). Any statement naming one meter as the culprit would be unsupported. The largest correction falls on the product meter only because it has the largest σ\sigma, i.e. the scheme trusts it least — that is a property of the weights, not evidence against that meter.

Because the global test in §4 fails, the reconciled values in this section are a conditional least-squares answer ("if the noise model held, these flows"), not a validated estimate of the plant flows. Presenting them without §4 would be a misuse.

Checks performed; failures are reported, not repaired.

It returned reconciled flows 96.8847, 49.2212, 146.105996.8847,\ 49.2212,\ 146.1059 flow units, χ2=7.788\chi^2=7.788, z=2.791z=2.791, two-sided p=0.00526p=0.00526, and measurement-test values −2.791,−2.791,+2.791-2.791,-2.791,+2.791 — agreeing with the hand algebra in §4–§6 to the digits shown.

8. Audit as an experienced plant engineer (Prompt 4); primary sources (Checklist item 5)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. An unmetered material path, not a meter, causes the residual. Direction: a leak, vent, drain, or unmetered feed on the inlet side, or product retained as hold-up despite the nominal steady state, produces a positive rr of exactly this sign (feeds read more than product out). Rough size: fully sufficient — 10 flow units is 6.7 % of total feed (measured basis), a small leak or a modest level drift over the averaging period. Settling record: the unit piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) and a line-by-line stream inventory, plus tank/level records over the reading period. Primary source: the plant P&ID and historian level records for the actual unit — unverified; not seen for this solution.
  2. Meter bias from installation or fluid state, largest on the product meter. Direction: a volumetric product meter (orifice, turbine, vortex) reading low — fouling, a wrong density or discharge-coefficient correction, or operation off its calibrated range — inflates rr positively, matching the sign observed. Rough size: biases of 2–7 % of reading are the scale needed (the whole residual is 7.1 % of the product reading). Settling document/test: the meter calibration/proving certificates and the vendor datasheet for the installed meter, plus an in-situ proving or a check measurement with a reference meter. Primary source: vendor document and calibration certificate for the actual installed meters — unverified; the generic "2 %" in the problem is not a substitute for them.
  3. The stated σ\sigma understates field error, or the errors are correlated. Direction: common calibration rigs, a shared density/temperature correction, or drift since calibration make the true σr\sigma_r larger (or, with adverse correlation, the effective σr\sigma_r different in either direction, §5), which weakens or removes the gross-error verdict. Rough size: a true σ\sigma of 3 % of reading instead of 2 % already flips the 95 % verdict (§5). Settling record: the meters' calibration history and repeatability data, and the plant data-reconciliation or historian record for this balance over many periods — a persistent ≈\approx10-unit residual is bias; a residual scattering around zero with standard deviation ≈3.6\approx3.6 flow units is noise. Primary source: plant historian time series and calibration records — unverified.

In short: the single most decisive real-world check is the historian. One snapshot cannot separate bias from noise; a time series can.

9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: meter bias and drift (only random error is modelled); non-normal and time-correlated errors; process dynamics and hold-up change within the reading window; reaction generation/consumption if the flows are component flows; density/temperature/pressure corrections if the flows are volumetric; fouling and two-phase or off-range meter operation.
  • Information not available here: the installed meter types, sizes, and calibrated ranges; calibration dates and certificates; the P&ID and stream inventory; historian data; fluid identity and properties. These are plant/vendor records, some held in restricted databanks, and none were seen. Every plant-level claim in §8 is unverified until checked against them (Checklist item 5).
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: leaks under pressure, passing valves, level drift, meter fouling over time, and sampling/averaging artefacts in the control system.
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10 %: (i) true σ\sigma of 3 % of reading or more — flips the significance verdict and widens all intervals by 50 %; (ii) one meter carrying the whole error — moves a reconciled flow by up to ≈\approx10 % (feed 2: 49.2 vs 40 in its single-fault case, a 19 % change); (iii) volumetric readings at uncorrected differing conditions, or an unmetered stream of ≥\geq15 flow units — either exceeds 10 % of total feed; (iv) strongly correlated errors (§5), which move zz by far more than 10 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. What is the explicit question — significance test, reconciled flows for accounting, or fault isolation (which these data cannot do)?
  2. Are the flow units mass, molar, or volumetric, and if volumetric, at what common reference conditions?
  3. Is "2 %" a certified 1σ1\sigma from the installed meters' calibration certificates, or a catalogue figure?
  4. Does the historian show this residual as persistent (bias/leak) or as zero-centred scatter (noise)?
  5. Has every stream on the P&ID been accounted for, including vents, drains, and recycle?
  6. When were the three meters last proved, and did any read off its calibrated range during the period?

F3. Corrosion and Remaining Life

Response without the skill

Remaining Life of a Vessel — Corrosion Allowance Calculation

Definitions
  • Measured wall thickness, tmeasuredt_{\mathrm{measured}} (millimetres, mm): the current wall thickness of the vessel, measured as 12 mm.
  • Minimum required thickness, tmint_{\mathrm{min}} (millimetres, mm): the smallest wall thickness at which the vessel still meets its design requirements, given as 8 mm.
  • Available metal loss, tavailt_{\mathrm{avail}} (millimetres, mm): the thickness that can be lost by corrosion before the minimum required thickness is reached.
  • General corrosion rate, rr (millimetres per year, mm/year): the uniform rate of wall thinning, given as 0.15 mm/year.
  • Remaining life, LL (years, year): the time until the wall thickness falls to the minimum required thickness, if corrosion continues at the rate rr.
Method

The available metal loss, tavailt_{\mathrm{avail}}, is the difference between the measured wall thickness, tmeasuredt_{\mathrm{measured}}, and the minimum required thickness, tmint_{\mathrm{min}}:

tavail=tmeasured−tmint_{\mathrm{avail}} = t_{\mathrm{measured}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}

The remaining life, LL, is the available metal loss, tavailt_{\mathrm{avail}}, divided by the general corrosion rate, rr:

L=tavail/rL = t_{\mathrm{avail}} / r

This method assumes uniform (general) corrosion, a constant corrosion rate rr over the remaining life, and no other thinning mechanism.

Calculation

Available metal loss:

tavail=12 mm−8 mm=4 mmt_{\mathrm{avail}} = 12\ \mathrm{mm} - 8\ \mathrm{mm} = 4\ \mathrm{mm}

Remaining life:

L=4 mm/0.15 mm/year=26.666… yearL = 4\ \mathrm{mm} / 0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year} = 26.666\ldots\ \mathrm{year}

Result

The remaining life is approximately 26.7 years (26.67 years before rounding).

At the stated general corrosion rate of 0.15 mm/year, the vessel is expected to reach its minimum required thickness of 8 mm after about 26.7 years, at which point it must be retired, repaired, re-rated, or taken out of service in accordance with the applicable inspection code.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Remaining Life of a Corroding Vessel

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: the arithmetic is exact, but the model is a single linear, uniform (general) corrosion rate applied into the future. Real remaining life is controlled by whether that rate stays constant, whether loss is uniform rather than localised (pitting, crevice, erosion-corrosion), and whether the stated minimum required thickness already contains all allowances. A small error in the rate produces a proportionally large error in life because life varies as 1 divided by the rate.

Confidence rating: high for the arithmetic, low-to-moderate for the prediction. The central value below is a conditional estimate — correct if the inputs and the linear model hold — not a fitness-for-service determination.

2. Inputs, labelled at point of use
  • Measured wall thickness, tactualt_{actual} = 12 mm — measured (stated in the problem as measured; instrument, location, number of readings, and measurement uncertainty not supplied).
  • Minimum required thickness, tmint_{min} = 8 mm — given (basis not supplied: see Section 4).
  • Available metal loss, Δt=tactual−tmin\Delta t = t_{actual} - t_{min} = 12 − 8 = 4 mm — derived from a measured value and a given value.
  • General corrosion rate, rr = 0.15 mm/year — given (provenance not supplied: whether it is measured from successive thickness surveys, fitted to survey data, estimated from a corrosion table, or assumed is not stated; it is treated here as given, and a plausible range is carried in Section 3).
  • Model: remaining life L=Δt/rL = \Delta t / r, with LL in years, Δt\Delta t in mm, and rr in mm/year — assumed linear, uniform, time-invariant loss. This is the standard remaining-life form used in in-service inspection practice (e.g. API 510 / API 570 style remaining-life calculations); that attribution is unverified against the current code edition in this solution (see Section 5).

No thermophysical properties, fitted correlations, or rules of thumb beyond the linear model above are used.

3. Solution and range

Central value, using the given rate:

L=Δtr=4 mm0.15 mm/year=26.7 yearsL = \frac{\Delta t}{r} = \frac{4\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 26.7\ \mathrm{years}

Range, not a single value (Prompt 1). The dominant uncertainty is rr. No uncertainty for rr was supplied, so an assumed plausible band of ±33 % about the given value, i.e. rr = 0.10 to 0.20 mm/year, is carried explicitly as an assumption, not as data:

Case rr (mm/year), status L=4/rL = 4 / r (years) Change from central
Low rate 0.10, assumed end of band 40.0 +50 %
Central 0.15, given 26.7 0 %
High rate 0.20, assumed end of band 20.0 −25 %

Reported result: LL = 26.7 years central, with a plausible range of 20 to 40 years for rr in 0.10–0.20 mm/year.

If the rate uncertainty is larger, the range widens asymmetrically (because L∝1/rL \propto 1/r): rr = 0.075 mm/year (half the given rate) gives 53.3 years (+100 %); rr = 0.225 mm/year (1.5 times the given rate) gives 17.8 years (−33 %).

Sensitivity of the result to each guess / input

Executed in Python (Section 6 gives the check):

  • Rate rr: −20 % in rr (0.12 mm/year) → 33.3 years, +25 %; +33 % in rr (0.20 mm/year) → 20.0 years, −25 %. Life is inversely proportional to rr, so a percentage error in rr moves life by roughly the same percentage, in the opposite direction, and more on the low-rate side.
  • Available metal Δt\Delta t: ±0.5 mm on the measured thickness (an assumed survey tolerance, not supplied) gives Δt\Delta t = 3.5–4.5 mm → LL = 23.3–30.0 years, −12.5 % to +12.5 %. Δt\Delta t = 3.0 mm → 20.0 years (−25 %); Δt\Delta t = 5.0 mm → 33.3 years (+25 %). Life is directly proportional to Δt\Delta t.

Combined adverse case (assumed): Δt\Delta t = 3.5 mm and rr = 0.20 mm/year → LL = 17.5 years. Combined favourable case: Δt\Delta t = 4.5 mm and rr = 0.10 mm/year → LL = 45.0 years. These bound the calculation but do not bound localised attack (Section 7).

4. Missing quantities — not taken in silence (Prompt 2)

The problem as stated is solvable only under the assumptions below. Each missing quantity is listed, with the alternative(s) solved or flagged:

  1. Basis of tmint_{min} (8 mm, given). Not stated whether it is the pressure-design minimum alone, or whether it already includes structural, external-load, and future corrosion allowances, and whether a retirement thickness above tmint_{min} applies. - If 8 mm is the true retirement thickness: result as above, 20–40 years. - If a further allowance must be added to 8 mm, Δt\Delta t falls by that allowance and life falls proportionally (e.g. 1 mm extra allowance → Δt\Delta t = 3 mm → 20.0 years at the given rate).
  2. Reference state / location of the 12 mm reading. Not stated whether 12 mm is the minimum reading over the vessel, a single-point reading, or a nominal/average value; nor the corrosion monitoring location it represents. Life must be governed by the thinnest relevant location. If 12 mm is an average and the local minimum is lower, life is shorter in direct proportion to the lower Δt\Delta t.
  3. Provenance and time basis of rr. Not stated whether rr is a long-term rate (from original thickness), a short-term rate (between the last two surveys), or a table value. Inspection practice normally uses the greater of the short- and long-term rates; if the supplied 0.15 mm/year is only one of them and the other is higher, life is overestimated. Solved here with 0.15 as given, with the band in Section 3 covering rates up to 0.20 mm/year.
  4. Pressure / operating basis. No design or operating pressure, temperature, or contents are given, so tmint_{min} cannot be independently recomputed and no check of it is possible in this solution. tmint_{min} is accepted as given — unverified.
  5. Composition / material basis. Material grade and process composition are not given, so whether a "general" rate is the correct damage model cannot be judged. If the mechanism is localised, the general-rate calculation does not apply (Section 7).
  6. Per-pass / overall, conversion bases: not applicable to this problem; no reaction or separation is involved.
  7. Inspection-interval rule. Not asked for, but commonly the next inspection is set at a fraction of remaining life (often half in API 510 style practice — unverified against the current edition here). Half of the central life is 13.3 years; half of the low end of the range (20 years) is 10.0 years.
5. Primary source that settles the point

The settling sources are: (a) the vessel's thickness survey records on the actual equipment (successive ultrasonic thickness readings at defined monitoring locations), which settle tactualt_{actual} and the measured short- and long-term rates; (b) the vessel design record / code calculation (the applicable construction code edition, e.g. ASME BPVC Section VIII, and the in-service code, e.g. API 510 for vessels) which settles tmint_{min} and any retirement thickness; and (c) a damage-mechanism review (e.g. API 571) for whether general corrosion is the governing mechanism. Every claim in this solution that rests on those sources — the linear remaining-life form, the short- vs long-term rate convention, and any half-life inspection interval — is marked unverified until checked against the current editions and the actual survey records. No agreement with any other AI model is offered or used as verification.

6. Independent verification (Prompt 3)

Checks performed, by routes independent of the headline division:

  1. Executed code. Python: 4.0 / 0.15 = 26.6667 years; the table in Section 3 and all sensitivity values in Section 3 were computed in the same run and match the hand values. Check passes.
  2. Dimensional check. mm divided by (mm/year) gives years. Passes.
  3. Limiting cases (known by sight). r→0r \to 0 → L→∞L \to \infty (no corrosion, no life limit from this mechanism): the formula gives this. Δt=0\Delta t = 0 (already at tmint_{min}) → L=0L = 0: the formula gives this. Doubling Δt\Delta t doubles LL; doubling rr halves LL (26.7 → 13.3 years at rr = 0.30 mm/year). All pass.
  4. Balance closure. Not applicable as a material/energy balance; the analogous closure here is arithmetic: $r \times L = 0.15 \times 26.6667 = 4.0mm,recoveringmm, recovering\Delta t$ exactly (closure error 0 mm). Passes.
  5. Correlation valid range. No fitted correlation is used; the linear model itself is valid only while the mechanism, environment, temperature, and operating conditions that produced the historical rate persist, and only for uniform loss. That condition cannot be checked from the data supplied — reported as an open check, not passed silently.

No check that was run failed. The model-validity check in item 5 is open, for the reason stated.

7. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from how the built vessel behaves:

  1. Localised rather than general loss. A general rate averages loss; pits, weld-area attack, or under-deposit corrosion can penetrate locally much faster. Direction: true life shorter, potentially by a large factor at the deepest local site — a local rate twice the general rate halves the local life to about 13 years at the central numbers. Settled by: a thickness survey grid / ultrasonic scan at monitoring locations, pit-depth measurement, and the damage-mechanism review (API 571; API 579-1 / ASME FFS-1 for local metal loss assessment).
  2. Rate change with time and operation. The historical rate may not persist after changes in feed composition, temperature, inhibitor dosing, or duty; corrosion is often not linear in time (protective scales can slow it; scale loss or an upset can accelerate it). Direction: either way; acceleration is the safety-relevant case. A sustained rate of 0.30 mm/year would give 13.3 years, half the central value. Settled by: successive survey history on this vessel showing the rate trend, plus process / operating records for the survey period.
  3. tmint_{min} and measurement reality in the built vessel. The as-built vessel has forming tolerances, welds, nozzles, and stress concentrations; the governing location may not be the surveyed shell location, and ultrasonic readings carry instrument and surface-condition error (an assumed ±0.5 mm here moves life by ±12.5 %). Direction: governing life usually shorter than a single-location shell calculation suggests. Settled by: the design calculation and data report for the vessel, the survey procedure and calibration record, and readings at nozzles and other governing locations.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: localised corrosion, erosion-corrosion, corrosion under insulation, fatigue, creep (if at elevated temperature), brittle fracture, external corrosion, and any damage at welds, nozzles, and supports; future process changes; inspection uncertainty beyond the assumed tolerance above.
  • Information not accessible here: the vessel's design code edition and calculation, its survey history, material certification, and operating records — held in plant / vendor records and in restricted code documents not consulted for this solution.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: upsets, excursions, inhibitor interruptions, and start-up / shut-down conditions, none of which a steady historical rate represents.
  • Conditions changing the answer by more than 10 %: any change of about 10 % or more in rr (≈ 0.015 mm/year or more) or in Δt\Delta t (0.4 mm or more) changes life by roughly 10 % or more; a change of damage mechanism, or discovery of a thinner governing location, changes it by far more. Specifically: rr at 0.20 mm/year gives −25 %; 1 mm less available metal gives −25 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is 12 mm the minimum reading at the governing location, from a calibrated survey, and what is its uncertainty?
  2. What does the 8 mm minimum consist of, which code edition produced it, and is a retirement thickness above it required?
  3. Is 0.15 mm/year the short-term rate, the long-term rate, or a table value — and what is the other rate from the survey history?
  4. Has a damage-mechanism review confirmed general corrosion as the governing mechanism, with no localised attack found?
  5. Have operating conditions since the rate was established changed in any way that would change the rate?
  6. What inspection interval and retirement criterion will actually be applied, and under which in-service code?
Result

Available metal loss Δt\Delta t = 4 mm (derived from a measured 12 mm and a given 8 mm minimum). At the given general corrosion rate rr = 0.15 mm/year, remaining life L=Δt/rL = \Delta t / r = 26.7 years central, 20–40 years over the assumed rate band of 0.10–0.20 mm/year, conditional on uniform, linear corrosion at an unchanged rate and on the 8 mm value being the true retirement thickness — all unverified against the vessel's survey records and the current code editions named in Section 5.

G1. Cost of Building a Plant

Response without the skill

Capital Cost Estimate by Capacity Scaling

Given data
  • C1C_1 is the known capital cost of the reference unit, in million United States dollars (USD), where C1=10C_1 = 10 million USD.
  • S1S_1 is the capacity of the reference unit, in kilotonnes per year (kt yr−1\mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}), where S1=50 kt yr−1S_1 = 50\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}.
  • S2S_2 is the capacity of the new unit, in kilotonnes per year (kt yr−1\mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}), where S2=100 kt yr−1S_2 = 100\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}.
  • C2C_2 is the capital cost of the new unit to be estimated, in million United States dollars (USD).
  • nn is the capacity scaling exponent, dimensionless, where n=0.6n = 0.6.

The two units are for the same process.

Method

Capital cost scaling by the six-tenths rule, for n=0.6n = 0.6, is:

C2=C1(S2S1)nC_2 = C_1 \left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^n

where every symbol in the equation has been defined above: C2C_2 and C1C_1 are in million USD, S2S_2 and S1S_1 are in kt yr−1\mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}, and nn is dimensionless. The ratio S2/S1S_2/S_1 is dimensionless, so the units of C2C_2 are the same as the units of C1C_1.

Calculation

First, the capacity ratio, dimensionless:

S2S1=100 kt yr−150 kt yr−1=2.0\frac{S_2}{S_1} = \frac{100\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}}{50\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}}} = 2.0

Next, the ratio raised to the exponent nn, dimensionless:

(S2S1)n=2.00.6=1.516\left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^n = 2.0^{0.6} = 1.516

Then:

C2=10 million USD×1.516=15.16 million USDC_2 = 10\ \text{million USD} \times 1.516 = 15.16\ \text{million USD}

Rounded to three significant figures, consistent with the input data:

C2≈15.2 million USDC_2 \approx 15.2\ \text{million USD}

Adjustment for year and location

The problem statement states that the new unit is in a different year and location from the reference unit, but it supplies no cost index values and no location factors. A year and location adjustment therefore cannot be evaluated numerically from the data given.

In general, the scaled cost above would be adjusted as:

C2,adjusted=C2×I2I1×L2L1C_{2,\mathrm{adjusted}} = C_2 \times \frac{I_2}{I_1} \times \frac{L_2}{L_1}

where C2,adjustedC_{2,\mathrm{adjusted}} is the adjusted capital cost of the new unit, in million USD; C2C_2 is the scaled capital cost calculated above, in million USD; I1I_1 is the cost index (for example, a plant cost index) at the year of the reference cost, dimensionless; I2I_2 is the cost index at the year of the new estimate, dimensionless; L1L_1 is the location factor for the reference location, dimensionless; and L2L_2 is the location factor for the new location, dimensionless.

With no values of I2I_2, I1I_1, L2L_2, or L1L_1 provided, the ratios I2/I1I_2/I_1 and L2/L1L_2/L_1 cannot be computed, and no numerical value for C2,adjustedC_{2,\mathrm{adjusted}} can be stated. Inventing index or location values would be unsupported.

Result

The capacity-scaled capital cost of the 100 kt yr−1100\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}} unit is approximately 15.2 million USD, on the same year and location basis as the 1010 million USD reference cost for the 50 kt yr−150\ \mathrm{kt\,yr^{-1}} unit.

This is an order-of-magnitude / study estimate based solely on capacity scaling with n=0.6n = 0.6. It assumes the same process, same scope, and same technology for both units, and it does not include any escalation for a different year or any correction for a different location, for which no data were given.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Capital Cost Estimate — Capacity Scaling from 50 to 100 kilotonnes per year

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The calculation transfers a capital cost across capacity, time, and place with a single generic power law. Two corrections that the problem statement says are relevant — a cost-index correction for the change of year and a location-factor correction for the change of place — are named by the words "in a different year and location" but no values for them are supplied. The scaling exponent is a rule of thumb, not a relation fitted to this process or to the equipment that dominates its cost. The result is therefore a screening estimate, not a design or sanction estimate.

Confidence rating: low. Confidence is high in the arithmetic for a stated set of inputs (Section 4, verified in code). Confidence is low in the numerical result as a prediction of the built cost, because the year, location, and scope corrections are missing and each can move the result by more than the capacity correction itself is precise to. No value in this solution that rests on a cost index, a location factor, or a fitted exponent for this specific process has been checked against the primary source for that quantity; all such values are marked unverified below.

Property values, rules of thumb, and fitted relations used:

  • The power law in Section 4. Source: the standard capacity-scaling relation used in process economics textbooks and cost-engineering practice. Valid range: it is a screening relation, normally applied for capacity ratios of roughly 0.5 to 2 for the same process, same technology, and same cost scope, with no change in the number of parallel trains. The ratio here, S2/S1=2S_2/S_1 = 2, is at the upper end of that customary range. Unverified against a databank for this specific process.
  • Plausible range for nn: 0.5 to 0.7 is used for the main range in Section 5, with 0.4 to 0.9 shown as a wider sensitivity. Individual equipment items commonly scale with exponents from about 0.4 to about 0.9 depending on equipment type; a whole plant is a cost-weighted mix. This range is estimated from general cost-engineering practice, not fitted to this process. Unverified against the primary source named in Section 7.

The solution needs the following quantities, none of which is supplied. No value is taken in silence; each is either carried symbolically or solved under stated alternatives in Sections 4 and 5.

Whether C1C_1 is purchased-equipment cost, total installed cost, inside-battery-limits cost, or total plant cost including offsites, utilities, land, and contingency. C2C_2 can only inherit the same basis; a comparison or a funding request normally needs total plant cost, which cannot be obtained from this calculation if C1C_1 is on a narrower basis.
  4. Capacity basis. Whether kt yr−1^{-1} is nameplate capacity, design capacity, or sustained achieved throughput, and whether the tonne is a metric tonne (the normal reading of kilotonne; assumed here). 4. Base calculation — capacity correction alone

The scaling relation, with the year and location corrections carried explicitly so that their absence is visible, is

C2=C1(S2S1)n(I2I1)FC_2 = C_1 \left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^{n} \left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right) F

Setting the two missing corrections to 1 (an assumption, stated here, not a given) gives the capacity-only value:

C2=10×(10050)0.6=10×20.6=10×1.516=15.16 USD millionC_2 = 10 \times \left(\frac{100}{50}\right)^{0.6} = 10 \times 2^{0.6} = 10 \times 1.516 = 15.16\ \text{USD million}

Base result (assumed I2/I1=1I_2/I_1 = 1, assumed F=1F = 1): approximately 15.2 USD million, on the same cost basis, scope, year price level, and location cost level as the known unit.

This is the only single value the supplied data support, and it answers a narrower question than the one posed: it is the cost at the old year's prices and the old location's cost level. It must not be quoted without that qualification.

Sensitivity of this value to each guess, in percent:

  • I2/I1I_2/I_1: linear. A ratio of 1.10 in place of the assumed 1.00 moves the result +10%+10\%; a ratio of 0.90 moves it −10%-10\%.
  • FF: linear, in the same way as the index ratio.
  • C1C_1: linear. Any error or scope difference in the given 10 USD million carries through at the same percentage.
  • Capacity basis: no effect on the ratio if both capacities share a basis; if the 100 kt yr−1^{-1} figure is nameplate and the 50 kt yr−1^{-1} figure is achieved throughput (or the reverse), the true ratio differs from 2 and the result moves as (true ratio / 2)0.6^{0.6}.

7. Primary sources that settle the open points

Each claim below rests on the named source and is unverified until checked against it:

  • Exponent for this process: the owner's or licensor's cost databank for built units of the same process at different capacities, or an itemised equipment-cost build-up for both sizes. This settles nn and whether a single train reaches 100 kt yr−1^{-1}.
  • Year correction: the cost index specified for the estimate — for example the Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index (CEPCI), published in Chemical Engineering magazine — read in the two relevant years from the publisher's record, not from a secondary summary.
  • Location correction: a current location-factor source for the two named locations (for example a published cost-engineering location- factor compilation, or contractor rates for the actual site), or vendor and contractor quotations at the new location.
  • Scope and basis of C1C_1: the original estimate document for the 50 kt yr−1^{-1} unit, stating its battery limits, inclusions, contingency, and price date.
8. Audit by a skilled engineer — Prompt 4

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Train limit and discrete equipment sizes. The power law assumes smooth growth of one train. If the largest available item of a key equipment type (compressor, reactor, column internals, heat exchanger) is reached before 100 kt yr−1^{-1}, the plant is built as two parallel trains and cost rises in a step toward proportionality (nn effectively near 1 for the duplicated section). Direction: built cost higher than the estimate. Rough size: +10%+10\% to +30%+30\% on the affected scope if full duplication is required. Settled by: vendor size limits and quotations for the largest items at both capacities.
  2. Change of standards and technology between the two years. The index corrects prices, not requirements. Environmental, safety, and code requirements in force at the new year and location can add scope that the old unit does not contain. Direction: built cost higher. Rough size: commonly several percent, and above 10%10\% where a new emissions or safety system is required. Settled by: the code and permit requirements in force at the new site and date, compared item by item with the scope of the original estimate.
  3. Site and location reality versus a single factor FF. A single factor averages labour rate and productivity, ground conditions, weather window, logistics, and local content rules. Any one of these can dominate on a specific site. Direction: either direction; adverse ground or low labour productivity is the common overrun case. Rough size: ±10%\pm 10\% to 20%20\% of installed cost. Settled by: a site survey and geotechnical record, and contractor labour rates and productivity data for the actual location.
9. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model:

  • Escalation and location effects (treated only as assumed multipliers in Section 5, because the data are missing).
  • Change in number of trains, equipment size steps, sparing philosophy, materials of construction, design pressure or temperature, and process conditions.
  • Scope items that may or may not be in C1C_1: offsites, utilities, land, owner's costs, licensing fees, start-up, working capital, financing during construction, taxes and duties, and contingency.
  • Schedule effects: construction duration, weather, and market conditions for equipment and labour at the time of purchase.

Information not available here: the owner's cost databank for this process, vendor quotations, the original estimate document for the known unit, and any restricted cost-index or location-factor databank beyond published summary values. None of these was consulted; claims resting on them are marked unverified in Section 7.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: achieved throughput relative to nameplate (which changes the effective capacity ratio), fouling and degradation allowances, and maintenance-driven sparing — all of which can change the built scope relative to a nameplate scaling.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 percent:

  • I2/I1I_2/I_1 above 1.10 or below 0.90 (a few years of typical escalation is sufficient).
  • FF above 1.10 or below 0.90.
  • True nn above about 0.75 (gives more than +10%+10\% against the base) or a step to two trains.
  • C1C_1 found to be on a different scope basis from the cost required (for example equipment-only versus total installed), which changes the result by far more than 10%10\%.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What are the year, price basis, location, and exact scope of the 10 USD million figure, per its original estimate document?
  2. What are the target year and location, and what index ratio and location factor, from which named primary sources, apply?
  3. Is 100 kt yr−1^{-1} achievable in a single train of this process, per vendor size limits?
  4. Is the exponent 0.6 supported by cost data for this process, or is it the generic rule of thumb?
  5. What accuracy class and contingency are required for the decision this estimate supports, and does a screening power-law estimate meet that class?
