G2. Heat Recovery and Energy Cost

Response without the skill

Annual Hot-Utility Cost

Given data
  • ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} is the minimum temperature approach in heat recovery, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}): ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}.
  • QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} is the hot-utility duty at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}, in megawatts (MW\mathrm{MW}): QH=20 MWQ_{\mathrm{H}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW}.
  • pHp_{\mathrm{H}} is the hot-utility price, in United States dollars per megawatt hour (USD/MWh\mathrm{USD/MWh}): pH=25 USD/MWhp_{\mathrm{H}} = 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh}.
  • topt_{\mathrm{op}} is the operating time, in hours per year (h/year\mathrm{h/year}): top=8,000 h/yeart_{\mathrm{op}} = 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year}.
Method

CHC_{\mathrm{H}} is the annual hot-utility cost, in United States dollars per year (USD/year\mathrm{USD/year}). It is the product of the hot-utility duty, the utility price, and the operating time:

CH=QH×pH×topC_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \times p_{\mathrm{H}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}}

The value of QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} is already stated at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}, so no further heat-recovery calculation is required.

Calculation

CH=20 MW×25 USD/MWh×8,000 h/yearC_{\mathrm{H}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW} \times 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} \times 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year}

CH=4,000,000 USD/yearC_{\mathrm{H}} = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}

Unit check: MW×USD/MWh×h/year=USD/year\mathrm{MW} \times \mathrm{USD/MWh} \times \mathrm{h/year} = \mathrm{USD/year}, as required.

Result

The annual hot-utility cost at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K} is 4,000,000 USD/year4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}, i.e. 4.0 million United States dollars per year.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Annual Hot-Utility Cost at a Minimum Temperature Approach of 10 K

Symbols
  • Minimum temperature approach in heat recovery, ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (kelvin, K): the smallest permitted temperature difference between hot and cold streams in the heat-recovery design.
  • Hot-utility duty, QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (megawatts, MW; 1 MW = 10610^{6} watts, W): the rate at which heat is supplied by the hot utility.
  • Utility price, pp (United States dollars per megawatt hour, USD/MWh): the unit price charged for hot-utility energy.
  • Operating time, topt_{\mathrm{op}} (hours per year, h/year): the time per year over which the stated duty is supplied.
  • Annual hot-utility energy, EHE_{\mathrm{H}} (megawatt hours per year, MWh/year): the hot-utility energy supplied in one year.
  • Annual hot-utility cost, CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (United States dollars per year, USD/year): the cost sought.
  • Fractional change, δ\delta (dimensionless, expressed as a percentage, %): the fractional change in CHC_{\mathrm{H}} caused by a fractional change in one input.
1. Weakness and Confidence

Weakness: the arithmetic is exact, but the representation of a real plant is weak. The stated QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) is a single duty figure at the stated ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K). No information is given on whether QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) is a pinch-analysis target, a design duty, a time-averaged operating duty, or a peak duty; on whether pp (USD/MWh) is a delivered, marginal, or fuel-only price; or on whether topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) is already the effective full-duty operating time. The result is therefore an exact product of the stated inputs and, at the same time, only an estimate of an actual annual utility bill.

Confidence rating:

  • Confidence in the arithmetic, conditional on the stated inputs: high (9/10). The relation is a direct product with no fitted relation, no property value, and no correlation.
  • Confidence that the result equals an actual plant's annual hot-utility expenditure in a given year: low to moderate (4/10), because duty variation with time, price variation, boiler or heater efficiency if pp (USD/MWh) is a fuel price, start-up and shutdown, and off-design operation are not specified.

No claim in this solution rests on agreement with another model or another AI system; agreement of that kind is not used as verification.

No thermophysical property, rule of thumb, or fitted relation is used: cost follows from the definition of energy as power multiplied by time, and from the definition of total price as unit price multiplied by quantity.

Role of ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K): ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K), given, does not enter the cost product directly. Its role is already contained in QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), given, because a hot-utility duty in a heat-recovery study is normally the duty that remains after heat recovery at the stated ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K). A different ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) would give a different QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) and therefore a different CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year), but the function relating QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) to ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) depends on the process stream data, which are not supplied. No such function is invented here.

3. Missing Quantities

The problem as stated can be solved as a product, but the following quantities, needed to interpret the product as a real annual bill, are missing. None is taken in silence; the base case uses the interpretation stated, and Section 5 solves under plausible alternatives.

  1. Basis of QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW): target (pinch), design, nameplate, peak, or time-averaged operating duty. Missing. Base case assumption: QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) is the constant, time-averaged duty over topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year). Alternative solved in Section 5: duty 10% below or above the stated value.
  2. Basis of pp (USD/MWh): delivered steam or hot-oil energy at the battery limit, or fuel energy into a boiler or fired heater. Missing. Base case assumption: pp (USD/MWh) is the price per unit of delivered hot-utility energy, so no efficiency factor applies. Alternative in Section 5 and Section 7: if pp (USD/MWh) is a fuel price, cost must be divided by the generation efficiency.
  3. Reference state: not applicable to a cost product. No enthalpy, no composition, and no conversion appears, so no thermodynamic reference state, composition basis, or per-pass versus overall distinction is required for the arithmetic. These bases would be required to recompute QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) from stream data, and those stream data are absent.
  4. Pressure basis: not applicable to the cost product for the same reason; it would be required to recompute QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) from steam tables or stream data.
  5. Price constancy and inclusions: whether pp (USD/MWh) is constant over the year and whether it includes delivery losses, demand or capacity charges, taxes, carbon charges, water treatment, and boiler blowdown losses. Missing. Base case assumption: pp (USD/MWh) is constant and all-inclusive for delivered energy.
  6. Effective operating time: whether topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) already excludes downtime and part-load periods. Missing. Base case assumption: topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) is the effective full-duty time. Alternative in Section 5: 7,500 h/year.
  7. Utility identity: steam, hot oil, or direct firing. Missing. It does not change the product, but it changes which of the exclusions in Section 8 matter and which primary source in Section 6 settles the price basis.
4. Calculation

Annual hot-utility energy, from the definition of energy as power multiplied by time, with QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) given and topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) given:

EH=QH×top=20 MW×8,000 h/year=160,000 MWh/yearE_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW} \times 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year} = 160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year}

Annual hot-utility cost, from the definition of total price as unit price multiplied by quantity, with pp (USD/MWh) given:

CH=EH×p=160,000 MWh/year×25 USD/MWh=4,000,000 USD/yearC_{\mathrm{H}} = E_{\mathrm{H}} \times p = 160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year} \times 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}

Point result, conditional on the stated inputs and the base-case assumptions in Section 3:

CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) = 4.0 million USD/year (4,000,000 USD/year).

Unit check: MW multiplied by h/year gives MWh/year; MWh/year multiplied by USD/MWh gives USD/year. Units close.

5. Result as a Range, and Sensitivity to Each Guess

The point result in Section 4 is reported with ranges because the interpretive inputs in Section 3 are assumed, not given.

5.1 Rounding range of the stated inputs

The stated values carry two significant figures. Treating QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), given, as 19.5 MW to 20.5 MW and pp (USD/MWh), given, as 24.5 USD/MWh to 25.5 USD/MWh, with topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year), given, held at 8,000 h/year:

  • Low end: 19.5 MW ×\times 8,000 h/year ×\times 24.5 USD/MWh = 3,822,000 USD/year.
  • High end: 20.5 MW ×\times 8,000 h/year ×\times 25.5 USD/MWh = 4,182,000 USD/year.

Rounding range: 3.8 million USD/year to 4.2 million USD/year.

5.2 Plausible operating range

Assumed ranges, each labelled assumed and chosen as plausible plant variation, not as data: QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), assumed range 18 MW to 22 MW (the stated value ±\pm10%); pp (USD/MWh), assumed range 20 USD/MWh to 30 USD/MWh (the stated value ±\pm20%); topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year), assumed range 7,500 h/year to 8,000 h/year (the stated value, with a lower end allowing for downtime or part-load operation not already excluded).

  • Low end: 18 MW ×\times 7,500 h/year ×\times 20 USD/MWh = 2,700,000 USD/year.
  • High end: 22 MW ×\times 8,000 h/year ×\times 30 USD/MWh = 5,280,000 USD/year.

Plausible operating range: 2.7 million USD/year to 5.3 million USD/year, with the conditional point value 4.0 million USD/year inside it. This range is a scenario range built from the assumed end values stated in this section; it is not a statistical confidence interval, because no distribution for any input is supplied.

5.3 Sensitivity: how much each guess moves the result

CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) is proportional to each of QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), pp (USD/MWh), and topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) separately, so a fractional change δ\delta (%) in any one input, the others held constant, produces the same fractional change δ\delta (%) in CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year). There is no damping and no amplification.

6. Primary Source That Settles the Point

Unverified until checked against the primary source: the claim that 4.0 million USD/year is the plant's actual annual hot-utility cost.

The sources that settle each open point are:

  • The utility supply contract, tariff sheet, or vendor quotation for the actual utility at the actual site: settles pp (USD/MWh), its basis (delivered energy or fuel), and its inclusions. Status: not supplied; unverified.
  • The plant historian or utility meter records for the actual unit: settle the time-averaged QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) and the effective topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year). Status: not supplied; unverified.
  • The pinch-analysis or heat-exchanger-network design record for the process: settles whether QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) is a target at ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) of 10 K or a built-network duty, and how QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) changes with ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K). Status: not supplied; unverified.

Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor for the case in question supersede the assumed ranges in Section 5.

7. Verification by an Independent Route

Checks performed in executed code (Python, direct arithmetic), independent of the hand calculation in Section 4 in the sense that the product was recomputed by a second route and the limiting cases were evaluated separately:

  1. Direct product, executed: 20 MW ×\times 8,000 h/year = 160,000 MWh/year; 160,000 MWh/year ×\times 25 USD/MWh = 4,000,000 USD/year. Matches Section 4.
  2. Independent route, hourly cost: cost rate = QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), given, ×\times pp (USD/MWh), given, = 20 ×\times 25 = 500 USD/h. Annual cost = 500 USD/h ×\times 8,000 h/year = 4,000,000 USD/year. Matches Section 4. A daily cross-check gives 500 USD/h ×\times 24 h = 12,000 USD per operating day, and 8,000 h/year corresponds to 333.3 operating days per year; 12,000 USD per day ×\times 333.3 days per year = 4,000,000 USD/year, within rounding.
  3. Limiting case, zero duty: QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) = 0 MW gives CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) = 0 USD/year, as required.
  4. Limiting case, zero time: topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) = 0 h/year gives CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) = 0 USD/year, as required.
  5. Limiting case, unit price and unit time: QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) = 20 MW, pp (USD/MWh) = 1 USD/MWh, topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) = 1 h/year gives 20 USD/year, as required by the definitions.
  6. Balance closure: no material balance applies. The energy statement is the definition EH=QH×topE_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}} (MWh/year, MW, h/year respectively); it closes exactly, with zero residual, because no conversion or loss term is in the base-case model. The absence of a loss term is an assumption (Section 3, item 2), not a verified closure against plant data.
  7. Correlation range check: no fitted relation or correlation is used, so no validity range applies. The linear product holds for any non-negative values of the three inputs.

No check failed. The checks verify the arithmetic and the definitions only; they do not verify that the inputs describe a real plant, which is the unverified part identified in Section 6.

8. Audit: Points Most Likely to Differ in Built Equipment

Three points, as a plant engineer would raise them:

  1. Target duty versus built-network duty. A QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) obtained as a pinch target at ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) of 10 K is a minimum for an ideal network. A built network with a finite number of exchangers, forbidden or required matches, fouling allowances, and control margins normally uses more hot utility. Direction: actual cost higher than the point result. Rough size: commonly of the order of 5% to 20% above target for the utility duty, i.e. about 200,000 USD/year to 800,000 USD/year on this case, stated as an estimated range, not a measured value. Settling document: the built network's design record and the unit's utility meter records.
  2. Duty is not constant in operation. Feed rate and composition, ambient conditions, exchanger fouling, and start-ups move the instantaneous duty; an annual bill follows the time integral of duty, not a single duty multiplied by calendar-based hours unless topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) is already the effective full-duty time. Direction: either direction; part-load and downtime lower the integral, fouling and off-design operation raise the duty per unit of throughput. Rough size: ±\pm10% on CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) is a plausible assumed band, as used in Section 5. Settling record: historian trends of utility flow integrated over a representative year.
  3. Price basis and generation efficiency. If pp (USD/MWh), given, is a fuel price rather than a delivered-energy price, boiler or heater efficiency, blowdown, condensate loss, and distribution loss raise the cost per unit of delivered heat. Direction: actual cost higher. Rough size: at an assumed efficiency of 0.85 (dimensionless), ++17.6%, i.e. about 4,710,000 USD/year; at an assumed efficiency of 0.80 (dimensionless), ++25%, i.e. 5,000,000 USD/year. Settling document: the utility contract or tariff stating the basis, and the boiler or heater performance test record stating the efficiency on the same basis (lower or higher heating value) as the price.
9. What Is Not Covered

Effects not in the model:

  • Capital cost of the heat-exchanger network, and the trade-off between capital and utility cost as ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) changes. Only the utility operating cost at one ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) is computed; no optimum ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) can be obtained from this calculation.
  • Cold-utility cost, electricity, and any refrigeration cost.
  • Boiler or heater efficiency, distribution and condensate losses, blowdown, water treatment, and maintenance, except as the sensitivity in Sections 5.3 and 8.
  • Price escalation, price volatility within the year, demand or capacity charges, taxes, and carbon charges, except insofar as pp (USD/MWh), given, is assumed all-inclusive.
  • Start-up, shutdown, turndown, fouling transients, and control behaviour.
  • Environmental emissions and their cost, and any credit for exported steam or power.

Information not available to this calculation: the utility contract and tariff, the stream data behind QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), the network design record, and metered operating data. These are held by the plant or vendor and are listed in Section 6.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%:

  • pp (USD/MWh) moves by more than 10% from 25 USD/MWh, i.e. outside 22.5 USD/MWh to 27.5 USD/MWh.
  • The time-averaged QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) differs by more than 10% from 20 MW, i.e. outside 18 MW to 22 MW, for any of the reasons in Section 8.
  • topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) falls below 7,200 h/year on an effective full-duty basis.
  • pp (USD/MWh) proves to be a fuel price with a generation efficiency below about 0.91 (dimensionless), which alone raises the cost by more than 10%.
  • ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) is changed and QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) is recomputed from stream data: the size of this effect cannot be stated without those data, and it can exceed 10%.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW), given as 20 MW, a pinch target, a design duty, or a metered time average, and at what ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) was it obtained?
  2. Is pp (USD/MWh), given as 25 USD/MWh, priced per unit of delivered heat or per unit of fuel, on which heating-value basis, and what does it include?
  3. Is topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year), given as 8,000 h/year, the effective full-duty time, or a calendar-based figure from which downtime and part-load periods must still be removed?
  4. Is a utility operating cost alone sufficient for the decision, or is the network capital cost at this ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) also required?
  5. Which primary source in Section 6 has been checked, and does its value replace any assumed range in Section 5?
Result

Conditional on the given inputs QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) = 20 MW, pp (USD/MWh) = 25 USD/MWh, and topt_{\mathrm{op}} (h/year) = 8,000 h/year, the annual hot-utility cost at ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) = 10 K is 4,000,000 USD/year. Reported as a range: 3.8 million USD/year to 4.2 million USD/year on the rounding of the stated inputs, and 2.7 million USD/year to 5.3 million USD/year over the assumed plausible operating ranges in Section 5.2.

G3. Carbon Emissions per Tonne

Response without the skill

Annual Emissions and Product Carbon Intensity

Given data and boundary

All masses below are per year. A kilotonne (kt) is 10310^3 metric tonnes (t).

Quantity Symbol Value
Direct carbon dioxide (CO2\mathrm{CO_2}) emitted mCO2m_{\mathrm{CO_2}}, in kt CO2\mathrm{CO_2} yr−1^{-1} 100
Methane (CH4\mathrm{CH_4}) leaked mCH4m_{\mathrm{CH_4}}, in kt CH4\mathrm{CH_4} yr−1^{-1} 2
Principal product made mpm_p, in kt product yr−1^{-1} 80
Co-product made not stated —

Boundary used here: direct plant emissions only. In Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol terms these are Scope 1 emissions: the direct CO2\mathrm{CO_2} plus the fugitive (leaked) CH4\mathrm{CH_4}. No purchased-energy (Scope 2) emissions and no upstream or downstream (Scope 3) emissions are given, so no total life-cycle footprint can be calculated from these data. The intensity calculated below is therefore a direct-emissions (Scope 1) intensity, not a cradle-to-grave product footprint.

Method

The 100-year global warming potential GWP100\mathrm{GWP}_{100} (dimensionless, kg CO2\mathrm{CO_2}-equivalent per kg of gas, abbreviated kg CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} kg−1^{-1}) converts a gas mass to carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e}) mass. By definition GWP100\mathrm{GWP}_{100} of CO2\mathrm{CO_2} is 1.

The total direct emissions EE, in kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}, are

E=mCO2×1  +  mCH4×GWP100,CH4E = m_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \times 1 \;+\; m_{\mathrm{CH_4}} \times \mathrm{GWP}_{100,\mathrm{CH_4}}

where GWP100,CH4\mathrm{GWP}_{100,\mathrm{CH_4}} is the 100-year global warming potential of methane (dimensionless).

The two gas masses must not be added directly (100+2=102100 + 2 = 102 kt is a mass of mixed gas, not a climate metric), because 1 kg of CH4\mathrm{CH_4} warms far more than 1 kg of CO2\mathrm{CO_2} over a stated period.

Choice of methane factor — stated, because the data do not state it

The problem does not state the origin of the leaked methane or the reporting convention to be used, and GWP100,CH4\mathrm{GWP}_{100,\mathrm{CH_4}} depends on both:

  • Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), Working Group I, Chapter 7, Table 7.15: GWP100,CH4=29.8\mathrm{GWP}_{100,\mathrm{CH_4}} = 29.8 for fossil methane and 27.027.0 for non-fossil (biogenic) methane. Fossil methane is higher because its oxidation in the air adds fossil CO2\mathrm{CO_2}.
  • IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5), still used in many regulatory and corporate inventories (for example the United States Environmental Protection Agency Greenhouse Gas Emission Factors Hub): a single value of 2828, with no fossil / non-fossil split.

A plant leak is taken as fossil methane (a fuel or fossil feedstock leak) for the headline result. The other conventions are carried as sensitivities so that the dependence is visible. The 100-year horizon is the standard inventory horizon; a 20-year sensitivity is also given because methane is short-lived (atmospheric lifetime about 12 years).

Annual emissions

Headline case, AR6 fossil GWP100,CH4=29.8\mathrm{GWP}_{100,\mathrm{CH_4}} = 29.8:

  • CO2\mathrm{CO_2} term: 100 kt×1=100.0100 \ \mathrm{kt} \times 1 = 100.0 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}
  • CH4\mathrm{CH_4} term: 2 kt×29.8=59.62 \ \mathrm{kt} \times 29.8 = 59.6 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}
  • Total: E=100.0+59.6=159.6E = 100.0 + 59.6 = 159.6 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} ≈\approx 160 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}

Methane is 2% of the emitted gas mass but 59.6/159.6=37%59.6 / 159.6 = 37\% of the CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} total. Cutting the leak is therefore worth about 0.60 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} per 0.02 kt (20 t) of CH4\mathrm{CH_4} yr−1^{-1} avoided on this basis, i.e. 29.8 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per kt CH4\mathrm{CH_4}.

Basis GWP\mathrm{GWP} of CH4\mathrm{CH_4} used (dimensionless) CH4\mathrm{CH_4} term (kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}) Total EE (kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1})

The spread from the time horizon is much larger: on a 20-year basis the same physical emissions are 265 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}. Any reported figure must state its horizon and its assessment-report source; "about 1.6×1021.6 \times 10^2 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} (100-year)" is the defensible summary.

Carbon intensity of the principal product

The carbon intensity of the principal product, CIp\mathrm{CI}_p in t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per t product (numerically equal to kg CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per kg product), is

CIp=fp Emp\mathrm{CI}_p = \frac{f_p \, E}{m_p}

where fpf_p is the fraction of the plant emissions allocated to the principal product (dimensionless, 0≤fp≤10 \le f_p \le 1), EE is the total direct emissions defined above (kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}), and mpm_p is the principal product rate defined above (kt product yr−1^{-1}).

Upper bound: no allocation to the co-product

Setting fp=1f_p = 1, i.e. charging all plant emissions to the principal product:

CIp=159.6 kt CO2e yr−180 kt product yr−1=1.995 t CO2e t−1≈2.0 kg CO2e per kg product\mathrm{CI}_p = \frac{159.6 \ \mathrm{kt \ CO_2e \ yr^{-1}}}{80 \ \mathrm{kt \ product \ yr^{-1}}} = 1.995 \ \mathrm{t \ CO_2e \ t^{-1}} \approx \mathbf{2.0 \ kg \ CO_2e \ per \ kg \ product}

On the AR5 factor the same calculation gives 156.0/80=1.95156.0 / 80 = 1.95 t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} t−1^{-1}; on AR6 non-fossil, 154.0/80=1.93154.0 / 80 = 1.93 t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} t−1^{-1}; on a 20-year fossil basis, 265.0/80=3.31265.0 / 80 = 3.31 t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} t−1^{-1}.

Why a single allocated intensity cannot be given from these data

A co-product is stated to exist, but neither its identity, its production rate, its value, nor the product it displaces is given. Allocation therefore cannot be completed:

  1. Avoidance first. ISO 14044 (environmental management — life cycle assessment) requires allocation to be avoided where possible, by subdividing the process so that emissions are measured per product, or by system expansion (crediting the co-product with the emissions of the production it displaces). Neither route is possible here: no sub-process emissions and no displaced product are given.
  2. Physical allocation. If allocation is unavoidable, a physical basis (mass, energy content, or another physical relation) is used next. That needs the co-product rate, which is not given.
  3. Economic allocation. Failing a physical basis, value shares are used. That needs prices or revenues for both products, which are not given.

The allocated intensity is therefore reported as a function of fpf_p, on the headline (AR6 fossil, 100-year) basis CIp=1.995 fp\mathrm{CI}_p = 1.995 \, f_p t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} t−1^{-1}:

fpf_p (dimensionless) CIp\mathrm{CI}_p (t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per t product)
1.00 (no credit to co-product) 2.00
0.90 1.80
0.80 1.60
0.50 1.00

These rows are a sensitivity, not alternative answers: fpf_p must come from a stated allocation rule and from co-product data. Reporting 2.0 kg CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} kg−1^{-1} without qualification would overstate the principal product's share whenever the co-product carries any share, and reporting a lower value without stating fpf_p and its basis would be unverifiable. For comparison between products, the allocation rule, the GWP\mathrm{GWP} source and horizon, and the Scope 1-only boundary must all match.

Result
  • Annual direct emissions: about 160 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} — 100.0 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} from CO2\mathrm{CO_2} plus 59.6 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} from 2 kt yr−1^{-1} of leaked CH4\mathrm{CH_4} at AR6 fossil GWP100=29.8\mathrm{GWP}_{100} = 29.8. Range across current 100-year conventions: 154–160 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1}; 265 kt CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} yr−1^{-1} on a 20-year basis.
  • Direct carbon intensity, all emissions charged to the principal product: about 2.0 t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per t product (2.0 kg CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} per kg), Scope 1 only.
  • Allocated intensity: CIp=1.995 fp\mathrm{CI}_p = 1.995 \, f_p t CO2e\mathrm{CO_2e} t−1^{-1}, with fpf_p undetermined from the data given. The co-product rate (for mass or energy allocation), product values (for economic allocation), or the displaced product (for system expansion) is required to fix a single allocated value.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Annual Emissions and Product Carbon Intensity — Estimate Under Underspecification

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness: the arithmetic is exact, but the result is convention-dependent. Two conventions not specified in the problem dominate the answer:

  1. the global warming potential (GWP, the mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂, that gives the same integrated radiative forcing as 1 unit mass of the gas in question over a stated time horizon) and its time horizon; and
  2. the allocation rule (the rule that divides shared emissions between a principal product and a co-product).

A third weakness is measurement: a methane (CH₄) leak rate is rarely measured continuously over a whole plant; it is usually estimated from surveys, factors, or a short campaign and extrapolated to a year.

Confidence rating: low for a single reported value; moderate for a range stated with its horizon and allocation rule. The range in §4 is defensible. Any single value taken from it without its horizon and allocation rule is not.

No agreement with another AI model is used as verification (Checklist item 7).

Allocation shares in §4.2 100 %, 90 %, 80 %, 70 %, 50 % assumed illustrative scenarios, not data for this plant

Property / factor provenance (Prompt 1): the only fitted or assessed relation used is GWP. Source: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), Working Group I, Chapter 7, Table 7.15 — CH₄ GWP-100 of 27.9 (non-fossil) and 29.8 (fossil), GWP-20 of about 81.2; Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) gave 28, or 34 with climate–carbon feedbacks. Valid range: these are global, horizon-dependent integrated values for a pulse emission; they are not plant-specific and do not describe temperature outcome at a specific year. Unverified until checked against that table in the current edition (Checklist item 5). No other correlation, rule of thumb, or physical property is used.

4. Calculation and results — ranges, not single values

Definition used, with every symbol defined at first use: total annual emission in CO₂e, E (kt CO₂e/yr), is

E = ECO₂ + mCH₄ × GWPCH₄

where ECO₂ is the direct CO₂ rate (kt/yr, given), mCH₄ is the CH₄ leak rate (kt/yr, given), and GWPCH₄ is dimensionless (t CO₂e per t CH₄, estimated, §3).

Carbon intensity of the principal product, I (t CO₂e per t product), is

I = f × E / mp

where f is the allocation fraction assigned to the principal product (dimensionless, assumed per scenario), and mp is the principal product rate (80 kt/yr, given). Units check: kt CO₂e/yr divided by kt product/yr gives t CO₂e per t product.

4.1 Total annual emissions, Scope 1 only
Case GWPCH₄ E (kt CO₂e/yr) CH₄ share of E
Old prescribed value 25 (assumed) 150.0 33 %
AR6, non-fossil, 100 yr 27.9 (estimated) 155.8 36 %
AR5, 100 yr 28 (estimated) 156.0 36 %
AR6, fossil, 100 yr 29.8 (estimated) 159.6 37 %
AR5 with feedbacks, 100 yr 34 (estimated) 168.0 41 %
AR6, 20 yr 81.2 (estimated) 262.4 62 %

Reportable result (100 year horizon): 150–160 kt CO₂e/yr for the central published values, 150–168 kt CO₂e/yr if the feedback-inclusive value is admitted. On a 20 year horizon: about 260 kt CO₂e/yr. The horizon must be reported with the number; the two horizons are not interchangeable and must not be averaged.

4.2 Carbon intensity of the principal product (80 kt/yr, given)

At the AR6 non-fossil 100 year total, E = 155.8 kt CO₂e/yr (estimated GWP):

Reportable result: 1.95 t CO₂e/t with no allocation on a 100 year horizon (range 1.88–2.00 for GWPCH₄ 25–29.8); 0.97–1.75 t CO₂e/t under the illustrative allocation scenarios; 3.28 t CO₂e/t with no allocation on a 20 year horizon. A single intensity cannot be stated for this plant until the co-product rate or value and the prescribed allocation rule are supplied. The formula above, with the plant's actual f, gives the value directly.

5. Sensitivity — how much each guess moves the result (Prompt 1)

Relative to the base case E = 155.8 kt CO₂e/yr (GWPCH₄ = 27.9):

  • GWPCH₄ 25 instead of 27.9: −3.7 % on E and on I.
  • GWPCH₄ 29.8 (fossil) instead of 27.9: +2.4 % (159.6 kt CO₂e/yr).
  • GWPCH₄ 34 instead of 27.9: +7.8 %.
  • Horizon changed to 20 year (81.2): +68 %. This is the largest single convention effect.
  • CH₄ leak ±50 % (1–3 kt/yr, assumed uncertainty for an extrapolated leak estimate) at GWPCH₄ = 27.9: E = 127.9–183.7 kt CO₂e/yr, i.e. −18 % to +18 %; I (no allocation) = 1.60–2.30 t CO₂e/t. Leak uncertainty moves the result more than the choice among current 100 year GWP values.
  • Allocation: f from 1.00 to 0.50 moves I by −50 %, with no change in E.
  • Direct CO₂: a ±10 % error in the given 100 kt/yr would move E by ±6.4 % (10/155.8). The state of that figure (metered fuel × factor, or stack measurement) was not given.
6. Primary sources that settle the open points

Each claim resting on these sources is unverified until checked against it (Checklist item 5):

  1. GWP values and horizon prescribed for the intended report: IPCC AR6 Working Group I Table 7.15 for the scientific values; the applicable reporting rule — GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, ISO 14064-1:2018, or the regulator's current prescribed factor set (for example a national inventory or emissions-trading factor list) — for the value that must legally be used. A prescribed value supersedes the scientific range for that report.
  2. Allocation rule: ISO 14044:2006 §4.3.4 (hierarchy: avoid allocation by subdivision or system expansion first, then physical, then economic) and ISO 14067:2018 for product carbon footprints, plus any product-category rule for this specific product.
  3. CH₄ leak rate: a measurement on the actual plant — continuous monitoring records, an optical gas imaging survey report, or a reconciled top-down (for example airborne or satellite) measurement — not an emission-factor estimate.
  4. Direct CO₂: the plant's fuel metering and carbon-content records, or continuous emissions monitoring records, for the reporting year.

Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor for this plant supersede the ranges above for this case.

7. Verification by an independent route — Prompt 3

Checks executed in Python (code run for this solution; results reproduced below):

  1. Recomputation. E recomputed for each GWP in §4.1: 150.0, 155.8, 156.0, 159.6, 168.0, 262.4 kt CO₂e/yr — matches the hand arithmetic 100 + 2 × GWP in every case. Check passes.
  2. Balance closure. The inventory has only two source terms and no transformation, so closure is definitional: CO₂ term (100 kt/yr) + CH₄ term in CO₂e (55.8 kt/yr at GWP 27.9) = 155.8 kt CO₂e/yr, residual 0. No material or energy balance exists in the problem to close independently; that absence is reported, not concealed. Check passes trivially and provides no independent assurance on the input figures.
  3. Limiting cases, known by sight. (a) GWPCH₄ = 1 would give E = 102 kt CO₂e/yr — recovered by the formula. (b) Zero leak gives E = 100 kt CO₂e/yr and I = 1.25 t/t with no allocation — recovered. (c) Allocation fractions for principal product and co-product must sum to 1; every scenario in §4.2 satisfies this by construction. Checks pass.
  4. Valid range of the fitted/assessed relation. GWP is applied only as published — as a pulse-emission, global, horizon-specific weighting. It is not used to predict a temperature change, a damage cost, or a year-by-year emission trajectory, which would be outside its range. Check passes with that restriction.
  5. Dimensional check. kt/yr × dimensionless = kt/yr; kt CO₂e/yr ÷ kt product/yr = t CO₂e/t product. Check passes.

No check failed. The checks verify the arithmetic and the conventions, not the truth of the given 100 and 2 kt/yr figures, which no independent data in the problem can test.

8. Audit by a skilled engineer — Prompt 4

Three points most likely to differ from how the built plant behaves:

  1. The CH₄ leak is not steady. Real leaks are dominated by a small number of large sources (a passing valve, a compressor seal, a tank vent) and by episodic events (start-ups, upsets, maintenance venting). An annual figure built from a periodic survey will typically understate the year, plausibly by tens of percent, and a ±50 % band (§5) may still be narrow. Settled by: continuous or repeated survey records over a full year, reconciled against a top-down measurement.
  2. Direct CO₂ from fuel factors differs from stack reality. If 100 kt/yr (given) comes from fuel use × a standard carbon factor, actual carbon content, incomplete accounting of flaring, pilot and purge gas, and start-up fuel move the figure, typically by a few percent in either direction, larger if flaring is material and unmetered. Settled by: continuous emissions monitoring records and the flare meter record, cross-checked against fuel purchase and metering records.
  3. Nameplate product rate is not sold product rate. If 80 kt/yr (given) is production including off-specification, recycled, or internally consumed material, the intensity per tonne sold is higher than §4.2, in inverse proportion to the saleable fraction (for example 90 % saleable raises I by 11 %). Settled by: the plant's production and sales/shipping records for the same year as the emissions.
9. What is not covered — Prompt 5
  • Scopes excluded: purchased electricity, steam and hydrogen (Scope 2); feedstock and product transport, upstream fuel and chemical supply, product use and end-of-life (Scope 3). For many products Scope 3 is larger than Scope 1; the intensity in §4.2 is a gate-to-gate, Scope 1 figure only and must not be compared with cradle-to-grave intensities.
  • Gases excluded: only CO₂ and CH₄ are given. Nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases, and black carbon are not in the model; if present, they are omitted, not zero by evidence.
  • Effects not in the model: time profile of emissions (GWP compresses it into one number); the difference between a sustained CH₄ leak and a one-off pulse, which a sustained-emission metric would weight differently; CO₂ capture, utilisation, offsets, and renewable-energy certificates, none of which were specified.
  • Restricted information not visible here: the plant's actual metering, survey and production records (§6, items 3–4); any product-category rule or customer specification that prescribes the allocation rule and GWP edition for this product.
  • Running-equipment effects: fouling, catalyst ageing, turndown operation, and upset flaring change fuel use and leaks year to year; a single-year figure does not show the trend or the spread.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: horizon switched to 20 year (+68 %); allocation applied at f ≤ 0.90 (−10 % or more on I); CH₄ leak revised by more than about ±28 % (about ±0.56 kt/yr) at GWP 27.9; Scope 2 or Scope 3 added for most real plants; a regulator prescribing the feedback-inclusive or an updated GWP combined with a fossil-CH₄ designation in the same direction.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Which reporting standard governs, and which GWP edition and horizon does it prescribe?
  2. How was the 2 kt/yr CH₄ figure obtained, over what period, and has it been reconciled top-down?
  3. Is the co-product sold, used internally, or disposed of — and what allocation rule does the product's category rule require?
  4. Is the intensity to be compared against a Scope 1-only or a cradle-to-grave figure?
  5. Are the emissions year and the product-rate year the same year, and is the product rate as produced or as sold?
  6. Has any CO₂ been captured, any offset applied, or any biogenic CO₂ included in the 100 kt/yr?
10. Summary for reporting
  • Total, Scope 1, 100 year horizon: 150–160 kt CO₂e/yr (155.8 kt CO₂e/yr at AR6 non-fossil GWPCH₄ = 27.9, estimated), stated always with its horizon.
  • Total, Scope 1, 20 year horizon: about 260 kt CO₂e/yr.
  • Carbon intensity, principal product: 1.95 t CO₂e/t with no allocation (100 year, AR6 non-fossil); 0.97–1.75 t CO₂e/t under the illustrative allocation scenarios in §4.2. Not reportable as a single plant value until the co-product quantity and the prescribed allocation rule are supplied (§2, §6).

Third test: the held-out problems

The 64 responses of the third test, on the 32 new problems written for that test.

A1. Henry's Law Conventions — Carbon Dioxide in Water

Response without the skill

Dissolved Carbon Dioxide in Water in Contact with Air

Symbols
  • TT is the temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K).
  • PP is the total gas pressure, in atmospheres (atm).
  • yCO2y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the mole fraction of carbon dioxide (CO2\mathrm{CO_2}) in the gas phase, dimensionless.
  • pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the gas phase, in atmospheres (atm).
  • HpcH_{pc} is the Henry's law constant in the pressure–concentration form, in litres atmosphere per mole (L atm mol−1\mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}}).
  • cCO2c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the concentration of dissolved molecular carbon dioxide in the liquid phase, in moles per litre (mol L−1\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}).
  • MCO2M_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the molar mass of carbon dioxide, in grams per mole (g mol−1\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}).
  • ρCO2\rho_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the mass concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide, in milligrams per litre (mg L−1\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}).
  • cH2Oc_{\mathrm{H_2O}} is the molar concentration of water in liquid water, in moles per litre (mol L−1\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}).
  • xCO2x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the mole fraction of dissolved carbon dioxide in the liquid phase, dimensionless.
  • kcpk_{cp} is the Henry's law constant in the concentration–pressure form, in moles per litre per atmosphere (mol L−1 atm−1\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,atm^{-1}}).
Given data
  • T=25 ∘CT = 25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  • P=1 atmP = 1\ \mathrm{atm}.
  • yCO2=0.00042y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.00042.
  • Hpc=29.4 L atm mol−1H_{pc} = 29.4\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}} at 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}.

The state considered is saturation equilibrium: the water has taken up carbon dioxide until no net transfer between the gas and the liquid occurs.

Identification of the Henry's law convention

The units of the quoted constant determine its convention.

A unit of L atm mol−1\mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}} is

atmmol L−1\frac{\mathrm{atm}}{\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}}

that is, pressure divided by molar concentration. The constant therefore belongs to the form in which pressure is proportional to concentration:

pCO2=Hpc cCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = H_{pc}\, c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}

Equivalently, solving for concentration gives

cCO2=pCO2Hpc=kcp pCO2c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{H_{pc}} = k_{cp}\, p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}

where kcpk_{cp} is the reciprocal of HpcH_{pc}:

kcp=1Hpc=129.4 L atm mol−1=0.0340 mol L−1 atm−1k_{cp} = \frac{1}{H_{pc}} = \frac{1}{29.4\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}}} = 0.0340\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,atm^{-1}}

A dimensionless Henry constant, or a constant expressed in atmospheres for the pressure–mole-fraction form, would have different units and would be used differently. No such conversion is required here, because the quoted units match the pressure–concentration form directly.

Partial pressure of carbon dioxide

For an ideal-gas mixture, the partial pressure pCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the gas mole fraction yCO2y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} multiplied by the total pressure PP:

pCO2=yCO2 P=(0.00042)(1 atm)=4.2×10−4 atmp_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = y_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\, P = (0.00042)(1\ \mathrm{atm}) = 4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{atm}

Saturated concentration

Substitution of pCO2=4.2×10−4 atmp_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{atm} and Hpc=29.4 L atm mol−1H_{pc} = 29.4\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}} into the Henry's law relation gives

cCO2=pCO2Hpc=4.2×10−4 atm29.4 L atm mol−1=1.43×10−5 mol L−1c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{H_{pc}} = \frac{4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{atm}}{29.4\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,mol^{-1}}} = 1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}

In micromoles per litre, where 1 mol L−1=106 μmol L−11\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{\mu mol\,L^{-1}}:

cCO2≈14 μmol L−1c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \approx 14\ \mathrm{\mu mol\,L^{-1}}

Equivalent expressions of the result
Mass concentration

With MCO2=44.01 g mol−1M_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 44.01\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}, the mass concentration ρCO2\rho_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is

ρCO2=cCO2 MCO2=(1.43×10−5 mol L−1)(44.01 g mol−1)=6.3×10−4 g L−1\rho_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\, M_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = (1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}})(44.01\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}) = 6.3 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}

ρCO2≈0.63 mg L−1\rho_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \approx 0.63\ \mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}

Liquid mole fraction

The molar concentration of water, cH2Oc_{\mathrm{H_2O}}, is approximately 55.5 mol L−155.5\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}} at 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}. The liquid mole fraction xCO2x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is therefore

xCO2=cCO2cCO2+cH2O≈1.43×10−555.5≈2.6×10−7x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} + c_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} \approx \frac{1.43 \times 10^{-5}}{55.5} \approx 2.6 \times 10^{-7}

Result

At 25 ∘C25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}, water in equilibrium with air at 1 atm1\ \mathrm{atm} containing a carbon dioxide mole fraction of 0.000420.00042 holds, at saturation,

cCO2≈1.4×10−5 mol L−1c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}

that is, approximately 14 μmol L−114\ \mathrm{\mu mol\,L^{-1}}, 0.63 mg L−10.63\ \mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}, or a liquid mole fraction of approximately 2.6×10−72.6 \times 10^{-7}.

Scope

The value above is the concentration of dissolved molecular carbon dioxide given by Henry's law. A small part of dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with water to form bicarbonate and hydrogen ions. That reacted fraction is additional dissolved inorganic carbon, is not counted in the Henry's law concentration above, and does not change the stated order of magnitude.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Dissolved Carbon Dioxide in Water in Equilibrium with Air at 25 °C and 1 atm

Definitions of symbols

Every symbol is defined here, at or before its first use elsewhere in the document.

  • T — temperature, in kelvin (K) or degrees Celsius (°C); the stated state is 25 °C = 298.15 K.
  • P — total gas pressure, in atmospheres (atm); 1 atm = 101 325 pascals (Pa).
  • y(CO₂) — mole fraction of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the gas phase, dimensionless.
  • p(CO₂) — partial pressure of CO₂ in the gas phase, in atm, defined by p(CO₂) = y(CO₂) × P.
  • Hpc — Henry's law constant in the pressure–concentration form, in litre·atmosphere per mole (L·atm/mol), defined by p(CO₂) = Hpc × C(CO₂).
  • C(CO₂) — concentration of physically dissolved, unreacted CO₂ in the liquid, in mole per litre (mol/L); the lumped species CO₂(aq) plus the small amount of true carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) formed from it is denoted CO₂(aq)* where the distinction matters.
  • kH — Henry's law constant in the solubility form, in mol/(L·atm), defined by C(CO₂) = kH × p(CO₂); kH = 1 / Hpc.
  • Hx — Henry's law constant in the pressure–mole-fraction form, in atm, defined by p(CO₂) = Hx × x(CO₂).
  • x(CO₂) — mole fraction of CO₂ in the liquid phase, dimensionless.
  • M(CO₂) — molar mass of CO₂, in gram per mole (g/mol); M(CO₂) = 44.01 g/mol.
  • C(water) — molar concentration of water in nearly pure water, in mol/L, approximately 55.5 mol/L.
  • DIC — dissolved inorganic carbon, in mol/L, defined as DIC = C(CO₂) + concentration of bicarbonate ion (HCO₃⁻) + concentration of carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻), all in mol/L.
  • Ka1 — first acid dissociation constant of carbonic acid, dimensionless (activities basis), with the negative base-10 logarithm pKa1 = 6.35 at 25 °C.
  • Ka2 — second acid dissociation constant of carbonic acid, dimensionless, with pKa2 = 10.33 at 25 °C.
  • pH — negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen-ion activity, dimensionless.
  • p(H₂O) — saturation vapour pressure of water at 25 °C, in atm, approximately 0.0317 atm.
Headline result

Physically dissolved CO₂, at saturation (gas–liquid equilibrium, no more will dissolve):

  • Range: 13 × 10⁻⁶ to 15 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L (13–15 µmol/L), i.e. 0.57–0.66 mg/L as CO₂, liquid mole fraction x(CO₂) ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ to 2.7 × 10⁻⁷.
  • Nominal value, from the quoted constant alone: C(CO₂) = 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L = 14.3 µmol/L = 0.63 mg/L; x(CO₂) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁷.

Total carbon absorbed, if "dissolved CO₂" is instead read as DIC in initially pure water: nominal 16.8 µmol/L, range approximately 15–18 µmol/L (Section 5). The two numbers answer two different questions; they must not be interchanged.

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. This problem type — a one-line Henry's law calculation — is numerically trivial but definitionally fragile. Three weaknesses carry the result:

  1. The convention of the quoted Henry's law constant is not stated. Henry's law is published in at least four mutually reciprocal or rescaled forms (pressure–concentration, solubility, pressure–mole-fraction, dimensionless gas/liquid ratio). Selecting the wrong form changes the answer by a factor of 55.5 or by a factor of about 864 (Section 4), not by a few percent.
  2. "How much CO₂ is dissolved" does not state whether the quantity wanted is physically dissolved CO₂(aq)* or total absorbed carbon (DIC). In pure water the difference is about +18 %; in alkaline water it is a factor of 5 to 58 (Section 5).
  3. The water is not characterised: its pH (the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity), alkalinity, and salinity are not given, and the gas basis (dry or water-saturated) is not given.

Confidence rating. High confidence, approximately 85–90 %, in the physical-solubility range 13–15 µmol/L, conditional on the quoted units L·atm/mol being correct, because the units themselves select the convention (Section 3). Low-to-medium confidence, approximately 40 %, that this range is the quantity a downstream user intends if the intended quantity is total CO₂ uptake by a real water of unstated composition. No higher rating is justified until the primary databank named in Section 7 is checked directly and the water composition is supplied.

2. Missing quantities, listed before solving (Prompt 2; Checklist item 4)

No missing quantity is taken in silence. Each item below is either given, resolved from the units, or solved under the plausible alternatives.

Missing quantity Status and treatment
Basis of the result (per what amount of water?) Not stated. Assumed: per litre of liquid solution, which at 10⁻⁵ mol/L is indistinguishable from per litre of water (difference below 0.1 %). A mass basis is also reported (mg/L) and a mole-fraction basis, so the basis can be converted.
Reference state Not stated. Assumed: Henry's law reference state of infinite dilution in water at 298.15 K and the stated partial pressure, which is the reference state attached to tabulated Henry constants.
Pressure basis Not stated whether 1 atm is absolute or gauge. Assumed absolute: a gauge reading of 1 atm would mean 2 atm absolute and would double the answer. Contact with air at ambient conditions makes absolute the only plausible reading.
Composition basis of the gas Not stated whether y(CO₂) = 0.00042 is on a dry-air basis or on a wet (water-saturated) gas basis. Solved both ways: wet basis as the headline (Section 3); dry basis corrected for water vapour gives −3.2 % (Section 4).
Composition of the water (pH, alkalinity, salinity, dissolved solids) Not stated. Assumed pure water for the headline. The alkaline and saline alternatives are quantified in Sections 5 and 8. This is the largest open gap.
Per-pass or overall conversion Not applicable in the process sense: the stated state is a single equilibrium contact (saturation), not a reactor or a staged absorber. No conversion is defined. If the question were about a flowing absorber, contact time and a mass-transfer coefficient would be missing and the equilibrium answer would be an upper bound only.
Definition of "dissolved CO₂" Not stated. Solved both ways: physical CO₂(aq)* (headline) and DIC (Section 5).
Activity / fugacity corrections Not stated. Assumed ideal gas and unit activity coefficient at infinite dilution. At p(CO₂) = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm the fugacity correction is below 0.5 % (estimated).
Whether the gas is replenished Implied by "in contact with air": the gas reservoir is effectively infinite, so p(CO₂) is held constant while CO₂ dissolves. In a small sealed headspace the partial pressure would fall as dissolution proceeded and the answer would be lower; that case cannot be solved without the headspace-to-liquid volume ratio, which is not given.
3. Solution
3.1 Inputs, labelled at the point of use (Prompt 1; Checklist item 3)
Input Value Label Source / remark
T 25 °C given Stated in the problem.
P 1 atm given (pressure basis assumed absolute; Section 2) Stated in the problem.
y(CO₂) 0.00042, dimensionless given Stated in the problem; consistent with approximately 420 parts per million by mole in current ambient air.
Hpc 29.4 L·atm/mol given (convention not stated; resolved in Section 3.2) Stated in the problem.
M(CO₂) 44.01 g/mol measured (tabulated atomic masses) Used only for the mg/L conversion.
C(water) 55.5 mol/L estimated From the density of water at 25 °C, approximately 997 g/L, divided by the molar mass of water, 18.015 g/mol, giving 55.3 mol/L; 55.5 mol/L (density 1000 g/L) changes x(CO₂) by under 0.5 %. Used only for the mole-fraction conversion.
pKa1, pKa2 6.35, 10.33 measured / fitted (tabulated equilibrium data at 25 °C) Used only in the DIC alternative, Section 5.
p(H₂O) 0.0317 atm measured (tabulated vapour pressure at 25 °C) Used only in the dry-gas alternative, Section 4.
3.2 Resolving the unstated convention from the units

The units are the deciding evidence. Hpc in L·atm/mol is a pressure divided by a concentration: atm / (mol/L) = L·atm/mol. The quoted value therefore belongs to the form p(CO₂) = Hpc × C(CO₂), and its reciprocal is kH = 1 / 29.4 L·atm/mol = 0.0340 mol/(L·atm), the solubility-form value tabulated for CO₂ in water at 25 °C. The alternative pressure–mole-fraction constant for this system is approximately 1.6 × 10³ atm (a different number, not merely a different label), and the dimensionless gas/liquid form is approximately 0.83, so neither matches 29.4 in value or in units. Conclusion: the convention is settled by the units, provided the units as quoted are correct. If the units themselves were mistyped, the problem is unsolvable as stated and must be returned for the source of the constant; that residual risk is part of the confidence rating in Section 1.

3.3 Calculation (executed in code; Section 6)

Step 1 — partial pressure:

p(CO₂) = y(CO₂) × P = 0.00042 × 1 atm = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm.

Step 2 — Henry's law, pressure–concentration form, solved for concentration:

C(CO₂) = p(CO₂) / Hpc = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm / 29.4 L·atm/mol = 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

Step 3 — conversions:

  • Mass concentration: 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L × 44.01 g/mol = 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ g/L = 0.63 mg/L.
  • Liquid mole fraction: x(CO₂) = C(CO₂) / (C(CO₂) + C(water)) = 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ / 55.5 ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁷. The denominator approximation introduces under 0.5 % error (estimated).
4. Range, guesses, and sensitivity (Prompt 1; Checklist item 2)

A single value is not reported for any quantity that rests on a fitted, estimated, or assumed input. The range is computed at the ends of the plausible range of the input that carries the weakness — here, the scatter in the tabulated Henry constant.

Range from the Henry constant. Tabulated solubility-form values for CO₂ in water at 298.15 K span approximately 0.032–0.035 mol/(kg·bar) across the entries of the primary compilation named in Section 7 (1 bar versus 1 atm and kilogram versus litre of water shift these by about 1–2 %, inside the stated span). In pressure–concentration form that span is Hpc = 28.6–31.3 L·atm/mol. Evaluating C(CO₂) = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ / Hpc at both ends:

  • At Hpc = 28.6 L·atm/mol: C(CO₂) = 1.47 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
  • At Hpc = 31.3 L·atm/mol: C(CO₂) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

Rounded to the two significant figures the inputs support: 13–15 µmol/L (0.57–0.66 mg/L). This range, not the nominal 14.3 µmol/L, is the deliverable answer for physically dissolved CO₂.

Effect of each guess or assumption, in percent of the nominal result:

Guess / assumption Plausible alternative Effect on C(CO₂)
Hpc taken as exactly 29.4 L·atm/mol (given, but a fitted/tabulated value) Tabulated span 28.6–31.3 L·atm/mol −6 % to +3 %
y(CO₂) = 0.00042 read as the wet-gas mole fraction (assumed) Dry-air basis, gas saturated with water vapour over the liquid: p(CO₂) = y(CO₂) × (P − p(H₂O)) = 0.00042 × 0.9683 atm −3.2 % (nominal value becomes 13.8 µmol/L)

The two catastrophic misreadings, for the record. These are not included in the range because the units exclude them, but they are the errors this problem type actually produces in practice:

  • Treating 29.4 as if it were kH in mol/(L·atm): C(CO₂) = 29.4 × 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.23 × 10⁻² mol/L — about 864 times too high.
  • Treating 29.4 as if it were Hx in atm: x(CO₂) = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ / 29.4 = 1.43 × 10⁻⁵, hence C(CO₂) ≈ 55.5 × 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ = 7.9 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L — 55.5 times too high.
5. Alternative reading: total dissolved inorganic carbon

Dissolved CO₂ reacts: CO₂(aq)* dissociates with constant Ka1 to bicarbonate ion (HCO₃⁻) and a hydrogen ion, and bicarbonate dissociates with constant Ka2 to carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻). Henry's law fixes only CO₂(aq)*; the total carbon absorbed is DIC, defined in the Definitions section.

Initially pure water, no other acid, base, or salt (assumed). Charge balance in the liquid, hydrogen-ion concentration = bicarbonate concentration to leading order, with Ka1 = 10^(−6.35) (measured/fitted, tabulated), gives a hydrogen-ion concentration of approximately 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L, i.e. pH ≈ 5.60. Bicarbonate is then approximately 2.5 µmol/L, carbonate is negligible at this pH (below 0.01 µmol/L), and:

DIC ≈ 14.3 + 2.5 = 16.8 µmol/L nominal; approximately 15–18 µmol/L over the Henry-constant range of Section 4 (0.74 mg/L nominal, expressed as CO₂).

Water held at a fixed higher pH (assumed values, for scale). With pH imposed by alkalinity, DIC = C(CO₂) × (1 + Ka1/[H⁺] + Ka1Ka2/[H⁺]²), where [H⁺] denotes hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L. Evaluated in code at the nominal C(CO₂):

  • pH 6: factor 1.45, DIC ≈ 21 µmol/L.
  • pH 7: factor 5.5, DIC ≈ 78 µmol/L.
  • pH 8: factor 46, DIC ≈ 655 µmol/L.
  • pH 8.1 (typical seawater pH, stated for scale only): factor 58, DIC ≈ 822 µmol/L — before any salinity correction to Hpc itself.

Any use of the headline number for a water whose pH is at or above 7 is therefore wrong by a factor of 5 or more.

6. Independent checks (Prompt 3; Checklist item 6)

All arithmetic was executed in code (Python) rather than by hand; the values quoted below are the code outputs. Checks that fail are reported as failures; the solution was not altered to make any check pass.

  1. Dimensional check — passes. atm / (L·atm/mol) = mol/L. The two misreadings in Section 4 fail this check, which is the mechanical reason they are excluded.
  2. Limiting case, zero partial pressure — passes. p(CO₂) = 0 gives C(CO₂) = 0, as required.
  3. Limiting case, pure CO₂ at 1 atm — passes within approximately 3 %. The model predicts C(CO₂) = 1 / 29.4 = 0.0340 mol/L = 1.50 g/L. Independently tabulated solubility of CO₂ in water at 25 °C and approximately 1 atm partial pressure (100 kPa) is 1.45 g/L, for which the model predicts 1.48 g/L at that partial pressure. Agreement within approximately 2–3 %, inside the Henry-constant range of Section 4.
  4. Independent route through the solubility form — passes. A separate textbook treatment of rainwater equilibrium uses kH = 3.4 × 10⁻² mol/(kg·atm) and a CO₂ partial pressure of 420 × 10⁻⁶ atm and obtains carbonic-acid concentration 1.42 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. The present route obtains 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. The routes use differently expressed constants and agree to under 1 %. This is agreement with published data, not with another AI model; agreement with another AI model is not used as verification anywhere in this solution (Checklist item 7).
  5. Speciation and charge-balance check — passes. Solving the charge balance for initially pure water (hydrogen-ion concentration = bicarbonate concentration + hydroxide concentration) gives pH 5.60 and bicarbonate 2.5 µmol/L, with the charge-balance residual zero by construction of the solved equation and the resulting pH matching the standard value of approximately 5.6 for unpolluted water in equilibrium with air. A materially different pH from this calculation would have indicated an error in the Henry step, because the pH depends on the square root of C(CO₂).
  6. Valid-range check for the fitted relation — passes. Henry's law in the linear form used here holds for dilute solutions and moderate partial pressures. Here x(CO₂) ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁷ (extremely dilute) and p(CO₂) = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm (far below the range, of order tens of atmospheres, where gas-phase non-ideality and pressure dependence of the constant become material for this system). The temperature dependence used for the sensitivity in Section 4 is the van 't Hoff form with the tabulated coefficient d(ln kH)/d(1/T) = 2400 K (fitted, from the primary compilation named in Section 7), valid over approximately 15–35 °C for the ±5 °C excursions evaluated; it predicts 16.4 µmol/L at 20 °C and 12.5 µmol/L at 30 °C.
  7. Material balance closure — not applicable, and stated as such. There is no process with inlet and outlet streams to close; the system is one liquid in equilibrium with an effectively infinite gas reservoir. The only closable balance is the liquid-phase charge balance, closed in check 5. Reporting a spurious "balance closure" percentage for a system with no streams would be a false check.
  8. Failed check — the dry-gas reading. If y(CO₂) = 0.00042 is a dry-air value and the gas over the liquid is water-saturated, the headline calculation overstates p(CO₂) by 3.2 %. This is a genuine unresolved ambiguity in the statement (Section 2), carried in the sensitivity table rather than absorbed silently into the result.
7. Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5)

The point — the value and convention of the Henry constant — is settled by: Sander, R., "Compilation of Henry's law constants (version 4.0) for water as solvent", Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 15, 4399–4981 (2015), and its mirror in the NIST Chemistry WebBook Henry's law data for CO₂ (data compiled by Sander), which tabulate the solubility-form constant at 298.15 K as approximately 0.034 mol/(kg·bar) with individual entries spanning 0.032–0.035, and the temperature coefficient 2400 K.

Verification status: unverified against the primary source in full. The span 0.032–0.035 and the coefficient 2400 K were seen in the NIST WebBook listing returned by search, and the value 3.4 × 10⁻² mol/(kg·atm) in a published textbook treatment; the Sander compilation paper itself was not retrieved and read in full for this solution. Every claim in Sections 4–6 that rests on the tabulated span, on pKa values, or on the 1.45 g/L pure-CO₂ solubility is therefore marked unverified until checked against that compilation or against the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics. The headline calculation itself rests only on inputs labelled "given" in Section 3.1 and does not depend on the unverified claims; only the width of the reported range does.

For a specific real water, the settling source is not a databank at all: it is a measurement on the actual water — a dissolved-inorganic-carbon / total-alkalinity titration and a pH measurement on the sample in question.

8. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this equilibrium calculation and built equipment or a real water body:

  1. The water is not pure; alkalinity dominates the uptake. Direction: total absorbed carbon higher, by a large factor. Size: factor 5.5 at pH 7, factor 46 at pH 8 (Section 5); a process water, a scrubber liquor, or seawater will absorb far more carbon per litre than 14 µmol/L while its physically dissolved CO₂(aq)* stays near the Henry value. Settling document/test: alkalinity titration and pH measurement on the actual water; a DIC analysis of an equilibrated sample.
  2. Real contact is not at equilibrium. Direction: dissolved concentration lower than the saturation value in a finite contact (short residence time, coarse bubbles, low interfacial area), or temporarily higher in a supersaturated stream leaving a pressurised contactor. Size: routinely 10–50 % below saturation in an un-designed contact; unbounded supersaturation is not possible, but 5–20 % supersaturation after pressure let-down is common before degassing completes. Settling document/test: dissolved-CO₂ measurement (or pH plus alkalinity, back-calculated) on samples at the actual contactor outlet, against the equilibrium value computed here.
  3. Salinity and temperature in service differ from the stated state. Direction: salts lower physical solubility (salting-out); higher temperature lowers it, lower temperature raises it. Size: seawater at 25 °C has a solubility-form constant roughly 15–20 % below the pure-water value (estimated, from the seawater Henry literature; unverified per Section 7); a ±5 °C excursion changes the result by approximately +15 % / −13 % (Section 4). Settling document/test: the water analysis (conductivity/salinity) and the operating temperature record; the Weiss correlation for CO₂ solubility in seawater where seawater is the actual solvent.
9. What this calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model.

  • Reaction of dissolved CO₂ beyond the DIC correction of Section 5: reaction with ammonia, amines, hydroxide liquors, or suspended carbonate solids (e.g. limestone), each of which can raise total uptake by orders of magnitude.
  • Mass transfer: rate of approach to saturation, interfacial area, bubble size, mixing. The result is an equilibrium end-point only.
  • Salting-out / salting-in by dissolved electrolytes, except as flagged in Section 8.
  • Pressure dependence of the Henry constant itself (the Krichevsky–Kasarnovsky correction) — negligible at 1 atm, material at high pressure.
  • Other dissolved gases competing for nothing in particular: Henry's law treats each gas independently at these dilutions, so oxygen and nitrogen dissolution does not change the CO₂ result; stated explicitly because the point is often raised.
  • Biological production or consumption of CO₂ in a real water, which can hold a natural water far from air equilibrium in either direction.

Information not available to this calculation.

  • The source document from which the quoted constant 29.4 L·atm/mol was taken, which would remove the convention question entirely.
  • Any analysis of the actual water (pH, alkalinity, salinity) — in industrial practice often held in plant laboratory records or a licensed databank (e.g. a process simulator's electrolyte property package) that this calculation cannot see.

Effects that appear only in running equipment. Fouling or surfactants at the gas–liquid interface reducing transfer rate; entrainment and degassing at pumps and let-down valves; local hot spots reducing solubility near heat-transfer surfaces; indoor or process-area air with CO₂ well above 420 parts per million (occupied buildings routinely 800–1000 parts per million, which would raise the result by a factor of approximately 2–2.4).

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %.

  • Reading "dissolved CO₂" as DIC in initially pure water: +18 %.
  • Water at pH 7 or above: factor 5.5 or more.
  • Temperature at or below 20 °C, or at or above 30 °C: approximately +15 % / −13 %.
  • Gas-phase CO₂ at or above approximately 465 parts per million in place of 420: +10 % or more, linearly.
  • Seawater in place of pure water (physical solubility only): approximately −15 to −20 % (estimated, unverified per Section 7).

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used.

  1. Is the quantity needed physically dissolved CO₂(aq)*, or total absorbed carbon (DIC)? If DIC, what are the pH and alkalinity of the actual water?
  2. From which source, in which convention, was the constant 29.4 L·atm/mol taken, and has it been checked against the Sander compilation or the NIST WebBook entry?
  3. Is the gas composition on a dry or a wet basis, and is the gas in fact ambient air, or local air with an elevated CO₂ level?
  4. Is the water at equilibrium with the gas, or is a measured outlet concentration from a finite contact required instead?
  5. What are the actual temperature and salinity, and do they move the result outside the 13–15 µmol/L range by the amounts listed above?
  6. Is 1 atm an absolute pressure at the actual site elevation and weather, or a nominal value?

A2. Non-Ideal Vapour–Liquid Equilibrium — Bubble Pressure, Second Case

Response without the skill

Bubble-Point Pressure for a Strongly Non-Ideal Binary Liquid

Result

No unique bubble-point pressure can be estimated from the data given.

The value obtained from ideal-solution theory is 82 kPa, but that value is not a valid estimate for a system stated to be strongly non-ideal. A numerical result requires the activity coefficients at the stated temperature and composition, or a model and parameters from which those activity coefficients can be calculated. None are supplied.

Symbols
  • x1x_1 is the liquid mole fraction of component 1, dimensionless.
  • x2x_2 is the liquid mole fraction of component 2, dimensionless.
  • y1y_1 is the vapour mole fraction of component 1, dimensionless.
  • y2y_2 is the vapour mole fraction of component 2, dimensionless.
  • PP is the total pressure, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • PbubbleP_{\text{bubble}} is the bubble-point pressure at the fixed temperature, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • P1satP_1^{\text{sat}} is the pure-component vapour pressure of component 1 at the fixed temperature, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • P2satP_2^{\text{sat}} is the pure-component vapour pressure of component 2 at the fixed temperature, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • γ1\gamma_1 is the liquid-phase activity coefficient of component 1, dimensionless.
  • γ2\gamma_2 is the liquid-phase activity coefficient of component 2, dimensionless.
Given data
  • x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30
  • P1sat=180 kPaP_1^{\text{sat}} = 180\ \text{kPa}
  • P2sat=40 kPaP_2^{\text{sat}} = 40\ \text{kPa}

Hence

x2=1−x1=1−0.30=0.70x_2 = 1 - x_1 = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70

No value is given for γ1\gamma_1, for γ2\gamma_2, or for any parameter that determines them.

Governing relation

At the bubble point the first vapour formed is in equilibrium with the liquid of composition x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30, x2=0.70x_2 = 0.70.

Under the usual low-to-moderate pressure approximation — ideal vapour phase and a Poynting correction of approximately one — equilibrium for each component is the modified Raoult relation:

y1P=x1γ1P1saty_1 P = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\text{sat}}

y2P=x2γ2P2saty_2 P = x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\text{sat}}

Adding the two relations and using y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1 gives

Pbubble=x1γ1P1sat+x2γ2P2satP_{\text{bubble}} = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\text{sat}} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\text{sat}}

Substituting the given data:

Pbubble=(0.30)(γ1)(180 kPa)+(0.70)(γ2)(40 kPa)P_{\text{bubble}} = (0.30)(\gamma_1)(180\ \text{kPa}) + (0.70)(\gamma_2)(40\ \text{kPa})

Pbubble=54 γ1+28 γ2kPaP_{\text{bubble}} = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2 \quad \text{kPa}

This is one equation containing the two unknowns γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 in addition to PbubbleP_{\text{bubble}}. It cannot be solved for PbubbleP_{\text{bubble}} without further information.

The ideal-solution value, and why it does not apply here

If, contrary to the stated strong non-ideality, the liquid were ideal, then γ1=1\gamma_1 = 1 and γ2=1\gamma_2 = 1, and

Pbubble, ideal=54+28=82 kPaP_{\text{bubble, ideal}} = 54 + 28 = 82\ \text{kPa}

with a first-vapour composition

y1=x1P1satPbubble, ideal=5482=0.66y_1 = \frac{x_1 P_1^{\text{sat}}}{P_{\text{bubble, ideal}}} = \frac{54}{82} = 0.66

This 82 kPa is the Raoult's-law result only. For a strongly non-ideal liquid, γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 differ substantially from one, so 82 kPa has no standing as an estimate for this system. Reporting it as the answer would contradict the premise of the problem.

Demonstration that different admissible values give different answers

The following pairs of activity coefficients are both consistent with all the data given, yet they give materially different bubble pressures from the relation Pbubble=54 γ1+28 γ2P_{\text{bubble}} = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2 kPa:

  1. Positive deviation, for example γ1=2.0\gamma_1 = 2.0, γ2=1.2\gamma_2 = 1.2:

Pbubble=54(2.0)+28(1.2)=108.0+33.6=141.6 kPaP_{\text{bubble}} = 54(2.0) + 28(1.2) = 108.0 + 33.6 = 141.6\ \text{kPa}

  1. Negative deviation, for example γ1=0.5\gamma_1 = 0.5, γ2=0.8\gamma_2 = 0.8:

Pbubble=54(0.5)+28(0.8)=27.0+22.4=49.4 kPaP_{\text{bubble}} = 54(0.5) + 28(0.8) = 27.0 + 22.4 = 49.4\ \text{kPa}

Both cases satisfy x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30, P1sat=180P_1^{\text{sat}} = 180 kPa, and P2sat=40P_2^{\text{sat}} = 40 kPa. The given data therefore do not select 141.6 kPa, 49.4 kPa, 82 kPa, or any other single value. Strong non-ideality also permits behaviour not present in the ideal case, such as a maximum- or minimum-pressure azeotrope, which likewise cannot be detected from the pure-component vapour pressures alone.

The examples above are illustrations of indeterminacy, not proposed estimates. No activity-coefficient values may be assumed, invented, or taken from a different system or a different temperature.

Information required for a numerical estimate

Any one of the following, at the same temperature as the stated vapour pressures, would close the problem:

  • measured values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30; or
  • parameters of an activity-coefficient model fitted to this binary at that temperature, for example the two Margules parameters, the van Laar parameters, the Wilson parameters, the Non-Random Two-Liquid (NRTL) parameters, or the Universal Quasi-Chemical (UNIQUAC) parameters, from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30 can be calculated; or
  • experimental vapour–liquid equilibrium data for this binary at that temperature from which γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 can be obtained.

At higher pressures, vapour-phase fugacity coefficients and the Poynting correction would also be required, but those refinements do not remove the primary gap: the liquid-phase activity coefficients are missing.

Conclusion

Pbubble=54 γ1+28 γ2 kPaP_{\text{bubble}} = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2 \ \text{kPa}

with γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 unknown. The bubble-point pressure is therefore indeterminate from the stated data. The Raoult's-law value of 82 kPa applies only to an ideal liquid and is not an estimate for the strongly non-ideal liquid specified.

1. Weakness and confidence rating — Prompt 1

Weakness: The governing quantities for a non-ideal liquid, γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2, are not supplied, and no activity-coefficient model, model parameters, component identities, or measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data are supplied. For a liquid described as strongly non-ideal, γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 differ from 1 by a large factor, so the missing quantities do not cause a small correction: they control the answer.

Confidence rating: Low. The ideal-solution reference value below is exact arithmetic on the given numbers. Any single non-ideal value would be a guess. Only a range, conditional on an explicitly stated range for γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 (or for AA), is defensible. No numerical result in this answer should be used for design, relief sizing, or operation.

3. Missing quantities — Prompt 2

No value is taken in silence. The solution needs, and does not have:

  1. Component identities. Without them, no databank activity-coefficient correlation can be selected or checked.
  2. γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30 and at the stated temperature, or a named model (Margules, van Laar, Wilson, NRTL, UNIQUAC) with its fitted binary parameters and the temperature at which they were fitted.

  4. Basis — pressure: Absolute is assumed (see Section 2). If the given vapour pressures were gauge, they would first have to be converted, and the reported PP would shift by the local atmospheric pressure, about 101 kPa — a change larger than the ideal-solution result itself.
  5. Reference state for the activity coefficients: The standard symmetric (Raoult's law) convention is assumed, i.e. γi→1\gamma_i \to 1 as xi→1x_i \to 1 for each component ii. An unsymmetric (Henry's law) convention would give different numerical γ\gamma values and must not be mixed with the equation used here.

  7. Vapour-phase model: Fugacity coefficients and, at elevated pressure, the Poynting correction are omitted. Their size cannot be assessed without component identities and the actual pressure.

Because items 1–3 cannot be obtained from the statement, the problem is solved under the plausible alternatives in Section 5 instead of under one assumed value.

4. Governing equation and the ideal-solution reference value

With the symmetric reference state and an ideal vapour phase (both assumed, see Sections 2–3), the modified Raoult's law gives, for each component ii:

yiP=xiγiPisaty_i P = x_i \gamma_i P_i^{\mathrm{sat}}

Summing over the two components and using y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1:

P=x1γ1P1sat+x2γ2P2satP = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}

Ideal-solution reference (γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1, assumed for reference only — it contradicts the stated strong non-ideality):

Pideal=(0.30)(180 kPa)+(0.70)(40 kPa)=54+28=82 kPaP_{\mathrm{ideal}} = (0.30)(180\ \mathrm{kPa}) + (0.70)(40\ \mathrm{kPa}) = 54 + 28 = 82\ \mathrm{kPa}

82 kPa is a reference point, not the answer for a strongly non-ideal liquid. Presenting it alone would be the silent completion this problem must not receive.

Sensitivity of PP to each guess, from the governing equation (executed in code, Section 6):

  • Increasing γ1\gamma_1 by 1.0, at fixed γ2\gamma_2, increases PP by x1P1sat=54x_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 54 kPa, i.e. by 66 % of PidealP_{\mathrm{ideal}}.
  • Increasing γ2\gamma_2 by 1.0, at fixed γ1\gamma_1, increases PP by x2P2sat=28x_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 28 kPa, i.e. by 34 % of PidealP_{\mathrm{ideal}}.
