6. Independent checks — Prompt 3

Checks were executed in Python from the governing equation; the arithmetic in Sections 4–5 is the code output, not hand calculation.

  1. Composition closure: y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1 holds by construction in every row of Section 5.1, and the computed y1y_1 values lie between 0 and 1. Pass.
  2. Limiting case, x1→0x_1 \to 0: P→γ2P2satP \to \gamma_2 P_2^{\mathrm{sat}} with γ2→1\gamma_2 \to 1 under the symmetric convention, so P→40P \to 40 kPa =P2sat= P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}. Pass, by sight and by the equation.
  3. Limiting case, x1→1x_1 \to 1: P→P1sat=180P \to P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 180 kPa by the same argument. Pass.
  4. Limiting case, γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1: The equation reduces to Raoult's law and returns 82 kPa, matching direct hand arithmetic (54+2854 + 28). Pass.
  5. Monotonicity / direction check: For all positive-deviation cases P>82P > 82 kPa and for all negative-deviation cases P<82P < 82 kPa, as the sign of ln⁡γ\ln \gamma requires. Pass.
  6. Correlation valid range check: Fails — cannot be performed. No fitted correlation is supplied, so there is no stated valid range to check against. This failure is a property of the problem statement, not of the arithmetic, and the solution has not been altered to conceal it.
  7. Material and energy balance closure: Not applicable beyond item 1 — a bubble point is a single equilibrium condition, with no flows, no conversion, and no energy balance. Stated explicitly rather than left silent.
  8. Liquid-phase stability check: For the symmetric Margules model, A>2A > 2 is the classical condition under which a single liquid phase can become unstable toward liquid–liquid splitting. The A=+2.5A = +2.5 and +3+3 rows, and the larger assumed γ\gamma pairs, may therefore describe a liquid that would not exist as one phase at this composition. Flagged, not removed: those rows bound the arithmetic but may not be physically realisable as a single-phase bubble point.

Agreement with any other AI model was not used as a check, and is not verification for this problem type.

7. Audit as a skilled plant engineer would — Prompt 4

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Azeotrope formation. Strong positive or negative deviation commonly produces a maximum- or minimum-pressure azeotrope. Near an azeotropic composition y1=x1y_1 = x_1, the bubble pressure passes through an extremum and small composition errors in the plant produce larger-than-expected pressure changes. Direction: either way, depending on the sign of the deviation; rough size: the extremum can differ from both pure vapour pressures' interpolation by tens of percent. Settled by: measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data for the actual pair (DECHEMA / NIST, see Section 5.3) showing whether y1−x1y_1 - x_1 changes sign.
  2. Liquid–liquid phase splitting. If the positive deviation is large enough (Section 6, item 8), the feed liquid in a real vessel forms two liquid phases; the observed pressure is then the three-phase pressure, essentially constant over a composition range, not the single-phase bubble pressure computed here. Direction: the single-phase calculation overstates the dependence of PP on x1x_1 and can overstate or understate PP itself. Settled by: a miscibility / cloud-point measurement on the actual liquid at the operating temperature, or databank liquid–liquid equilibrium data for the pair.
  3. Vapour-phase non-ideality and temperature error in PisatP_i^{\mathrm{sat}}. At the upper end of the range (200–300 kPa and above) fugacity coefficients depart from 1, and vapour pressures are steeply temperature-dependent (typically several percent per kelvin). A temperature offset of a few kelvin between the stated condition and the vessel, or PisatP_i^{\mathrm{sat}} values taken at a different temperature, moves PP by more than the whole ideal-to-moderate correction. Direction: PP rises with temperature; fugacity corrections usually lower the effective pressure contribution modestly. Rough size: 5–20 % for a few kelvin. Settled by: the Antoine or DIPPR vapour-pressure correlation for each named component evaluated at a measured vessel temperature, and an equation of state appropriate to the named components.
8. What this calculation leaves out — Prompt 5
  • Effects not in the model: vapour-phase fugacity coefficients; the Poynting correction; temperature dependence of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2; composition dependence beyond the illustrative Margules form; azeotropy and liquid–liquid splitting (treated as flags in Sections 6–7, not modelled); any third component, dissolved gas, water, or impurity; reaction between the components.
  • Information not available here: the identity of the components and any fitted binary parameters held in primary databanks (DECHEMA, NIST ThermoData Engine, DIPPR) or in vendor / licensed process-simulator databanks. Without access to a checked entry for the actual pair, no γ\gamma value can be stated as measured or fitted.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: temperature gradients and superheat in a real vessel; entrainment and foaming near the bubble point; composition drift from preferential vaporisation; pressure drop between the liquid surface and the pressure instrument; instrument basis (gauge versus absolute) and calibration.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any of — γ1\gamma_1 differing from the assumed value by about 0.15 or more (Section 4 sensitivity); a temperature change of roughly 2–3 K for typical vapour-pressure slopes; the pressure basis being gauge rather than absolute (a change of about 101 kPa); the composition 0.30 being a mass rather than a mole fraction for components of unlike molar mass; the liquid splitting into two phases.
  • Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used: 1. What are the two components, and what measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data exist for them at this temperature? 2. Which activity-coefficient model and parameter set are being used, from which databank or fit, and over what composition and temperature range were they fitted? 3. Is the stated pressure basis absolute, and are P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} and P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} evaluated at the same, stated temperature? 4. Is the liquid a single phase at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30, and is the composition near an azeotrope? 5. What pressure accuracy does the intended use require, and does the 44–219 kPa unverified range meet it? (For any design or safety use, it does not.)
Summary

The ideal-solution reference pressure is 82 kPa (given inputs; γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1 assumed for reference only). For the strongly non-ideal liquid actually described, no single value is supported by the data supplied. The defensible result is a conditional range: approximately 44 to 219 kPa over the assumed Margules range A=−2A = -2 to +2.5+2.5 (119 to 219 kPa if positive deviation is intended; 44 to 59 kPa if negative deviation is intended), unverified until γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 for the named pair are taken from a primary databank or measured on the actual liquid. Confidence: low.

A3. Reactive Absorption Capacity — Hydrogen Sulfide Removal

Response without the skill

Amine Solvent Flow for Hydrogen Sulfide Removal

Result

No unique solvent flow can be calculated from the data given. The hydrogen sulfide (H2S) removal rate and the lean loading alone do not fix the circulation rate. The rich loading, the identity of the amine, and the amine concentration in the water-based solvent are also required. The material balance below gives the exact relation that the missing data must satisfy, and a parametric set of values showing the range of flows consistent with the stated data.

Data given
  • RR, the molar rate at which H2S is to be removed, in kilomoles per hour (kmol h−1^{-1}): R=60 kmol h−1R = 60\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}}.
  • αlean\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}, the lean loading, in moles of H2S per mole of amine (mol mol−1^{-1}), for the solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber: αlean=0.05 mol mol−1\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ mol^{-1}}.
Symbols defined before use
  • AA, the molar flow rate of amine itself (the active component only, not the total solution), in kilomoles of amine per hour (kmol h−1^{-1}).
  • αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, the rich loading, in moles of H2S per mole of amine (mol mol−1^{-1}), for the solvent leaving the absorber.
  • Δα\Delta\alpha, the working loading difference, in moles of H2S per mole of amine (mol mol−1^{-1}): Δα=αrich−αlean\Delta\alpha = \alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}.
  • MM, the molar mass of the amine, in kilograms per kilomole (kg kmol−1^{-1}).
  • ww, the mass fraction of amine in the water-based solvent, dimensionless.
  • SS, the mass flow rate of the total solvent solution (amine plus water), in kilograms per hour (kg h−1^{-1}).
  • ρ\rho, the density of the solvent solution, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3^{-3}).
  • QQ, the volumetric flow rate of the total solvent solution, in cubic metres per hour (m3^{3} h−1^{-1}).
Material balance

Amine is conserved around the absorber: the same amine flow AA enters in the lean solvent and leaves in the rich solvent. H2S enters the solvent at the rate at which it is removed from the gas. A steady-state H2S balance on the absorber therefore gives

R=A αrich−A αlean=A (αrich−αlean)=A Δα.R = A\,\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - A\,\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = A\,(\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{lean}}) = A\,\Delta\alpha.

Rearranged for the amine flow:

A=RΔα=60αrich−0.05 kmol h−1,A = \dfrac{R}{\Delta\alpha} = \dfrac{60}{\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - 0.05}\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}},

with αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} in mol mol−1^{-1}.

The total solvent solution flow, which is the quantity normally specified as "solvent flow", follows from AA only after the amine and its concentration are known:

S=A Mw,Q=Sρ=A Mw ρ.S = \dfrac{A\,M}{w}, \qquad Q = \dfrac{S}{\rho} = \dfrac{A\,M}{w\,\rho}.

Why the problem is underdetermined
  1. αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} is not given. It is set by the equilibrium between H2S and the loaded amine at the absorber bottom conditions: the absorber temperature, the H2S partial pressure in the feed gas, and the specific amine. None of these is stated. It is also subject to practical limits, such as a maximum loading imposed to control corrosion. Different admissible values of αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} give different values of AA from the same stated data.
  2. The amine is not identified. Monoethanolamine, diethanolamine, methyldiethanolamine, and other amines have different values of MM, different equilibrium loadings, different reaction stoichiometries and heats of reaction, and different customary concentrations. MM is therefore unknown.
  3. The concentration ww is not given. Even if AA were known, the total solution flow SS and the volumetric flow QQ scale as 1/w1/w. A 20 mass % solution requires 2.5 times the total circulation of a 50 mass % solution at the same amine molar flow.
  4. ρ\rho is not given. Conversion from mass flow to volumetric flow requires the solution density, which depends on the amine, the concentration, the loading, and the temperature.

Counting confirms the deficit: the balance is one equation, R=A ΔαR = A\,\Delta\alpha, in the two unknowns AA and αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}; the conversion to total solvent flow adds the further unknowns MM, ww, and ρ\rho.

Parametric values consistent with the stated data

The following values of AA all satisfy R=60 kmol h−1R = 60\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}} and αlean=0.05 mol mol−1\alpha_{\mathrm{lean}} = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ mol^{-1}} exactly. They differ only in the assumed αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, which is not a result and must not be read as one.

αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} (mol mol−1^{-1}) Δα\Delta\alpha (mol mol−1^{-1}) A=60/ΔαA = 60/\Delta\alpha (kmol h−1^{-1})
0.15 0.10 600
0.25 0.20 300
0.35 0.30 200
0.45 0.40 150
0.55 0.50 120

The amine flow varies by a factor of five across this illustrative range alone, and the total solution flow varies further with ww.

For scale only, and not as an answer: if αrich=0.45 mol mol−1\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} = 0.45\ \mathrm{mol\ mol^{-1}} were supplied, so that A=150 kmol h−1A = 150\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}}, and if the amine were methyldiethanolamine with M=119.16 kg kmol−1M = 119.16\ \mathrm{kg\ kmol^{-1}} at w=0.30w = 0.30, then S=150×119.16/0.30=59 580 kg h−1S = 150 \times 119.16 / 0.30 = 59\,580\ \mathrm{kg\ h^{-1}}, corresponding to Q≈60 m3 h−1Q \approx 60\ \mathrm{m^{3}\ h^{-1}} at ρ≈1 000 kg m−3\rho \approx 1\,000\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}. Changing any one of the assumed quantities αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, MM, ww, or ρ\rho changes this figure.

Data required for a unique answer
  • Amine identity, fixing MM and the equilibrium behaviour.
  • Amine concentration ww in the water-based solvent.
  • Rich loading αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, or the data from which it is obtained: absorber temperature and pressure, feed-gas H2S partial pressure, and an equilibrium (vapour–liquid equilibrium) relation or design loading limit for the chosen amine.
  • Solution density ρ\rho at the circulation temperature, if a volumetric flow is required.
  • Confirmation that R=60 kmol h−1R = 60\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}} is the net absorbed H2S rate (feed H2S minus treated-gas H2S), with no other acid gas, such as carbon dioxide co-absorption, consuming amine capacity; co-absorption would require an additional balance and would increase the required circulation.
Conclusion

The required amine molar flow is A=60 / (αrich−0.05) kmol h−1A = 60\,/\,(\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}} - 0.05)\ \mathrm{kmol\ h^{-1}}, and the total solvent flow is S=A M/wS = A\,M/w (mass) or Q=A M/(wρ)Q = A\,M/(w\rho) (volumetric). A single numerical solvent flow cannot be stated until αrich\alpha_{\mathrm{rich}}, the amine identity, and the amine concentration are supplied.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Amine Solvent Flow to Remove Hydrogen Sulfide at 60 kmol/h

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) absorption into an amine is an equilibrium- and kinetics-limited reactive absorption. The circulation rate is set almost entirely by the difference between the rich loading leaving the absorber and the lean loading entering it. Only the lean loading is supplied. The rich loading depends on the amine identity, the absorber temperature in degrees Celsius (°C), the absorber pressure in kilopascals absolute (kPa abs), the H2S partial pressure in the feed gas in kPa abs, the carbon dioxide (CO2) content of the feed gas, and how closely the absorber approaches equilibrium. None of those quantities is supplied. A single flow value computed from the supplied data alone would therefore be false precision.

Confidence rating: low — 2 out of 5 for any absolute circulation rate, and high for the form of the balance in Section 3, which is an exact material balance and does not depend on any fitted relation. The amine molar flow in Section 4 is reliable only within the stated rich-loading range. The solution mass and volume flows are illustrative only, because the amine identity and concentration are not supplied.

Amine identity (for example monoethanolamine, MEA; diethanolamine, DEA; methyldiethanolamine, MDEA) Sets the molar mass in kilograms per kilomole (kg/kmol), the usable loading range, the reaction rate, and CO2 selectivity Amine molar flow reported independently of identity; mass and volume flows reported separately for three illustrative amines (assumed cases)

Pressure basis Not needed for the balance itself; needed for any equilibrium check No pressure used in the balance; any equilibrium value quoted for a named pressure would be absolute pressure (kPa abs)

No missing quantity has been filled silently. Every substituted value is labelled assumed or estimated at its point of use and is carried through a range calculation.

3. Governing balance and symbol definitions

Symbols, each defined before first use, with SI units:

  • F_H2S = rate at which H2S is removed from the gas and absorbed in the solvent, in kilomoles per hour (kmol/h).
  • alpha_L = lean loading, in moles of H2S per mole of amine (mol/mol), in the solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber.
  • alpha_R = rich loading, in mol/mol, in the solvent leaving the absorber.
  • Delta_alpha = net loading rise across the absorber, in mol/mol, defined as Delta_alpha = alpha_R − alpha_L.
  • N_amine = molar circulation rate of amine itself (not of solution), in kmol/h.
  • M_amine = molar mass of the amine, in kg/kmol.
  • w_amine = mass fraction of amine in the aqueous solution, dimensionless (wt% divided by 100).
  • m_solution = mass circulation rate of aqueous solution, in kilograms per hour (kg/h).
  • rho_solution = density of the aqueous solution, in kg/m3.
  • V_solution = volume circulation rate of aqueous solution, in cubic metres per hour (m3/h).

Steady-state H2S balance over the absorber, with no H2S generation or loss in the absorber:

F_H2S = N_amine × Delta_alpha = N_amine × (alpha_R − alpha_L)

so

N_amine = F_H2S / (alpha_R − alpha_L)

m_solution = N_amine × M_amine / w_amine

V_solution = m_solution / rho_solution

The first relation is exact if alpha_L and alpha_R are the actual loadings of the circulating solvent and if F_H2S is the net absorbed rate. All uncertainty in the result enters through alpha_R, and, for mass and volume flows, through M_amine, w_amine, and rho_solution.

5.3 How much each guess moves the result (Prompt 1)

Reference point for percentages: N_amine = 171 kmol/h at alpha_R = 0.40 mol/mol.

  • alpha_R = 0.35 instead of 0.40 mol/mol: N_amine rises to 200 kmol/h, +17 percent.
  • alpha_R = 0.50 instead of 0.40 mol/mol: N_amine falls to 133 kmol/h, −22 percent.
  • alpha_R (extended) = 0.30 or 0.60 mol/mol: N_amine = 240 kmol/h (+40 percent) or 109 kmol/h (−36 percent).
  • alpha_L in error by ±0.01 mol/mol (for example regenerator under-stripping giving 0.06 instead of the given 0.05): at alpha_R = 0.40, Delta_alpha changes from 0.35 to 0.34 or 0.36, moving N_amine by about +3 percent or −3 percent.
  • Amine identity and concentration (mass and volume flows only; no effect on N_amine): switching the assumed case from 30 wt% MEA to 35 wt% DEA at the same rich loading raises m_solution by about +48 percent (40,700 to 60,100 kg/h at alpha_R = 0.35), because DEA has the larger molar mass and only a modestly higher assumed concentration.
  • rho_solution in error by ±2 percent: V_solution moves by about ∓2 percent; density is a minor contributor next to alpha_R.
  • F_H2S: N_amine is directly proportional to F_H2S, so a 10 percent error in the removal rate moves every flow in this solution by exactly 10 percent.
6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run as stated. The solution was not altered to make any check pass.

  1. Material balance closure. Substituting each tabulated N_amine back into F_H2S = N_amine × (alpha_R − alpha_L) returns exactly 60 kmol/h for every row of the table in Section 5.1 (for example 200 × 0.30 = 60; 133.3 × 0.45 = 60). Closure error: 0 kmol/h, 0 percent. Note the limit of this check: closure is exact by construction, because one equation was solved for one unknown. It verifies the arithmetic only. It does not verify alpha_R, which carries essentially all of the real uncertainty. This check passes on arithmetic and provides no evidence on the loading assumption.
  2. Limiting cases, known by sight. - If alpha_R approaches alpha_L, Delta_alpha approaches zero and N_amine grows without bound. Correct: a solvent that picks up no net H2S per pass must circulate at an unbounded rate to remove a finite amount. - If F_H2S = 0, the balance gives N_amine = 0. Correct for the balance, with a practical caveat: a real absorber still needs a minimum circulation for liquid distribution and tray or packing wetting, which this balance does not contain. - Doubling F_H2S doubles N_amine at fixed loadings. Correct: the balance is linear in the removal rate. All three limiting cases behave as required.
  3. Executed code. All numbers in Sections 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 were computed by a short Python script evaluating the three relations of Section 3 over the stated ranges, not by hand arithmetic. The script output reproduces the tabulated values (for example rich 0.35 → 200.0 kmol/h; rich 0.50 → 133.3 kmol/h; MDEA 50 wt% case → 47,664 kg/h and 45.8 m3/h at rich 0.35). Pass.
  4. Valid-range check on the only empirical input. The estimated rich-loading range 0.35 to 0.50 mol/mol sits inside commonly reported operating rich loadings for aqueous amines in H2S service and below reported maximum (equilibrium, high partial pressure) loadings; it is not extrapolated beyond reported practice. However, this is a range check against general practice, unverified against the primary sources named in Section 5.1 for any specific amine, temperature, or pressure. At low H2S partial pressure (for example a low-pressure or already-lean feed gas) the equilibrium rich loading can fall below 0.35 mol/mol, in which case the headline range understates the required flow. Recorded as a conditional pass with that stated exception.
  5. Check that fails / cannot be run. No energy balance can be closed: absorber and regenerator temperatures, the heat of absorption, and the gas flow are not supplied, so the regenerator steam rate and the absorber temperature rise cannot be computed or checked. No check against a treated-gas H2S specification can be run: no specification or feed condition is supplied, so it cannot be confirmed that a lean loading of 0.05 mol/mol is low enough to meet any outlet specification. Both checks are reported as not runnable, not as passed.
7. Audit as an experienced plant engineer would (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this balance and built equipment:

  1. The absorber does not reach equilibrium rich loading. Trays or packing give a finite approach to equilibrium, set by mass-transfer rate, liquid distribution, and contact time. Direction: the actual rich loading is lower than the equilibrium value, so the actual circulation is higher than a flow computed from an equilibrium rich loading. Rough size: an approach corresponding to a rich loading 0.03 to 0.10 mol/mol below equilibrium moves the flow by roughly +10 to +40 percent at the loadings in Section 5.1. Settled by: absorber outlet (rich) solvent sampling with loading titration on the operating unit, or the absorber vendor's rated simulation for the installed internals.
  2. CO2 co-absorption competes for the amine. With MEA and DEA, CO2 reacts with the same amine; the circulation must then carry both acid gases, and the H2S-only balance understates the flow. With MDEA the effect is smaller and partly selective, but not zero at long contact time. Direction: actual flow higher than the H2S-only figure. Rough size: from a few percent for a selective MDEA case to +50 percent or more where the CO2 removal duty is comparable to the H2S duty on a non-selective amine. Settled by: feed gas analysis (H2S and CO2 mole fractions) and rich-solvent acid-gas analysis (both loadings) from plant samples or the design gas composition in the process design package.
  3. Solvent condition in service differs from nameplate solvent. Heat-stable salts, degradation products, hydrocarbon contamination, and foaming reduce the effective active amine concentration and the effective capacity; regenerator under-performance raises the actual lean loading above 0.05 mol/mol. Direction: effective Delta_alpha smaller, so actual flow higher, and the treated gas can go off specification before the flow shortfall is obvious. Rough size: commonly 5 to 20 percent of capacity in a degraded solvent; larger in a foaming or severely contaminated unit. Settled by: full solvent analysis (active amine assay, heat-stable salt content, lean and rich loadings) from the solvent supplier's or plant laboratory's routine sample reports.

Agreement with any other AI model's circulation figure is not used as verification anywhere in this solution, and would not settle any of the three points above.

8. What this calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model

  • Mass-transfer kinetics and absorber internals: tray efficiency, packing height, liquid distribution, wetting minimum, entrainment, and foaming.
  • CO2 absorption and any CO2 outlet specification; carbonyl sulfide and mercaptan removal, if required.
  • Energy balance: heat of absorption, absorber temperature bulge (which lowers the equilibrium loading partway up the column), regenerator steam consumption, lean/rich heat exchange, and condenser and reboiler duties.
  • Water balance: water picked up or lost with the gas, which drifts the amine concentration and therefore the solution flow at fixed amine flow.
  • Amine losses (volatility, entrainment, degradation) and make-up rate.
  • Hydraulics and equipment sizing: column diameter, pump head, and line sizes do not follow from the circulation rate alone.

Information not available to this calculation

  • The amine vendor's proprietary equilibrium and kinetic data packages and the fitted parameters of commercial rate-based simulators for the specific solvent formulation (promoted or inhibited solvents are not pure MEA, DEA, or MDEA).
  • The plant's design gas analysis, solvent sample history, and operating records.
  • Any site specification for treated-gas H2S content.

Effects that appear only in running equipment

  • Foaming episodes, fouling of the lean/rich exchanger, corrosion-product loading, and seasonal cooling-water temperature changes that move the lean solvent temperature and hence the equilibrium at both ends of the loop.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 percent

  • Actual rich loading outside 0.39 to 0.51 mol/mol when judged against the midpoint case (Section 5.3: ±0.05 mol/mol in alpha_R moves the flow by roughly −22 to +17 percent).
  • Any material CO2 co-absorption duty on a non-selective amine (Section 7, point 2).
  • Actual lean loading of 0.08 mol/mol or higher instead of the given 0.05 mol/mol (at alpha_R = 0.40, Delta_alpha falls to 0.32 and the flow rises by about +9 percent; at 0.10 mol/mol it rises by about +17 percent).
  • The 60 kmol/h figure being feed-gas H2S content at less than complete removal, or being total acid gas rather than H2S alone: the flow scales in direct proportion to the true absorbed H2S rate.
  • Absorber operation at low H2S partial pressure, where the equilibrium rich loading, and not the balance, becomes the binding constraint.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used

  1. Which amine, at what concentration, and is the formulation proprietary?
  2. What are the feed gas flow, H2S and CO2 contents, temperature, and pressure, and what is the treated-gas H2S specification?
  3. What rich loading was measured on this solvent, or predicted by which equilibrium model fitted to which data, at the actual absorber conditions?
  4. Is the 60 kmol/h an absorbed rate, a feed rate, or a design margin over either?
  5. What lean loading does the regenerator actually hold in service, from samples, rather than the design figure of 0.05 mol/mol?
  6. Has a rate-based absorber rating, with the installed internals, confirmed that the assumed rich loading is approached closely enough at the chosen circulation?
  7. Has the energy balance (regenerator steam, exchanger approach) been closed at the chosen circulation, and does the water balance hold the concentration?
Final answer
  • Amine circulation, headline range: 133 to 200 kmol of amine per hour (rich loading 0.50 to 0.35 mol/mol, estimated; lean loading 0.05 mol/mol, given; H2S removal 60 kmol/h, given). Extended screening range: 109 to 240 kmol/h.
  • Solution circulation cannot be fixed without the amine identity and concentration. For the three assumed illustrative cases of Section 5.2 it spans roughly 27 to 58 m3/h (27,000 to 60,000 kg/h).
  • Confidence: low (2 out of 5) for the absolute rate, pending a measured or properly modelled rich loading for the named amine at the actual absorber conditions. Unverified items are marked as such in Sections 4, 5.1, and 6.

A4. Estimated Properties and Compressibility — Second Gas

Response without the skill

Density of a Gas at 60 bar and 350 K

Symbols
  • ρ\rho = mass density of the gas, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3})
  • PP = absolute pressure, in pascals (Pa\mathrm{Pa}); 1 bar=105 Pa1\ \mathrm{bar} = 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}
  • TT = absolute temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K})
  • MM = molar mass, in kilograms per mole (kg/mol\mathrm{kg/mol})
  • RR = universal gas constant, R=8.314 J/(mol K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}, where J\mathrm{J} denotes joule
  • nn = amount of substance, in moles (mol\mathrm{mol})
  • VV = volume, in cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^3})
  • mm = mass, in kilograms (kg\mathrm{kg})
  • ZZ = compressibility factor, dimensionless
Given data
  • P=60 bar=60×105 Pa=6.0×106 PaP = 60\ \mathrm{bar} = 60 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{Pa} = 6.0 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{Pa}
  • T=350 KT = 350\ \mathrm{K}
  • M=0.044 kg/molM = 0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol}

The gas is not named. No critical temperature, critical pressure, acentric factor, virial coefficients, or other equation-of-state parameters are given.

Method

With the data given, the only density that can be calculated without adding an unstated assumption about the identity of the gas is the ideal-gas density. A real-gas correction would require ZZ, and ZZ at 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} cannot be obtained from MM alone.

For an ideal gas:

PV=nRTP V = n R T

The mass is m=nMm = n M, and the density is ρ=m/V\rho = m/V. Eliminating nn and VV:

ρ=PMRT\rho = \frac{P M}{R T}

Calculation

ρ=(6.0×106 Pa)(0.044 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol K))(350 K)\rho = \frac{(6.0 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{Pa})(0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)})(350\ \mathrm{K})}

Using 1 Pa=1 J/m31\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{J/m^3} for dimensional consistency:

ρ=2.64×1052.91×103 kg/m3≈90.7 kg/m3\rho = \frac{2.64 \times 10^5}{2.91 \times 10^3}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \approx 90.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

ρ≈91 kg/m3\rho \approx 91\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

The corresponding ideal-gas molar volume, RT/PR T / P, is 4.85×10−4 m3/mol4.85 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3/mol}.

Scope and limitation

60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} is a high pressure, so a real gas at these conditions will in general deviate from ideal-gas behaviour, i.e. Z≠1Z \ne 1 in the real-gas relation ρ=PM/(ZRT)\rho = P M / (Z R T). The size and even the practical importance of the deviation depend on the identity of the gas, in particular on its critical temperature and critical pressure relative to 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} and 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar}:

  • For a gas well above its critical temperature at 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar}, ZZ may be close to 1 and the ideal-gas value above may be within a few to about ten percent.
  • For a gas near its critical point, or below its critical temperature at 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar}, ZZ can differ substantially from 1, and the gas may not even exist as a single-phase gas at these conditions; it could condense.

A molar mass of 0.044 kg/mol0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol} alone does not identify the gas — for example, different gases with molar masses near 44 g/mol44\ \mathrm{g/mol} have very different critical properties — so no unique real-gas correction can be assigned from the stated data.

Result

Ideal-gas estimate:

ρ≈91 kg/m3 at 60 bar and 350 K\rho \approx 91\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}\ \text{at}\ 60\ \mathrm{bar}\ \text{and}\ 350\ \mathrm{K}

This value should be reported as an estimate, not as an accurate real-gas density. A more accurate value requires the identity of the gas, or equivalently its ZZ at 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} and 350 K350\ \mathrm{K}, or the parameters needed to calculate ZZ from a real-gas equation of state or a generalised compressibility chart.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Density of a Gas at 60 bar and 350 K — Underspecified Estimate

Symbols, defined before first use
  • ρ\rho (rho) = mass density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³) — the quantity sought
  • PP = absolute pressure, in pascals (Pa); 1 bar = 10510^{5} Pa
  • TT = absolute temperature, in kelvin (K)

  • RR = universal gas constant, R=8.314 J mol−1 K−1R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} (given constant, exact for this calculation to the precision shown)
  • ZZ = compressibility factor, dimensionless, defined by Z=PVm/(RT)Z = PV_{\mathrm{m}}/(RT), where VmV_{\mathrm{m}} is molar volume in cubic metres per mole (m³/mol); Z=1Z = 1 for an ideal gas
  • TcT_{\mathrm{c}} = critical temperature (K); PcP_{\mathrm{c}} = critical pressure (bar); ω\omega (omega) = acentric factor, dimensionless
  • Tr=T/TcT_{\mathrm{r}} = T/T_{\mathrm{c}} = reduced temperature, dimensionless; Pr=P/PcP_{\mathrm{r}} = P/P_{\mathrm{c}} = reduced pressure, dimensionless

Density follows from the definition of ZZ:

ρ=PMZRT\rho = \frac{PM}{ZRT}

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Prompt 1; Checklist items 1–2)

Weakness. The gas is not named. At 60 bar, non-ideality is not a small correction, and ZZ is a property of the specific gas (through TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, PcP_{\mathrm{c}} and ω\omega), not of MM alone. Several common pure fluids have M≈0.044M \approx 0.044 kg/mol and behave completely differently at 350 K and 60 bar: carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) are supercritical fluids there, whereas propane is below its critical temperature and above its saturation pressure there, i.e. a compressed liquid, not a gas at all. No value of ZZ, and therefore no single density, can be obtained from PP, TT and MM alone.

Confidence rating: low — 2 out of 10 for any single unconditional value; 5 out of 10 for the conditional gas-phase range in §4. Agreement with another AI model would not raise this rating (Checklist item 7); only the identity of the gas, checked against a primary databank, settles it.

7. Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5)

The identity of the gas, plus NIST REFPROP (or the NIST Chemistry WebBook for TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, PcP_{\mathrm{c}}, ω\omega) for that named gas, settles the density to better than ≈ 0.1–1 % at this state. All candidate critical constants and all Peng–Robinson densities in §4 are marked unverified until checked against NIST REFPROP / the WebBook for the actual gas. Data supplied by the user for the actual gas (plant, vendor, or measured) would supersede the ranges here.

8. Audit by a skilled engineer (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Phase in the actual vessel or line. A fluid handled as "gas" at 60 bar may be a dense supercritical fluid (CO₂-like, ρ≈114\rho \approx 114 kg/m³) or may condense on cooling in dead legs, instrument lines or during depressurisation (propane-like behaviour). Direction: inventory, hold-up and relief loads larger than a gas calculation suggests. Settled by: a phase envelope / flash calculation for the actual composition in NIST REFPROP, and the operating record for the line in question.
  2. Mixture, not pure. A real stream with mean M=0.044M = 0.044 kg/mol is usually a mixture; mixture ZZ and condensation behaviour are not the pure-component values, and the mean MM shifts with composition drift. Direction: either way, typically 5–30 %. Settled by: a current laboratory composition analysis of the actual stream.
  3. Local state differs from nominal state. Pressure drop, Joule–Thomson cooling across valves, and temperature gradients move the local PP and TT; near the critical region a few kelvin moves density by several percent (for CO₂ near Tr≈1.15T_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1.15, of order 1 % per kelvin). Direction: local density higher in cold, high-pressure pockets. Settled by: calibrated pressure and temperature measurements at the point of use, not nameplate conditions.
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5; Checklist items 4–5)
  • Effects not in the model: mixture non-ideality and composition variation; two-phase behaviour and condensation; adsorption, solubility in any liquid present, and reaction; real-gas effects beyond a cubic equation of state (association, polarity, quantum effects — minor for the candidates considered, unquantified for an unnamed gas).
  • Information not accessible here: the actual gas identity and composition; any restricted databank values (e.g. a licensed REFPROP installation or vendor property package) for the actual material; plant measurements on the actual stream.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling and liquid accumulation changing effective volume; transient condensation during start-up, shutdown and depressurisation; instrument error at high pressure.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: any change of gas identity (up to +357 % shown); crossing a saturation boundary; moving within ≈ 20 K or ≈ 20 bar of the critical point of the actual gas; pressure basis error combined with a near-critical state; composition drift in a mixture.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Which gas (or which analysed composition) is this, and what is its ZZ at 350 K and 60 bar from NIST REFPROP?
  2. Is 60 bar absolute or gauge, and is it the pressure at the point where density is needed?
  3. Has a flash calculation confirmed a single gas-like phase at the coldest and highest-pressure point in the system, not only at the nominal state?
  4. What tolerance does the downstream use (sizing, inventory, relief) actually require — is a ±30 % conditional range acceptable, or is a databank value mandatory?
  5. Is M=0.044M = 0.044 kg/mol a pure-component value or a mixture mean, and how current is the analysis behind it?
Final answer

As stated, the problem has no single defensible answer. Ideal gas (assumed Z=1Z = 1): ρ=90.7\rho = 90.7 kg/m³. For a gas-like pure fluid of this molar mass, the defensible conditional range is ρ≈95\rho \approx 95–130130 kg/m³ (≈ 114 kg/m³ if the gas is CO₂, ≈ 118 kg/m³ if N₂O — both estimated by Peng–Robinson, unverified against NIST REFPROP). Across all common fluids with M≈0.044M \approx 0.044 kg/mol the span is ≈ 90–420 kg/m³, because propane at this state is a compressed liquid at ≈ 415 kg/m³, not a gas. Confidence: low (2/10 unconditional). Naming the gas and taking ZZ from NIST REFPROP is the step that settles the value.

A5. Crystallisation Yield — Second Solute

Response without the skill

Crystal Yield from Cooling a Saturated Solution

Problem

Estimate the crystal yield from cooling a saturated solution from 80 °C to 25 °C, per 100 g of solvent.

Solubility of the solute:

  • 45 g of solute per 100 g of solvent at 80 °C
  • 18 g of solute per 100 g of solvent at 25 °C

Here, °C denotes degrees Celsius, g denotes grams, solubility denotes the maximum mass of solute dissolved in a given mass of solvent at equilibrium at the stated temperature, and crystal yield denotes the mass of solute that crystallizes from solution on cooling, on the stated basis.

Basis and assumptions

Basis: 100 g of solvent.

Assumptions:

  1. The solution is saturated at 80 °C at the start.
  2. The solution is saturated, that is, at equilibrium with solid solute, at 25 °C at the end.
  3. No solvent is lost by evaporation and no solvent is gained during cooling, so the mass of solvent remains 100 g.
  4. The crystals are pure solute, with no solvent incorporated in the crystal (no solvate or hydrate formation) and no mother liquor retained with the crystals.
  5. All solute that can no longer be held in solution at 25 °C crystallizes.
Calculation

Let m80m_{80} be the mass of solute dissolved at 80 °C, in g per 100 g of solvent; let m25m_{25} be the mass of solute that remains dissolved at 25 °C, in g per 100 g of solvent; and let mcrystalm_{\text{crystal}} be the mass of crystals formed, in g per 100 g of solvent.

Given values:

  • m80=45 g per 100 g of solventm_{80} = 45\ \text{g per 100 g of solvent}
  • m25=18 g per 100 g of solventm_{25} = 18\ \text{g per 100 g of solvent}

Solute balance on the basis of 100 g of solvent:

mcrystal=m80−m25m_{\text{crystal}} = m_{80} - m_{25}

mcrystal=45−18=27 g per 100 g of solventm_{\text{crystal}} = 45 - 18 = 27\ \text{g per 100 g of solvent}

Fraction of the initially dissolved solute recovered as crystals:

mcrystalm80=2745=0.60\frac{m_{\text{crystal}}}{m_{80}} = \frac{27}{45} = 0.60

That is, 60% of the initially dissolved solute is recovered as crystals.

Result

27 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, corresponding to 60% recovery of the solute dissolved at 80 °C.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution — 80 °C to 25 °C

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is trivial, but the problem is underspecified for any real material. The crystal form (anhydrous or hydrate/solvate), whether the system is closed to solvent loss, whether equilibrium is reached at 25 °C, and whether the reported yield is pure dry crystals, a wet filter cake, or solute contained in crystals are all unstated. Each of these changes the answer by several percent, and the hydrate case changes it by more than 10 %. Solubility alone does not determine a plant yield.

Confidence.

  • Idealised (textbook) yield under the assumptions stated in §3: high, 9/10 — a direct difference of two given solubilities, verified by balance closure in §5.
  • Yield from built equipment for an unspecified solute: low to moderate, 4/10 — rests on assumed, unverified values for evaporation, residual supersaturation, and crystal form.

No agreement with another AI model is used as verification anywhere in this solution (Checklist item 7).

2. Result

Let S80S_{80} be the solubility at 80 °C, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent; S25S_{25} be the solubility at 25 °C, in the same units; and YY be the crystal yield, in grams of crystals per 100 g of (initial) solvent.

  • Idealised yield: Y=27.0Y = 27.0 g per 100 g of solvent.
  • Plausible operating range (assumed scenarios in §4, anhydrous crystals): 25.2 to 27.9 g per 100 g of solvent, i.e. −6.7 % to +3.3 % about the idealised value.
  • Range from solubility uncertainty alone (§4): 25 to 29 g per 100 g of solvent, if each given solubility carries ±1 g per 100 g.
  • Alternative crystal form (§3, Prompt 2): if the crystals contain 10 % by mass of water of crystallisation (assumed, illustrative), the crystal mass is 30.6 g per 100 g of solvent, containing 27.6 g of solute. This is not the same quantity as the anhydrous yield and must not be interchanged with it.

All checks were executed in Python; results are reported as computed, including no failures.

6. Prompt 4 — Audit as for built equipment

Three points most likely to differ in operating equipment:

  1. Equilibrium is not reached. Finite cooling rate, no or late seeding, and slow growth kinetics leave the mother liquor supersaturated and fines unripened. Direction: actual yield lower, typically by the order of the −6.7 % computed for 10 % residual supersaturation, and worse for fast unseeded cooling. Settled by: a laboratory or plant batch record with mother-liquor concentration (e.g. by density, refractive index, or assay) measured against time at 25 °C on the actual material.
  2. The isolated product is a wet cake, not dry pure crystals. Mother liquor retained in the cake (commonly several percent to tens of percent of cake mass, depending on crystal size and the centrifuge or filter) adds liquor mass and, after drying, leaves its dissolved solute as impurity rather than as clean yield; washing removes it at the cost of dissolving some product. Direction: apparent wet yield higher, dry pure yield lower, purity lower. Settled by: cake moisture / loss-on-drying and assay records from the actual filter or centrifuge, and the equipment vendor's cake-washing data.
  3. Solvent loss and encrustation. Open or vacuum cooling evaporates solvent (direction: yield higher, +3.3 % for 5 % loss, §4), and scale on cooled surfaces removes solute from the recovered product while fouling heat transfer (direction: recovered yield lower). Net sign is equipment-specific. Settled by: plant solvent inventory / condensate records and crystalliser inspection and cleaning records for the actual vessel.
7. Prompt 5 — What is not covered
  • Not in the model: nucleation and growth kinetics, metastable zone width, crystal size distribution, polymorphism, hydrate or solvate transitions between 80 °C and 25 °C, impurity incorporation and its effect on solubility, mother-liquor recycle, wash and handling losses, energy balance and cooling duty, and heat-transfer fouling. Energy is not balanced here because no heat capacity, heat of crystallisation, or cooling duty was asked for or given.
  • Information not accessible here: proprietary solubility and metastable-zone data in commercial databanks and vendor crystalliser design files, and any data for the actual (unnamed) solute.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: encrustation, attrition and secondary nucleation, classification in the vessel, and cake behaviour in filtration and drying (§6).
  • Conditions changing the answer by more than 10 %: hydrate or solvate formation (§4, +13.4 % on crystal mass for the illustrative 0.10 mass fraction case, and larger for higher solvent content); combined solubility error and supersaturation acting together; reporting wet-cake mass instead of dry crystal mass.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. What is the solute, and do its crystals at 25 °C contain water or solvent of crystallisation? Has that been checked against a primary databank or a test on the actual material (unverified here)?
  2. Is the required number dry pure crystals, wet cake, or solute recovered — and on a solvent, solution, or charge basis?
  3. Was equilibrium at 25 °C demonstrated (mother-liquor assay), or is a supersaturation allowance needed?
  4. Is the cooler closed, and what is the measured solvent loss?
  5. Are the two solubilities measured values for this material and solvent purity, and what is their uncertainty?
8. Summary

Under the stated assumptions — closed system (assumed), equilibrium at both temperatures (assumed), anhydrous pure crystals (assumed), no entrainment or losses (assumed) — the yield is the difference of the two given solubilities: 27.0 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, plausible range 25.2–27.9 g under the assumed operating scenarios, 25–29 g allowing ±1 g per 100 g on each solubility. Balance closure is exact and both limiting cases pass. The result is unverified against any primary source for a specific material, because the solute is not named.

A6. Polymer Viscosity — Second Polymer System

Response without the skill

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Symbols and given data
  • The intrinsic viscosity, denoted by [η][\eta] (decilitres per gram, dL/g), is the quantity to be estimated.
  • The Mark–Houwink constant, denoted by KK (decilitres per gram, dL/g), is K=5×10−4 dL/gK = 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}.
  • The molar mass, denoted by MM (grams per mole, g/mol), is M=80,000 g/molM = 80{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol}.
  • The Mark–Houwink exponent, denoted by aa (dimensionless), is a second constant in the relation. No value of aa is given in the problem statement.
Relation

The Mark–Houwink relation is

[η]=KMa[\eta] = K M^{a}

where [η][\eta], KK, MM, and aa are as defined above.

Assessment of the data

A unique numerical value of [η][\eta] cannot be obtained from KK and MM alone. The relation contains two constants, KK and aa, and only KK is supplied. The result depends strongly on aa, because MM is large: M=8.0×104 g/molM = 8.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{g/mol}. Assigning a value to aa without a stated source — for example, for a specified polymer, solvent, and temperature — would be an added assumption, not a consequence of the given data.

The calculation can therefore be completed only in parametric form, with illustrative values shown for a stated range of aa.

Parametric calculation

Substitution of the given values of KK and MM gives

[η]=(5×10−4 dL/g)(80,000)a[\eta] = \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}\right) \left(80{,}000\right)^{a}

where 80,00080{,}000 is the numerical value of MM in grams per mole (g/mol). Equivalently, using ln⁡(80,000)=11.29\ln(80{,}000) = 11.29, where ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm,

[η]=(5×10−4)exp⁡(11.29 a) dL/g[\eta] = \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\right) \exp\left(11.29\,a\right)\ \mathrm{dL/g}

where exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function.

Illustrative values

The following values are evaluations of the parametric expression above at selected values of aa. The values a=0.5a = 0.5 and a=0.8a = 0.8 are commonly used to represent, respectively, a flexible polymer under theta conditions and in a good solvent; the intermediate values are shown to display the sensitivity to aa. None of these values is selected as the answer, because no condition that fixes aa is stated.

aa (dimensionless) MaM^{a} (dimensionless, for MM in g/mol as above) [η][\eta] (dL/g)
0.5 283 0.14
0.6 875 0.44
0.7 2,705 1.35
0.8 8,365 4.18

Sample check at a=0.7a = 0.7:

[η]=(5×10−4 dL/g)(80,000)0.7=(5×10−4)(2,705) dL/g≈1.35 dL/g[\eta] = \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}\right)(80{,}000)^{0.7} = \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\right)(2{,}705)\ \mathrm{dL/g} \approx 1.35\ \mathrm{dL/g}

The tabulated values span a factor of about 30 between a=0.5a = 0.5 and a=0.8a = 0.8, which quantifies the effect of the missing datum.

Result

No single intrinsic viscosity is determined by the stated data. The result determined by the given KK and MM is

[η]=(5×10−4)(80,000)a dL/g[\eta] = \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\right) (80{,}000)^{a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

A numerical estimate requires one additional datum: the Mark–Houwink exponent aa for the polymer, solvent, and temperature of interest (or, equivalently, a paired value of KK and aa from a table for that system). With such a value, substitution into the expression above gives [η][\eta] directly; for illustration, a=0.7a = 0.7 would give [η]≈1.35 dL/g[\eta] \approx 1.35\ \mathrm{dL/g}, and a=0.5a = 0.5 would give [η]≈0.14 dL/g[\eta] \approx 0.14\ \mathrm{dL/g}.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation — No Single Value Can Be Given

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: The problem is underspecified in the quantity to which the result is most sensitive. The Mark–Houwink relation needs two fitted constants, and only one of them is supplied. The missing exponent changes the answer by a factor of about 30 across its normal range for flexible polymers (Section 4). No polymer, solvent, or temperature is named, so no published pair of constants can be selected to fill the gap.

Confidence rating: Low. The arithmetic, conditional on stated values of the missing exponent, is exact and code-checked (Section 6). Confidence in any single numerical value as an estimate for a real polymer is low, because that value is not determined by the data supplied.

Symbols are defined at first use: [η][\eta], in decilitres per gram (dL/g), is the intrinsic viscosity, the limit of reduced viscosity as concentration approaches zero; KK, in dL/g as stated in the problem (see the dimensional note in Section 6), is the Mark–Houwink constant; MM, in grams per mole (g/mol), is the molar mass; aa, dimensionless, is the Mark–Houwink exponent.

Checks were run in code and are reported as they came out; the solution was not altered to make a check pass.

  1. Executed code. [η]=5×10−4×80,000a[\eta] = 5\times10^{-4}\times 80{,}000^{a} evaluated numerically reproduces every value in the table in Section 4 (0.141, 0.437, 1.353, 4.183 dL/g at a=0.5a = 0.5, 0.60.6, 0.70.7, 0.80.8). Check passes.

The check shows the calculation has no internal guard against an inapplicable aa: the formula returns a number for any exponent supplied.
  4. Dimensional check — fails as stated. For [η]=KMa[\eta] = K M^{a} to be dimensionally consistent, the units of KK must depend on aa: KK carries units of (dL/g)·(g/mol)−a^{-a}, reducing to plain dL/g only when a=0a = 0. Quoting KK simply as 5×10−45\times10^{-4} dL/g with an unstated, non-zero aa is the conventional shorthand in polymer tables, but strictly the stated units are incomplete, and they cannot be completed until aa is known. Reported as a failure of the problem statement, not adjusted away.
  5. Correlation valid range — cannot be performed, reported as failed. A fitted (K,a)(K, a) pair is valid only for its polymer, its solvent, its temperature, and the molar-mass range of the fit. None of the first three is given, so whether M=80,000M = 80{,}000 g/mol (given) lies inside the fit range is unknown.

No agreement with any other AI model is offered as verification, and none was used.

7. Primary source that settles the point

The point is settled by the Mark–Houwink parameter table for the actual polymer–solvent–temperature system in the Polymer Handbook (Brandrup, Immergut and Grulke, eds., Wiley), which lists KK and aa as a pair, with the temperature and the molar-mass range of the fit; failing a tabulated entry, it is settled by viscometry on the actual material (measurement of reduced viscosity at several low concentrations, extrapolated to zero concentration) in the actual solvent at the actual temperature. Every statement in this solution that rests on typical aa ranges (0.50.5 theta, 0.80.8 good solvent, higher for rods, lower for compact structures) is a general textbook statement and is unverified against that primary source for any specific polymer, because no polymer has been named.

8. Audit points: where real material is most likely to differ (Prompt 4)
  1. Solvent quality and temperature in use differ from the fit conditions. Direction: a better solvent or a temperature change that improves solvent quality raises aa and the coil size, raising [η][\eta]; the reverse lowers it. Rough size: the full theta-to-good-solvent swing at this MM is the factor of about 3030 in Section 4 if KK were held fixed, and a factor of several with correctly paired constants. Settled by: the Polymer Handbook entry at the use temperature, or a viscometric measurement in the use solvent at the use temperature.
  2. Molar-mass average and distribution. Direction: using a weight-average MM where the viscosity-average belongs overstates [η][\eta]; a broad distribution widens the gap. Rough size: commonly 1010 to 50%50 \% for broad distributions, unbounded without the distribution. Settled by: a molar-mass distribution measurement on the actual sample (size-exclusion chromatography with an absolute detector, e.g. multi-angle light scattering), from which the viscosity-average is computed.
  3. Branching and architecture. Direction: branched chains are more compact, so [η][\eta] at given MM is lower than the linear-chain relation gives, and the apparent aa falls. Rough size: tens of percent for light branching; a factor of two or more for heavy branching. Settled by: the branching characterisation of the actual material (manufacturer's data sheet or a combined viscometry and light-scattering measurement giving the branching contraction factor).
9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects outside the model: chain branching, copolymer composition and composition drift, electrostatic (polyelectrolyte) expansion in low-ionic-strength solvents, specific solvent binding, aggregation, degradation during handling, and any shear-rate dependence in the measurement used to obtain [η][\eta].
  • Information not visible here: the fitted (K,a)(K, a) pair, its fit range, and its scatter for the unnamed polymer, held in the Polymer Handbook and in manufacturers' data; no tabulated value was consulted for a specific polymer because none was named.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: dissolution state and history (incompletely dissolved or partially degraded polymer in a process solution has a different [η][\eta] from a carefully prepared laboratory sample), fouling or filtration removing the highest-molar-mass fraction, and temperature excursions changing solvent quality in the vessel.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%10 \%: an error or change in aa greater than 0.00840.0084; a change of solvent, or a temperature change sufficient to shift aa by that amount; a 1313 to 18%18 \% error in MM (at a=0.8a = 0.8 to 0.50.5); any error in KK greater than 10%10 \%; substitution of a different molar-mass average for a sample of broad distribution; onset of branching.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Which polymer, which solvent, and which temperature does the quoted KK belong to, and what is the aa fitted with it?
  2. Is 80,00080{,}000 g/mol a viscosity-average, a weight-average, or a number-average molar mass, and what is the distribution width?
  3. Does 80,00080{,}000 g/mol lie inside the molar-mass range over which that (K,a)(K, a) pair was fitted?
  4. Is the chain linear, and is the material a homopolymer?
  5. Has [η][\eta] been measured on the actual material in the actual solvent, and does it fall inside the range reported here?
10. Answer

No single intrinsic viscosity is determined by the data supplied. Conditional on the given K=5×10−4K = 5\times10^{-4} dL/g, the given M=80,000M = 80{,}000 g/mol, and an assumed Mark–Houwink exponent aa between 0.50.5 (theta solvent) and 0.80.8 (good solvent) for a flexible linear polymer, the intrinsic viscosity [η][\eta] lies in the range 0.140.14 to 4.184.18 dL/g. A usable single value requires the exponent aa and the (K,a)(K, a) pair for the named polymer, solvent, and temperature, checked against the primary source named in Section 7.

B1. Arrhenius Extrapolation — Second Reaction

Response without the skill

Rate constant at 450 K from an Arrhenius fit

Given data and symbols
  • kk is the rate constant, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}).
  • TT is the absolute temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}).
  • k1k_1 is the known rate constant at the reference temperature T1T_1: k1=0.020 s−1k_1 = 0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} at T1=350 KT_1 = 350\ \mathrm{K}.
  • k2k_2 is the rate constant to be estimated at the target temperature T2T_2: T2=450 KT_2 = 450\ \mathrm{K}.
  • EaE_a is the activation energy, in joules per mole (J mol−1\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}) in the calculation: Ea=95 kJ mol−1=95,000 J mol−1E_a = 95\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} = 95{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}.
  • RR is the ideal gas constant: R=8.314 J mol−1 K−1R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}.
  • AA is the pre-exponential factor, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}); it is eliminated below and does not need to be evaluated separately.

The value of EaE_a was fitted over 340340 to 370 K370\ \mathrm{K}. That fit range is part of the data, and it limits the reliability of the result, as discussed after the calculation.

Method

The Arrhenius equation is

k=Aexp⁡(−EaRT)k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)

where exp⁡\exp is the exponential function. Writing the equation at T1T_1 and at T2T_2 and dividing the second form by the first removes AA:

ln⁡(k2k1)=−EaR(1T2−1T1)=EaR(1T1−1T2)\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)

where ln⁡\ln is the natural logarithm. This ratio form uses only the given reference point and EaE_a, so no separate value of AA is required.

Calculation

First, the temperature-independent group Ea/RE_a/R, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}):

EaR=95,000 J mol−18.314 J mol−1 K−1=11,427 K\frac{E_a}{R} = \frac{95{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}} = 11{,}427\ \mathrm{K}

Next, the reciprocal-temperature difference, in reciprocal kelvin (K−1\mathrm{K^{-1}}):

1T1−1T2=1350 K−1450 K=2.8571×10−3−2.2222×10−3=6.349×10−4 K−1\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{350\ \mathrm{K}} - \frac{1}{450\ \mathrm{K}} = 2.8571\times10^{-3} - 2.2222\times10^{-3} = 6.349\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}

Then

ln⁡(k2k1)=(11,427 K)(6.349×10−4 K−1)=7.25\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = (11{,}427\ \mathrm{K})(6.349\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}) = 7.25

The units cancel, as required for the argument of a logarithm's output in this form. Hence

k2k1=exp⁡(7.25)=1.42×103\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp(7.25) = 1.42\times10^{3}

k2=(0.020 s−1)(1.42×103)=28 s−1k_2 = (0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})(1.42\times10^{3}) = 28\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

To two significant figures, consistent with k1=0.020 s−1k_1 = 0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} and Ea=95 kJ mol−1E_a = 95\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}:

k(450 K)≈28 s−1(formal Arrhenius extrapolation)k(450\ \mathrm{K}) \approx 28\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \quad \text{(formal Arrhenius extrapolation)}

Checks: T2>T1T_2 > T_1 and Ea>0E_a > 0, so k2>k1k_2 > k_1, as obtained. As a scale check inside the fit range, the same formula gives k≈0.12 s−1k \approx 0.12\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} at 370 K370\ \mathrm{K}, a factor of about 66 over 20 K20\ \mathrm{K} — already a steep temperature dependence, which is why a further 80 K80\ \mathrm{K} produces a factor of about 1,4001{,}400.

Reliability: this is a long extrapolation, not an interpolation

The number above is the value the fitted Arrhenius line gives at 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} if EaE_a and AA remain constant all the way from 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} to 450 K450\ \mathrm{K}. That condition is not established by the data given:

  1. Distance outside the fit range. The fit covers 340340–370 K370\ \mathrm{K}, a span of 30 K30\ \mathrm{K}. The target 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} is 80 K80\ \mathrm{K} above the top of the fit range — nearly three times the whole fitted span beyond the data. The reference point 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} lies inside the fit range; 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} does not.

  2. Error in EaE_a is amplified. An error ΔEa\Delta E_a in the activation energy changes ln⁡(k2/k1)\ln(k_2/k_1) by (ΔEa/R)(1/T1−1/T2)(\Delta E_a/R)(1/T_1 - 1/T_2). For example, an error of only 5 kJ mol−15\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} (about 5%5\% of 95 kJ mol−195\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) changes k2k_2 by a factor of exp⁡(0.38)≈1.5\exp(0.38) \approx 1.5, and an error of 10 kJ mol−110\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} changes it by a factor of about 2.12.1. No uncertainty in EaE_a was supplied, so no defensible uncertainty band on k2k_2 can be stated.

  3. The underlying behaviour can change. A change of reaction mechanism or rate-determining step, a temperature-dependent EaE_a or AA, catalyst deactivation or sintering, a phase change, or the onset of mass-transfer (diffusion) limitation at the much higher rate would all make a constant-EaE_a extrapolation fail, and none of these can be ruled in or out from the three numbers given.

  4. Temperature sensitivity is large at 450 K450\ \mathrm{K}. From the Arrhenius equation, the fractional change of kk per kelvin at 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} is Ea/(RT22)≈0.056 K−1E_a/(RT_2^{2}) \approx 0.056\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}, i.e. about 55–6%6\% per kelvin, so even a few kelvin of temperature error or non-uniformity matters.

Answer

Formal Arrhenius extrapolation from k=0.020 s−1k = 0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} at 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} with Ea=95 kJ mol−1E_a = 95\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} gives

k(450 K)≈28 s−1k(450\ \mathrm{K}) \approx 28\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

This value should be reported and used only as an unvalidated extrapolation. It is not a measured or reliably predicted rate constant at 450 K450\ \mathrm{K}, because 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} lies far outside the 340340–370 K370\ \mathrm{K} range over which EaE_a was fitted. A value for design or safety use would require rate data at, or at least much nearer to, 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} to confirm that the same Arrhenius line still applies.

Rate constant at 450 K — extrapolated estimate

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness (stated first, per Prompt 1): extrapolation far outside the fitted range. The activation energy, denoted EaE_a, was fitted over 340 K to 370 K. The target temperature, denoted T2T_2, is 450 K: 80 K above the top of the fitted range, i.e. 2.7 times the entire fitted span (30 K) beyond it. The Arrhenius relation is an empirical fitted relation, not a law that guarantees constant EaE_a, a single rate-determining step, or a single mechanism outside its fitted range. Any of those can change between 370 K and 450 K, and the exponential amplifies small changes in EaE_a into large changes in the result (Section 4).

Confidence rating: Low. The arithmetic of the extrapolation is exact (Section 6, checks pass), but confidence that the extrapolated value describes the real reaction at 450 K is low — roughly, the nominal value should be read as correct only to within a factor of about 2–10, and a larger error cannot be excluded (estimated judgement, not a measured statistic). No value in this solution should be used for design, sizing, safety, or runaway assessment without a measurement at or near 450 K (Section 5).

Two-point Arrhenius form, with every symbol defined in Section 3:

5. Missing quantities (Prompt 2) and primary source

The problem was not completed silently. Missing quantities, none of which was supplied:

  • Uncertainty (standard error / confidence interval) of the fitted EaE_a, and of k1k_1 — needed for a real range; replaced here by assumed bands (Section 4, item 1).
  • The underlying kinetic data set and fit: number of points, residuals, whether k1k_1 at 350 K is a measured point or a fit value.
  • Reaction identity, order, and rate law; phase; solvent or medium; catalyst identity and state, if any.
  • Pressure basis and composition basis: pressure, concentrations/reactant composition at which k1k_1 applies, and whether either changes the rate constant (for a true elementary first-order constant they should not; for an apparent constant they can).

  • Evidence on mechanism stability between 370 K and 450 K: no phase change, no catalyst change, no onset of a parallel reaction, no equilibrium limitation.

Because none of these could be obtained here, the solution was carried through under the two most likely alternatives where it matters: (a) plain Arrhenius with constant EaE_a (nominal, Sections 2 and 4), and (b) Arrhenius with a reduced or changed effective EaE_a above the fitted range (scenario rows, Section 2).

Primary source that settles the point: a rate measurement on the actual reaction, material, catalyst, and medium at or bracketing 450 K (for example 430 K, 450 K, 470 K), together with the original fitted data set and fit report behind the supplied EaE_a. Every claim in this solution that the Arrhenius relation holds at 450 K is unverified until checked against that source. Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor for the actual system would supersede the assumed ranges used here.

Checks were run in executed Python code; results reported as found, not adjusted:

7. Audit as an experienced plant engineer would (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ in built/running equipment:

  1. Rate-determining step or mechanism change between 370 K and 450 K. Direction: either way; a new parallel path usually raises the observed rate, loss of the original path lowers it. Rough size: factor of 2 to 30 (the scenario rows span 0.91 to 191 1/s). Settled by: kinetic measurements at several temperatures bracketing 450 K on the actual system, checked for a break in the Arrhenius plot (a plot of the natural logarithm of kk against 1/TT).
  2. Transport masking at the higher rate. At 28 1/s the characteristic reaction time is about 0.035 s; in real equipment, mixing, heat transfer, or pore/bulk diffusion can become limiting, so the observed rate is lower than the intrinsic constant and the apparent EaE_a falls, often to about half. Direction: observed rate below the extrapolated value. Rough size: the halved-EaE_a scenario gives 1.8 1/s, about 94 % below nominal. Settled by: transport criteria and tests on the actual equipment/material (for example varying particle size, agitation, or flow rate and confirming the rate is unchanged), plus the equipment design and operating records.
  3. Temperature actually experienced by the reacting material differs from the nominal 450 K. An exothermic reaction at this rate can self-heat; a 10 K local excess at 450 K corresponds, at EaE_a = 95 kJ/mol, to a rate about 1.75 times the nominal-temperature value; a cold spot gives the reverse. Direction: both ways, hot spots dominate risk. Rough size: tens of percent per 5–10 K. Settled by: thermocouple/temperature-profile records and the heat-removal design calculation for the actual vessel.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: change of mechanism or rate-determining step; temperature dependence of EaE_a and of AA; reverse reaction and approach to equilibrium at 450 K; parallel/side reactions and selectivity; catalyst deactivation, sintering, poisoning, or phase change; solvent/medium change or phase change; pressure and composition dependence of an apparent constant; transport limitations; self-heating.
  • Information not available here: the original kinetic data and fit statistics; any proprietary/vendor databank values for this reaction; the identity of the reaction itself. Nothing private or restricted was accessed.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: hot spots, fouling, ageing, feed impurities, and control excursions (Section 7).
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: an EaE_a error of only about 1.3 kJ/mol (from the sensitivity in Section 4, item 1); a temperature error of about 2 K at 450 K; any mechanism, catalyst, phase, or transport change above 370 K; a modified-Arrhenius exponent ∣n∣≳0.4|n| \gtrsim 0.4. In short, almost any realistic deviation moves the answer by more than 10 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the standard error of the fitted EaE_a, and what does the raw Arrhenius plot look like — is it straight even to 370 K?
  2. Has the rate been measured anywhere above 370 K, on this material, catalyst, and medium?
  3. Is the supplied constant intrinsic or an overall/apparent constant from a reactor?
  4. Is the equipment at 450 K in the kinetic regime, demonstrated by a transport test?
  5. What is the consequence if the true constant is 10 times the nominal value (thermal/runaway assessment) or one-tenth of it (conversion shortfall)?
  6. Is this value being used inside or outside the fitted range in any downstream calculation, and is that use flagged as extrapolated?
9. Bottom line

Arithmetic result of the Arrhenius extrapolation: k2k_2 = 28 1/s at 450 K. Status of that number: an unverified extrapolation, low confidence, reported range about 13 to 61 1/s on assumed EaE_a uncertainty alone and roughly 1 to 200 1/s under admitted model-change scenarios. A measurement at or near 450 K is the primary source required before reliance.

B2. Catalyst Deactivation — Second Catalyst

Response without the skill

Conversion in a Plug-Flow Reactor with Exponential Catalyst Deactivation

Given data and definitions
  • XX is the fractional conversion of the reactant, dimensionless. X=0X = 0 means no reactant converted and X=1X = 1 means complete conversion.
  • tt is the time on stream, in days (d\mathrm{d}). The value required is t=240 dt = 240\ \mathrm{d}.
  • kk is the first-order rate constant for the fresh catalyst, in reciprocal time (time−1\mathrm{time^{-1}}).
  • τ\tau is the reactor residence time, in time (time\mathrm{time}). The product kτk\tau is therefore dimensionless.
  • (kτ)0(k\tau)_0 is the value of kτk\tau for fresh catalyst, dimensionless. The given value is (kτ)0=1.6(k\tau)_0 = 1.6.
  • a(t)a(t) is the catalyst activity at time on stream tt, dimensionless. a=1a = 1 for fresh catalyst and aa decreases as the catalyst deactivates.
  • kdk_{\mathrm{d}} is the catalyst deactivation constant, in reciprocal days (d−1\mathrm{d^{-1}}). The given value is kd=0.003 d−1k_{\mathrm{d}} = 0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}.
Model

For an isothermal plug-flow reactor with constant density and a first-order reaction, the conversion for a catalyst of uniform activity a(t)a(t) is

X=1−exp⁡[−(kτ)0 a(t)]X = 1 - \exp\left[-(k\tau)_0\, a(t)\right]

where exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function. The expression uses the fresh-catalyst value (kτ)0(k\tau)_0 multiplied by the current activity a(t)a(t), because the effective rate constant at time tt is k a(t)k\,a(t).

Exponential deactivation means the activity is

a(t)=exp⁡(−kdt)a(t) = \exp(-k_{\mathrm{d}} t)

The deactivation is slow compared with the residence time τ\tau, so the reactor is treated as being in quasi-steady state at the activity corresponding to t=240 dt = 240\ \mathrm{d}: the activity is taken as uniform in the reactor and constant during one pass through the reactor.

Calculation

Activity after 240 d240\ \mathrm{d}:

kdt=(0.003 d−1)(240 d)=0.72k_{\mathrm{d}} t = (0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}})(240\ \mathrm{d}) = 0.72

The product kdtk_{\mathrm{d}} t is dimensionless, as required for an exponent.

a(240 d)=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a(240\ \mathrm{d}) = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487

Effective dimensionless rate constant at 240 d240\ \mathrm{d}:

(kτ)eff=(kτ)0 a(240 d)=(1.6)(0.487)=0.779(k\tau)_{\mathrm{eff}} = (k\tau)_0\, a(240\ \mathrm{d}) = (1.6)(0.487) = 0.779

where (kτ)eff(k\tau)_{\mathrm{eff}} is the effective value of kτk\tau at t=240 dt = 240\ \mathrm{d}, dimensionless.

Conversion at 240 d240\ \mathrm{d}:
