Response with the skill (generic layer)

Conversion in a Plug-Flow Reactor with Exponential Catalyst Deactivation

Symbols and result in brief

The symbols used in this solution are defined here, before first use elsewhere. XX is the fractional conversion of the limiting reactant, dimensionless. X0X_0 is the fractional conversion with fresh catalyst, dimensionless. kk is the first-order rate constant for fresh catalyst, in reciprocal time (1/time, in the same time unit as the residence time). keffk_{\mathrm{eff}} is the effective rate constant at a stated time on stream, in reciprocal time (1/time). τ\tau is the mean residence time in the reactor, in time (the same time unit as in 1/k1/k). kτk\tau is the dimensionless product of rate constant and residence time for fresh catalyst. keffτk_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau is the corresponding dimensionless product at a stated time on stream. aa is the catalyst activity, dimensionless, defined as the ratio of the rate on the aged catalyst to the rate on fresh catalyst under the same conditions, so that a=1a = 1 for fresh catalyst. tt is the time on stream, in days (d). kdk_d is the deactivation constant, in reciprocal days (1/d). CA0C_{A0} is the inlet concentration of the limiting reactant AA, in amount per unit volume (for example mol/m3^3). CAC_A is the outlet concentration of AA, in the same units as CA0C_{A0}.

Result, under the stated ideal model and the instantaneous, per-pass interpretation set out below: X=0.54X = 0.54, that is about 54% at 240 d, with a defensible reporting range of 49–60% from the rounding of the given numbers alone, and 42–67% if kdk_d carries a ±50%\pm 50\% fitted uncertainty (Section 4). The time-averaged conversion over the whole 240 d, a different quantity, is 0.67 (67%; Section 3).

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is elementary and exact once a model is chosen. The weakness is the model and the wording, not the arithmetic: the problem does not state (i) whether the conversion wanted is the instantaneous conversion at 240 d or the conversion averaged over the 240 d, (ii) whether conversion is per pass or overall, (iii) whether activity is uniform through the bed at each instant, or (iv) any uncertainty or fitted range for kdk_d. An answer for built equipment also depends on effects absent from the ideal plug-flow, separable-deactivation model (Section 7). This is a problem type in which a single unqualified number is not justified.

Confidence rating.

  • Conditional on the ideal model and the instantaneous, per-pass interpretation in Section 2: high, about 9/10 — the result is an exact closed-form evaluation, verified by independent numerical integration (Section 6).
  • As a prediction for a real reactor on stream for 240 d: low to moderate, about 4/10 — no plant data, vendor deactivation data, fitted range for kdk_d, temperature history, or residence-time distribution were supplied, and those items carry the result (Sections 5, 7 and 8). All claims that rest on such sources are marked unverified until checked against them (Section 5).

No agreement with any other AI model is used as verification anywhere in this solution.

2. Model, inputs at the point of use, and calculation
2.1 Relations used, their source and their range
  1. Plug-flow design relation for an irreversible first-order reaction. For ideal plug flow, constant τ\tau, and a first-order rate in AA, integration of the plug-flow balance gives CA/CA0=exp⁡(−keffτ)C_A/C_{A0} = \exp(-k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau), hence X=1−exp⁡(−keffτ)X = 1 - \exp(-k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau). Source: the standard plug-flow reactor design equation as given in standard reaction-engineering texts (for example Levenspiel, Chemical Reaction Engineering; Fogler, Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering) — unverified against those texts in this solution; the relation is re-derived by direct integration of the balance in the check in Section 6, which is the verification actually relied on here. Range of validity: ideal plug flow (no axial dispersion, no bypassing), constant density or τ\tau defined consistently with the concentration basis, irreversible first-order kinetics, no equilibrium limit, isothermal operation or kk understood as the value at the operating temperature.
  2. Separable deactivation. keff=a kk_{\mathrm{eff}} = a\,k, that is, deactivation multiplies the fresh-catalyst rate constant without changing the reaction order. Source: the standard separable-deactivation assumption in the same texts — unverified, as above. Range of validity: deactivation that affects all active sites in the same proportion and does not change the mechanism, the order, or diffusion resistance.
  3. Exponential activity decay. a=exp⁡(−kdt)a = \exp(-k_d t), with a=1a = 1 at t=0t = 0. Source: this is the form stated in the problem ("activity falls exponentially with time"), with the normalisation a(0)=1a(0)=1 assumed (see Section 3). Range of validity: only the time interval over which exponential decay was fitted or observed; no such interval was supplied, so validity at t=240t = 240 d, where kdt=0.72k_d t = 0.72, is unverified.
2.2 Inputs, labelled by state
  • kτ=1.6k\tau = 1.6, dimensionless — given. No uncertainty stated; it carries two significant figures.
  • kd=0.003k_d = 0.003 1/d — given. No uncertainty or fitted range stated; it carries one significant figure.
  • t=240t = 240 d — given.
  • a(0)=1a(0) = 1 — assumed (fresh catalyst defines activity 1; the standard normalisation).
  • τ\tau constant over the 240 d (constant flow rate and hold-up) — assumed; neither kk nor τ\tau is given separately, only their product, so any separate drift in either is invisible in the data supplied.
  • Temperature, pressure and feed composition constant, so that kk itself does not drift — assumed.
  • Activity uniform through the bed at each instant, and constant during the passage of one fluid element (deactivation time scale 1/kd≈3331/k_d \approx 333 d, estimated from the given kdk_d, much longer than any normal τ\tau) — assumed.
  • All catalyst of the same age (single fresh load at t=0t = 0, no partial replacement, make-up or regeneration) — assumed.
2.3 Calculation

Activity at 240 d, from relation 3 with the inputs labelled in Section 2.2:

a=exp⁡(−kdt)=exp⁡[−(0.003 1/d)(240 d)]=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a = \exp(-k_d t) = \exp[-(0.003\ \mathrm{1/d})(240\ \mathrm{d})] = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487

Dimensionless rate product at 240 d, from relation 2:

keffτ=a (kτ)=(0.487)(1.6)=0.779k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau = a\,(k\tau) = (0.487)(1.6) = 0.779

Conversion at 240 d, from relation 1:

X=1−exp⁡(−keffτ)=1−exp⁡(−0.779)=1−0.459=0.541X = 1 - \exp(-k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau) = 1 - \exp(-0.779) = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541

X≈0.54X \approx 0.54 (54%) at 240 d, instantaneous and per pass, under the assumptions of Section 2.2.

For reference, the fresh-catalyst conversion is X0=1−exp⁡(−1.6)=0.798X_0 = 1 - \exp(-1.6) = 0.798 (79.8%). Deactivation to a=0.487a = 0.487 therefore removes about one third of the fresh conversion on a relative basis.

7. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to make built equipment differ from the calculation in Section 2, each with direction, rough size, and the record that would settle it. Sizes not taken from the computed sensitivities in Section 4 are estimated and unverified.

  1. Non-uniform deactivation through the bed. In a real bed the inlet sees the highest reactant and poison concentrations and commonly deactivates fastest, so activity varies with position rather than taking the single value a=0.487a = 0.487 used here. Because XX as a function of local activity is concave, a bed with a given mean activity but activity spread along its length gives a lower conversion than a uniform bed of the same mean activity; the uniform model also takes no account of the mean itself being lower than a fresh-sample kdk_d suggests. Direction: real XX lower than 0.541. Rough size: estimated at several percentage points, of order 5–15% relative. Settling record: activity or coke profiling of spent catalyst by bed section (vendor or laboratory post-mortem), and axial temperature-profile history from the DCS.
  2. Flow maldistribution, fouling and loss of effective residence time. Fouling and coking raise pressure drop and promote channelling and bypassing, so part of the feed sees an effective kτk\tau below 1.6 even before chemical deactivation. Direction: real XX lower. Rough size: anchored to Section 4 — a 10% loss of effective kτk\tau lowers XX by 6.9% relative (to about 0.504); larger maldistribution scales accordingly. Settling record: a tracer residence-time-distribution test on the actual reactor, and the pressure-drop trend in the plant historian.
  3. Operating policy over 240 d is not constant-condition operation. Plants commonly raise inlet temperature, or cut feed rate, as activity falls. Either action raises the conversion above the constant-condition figure; conversely, hot spots formed during such operation can accelerate local deactivation and lower it. Direction: either direction, with temperature compensation the more common plant response, hence real XX more likely higher than 0.541. Rough size: bounded by Section 3 — full compensation restores X=0.798X = 0.798, +47.5% relative; partial compensation lies between. Settling record: DCS temperature, feed-rate and product-composition history for the 240 d, with the unit operating procedure for end-of-run criteria.
8. What the calculation does not cover (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model.

  • Axial dispersion, bypassing, and any deviation from plug flow.
  • Reversibility and equilibrium limitation; product inhibition; side reactions and selectivity change as the catalyst ages.
  • Change of reaction order or mechanism with ageing; non-separable deactivation, in which deactivation depends on local concentration or on the reaction itself rather than on time alone.
  • Pore-diffusion resistance and its growth with fouling or coking, which make the observed deactivation faster than the intrinsic activity decay.
  • Temperature and pressure gradients, hot spots, and any drift of kk or τ\tau with operating changes.
  • Poison fronts from feed contaminants, sulphur or metals breakthrough, and step changes from feedstock changes.
  • Catalyst replacement, make-up, regeneration, attrition and loss of catalyst inventory.
  • Recycle, separation and purge, and hence overall plant conversion.

Information not available to this calculation. The vendor's proprietary deactivation data and ageing-test results for the specific catalyst; the plant historian record for the specific unit; and the fitted range and raw data behind the given kdk_d. Each of these is held outside the problem statement, and the claims that depend on them are marked unverified in Section 5.

Effects appearing only in running equipment. Channelling after fouling, flow redistribution after pressure-drop growth, deactivation accelerated by upsets, condensation or hot spots, and activity loss during shutdowns and restarts. None of these appears in a time-only exponential law.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%. From the computed sensitivities in Section 4, a change of more than 10% relative in XX (that is, XX outside about 0.49–0.60) follows from any one of: kdk_d in error by more than about ±22%\pm 22\%; kτk\tau in error by more than about ±16%\pm 16\%; the question meaning time-averaged rather than instantaneous conversion (+24%); any substantial temperature compensation (up to +48%); a bed activity profile or age distribution materially different from the uniform, single-age assumption; or deactivation during shutdowns being counted in the 240 d when it does not occur, or the reverse.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used.

  1. Is the required quantity the instantaneous conversion at 240 d, the time-averaged conversion over the run, or the cumulative product composition, and is it per pass or overall?
  2. What is the source of kd=0.003k_d = 0.003 1/d, over what time and activity range was it fitted, and what is its uncertainty on the actual catalyst batch?
  3. Was the catalyst a single fresh load at t=0t = 0, and has any catalyst been added, removed, or regenerated since?
  4. What were the temperature, pressure, feed rate and feed composition histories over the 240 d, and was temperature raised to compensate for deactivation?
  5. Does measured plant conversion at any earlier time on stream agree with the exponential law, and at what activity was the last check made?
  6. Is there evidence of channelling, abnormal pressure-drop growth, or an axial activity gradient in the bed?
  7. Is the reaction in fact irreversible and first order over the whole composition range in the reactor at end-of-run conditions?
9. Final answer

Under the ideal plug-flow model with separable, exponential deactivation, activity a=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487 at 240 d, an effective dimensionless rate product keffτ=0.779k_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau = 0.779, and an instantaneous, per-pass conversion X=0.541X = 0.541, reported as 54% with a range of 49–60% from the rounding of the given data, widening to 42–67% under a ±50%\pm 50\% fitted uncertainty in kdk_d. The time-averaged conversion over the 240 d, if that is the quantity required, is 67%. The fresh-catalyst conversion is 80%.

B3. Reactor Heat Removal — Second Duty

Response without the skill

Reactor Cooling Area

Symbols and given data
  • QQ — heat release rate to be removed by cooling, in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW): Q=800 kW=800,000 WQ = 800\ \mathrm{kW} = 800{,}000\ \mathrm{W}
  • ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} — mean temperature difference between the reaction mass and the coolant, in kelvin (K): ΔTm=30 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 30\ \mathrm{K}. A temperature difference of 1 K1\ \mathrm{K} is equal to a temperature difference of 1 ∘C1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}, so no numerical conversion is required.
  • UU — overall heat transfer coefficient for the cooling surface, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}): not given, estimated in the next section
  • AA — cooling heat transfer area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}): to be estimated
Governing equation

At steady operation, with the reaction mass held at constant temperature, the heat released must be removed at the same rate through the cooling surface. Neglecting heat losses to the surroundings, which are small compared with 800 kW800\ \mathrm{kW} and which act in the direction of cooling in any case:

Q=UAΔTmQ = U A \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}

Rearrangement for the unknown area gives:

A=QUΔTmA = \dfrac{Q}{U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}}

The data given are therefore not sufficient for a unique answer: QQ and ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} are specified, but UU is not. UU depends on the reaction-mass viscosity and agitation, the coolant and its velocity, the wall material and thickness, and fouling. An estimate must use a published typical value of UU for a jacketed agitated reactor and must state the sensitivity to that choice.

Estimate of the overall heat transfer coefficient

Typical overall coefficients for agitated jacketed vessels, as tabulated by Carpenter, "Agitated Vessel Heat Transfer", Heat Transfer Engineering / AtoZ of Thermal Processing, and reproduced in standard texts, are:

Cooling arrangement UU (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}})
Jacketed glass-lined steel vessel, cooling 200
Jacketed glass-lined steel vessel, chilled service 100
Jacketed carbon or stainless steel vessel, cooling 350
Jacketed carbon or stainless steel vessel, chilled service 150
Internal coil, well designed 400–600

General tables for jacketed stainless-steel vessels with water-like fluids on both sides give a similar range, 300300–500 W m−2 K−1500\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} for a standard jacket, falling to about 100 W m−2 K−1100\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} for viscous batches of several thousand centipoise.

Base case adopted: a jacketed carbon or stainless steel reactor, a water-like reaction mass of low to moderate viscosity, good agitation, and a liquid coolant, for which the tabulated cooling value is

U=350 W m−2 K−1U = 350\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}

Calculation

Heat flux through the cooling surface, defined as the heat rate per unit area, Q/AQ/A, in kilowatts per square metre (kW m−2\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}}):

QA=UΔTm=350×30=10,500 W m−2=10.5 kW m−2\frac{Q}{A} = U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 350 \times 30 = 10{,}500\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} = 10.5\ \mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}}

Required area:

A=QUΔTm=800,000 W350 W m−2 K−1×30 K=800,00010,500 m2=76.2 m2A = \frac{Q}{U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}} = \frac{800{,}000\ \mathrm{W}}{350\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} \times 30\ \mathrm{K}} = \frac{800{,}000}{10{,}500}\ \mathrm{m^{2}} = 76.2\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

Unit check: W/[(W m−2 K−1)(K)]=m2\mathrm{W} / [(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}})(\mathrm{K})] = \mathrm{m^{2}}, as required.

Sensitivity to the assumed coefficient

The same calculation, A=Q/(UΔTm)A = Q/(U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}) with Q=800,000 WQ = 800{,}000\ \mathrm{W} and ΔTm=30 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 30\ \mathrm{K}, over the published range of UU:

Case UU (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}) AA (m2\mathrm{m^{2}})
Chilled or heavily fouled / viscous service 150 178
Glass-lined vessel, cooling 200 133
Conservative steel vessel, some fouling or moderate viscosity 250 107
Steel vessel, lower end of standard-jacket range 300 89
Base case: steel vessel, cooling (tabulated value) 350 76
Steel vessel, cooling, favourable conditions 500 53
Internal coil, upper tabulated value 600 44

The area is inversely proportional to UU: halving UU doubles AA. No value in the credible range changes the order of magnitude. The required area is of order 102 m210^{2}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}.

Design allowance and practical implication
  1. Fouling and uncertainty in UU. The tabulated value of UU is a clean, typical value. A design allowance of about 2020–30%30\% on area for fouling, viscosity variation, and uncertainty in UU applied to the base case gives 76.2×1.25≈95 m276.2 \times 1.25 \approx 95\ \mathrm{m^{2}}, i.e. about 100 m2100\ \mathrm{m^{2}} to specify.
  2. Attainability by a jacket alone. A jacket covers only the cylindrical wall and bottom head of a vessel. A vessel of, for example, 10 m310\ \mathrm{m^{3}} working volume has a jacketed area of only roughly 1515–20 m220\ \mathrm{m^{2}}. An area of about 7676–100 m2100\ \mathrm{m^{2}} therefore cannot normally be provided by a jacket on a single conventional reactor of ordinary size. Practical options are internal cooling coils in addition to the jacket, a pumped external loop through a shell-and-tube heat exchanger, or a larger mean temperature difference obtained with a colder coolant — noting that reducing the coolant temperature also reduces UU in chilled service, per the table in the sensitivity section, and partly cancels the gain.
  3. Coolant duty check (order of magnitude). The coolant flow implied by QQ is large but not exceptional; it is set by the coolant specific heat capacity and its permitted temperature rise, quantities not specified in the problem, and does not affect the area estimate above because ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} is already given as the mean driving force.
Result

With a typical overall coefficient for a jacketed steel reactor in cooling service, U=350 W m−2 K−1U = 350\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}:

A≈76 m2A \approx 76\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

Allowing for fouling and uncertainty, about 100 m2100\ \mathrm{m^{2}} of cooling area should be specified. Over the full published range of UU for jacketed reactors and coils, 150150–600 W m−2 K−1600\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}, the required area lies between about 44 m244\ \mathrm{m^{2}} and 178 m2178\ \mathrm{m^{2}}. The robust conclusion, independent of the exact value of UU adopted, is that the required cooling area is of order 100 m2100\ \mathrm{m^{2}}, substantially more than a reactor jacket alone normally provides.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Cooling Area Estimate for an 800 kW Reactor

Symbols and definitions

Every symbol is defined here, at or before its first use elsewhere in this document.

  • A — cooling (heat-transfer) area, in square metres (m²). The quantity to be estimated.
  • Q — heat-removal rate (heat duty) that the cooling surface must remove, in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW); 1 kW = 1000 W.
  • U — overall heat-transfer coefficient, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W/(m²·K)). A single coefficient that combines the process-side film, the wall, fouling, and the coolant-side film resistances.
  • ΔT_m — mean temperature difference between the reaction mass and the coolant, in kelvin (K).
  • h_i — process-side (inside) film heat-transfer coefficient, in W/(m²·K).
  • h_o — coolant-side (outside) film heat-transfer coefficient, in W/(m²·K).
  • x_w — wall thickness, in metres (m).
  • k_w — thermal conductivity of the wall material, in watts per metre per kelvin (W/(m·K)).
  • R_f — combined fouling resistance (process side plus coolant side), in square metres kelvin per watt (m²·K/W).
  • m_dot_cool — coolant mass flow rate, in kilograms per second (kg/s).
  • c_p,cool — specific heat capacity of the coolant at constant pressure, in joules per kilogram per kelvin (J/(kg·K)).
  • ΔT_cool — temperature rise of the coolant from inlet to outlet, in kelvin (K).
  • F — design margin factor (dimensionless), a multiplier greater than 1 applied to a calculated area if a margin is specified. No value is given in this problem.
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The governing relation needs three quantities: Q, U, and ΔT_m. Only two are supplied. U is not supplied, is not a property of a single substance, and cannot be calculated from the information given: U depends on the reactor type (jacket, internal coil, or external heat-exchanger loop), the wall material and thickness, whether the wall is glass-lined, the viscosity and other properties of the reaction mass, the degree of agitation, the coolant and its flow rate, and the fouling state. Across ordinary reactor cooling equipment, published U values span roughly a factor of five, and across all plausible cases roughly a factor of ten. Because A is inversely proportional to U, that factor passes directly into A.

Confidence rating: Low. Confidence in the arithmetic is high (Section 6). Confidence in any single numerical area is low, because the result is dominated by one input, U, that is entirely assumed. Confidence in the reported range is moderate, conditional on the reactor being a liquid-filled, agitated, water-cooled vessel (see Section 2). The range is an estimate for screening and for stating what must be measured or specified next. It is not a design area.

No agreement with any other model is used as verification in this solution. Verification is by dimensional check, limiting cases, a resistance-sum calculation, and executed arithmetic only (Section 6).

2. Missing quantities — Prompt 2: fill the gaps first

The problem as stated is underspecified. The following quantities are needed and are not given. No value is taken in silence: each item states the assumption used for the screening range and the alternative that changes the answer.

# Missing quantity Why it is needed Treatment in this solution
1 U, in W/(m²·K) Directly sets A Assumed from published typical ranges for jacketed vessels; solved at both ends (Section 4). This is the dominant gap.
2 Reactor / cooler type: jacket, internal coil, external loop, or shell-and-tube exchanger Each type has a different typical U range and a different meaning of A Main range assumes a jacketed agitated vessel. A wider range covering coils and glass-lined and chilled service is also reported.
3 Reaction-mass identity, phase, and composition basis (mass, mole, or volume basis if a mixture) Sets viscosity, and through viscosity sets h_i and hence U Assumed: a single-phase liquid of low to moderate viscosity. Gas-phase, boiling, condensing, polymerising, or highly viscous masses fall outside the main range.
4 Reaction-mass viscosity and its change with temperature and conversion h_i falls sharply as viscosity rises; U can fall by a factor of 2–5 Not modelled. Listed as a condition that moves the answer by more than 10 % (Section 8).
5 Coolant identity, inlet temperature, flow rate, and whether ΔT_m is a log-mean, an arithmetic mean, or a stated bulk difference Determines whether the stated ΔT_m = 30 K can actually be held and whether the coolant side limits U Assumed: liquid water coolant, and ΔT_m taken exactly as given. ΔT_m is not recalculated, because the terminal temperatures are not given.
6 Pressure basis and operating pressure Affects coolant choice (for example brine or glycol under chilled service), wall thickness, and whether boiling occurs Not used in the area arithmetic, because Q and ΔT_m are already given. Still required for any real design. Not supplied.
7 Reference state / basis of Q: peak, time-averaged, or steady-state duty; per pass or overall for a recirculating loop A peak duty larger than an average duty requires proportionally larger A Assumed: Q = 800 kW is the duty the surface must remove at the condition where ΔT_m = 30 K (given). If 800 kW is an average and the peak is higher, A scales in direct proportion to the peak.
8 Vessel material, wall thickness, glass lining Wall resistance enters U; glass lining lowers U materially Reflected only through the spread of the assumed U range (glass-lined values at the low end).
9 Agitation: impeller type, speed, baffling Sets h_i for a stirred vessel Not modelled. Reflected only in the spread of U.
10 Fouling allowance and service age (clean or fouled U) Fouled U is lower than clean U Not separated. Published "typical" U values are normally in-service values, but this is unverified for any specific plant (Section 5).

12 Design margin F, and any safety factor required by the site standard Multiplies the calculated area None applied, because none is given. Applying F = 1.20 (assumed, illustrative only) would multiply every area below by 1.20 (+20 %).
13 Whether A must be available in one vessel Jacket area grows more slowly than vessel volume on scale-up; a large required A may not exist as jacket area Checked qualitatively in Section 7. A total area is reported, not a vessel size.

Quantities that are not missing for this narrow calculation: a material balance and a reaction enthalpy are not needed, because Q is given directly rather than calculated from a feed rate and a heat of reaction. Conversion, per pass or overall, therefore does not enter, except through item 7 if Q was itself derived elsewhere on a per-pass basis — that derivation is not supplied and is unverified.

3. Inputs, labelled at the point of use
Input Value State
Q 800 kW = 800 000 W Given
ΔT_m 30 K Given. Whether it is a log-mean or another mean is not stated (assumed: usable directly in the relation in Section 4).
U 200 to 500 W/(m²·K) for the main range Assumed / estimated from published typical values for water-cooled jacketed vessels (Section 5). Not measured, not fitted to this reactor.
U 100 to 600 W/(m²·K) for the wider range Assumed / estimated, covering glass-lined chilled service at the low end and well-designed internal coils at the high end (Section 5).
F 1.00 (no margin) Assumed, because no margin was specified.
4. Model and result — Prompt 1: range, not a single value

Model (steady heat transfer through a surface, no other terms):

Q = U × A × ΔT_m so A = Q / (U × ΔT_m)

with Q in W, U in W/(m²·K), ΔT_m in K, giving A in m². The model assumes steady state, a uniform U over the surface, a uniform ΔT_m as given, no heat loss to the surroundings, no agitator power input, and no separate correction factor. Each of these is an assumption; Section 8 lists what they omit.

4.1 Main result

For a jacketed, agitated vessel, liquid reaction mass, water coolant:

  • Q = 800 000 W — given.
  • ΔT_m = 30 K — given.
  • U = 200 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, low end: A = 800 000 / (200 × 30) = 133 m².
  • U = 500 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, high end: A = 800 000 / (500 × 30) = 53 m².

Reported result (main range): A = 53 to 133 m².

Two illustrative mid-range values, reported only to show position inside the range and not as the answer: at U = 350 W/(m²·K) (assumed, a commonly tabulated single figure for cooling in a carbon- or stainless-steel jacketed vessel), A = 76 m²; at U = 300 W/(m²·K) (assumed), A = 89 m².

4.2 Wider range if the equipment type is not assumed

If the glass-lined, chilled-service, coil, and external-loop cases are not excluded:

  • U = 100 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, low end: A = 267 m².
  • U = 600 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, high end: A = 44 m².

Reported result (wide range): A = 44 to 267 m².

Outside even the wide range: a viscous or gas-phase system at U = 50 W/(m²·K) (assumed, for illustration of the failure mode) would need A = 533 m², and no jacketed vessel of ordinary size provides that area. A required area in the hundreds of square metres is itself a finding: the cooling concept, not only the number, would have to change (internal coils or an external pumped loop through a heat exchanger).

4.3 Calculated table (executed)

Arithmetic was executed in Python (Section 6.4). Values of A, in m², at Q = 800 000 W (given) and ΔT_m = 30 K (given), as U (assumed) varies:

U, W/(m²·K) 100 150 200 250 300 350 400 500 600 800
A, m² 267 178 133 107 89 76 67 53 44 33

Values at U = 800 W/(m²·K) and above are shown for completeness of the sensitivity table only; they belong to high-performance external exchangers, not to a plain jacket, and are not part of either reported range.

4.4 Sensitivity: how much each guess moves the result

A is exactly proportional to Q and exactly inversely proportional to U and to ΔT_m. Therefore:

Change in an input Change in A
U +10 % A −9 % (A multiplied by 1/1.10)
U −10 % A +11 %
U doubled (200 → 400 W/(m²·K)) A halved (133 → 67 m²)
U halved (400 → 200 W/(m²·K)) A doubled (67 → 133 m²)
ΔT_m 30 → 20 K (−33 %) A +50 % at any fixed U
ΔT_m 30 → 15 K (−50 %) A +100 % (doubled)
ΔT_m 30 → 40 K (+33 %) A −25 %
Q 800 → 880 kW (+10 %, for example a peak above an average) A +10 % at any fixed U and ΔT_m
Margin F = 1.20 applied (assumed, illustrative) A +20 %
Area basis changed from outside to inside for a thin vessel wall A changes by a few percent (estimated); small against the U spread

Ranking of guesses by effect on A: (1) U, including everything inside it — equipment type, viscosity, agitation, fouling — a factor of about 2.5 across the main range and about 6 across the wide range; (2) the true ΔT_m in service, if it differs from the given 30 K — tens of percent, up to a doubling; (3) whether Q is a peak or an average — directly proportional; (4) margin and area basis — percent to tens of percent.

5. Property values, rules of thumb, and sources — with validity ranges

No thermophysical property of a specific substance is used: Q and ΔT_m are given, so no density, heat capacity, or heat of reaction enters the main calculation. The only property-type input is U, a fitted / tabulated quantity, not a true property.

Value used Source type Range where it holds Status
Jacketed vessel, water coolant, dilute aqueous solutions: U = 200 to 500 W/(m²·K) Typical-values table for overall coefficients, jacketed vessels section, in Sinnott and Towler, Chemical Engineering Design (Table 12.1 in the edition consulted in secondary copies) Jacketed vessels, aqueous liquids, liquid coolant Unverified against the current publisher edition in this solution; checked only against secondary copies found by web search
Jacketed vessel, water coolant, light organics: U = 200 to 300 W/(m²·K) Same table as above Jacketed vessels, light organic liquids Unverified as above; this is why the main range is not narrowed below a low end of 200 W/(m²·K)
Jacketed carbon / stainless steel vessel, cooling duty: U ≈ 350 W/(m²·K); glass-lined steel, cooling: U ≈ 200 W/(m²·K); glass-lined, chilled service: U ≈ 100 W/(m²·K); well-designed coil: U = 400 to 600 W/(m²·K) Carpenter, "Agitated Vessel Heat Transfer", typical-coefficient tables for jacketed vessels Agitated jacketed vessels and coils, liquid service, moderate agitation Unverified against the primary text in this solution; values taken from secondary copies found by web search
Stainless-steel standard jacket: U = 300 to 500 W/(m²·K) Secondary industry summary of jacketed-vessel coefficients Stainless vessels, standard jackets, low-viscosity liquids Unverified; used only as a consistency indication that the main range is of the right order, not as verification

Primary sources that settle the point. In order of authority for a real case:

  1. A measurement on the actual equipment and material: a heat-balance trial on the vessel in question, from which U is calculated as Q divided by (A × ΔT_m), with A the installed area (known), Q from the coolant side (flow rate and temperature rise), and ΔT_m from measured terminal temperatures. This settles U for that vessel, fluid, agitation, and fouling state.
  2. The vessel vendor's rating document or guaranteed U for the specified vessel, lining, agitator, and services.
  3. The current edition of Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook, section on heat transfer in agitated vessels, or the current edition of Sinnott and Towler, Chemical Engineering Design, typical overall coefficients table — the primary databank for a screening value when no measurement exists.

Every tabulated U claim in this solution rests on sources of type 3 as seen in secondary copies and is marked unverified until checked against the current edition of the primary text or replaced by a source of type 1 or 2. Data supplied by the user, the plant, or a vendor for the actual case supersede these ranges for that case.

6. Independent checks — Prompt 3: check the work

Checks were performed by routes separate from the main division. Failed or unperformable checks are reported as such; the solution was not altered to make a check pass.

6.1 Dimensional check — passes

W / [W/(m²·K) × K] = W / (W/m²) = m². The relation returns an area.

6.2 Limiting cases — passes
  • As U increases without limit at fixed Q and ΔT_m, A tends to zero. Correct behaviour for the model.
  • As ΔT_m tends to zero at fixed Q and U, A tends to infinity. Correct: no temperature driving force removes no heat through any finite area.
  • At U = 300 W/(m²·K) (assumed) and ΔT_m = 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 K, executed values of A are 267, 178, 133, 89, 67 m² respectively, monotone decreasing in ΔT_m as the model requires.
6.3 Independent route: resistance sum — consistent, not a verification of U

U was rebuilt from separate resistances using assumed film coefficients, to test whether the assumed range is physically decomposable rather than arbitrary:

  • h_i = 1000 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, agitated low-viscosity liquid.
  • h_o = 1500 W/(m²·K) — assumed / estimated, flowing water in a jacket.
  • x_w = 0.005 m and k_w = 16 W/(m·K) — assumed / estimated, a 5 mm stainless-steel wall.
  • R_f = 0.0004 m²·K/W — assumed / estimated, combined fouling.

U = 1 / (1/h_i + 1/h_o + x_w/k_w + R_f) = 1 / (0.001000 + 0.000667 + 0.000313 + 0.000400) ≈ 420 W/(m²·K), giving A ≈ 63 m², inside the main range. This shows a plausible set of film and wall resistances lands inside the tabulated range. It does not verify U for the unstated reactor, because every resistance in it is also assumed. If h_i is instead 250 W/(m²·K) (assumed, a viscous or poorly agitated liquid), the same calculation gives U ≈ 175 W/(m²·K) and A ≈ 152 m², outside the main range — which is the expected failure mode, not a contradiction.

6.4 Executed arithmetic — passes

The table in Section 4.3 was computed in Python as A = 800000 / (U * 30). Spot values agree with hand arithmetic: at U = 200 W/(m²·K), 800 000 / 6000 = 133.3 m²; at U = 350 W/(m²·K), 800 000 / 10 500 = 76.2 m²; at U = 500 W/(m²·K), 800 000 / 15 000 = 53.3 m².

6.5 Energy-balance closure on the coolant side — cannot be closed; reported as a failed check

A coolant-side balance needs m_dot_cool, c_p,cool, and ΔT_cool, none of which is given. The check therefore cannot be performed on the problem as stated, and that is recorded here as an unclosed balance, not passed over. What can be shown is the flow the stated duty implies, using assumed water values (c_p,cool = 4180 J/(kg·K), estimated for liquid water near ambient temperature; ΔT_cool assumed):

ΔT_cool, K (assumed) 5 10 15
m_dot_cool = Q / (c_p,cool × ΔT_cool), kg/s 38.3 19.1 12.8
Approximate volume flow, m³/h (estimated, water density ≈ 1000 kg/m³, assumed) 138 69 46

These are large but industrially plausible cooling-water flows, so the stated Q is not internally absurd. They also show that holding ΔT_m = 30 K (given) requires a coolant supply of this size; a plant that cannot deliver it will see ΔT_m fall and A rise (Section 4.4). A material balance likewise cannot be closed: no feed, product, or reaction quantities are given, and none is needed for the area arithmetic because Q is given.

6.6 Correlation / table valid-range check — conditional pass

The tabulated U ranges used hold for liquid-filled agitated vessels with liquid coolants and moderate agitation. The problem does not state that the reactor meets those conditions. The range therefore passes its validity check only under the assumptions listed in Section 2, items 2, 3, and 9. For a gas-phase, boiling, condensing, non-Newtonian, or very viscous system the table is outside its range and the reported area range does not apply.

7. Audit as built equipment behaves — Prompt 4

The three points most likely to make built equipment differ from this calculation:

7.1 Fouling and ageing lower U in service
  • Direction: real U falls below the clean or new-equipment value, so the real area needed is larger than calculated, or a fixed installed area removes less than 800 kW.
  • Rough size: a combined fouling resistance R_f of 0.0005 to 0.001 m²·K/W (estimated, typical cooling-water and organic-service range) added to a clean U of 400 W/(m²·K) lowers U to about 286 to 222 W/(m²·K), a fall of about 29 to 44 %, which raises the required A by about 40 to 80 %.
  • Settling document / test / record: the plant historian record of coolant flow and inlet / outlet temperatures together with process temperature for the actual vessel, reduced to an in-service U and trended over a campaign; or the site fouling allowances in the vessel datasheet.
7.2 The process-side film controls, and it depends on viscosity and agitation in the real vessel
  • Direction: if the reaction mass is more viscous than the low-viscosity liquids behind the tabulated values, or is poorly agitated, has dead zones, or thickens during reaction, h_i falls, U falls, and the required A rises. Agitator failure is the extreme case.
  • Rough size: a factor of 2 to 5 on U between a mobile liquid under good agitation and a viscous or poorly mixed one (Sections 5 and 6.3), hence a factor of 2 to 5 on A — larger than every other correction in this solution.
  • Settling document / test / record: a measured viscosity (in pascal-seconds, Pa·s; 1 Pa·s = 1000 centipoise) of the actual reaction mass at reaction temperature and at end-of-reaction composition, the agitator datasheet and power / speed record, and a heat-balance trial on the actual vessel (Section 5, source type 1).
7.3 The duty and the driving force in an upset or a batch peak are not the stated steady values
  • Direction: the calculation treats Q = 800 kW (given) and ΔT_m = 30 K (given) as simultaneous and steady. In a batch, the heat-release rate peaks and then falls; in any system, a high coolant inlet temperature on a hot day, or a falling coolant flow, reduces ΔT_m. Both effects act in the unsafe direction: a peak Q above 800 kW needs proportionally more area, and a ΔT_m below 30 K needs proportionally more area, and they can occur together.
  • Rough size: a peak-to-average ratio of 1.5 (assumed, illustrative) combined with ΔT_m falling from 30 K to 20 K multiplies the required A by 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. The main-range top end of 133 m² becomes about 300 m² on that combined basis.
  • Settling document / test / record: reaction calorimetry or a plant heat-release profile over time for the actual chemistry (peak and time-averaged rates stated separately), the cooling-water supply temperature record for the warmest design month, and the relief / thermal-stability assessment that states the maximum credible heat-release rate.

A fourth point, noted because it decides feasibility rather than size of the number: jacket area on a single vessel is fixed by vessel geometry and grows more slowly than volume. A required A of 53 to 133 m² corresponds to a large vessel if it is jacket area alone; if the intended vessel is smaller, the area must come from coils or an external loop, each with its own U — settled by the vessel general-arrangement drawing and the piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID), where P&ID means piping and instrumentation diagram.

8. What this calculation does not cover — Prompt 5
8.1 Effects not in the model
  • Fouling growth over time, and cleaning state (treated only as a sensitivity in Section 7.1).
  • Variation of viscosity, density, and other properties with temperature, composition, and conversion, including non-Newtonian behaviour and polymer formation.
  • Phase change on either side: boiling or condensing process fluid, boiling coolant, gas evolution, and solids formation or settling.
  • Agitator power dissipated as heat into the reaction mass (adds to the load), heat loss to the surroundings (reduces it), and heat capacity of the vessel and contents, which govern transient temperature rise if cooling is lost.
  • Control behaviour: coolant valve and supply limits, jacket temperature dynamics, cascade control, and the response to coolant failure. Nothing here is a runaway or relief calculation; thermal stability, maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction, and vent sizing require separate methods and the actual reaction kinetics.
  • Coolant-side hydraulics: pressure drop, pump capacity, jacket or coil flow distribution, and whether the flows implied in Section 6.5 are deliverable.
  • Mechanical and materials matters: pressure rating, corrosion, erosion, glass-lining thermal-shock limits, and code compliance of any vessel that would be built to provide the area.
8.2 Information not visible here
  • Current-edition databank values (Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook; Sinnott and Towler, Chemical Engineering Design) and proprietary databanks and rating software (for example HTRI, where HTRI means Heat Transfer Research, Inc.) — the tabulated U values used here come from secondary copies and are unverified (Section 5).
  • Vendor guarantees, vessel datasheets, and plant historian and laboratory records for the actual material and equipment. These are held by the plant and the vendor and supersede every range here.
  • Site design standards: required margin, fouling allowances, design coolant temperature, and the standard that decides whether a screening estimate may be used at all.
8.3 Effects that appear only in running equipment
  • Real flow maldistribution in the jacket, air binding, scaling on the coolant side, agitator dead zones, and batch-to-batch variation in charge and composition.
  • Ageing of the lining or wall, gasket and nozzle restrictions, and the difference between the nameplate area and the wetted, effective area at the actual working liquid level. A partially filled vessel has less jacket area in contact with liquid than its nominal jacket area.
8.4 Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %

The answer changes by more than 10 % under any one of the following, each of which is plausible without further data:

  • U differs from any chosen single value by more than about 10 % — near-certain, since U is assumed and its published spread is a factor of about 2.5 to 6 (A then moves by about 11 % to several hundred percent).
  • ΔT_m in service differs from 30 K by more than about 3 K.
  • The duty to be removed at design conditions exceeds 880 kW, for example if 800 kW is an average rather than a peak.
  • A design margin or fouling allowance of 10 % or more is imposed by the site standard.
  • The coolant is brine or glycol rather than water (chilled service), which moves U toward the low end of the wide range.
  • The reaction mass is viscous, gas-phase, boiling, or poorly agitated (Sections 6.6, 7.2).
8.5 Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used
  1. What is the reactor: jacket, coil, or external loop — and what area, on what area basis, is actually installed or proposed?
  2. What is the measured or vendor-guaranteed U for this vessel, this material, this agitator, and this coolant, in its fouled state?
  3. Is 800 kW a peak, an average, or a steady value, on what basis was it derived, and what is the maximum credible heat-release rate?
  4. How was ΔT_m = 30 K obtained: from which four terminal temperatures, is it a log-mean, and can the coolant supply hold it in the warmest month?
  5. What are the reaction mass viscosity (at start and at end of reaction), phase, and composition basis?
  6. What coolant, at what flow rate and pressure drop, and is the flow implied by Section 6.5 available?
  7. What margin and fouling allowance does the site standard require, and has the margin been applied once, not twice or not at all?
  8. What happens on loss of cooling or loss of agitation, and where is that case calculated? This area estimate does not answer it.
9. Answer, restated
  • Q = 800 kW — given.
  • ΔT_m = 30 K — given.
  • U — not given; assumed / estimated.

Cooling area A = 53 to 133 m² for a jacketed, agitated, water-cooled vessel with a liquid reaction mass (U = 500 to 200 W/(m²·K), assumed), with no design margin applied.

Cooling area A = 44 to 267 m² if the equipment type, lining, and service are left open (U = 600 to 100 W/(m²·K), assumed).

Confidence: low for any single value; moderate for the main range under the assumptions stated in Sections 2 and 3. The value that settles the estimate is a measured or vendor-guaranteed U for the actual vessel and material (Section 5). Any user-, plant-, or vendor-supplied U for the actual case replaces the assumed range and the area must then be recomputed from A = Q / (U × ΔT_m) with Q and ΔT_m as given.

B4. Mixing Scale-Up — Second Vessel

Response without the skill

Stirred Vessel Scale-Up

Result

No unique stirrer speed for the large vessel can be obtained from the information given. Geometric similarity and the small-vessel speed fix the size ratio, but a scale-up criterion must also be stated. Different standard criteria, all in routine use, give large-vessel speeds from about 26 revolutions per minute (rpm) to 300 rpm, a range of more than a factor of ten. Conditional results for the standard criteria are given below.

Given Data and Definitions
  • V1V_1 is the working volume of the small vessel, V1=0.05 m3V_1 = 0.05\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • V2V_2 is the working volume of the large vessel, V2=2 m3V_2 = 2\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • N1N_1 is the stirrer speed in the small vessel, N1=300 rpmN_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}.
  • N2N_2 is the stirrer speed in the large vessel, in rpm, to be determined.
  • D1D_1 is a characteristic linear dimension of the small vessel (for example the vessel diameter, or the impeller diameter), in metres (m).
  • D2D_2 is the corresponding linear dimension of the large vessel, in m.
  • SS is the linear scale ratio, S=D2/D1S = D_2/D_1, dimensionless.

No fluid properties, impeller type, flow regime, or process duty (blending, solids suspension, gas dispersion, heat transfer, or reaction) are specified.

Geometric Scale Ratio

Geometric similarity means that every length scales by the same ratio SS, so volume scales as S3S^3:

V2V1=S3\frac{V_2}{V_1} = S^3

S=(V2V1)1/3=(20.05)1/3=401/3=3.42S = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{2}{0.05}\right)^{1/3} = 40^{1/3} = 3.42

Hence D2=3.42 D1D_2 = 3.42\,D_1: the large vessel is 3.42 times the small vessel in every linear dimension, and 40 times it in volume. This is the only result that follows from the stated data alone.

Why a Criterion Is Required

Scale-up holds one chosen quantity constant and lets the others change. The quantities cannot all be held constant at once, because they depend on N2N_2 and D2D_2 in different ways. The definitions used below are stated before use:

  • ρ\rho is the liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}).
  • μ\mu is the liquid dynamic viscosity, in pascal-seconds (Pa s\mathrm{Pa\,s}).
  • ReRe is the impeller Reynolds number, Re=ρND2/μRe = \rho N D^2/\mu, dimensionless, where NN is the stirrer speed in revolutions per second and DD is the impeller diameter in m. Ratios of speeds may be evaluated in rpm, since the unit conversion cancels.
  • utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} is the impeller tip speed, in metres per second (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}), utip=πDNu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N.
  • PP is the power drawn by the impeller, in watts (W).
  • NPN_P is the power number, dimensionless. In fully turbulent flow in a baffled vessel NPN_P is approximately constant for a given impeller, and P=NP ρN3D5P = N_P\,\rho N^3 D^5.
  • VV is the vessel working volume, in m3\mathrm{m^3}, with V∝D3V \propto D^3 under geometric similarity.
  • θm\theta_m is the blending (mixing) time, in seconds (s). In turbulent flow under geometric similarity the dimensionless product NθmN\theta_m is approximately constant.
Conditional Results
1. Constant impeller Reynolds number

Holding ReRe constant, with the same liquid (ρ\rho and μ\mu unchanged), gives N∝D−2N \propto D^{-2}:

N2=N1S−2=300×3.42−2=25.6 rpmN_2 = N_1 S^{-2} = 300 \times 3.42^{-2} = 25.6\ \mathrm{rpm}

2. Constant impeller tip speed

Holding utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} constant gives N∝D−1N \propto D^{-1}. This criterion is used where tip speed controls the process, for example shear-sensitive dispersion or a maximum-shear limit:

N2=N1S−1=300/3.42=87.7 rpmN_2 = N_1 S^{-1} = 300 / 3.42 = 87.7\ \mathrm{rpm}

Constant torque per unit volume in turbulent flow leads to the same N∝D−1N \propto D^{-1} dependence.

3. Constant power per unit volume, turbulent flow

From P=NP ρN3D5P = N_P\,\rho N^3 D^5 and V∝D3V \propto D^3, the power per unit volume P/VP/V, in watts per cubic metre (W m−3\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}), satisfies P/V∝N3D2P/V \propto N^3 D^2. Holding P/VP/V constant gives N∝D−2/3N \propto D^{-2/3}:

N2=N1S−2/3=300×3.42−2/3=132 rpmN_2 = N_1 S^{-2/3} = 300 \times 3.42^{-2/3} = 132\ \mathrm{rpm}

This is the most commonly used first estimate for blending and for solids suspension duties. The exponent is regime-dependent: in laminar flow NP∝Re−1N_P \propto Re^{-1}, so P/V∝N2P/V \propto N^2 with no dependence on DD, and constant P/VP/V would instead give N2=N1=300 rpmN_2 = N_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}. The flow regime is therefore part of the missing information.

4. Constant blending time

Holding θm\theta_m constant, with NθmN\theta_m approximately constant in turbulent flow, gives NN constant:

N2=N1=300 rpmN_2 = N_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}

Summary Table
Quantity held constant Scaling of NN with DD N2N_2 (rpm)
Impeller Reynolds number ReRe N∝D−2N \propto D^{-2} 26
Impeller tip speed utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} N∝D−1N \propto D^{-1} 88
Power per unit volume P/VP/V, turbulent N∝D−2/3N \propto D^{-2/3} 132
Blending time θm\theta_m, turbulent N∝D0N \propto D^{0} 300
Incompatibility of the Criteria

The criteria conflict quantitatively. At the constant-P/VP/V speed of 132 rpm, for example:

  • the tip speed is 132/300×3.42=1.51132/300 \times 3.42 = 1.51 times the small-vessel value;
  • the impeller Reynolds number is 132/300×3.422=5.15132/300 \times 3.42^2 = 5.15 times the small-vessel value.

Conversely, at the constant-ReRe speed of 25.6 rpm, the turbulent power per unit volume falls to (25.6/300)3×3.422=0.0073(25.6/300)^3 \times 3.42^2 = 0.0073 of the small-vessel value, a reduction by a factor of about 137. No single speed preserves ReRe, utipu_{\mathrm{tip}}, P/VP/V, and θm\theta_m simultaneously at S=3.42S = 3.42.

Information Required for a Definite Answer

A definite value of N2N_2 requires, at minimum:

  1. the scale-up criterion, selected from the process duty — for example P/VP/V for general blending or suspension, utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} where shear or drop or bubble size controls, or a just-suspended speed correlation where solids suspension controls;
  2. the flow regime (or the fluid density ρ\rho and viscosity μ\mu, together with D1D_1 and the impeller type, so that the regime and NPN_P can be established);
  3. any operating limits that may override the selected criterion, such as maximum tip speed, motor power, or shaft torque.

If a single provisional figure must be quoted before that information is available, the conventional turbulent constant-P/VP/V estimate, N2≈132 rpmN_2 \approx 132\ \mathrm{rpm}, is the usual starting point for blending duties. It is a conditional estimate under criteria 3 above, not a result implied by the stated data.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Scale-up of a Stirred Vessel — 0.05 m³ to 2 m³

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: Stirred-vessel scale-up has no single governing rule. The large-vessel stirrer speed depends entirely on the scale-up criterion — what is held constant on scale-up (power per unit volume, impeller tip speed, Reynolds number, mixing time, solids suspension, gas dispersion, heat transfer, and others). The problem states no criterion and no process duty. Different standard criteria give speeds differing by more than a factor of ten for this size change, so any single-value answer would be an artefact of an unstated assumption, not of the data.

Confidence rating: Low for a single speed; High for the arithmetic conditional on a stated criterion. The geometric scale ratio is exact from the given volumes. Each conditional speed below is exact algebra given its criterion. Which criterion is correct for this duty is not knowable from the problem statement.

2. Missing quantities — Prompt 2: fill the gaps first

No value is taken in silence. The following are needed and are not supplied:

  1. Scale-up criterion / process duty — missing. This is the decisive gap. Solved below under the plausible alternatives and all results reported (Section 4).
  2. Fluid properties — density, in kg/m³; dynamic viscosity, in Pa·s; whether Newtonian; whether single-phase, solid–liquid, gas–liquid, or liquid–liquid — all missing. They decide whether the flow is turbulent, transitional, or laminar, and therefore whether the turbulent power relation used for the power-per-volume criterion holds.
  3. Impeller and vessel geometry beyond "geometric similarity" — impeller type (Rushton turbine, pitched-blade, anchor, etc.), impeller diameter to vessel diameter ratio, baffling, fill level — missing except that all lengths scale in one ratio (given). The absolute power, not computed here, cannot be obtained without them.
  4. Power number and its regime — the power number, a dimensionless group defined as shaft power divided by (fluid density × stirrer speed cubed × impeller diameter to the fifth power) — missing / not needed for speed ratios at constant criterion in the turbulent regime, but needed for any motor sizing.
  5. Basis notes: volumes are taken as working (liquid) volumes — assumed, not given; if they are total vessel volumes at different fill fractions, the scale ratio changes. Pressure basis, composition basis, reference state, and per-pass versus overall conversion do not arise: no pressure, composition, reaction, or conversion is stated or computed. Their absence is recorded here rather than passed over.

Primary source that settles the decisive point (Checklist item 5): the process duty specification and pilot-plant mixing trials on the actual fluid and solids/gas system, interpreted with the impeller vendor's power and pumping curves for the actual impeller. Textbook scale-up exponents (e.g. in Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook, agitation chapter, and in Oldshue, Fluid Mixing Technology) are secondary compilations. Any claim resting on a textbook exponent is unverified until checked against that duty specification and those vendor curves. No such document was supplied or consulted for this solution; the exponents below are the standard textbook forms, stated with their regimes.

3. Inputs, labelled at point of use
Quantity Value State
Small-vessel volume, V₁ (volume of vessel 1, in m³) 0.05 m³ given
Large-vessel volume, V₂ (volume of vessel 2, in m³) 2 m³ given
Small-vessel stirrer speed, N₁ (stirrer speed in vessel 1, in rpm) 300 rpm given
Geometric similarity (all lengths in one ratio) — given
Volumes are working volumes at equal fill fraction — assumed — see sensitivity, Section 5
Large-vessel stirrer speed, N₂ (stirrer speed in vessel 2, in rpm) to be found —
Linear scale ratio, S (ratio of any large-vessel length to the corresponding small-vessel length, dimensionless) computed below derived from given values
Impeller diameter in vessel 1, D₁ (in m), and in vessel 2, D₂ (in m) not supplied; only the ratio D₂/D₁ = S is used ratio derived; absolute values missing
4. Calculation and results as a range
4.1 Linear scale ratio

With geometric similarity, volume scales as length cubed, so

S = (V₂ / V₁)^(1/3) = (2 / 0.05)^(1/3) = 40^(1/3) = 3.42

That is, every length in the large vessel — vessel diameter, liquid depth, impeller diameter D₂ = S × D₁ — is 3.42 times the small-vessel length. This step uses only given values; it carries no fitted or estimated input.

4.2 Speed under each standard criterion

Each criterion has the form N₂ = N₁ × S^(−a), where a (a dimensionless exponent set by the criterion, defined here at first use) differs by criterion:

Criterion held constant a Relation / where it holds N₂ (rpm)
Mixing time (N itself constant) 0 Definition of constant mixing time in the turbulent regime; fitted/textbook relation 300
Froude number (impeller speed squared × impeller diameter / gravitational acceleration) — vortex / surface behaviour 0.5 Dimensionless-group constancy 162
Power per unit volume, P/V (shaft power P, in W, divided by volume, in m³), turbulent 2/3 Derived below; holds only for turbulent flow, constant power number 132
Just-suspended speed, Zwietering form ≈0.85 Fitted correlation for solid–liquid suspension; exponent fitted, valid only within the correlation's tested solids, particle, and geometry range — unverified here 106
Impeller tip speed (π × impeller diameter × stirrer speed) — shear-sensitive duties 1 Dimensionless/kinematic constancy 88
Reynolds number (fluid density × stirrer speed × impeller diameter squared / dynamic viscosity) 2 Dimensionless-group constancy 26

Derivation of the power-per-volume row: in turbulent flow with a constant power number, P is proportional to N³ × D⁵, where N is stirrer speed and D is impeller diameter. Since V is proportional to D³, P/V is proportional to N³ × D². Holding P/V constant gives N proportional to D^(−2/3), i.e. a = 2/3, hence N₂ = 300 × 3.42^(−2/3) = 132 rpm.

4.3 Answer
  • Reported range (Checklist item 2): N₂ = 26 to 300 rpm across all standard criteria above; 88 to 162 rpm across the criteria most commonly used for blending, suspension, and surface duties.
  • If — and only if — the intended criterion is the most common default, constant power per unit volume in turbulent flow (assumed, not given): N₂ ≈ 132 rpm.
  • No single value is presented as "the" answer. Selecting one requires the missing duty in Section 2, item 1.

Consequences that follow whichever criterion is chosen, and that a single-criterion answer hides: at constant P/V, tip speed rises by a factor of 1.51 (higher maximum shear in the large vessel); at constant tip speed, P/V falls by a factor of S = 3.42 (much weaker bulk mixing per unit volume); Reynolds number cannot be held constant together with any of the others. Geometric similarity plus one criterion necessarily breaks the others.

5. Every guess and its effect — Prompt 1
Guess / assumed or fitted input State Effect on N₂
Scale-up criterion (exponent a from 0 to 2) assumed — not given Dominant: moves N₂ from 300 rpm to 26 rpm, i.e. −91 % to 0 % relative to N₁. No other input matters by comparison.
Choice of constant P/V as the "default" assumed Gives 132 rpm; choosing tip speed instead changes the result by −34 % (to 88 rpm); choosing constant mixing time changes it by +127 % (to 300 rpm).

Turbulent regime, constant power number (for the P/V row) assumed — no viscosity or density given If the large vessel (or the small one) is in transitional or laminar flow, the P/V exponent is not 2/3; in laminar flow P is proportional to N² × D³, so constant P/V gives a = 1/3 and N₂ ≈ 199 rpm, +51 % versus 132 rpm.
Zwietering exponent 0.85 fitted ±0.1 in the exponent moves N₂ by about ∓13 % (S^0.1 ≈ 1.13). Correlation range unverified — no solids data supplied.

Property values, rules of thumb, and fitted relations used: only the power relation P proportional to N³D⁵ (turbulent, constant power number; textbook agitation theory, holds for Reynolds number above roughly 10⁴ for a baffled turbine — unverified here because no fluid properties were supplied), its laminar counterpart P proportional to N²D³, and the Zwietering exponent ≈0.85 (fitted correlation, range unverified here). No fluid property value was used or invented.

6. Independent verification — Prompt 3

Checks performed by a route independent of the table algebra — executed code (Python) recomputing S and every row, plus the checks below. No agreement with another AI model is used as verification (Checklist item 7).

  1. Executed code: S = 40^(1/3) = 3.41995; N₂ values 300, 162.2, 132.2, 105.5, 87.7, 25.6 rpm for a = 0, 0.5, 2/3, 0.85, 1, 2 — matches the table (rounded). Pass.
  2. Balance / invariant closure: for the P/V row, (N₂/N₁)³ × (D₂/D₁)² = (132.2/300)³ × 3.42² = 1.000 to three figures, i.e. P/V is in fact conserved by the computed speed. Pass. No material or energy balance exists in this problem; the conserved quantity of the chosen criterion is the applicable closure.
  3. Limiting cases known by sight: if V₂ = V₁, then S = 1 and every criterion gives N₂ = N₁ — the formula satisfies this. If a = 0 the formula returns N₁ for any S — correct by definition of that criterion. Pass.
  4. Dimensional check: S is a ratio of volumes to the one-third power, hence dimensionless; N₂ inherits rpm from N₁. Pass.
  5. Correlation valid-range check: fails / cannot be completed — the turbulent power relation and the Zwietering correlation cannot be checked against their valid Reynolds-number and solids ranges because density, viscosity, impeller type, and solids data are missing. This failure is reported, not repaired by changing the solution (Prompt 3 instruction).
7. Audit as built equipment behaves — Prompt 4

Three points most likely to differ in built equipment, as a 25-year plant engineer would flag them:

  1. Regime shift on scale-up. Direction: at constant P/V the large vessel's Reynolds number rises by S^(4/3) ≈ 5.2 (at the same fluid properties, assumed), so a small vessel that was transitional may be fully turbulent at scale — or, with a viscous fluid, neither is turbulent and the 2/3 exponent is simply wrong (see Section 5, +51 % case). Size: tens of percent in speed, factor-level in power. Settled by: measured viscosity and density of the actual fluid and the vendor power curve (power number versus Reynolds number) for the actual impeller — unverified until checked.
  2. Motor, gearbox, and standard sizes. Built drives come in discrete ratings and gear ratios; the installed speed will be a catalogue step near, not at, 132 rpm (or whichever target), and start-up torque in an unmixed, settled, or cold vessel can size the drive, not running power. Direction: installed speed typically rounded to the nearest available ratio, commonly ±5–15 %. Settled by: the vendor drive selection document for the large vessel.
  3. Non-ideal geometry and contents behaviour. Standard head shapes, a nearest-standard impeller diameter, baffles omitted or added, surface vortexing, solids settling in dead zones, and gas hold-up (if gassed) all break exact geometric similarity and the single-phase power relation; gassed power can fall to roughly half the ungassed value for a Rushton turbine (textbook range, unverified here). Settled by: the vessel fabrication drawing, and a mixing trial or torque measurement on the built vessel.
8. What is not covered — Prompt 5
  • Effects not in the model: absolute shaft power, motor size, torque, heat-transfer rate, blend time in absolute seconds, shear damage to product, solids distribution quality, gas dispersion, foaming, vortexing, mechanical design (shaft, seals, critical speed). None can be computed from the supplied data.
  • Information not accessible here: the actual fluid properties, the duty specification, vendor power/pumping curves, and any site standards — private or vendor-held documents not supplied.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: start-up and settled-solids torque, viscosity change during a batch (e.g. with temperature or reaction), fouling, and level variation during filling/emptying.
  • Conditions changing the answer by more than 10 %: any change of scale-up criterion (up to a factor of ~11 across the table); laminar or transitional instead of turbulent flow (+51 % on the P/V row); a volume-ratio error or fill difference of about ±25 % (≈∓7 % on the P/V row — below 10 % alone, but compounding with the above); a departure of D₂/D₁ from S by more than about 15 %.
  • Questions a reviewer should ask before use: (1) What duty is the vessel for, and which quantity must be preserved on scale-up? (2) What are the fluid density, viscosity (over the batch), and phases present? (3) What impeller, baffling, and fill level, in both vessels? (4) Is 132 rpm (or the chosen target) an available drive speed, and is the drive sized for start-up torque? (5) Has the chosen criterion been confirmed on a pilot trial with the actual material?
9. Bottom line

Geometric scale ratio S = 3.42 (derived, from given volumes). Large-vessel speed: 26–300 rpm depending on the unstated scale-up criterion; 132 rpm under the assumed default of constant turbulent power per unit volume. The criterion, fluid properties, and duty must be supplied before a single design speed can be stated.

B5. Non-Ideal Flow — Second Reactor

Response without the skill

Conversion of a First-Order Reaction in a Continuous Reactor

Statement

Estimate the conversion for a first-order reaction in a continuous reactor, given that the product of the rate constant and the nominal residence time is 1.5.

Symbols
  • XX is the fractional conversion of the limiting reactant, dimensionless, defined as the molar flow rate of reactant consumed divided by the molar flow rate of reactant fed.
  • kk is the first-order rate constant, with units of reciprocal time, s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}} (any reciprocal-time unit may be used, provided the same unit is used for the residence time defined below).
  • τ\tau is the nominal residence time, with units of time, s\mathrm{s}, defined as the reactor volume divided by the inlet volumetric flow rate.
  • DaDa is the Damköhler number, dimensionless, defined here as Da=kτDa = k\tau.

The given value is

Da=kτ=1.5Da = k\tau = 1.5

Qualification: the reactor type is not specified

A single numerical value of conversion cannot be obtained from Da=1.5Da = 1.5 alone. For a first-order reaction the conversion at a given DaDa depends on the residence-time distribution, that is, on the flow pattern in the reactor. The two standard ideal limits are the continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR, perfect mixing) and the plug-flow reactor (PFR, no axial mixing). Both are derived below. For a first-order reaction these two limits give the practical range for an ideal continuous reactor, and any real reactor with partial mixing lies between them unless bypassing or dead volume is present.

Case 1: Ideal CSTR

For a steady-state CSTR with constant density, the mole balance on the reactant over the whole reactor is: inlet molar flow rate minus outlet molar flow rate minus rate of consumption by reaction equals zero. For a first-order reaction the consumption term is kk multiplied by the (uniform, outlet) reactant concentration and by the reactor volume. Dividing by the inlet molar flow rate and using τ\tau as defined above gives

XCSTR=kτ1+kτ=Da1+DaX_{\mathrm{CSTR}} = \frac{k\tau}{1 + k\tau} = \frac{Da}{1 + Da}

Substitution of Da=1.5Da = 1.5 gives

XCSTR=1.51+1.5=1.52.5=0.60X_{\mathrm{CSTR}} = \frac{1.5}{1 + 1.5} = \frac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.60

That is, a conversion of 60%.

Case 2: Ideal PFR

For a steady-state PFR with constant density, the differential mole balance on the reactant over a differential reactor volume gives, after integration from inlet (X=0X = 0) to outlet and use of τ\tau as defined above,

XPFR=1−exp⁡(−kτ)=1−exp⁡(−Da)X_{\mathrm{PFR}} = 1 - \exp(-k\tau) = 1 - \exp(-Da)

where exp⁡\exp is the exponential function. Substitution of Da=1.5Da = 1.5 gives

XPFR=1−exp⁡(−1.5)=1−0.2231=0.7769X_{\mathrm{PFR}} = 1 - \exp(-1.5) = 1 - 0.2231 = 0.7769

That is, a conversion of approximately 77.7%.

Result
  • Ideal CSTR: X=0.60X = 0.60, i.e. 60% conversion.
  • Ideal PFR: X=0.777X = 0.777, i.e. approximately 77.7% conversion.

With no reactor type stated, the defensible estimate is the range 0.60≤X≤0.780.60 \le X \le 0.78, with the endpoint selected by the flow pattern: 0.60 for a perfectly mixed continuous reactor and 0.78 for a plug-flow continuous reactor. If a single conventional textbook value is required and a stirred tank is intended, the answer is 60%; if a tubular plug-flow reactor is intended, the answer is approximately 78%. The difference is physical, not numerical error: in a CSTR the feed is diluted immediately to the low outlet concentration, so the reaction rate throughout the vessel is the low outlet rate, whereas in a PFR the concentration declines gradually and the average rate is higher.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Weakness. The problem does not state the reactor type or its residence-time distribution (RTD). No choice between those models is given, measured, or inferable from the statement.

Confidence rating.

  • In the arithmetic, given a named ideal model: high. Both model results below are closed-form, were recomputed in code, and pass limiting-case checks (Section 6).

  • In the range 0.60–0.78 as the span of the two ideal limiting models under the stated assumptions of Section 3: moderate to high — subject to the caution in Section 7 that this is a span across two ideal models, not a guaranteed bound for built equipment.

X=0.60 (ideal stirred tank)toX=0.78 (ideal plug flow)X = 0.60 \text{ (ideal stirred tank)} \quad\text{to}\quad X = 0.78 \text{ (ideal plug flow)}

3. Inputs, labelled at the point of use (Checklist item 3; Prompt 1)
  • Da=kτ=1.5Da = k\tau = 1.5 — given, dimensionless.

  • Reactor is continuous — given.

4. Solution
4.1 Ideal plug flow reactor (PFR)

For plug flow, every fluid element spends exactly τ\tau in the reactor and the first-order balance integrates to

CA,outCA,0=exp⁡(−kτ)=exp⁡(−Da),X=1−exp⁡(−Da).\frac{C_{A,\mathrm{out}}}{C_{A,0}} = \exp(-k\tau) = \exp(-Da), \qquad X = 1 - \exp(-Da).

With Da=1.5Da = 1.5 (given):

XPFR=1−exp⁡(−1.5)=1−0.2231=0.7769≈0.78.X_{\mathrm{PFR}} = 1 - \exp(-1.5) = 1 - 0.2231 = 0.7769 \approx 0.78.

4.2 Ideal continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR)

For a perfectly mixed stirred tank at steady state, the balance over the whole vessel gives

CA,outCA,0=11+kτ=11+Da,X=Da1+Da.\frac{C_{A,\mathrm{out}}}{C_{A,0}} = \frac{1}{1 + k\tau} = \frac{1}{1 + Da}, \qquad X = \frac{Da}{1 + Da}.

With Da=1.5Da = 1.5 (given):

XCSTR=1.51+1.5=1.52.5=0.6000≈0.60.X_{\mathrm{CSTR}} = \frac{1.5}{1 + 1.5} = \frac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.6000 \approx 0.60.

4.3 Result

0.60  ≤  X  ≤  0.78across the two ideal models, at Da=1.5.0.60 \;\le\; X \;\le\; 0.78 \quad\text{across the two ideal models, at } Da = 1.5.

Intermediate RTD models fall inside this span (Section 6), which is why the span is reported rather than either endpoint alone.

All numerical values in Sections 4–6 were computed in code (Python, mpmath quadrature for the laminar case); the code output is the basis for the figures quoted. No agreement with any other AI model is used as verification (Checklist item 7); none was consulted.
