7. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to make built equipment differ from either ideal model, with direction, rough size, and the record that would settle each. All three are unverified — no plant, vendor, or equipment document was supplied or consulted (Checklist item 5).

  1. Short-circuiting, bypassing, and dead volume. Real vessels rarely realise either ideal RTD; stagnant zones reduce the effective volume (hence the effective τ\tau and DaDa) and a bypass fraction passes almost unreacted. Direction: conversion below the value computed with the nominal τ\tau, and possibly below the CSTR endpoint 0.60 — the headline span is a span across ideal models, not a lower bound for a real vessel. Rough size: a 20 % dead volume acts like a 20 % reduction in DaDa, which Section 5 shows moves XX by about 0.03–0.08; gross bypassing can move it by more. Settling record: a tracer RTD test (pulse or step) on the actual vessel at operating flow rate, plus the vessel drawing / vendor datasheet giving the reactor type and internals. Primary source that settles the model question for this problem: the reactor specification (type, internals) and a measured RTD on the actual equipment. Unverified until checked against them.
  2. Non-isothermal operation. If the reaction is exothermic, a stirred tank is near-uniform in temperature but a tubular reactor develops axial and radial profiles; kk varies exponentially with temperature (Arrhenius dependence), so DaDa is not uniform and the isothermal Da=1.5Da = 1.5 (given, at an unstated temperature) may not hold locally. Direction: hot regions react faster (higher local conversion, with runaway risk in extreme cases); cooled or cold-feed regions react slower. Net direction cannot be stated without the heat of reaction, the activation energy, and the cooling arrangement — none supplied. Rough size: for many liquid-phase reactions kk roughly doubles per 10 K, which would change DaDa by far more than the ±20 %\pm 20\,\% band in Section 5. Settling record: measured temperature profile / distributed temperature points from the plant data historian for the actual run, with the kinetic parameters from the vendor or licensor kinetics package for the actual feed.
  3. Effective rate constant lower than the nominal kk — catalyst deactivation or fouling (if catalytic), poisoning by trace feed contaminants, or interphase / pore mass-transfer limitation making the observed rate slower than the intrinsic first-order rate. Direction: conversion lower than either ideal-model value at the nominal DaDa. Rough size: an effectiveness or activity factor of 0.7 acts like Da=1.05Da = 1.05, giving X≈0.51X \approx 0.51 (CSTR) to 0.650.65 (PFR) by the equations of Section 4 — i.e. a change well above 10 %. Settling record: laboratory rate measurement on the actual (aged) catalyst or actual feed, plant conversion samples (inlet/outlet analyses from the laboratory information system) for the run in question, and the catalyst vendor's deactivation / life data.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model.

  • Reversibility / equilibrium limitation: a reversible first-order reaction has XX capped below the values here; the equilibrium conversion was not given and is not accounted for.
  • Selectivity and side reactions: conversion of AA is reported; yield of any desired product is a different quantity and is not computed.
  • Gas-phase density change on reaction (mole-number change, pressure drop along a tube): changes the local residence time and can move a tubular reactor's conversion outside the constant-density figures.
  • Non-isothermal behaviour, hot spots, and thermal stability (Section 7, item 2).
  • Start-up, transients, control action, and flow maldistribution between parallel trains or tubes.
  • Fouling, deactivation, and ageing over a run (Section 7, item 3).

Information not available to this solution. The reactor type and internals, any tracer/RTD data, the kinetic source for kk (intrinsic or effective, and at what temperature), and any plant operating data are all held, if anywhere, in the equipment datasheet, the licensor or catalyst vendor's kinetics package, and plant records. None was supplied; every claim in Section 7 that rests on such a source is marked unverified.

Effects that appear only in running equipment. Bypassing around internals, fouling layers, catalyst ageing, feed contaminants, mal-distribution, and instrument error in the flows from which τ\tau is computed. None is observable from the problem statement.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %.

  • Changing the reactor model alone: CSTR in place of PFR (or the reverse) changes XX by 23–30 % relative — already satisfied by the ambiguity in the statement.
  • A change of about ±25 %\pm 25\,\% or more in the effective DaDa (through temperature, deactivation, dead volume, or a flow-rate error in τ\tau) moves XX by roughly 10 % relative near Da=1.5Da = 1.5, by the sensitivity computed in Section 5.
  • Adding recycle with separation: overall conversion then differs from the per-pass values here by far more than 10 % and can approach 1.0.
  • An equilibrium cap below about 0.70, if the reaction is in fact reversible, would put the achievable conversion below the PFR endpoint by more than 10 % relative.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used.

  1. Which reactor is this — stirred tank, tubular, or other — and what RTD or tracer evidence supports that choice?
  2. Is the required figure per-pass or overall (plant, with recycle) conversion, and on what molar basis?
  3. At what temperature was kk obtained, is it intrinsic or effective (mass transfer, catalyst age) for the actual feed, and is operation close enough to isothermal for a single DaDa to apply?
  4. Is the reaction treated as irreversible, and what is the equilibrium conversion at operating conditions?
  5. Is the flow gas or liquid, and does the mole number (hence density and residence time) change on reaction?
  6. What measured inlet/outlet compositions exist for the actual equipment against which 0.60–0.78 can be checked?
9. Answer in one line

At Da=kτ=1.5Da = k\tau = 1.5 (given), a first-order reaction in a continuous reactor converts X=0.60X = 0.60 in an ideal stirred tank and X=0.78X = 0.78 in ideal plug flow; with the reactor type unstated, the defensible estimate is the range X≈0.60X \approx 0.60–0.780.78 (widening to about 0.57–0.81 if DaDa itself carries an assumed ±10 %\pm 10\,\% uncertainty), and a single value should not be quoted without naming the reactor model it belongs to.

C1. Relative Volatility Near Unity — Second Separation

Response without the skill

Minimum Number of Theoretical Stages — Fenske Equation

Definitions
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min}: the minimum number of theoretical stages for the separation, dimensionless, obtained at total reflux.
  • α\alpha: the relative volatility of the more volatile component with respect to the less volatile component, dimensionless. Here α=1.22\alpha = 1.22.
  • xDx_D: the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the distillate, dimensionless.
  • xBx_B: the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the bottoms, dimensionless.
  • RR: the product of the distillate and bottoms composition ratios in the Fenske equation, dimensionless, defined by

R=(xD1−xD)(1−xBxB)R = \left(\frac{x_D}{1-x_D}\right)\left(\frac{1-x_B}{x_B}\right)

Here R=24,000R = 24{,}000.

In these definitions, 1−xD1-x_D is the mole fraction of the less volatile component in the distillate, and 1−xB1-x_B is the mole fraction of the less volatile component in the bottoms.

Method

For a binary separation at total reflux with constant relative volatility α\alpha, the Fenske equation is

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Rln⁡αN_{\min} = \frac{\ln R}{\ln \alpha}

where ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm. Any logarithm base gives the same result, since the base cancels in the ratio.

Calculation

Substitution of R=24,000R = 24{,}000 and α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 gives

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)ln⁡(1.22)=10.0860.1989=50.7N_{\min} = \frac{\ln(24{,}000)}{\ln(1.22)} = \frac{10.086}{0.1989} = 50.7

A check with base-10 logarithms gives the same value:

Nmin⁡=log⁡10(24,000)log⁡10(1.22)=4.38020.08636=50.7N_{\min} = \frac{\log_{10}(24{,}000)}{\log_{10}(1.22)} = \frac{4.3802}{0.08636} = 50.7

Consistency check: 1.2250.7≈24,0001.22^{50.7} \approx 24{,}000, which recovers RR.

Result

The minimum number of theoretical stages is 50.750.7. Since a stage count in a physical column must be a whole number, at least 5151 theoretical stages are required.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Minimum theoretical stages — Fenske equation

Result

The minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux, denoted Nmin⁡N_{\min} and dimensionless (a count), is

Nmin⁡=50.7N_{\min} = 50.7

i.e. 51 theoretical stages when rounded up to a whole count, on the usual convention that Nmin⁡N_{\min} from the Fenske equation includes the reboiler as one theoretical stage.

Reported as a range, not a single value, for the plausible uncertainty in the relative volatility (see Weakness and Range below): 47 to 55 stages for a relative volatility of 1.24 to 1.20, and 42 to 64 stages for a wider relative-volatility band of 1.27 to 1.17.

Symbols and inputs, labelled at point of use
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min} — minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux, dimensionless count. Sought.
  • α\alpha — relative volatility, the ratio of the vapour–liquid equilibrium ratios (KK-values) of the light and heavy components, α=Klight/Kheavy\alpha = K_{\mathrm{light}}/K_{\mathrm{heavy}}, dimensionless. Given: α=1.22\alpha = 1.22. No source, measurement method, temperature, pressure, or composition range for this value was supplied, so its state in any real application would be estimated or assumed, not measured, until checked.
  • SS — the separation factor appearing in the Fenske equation, defined here as the product of the distillate composition ratio and the bottoms composition ratio, S=[xD/(1−xD)][(1−xB)/xB]S = \left[x_D/(1-x_D)\right]\left[(1-x_B)/x_B\right], where xDx_D is the mole fraction of the light component in the distillate, dimensionless, and xBx_B is the mole fraction of the light component in the bottoms, dimensionless. Given: S=24,000S = 24{,}000, dimensionless. The individual values of xDx_D and xBx_B were not given; they are not needed once SS is given.
  • No physical property value, fitted relation, correlation, or rule of thumb other than the Fenske equation itself is used in the central calculation.
Calculation

The Fenske equation for a binary separation at total reflux, with constant α\alpha, is

Nmin⁡=log⁡Slog⁡αN_{\min} = \dfrac{\log S}{\log \alpha}

where log⁡\log may be the natural logarithm or the base-10 logarithm, provided the same base is used in numerator and denominator.

Substitution of the given values:

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)ln⁡(1.22)=10.08580.19885=50.72N_{\min} = \dfrac{\ln(24{,}000)}{\ln(1.22)} = \dfrac{10.0858}{0.19885} = 50.72

Rounded up, because a fractional stage cannot be built and rounding down would not meet the stated separation: 51 theoretical stages in total, including the reboiler; 49.72, i.e. 50, theoretical stages in the column proper if the reboiler is counted separately. A partial condenser, if present and counted as a stage, would change the allocation between column and auxiliaries, not the total of 50.72.

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is exact given SS and α\alpha; the weakness is in the model and in α\alpha, not in the logarithm. The Fenske equation assumes (i) total reflux, (ii) constant α\alpha over the whole column, (iii) a binary system (or a light-key/heavy-key pair treated as binary), and (iv) theoretical (100 % efficient) stages. Because α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 is close to 1, ln⁡α\ln\alpha is small, so Nmin⁡N_{\min} is highly sensitive to α\alpha: the sensitivity is

dNmin⁡Nmin⁡≈− dαα ln⁡α\frac{\mathrm{d}N_{\min}}{N_{\min}} \approx -\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha}{\alpha\,\ln\alpha}

so an absolute change of +0.01+0.01 in α\alpha (a +0.82%+0.82\% relative change) moves Nmin⁡N_{\min} by about −4%-4\% (computed exactly below: −3.9%-3.9\%). No uncertainty, temperature, pressure, or composition range was supplied for α\alpha, so no measured uncertainty band can be stated; the ranges below are scenario ranges, labelled as such.

Confidence rating. High for the arithmetic result 50.72 conditional on the two given inputs and on the Fenske assumptions. Low to moderate for any use of 51 as a design stage count for real equipment, because α\alpha is unverified for any named pair, its constancy is untested, and Nmin⁡N_{\min} is a total-reflux lower bound, not an operating stage count.

Effect of the other input: SS enters only logarithmically, so it moves the result weakly. At α=1.22\alpha = 1.22, S=20,000S = 20{,}000 gives Nmin⁡=49.80N_{\min} = 49.80 (−1.8 %) and S=28,000S = 28{,}000 gives Nmin⁡=51.50N_{\min} = 51.50 (+1.5 %).

Guesses made, and their effect: (a) the convention that Nmin⁡N_{\min} includes the reboiler — moves the column-only count by exactly 1 stage, about 2 %; (b) the plausible α\alpha bands in the table — assumed scenario bands, not supplied data, moving the result as tabulated; (c) no other guess is made in the central calculation. Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor for the actual system would supersede these scenario bands.

Property values, rules, and fitted relations used, with source and valid range: only the Fenske equation (Fenske, 1932, binary/multicomponent minimum-stage relation at total reflux). It holds for constant (or geometric-mean) α\alpha, total reflux, and equilibrium stages; it does not hold at finite reflux, for strongly varying α\alpha, or for real (non-equilibrium) trays without an efficiency correction. No Antoine, activity-coefficient, or other fitted relation is used, because no component pair, temperature, or pressure was given.

3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2) — not completed silently

The two numbers given are sufficient for the Fenske arithmetic. They are not sufficient to specify, check, or build the separation. Missing, with the treatment adopted:

  1. Individual compositions xDx_D and xBx_B — missing. Only their combined product SS is given. Many pairs (xD,xB)(x_D, x_B) give S=24,000S = 24{,}000; component recoveries, product purities individually, and any material-balance check need the pair separately. Solved here only for Nmin⁡N_{\min}, which depends on SS alone.
  2. Basis — missing. Feed rate and whether compositions are mole, mass, or volume fractions are not stated. The Fenske form above assumes mole fractions. If the given ratios were mass-fraction ratios, SS and hence Nmin⁡N_{\min} would differ; no conversion is possible without molecular weights, which were also not given. Assumed: mole basis, as is standard for the Fenske equation, stated here rather than taken in silence.
  3. Reference conditions for α\alpha — missing. The pressure basis, the temperature and composition range over which α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 applies, and whether 1.22 is a point value or a geometric mean between top and bottom conditions are not stated. Alternative treatments are the scenario bands in Section 2 (point value at 1.20–1.24, wide band 1.17–1.27).
  4. Condenser type and stage-counting convention — missing. Treated under both conventions in the Calculation section: 50.72 total including the reboiler; 49.72 excluding it.
  5. Per-pass or overall, and reflux condition — the Fenske result is by definition the total-reflux (minimum-stage) limit. No finite reflux ratio was given, so no operating stage count can be obtained from these data alone; a finite-reflux count would additionally require the reflux ratio or a Gilliland-type correlation and feed condition (feed composition and thermal state), all missing.
  6. Component identities — missing. Without them, α\alpha cannot be checked against any databank (see Section 4).
4. Primary source that settles the point

The point that would settle the real-system value is α\alpha for the actual pair at the actual column conditions. The primary sources are, in order: vapour–liquid equilibrium data for the named pair in a primary databank (DIPPR, NIST ThermoData Engine, or the DECHEMA Chemistry Data Series), or a measurement on the actual mixture; and the primary statement of the method, Fenske (1932), as reproduced in standard design texts (e.g. Seader, Henley and Roper, Separation Process Principles). Any claim here about a real pair's α\alpha is unverified until checked against such a source — no pair is named in the problem, so no such check was possible, and none is claimed. Agreement with another AI model is not used as verification at any point in this solution.

6. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. α\alpha is not constant down a real column. Temperature, pressure, and composition change from top to bottom, so α\alpha changes; if the bottom α\alpha is lower than the top value, the geometric-mean α\alpha is lower than a top-condition value and the true minimum stage count is higher. Direction: usually upward in Nmin⁡N_{\min} if a favourable (top or feed-condition) α\alpha was used; size: from the table, a mean α\alpha of 1.20 instead of 1.22 already raises Nmin⁡N_{\min} by 9 %. Settled by: databank or measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data at top and bottom conditions for the actual mixture.
  2. Real trays are not theoretical stages. Tray efficiency (Murphree or overall column efficiency) for a close-boiling system is commonly well below 100 %, so the number of actual trays exceeds Nmin⁡N_{\min} roughly by division by the efficiency (e.g. at an overall efficiency of 0.7, a factor of about 1.43). Direction: actual count higher. Settled by: efficiency data or a vendor rating for the actual internals and system (e.g. vendor hydraulic/efficiency documentation, or operating data from a comparable column).
  3. Total reflux is not an operating condition. Nmin⁡N_{\min} is the lower bound at infinite reflux, where no product is withdrawn. Any finite reflux ratio requires more stages than Nmin⁡N_{\min} — commonly of order 1.5 to 2 times Nmin⁡N_{\min} at an economic reflux ratio, via a Gilliland-type relation — plus allowance for pressure drop, which shifts temperatures and α\alpha. Direction: operating count higher. Settled by: a rated simulation or design calculation at the specified reflux ratio, feed condition, and column pressure profile.
7. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: variation of α\alpha with temperature, pressure, and composition; non-ideal vapour and liquid behaviour; tray or packing efficiency; hydraulics, flooding, weeping, and pressure drop; fouling; control and start-up; any third component, azeotrope, or reaction.
  • Information not accessible here: proprietary or databank-held equilibrium data for the unnamed pair; vendor efficiency and hydraulic ratings for specific internals; any plant operating record for this separation.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: efficiency loss from foaming, entrainment, and maldistribution; α\alpha drift with feed-composition changes; degradation of separation under turndown.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: because of the sensitivity in Section 1, a fall in the effective (geometric-mean) α\alpha from 1.22 to about 1.20 raises Nmin⁡N_{\min} by about 9–10 %, and to about 1.198 raises it by a full 10 %; a rise to about 1.247 lowers it by 10 %. Any change of basis (mass instead of mole fractions), a partial condenser counted differently combined with low efficiency, or operation at finite reflux also changes a stage count derived from this result by well over 10 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. For which named pair, at which pressure, and over which temperature and composition range is α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 stated, and is it a point value or a geometric mean?
  2. What are xDx_D and xBx_B individually, on a stated mole basis, and do the implied recoveries close a material balance on a stated feed?
  3. Is the count required at total reflux (a bound) or at a specified finite reflux ratio, and what efficiency converts theoretical stages to actual trays or packing height?
  4. Does the quoted count include the reboiler, and is the condenser total or partial?
Final answer

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)/ln⁡(1.22)=50.72N_{\min} = \ln(24{,}000)/\ln(1.22) = 50.72, i.e. 51 theoretical stages including the reboiler, conditional on the given S=24,000S = 24{,}000 (given) and α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 (given, unverified for any real pair), with a scenario range of 47–55 stages for α\alpha between 1.24 and 1.20.

C2. Flooding and Diameter — Second Column

Response without the skill

Packed Column Diameter

Given data
  • QQ = volumetric gas flow rate, in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}): Q=1.8 m3/sQ = 1.8\ \mathrm{m^3/s}
  • uu = flooding superficial gas velocity, in metres per second (m/s\mathrm{m/s}): u=1.5 m/su = 1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}

The flooding superficial gas velocity uu is stated to be the maximum usable velocity, so the column is sized at uu.

Definitions
  • AA = cross-sectional area of the column, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2})
  • DD = internal diameter of the column, in metres (m\mathrm{m})
  • π\pi = ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, dimensionless: π≈3.1416\pi \approx 3.1416

The superficial gas velocity uu is defined as the volumetric gas flow rate QQ divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area AA:

u=QAu = \frac{Q}{A}

For a circular column, the cross-sectional area AA is related to the internal diameter DD by:

A=πD24A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4}

Calculation

Rearranging u=Q/Au = Q/A for the cross-sectional area AA:

A=Qu=1.8 m3/s1.5 m/s=1.2 m2A = \frac{Q}{u} = \frac{1.8\ \mathrm{m^3/s}}{1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 1.2\ \mathrm{m^2}

Rearranging A=πD2/4A = \pi D^2/4 for the internal diameter DD:

D=4Aπ=4×1.2 m2π=1.528 m2≈1.24 mD = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 1.2\ \mathrm{m^2}}{\pi}} = \sqrt{1.528\ \mathrm{m^2}} \approx 1.24\ \mathrm{m}

Result

The required internal diameter is approximately 1.24 m1.24\ \mathrm{m}, corresponding to a cross-sectional area of 1.2 m21.2\ \mathrm{m^2} at the flooding superficial gas velocity of 1.5 m/s1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}. In practice the next available standard size at or above 1.24 m1.24\ \mathrm{m} would be selected.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Packed Column Diameter Sizing

1. Weakness and confidence

Weakness. The arithmetic is a single continuity relation and is exact. The weakness is not the arithmetic; it is the design meaning of the supplied velocity. A flooding velocity is, in normal packed-column usage, the velocity at which the column ceases to operate usefully (liquid is carried up, pressure drop rises steeply, separation collapses), not a velocity at which a column is operated. The problem statement calls the flooding velocity the "maximum usable" velocity. Those two readings give different diameters, and no packing type, liquid rate, or physical properties are supplied to check which reading is intended, or to check the stated flooding velocity itself.

Confidence rating. - Arithmetic, conditional on the two supplied numbers and on the literal reading: high, 9/10. - Adequacy of the resulting diameter for built, operable equipment: low, 3/10, for the reasons in Sections 2, 6, and 7. Any claim about operability resting on vendor packing data or on a flooding correlation is unverified until checked against that source (Section 5).

Its origin (measured, vendor, or correlation) is not stated, so for design purposes it is treated as estimated, with the plausible range in Section 4.

4. Calculation and range of results

Symbols: A is the required free cross-sectional area of the column, in square metres (m²); D is the required column inside diameter, in metres (m); u_op is the operating superficial gas velocity, in metres per second (m/s), defined by u_op = f × u_f.

Step 1 — area from continuity:

A = Q / u_op

Step 2 — diameter from the area of a circle:

D = sqrt(4 × A / π), where π is the mathematical constant pi (dimensionless) and sqrt denotes the square root.

Literal reading (f = 1.00, both inputs as given):

A = 1.8 m³/s / 1.5 m/s = 1.20 m²

D = sqrt(4 × 1.20 m² / π) = sqrt(1.528 m²) = 1.24 m

This is a minimum diameter at the flooding limit, not an operating design diameter.

Range over the design fraction f (inputs otherwise as given, computed in code, Section 6):

f (dimensionless, assumed/estimated) u_op (m/s) A (m²) D (m) Change in D vs. f = 1
1.00 1.500 1.200 1.236 0 %

Range over the flooding velocity itself. Because u_f is treated as estimated, taking a plausible ±20 % band, u_f = 1.2–1.8 m/s (estimated), at f = 1 gives D = 1.38 m down to 1.13 m. Combined with the usual design fraction, the plausible design range is wider still.

Sensitivity of the result to each guess (Prompt 1). From D = sqrt(4Q/(π f u_f)), the diameter varies as the square root of each input: a ±10 % change in Q moves D by ∓/+5 % (computed: Q = 1.62 m³/s gives D = 1.17 m; Q = 1.98 m³/s gives D = 1.30 m); a ±10 % change in ufor in f moves D by about ∓5 % in the opposite sense. The single largest lever is the interpretation of f: moving from 1.00 to 0.70 moves D by +19.5 %, and to 0.50 by +41.4 %. A flow-basis error is comparable: if the stated Q were a standard-state value and the actual volume at column conditions were twice the stated value (assumed illustrative factor of 2), D at f = 1 would be 1.75 m, not 1.24 m (+41 %); if the actual volume were half, D would be 0.87 m (−29 %).

Reported result, as a range, not a single value: - Minimum diameter at the stated flooding limit: 1.24 m (select no shell smaller than this under any reading). - Plausible operating design diameter, at f = 0.70–0.80 on the given flooding velocity: 1.38–1.48 m, i.e. a nominal 1.4–1.5 m inside diameter before vendor confirmation. - Full plausible envelope over f = 0.50–1.00 and u_f = 1.2–1.8 m/s: approximately 1.1–1.9 m. The envelope, not the point value, is the deliverable until the items in Section 2 are supplied.

5. Sources and validity (Prompt 1)
  • Continuity, A = Q/u: a definition of superficial velocity. No source needed; no validity range beyond a consistent basis for Q and u.
  • Design fraction f = 0.70–0.80 of flooding: a rule of thumb from standard packed-column design practice, as summarised in general references such as Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook (packed-column design sections) and Kister, Distillation Design. Unverified against the current edition in this solution, and it is a practice range, not a physical limit; foaming, high liquid rate, high pressure drop limits, or a required turndown can push the appropriate f lower.
  • Flooding velocity of a specific packing: the primary source that settles it is the packing vendor's capacity and pressure-drop data for the named packing, size, and material, at the actual liquid rate and physical properties, or a flooding correlation of the generalised pressure-drop correlation (GPDC / Sherwood–Eckert) family applied with those properties. Neither was available here. The supplied 1.5 m/s is therefore unverified as a flooding velocity for any real packing and system.
6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

All numbers in Section 4 were recomputed in executed Python code (continuity and the circle-area relation only); the code output agrees with the hand values above to the figures shown (area 1.2000 m², diameter 1.2361 m at f = 1).

  • Dimensional check. (m³/s) / (m/s) = m² for A; sqrt(m²) = m for D. Pass.
  • Limiting case 1. As Q tends to zero, D tends to zero. The relation shows this. Pass.
  • Limiting case 2. Doubling Q at fixed velocity must multiply D by sqrt(2) = 1.414, not by 2. The formula shows this, and the factor-of-2 flow-basis illustration in Section 4 uses it (1.236 m × 1.414 = 1.748 m). Pass.
  • Back-substitution. At D = 1.236 m, A = πD²/4 = 1.20 m² and Q/A = 1.5 m/s, recovering u_f exactly. Pass.
  • Material and energy balance closure. Fails / cannot be performed. No liquid rate, compositions, temperatures, or enthalpies are supplied, so no balance exists to close. This is reported, not repaired: the diameter rests on the supplied velocity alone.
  • Correlation valid-range check. Cannot be performed. No correlation was used, and the packing and properties needed to test whether 1.5 m/s lies inside any correlation's valid range were not supplied. Reported as an open check, not a pass.
  • No check result was used to alter the solution. Agreement with any other AI model is not claimed as verification, and none was sought.
7. Audit as built equipment would behave (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ between this calculation and a built column, each with direction, rough size, and the record that settles it:

  1. Operation at flooding is not operable. A column sized at f = 1 will flood on any upward excursion in gas or liquid rate, with a steep rise in pressure drop in pascals per metre (Pa/m) and loss of separation. Direction: the built column needs a larger diameter than 1.24 m. Rough size: +12 % to +20 % in diameter for f = 0.80–0.70 (Section 4), more for foaming systems. Settled by: the vendor's flood and pressure-drop curves for the named packing, and the plant's required operating envelope and turndown.
  2. Liquid maldistribution and wall flow grow with diameter. The calculation assumes uniform gas and liquid distribution over the whole cross-section. In a built column of about 1.4 m diameter, distributor quality, packing settling, and fouling reduce the effective area, so the effective local velocity is higher than the superficial value. Direction: a larger diameter, or a specified high-quality liquid distributor and redistribution, is needed for the calculated performance. Rough size: commonly of the order of 5–15 % of effective capacity (estimated, unverified for this service). Settled by: vendor distributor specifications and, after construction, a gamma scan or tracer test on the actual column.
  3. The stated flooding velocity may not belong to this system. Flooding velocity falls as liquid rate, liquid density relative to gas density, viscosity, and foaming tendency change, and it is packing-specific. If the actual system floods below 1.5 m/s, a column sized on 1.5 m/s is undersized in direct proportion (Section 4: at a true flooding velocity of 1.2 m/s the flood-limit diameter is already 1.38 m). Direction: unknown until properties are supplied; the error is one-sided in risk, because an oversized column still operates (with some loss of wetting at very low rates) while an undersized one floods. Settled by: measured physical properties of the actual fluids and the vendor document or a GPDC calculation using them.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: pressure drop and its limit; liquid hold-up; mass-transfer performance (no height, stage, or transfer-unit calculation is possible from the data given, and none is implied by this diameter); minimum wetting rate at turndown; foaming; entrainment below nominal flooding; thermal effects; and mechanical design (shell thickness, supports, distributors, wind and seismic loads).
  • Information not visible here: vendor-proprietary packing capacity data held in vendor documents and rating programs; any site standards or current code editions that fix design fractions, corrosion allowance, or standard shell sizes for this plant.
  • Effects that appear only in running equipment: maldistribution after fouling or packing damage, distributor plugging, surge behaviour under plant rate changes, and flooding initiated by liquid-rate excursions rather than gas rate.
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: a design fraction at or below about 0.83 (diameter change exceeds +10 % relative to f = 1); a true flooding velocity below about 1.24 m/s or above about 1.86 m/s (± about 20 %); a flow-basis conversion factor outside about 0.83–1.21 in actual-to-stated volume; or a gas rate more than about 21 % above 1.8 m³/s.
  • Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used: 1. Is 1.5 m/s a measured or vendor flooding velocity for the named packing at the design liquid rate, or a placeholder? 2. Is 1.8 m³/s an actual volume at column temperature and pressure, and what are that temperature and pressure? 3. What design fraction of flooding, pressure-drop limit, and turndown does the site standard require? 4. What are the liquid rate and the gas and liquid densities, viscosities, and surface tension, and does a GPDC or vendor check reproduce 1.5 m/s? 5. Which standard shell size at or above 1.38–1.48 m is available, and do the distributor and support designs suit that diameter?
9. Conclusion

On the data as given and read literally, the required cross-sectional area A is 1.20 m² and the minimum inside diameter D is 1.24 m. Read as a design for operable equipment, the diameter should be reported as a range, 1.38–1.48 m at a design fraction f of 0.70–0.80 of the given flooding velocity, within a full plausible envelope of approximately 1.1–1.9 m, and should not be fixed until the liquid rate, physical properties, packing identity, flow basis, and required design fraction listed in Section 2 are supplied and checked against the packing vendor's data.

C3. Liquid–Liquid Extraction — Second Solute

Response without the skill

Multistage Extraction: Stage Number

Symbols and given values
  • NN (dimensionless): number of equilibrium stages in a countercurrent cascade.
  • φ\varphi (dimensionless): fraction of solute remaining in the final raffinate, defined as the solute concentration in the final raffinate divided by the solute concentration in the feed. The required value is φ=0.01\varphi = 0.01.
  • FF (amount per unit time): flow rate of the feed (raffinate) phase, taken as constant through the cascade.
  • SS (amount per unit time, in the same units as FF): flow rate of the solvent (extract) phase, taken as constant through the cascade. The given solvent-to-feed ratio is S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2 (dimensionless).
  • xFx_F (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase): solute concentration in the feed.
  • xNx_N (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase, in the same units as xFx_F): solute concentration in the final raffinate leaving stage NN, so that φ=xN/xF\varphi = x_N / x_F.
  • DD (dimensionless): distribution coefficient, defined as the solute concentration in the extract phase at equilibrium divided by the solute concentration in the raffinate phase at equilibrium. The given value is D=1.8D = 1.8.
  • EE (dimensionless): extraction factor, defined in the next section.
Assumptions
  1. The carrier liquid in the feed and the solvent are effectively immiscible, so FF (amount per unit time) and SS (amount per unit time) are constant from stage to stage.
  2. DD (dimensionless), as defined above, is constant, independent of concentration.
  3. The solvent entering the cascade is fresh, that is, it contains no solute.
  4. The cascade is countercurrent, and each stage reaches equilibrium.
  5. The feed phase and the extract phase leave each stage in equilibrium with each other.
Extraction factor

The extraction factor EE (dimensionless) is defined by

E=DSFE = D \frac{S}{F}

Substitution of D=1.8D = 1.8 (dimensionless) and S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2 (dimensionless) gives

E=1.8×1.2=2.16E = 1.8 \times 1.2 = 2.16

Stage relation

Let ii (dimensionless) denote a stage index, running from 11 to NN (dimensionless). Let xix_i (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase) denote the solute concentration in the raffinate leaving stage ii (dimensionless index), with x0x_0 (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase) denoting the feed concentration, that is, x0=xFx_0 = x_F. Let yiy_i (solute amount per unit amount of extract phase) denote the solute concentration in the extract leaving stage ii (dimensionless index). Equilibrium at stage ii (dimensionless index) gives yi=Dxiy_i = D x_i, with DD (dimensionless) and xix_i and yiy_i as defined above and in the symbols list.

A solute balance on stage ii (dimensionless index), with FF (amount per unit time), SS (amount per unit time), xi−1x_{i-1} (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase), xix_i (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase), yiy_i (solute amount per unit amount of extract phase), and yi+1y_{i+1} (solute amount per unit amount of extract phase) as defined above, is

Fxi−1+Syi+1=Fxi+SyiF x_{i-1} + S y_{i+1} = F x_i + S y_i

Substitution of yi=Dxiy_i = D x_i and yi+1=Dxi+1y_{i+1} = D x_{i+1}, with the symbols as defined above, and division by FF (amount per unit time) gives

xi−1−xi=E(xi−xi+1)x_{i-1} - x_i = E \left(x_i - x_{i+1}\right)

where xi+1x_{i+1} (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase) is the raffinate concentration leaving the next stage, and a dummy value xN+1=0x_{N+1} = 0 (solute amount per unit amount of raffinate phase) represents the fresh, solute-free solvent entering stage NN (dimensionless).

The successive concentration differences therefore form a geometric series with ratio EE (dimensionless). Summation of the differences from the feed to the final raffinate gives the Kremser relation for this case:

φ=xNxF=E−1EN+1−1,E≠1\varphi = \frac{x_N}{x_F} = \frac{E - 1}{E^{N+1} - 1}, \qquad E \ne 1

Check for a single stage: for N=1N = 1 (dimensionless), the relation above gives φ=(2.16−1)/(2.162−1)=0.316\varphi = (2.16 - 1)/(2.16^{2} - 1) = 0.316 (dimensionless), which is equal to 1/(1+E)=1/3.16=0.3161/(1 + E) = 1/3.16 = 0.316 (dimensionless) from a direct single-stage balance. The relation is consistent.

Solution for the stage number

Set φ=0.01\varphi = 0.01 (dimensionless) and E=2.16E = 2.16 (dimensionless) in the Kremser relation above, with φ\varphi, EE, and NN (dimensionless) as defined above:

0.01=2.16−12.16N+1−10.01 = \frac{2.16 - 1}{2.16^{N+1} - 1}

2.16N+1−1=1.160.01=1162.16^{N+1} - 1 = \frac{1.16}{0.01} = 116

2.16N+1=1172.16^{N+1} = 117

N+1=ln⁡117ln⁡2.16=4.7620.770=6.18N + 1 = \frac{\ln 117}{\ln 2.16} = \frac{4.762}{0.770} = 6.18

N=5.18N = 5.18

Here ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm (dimensionless argument and result).

The theoretical requirement is N=5.18N = 5.18 (dimensionless) equilibrium stages. A physical cascade must contain a whole number of stages, so N=6N = 6 equilibrium stages are required to reduce the fraction of solute remaining in the raffinate to 0.010.01 (1%1\%) or below, at a solvent-to-feed ratio of 1.21.2 (dimensionless) and a distribution coefficient of 1.81.8 (dimensionless).

Equilibrium Stages for Liquid–Liquid Extraction — Estimate and Audit

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. This problem type is a low-confidence type for a closed-form answer. The arithmetic is simple, but the result rests entirely on an idealised model: constant distribution coefficient, immiscible carrier and solvent, equilibrium (theoretical) stages, constant phase flow rates, and a countercurrent cascade fed with solute-free solvent. None of those conditions is stated in the problem, and in real liquid–liquid extraction the distribution coefficient varies with concentration, temperature, and composition, the phases are partly miscible so the phase flow rates change from stage to stage, and real stages do not reach equilibrium. A single stage count quoted without those qualifications would overstate what the supplied numbers support.

Confidence rating.

  • Conditional arithmetic, given the model and the inputs in §3: high, about 90 % — verified by two independent routes in §7, which agree to numerical precision.
  • Applicability of that stage count to built equipment: low to moderate, about 40–50 % — it depends on unmeasured equilibrium data and unmeasured stage efficiency for the actual system. See §8 and §9.

Headline result (range, not a single value — Checklist item 2). Under the base-case model in §4, the number of equilibrium stages, denoted NN and dimensionless, is N=5.2N = 5.2, so 6 whole equilibrium stages are required. Over the plausible input range examined in §6, NN spans 4.3 to 6.9 (5 to 7 whole stages) for uncertainty in the distribution coefficient alone, and 4.0 to 8.1 (4 to 9 whole stages) when flow-ratio uncertainty is included as well. Real (non-equilibrium) stages would be more; see §8.

Countercurrent, crosscurrent, or repeated single-stage (batch) contact is not stated. - Countercurrent, fresh solvent (assumed, base case): N=5.2N = 5.2, i.e. 6 whole stages. - Crosscurrent, with the full S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2 (given) of fresh solvent used at each stage (assumed alternative): ϕ=(1/(1+E))N\phi = (1/(1+E))^{N} per stage, giving N=ln⁡(0.01)/ln⁡(1/3.16)=4.0N = \ln(0.01)/\ln(1/3.16) = 4.0, i.e. 4 whole stages — but at roughly NN times the total solvent use of the base case, so the two numbers are not on the same solvent basis and are not interchangeable. - If the total solvent is instead split equally among crosscurrent stages, NN is larger than 4.0 and must be found by stage-by-stage calculation; no single closed-form value is quoted for that sub-case.
  2. Basis of S/FS/F — missing. Molar, mass, or volumetric; and whether FF is total feed or solute-free carrier. The base case assumes a basis consistent with the basis of DD, with FF as the raffinate-carrier flow. If DD is on a molar basis and S/FS/F on a volumetric basis (or vice versa), EE — and therefore NN — is wrong by the corresponding density / molar-mass ratio, which is not supplied.
  3. Composition basis of DD — missing. Mole fraction, mass fraction, or concentration (amount per volume) give different numerical DD values for the same physical system. Assumed: DD and S/FS/F are on mutually consistent bases, so that E=D(S/F)E = D(S/F) is valid.
  4. Reference state / entering solvent composition — missing. Assumed solute-free fresh solvent. Solvent recycled with residual solute raises ϕ\phi at fixed NN, or raises the NN needed at fixed ϕ\phi; the size cannot be computed without the residual solute concentration.
  5. Temperature and pressure — missing. Pressure has a small effect on liquid–liquid equilibrium in most systems at moderate pressure (estimated qualitative statement); temperature can change DD substantially. No values are supplied, so D=1.8D = 1.8 (given) is taken to apply at the (unstated) operating temperature.
  6. Concentration dependence of DD — missing. Assumed constant at 1.8 from feed concentration down to 1 % of feed concentration. If DD falls at low concentration, the last stages do less work and NN rises; §6 bounds this by lowering DD.
  7. Per-pass versus overall — not applicable in the usual sense, but the equivalent ambiguity is item 1: ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01 is read as overall, feed to final raffinate, across the whole cascade (assumed reading of the given target).
  8. Stage efficiency — missing for real equipment. The question asks for equilibrium stages, so efficiency is 100 % by definition in the base case. A real-stage estimate needs a measured or vendor efficiency; §8 gives an estimated range only.

Primary source that would settle the open points (Checklist item 5): measured liquid–liquid equilibrium (tie-line) data for the actual feed–solvent pair, at the actual temperature and over the actual concentration range, from a primary databank (for example the Dortmund Data Bank / DECHEMA liquid–liquid equilibrium collection) or from measurement on the actual material; and, for real stages, the equipment vendor's efficiency / pilot-test record for the actual contactor. Every claim in this solution that rests on D=1.8D = 1.8 holding for the real system is unverified until checked against such data. No such data were supplied or consulted here.

8. Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Stage efficiency below 100 %. Direction: more real stages than equilibrium stages. Rough size (estimated): at a Murphree-type efficiency of 0.8, 0.6, or 0.5 — a plausible estimated range for liquid–liquid contactors, not a measured value for this system — the real stage count corresponding to N=5.18N = 5.18 equilibrium stages is approximately 6.5, 8.6, or 10.4, i.e. about 7, 9, or 11 whole real stages (simple division, estimated approximation). Settling document: vendor efficiency data or a pilot-column test on the actual system. Unverified for this system.
  2. DD varying with concentration and temperature. Direction: if DD falls toward the dilute end — a common pattern, stated here as an estimated qualitative expectation, not a fact about this unnamed system — the dilute stages contribute less, and NN rises toward the low-DD rows of §6 (up to +32 % for a 20 % fall, and more if the fall is larger). Opposite movement is possible for other systems. Settling source: measured tie-line data over the full concentration range (see §5). Unverified.
  3. Partial miscibility and flow-rate change; entrainment and back-mixing. Direction: carrier dissolving in the extract and solvent dissolving in the raffinate change SS and FF from stage to stage, so the constant-EE model misstates each stage; entrainment and axial back-mixing in a column move solute backwards and raise the stage count needed. Rough size: system-specific; a change of more than 10 % in NN is plausible (estimated) for appreciably miscible pairs, and cannot be bounded from the supplied data. Settling sources: mutual-solubility data for the actual pair, and the contactor vendor's hydraulic / back-mixing rating or pilot record. Unverified.

C4. Adsorption Breakthrough — Second Bed

Response without the skill

Breakthrough Time of an Adsorption Bed

Problem statement

An adsorption bed contains an adsorbent mass, denoted (M), in kilograms (kg), of (M = 5{,}000\ \text{kg}). The feed stream carries adsorbate at a mass flow rate, denoted (F), in kilograms per hour (kg/h), of (F = 6\ \text{kg/h}). The equilibrium capacity of the adsorbent, denoted (q), in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg), is (q = 0.15\ \text{kg/kg}). The breakthrough time, denoted (t_b), in hours (h), is to be estimated.

Assumptions
  1. The feed rate (F) is constant in time.
  2. All adsorbate in the feed is captured by the bed up to breakthrough; no adsorbate leaves with the treated stream before breakthrough.
  3. The full equilibrium capacity (q) is usable, i.e. the mass-transfer zone is neglected and breakthrough is taken as sharp. This is the ideal, stoichiometric estimate; in a real bed breakthrough occurs earlier because a portion of the bed in the mass-transfer zone is not fully saturated at breakthrough.
  4. No adsorbate is lost, desorbed, or degraded during loading.
Method

The total mass of adsorbate the bed can hold at saturation, denoted (W), in kilograms (kg), is the adsorbent mass (M) multiplied by the equilibrium capacity (q):

[ W = M q ]

At a constant capture rate equal to the feed rate (F), the time required to accumulate the mass (W) is:

[ t_b = \frac{W}{F} = \frac{M q}{F} ]

Calculation

Total capacity:

[ W = (5{,}000\ \text{kg})(0.15\ \text{kg/kg}) = 750\ \text{kg} ]

Breakthrough time:

[ t_b = \frac{750\ \text{kg}}{6\ \text{kg/h}} = 125\ \text{h} ]

Unit check: (\text{kg} / (\text{kg/h}) = \text{h}), as required.

Result

The ideal (stoichiometric) breakthrough time is approximately 125 h, i.e. about 5.2 days of continuous operation. In practice the usable breakthrough time will be shorter than 125 h because the mass-transfer zone leaves part of the bed unsaturated at breakthrough; 125 h is therefore an upper-bound estimate based on equilibrium capacity alone.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Breakthrough Time of an Adsorption Bed — Estimate

1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1)

Weakness. An equilibrium capacity alone does not determine a breakthrough time. Equilibrium gives only the total inventory the bed can hold at saturation — an upper bound on the time. The actual breakthrough time is set by kinetics and hydrodynamics that are not supplied: the length of the mass-transfer zone (MTZ), the isotherm shape, the superficial velocity, and the concentration at which "breakthrough" is declared. Any single number produced from the supplied data alone would conceal that gap.

Confidence rating.

  • Stoichiometric (ideal, fully saturated) time, §3: high — it is arithmetic on the given numbers and closes a material balance exactly (§6).
  • Actual breakthrough time, §4: low — it rests on an assumed bed-utilisation fraction, not on measured data for this adsorbent, adsorbate, or bed. It is reported as a range only.

Agreement with another AI model would not raise this rating and is not used as verification (Checklist item 7).

2. Inputs, labelled at the point of use (Prompt 1; Checklist item 3)
Quantity Symbol used here Value State
Mass of adsorbent in the bed MM 5,000 kg given
Equilibrium capacity (kg adsorbate per kg adsorbent) qq 0.15 kg/kg given
Adsorbate feed rate (mass of adsorbate carried in per unit time) FF 6 kg/h given
Fraction of equilibrium capacity used at breakthrough ff 0.5–0.9 assumed — rule-of-thumb range, see §4
Capture before breakthrough (no adsorbate slip) — 100 % until breakthrough assumed — idealisation, see §7

No property value, fitted correlation, or isotherm relation is used. The only relation used is a material balance (§3), which holds whenever the bed is the only sink for the adsorbate and no adsorbate is created or destroyed in the bed. No measured, fitted, or estimated input was supplied; every quantity beyond the three given values is labelled assumed above.

3. Ideal (stoichiometric) solution

Total equilibrium inventory:

M q=5,000 kg×0.15 kg/kg=750 kg of adsorbateM \, q = 5{,}000\ \text{kg} \times 0.15\ \text{kg/kg} = 750\ \text{kg of adsorbate}

where MM (given) is the adsorbent mass, in kilograms (kg), and qq (given) is the equilibrium capacity, in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg).

Stoichiometric time — the time to deliver that inventory at the given feed rate:

tstoich=MqF=750 kg6 kg/h=125 h≈5.2 dayst_{\text{stoich}} = \frac{M q}{F} = \frac{750\ \text{kg}}{6\ \text{kg/h}} = 125\ \text{h} \approx 5.2\ \text{days}

where FF (given) is the adsorbate feed rate, in kilograms per hour (kg/h), and tstoicht_{\text{stoich}} is the stoichiometric time, in hours (h).

125 h is an upper bound, not a breakthrough prediction. It holds only for a sharp (shock) front, complete capture until the bed is fully saturated, a constant feed rate, and a capacity qq that is actually reached at the bed's operating temperature and at the inlet adsorbate partial pressure or concentration.

4. Realistic breakthrough range (Checklist item 2)

In a real bed a mass-transfer zone forms: part of the bed is saturated, part is in the zone and only partly loaded, and part is still fresh when the leading edge of the zone reaches the outlet. Breakthrough — first appearance, or a specified fraction of inlet concentration, at the outlet — therefore occurs before the bed is fully saturated.

tb=f tstoicht_b = f \, t_{\text{stoich}}

where tbt_b is the breakthrough time, in hours (h), and ff (assumed) is the fraction of the equilibrium capacity used at breakthrough, dimensionless.

Computed at the ends of the assumed plausible range of ff (code check, §6):

ff (assumed) tbt_b
0.5 62.5 h
0.6 75.0 h
0.7 87.5 h
0.8 100.0 h
0.9 112.5 h
1.0 (ideal limit) 125.0 h

Reported result: breakthrough in approximately 60–115 h (about 2.5–4.7 days) under the assumed utilisation range f=0.5f = 0.5–0.90.9, with 125 h as the hard equilibrium upper bound. A central planning figure of about 85–90 h corresponds to f=0.7f = 0.7 (assumed), but it carries no more evidential weight than the range.

If q=0.15q = 0.15 kg/kg (given) is an equilibrium value at a higher concentration or lower temperature than the bed actually sees, the working capacity will be lower. At q=0.10q = 0.10 kg/kg (assumed alternative) with the same ff range, tbt_b falls to 42–75 h. That combined downside — about 40 h — cannot be excluded on the supplied data.

5. Missing quantities — not completed silently (Prompt 2; Checklist item 4)

The following are needed for a defensible breakthrough prediction and were not supplied. No value has been taken in silence; the solution above proceeds only under the alternatives stated.

  1. Breakthrough criterion — missing. First detectable slip, 1 %, 5 %, or 10 % of inlet concentration, or a discharge limit each give a different tbt_b. Solved here as "leading edge of the MTZ reaches the outlet", folded into the assumed ff range.
  2. Basis of qq — missing. Whether 0.15 kg/kg is equilibrium at the inlet concentration (the favourable reading, used here) or a nominal/vendor maximum; the dry- or wet-adsorbent mass basis; and the temperature and pressure at which it was obtained. Alternative solved: q=0.10q = 0.10 kg/kg, §4.
  3. Composition basis and inlet concentration — missing. Only the adsorbate mass rate (6 kg/h, given) is known; the total stream flow, adsorbate concentration, and carrier are unknown, so the isotherm operating point and velocity cannot be checked.
  4. Bed geometry and flow — missing. Bed length, diameter, particle size, and superficial velocity set the MTZ length and hence ff. Without them ff can only be assumed (0.5–0.9).
  5. Isotherm shape and kinetics — missing. A favourable isotherm gives a self-sharpening front (high ff); a linear or unfavourable isotherm, or slow intraparticle diffusion, gives a long MTZ (low ff).
  6. Operating conditions and competing species — missing. Temperature, pressure (and its basis, absolute or gauge — not needed for the balance here, but needed to use any isotherm), humidity, and co-adsorbing components all reduce working capacity.
  7. Per-pass or overall — not applicable to a once-through bed charged to breakthrough, but regeneration history and residual loading ("heel") after regeneration are missing and would reduce the usable capacity of a cycled bed below the fresh-bed value.

Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5): a breakthrough curve measured on the actual adsorbent with the actual feed at the actual temperature, flow, and concentration — or, failing that, the adsorbent vendor's isotherm and MTZ / length-of- unused-bed data for that grade. Standard textbook treatments (for example the adsorption chapters of Seader, Henley and Roper, Separation Process Principles, or Treybal, Mass-Transfer Operations) state the stoichiometric-time and unused-bed framework used here. Any claim about ff, or about qq at operating conditions, is unverified until checked against the measured curve or the vendor document for the actual material.

6. Independent checks (Prompt 3; Checklist item 6)

Checks were executed in code (Python) rather than by hand arithmetic alone. Results:

  • Material-balance closure. At tstoicht_{\text{stoich}}: adsorbate fed =6×125=750= 6 \times 125 = 750 kg; adsorbate stored =Mq=750= M q = 750 kg. Closure error 0.0 kg — passes.
  • Limiting case 1. f=1f = 1 recovers the stoichiometric time, 125 h — passes by construction and by the code output.
  • Limiting case 2. q→0q \to 0 or F→∞F \to \infty gives tb→0t_b \to 0, and doubling FF halves tbt_b — the formula behaves correctly at both extremes.
  • Sensitivity (Prompt 1 — how much each guess moves the result).
  • ff from 1.0 to 0.5: −50 % on tbt_b. This is the dominant uncertainty.
  • FF (given) varied ±10 % for illustration: 6.6 kg/h gives 113.6 h (−9 %); 5.4 kg/h gives 138.9 h (+11 %).
  • qq from 0.15 to 0.10 kg/kg (assumed alternative): −33 % on every time in §4.
  • Correlation valid range. No fitted correlation was used, so there is no valid-range check to fail; the ff range is a rule-of-thumb band for fixed beds, not a correlation, and is labelled assumed accordingly.
  • Failed checks. None of the arithmetic checks failed. The check that cannot be run on the supplied data — comparison against a measured breakthrough curve — is the material gap, and is reported here rather than passed over.
7. Audit as a practised plant engineer would (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. Early leakage through the mass-transfer zone. Real beds leak adsorbate well before the stoichiometric time, especially with slow diffusion (large particles, microporous adsorbent) or a high velocity. Direction: breakthrough earlier, by the full ff effect — 10–50 % below 125 h. Settled by: a pilot or plant breakthrough curve at operating velocity, or vendor MTZ data.
  2. Channelling and maldistribution. Uneven packing, settling, or a poor inlet distributor lets part of the stream bypass most of the bed while the rest is under-used. Direction: breakthrough earlier, commonly a further 10–30 % in a poorly distributed bed, with a long tail rather than a sharp rise. Settled by: bed pressure-drop records, distributor design drawings, and the shape of a measured outlet-concentration history.
  3. Working capacity below the equilibrium figure. Competition from water or other adsorbables, a higher bed temperature (including the heat of adsorption raising the front temperature), fouling, and ageing across regeneration cycles all cut capacity. Direction: breakthrough earlier, 10–40 % over a campaign is plausible for a cycled bed. Settled by: the vendor isotherm at the actual temperature and feed composition, feed analysis (including moisture), and cycle-by-cycle breakthrough records from the operating unit.
8. What this calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: MTZ shape and its movement, axial dispersion, heat of adsorption and any temperature front, pressure drop, particle-size distribution, adsorbent attrition, and any reaction or polymerisation of the adsorbate in the bed.
  • Information not available here: the vendor's isotherm, kinetic, and unused-bed data for the specific adsorbent grade (commercial data, not public), and any plant historian records for an existing unit. Neither was consulted; claims resting on such sources are marked unverified in §5.
  • Effects seen only in running equipment: channelling after settling, fouling, moisture excursions, feed-rate and feed- composition swings, and capacity loss over regeneration cycles.
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10 %: any of — utilisation ff below 0.9; working qq below about 0.135 kg/kg; sustained feed rate above 6.6 kg/h; a breakthrough criterion tighter than first slip (for example a low discharge limit); significant co-adsorption or a bed temperature above the temperature at which qq was obtained.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. At what outlet concentration is breakthrough declared, and is that a process, product-quality, or discharge requirement?
  2. Is 0.15 kg/kg the equilibrium capacity at the actual inlet concentration and bed temperature, on a dry-mass basis — and what document states it?
  3. What are the bed dimensions, particle size, and superficial velocity, and what MTZ or unused-bed length follows from them?
  4. What else is in the feed — in particular water — and does it compete for the adsorbent?
  5. Is the bed fresh or regenerated, and what residual loading and cycle history apply?
  6. Has any breakthrough curve, pilot or plant, been measured for this system, and does the 60–115 h range survive comparison with it?
9. Result
  • Equilibrium inventory: 750 kg of adsorbate (M=5,000M = 5{,}000 kg, given; q=0.15q = 0.15 kg/kg, given).
  • Stoichiometric (ideal) time: 125 h — a verified upper bound.
  • Estimated breakthrough time: approximately 60–115 h, on an assumed utilisation f=0.5f = 0.5–0.90.9; a downside near 40 h if the working capacity is 0.10 kg/kg rather than 0.15 kg/kg.
  • Confidence: high for the upper bound; low for the breakthrough range, pending a measured breakthrough curve or vendor MTZ data for the actual adsorbent and feed.

C5. Membrane Ageing and Fouling — Second Plant

Response without the skill

Membrane Area Sizing

Given data
  • QpQ_{\mathrm{p}} is the required permeate volumetric flow rate, in cubic metres per hour (m3 h−1\mathrm{m^{3}\,h^{-1}}): Qp=60 m3 h−1Q_{\mathrm{p}} = 60\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,h^{-1}}.
  • JJ is the design permeate flux, in litres per square metre per hour (L m−2 h−1\mathrm{L\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}): J=35 L m−2 h−1J = 35\ \mathrm{L\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}.
Required quantity
  • AA is the required membrane area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}).
Relation

For a pressure-driven liquid separation operated at a uniform design flux, the permeate volumetric flow rate is the product of the flux and the membrane area. In consistent units:

Qp=J AQ_{\mathrm{p}} = J \, A

Rearranged for the area:

A=QpJA = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{p}}}{J}

Unit conversion

The flux JJ is expressed in litres per square metre per hour (L m−2 h−1\mathrm{L\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}), while the permeate flow rate QpQ_{\mathrm{p}} is given in cubic metres per hour (m3 h−1\mathrm{m^{3}\,h^{-1}}). One cubic metre (1 m31\ \mathrm{m^{3}}) equals 10001000 litres (1000 L1000\ \mathrm{L}), so:

Qp=60 m3 h−1×1000 L m−3=60,000 L h−1Q_{\mathrm{p}} = 60\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,h^{-1}} \times 1000\ \mathrm{L\,m^{-3}} = 60{,}000\ \mathrm{L\,h^{-1}}

Calculation

A=QpJ=60,000 L h−135 L m−2 h−1=1714.2857… m2A = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{p}}}{J} = \frac{60{,}000\ \mathrm{L\,h^{-1}}}{35\ \mathrm{L\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}} = 1714.2857\ldots\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

The units check: litres per hour (L h−1\mathrm{L\,h^{-1}}) divided by litres per square metre per hour (L m−2 h−1\mathrm{L\,m^{-2}\,h^{-1}}) gives square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}), as required for an area.

Result

A≈1.71×103 m2A \approx 1.71 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

In practical terms, at least 1715 m21715\ \mathrm{m^{2}} of membrane area is required, before any additional allowance for fouling, ageing, downtime, or module rounding in a detailed design.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Membrane Area Sizing — Permeate Production at a Stated Design Flux

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The area follows from a single division, but the result is only as good as the flux. The flux, denoted JJ and expressed in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m²·h)), is not a material constant: in a pressure-driven liquid separation it depends on transmembrane pressure, feed composition and concentration along the module, temperature (through viscosity), fouling, scaling and ageing, recovery, and cleaning state. A flux measured on clean water or on a short pilot run is systematically higher than the sustained flux on the actual feed. The problem states a design flux without stating whether it is clean-water, initial, time-averaged, or vendor-guaranteed sustained flux, and without feed, recovery, temperature, or membrane type (microfiltration, ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, or reverse osmosis).

Confidence rating. - Arithmetic: high — verified by two independent routes and by executed code (Section 5). - That the nominal area suffices in built equipment: low — it rests on the unstated meaning of the design flux. The nominal value is a calculation result, not a procurement recommendation.

2. Symbols and inputs, labelled at the point of use

Symbols, defined before use:

  • AA — required membrane area, in square metres (m²).
  • QpQ_\mathrm{p} — permeate volumetric production rate, in cubic metres per hour (m³/h) or litres per hour (L/h).
  • JJ — (average, area-averaged) permeate flux, in L/(m²·h).

Inputs:

Quantity Value State
QpQ_\mathrm{p} 60 m³/h = 60,000 L/h given
JJ (design) 35 L/(m²·h) given as a design value; its basis (clean, initial, or sustained) is not stated — see Section 3
Safety / fouling margin on area none stated assumed = 0 for the nominal result; varied in Section 4
Availability (fraction of time producing) not stated assumed = 1.00 for the nominal result; varied in Section 4
Net vs. gross permeate (backwash / cleaning consumption) not stated assumed gross = net for the nominal result

No property value, fitted relation, correlation, or rule of thumb is used. The only relation used is the definition of area-averaged flux, J=Qp/AJ = Q_\mathrm{p} / A, which holds by definition and has no validity range of its own; the validity question attaches entirely to the value of JJ, not to the relation.

3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — gaps filled before solving)

The following quantities are needed for a design-grade sizing and are not supplied. None has been taken in silence; the nominal solution proceeds under the stated assumption in the right-hand column, and the consequential alternatives are quantified in Section 4.

  1. Membrane / process type (microfiltration, ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, reverse osmosis) — missing. A flux of 35 L/(m²·h) is plausible for all four, but the drivers of flux decline differ. Assumption for the nominal result: none needed for the arithmetic.
  2. Basis of JJ — clean-water, initial on feed, time-averaged over a cleaning cycle, or guaranteed sustained: missing. Assumption: JJ is the sustained average flux. This is the single most consequential assumption.
  3. Basis of QpQ_\mathrm{p} — instantaneous rate while running, or average over a day including cleaning and downtime: missing. Assumption: instantaneous continuous rate (availability 1.00).
  4. Reference state / temperature — feed temperature at which JJ applies, and any temperature (viscosity) correction: missing. Assumption: JJ applies at the actual operating temperature.
  5. Pressure basis — transmembrane pressure at which JJ was obtained, and whether pressure is gauge or absolute: missing, and not needed for the area division, but needed to check that JJ is attainable in the built unit.
  6. Composition basis — feed composition, and permeate quantity as gross produced or net delivered (after backwash and cleaning use): missing. Assumption: gross = net.
  7. Per-pass or overall — recovery and staging: JJ may be a local (lead-element) flux or a system-average flux over all stages at the design recovery. Missing. Assumption: JJ is the system-average flux. A lead-element flux used as a system average undersizes the unit.
  8. Module discreteness — area per module / element and housing configuration: missing. Installed area must be rounded up to whole modules, so installed area will exceed the nominal area by up to one module increment.
  9. End-of-run criterion — design life, flux-decline allowance, and cleaning interval: missing.
4. Solution (Prompt 1 — result as a range, with sensitivities)

By the definition of JJ,

A=QpJ=60,000 L/h35 L/(m2⋅h)=1,714.3 m2A = \frac{Q_\mathrm{p}}{J} = \frac{60{,}000\ \mathrm{L/h}}{35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}} = 1{,}714.3\ \mathrm{m^2}

Nominal result: A=1,714 m2A = 1{,}714\ \mathrm{m^2} (no margin, availability 1.00, JJ sustained and system-averaged).

Because JJ is the weak input, the answer is reported as a range over the plausible range of the effective sustained flux. The bounds below are assumed scenario bounds, not measured values:

Reported range: A≈1,300A \approx 1{,}300–2,400 m22{,}400\ \mathrm{m^2} over J=45J = 45–2525 L/(m²·h), with 1,714 m² at the stated design flux. A narrower operational band, J=40J = 40–3030 L/(m²·h), gives 1,500–2,000 m².

Area is inversely proportional to JJ and directly proportional to QpQ_\mathrm{p}: a 10 % error in either input moves AA by about 10 % (exactly −9.1 % for JJ 10 % high, +11.1 % for JJ 10 % low). Derating and availability effects compound multiplicatively, not additively.
