6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

All checks were run in code (Python, executed for this solution). Results are reported as found; no result was adjusted to make a check pass.

  1. Energy balance closure, second route. For an adiabatic steady-flow machine the shaft work equals the enthalpy rise, cp·(T2s − T1) = 1.435 × (454.7 − 300) = 222.0 kJ/kg. This matches the pressure-ratio formula value 222.0 kJ/kg to the figures shown. Closure error: 0.0 kJ/kg at the reported precision. Check passes.
  2. Limiting case, pressure ratio near 1. At rp = 1.01 the formula gives 0.858 kJ/kg; the small-change limit R·T1·ln(rp) gives 0.857 kJ/kg. At rp = 1.001 the two give 0.0861 and 0.0861 kJ/kg. The adiabatic formula reduces to the known small-change result, as it must. Check passes.
  3. Limiting case, rp = 1. The formula gives w = 0. Check passes by inspection of the term [rp^0.20 − 1].
  4. Ordering of models. Isothermal (179) < three-stage intercooled (192) < two-stage intercooled (199) < single-stage adiabatic (222) < actual at any ηs below 1 (261 to 317). This is the required ordering: cooling can only reduce work toward the isothermal limit, and irreversibility can only raise it. Check passes.
  5. Range of validity of the relations used. The isentropic relation and cp = kR/(k − 1) hold for an ideal gas with constant cp and cv. Two points fall outside safe use and are flagged, not corrected: (a) cp for a real gas changes between 300 K and 455–521 K, so constant cp is an approximation whose size cannot be computed without the gas identity; (b) at 8 bar most permanent gases remain near-ideal, but a gas near its critical point or a condensable vapour would not, and nothing in the problem excludes that case. Both are unverified (Section 7).
  6. Failed check. The consistency check on the given data fails: R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) implies a molar mass of 29.0 kg/kmol, i.e. an air-like gas, while k = 1.25 does not match air at 300 K (k near 1.40). The problem data are therefore either hypothetical or drawn from two different sources. This failure is reported, not repaired; the solution uses the values as given, and Section 5.2 prices the discrepancy at +10 % if k = 1.40 is the correct value.
7. Primary sources that settle the open points (all unverified)

Every claim below rests on a source not consulted for this solution and is marked unverified until checked against it.

  • Gas identity, cp as a function of temperature, and compressibility: the DIPPR 801 database or NIST REFPROP for the named gas. Unverified — no gas is named, so no look-up was possible.
  • Value of k for the actual gas at the actual temperatures: the same databanks, or a measured speed of sound or measured cp and cv on the actual gas. Unverified.
  • Efficiency and the real work at the duty point: the compressor vendor's performance curve (head and efficiency against flow at the stated inlet conditions) for the selected machine, confirmed after installation by a performance test to ASME PTC 10, Performance Test Code on Compressors and Exhausters, current edition. Unverified — no machine is selected.
  • Pressure basis: the plant piping and instrumentation diagram and the pressure-transmitter calibration records, which state whether the 1 bar and 8 bar figures are absolute or gauge. Unverified.
  • Discharge temperature limit: the machine vendor's datasheet and, for a gas containing reactive or polymerisable components, the process safety documentation for the actual composition. Unverified.
8. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Internal irreversibility. Direction: real work higher, outlet temperature higher. Size: +18 % to +43 % on work at the assumed ηs range of Section 5.1; outlet temperature 482–521 K against 455 K ideal. Settled by: the vendor performance curve and an ASME PTC 10 test on the installed machine (Section 7).
  2. Discharge temperature limit forcing a design change. A single-stage outlet at 455 K ideal, and above 480 K in practice, exceeds the temperature limits of many seals, lubricants, and gas services. Direction: the built plant is likely to use two stages with an intercooler, which lowers the work toward 199 kJ/kg ideal (about 235–285 kJ/kg at the Section 5.1 efficiencies applied stage by stage — estimated, not computed from a vendor model) and adds cooler pressure drop, which raises it again by a few percent. Size: of the order of −10 % on ideal work from staging, partly offset by pressure drops of typically 0.1–0.3 bar per cooler and filter (assumed range, unverified). Settled by: the vendor's staged design proposal and the plant pressure-drop records.
  3. Suction conditions at the machine flange differ from the stated conditions. Filters, strainers, and inlet piping lower the pressure at the flange below 1 bar, and a warm suction line raises T1. Direction: both raise the work, because the machine sees a larger pressure ratio from a warmer inlet. Size: a 0.05 bar suction loss at this duty raises the ratio from 8.00 to 8.42 and the ideal work by about +3 % (computed from the Section 3 formula); a 10 K warmer suction adds a further +3 %. Settled by: calibrated pressure and temperature measurements at the compressor flange during operation.
9. What the calculation leaves out (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model.

  • Temperature dependence of cp and cv, and any real-gas departure (compressibility factor different from 1) at up to 8 bar and 521 K.
  • Heat loss from the casing (lowers outlet temperature, small effect on shaft work) and internal leakage and recirculation in a real machine.
  • Pressure drops in inlet and outlet piping, filters, and intercoolers; pulsation losses in a reciprocating machine.
  • Mechanical efficiency of bearings and seals, and motor and variable-speed-drive efficiency; the electrical power drawn is higher than every shaft figure in this solution.
  • Moisture or condensable components dropping out during compression or intercooling, which changes both the gas properties and the machine duty, and corrosion and fouling over run time.
  • Transient behaviour: start-up, surge and its control system in a dynamic (centrifugal or axial) machine, recycle and anti-surge valve losses, and operation away from the design flow, where efficiency falls.

Information not available to this calculation. The gas identity and composition; the vendor's test data and efficiency maps, which are held by the manufacturer; the plant's actual suction conditions and transmitter bases; and any site limits on discharge temperature. Each is named with its settling source in Section 7.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %.

  • Isentropic efficiency below 0.90, which covers nearly all real machines (Section 5.1).
  • The pressures being gauge rather than absolute (−32 %, Section 4).
  • k being 1.40 (air) rather than 1.25 (+10 %, Section 5.2).
  • A closed-system (batch) device rather than a steady-flow machine (−20 %, Section 4).
  • Staging with intercooling (−10 % to −14 % ideal, Section 4).
  • Condensation during compression, or a gas with a compressibility factor departing from 1 by more than about 0.05 at the outlet state (size not computable without the gas identity).

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used.

  1. Is 222 kJ/kg being used as an ideal reference value, or as an expected plant consumption? Only the first use is supported.
  2. Which gas, at what composition, and what do DIPPR or NIST REFPROP give for its cp and compressibility between 300 K and the outlet temperature?
  3. Are the 1 bar and 8 bar figures absolute or gauge, on the plant documents?
  4. Which machine, and what does its vendor curve give for head and efficiency at the required flow and inlet state?
  5. What is the discharge temperature limit for the machine and the gas service, and does it force staging?
  6. Is the required figure shaft power or electrical power, and what mechanical and driver efficiencies apply?
  7. Has the sensitivity to k been resolved — is the gas the one R describes, the one k describes, or neither?

D5. Solids Drying — Second Dryer

Response without the skill

Drying Time for a Batch of Wet Solid

Symbols and given data

Each symbol is defined here, before its first use in a calculation.

  • LsL_s is the mass of dry solid, in kilograms (kg). Ls=400 kgL_s = 400\ \text{kg}.
  • X1X_1 is the initial moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg). X1=0.80 kg/kgX_1 = 0.80\ \text{kg/kg}.
  • X2X_2 is the final moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg). X2=0.10 kg/kgX_2 = 0.10\ \text{kg/kg}.
  • NN is the drying rate in the constant-rate period, in kilograms per square metre per hour (kg/(m²·h)). N=3.0 kg/(m2⋅h)N = 3.0\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·h)}.
  • AA is the drying area, in square metres (m²). A=15 m2A = 15\ \text{m}^2.
  • MwM_w is the total mass of water removed, in kilograms (kg).
  • RR is the total rate of water removal, in kilograms per hour (kg/h).
  • tt is the drying time, in hours (h).
Basis and assumption

The moisture contents X1X_1 and X2X_2 are stated on a dry basis, so the mass of dry solid LsL_s is constant during drying and is the correct basis for the water balance.

No critical moisture content, no equilibrium moisture content, and no falling-rate drying data are given. The calculation therefore uses the stated constant-rate value NN over the whole moisture interval from X1X_1 to X2X_2. The result is an estimate on that basis. If a falling-rate period occurs before X2X_2 is reached, the actual drying time is longer than the value calculated here, and the additional time cannot be calculated from the data given.

Step 1: Mass of water removed

The decrease in dry-basis moisture content, denoted ΔX\Delta X and measured in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg), is:

ΔX=X1−X2=0.80−0.10=0.70 kg/kg\Delta X = X_1 - X_2 = 0.80 - 0.10 = 0.70\ \text{kg/kg}

The total mass of water removed MwM_w is LsL_s multiplied by ΔX\Delta X:

Mw=Ls ΔX=400 kg×0.70 kg/kg=280 kgM_w = L_s \, \Delta X = 400\ \text{kg} \times 0.70\ \text{kg/kg} = 280\ \text{kg}

Step 2: Total rate of water removal

The total rate of water removal RR is the area-specific drying rate NN multiplied by the drying area AA:

R=N A=3.0 kg/(m2⋅h)×15 m2=45 kg/hR = N \, A = 3.0\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·h)} \times 15\ \text{m}^2 = 45\ \text{kg/h}

Step 3: Drying time

The drying time tt is the total mass of water removed MwM_w divided by the total rate of water removal RR:

t=MwR=280 kg45 kg/h=6.22 ht = \dfrac{M_w}{R} = \dfrac{280\ \text{kg}}{45\ \text{kg/h}} = 6.22\ \text{h}

The fractional part, 0.22 h0.22\ \text{h}, is 0.22×60=130.22 \times 60 = 13 minutes, so 6.22 h6.22\ \text{h} is 6 h 13 min.

Result

The estimated drying time is 6.22 h, approximately 6.2 h (6 h 13 min), on the stated constant-rate basis.

Units check: kilograms divided by kilograms per hour gives hours, as required for tt.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Batch Drying Time — Estimate with Stated Limitations

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: The problem supplies only the constant-rate drying rate. Drying of most wet solids has two periods: a constant-rate period, while the surface stays wet, and a falling-rate period, after the surface is no longer fully wet, in which the rate falls as moisture content falls. No falling-rate data are supplied. The total time therefore cannot be fixed from the supplied data alone. Any single value obtained by applying the constant rate over the whole moisture range is a lower bound, not an estimate of the total time, unless the final moisture content is still in the constant-rate period.

Confidence rating: Low for a total drying time (about 3 out of 10). High for the water mass to be removed and for the constant-rate-only lower bound, because those follow by arithmetic from given values. Confidence in any falling-rate total is low until the drying curve for the actual solid, at the actual air conditions, is measured.

Symbols are defined at first use, with units.

  • LsL_s is the mass of dry solid, in kilograms (kg).
  • XX is the moisture content on a dry basis, in kilograms of water per kilogram of dry solid (kg/kg dry solid); X1X_1 is its initial value and X2X_2 is its final value.
  • NN is the drying rate per unit area, in kilograms per square metre per hour (kg/(m²·h)); NcN_c is its constant-rate value.
  • AA is the exposed drying area, in square metres (m²).
  • tt is the drying time, in hours (h); tct_c is the time in the constant-rate period and tft_f is the time in the falling-rate period.
  • XcX_c is the critical moisture content, in kg/kg dry solid, at which the constant-rate period ends.
  • XeX_e is the equilibrium moisture content, in kg/kg dry solid, at the drying-air conditions; the rate tends to zero as XX approaches XeX_e.
  • WW is the total mass of water removed, in kg.
2. Inputs, labelled by state
Quantity Value State
LsL_s 400 kg given
X1X_1 0.80 kg/kg dry solid given; dry basis is stated in the problem
X2X_2 0.10 kg/kg dry solid given; dry basis as above
NcN_c 3.0 kg/(m²·h) given; whether measured, vendor, or nominal is not stated — unverified
AA 15 m² given; whether it is one-sided exposed area, tray area, or total particle area is not stated — unverified
XcX_c not supplied missing; plausible range used below: 0.10 to 0.60 kg/kg
XeX_e not supplied missing; plausible range used below: 0 to 0.05 kg/kg
Falling-rate relation NN as a function of XX not supplied missing; a linear form is assumed below only as an illustrative model
Air temperature, humidity, velocity not supplied missing; NcN_c is taken as already embodying them
Solid identity, particle size, bed depth, shrinkage, case-hardening not supplied missing

No property value, correlation, or fitted relation from a databank is used. The only relations used are the dry-basis mass balance and the definition of drying rate, which hold by definition, and, in the illustrative falling-rate cases only, a linear falling-rate relation whose range of validity is the actual material's measured curve — which is not available. That relation is assumed, unverified.

3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — fill the gaps first)

The solution needs, and the problem does not supply:

  1. XcX_c — without it, the split between constant-rate and falling-rate time is unknown.
  2. The falling-rate curve N(X)N(X), or equivalent data (for example a characteristic drying curve, or effective moisture diffusivity and particle size for a diffusion model).
  3. XeX_e and the air humidity that sets it — if X2X_2 is close to XeX_e, the falling-rate time grows without bound as X2→XeX_2 \to X_e; if Xe≥X2X_e \ge X_2, the target cannot be reached at those air conditions at all.
  4. Basis checks: moisture contents are stated per kg dry solid (dry basis), so no wet-basis conversion is needed — this basis is given, not assumed. AA basis (exposed surface, one side or two) is not stated. NcN_c basis (per exposed area as above) is presumed consistent with AA; if the two use different area definitions, the product NcAN_c A is wrong in proportion.
  5. Operating basis: batch operation is stated; whether NcN_c is constant in time (constant air conditions, no heat-up period) is not stated. Heat-up time, loading and unloading time, and any induction period are not supplied and are excluded.
  6. Per-pass or overall: not applicable to a batch dryer in the flow sense; the result is overall for the batch as charged.

Because these are missing, the problem is not completed silently. It is solved (a) exactly for the part the data do fix, and (b) under the plausible alternatives in Section 5.

4. Part fixed by the supplied data

Water removed, by dry-basis balance:

W=Ls(X1−X2)=400×(0.80−0.10)=280 kgW = L_s (X_1 - X_2) = 400 \times (0.80 - 0.10) = 280\ \text{kg}

Water removal rate in the constant-rate period:

NcA=3.0×15=45 kg/hN_c A = 3.0 \times 15 = 45\ \text{kg/h}

Time if the constant rate held over the whole range:

t=WNcA=28045=6.22 ht = \frac{W}{N_c A} = \frac{280}{45} = 6.22\ \text{h}

Result (lower bound): t≥6.22t \ge 6.22 h, with equality only if Xc≤X2=0.10X_c \le X_2 = 0.10 kg/kg, that is, only if the solid stays in the constant-rate period down to the final moisture content. For most granular, porous, or food-type solids XcX_c is well above 0.10 kg/kg, so equality is unlikely; it is retained as the bounding case, not as the expected case.

General split, when XcX_c lies between X2X_2 and X1X_1:

tc=LsANc (X1−Xc),LsANc=40045=8.889 h per unit Xt_c = \frac{L_s}{A N_c}\,(X_1 - X_c), \qquad \frac{L_s}{A N_c} = \frac{400}{45} = 8.889\ \text{h per unit } X

tf=LsA∫X2XcdXN(X)t_f = \frac{L_s}{A} \int_{X_2}^{X_c} \frac{dX}{N(X)}

The integral cannot be evaluated without N(X)N(X). This is the point at which the supplied data run out.

5. Range under plausible alternatives (Prompt 1)

Illustrative model for the falling-rate period, assumed: NN falls linearly with XX from NcN_c at XcX_c to zero at XeX_e,

N=Nc X−XeXc−Xe⟹tf=Ls(Xc−Xe)ANc ln⁡ ⁣(Xc−XeX2−Xe)N = N_c\,\frac{X - X_e}{X_c - X_e} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_f = \frac{L_s (X_c - X_e)}{A N_c}\, \ln\!\left(\frac{X_c - X_e}{X_2 - X_e}\right)

All cases below were computed in code (Section 7); LsL_s, X1X_1, X2X_2, NcN_c and AA are given in every case, XcX_c and XeX_e are assumed as labelled.

Reported result: a range, not a single value.

  • Defensible lower bound: 6.2 h.
  • Plausible total range under the linear falling-rate model: about 7.4 to 11.5 h, for XcX_c from 0.30 to 0.50 kg/kg and XeX_e from 0 to 0.05 kg/kg.
  • Central illustrative value: about 8.5 h (Case C). This value rests on assumed XcX_c and an assumed linear curve; it is not a measured or fitted result.
  • The true time can lie above 11.5 h: a concave (diffusion-controlled) falling-rate curve, a higher XcX_c, XeX_e closer to X2X_2, or a falling NcN_c all lengthen it. No upper bound can be defended from the supplied data; as Xe→X2X_e \to X_2 the time diverges.

  • XeX_e, assumed, 0 → 0.05 at Xc=0.40X_c = 0.40: total 8.48 → 9.61 h, +13 %.
  • Shape of N(X)N(X), assumed linear: a diffusion-type curve falling faster than linear at low XX would increase tft_f; the effect is of the same order as the XcX_c effect and is unquantifiable without data. Direction: longer time.
  • NcN_c, given but unverified, ±20 % (2.4 to 3.6 kg/(m²·h)): every time scales as 1/Nc1/N_c, so the lower bound moves 5.19 to 7.78 h, −17 % to +25 %. If the given NcN_c is a nominal or clean-surface value rather than a value for this bed, this error applies in full.

6. Primary source that would settle the point

The point is settled only by a measured drying curve for the actual solid: a laboratory or pilot batch drying test on the actual material, at the intended air temperature, humidity and velocity and at the intended bed depth or particle size, recording mass against time, from which XcX_c, XeX_e and N(X)N(X) are read directly. Textbook tabulations of XcX_c for other materials (for example in Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook or Geankoplis, Transport Processes and Separation Process Principles, drying chapter) give ranges for named materials only and do not settle the value for an unnamed solid. Every claim in Section 5 that rests on an assumed XcX_c, XeX_e, or curve shape is marked unverified until checked against such a test. The arithmetic in Section 4 rests on definitions and given values and needs no external source.

7. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run in code (Python) independently of the hand arithmetic; the code recomputed WW, NcAN_c A, the lower bound, and every case in the Section 5 table.

  1. Balance closure. Water in the solid initially: 400×0.80=320400 \times 0.80 = 320 kg (computed). Water finally: 400×0.10=40400 \times 0.10 = 40 kg (computed). Removed: 320−40=280320 - 40 = 280 kg, equal to WW from Section 4. Closure error: 0 kg (0 %). Check passes.
  2. Limiting case 1 — known by sight. If Xc≤X2X_c \le X_2, the falling-rate integral has zero width and the formula returns t=6.22t = 6.22 h, the constant-rate result. The code reproduces this (Case A). Check passes.
  3. Limiting case 2 — known by sight. If NcN_c doubles, every time must halve, because tt is proportional to 1/Nc1/N_c in both periods under the assumed model. In the code, Nc=2.4N_c = 2.4 and 3.63.6 kg/(m²·h) give lower bounds of 7.78 h and 5.19 h, in exact inverse proportion to 6.22 h. Check passes.
  4. Limiting case 3 — divergence. As Xe→X2X_e \to X_2 from below, the logarithm in tft_f diverges, as it must, because the rate tends to zero at the target. The formula shows this behaviour; no finite time is reported for Xe≥X2X_e \ge X_2. Check passes, and it flags a real risk: a target close to equilibrium is not a small correction.
  5. Dimensional check. Ls/(ANc)L_s/(A N_c) has units kg / (m² · kg/(m²·h)) = h, and it multiplies a dimensionless moisture difference or logarithm. All time expressions are in hours. Check passes.
  6. Correlation valid range. No correlation is used. The linear falling-rate relation is an assumed shape, valid only where the actual material's curve is approximately linear in XX; that condition is unverified and is the check that fails — not numerically, but as a matter of evidence. It is reported as failing, and the solution is not altered to make it pass: the range in Section 5 is presented as conditional on that shape.

No check was made by agreement with another AI model, and none is claimed as verification.

8. Audit against built-equipment behaviour (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. Effective area and bed behaviour. In a tray or through-circulation dryer the exposed area is not the nominal tray area: channeling, uneven bed depth, and shrinkage that pulls the solid away from tray edges reduce the effective AA and the local rate. Direction: longer time. Rough size: commonly 10–30 % on total time. Settled by: the plant or pilot drying log for the actual equipment (mass or outlet-air humidity against time), or a bed-depth and airflow survey.
  2. NcN_c does not stay constant. Heat-up of the cold wet charge, falling air temperature across a deep bed, rising outlet humidity, and fouling all reduce the realised rate below a nominal NcN_c measured under clean, steady conditions. Direction: longer time. Rough size: heat-up alone can add roughly 0.25–1 h on a batch of this size; sustained rate depression adds in proportion. Settled by: the dryer's air inlet and outlet temperature and humidity records over a comparable batch, and the vendor's rated duty for the actual unit — vendor document unverified here, as no vendor or unit is named.
  3. End-point non-uniformity. The batch average reaches X2=0.10X_2 = 0.10 kg/kg before the wettest zones do; drying to a specification on the wettest material, not the average, extends the batch, and case-hardening in some solids slows the late falling-rate period well below a linear curve. Direction: longer time. Rough size: 10–50 % on the falling-rate portion for non-uniform beds. Settled by: moisture measurements on samples taken from several bed locations at the end of a trial batch (oven-dry method on the actual material).

All three effects act in the same direction: the built-equipment time is expected to be longer than both the lower bound and the central illustrative value.

9. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: heat-up and cool-down periods; internal temperature gradients and any heat-sensitive degradation limit on air temperature; shrinkage and changes in AA during drying; diffusion, capillary and bound-water mechanisms in detail; rewetting from humid air at discharge; energy use, air flow requirement, and dryer thermal efficiency (no air data are supplied, so no energy balance is possible — this is an omission forced by the data, reported as such, not a closed balance).
  • Information not available here: the identity and measured drying characteristics of the solid, which are material-specific test data; any vendor rating for a specific dryer; site air conditions. None of these is in a public databank for an unnamed solid.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: channeling, fouling, tray warping, fan performance drift, and operator end-point judgement (Section 8).
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: XcX_c above about 0.25 kg/kg (already +19 % at 0.30); XeX_e above about 0.04 kg/kg at Xc=0.40X_c = 0.40; realised NcN_c more than about 10 % below the given value; effective AA more than about 10 % below the given value; a concave rather than linear falling-rate curve. Most realistic combinations of these exceed 10 %, which is why a single value is not reported.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the solid, and has a drying curve been measured on it at the intended air conditions and bed depth? What are its measured XcX_c and XeX_e?
  2. Is the target X2=0.10X_2 = 0.10 kg/kg an average or a maximum for any part of the batch, and how far is it above XeX_e at the actual outlet-air humidity?
  3. On what area basis were NcN_c and AA each stated, and were they measured on this equipment or taken from a rating?
  4. What schedule margin is carried for heat-up, non-uniformity, and end-point testing, given that every identified plant effect lengthens the time?
  5. Is 6.2 h being used anywhere as the planned batch time? If so, it should be replaced by a range with the lower bound labelled as a bound only.
10. Answer in brief
  • Water to be removed (given data, exact): 280 kg.
  • Constant-rate removal rate (given data): 45 kg/h.
  • Drying time, constant-rate only (lower bound): 6.22 h.
  • Drying time, total, with a falling-rate period under the stated assumed cases: about 7.4 to 11.5 h, central illustrative value about 8.5 h — low confidence, unverified until a drying curve for the actual solid is measured. Built equipment is expected to fall at or above the corresponding model value.

D6. Compressible-Cake Filtration — Second Filter

Response without the skill

Constant-Pressure Filtration — Time for a Given Filtrate Volume

Given data
  • VV is the filtrate volume to be obtained, in cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^3}): V=2 m3V = 2\ \mathrm{m^3}
  • ΔP\Delta P is the constant pressure difference across the filter, in pascals (Pa\mathrm{Pa}): ΔP=150 kPa=150×103 Pa=1.50×105 Pa\Delta P = 150\ \mathrm{kPa} = 150 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.50 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}
  • AA is the filter area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}): A=3 m2A = 3\ \mathrm{m^2}
  • μ\mu is the filtrate viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa⋅s\mathrm{Pa \cdot s}): μ=0.0012 Pa⋅s\mu = 0.0012\ \mathrm{Pa \cdot s}
  • cc is the mass of dry cake solids deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}): c=40 kg/m3c = 40\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}
  • α\alpha is the specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg\mathrm{m/kg}): α=8×1010 m/kg\alpha = 8 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg}

No value is given for the filter-medium resistance. The filter-medium resistance is therefore taken as negligible in comparison with the cake resistance. This is the standard form used when only α\alpha, cc, μ\mu, AA, and ΔP\Delta P are supplied.

Theory

tt is the filtration time, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}).

mm is the mass of dry cake deposited, in kilograms (kg\mathrm{kg}). By the definition of cc:

m=cVm = cV

RcR_{\mathrm{c}} is the cake resistance, in reciprocal metres (m−1\mathrm{m^{-1}}). By the definition of α\alpha as resistance per unit mass of cake per unit area:

Rc=αmA=αcVAR_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\alpha m}{A} = \frac{\alpha c V}{A}

The instantaneous filtration rate follows Darcy's law applied to flow through the cake. With the filter-medium resistance neglected, the rate of filtrate production dV/dt\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}t, in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}), is:

dVdt=A ΔPμRc=A ΔPμ αcV/A=A2ΔPμαcV\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{A \, \Delta P}{\mu R_{\mathrm{c}}} = \frac{A \, \Delta P}{\mu \, \alpha c V / A} = \frac{A^{2} \Delta P}{\mu \alpha c V}

The rate falls as VV increases, because the cake thickens and RcR_{\mathrm{c}} grows in proportion to VV.

For constant ΔP\Delta P, μ\mu, α\alpha, cc, and AA, separate variables and integrate from V=0V = 0 at t=0t = 0 to the target VV at time tt:

V dV=A2ΔPμαc dtV \, \mathrm{d}V = \frac{A^{2} \Delta P}{\mu \alpha c} \, \mathrm{d}t

∫0VV dV=A2ΔPμαc∫0tdt\int_{0}^{V} V \, \mathrm{d}V = \frac{A^{2} \Delta P}{\mu \alpha c} \int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{d}t

V22=A2ΔPμαc t\frac{V^{2}}{2} = \frac{A^{2} \Delta P}{\mu \alpha c} \, t

Hence:

t=μαc2A2ΔP V2t = \frac{\mu \alpha c}{2 A^{2} \Delta P} \, V^{2}

Dimensional check: μ\mu (Pa⋅s=kg/(m⋅s)\mathrm{Pa \cdot s} = \mathrm{kg/(m \cdot s)}) multiplied by α\alpha (m/kg\mathrm{m/kg}) multiplied by cc (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}) multiplied by V2V^{2} (m6\mathrm{m^6}), divided by A2A^{2} (m4\mathrm{m^4}) and ΔP\Delta P (Pa=kg/(m⋅s2)\mathrm{Pa} = \mathrm{kg/(m \cdot s^2)}), gives seconds (s\mathrm{s}), as required.

Calculation

Substitute the given values:

t=(0.0012 Pa⋅s)(8×1010 m/kg)(40 kg/m3)2 (3 m2)2 (1.50×105 Pa) (2 m3)2t = \frac{(0.0012\ \mathrm{Pa \cdot s})(8 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg})(40\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})}{2 \, (3\ \mathrm{m^2})^{2} \, (1.50 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa})} \, (2\ \mathrm{m^3})^{2}

Numerator factor before V2V^{2}:

μαc=(0.0012)(8×1010)(40)=3.84×109\mu \alpha c = (0.0012)(8 \times 10^{10})(40) = 3.84 \times 10^{9}

Denominator:

2A2ΔP=2×9×1.50×105=2.70×1062 A^{2} \Delta P = 2 \times 9 \times 1.50 \times 10^{5} = 2.70 \times 10^{6}

Therefore:

t=3.84×1092.70×106×4t = \frac{3.84 \times 10^{9}}{2.70 \times 10^{6}} \times 4

t=1422.2×4≈5689 st = 1422.2 \times 4 \approx 5689\ \mathrm{s}

Convert to minutes and hours, where 60 s=1 min60\ \mathrm{s} = 1\ \mathrm{min} and 3600 s=1 h3600\ \mathrm{s} = 1\ \mathrm{h}:

t=568960≈94.8 min≈1.58 ht = \frac{5689}{60} \approx 94.8\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.58\ \mathrm{h}

Result

The time required to obtain 2 m32\ \mathrm{m^3} of filtrate at a constant pressure difference of 150 kPa150\ \mathrm{kPa} through 3 m23\ \mathrm{m^2} of filter area, neglecting filter-medium resistance, is approximately 5.7×103 s5.7 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}, i.e. approximately 95 min95\ \mathrm{min} (approximately 1.6 h1.6\ \mathrm{h}).

If the filter-medium resistance is not negligible in practice, the actual time will be longer than this value, because an additional resistance term would appear in the denominator of the rate equation throughout the filtration.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Constant-pressure filtration — time to collect 2 m³ of filtrate

1. Weakness and confidence rating — stated first (Checklist 1)

Weakness. The problem is underspecified for the standard constant-pressure filtration equation: the filter-medium resistance is not supplied, and the provenance and pressure-dependence of the specific cake resistance are not supplied. The cake term can be computed exactly from the numbers given; the total time cannot, because the medium term is of unknown size relative to the cake term at the stated volume.

Confidence rating: Low for the total time as a prediction of built equipment; High for the arithmetic of the cake term alone, conditional on the given numbers. On a 0–10 scale: 4 / 10 for total time, 9 / 10 for the cake-only term. The missing quantity can change the total by roughly 0 % to roughly +94 % over its plausible range (Section 4), and by more if the medium blinds. No single value is therefore reported as the answer; a range is reported (Checklist 2).

Agreement with any other AI model would not raise this rating (Checklist 7). Verification below is by dimensions, limiting cases and executed code only (Checklist 6).

2. Symbols, defined before first use
  • tt — filtration time, in seconds (s), reported also in minutes (min) and hours (h).
  • VV — cumulative filtrate volume collected, in cubic metres (m³).
  • AA — filter area, in square metres (m²).
  • ΔP\Delta P — constant pressure difference across cake plus medium, in pascals (Pa); 1 kilopascal (kPa) = 1,000 Pa.
  • μ\mu — filtrate viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa·s).
  • cc — dry cake mass deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre of filtrate (kg/m³).
  • α\alpha — specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg).
  • RmR_m — filter-medium resistance, in reciprocal metres (1/m, i.e. m⁻¹). Not given — see Section 3.
  • ss — cake compressibility exponent (dimensionless), in α=α0 ΔP s\alpha = \alpha_0 \, \Delta P^{\,s}, where α0\alpha_0 is the specific cake resistance at unit pressure reference (m/kg in the stated convention). Not given — see Section 3.

4. Model, inputs at point of use, and result as a range
4.1 Model

For constant-pressure cake filtration (Ruth equation; standard form in e.g. Coulson & Richardson, Chemical Engineering, Vol. 2, and in Richardson & Harker — a textbook source, not the primary source for the actual material, see Section 6):

Differential form, with every symbol as defined in Section 2:

dtdV=μA ΔP(α c VA+Rm)\frac{dt}{dV} = \frac{\mu}{A\,\Delta P}\left(\frac{\alpha\,c\,V}{A} + R_m\right)

Integrated from V=0V = 0 at t=0t = 0:

t=μ α c V22 A2 ΔP  +  μ Rm VA ΔPt = \frac{\mu\,\alpha\,c\,V^{2}}{2\,A^{2}\,\Delta P} \;+\; \frac{\mu\,R_m\,V}{A\,\Delta P}

First term: cake resistance, growing as cake builds. Second term: medium resistance, constant. Validity: incompressible or constant-α\alpha cake at the stated ΔP\Delta P, laminar flow through cake and medium (Darcy regime), constant μ\mu, cc and AA. Outside that regime the equation is not claimed to hold.

  • α=8×1010\alpha = 8\times10^{10} m/kg — given as a number; its origin is in practice fitted from a laboratory filtration test, and its applicability at 150 kPa is assumed, unverified (Section 6).
  • RmR_m — not given; values used are estimated alternatives, Section 3.

6. Primary source that settles the point (Checklist 5)

The point — the true RmR_m and the true α\alpha at 150 kPa for this slurry and this medium — is settled only by:

  1. A filtration test on the actual slurry with the actual medium (laboratory leaf test or bomb-filter test) at ΔP=150\Delta P = 150 kPa: a plot of t/Vt/V against VV is a straight line under the model, with slope =μαc/(A2ΔP)= \mu\alpha c / (A^{2}\Delta P) and intercept =μRm/(A ΔP)= \mu R_m / (A\,\Delta P), giving α\alpha and RmR_m separately from the actual material. This is the primary measurement.
  2. The medium manufacturer's data sheet for the specified cloth / membrane, for a clean-medium RmR_m starting value only — it does not capture blinding by this slurry.

Every claim in this solution that rests on those sources — the RmR_m band, the applicability of α\alpha at 150 kPa, the ss band — is marked unverified until checked against them. The given numbers supplied in the problem supersede generic ranges for the quantities they actually specify (VV, ΔP\Delta P, AA, μ\mu, cc, α\alpha); they specify nothing about RmR_m, which is why the range stands.

8. Prompt 4 — Audit as an experienced plant engineer

The three points most likely to differ in built equipment:

  1. Medium resistance and blinding — direction: longer time; size: +10 % to +100 % or more. A clean-medium RmR_m from a data sheet does not survive contact with a real slurry: fines plug the cloth in the first minutes, and RmR_m then grows with cycles if cleaning is incomplete. This is exactly the missing term in Section 4.4. Settled by: the leaf / bomb test on the actual slurry and medium (Section 6), and by plant cycle records of t/Vt/V vs VV if the filter already exists.
  2. Cake compressibility and non-uniform cake — direction: longer time; size: typically +20 % to +50 % at elevated pressure for a compressible cake (estimated, unverified for this material). α\alpha rises through the cake depth as the solids compressive stress rises toward the medium, and feed distribution gives thicker cake — hence longer local filtration — on part of the area. Settled by: filtration tests at two or more pressures on the actual slurry (giving ss), and cake-thickness surveys on the built filter.
  3. Cycle dead time and pressure delivery — direction: longer elapsed time; size: minutes to tens of minutes per cycle. The equation times only filtration at full ΔP\Delta P. Ramp-up, fill, discharge, cloth wash and any pressure drop in feed piping are excluded, and a pump-fed (rather than truly constant-pressure) supply may not hold 150 kPa as the cake builds. Settled by: the vendor's cycle-time statement for the specified machine and the plant pressure record / pump curve at the duty point.
9. Prompt 5 — What is not covered
  • Effects not in the model: pore blocking before a cake forms; cake cracking or shrinkage (which would shorten time by opening channels); sedimentation in the feed; cake washing and deliquoring / air-blow time; cake moisture and discharge behaviour; cloth ageing over repeated cycles; temperature drift of μ\mu during the run; any gas evolution or flashing.
  • Information not visible here: the actual slurry's particle size distribution and solids identity; the specified medium and its vendor data; any laboratory filtration test report for this material; the machine type (press, leaf, rotary vacuum — the equation's constant- pressure form fits some better than others). These are held, if anywhere, in vendor documents and test records, not in the problem statement.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: progressive blinding, feed-composition swings moving cc, operator wash practice, and pressure-supply behaviour under load (Section 8, points 1 and 3).
  • Conditions that change the answer by more than 10 %: RmR_m above about 101110^{11} 1/m (+9 % and rising); α\alpha in error by more than about 10 % from pressure mismatch or fit scatter (proportional); μ\mu in error by more than 10 % (proportional); more than about 5 % of AA inactive (cake term, about +11 %); more than about 10 % of ΔP\Delta P lost outside cake + medium (about +11 %); any substantial wash or discharge time added to the cycle.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used:

  1. What is RmR_m for the actual medium with this slurry, from a test — not from a clean-water data sheet?
  2. At what pressure was α=8×1010\alpha = 8\times10^{10} m/kg measured, what is ss, and what was the scatter of the fit?
  3. Is c=40c = 40 kg/m³ dry cake per filtrate volume, confirmed against the feed solids concentration and cake moisture?
  4. Is 150 kPa held constant across cake + medium for the whole cycle, and what device holds it?
  5. Is the required figure filtration time only, or full cycle time including wash, discharge and cloth wash?
  6. Which end of the 95–184 min range will be used for sizing, and is the margin to the next-larger machine acceptable at the blinded- medium end?

E1. Relief Sizing — Second Valve

Response without the skill

Relief Orifice Sizing

Given data and definitions

The relieving rate, denoted WW, in kilograms per second (kg/s\mathrm{kg/s}), is the mass flow rate that the relief device must pass:

W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \mathrm{kg/s}

The orifice mass flux under a vapour-only assumption, denoted GG, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m2⋅s)\mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}), is the mass flow rate per unit orifice area:

G=900 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 900\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}

The required orifice area, denoted AreqA_{\mathrm{req}}, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}), is the area sought.

The equivalent circular orifice diameter, denoted dreqd_{\mathrm{req}}, in metres (m\mathrm{m}), is the diameter of a circle having area AreqA_{\mathrm{req}}.

The mathematical constant pi, denoted π\pi, is dimensionless and is approximately 3.14163.1416.

No other fluid, pressure, or temperature data are given. The stated value of GG is therefore taken as the complete vapour-only flux for the relieving condition. No discharge coefficient, back-pressure correction, or other correction factor is applied again, because any such factor applicable to the stated condition is already contained in the given value of GG.

Required area

By definition, GG is WW divided by the orifice area. Rearrangement for the required area gives:

Areq=WGA_{\mathrm{req}} = \frac{W}{G}

Substitution of the given values gives:

Areq=5 kg/s900 kg/(m2⋅s)=5.56×10−3 m2A_{\mathrm{req}} = \frac{5\ \mathrm{kg/s}}{900\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}

Unit conversions of AreqA_{\mathrm{req}} are:

  • Areq=5.56×10−3 m2A_{\mathrm{req}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}
  • Areq=55.6 cm2A_{\mathrm{req}} = 55.6\ \mathrm{cm^2}, where cm2\mathrm{cm^2} denotes square centimetres
  • Areq=5,556 mm2A_{\mathrm{req}} = 5{,}556\ \mathrm{mm^2}, where mm2\mathrm{mm^2} denotes square millimetres
  • Areq=8.61 in2A_{\mathrm{req}} = 8.61\ \mathrm{in^2}, where in2\mathrm{in^2} denotes square inches, using 1 in2=6.4516×10−4 m21\ \mathrm{in^2} = 6.4516 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}
Equivalent diameter

For a circular orifice, AreqA_{\mathrm{req}} and dreqd_{\mathrm{req}} are related by:

Areq=πdreq24A_{\mathrm{req}} = \frac{\pi d_{\mathrm{req}}^2}{4}

Rearrangement and substitution give:

dreq=4Areqπ=4×5.56×10−3 m2π=0.0841 md_{\mathrm{req}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 A_{\mathrm{req}}}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 5.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}}{\pi}} = 0.0841\ \mathrm{m}

That is, dreq=84.1 mmd_{\mathrm{req}} = 84.1\ \mathrm{mm}, where mm\mathrm{mm} denotes millimetres, or 3.31 in3.31\ \mathrm{in}, where in\mathrm{in} denotes inches.

The equivalent diameter is a geometric conversion of the required area. Commercial relief valves are selected by orifice area, not by this diameter alone.

Standard orifice selection

The American Petroleum Institute (API) Standard 526 letter series gives standard effective orifice areas. The two sizes bracketing AreqA_{\mathrm{req}} are:

Letter Standard area, in in2\mathrm{in^2} Standard area, in m2\mathrm{m^2} Capacity at G=900 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 900\ \mathrm{kg/(m^2 \cdot s)}, in kg/s\mathrm{kg/s}
P 6.38 4.12×10−34.12 \times 10^{-3} 3.70
Q 11.05 7.13×10−37.13 \times 10^{-3} 6.42

The capacity in the table is the product of the standard area and GG.

A P orifice is insufficient, because its capacity of 3.70 kg/s3.70\ \mathrm{kg/s} is less than W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \mathrm{kg/s}.

The selected standard orifice area, denoted AselA_{\mathrm{sel}}, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}), is therefore the Q orifice:

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Relief Orifice Sizing — Vapour-Only, Given Mass Flux

Symbols, defined before first use
  • WW = required relieving mass rate, in kilograms per second (kg/s).
  • GG = mass flux through the orifice, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m²·s)).
  • AA = required orifice flow area, in square metres (m²), also reported in square centimetres (cm²).
  • dd = diameter of a circular orifice having area AA, in metres (m), also reported in millimetres (mm).
  • KdK_d = discharge coefficient of the relief device, dimensionless.
  • KbK_b = backpressure correction factor, dimensionless.
  • KcK_c = combination correction factor for a rupture disc installed with the valve, dimensionless.
  • KvK_v = viscosity correction factor, dimensionless.
  • kk = ratio of specific heat capacities of the vapour, dimensionless.
1. Weakness and confidence rating (Checklist item 1; Prompt 1)

Weakness. The arithmetic in this problem is exact, but the engineering content is not in the arithmetic. It is carried entirely by two inputs whose provenance is not stated:

  1. Whether the stated value of GG is an ideal (theoretical critical-flow) flux, to which a discharge coefficient KdK_d and correction factors must still be applied, or an effective flux that already contains them. This single ambiguity moves AA by +2.6%+2.6\% to +11.1%+11.1\% (Section 4).
  2. The vapour-only assumption. If any liquid is present at, or forms by flashing in, the nozzle, GG for a vapour calculation does not apply, and the required area can be larger by far more than 10 % (Sections 6 and 7).

Confidence rating.

  • Confidence in AA as a consequence of the two stated inputs: high, 5/5. It is a definitional division, checked by back-substitution and by code (Section 5).
  • Confidence in AA as the size of a device that can be purchased and installed: low, 2/5. Set pressure, relieving temperature, fluid identity and composition, backpressure, and the correction factors are all missing (Section 3). No claim in this file that depends on a code, a databank, or vendor data should be used until it has been checked against the primary source named for it (Section 2). Agreement with any other AI model is not used as verification anywhere in this file (Checklist item 7).
2. Primary sources that settle the open points (Checklist item 5)

Every claim below that rests on one of these sources is unverified until checked against that source:

Choice of relieving scenario and the basis on which WW is calculated (fire, blocked outlet, tube rupture, and others) API Recommended Practice 521 (current edition), Pressure-Relieving and Depressuring Systems Unverified

3. Missing quantities — filled in by alternatives, not in silence (Prompt 2; Checklist item 4)

The problem as stated supplies WW and GG only. The following quantities are needed for a complete relief sizing. None has been taken silently; where the stated result depends on one, the plausible alternatives are solved in Section 4.

  1. Set pressure and relieving pressure — not given. Needed to establish that the flow is critical (choked), to recompute GG from properties if required, and to select a device. Pressure basis (gauge or absolute) is also not given; the two differ by about 101 kPa, which is a large fraction of a low set pressure.
  2. Relieving temperature — not given. Needed for any recomputation of GG.
  3. Fluid identity and composition, and its basis — not given. Neither the mass basis nor the mole basis is stated. Needed for molar mass, kk, and compressibility, and hence for GG.
  4. Backpressure — not given. Superimposed backpressure, built-up backpressure, and total backpressure at the rated flow are all missing, as is the total backpressure expressed as a percentage of set pressure. These decide whether flow remains critical and set the value of KbK_b.
  5. Whether GG already includes KdK_d, KbK_b, KcK_c, and KvK_v — not given. This is the largest identified numerical ambiguity in the stated problem and is treated as Alternatives A and B in Section 4.
  6. Inlet phase and quality — asserted as vapour-only, not demonstrated. The inlet liquid fraction, and whether the vapour is saturated (so that it flashes or condenses on expansion) or superheated, are not given.
  7. Basis of WW — not given. The scenario that produces WW, whether WW is per device or for the whole system, whether it is a peak or a sustained rate, and whether it already includes any code margin, are all unstated. There is no per-pass/overall conversion in a relief calculation, but the equivalent question — peak instantaneous rate versus rate at relieving conditions after accumulation — is open.
  8. Reference state for GG — not given. GG is meaningful only at a stated upstream stagnation pressure and temperature; neither is supplied.
  9. Installation quantities — not given. Inlet line pressure drop (against the customary 3 % of set pressure limit, unverified, API RP 520 Part II), outlet line pressure drop, presence of a rupture disc (sets KcK_c), and the number of installed devices (operating plus spare) are all missing.
  10. Fluid secondary properties — not given. Viscosity (sets KvK_v), fouling or polymerising tendency, and toxicity/flammability (which decide discharge destination, not area) are missing.

Consequence. What follows is the sizing implied by the two given numbers, plus the range produced by the plausible readings of those numbers. It is not a device selection, and it is not sufficient for construction.

4. Solution and range (Prompt 1)
4.1 Stated inputs, labelled at the point of use (Checklist item 3)
  • W=5W = 5 kg/s — given. Its derivation is not supplied, so its own uncertainty is unknown; a ±10 % sensitivity is shown in Section 4.3 only as a sensitivity, not as a stated property of the input.
  • G=900G = 900 kg/(m²·s) — given, under a vapour-only assumption that is assumed, not measured or demonstrated. Whether GG includes any correction factor is assumed differently in Alternatives A and B.
  • Circular orifice shape, used only to report dd — assumed; real valve nozzles are not plain circular sharp-edged holes, so dd is an equivalent diameter, not a machining dimension.
  • Value of Kd=0.90K_d = 0.90 to 0.9750.975 used in Alternative B — estimated from the range customarily used for vapour relief valves, unverified against API RP 520 Part I and against vendor certified data (Section 2).

4.5 Relation to standard orifice sizes — unverified

Standard effective orifice areas in API RP 520 (letter designations) are, from general knowledge and unverified against the current edition: "N" = 7.06 in² = 45.5 cm², capacity at G=900G = 900 kg/(m²·s) of 4.10 kg/s, which is below WW; "P" = 11.05 in² = 71.3 cm², capacity 6.42 kg/s, which exceeds WW by 28 %. On that basis the next standard size above the Alternative A–B range is the "P" orifice. This step must not be used until (a) the letter areas are confirmed in the current edition of API RP 520 Part I, and (b) it is confirmed whether those effective areas are to be combined with Kd=0.9K_d = 0.9, as the API effective-area method customarily does — mixing the effective-area method with the actual-area method, or applying KdK_d twice, is a common source of an error of about 11 % in either direction. Note also that an installed capacity 28 % above the required rate is a chattering and instability consideration (Section 6), not a free margin.

5. Independent checks (Prompt 3; Checklist item 6)

All arithmetic was executed in Python (code run for this solution); the figures below are its output, not hand arithmetic.

  1. Back-substitution (balance closure). G×A=900×5.556×10−3=5.00G \times A = 900 \times 5.556\times10^{-3} = 5.00 kg/s =W= W. Closure error 0.00 %. This is the only balance the problem contains — a single stream in, a single stream out — so closure is a check on arithmetic only, not on the model.
  2. Dimensional check. (kg/s) divided by (kg/(m²·s)) gives m². Pass.
  3. Independent route through other units. A=55.6A = 55.6 cm² =8.61= 8.61 in²; a circle of d=3.31d = 3.31 in has area π(3.31)2/4=8.61\pi (3.31)^2/4 = 8.61 in². The metric and imperial routes agree. Pass.
  4. Limiting cases, known by sight. Doubling GG to 1800 kg/(m²·s) halves AA to 27.8 cm²; doubling WW to 10 kg/s doubles AA to 111.1 cm²; as GG tends to zero, AA tends to infinity, as it must for a finite rate at vanishing flux. Pass.
  5. Monotonicity and square-root scaling. AA is proportional to WW and inversely proportional to GG; dd is proportional to the square root of AA, so a 10 % error in AA is a 5 % error in dd. Confirmed numerically in the sensitivity table of Section 4.4. Pass.
  6. Validity range of relations used. A=W/GA = W/G is a definition, not a fitted correlation, so it has no validity range to violate. No fitted relation was available to check — because GG was supplied rather than calculated, the critical-flow relation that would normally produce GG could not be checked against its range at all.

Checks that fail, reported without altering the solution:

  • Critical-flow check — cannot be performed, recorded as a failure of completeness. Critical flow requires the backpressure to be below the critical pressure, which for an ideal vapour is a fraction (2/(k+1))k/(k−1)(2/(k+1))^{k/(k-1)} of the upstream absolute pressure. Neither pressure nor kk is supplied, so the premise on which a single value of GG is normally quoted is untested. If the flow is in fact subcritical, GG falls and AA rises.
  • Two-phase check — cannot be performed. No inlet quality, saturation state, or liquid fraction is supplied (Section 3, item 6).
  • Scenario check on WW — cannot be performed. WW is accepted as given; whether it is the governing scenario, and whether it is a peak or a sustained rate, is untested.
6. Audit as an experienced design and operating engineer would (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this calculation and built equipment:

  1. Phase behaviour in the nozzle. A vapour that is saturated at inlet conditions, or a stream with any entrained liquid, does not behave as a dry vapour on expansion: flashing increases the specific volume sharply through the nozzle and the mass flux falls well below the vapour-only value. Direction: the required area is larger than calculated, and the shortfall is on the unsafe side. Rough size: routinely more than 10 %; for flashing-liquid service the required area can be several times the vapour-only figure. No tighter figure can be stated from the supplied data. Settled by: a rigorously calculated or measured inlet state (pressure, temperature, composition, quality) and a two-phase sizing by the API RP 520 Part I omega method or DIERS methodology (Section 2, unverified).
  2. Installed hydraulics: inlet pressure drop and backpressure. The calculation assumes the full relieving pressure is available at the nozzle and that the discharge is unimpeded. Built equipment has an inlet line, possibly a rupture disc and an isolation valve, and an outlet line or header shared with other valves. Inlet pressure drop reduces the effective relieving pressure and can make the valve chatter (rapid open–close cycling), which damages the seat and can reduce the effective capacity below nameplate; built-up backpressure in a shared header reduces capacity and can lift valves out of sequence. Direction: delivered capacity lower than calculated; stability worse. Rough size: a few percent on capacity for pressure drop alone, but chattering is a pass/fail failure mode, not a percentage. Settled by: an inlet and outlet pressure-drop calculation at rated flow against API RP 520 Part II criteria (unverified), the flare/header hydraulic study, and the manufacturer's stability guidance.
  3. nameplate (effective) area versus actual bore, and oversizing. The required area, 55.6–61.7 cm², falls between two standard sizes, so the installed device (Section 4.5, "P", 71.3 cm², unverified) delivers about 28 % more than required at the stated GG. An oversized vapour valve on a small relieving load is prone to chattering and simmer, and its certified KdK_d is established by test on that trim, not by the textbook value. Direction: installed capacity higher than required (favourable for capacity, unfavourable for stability, seat life, and reaction forces, which scale with the larger flow). Rough size: +28 % flow at the stated GG; reaction force and outlet-line loading rise in proportion. Settled by: the manufacturer's certified datasheet and capacity test record for the exact model, the certified KdK_d, and a check of the minimum relieving case (not only the governing case) against the valve's stable operating range.
7. What this calculation does not cover (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model

  • The calculation of WW itself: fire heat input, reaction runaway, blocked-outlet accumulation, heat-exchanger tube rupture, and every other scenario are outside it. WW is taken as given.
  • Transients: pressure accumulation in the protected vessel while the valve opens, valve opening time, and the peak (rather than steady) rate.
  • Subcritical flow, and any variation of GG with backpressure.
  • Two-phase, flashing, condensing, and reacting flow; non-equilibrium (delayed flashing) effects in short nozzles.
  • Real-gas behaviour, variation of kk and compressibility through the expansion, and Joule–Thomson cooling, with its consequences for low-temperature embrittlement of downstream materials, hydrate formation, and solid (dry-ice) formation for some fluids.
  • Viscous and non-Newtonian behaviour, fouling, polymerisation, scale, and debris partially obstructing the nozzle.
  • Discharge-side effects: reaction (thrust) forces on the valve and piping, acoustic fatigue and noise, flare capacity and radiation, dispersion of a toxic or flammable discharge, and erosion of the trim.
  • Mechanical selection: body and trim materials, flange ratings, temperature limits, seat leakage class, and set-pressure tolerance and blowdown.

Information not available to this calculation

  • Vendor certified data: tested KdK_d, actual bore areas, and certified capacities are manufacturer documents, partly proprietary.
  • Full text of API RP 520/521 and ASME Section VIII is restricted (paywalled); statements here about their content are unverified (Section 2).
  • Licensed thermophysical databanks (DIPPR, NIST REFPROP) and the plant's own relief-system design basis, flare study, and process safety information were not supplied and have not been seen.
  • Plant-specific data that exist only in site records: actual piping isometrics, existing header loadings, previous relief calculations, and inspection history.

Effects that appear only in running equipment

  • Chattering, simmering, and failure to reseat (leakage after a lift).
  • Inlet blockage by corrosion products, polymer, or a left-closed isolation valve; rupture-disc fragments obstructing the nozzle.
  • Set-pressure drift with temperature, spring relaxation, and bellows failure in balanced-bellows valves exposed to backpressure.
  • Simultaneous lifting of several valves into a common header during a plant-wide event, raising backpressure above the single-valve design value.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %

Since A=W/(G×product of correction factors)A = W/(G \times \text{product of correction factors}), AA rises by more than 10 % if any one of the following holds, and the effects multiply if several hold together:

  • the true effective GG is more than 9.1 % below 900 kg/(m²·s) (a 10 % fall in GG raises AA by 11.1 %);
  • KdK_d, or the product KdKbKcKvK_d K_b K_c K_v, is below 0.909 and has not already been included in GG;
  • the governing relieving rate is more than 10 % above 5 kg/s, for example because WW was quoted at normal rather than relieving conditions, or because a fire or runaway case governs instead of the case used;
  • backpressure is high enough to make the flow subcritical, or to require a material KbK_b correction;
  • any liquid is present, or the vapour flashes in the nozzle (change can be far larger than 10 %; Section 6, item 1);
  • WW must be met by one operating valve where the stated WW was a total for several, or the reverse.

Questions a reviewer should ask before this answer is used

  1. What scenario produces W=5W = 5 kg/s, is it the governing scenario, and is WW a peak or a sustained rate at relieving conditions? Where is that calculation?
  2. What are the set pressure, the relieving pressure (stated on an absolute basis), the relieving temperature, and the allowable accumulation, and under which code edition?
  3. What is the fluid, its composition and basis, and its state at the valve inlet — specifically, what evidence establishes that it is vapour-only and non-flashing?
  4. Does the quoted G=900G = 900 kg/(m²·s) already contain KdK_d, KbK_b, KcK_c, and KvK_v? Who calculated GG, from what properties, and at what upstream state?
  5. What are the superimposed and built-up backpressures at rated flow, and is the flow demonstrably critical?
  6. Is a rupture disc or an inlet isolation valve fitted, and what are the inlet and outlet pressure drops at rated flow?
  7. Which standard orifice and which manufacturer's model are proposed, what are its certified area and KdK_d, and what is its capacity at the minimum relieving case as well as at the governing case?
  8. Where does the discharge go, and has the flare or vent system been checked for the installed (not required) capacity of about 6.4 kg/s at the stated GG?
  9. Has the sizing been checked against the current editions of API RP 520 Part I, API RP 521, and the applicable pressure-equipment code by the engineer responsible for the relief system?
