Over the identified ambiguity in whether GG already contains the discharge coefficient KdK_d, the range is A=55.6A = 55.6 to 61.761.7 cm² (d=84.1d = 84.1 to 88.788.7 mm). The next standard API orifice above this range is reported, unverified, as "P" at 71.3 cm². Set pressure, temperature, composition, backpressure, phase evidence, and vendor certified data are all missing; the figures above size an area from two given numbers and do not, on their own, specify a relief device.

E2. Thermal Runaway Time — Second Reaction

Response without the skill

Time to Maximum Rate under Adiabatic Conditions

Symbols and Given Data

All symbols are defined at first use, with SI units where applicable.

  • TMRT_{\mathrm{MR}} (s) is the time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions, measured from the initial temperature defined below.
  • tt (s) is time.
  • TT (K) is the absolute temperature of the reaction mass. The initial temperature, denoted T0T_0, is T0=420 KT_0 = 420\ \mathrm{K}.
  • cpc_p (J/(kg·K)) is the specific heat capacity of the reaction mass. The given value is cp=2.2 kJ/(kg⋅K)=2200 J/(kg⋅K)c_p = 2.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)} = 2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}.
  • qq (W/kg, equivalently J/(s·kg)) is the specific heat release rate of the reaction. The given value at 420 K420\ \mathrm{K} is q0=6 W/kgq_0 = 6\ \mathrm{W/kg}, where the subscript 00 denotes evaluation at T0T_0.
  • EaE_a (J/mol) is the activation energy. The given value is Ea=110 kJ/mol=110,000 J/molE_a = 110\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 110{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}.
  • RR (J/(mol·K)) is the universal gas constant, R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}.
  • dT/dtdT/dt (K/s) is the self-heating rate, that is, the rate of temperature rise under adiabatic conditions.

Given data in SI units:

Quantity Value
T0T_0 420 K420\ \mathrm{K}
cpc_p 2200 J/(kg⋅K)2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}
q0q_0 6 J/(s⋅kg)6\ \mathrm{J/(s\cdot kg)}
EaE_a 110,000 J/mol110{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}
RR 8.314 J/(mol⋅K)8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}
Model and Assumptions

The estimate uses the standard adiabatic induction-time approximation:

  1. Adiabatic conditions: no heat is lost to the surroundings, so all heat released raises the temperature of the reaction mass.
  2. The specific heat capacity cpc_p is constant over the temperature interval of interest.
  3. Reactant consumption is neglected up to the maximum rate (zero-order approximation). The heat release rate therefore depends on temperature only, through the Arrhenius temperature dependence defined below.
  4. The reaction mass is at a uniform temperature.
  5. One exothermic reaction with a single activation energy EaE_a controls the heat release.
Derivation

Under adiabatic conditions, the energy balance per unit mass is

cpdTdt=q,c_p \frac{dT}{dt} = q,

so that the initial self-heating rate, denoted (dT/dt)0(dT/dt)_0 (K/s), is

(dTdt)0=q0cp.\left(\frac{dT}{dt}\right)_0 = \frac{q_0}{c_p}.

The Arrhenius temperature dependence of the heat release rate is

q=q0exp⁡[−EaR(1T−1T0)],q = q_0 \exp\left[-\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_0}\right)\right],

where 1/T1/T (1/K) is the reciprocal absolute temperature.

For a temperature rise that is small compared with T0T_0, the reciprocal temperature can be expanded about T0T_0:

1T−1T0≈−T−T0T02.\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_0} \approx -\frac{T - T_0}{T_0^{2}}.

The heat release rate then increases approximately exponentially with temperature rise:

q≈q0exp⁡[EaRT02 (T−T0)].q \approx q_0 \exp\left[\frac{E_a}{R T_0^{2}}\,(T - T_0)\right].

The temperature interval over which the rate increases by a factor of ee, denoted ΔTe\Delta T_e (K), follows from setting the exponent equal to 1:

ΔTe=RT02Ea.\Delta T_e = \frac{R T_0^{2}}{E_a}.

Combining the energy balance with the exponential rate increase gives exponential growth of the self-heating rate, with a characteristic time equal to the time needed, at the initial rate, to rise by ΔTe\Delta T_e. Integration of the energy balance from T0T_0 towards the runaway, with the integral dominated by the initial temperature region, gives the adiabatic induction-time formula

TMR≈ΔTe(dT/dt)0=RT02/Eaq0/cp=cpRT02Eaq0.T_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{\Delta T_e}{(dT/dt)_0} = \frac{R T_0^{2}/E_a}{q_0/c_p} = \frac{c_p R T_0^{2}}{E_a q_0}.

Dimensional check: cpRT02c_p R T_0^{2} has units (J/(kg⋅K))(J/(mol⋅K))(K2)(\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)})(\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)})(\mathrm{K^2}), and Eaq0E_a q_0 has units (J/mol)(J/(s⋅kg))(\mathrm{J/mol})(\mathrm{J/(s\cdot kg)}). The ratio therefore has units of seconds, as required for TMRT_{\mathrm{MR}}.

The approximation is self-consistent in this case because Ea/(RT0)=110,000/(8.314×420)≈31.5E_a/(R T_0) = 110{,}000/(8.314 \times 420) \approx 31.5, which is much larger than 1. The exponential expansion is therefore applicable, and ΔTe\Delta T_e is small compared with T0T_0.

Numerical Evaluation

Initial self-heating rate:

(dTdt)0=q0cp=6 J/(s⋅kg)2200 J/(kg⋅K)=2.73×10−3 K/s=9.82 K/h.\left(\frac{dT}{dt}\right)_0 = \frac{q_0}{c_p} = \frac{6\ \mathrm{J/(s\cdot kg)}}{2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}} = 2.73 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K/s} = 9.82\ \mathrm{K/h}.

Temperature interval for an ee-fold rate increase:

ΔTe=RT02Ea=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)×(420 K)2110,000 J/mol=8.314×176,400110,000 K≈13.3 K.\Delta T_e = \frac{R T_0^{2}}{E_a} = \frac{8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} \times (420\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{110{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}} = \frac{8.314 \times 176{,}400}{110{,}000}\ \mathrm{K} \approx 13.3\ \mathrm{K}.

Time to maximum rate:

TMR≈cpRT02Eaq0=2200×8.314×(420)2110,000×6 sT_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{c_p R T_0^{2}}{E_a q_0} = \frac{2200 \times 8.314 \times (420)^{2}}{110{,}000 \times 6}\ \mathrm{s}

TMR≈3.23×1096.60×105 s≈4.89×103 s.T_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{3.23 \times 10^{9}}{6.60 \times 10^{5}}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 4.89 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}.

Equivalently, from the two intermediate quantities:

TMR≈ΔTe(dT/dt)0=13.3 K2.73×10−3 K/s≈4.89×103 s,T_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{\Delta T_e}{(dT/dt)_0} = \frac{13.3\ \mathrm{K}}{2.73 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K/s}} \approx 4.89 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s},

which confirms the direct substitution.

Conversion to hours and minutes:

TMR≈4889 s3600 s/h≈1.36 h≈81 min.T_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx \frac{4889\ \mathrm{s}}{3600\ \mathrm{s/h}} \approx 1.36\ \mathrm{h} \approx 81\ \mathrm{min}.

Result

TMR≈4.9×103 s≈1.4 hT_{\mathrm{MR}} \approx 4.9 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 1.4\ \mathrm{h}

at an initial temperature of 420 K420\ \mathrm{K} under adiabatic conditions.

The value is an induction-time estimate: reactant consumption, heat losses, and any change in cpc_p with temperature are neglected. Consumption and heat losses, if present, lengthen the time to the maximum rate. On the stated adiabatic basis, the available time for corrective action after the reaction mass reaches 420 K420\ \mathrm{K} is of the order of one hour; it is well below a 24 h screening criterion commonly used for adiabatic runaway.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Time to Maximum Rate under Adiabatic Conditions

Nomenclature

All symbols are defined here, before first use in the text.

  • Time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions, in hours (h) or seconds (s): the time from a stated starting temperature to the temperature at which the self-heating rate is greatest, with no heat loss to the surroundings.
  • Temperature, in kelvin (K): the temperature of the reaction mass.
  • Starting temperature, in kelvin (K): the temperature at the start of the adiabatic period.
  • Specific heat capacity of the reaction mass, in joules per kilogram per kelvin (J/(kg·K)) or kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg·K)): the heat required to raise one kilogram of reaction mass by one kelvin.
  • Specific heat release rate, in watts per kilogram (W/kg): the heat released by reaction per kilogram of reaction mass per second; one watt (W) is one joule per second (J/s).
  • Specific heat release rate at a stated temperature, in watts per kilogram (W/kg): the value of the specific heat release rate evaluated at that temperature.
  • Activation energy, in joules per mole (J/mol) or kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol): the Arrhenius temperature-sensitivity parameter for the reaction rate.
  • Universal gas constant, equal to 8.314 J/(mol·K): the constant in the Arrhenius temperature relation.
  • Time, in seconds (s) or hours (h).
  • Self-heating rate, in kelvin per second (K/s) or kelvin per hour (K/h): the rate of temperature rise of the reaction mass.
  • Thermal inertia factor, dimensionless: the ratio of the total heat capacity of the sample plus its container to the heat capacity of the sample alone; a value of 1 corresponds to a plant vessel that absorbs a negligible share of the heat, and a larger value corresponds to a laboratory bomb that absorbs part of the heat.
  • Adiabatic temperature rise, in kelvin (K): the total temperature rise if all reaction heat is retained and the reaction runs to completion.
  • Characteristic temperature rise, in kelvin (K): the temperature interval over which the Arrhenius rate rises by a factor of about 2.7, computed from the starting temperature, the activation energy, and the universal gas constant.
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The estimate rests on a single heat release rate at one temperature and a single activation energy. No reaction order, no reactant consumption, no total heat of reaction, and no information on autocatalysis, gas generation, phase change, or the temperature range over which the activation energy was fitted are supplied. The standard closed-form relation used below is a zero-order, no-consumption approximation. It is reliable for order of magnitude and for screening; it is not a design value for relief sizing or for a safe operating limit on plant equipment.

Confidence rating: low for use as a plant value; moderate for order of magnitude. The arithmetic is exact for the stated inputs (confidence high). Confidence that the true adiabatic time for a real material lies within about a factor of two of the central value is moderate. Confidence that it lies within 10 % of the central value is low. Every range reported below reflects that rating.

2. Inputs, labelled by state
Quantity Value State
Starting temperature 420 K Given
Specific heat capacity 2.2 kJ/(kg·K) = 2200 J/(kg·K) Given; treated as constant (assumed — see Section 5)
Specific heat release rate at 420 K 6 W/kg Given; measurement method, sample, and uncertainty not supplied (unverified)
Activation energy 110 kJ/mol = 110 000 J/mol Given; fitted range and fitting method not supplied (unverified)
Universal gas constant 8.314 J/(mol·K) Standard constant
Thermal inertia factor 1 Assumed (ideal adiabatic, plant-scale vessel)
Reaction order / consumption Zero order, no consumption Assumed (built into the closed-form relation)
Heat loss None Assumed (part of "adiabatic")

No input is labelled measured or fitted on evidence in the problem statement: the two kinetic quantities are given, and whether they were measured, fitted to calorimetry, or estimated is not stated. That gap is itself a source of the low confidence rating.

3. Missing quantities (Prompt 2)

The following quantities are needed for a complete treatment and are not supplied. None is taken in silence; each is either assumed as stated or carried as an alternative in Section 4.

  1. Reaction order and reactant consumption. Missing. The closed-form relation assumes zero order with no depletion. First-order consumption lengthens the time to maximum rate because the rate falls as reactant is consumed.
  2. Total heat of reaction / adiabatic temperature rise. Missing. It sets the final temperature and whether a maximum rate is reached before depletion. Without it, the integration can only be run to unlimited temperature.
  3. Basis of the heat release rate. Missing: whether 6 W/kg is per kilogram of total reaction mass, of one reactant, or of sample as charged in a calorimeter. The calculation takes it as per kilogram of total reaction mass, matching the stated units.
  4. Reference state. The heat release rate is referenced to 420 K, as stated. No other reference state is needed for this rate-based estimate.
  5. Pressure and pressure basis. Missing and not used. The estimate gives a time only; it gives no pressure rise, no gas rate, and no relief load. Pressure basis (absolute or gauge) does not enter the thermal calculation.
  6. Composition basis. Missing: composition, conversion at 420 K, and whether the stated rate is at initial composition. The calculation takes the rate as the rate of the mass as it stands at 420 K.
  7. Per-pass or overall conversion. Not applicable to a batch adiabatic induction estimate; no conversion figure is used.
  8. Thermal inertia factor of the source measurement. Missing. If the heat release rate came from a laboratory bomb with a thermal inertia factor above 1 and was not corrected, the plant value differs (Section 7).
  9. Temperature dependence of the specific heat capacity and secondary reactions. Missing; constant specific heat capacity is assumed.
4. Calculation
4.1 Relation used, its source, and its range

The relation is the standard adiabatic induction-time approximation of thermal process safety (Semenov / Frank–Kamenetskii exponential approximation; the form tabulated in Stoessel, Thermal Safety of Chemical Processes, and in the Center for Chemical Process Safety guidelines on chemical reactivity hazards — unverified against those sources in this calculation, to be checked against the current editions before design use):

Time to maximum rate = (specific heat capacity × universal gas constant × starting temperature squared) / (specific heat release rate at the starting temperature × activation energy).

Where it holds: single exothermic reaction; Arrhenius temperature dependence with a constant activation energy; activation energy large compared with universal gas constant × temperature (here the ratio is 110 000 / (8.314 × 420) = 31.5, so the condition is met); negligible reactant consumption up to the point of maximum rate; constant specific heat capacity; no heat loss; no phase change or gas effect on the thermal balance. The characteristic temperature rise is universal gas constant × starting temperature squared / activation energy = 8.314 × 420² / 110 000 = 13.3 K, small compared with 420 K, which is the condition that makes the exponential approximation usable.

4.2 Central value

Time to maximum rate = (2200 J/(kg·K) × 8.314 J/(mol·K) × (420 K)²) / (6 W/kg × 110 000 J/mol) = 3.227 × 10⁹ / 6.60 × 10⁵ s = 4 889 s = 1.36 h, reported as about 1.4 h.

Initial self-heating rate at 420 K, for scale: specific heat release rate / specific heat capacity = 6 / 2200 = 0.00273 K/s = 0.164 K/min = 9.8 K/h.

4.3 Range, not a single value (Prompt 1)

Sensitivity of the central value to each input, one at a time:

Change (state: assumed plausible variation) Effect on the result
Specific heat capacity 2.0 instead of 2.2 kJ/(kg·K) −9 % (1.23 h)
Specific heat capacity 2.4 instead of 2.2 kJ/(kg·K) +9 % (1.48 h)
Activation energy 100 instead of 110 kJ/mol +10 % (1.49 h)
Activation energy 120 instead of 110 kJ/mol −8 % (1.24 h)
Heat release rate 5 instead of 6 W/kg +20 % (1.63 h)
Heat release rate 7 instead of 6 W/kg −14 % (1.16 h)
Heat release rate ±30 % (a plausible calorimetric uncertainty, assumed) −23 % to +43 %
Starting temperature 415 K instead of 420 K, with the heat release rate re-evaluated by the Arrhenius relation (computed value 4.11 W/kg) +43 % (1.94 h)
Starting temperature 425 K instead of 420 K, heat release rate re-evaluated the same way (computed value 8.69 W/kg) −29 % (0.96 h)
Thermal inertia factor 1.5 instead of 1 (laboratory bomb, assumed alternative) +50 % (about 2.0 h), because the time scales in proportion to the thermal inertia factor in this approximation

Combined plausible range, taking the specific heat capacity within ±10 %, the activation energy within ±10 kJ/mol, and the heat release rate within ±30 % simultaneously at their least favourable ends (all variations assumed, since no uncertainties were supplied):

Time to maximum rate: 0.86 h to 2.35 h, central value about 1.4 h.

A wider range follows if the heat release rate is uncertain by a factor of two, which is not unusual for a rate extrapolated from differential scanning calorimetry to a temperature outside the fitted range: about 0.6 h to 3.3 h when combined with the specific-heat-capacity and activation-energy ranges above. The temperature sensitivity is the dominant practical risk: a 5 K error in the starting temperature moves the result by roughly 30–40 %, more than any plausible error in the specific heat capacity.

5. Independent check (Prompt 3)

Checks were worked in code (Python, numerical quadrature of the rate equation) and are reported as run; none was used to adjust the answer.

  1. Independent route — direct numerical integration. Integrating the adiabatic energy balance, self-heating rate = specific heat release rate at temperature / specific heat capacity, with the heat release rate following the full Arrhenius factor referenced to 6 W/kg at 420 K, from 420 K to 2 000 K (the integrand is negligible beyond about 800 K), gives 5 233 s = 1.45 h. This is 7 % above the closed-form value of 1.36 h. Check passes within the expected error of the exponential approximation, and it fixes the sign of that error: the closed form slightly understates the time, i.e. it errs on the safe (short) side for this step.
  2. Dimensional check. (J/(kg·K) × J/(mol·K) × K²) / (W/kg × J/mol) reduces to seconds. Passes.
  3. Limiting cases. Heat release rate tending to zero gives time tending to infinity (no self-heating); activation energy tending to a larger value at fixed rate at 420 K shortens the time in the closed form through faster acceleration once heating starts, and both behaviours match the formula as written and physical expectation for a rate fixed at the starting temperature. Passes.
  4. Balance closure. The calculation is a rate integration, not a steady balance; the applicable closure is the energy balance itself, which is satisfied identically by the numerical integration in check 1 (heat released = sensible heat gained at every step, by construction of the integrand). No material balance can be closed because no stoichiometry, order, or total heat of reaction was supplied — this check cannot be run and is reported as a gap, not a pass.
  5. Valid-range check. Activation energy / (universal gas constant × temperature) = 31.5, well above 1; characteristic temperature rise 13.3 K, well below 420 K. The approximation is inside its stated range for these inputs. Passes, for the assumed single-step Arrhenius model only.
6. Audit against built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from built-equipment behaviour:

  1. Heat loss and thermal inertia in real vessels. A plant vessel is not perfectly adiabatic and its wall absorbs heat early. Direction: the real time is longer than 1.4 h near the starting temperature, but a vessel that has already self-heated retains the runaway. Rough size: tens of percent for a large, well-insulated vessel; a factor of two or more for a small or uninsulated one. Settled by: the vessel heat-loss characteristic (overall heat-transfer coefficient × area / mass) and a phi-corrected adiabatic calorimetry test (accelerating rate calorimetry or Phi-TEC) on the actual material.
  2. Temperature non-uniformity, hot spots, and scale. A hot spot, a stagnant zone, or a heating-medium fault puts part of the mass above 420 K. Direction: shorter time, strongly — 5 K higher locally cuts the time by about 30 % (Section 4.3), and 20 K higher would cut it by roughly a factor of four (computed value 0.36 h at 440 K by the same relation). Settled by: plant temperature records, mixing and heat-transfer assessment for the actual vessel and agitation state.
  3. Chemistry not in the single-step model. Autocatalysis, catalysis by impurities, corrosion products or aged material, and a second decomposition step all change the effective rate law. Direction: usually shorter, occasionally longer after an inhibitor is consumed; size can be a factor of several and is not bounded by the ranges in Section 4.3. Settled by: adiabatic and isothermal ageing calorimetry on the actual plant material (including recycled and contaminated samples), not on a fresh laboratory sample.

Primary source that settles the point (Checklist item 5): adiabatic calorimetry on the actual reaction mass in its actual composition and state of ageing (accelerating rate calorimeter, Phi-TEC, or vent-sizing package data), with the activation energy fitted over a stated temperature range, checked against Stoessel, Thermal Safety of Chemical Processes, and the current Center for Chemical Process Safety reactivity guidelines. All kinetic claims in this calculation rest on the two given numbers and are unverified against any such source.

7. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Pressure: no pressure rise, gas generation rate, vapour pressure, or relief load is computed. A time to maximum rate alone cannot size a vent; that requires the maximum pressure rate and a DIERS-type (Design Institute for Emergency Relief Systems) two-phase assessment.
  • Reactant consumption and the final temperature: without the adiabatic temperature rise, the temperature and pressure at the maximum rate are unknown.
  • Phase change, boiling, and two-phase discharge, which can remove heat (lengthening the time) or produce a violent pressure rise.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling, agitation failure, mischarging, wrong addition order, contamination, and loss of cooling before the adiabatic period begins.
  • Private or restricted data: the material's measured calorimetry, its fitted kinetics, and any vendor thermal-stability data are not available here; the two given kinetic numbers cannot be audited.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %: a starting-temperature change of about 2 K or more (with the rate following the Arrhenius relation); a heat release rate change of about 10 % or more; an activation-energy change of about 11 kJ/mol or more; a thermal inertia factor change of 0.1 or more; onset of autocatalysis or a second reaction at any level that raises the rate at 420 K by 10 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. From what instrument, sample, and temperature range do the heat release rate at 420 K and the activation energy come, and was the thermal inertia correction applied?
  2. Is 420 K the normal process temperature, the maximum attainable temperature on a fault, or already an excursion — and what margin does a time of about 1.4 h leave for detection and response?
  3. What are the adiabatic temperature rise, the maximum pressure rate, and the gas generation, and has relief been assessed separately?
  4. Has the material been tested aged, recycled, and contaminated, or only fresh?
  5. Is the value to be used for screening only, or is any safeguard, alarm response time, or operating limit being set from it? (On the confidence rating in Section 1, only screening use is supported.)
8. Result

Time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions at 420 K: about 1.4 h, with a plausible range of 0.86 h to 2.35 h for the stated plausible variations in the given inputs, and a wider range of about 0.6 h to 3.3 h if the heat release rate carries a factor-of-two extrapolation uncertainty. An independent numerical integration gives 1.45 h, 7 % above the closed-form central value. The value is a screening estimate under the assumed zero-order, no-consumption, perfectly adiabatic model; it is not verified against calorimetry on the actual material.

E3. Gas Dispersion — Second Release

Response without the skill

Ground-Level Centreline Concentration from a Continuous Release

Problem

Estimate the ground-level concentration on the centreline of the plume at a downwind distance of 400 m from a continuous gas release.

Data and definitions

Each symbol is defined at its first use, with its value where one is given.

  • QQ is the continuous mass release rate, in kilograms per second (kg/s): Q=0.8 kg/sQ = 0.8\ \mathrm{kg/s}.
  • uu is the mean wind speed, in metres per second (m/s): u=4 m/su = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  • xx is the downwind distance from the source, in metres (m): x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m}.
  • yy is the crosswind distance from the plume centreline, in metres (m). On the centreline, y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m}.
  • zz is the height above ground, in metres (m). At ground level, z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}.
  • HH is the effective release height above ground, in metres (m). No release height, stack height, or plume rise is stated in the problem. The only case that can be evaluated from the data given is a ground-level release, so H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m} is assumed. The dependence of the result on HH is stated in the Limitations section.
  • C(x,y,z)C(x, y, z) is the mean gas concentration at downwind distance xx, crosswind distance yy, and height zz, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}).
  • σy\sigma_y is the standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the crosswind direction, in metres (m), at downwind distance xx.
  • σz\sigma_z is the standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the vertical direction, in metres (m), at downwind distance xx.

Stability condition given: overcast, day or night. In the Pasquill classification of atmospheric stability, classes A to F run from very unstable (A) to very stable (F), and overcast conditions, day or night, correspond to class D (neutral stability). This also matches the stated wind speed: a wind speed of 4 m/s4\ \mathrm{m/s} under a complete cloud cover falls in class D. Class D is therefore used.

Model

The standard steady-state Gaussian plume model is used. It applies to a continuous point release, a constant mean wind, a flat and uniform surface, and a gas that is neither created nor removed during travel (no chemical reaction, no deposition, and no washout). Total reflection of the plume at the ground is assumed, which is represented by an image source below ground.

For a release at effective height HH, the model gives

C(x,y,z)=Q2πu σyσzexp⁡ ⁣(−y22σy2)[exp⁡ ⁣(−(z−H)22σz2)+exp⁡ ⁣(−(z+H)22σz2)],C(x, y, z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u \, \sigma_y \sigma_z} \exp\!\left(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right) \left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) + \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z+H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) \right],

where π\pi is the mathematical constant pi, approximately 3.14163.1416, and exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot) is the exponential function.

Reduction to ground level on the centreline

Set y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m}, z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}, and H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}:

  • The crosswind factor is exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0) = 1.
  • The two vertical terms are each exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0) = 1, so the bracket is 22.

The equation therefore reduces to

C(x,0,0)=Qπu σyσz.C(x, 0, 0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u \, \sigma_y \sigma_z}.

Dimensional check: QQ divided by (uu multiplied by σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z) has units $(\mathrm{kg/s}) / [(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})] = \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, as required for a concentration.

Dispersion coefficients at 400 m, class D

The values of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z are obtained from the Briggs formulas for open country, which are fits to the Pasquill–Gifford curves and are valid over downwind distances from about 100 m100\ \mathrm{m} to about 10 000 m10\,000\ \mathrm{m}. Open country is the default terrain in the absence of a stated urban setting; the effect of the urban formulas is given in the Limitations section.

For class D, open country, with xx in metres and the resulting standard deviations in metres:

σy=0.08 x(1+0.0001 x)1/2,σz=0.06 x(1+0.0015 x)1/2,\sigma_y = \frac{0.08\,x}{(1 + 0.0001\,x)^{1/2}}, \qquad \sigma_z = \frac{0.06\,x}{(1 + 0.0015\,x)^{1/2}},

where the numerical coefficients 0.080.08, 0.060.06, 0.00010.0001, and 0.00150.0015 are the empirical class D coefficients of these correlations, with 0.00010.0001 and 0.00150.0015 carrying units of reciprocal metres (m−1\mathrm{m^{-1}}) so that the terms in parentheses are dimensionless.

At x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m}:

σy=0.08×400(1+0.0001×400)1/2=32(1.04)1/2=321.020≈31.4 m,\sigma_y = \frac{0.08 \times 400}{(1 + 0.0001 \times 400)^{1/2}} = \frac{32}{(1.04)^{1/2}} = \frac{32}{1.020} \approx 31.4\ \mathrm{m},

σz=0.06×400(1+0.0015×400)1/2=24(1.60)1/2=241.265≈19.0 m.\sigma_z = \frac{0.06 \times 400}{(1 + 0.0015 \times 400)^{1/2}} = \frac{24}{(1.60)^{1/2}} = \frac{24}{1.265} \approx 19.0\ \mathrm{m}.

These values agree with a direct reading of the Pasquill–Gifford curves for class D at 400 m400\ \mathrm{m}, which give a crosswind standard deviation of roughly 30 m30\ \mathrm{m} and a vertical standard deviation of roughly 19 m19\ \mathrm{m}.

Calculation

C(400,0,0)=Qπu σyσz=0.8π×4×31.4×19.0 kg/m3.C(400, 0, 0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u \, \sigma_y \sigma_z} = \frac{0.8}{\pi \times 4 \times 31.4 \times 19.0} \ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

The denominator is

π×4×31.4×19.0≈7.48×103 m3/s,\pi \times 4 \times 31.4 \times 19.0 \approx 7.48 \times 10^{3} \ \mathrm{m^3/s},

so

C(400,0,0)≈0.87.48×103≈1.07×10−4 kg/m3.C(400, 0, 0) \approx \frac{0.8}{7.48 \times 10^{3}} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

In more convenient units:

  • 1.07×10−4 kg/m3=0.107 g/m31.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 0.107\ \mathrm{g/m^3}, where g\mathrm{g} denotes grams.
  • 0.107 g/m3≈107 mg/m30.107\ \mathrm{g/m^3} \approx 107\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}, where mg\mathrm{mg} denotes milligrams.
Checks
  1. Magnitude. The plume cross-section scale at the receptor is set by σyσz≈31.4×19.0≈596 m2\sigma_y \sigma_z \approx 31.4 \times 19.0 \approx 596\ \mathrm{m^2}. Spreading 0.8 kg/s0.8\ \mathrm{kg/s} carried at 4 m/s4\ \mathrm{m/s} over an area of this scale gives a concentration of order 10−4 kg/m310^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, consistent with the calculated value.
  2. Trend. σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z both increase with xx, so the centreline ground-level concentration decreases with downwind distance, as required for a dispersing plume with no source added along the path.
  3. Correlation range. x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} lies inside the stated range of the Briggs formulas, so no extrapolation is involved.
Result

The estimated mean ground-level concentration on the plume centreline, 400 m400\ \mathrm{m} downwind of a continuous ground-level release of 0.8 kg/s0.8\ \mathrm{kg/s} in a 4 m/s4\ \mathrm{m/s} wind under neutral (class D, overcast) conditions, is

C≈1.1×10−4 kg/m3≈0.11 g/m3≈110 mg/m3.C \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \approx 0.11\ \mathrm{g/m^3} \approx 110\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

Two significant figures are appropriate, given the accuracy of the dispersion correlations.

Limitations
  • Release height. The result rests on H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}, because no release height is given. For an elevated release the centreline ground-level value is multiplied by exp⁡[−H2/(2σz2)]\exp[-H^2 / (2\sigma_z^2)], with σz≈19.0 m\sigma_z \approx 19.0\ \mathrm{m} here, so even a modest effective height reduces the ground-level value substantially: for example, H=19.0 mH = 19.0\ \mathrm{m} gives a factor of exp⁡(−0.5)≈0.61\exp(-0.5) \approx 0.61, and H=38 mH = 38\ \mathrm{m} gives a factor of exp⁡(−2)≈0.14\exp(-2) \approx 0.14. An elevated source cannot be evaluated without a stated HH, including any plume rise.
  • Terrain. The Briggs urban formulas for class D give larger values, σy≈59 m\sigma_y \approx 59\ \mathrm{m} and σz≈53 m\sigma_z \approx 53\ \mathrm{m} at 400 m400\ \mathrm{m}, and hence a lower concentration of about 20 mg/m320\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}. The open-country value above is the appropriate estimate for the problem as stated, which specifies no urban surface.
  • Averaging time and meander. The Pasquill–Gifford and Briggs coefficients correspond to a mean over roughly 10 minutes. Over longer averaging times, lateral meander of the wind direction widens the mean plume and lowers the mean centreline concentration; short-term peak concentrations at a fixed point are higher than the mean value given.
  • Idealisation. Steady wind, flat terrain, no buildings in the near field, no deposition, no reaction, and a gas of near-neutral buoyancy are assumed. A dense gas, a building wake, or complex terrain would require a different model.
  • Accuracy. Gaussian plume estimates of this type are normally regarded as accurate only to within about a factor of two, even when the stability class is correctly assigned.
Response with the skill (generic layer)

Ground-Level Plume Centreline Concentration at 400 m — Stability Class D

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: the problem is underspecified for the model it requires, and the model itself uses fitted dispersion coefficients with a wide scatter. The effective release height — the quantity to which the ground-level result is most sensitive — is not given, and neither are the terrain (open country or urban), the averaging time, nor the height at which the wind speed applies. Different published fitted relations for the same stability class differ by a factor of about 2 to 5 in the predicted concentration at this distance.

Confidence rating: low for a single numerical value; moderate for an order of magnitude and for a range stated conditional on an assumed release height and terrain. A single value presented without those conditions would not be defensible.

All symbols are defined at first use below, with SI units where applicable.

  • CC — concentration, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}), reported also in milligrams per cubic metre (mg m−3\mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}}); 1 kg m−3=106 mg m−31\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}}.
  • xx — downwind distance from the source, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • yy — crosswind distance from the plume centreline, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • zz — height above ground, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • QQ — continuous release rate, in kilograms per second (kg s−1\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}).
  • uu — mean wind speed at release height, in metres per second (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}).
  • HH — effective release height (physical release height plus plume rise), in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • σy\sigma_y — standard deviation of the crosswind concentration distribution, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • σz\sigma_z — standard deviation of the vertical concentration distribution, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • π\pi — the mathematical constant pi, dimensionless, approximately 3.1416.
  • exp⁡\exp — the exponential function, dimensionless argument.

4. Model and fitted relations — Prompt 1

Model: the steady-state Gaussian plume model with total reflection at the ground, for a continuous point release:

C(x,y,z)=Q2πuσyσz{exp⁡ ⁣[−(z−H)22σz2]+exp⁡ ⁣[−(z+H)22σz2]}exp⁡ ⁣[−y22σy2]C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z} \left\{ \exp\!\left[-\frac{(z-H)^{2}}{2\sigma_z^{2}}\right] + \exp\!\left[-\frac{(z+H)^{2}}{2\sigma_z^{2}}\right] \right\} \exp\!\left[-\frac{y^{2}}{2\sigma_y^{2}}\right]

At the ground-level centreline, y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m} and z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}, the two vertical terms are equal and the expression reduces to:

C(x,0,0)=Qπuσyσz exp⁡ ⁣[−H22σz2]C(x,0,0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z}\, \exp\!\left[-\frac{H^{2}}{2\sigma_z^{2}}\right]

Property values, rules of thumb and fitted relations used, with source and valid range:

  1. Gaussian plume equation — standard textbook form (for example Beychok, Fundamentals of Stack Gas Dispersion; Seinfeld and Pandis, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics). Unverified against the primary text in this work. It holds for steady wind, homogeneous turbulence, a non-reacting, non-depositing plume, flat terrain, and distances where the plume has not yet filled the mixing layer — nominally from about 100 m100\ \mathrm{m} to about 10 km10\ \mathrm{km} downwind. x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} is inside that nominal range.
  2. Briggs (1973) fitted relations for σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z as a function of xx and stability class, as tabulated in Turner, Workbook of Atmospheric Dispersion Estimates, and in Gifford's summaries. Unverified against the primary source in this work. For class D: - Open country: σy=0.08 x (1+0.0001 x)−1/2\sigma_y = 0.08\,x\,(1+0.0001\,x)^{-1/2} and σz=0.06 x (1+0.0015 x)−1/2\sigma_z = 0.06\,x\,(1+0.0015\,x)^{-1/2}, with xx, σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z all in metres (m\mathrm{m}). Fitted coefficients 0.08 and 0.06 are dimensionless; 0.0001 and 0.0015 are in inverse metres (m−1\mathrm{m^{-1}}). - Urban: σy=0.16 x (1+0.0004 x)−1/2\sigma_y = 0.16\,x\,(1+0.0004\,x)^{-1/2} and σz=0.14 x (1+0.0003 x)−1/2\sigma_z = 0.14\,x\,(1+0.0003\,x)^{-1/2}, in the same units. These are fits to Pasquill–Gifford field data with scatter of roughly a factor of 2 in σz\sigma_z; they are not physical laws.
  3. No other property value, rule of thumb or fitted relation is used. In particular no density, viscosity or diffusivity is required by the model as posed — which is itself a limitation (Section 8).

The primary source that settles the fitted-relation point for regulatory use is the current edition of the applicable regulatory model guidance — for example the United States Environmental Protection Agency AERMOD guidance (40 CFR Part 51, Appendix W) in the United States, or the corresponding national guidance elsewhere — together with site meteorological data. Unverified in this work; the Briggs values above should be checked against that source before design or permit use.

6. What the answer means

107 mg m−3107\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} is a mean concentration over the assumed averaging time (about 10 min, assumed), not an instantaneous peak. Short-term peaks inside a meandering plume are commonly a factor of 2 to 5 above the mean at a fixed point (estimated from general dispersion practice; unverified against a primary source in this work). No comparison with an exposure limit or an odour threshold is made, because the gas is not identified.

Integrating u C(x,y,z)u\,C(x,y,z) over the crosswind–vertical plane at fixed xx for the base case returned 0.800 kg s−10.800\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}} against the given Q=0.8 kg s−1Q = 0.8\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}} — closure to within numerical error (<10−12<10^{-12} relative in the separable analytic–numeric comparison of the Gaussian integrals). 8. Audit as for built equipment — Prompt 4

The three points most likely to differ from how a built, operating source behaves:

  1. Building wake and downwash, and plume rise. A real release near a building, or from a stack with finite exit velocity and temperature, has an HH set by downwash and rise, not by the stack top alone. Direction: downwash lowers HH and raises ground CC, by up to the full HH sensitivity in Section 5.3 (tens of percent to a factor of several tens at 50 m50\ \mathrm{m} nominal height). Rise raises HH and lowers CC in the opposite sense. Settling document: the stack and building drawings, exit-condition design data, and a downwash assessment in the applicable regulatory model (for example AERMOD with its building-wake preprocessor). Unverified.
  2. Real wind field versus a single uu and a single class. Operating conditions vary over an hour; class D with u=4 m s−1u = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} is one hour of many. Low-wind, stable hours (classes E and F) at the same QQ give materially higher ground concentrations from a ground release, and wind direction variation moves the centreline off the receptor entirely. Direction: the stated case is not the worst case; a worst-hour value can be several times higher (estimated). Settling record: at least one year of hourly on-site meteorological data, processed through the regulatory model. Unverified.
  3. Losses and buoyancy absent from the model. A dense gas slumps and does not follow a Gaussian plume near the source; a soluble or reactive gas, or a particulate, deposits. Direction: deposition and reaction lower CC (the present result is conservative in that respect); dense-gas slumping raises ground CC near the source and invalidates the model form itself. Settling document: the gas identity and safety data sheet, release temperature and density, and, if the gas is dense, a dense-gas model assessment rather than a Gaussian one. Unverified — gas identity was not given.
9. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model:

  • Plume rise, downwash, dense-gas behaviour, buoyancy.
  • Deposition (dry and wet), chemical reaction, radioactive or biological decay, aerosol coagulation.
  • Terrain elevation, valley channelling, land–sea effects, building effects.
  • Inversion capping and fumigation (break-up of a nocturnal inversion bringing an elevated plume to ground at high concentration for a short period — a condition under which the answer can change by more than 10%10\%, by a large factor).
  • Time variation: gusts, meander, non-steady release rate, start-up and shut-down transients.
  • Short-averaging-time peak concentrations (Section 6).

Information not visible here:

  • Site meteorological measurements, source drawings, permit conditions and any dispersion study already performed for the site — held by the operator, not supplied.
  • The primary fitted-relation and regulatory-model documents named in Sections 4 and 8 — not checked in this work; claims resting on them are marked unverified above.
  • Any restricted databank values (for example licensed meteorological or terrain data sets) used by regulatory models.

Effects appearing only in running equipment:

  • Fouling, damper or fan degradation changing exit velocity and hence rise; simultaneous releases from neighbouring sources adding to CC; fugitive (non-point) releases not in QQ.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%10\%:

  • Any change in HH of more than about 8 m8\ \mathrm{m} at the base-case σz\sigma_z (open country); any terrain reclassification; a wind speed error of more than about 0.4 m s−10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}; a stability class change; an averaging-time change; onset of fumigation, downwash or dense-gas behaviour; a receptor moved 100 m100\ \mathrm{m} in xx.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What is the effective release height, from what exit conditions, and who measured or calculated it?
  2. Is the terrain open country or urban for this source, and what is the surface roughness?
  3. At what height and exposure was u=4 m s−1u = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} measured, and over what averaging time?
  4. What is the gas, and is it neutrally buoyant, depositing or reactive?
  5. Is the required result a 10-min mean, an hourly mean, or a short-term peak — and against which limit or threshold will it be compared?
  6. Has the applicable regulatory model and current guidance edition been run with on-site meteorological data, and how does this screening estimate compare with it?
  7. Are there buildings, terrain or neighbouring sources that the flat-terrain, single-source model omits?
10. Final answer

Conditional on a ground-level release (H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}, assumed — not given), open country (assumed), fitted Briggs class D coefficients, Q=0.8 kg s−1Q = 0.8\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}} (given), u=4 m s−1u = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} (given) and x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} (given):

C≈107 mg m−3C \approx 107\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}}, with a plausible range of 2020 to 130 mg m−3130\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} across terrain and fitted-relation choice.

If the release is in fact elevated, the value falls rapidly with HH (93 mg m−393\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} at H=10 mH = 10\ \mathrm{m}; 31 mg m−331\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} at H=30 mH = 30\ \mathrm{m}; 3.3 mg m−33.3\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} at H=50 mH = 50\ \mathrm{m}, open country) and the release height must be supplied before a narrower range is used. Confidence: low for a single value, for the reasons in Section 1.

F1. Control-Loop Tuning — Second Loop

Response without the skill

Proportional-Integral Controller Tuning for a First-Order-Plus-Dead-Time Process

Given data and symbols

The process gain is KpK_{\mathrm{p}}, dimensionless, defined as the steady-state change in the controlled variable divided by the steady-state change in the manipulated variable. The time constant is τ\tau, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}), defined as the time for the dead-time-free first-order response to reach 63.2%63.2\% of its final change after a step input. The dead time is θ\theta, in s\mathrm{s}, defined as the interval after a step input during which no response is observed. The Laplace variable is ss, in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}. The controller gain is KcK_{\mathrm{c}}, dimensionless on the same engineering-unit scaling as KpK_{\mathrm{p}}. The integral time is TiT_{\mathrm{i}}, in s\mathrm{s}. The integral gain is KiK_{\mathrm{i}}, in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}, defined as Ki=Kc/TiK_{\mathrm{i}} = K_{\mathrm{c}} / T_{\mathrm{i}}.

Given values:

  • Kp=1.8K_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.8, dimensionless
  • τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}
  • θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}
Process model

The transfer function of the process, Gp(s)G_{\mathrm{p}}(s), dimensionless per unit of ss-domain input scaling consistent with KpK_{\mathrm{p}}, is

Gp(s)=Kp e−θsτs+1=1.8 e−12s45s+1G_{\mathrm{p}}(s) = \frac{K_{\mathrm{p}}\, e^{-\theta s}}{\tau s + 1} = \frac{1.8\, e^{-12 s}}{45 s + 1}

where e−θse^{-\theta s} is the dead-time term.

The dead-time ratio, rr, dimensionless, defined as r=θ/τr = \theta / \tau, is

r=1245=0.267r = \frac{12}{45} = 0.267

A value of rr between 0.10.1 and 0.50.5 denotes a process that is controllable with a conventional proportional-integral (PI) controller, with dead time large enough that aggressive tuning produces oscillation, and small enough that a Smith predictor or derivative action is not required for acceptable performance. No derivative action is specified in this problem, and none is recommended: derivative action provides limited benefit at r=0.267r = 0.267 and amplifies measurement noise.

Controller form

The PI controller transfer function, Gc(s)G_{\mathrm{c}}(s), dimensionless, in the standard (non-interacting, ideal) form is

Gc(s)=Kc(1+1Tis)=Kc+KisG_{\mathrm{c}}(s) = K_{\mathrm{c}} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{i}} s} \right) = K_{\mathrm{c}} + \frac{K_{\mathrm{i}}}{s}

Tuning consists of selecting KcK_{\mathrm{c}} and TiT_{\mathrm{i}}. Direct (reverse) action is set by the sign of KpK_{\mathrm{p}}: Kp>0K_{\mathrm{p}} > 0, so the controller is reverse-acting in the usual convention, with the sign absorbed into the loop configuration and Kc>0K_{\mathrm{c}} > 0 reported here as a magnitude.

Method 1: Ziegler–Nichols open-loop (reaction-curve) rules for PI control

The Ziegler–Nichols open-loop rules for PI control are

Kc=0.9Kpτθ,Ti=θ0.3K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{0.9}{K_{\mathrm{p}}} \frac{\tau}{\theta}, \qquad T_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{\theta}{0.3}

Substitution gives

Kc=0.91.8×4512=0.50×3.75=1.88K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{0.9}{1.8} \times \frac{45}{12} = 0.50 \times 3.75 = 1.88

Ti=120.3=40 sT_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{12}{0.3} = 40\ \mathrm{s}

Ki=1.8840=0.047 s−1K_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1.88}{40} = 0.047\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

These rules target quarter-amplitude decay for a load disturbance. The resulting loop is fast but has low robustness margins and substantial overshoot for a set-point change.

Method 2: Cohen–Coon rules for PI control

The Cohen–Coon rules for PI control, in terms of r=θ/τ=0.267r = \theta / \tau = 0.267, are

Kc=1Kpτθ(0.9+r12),Ti=θ 30+3r9+20rK_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{K_{\mathrm{p}}} \frac{\tau}{\theta} \left( 0.9 + \frac{r}{12} \right), \qquad T_{\mathrm{i}} = \theta\, \frac{30 + 3r}{9 + 20r}

Substitution gives

Kc=11.8×3.75×(0.9+0.26712)=2.083×0.922=1.92K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{1.8} \times 3.75 \times \left( 0.9 + \frac{0.267}{12} \right) = 2.083 \times 0.922 = 1.92

Ti=12×30+3(0.267)9+20(0.267)=12×30.8014.33=25.8 sT_{\mathrm{i}} = 12 \times \frac{30 + 3(0.267)}{9 + 20(0.267)} = 12 \times \frac{30.80}{14.33} = 25.8\ \mathrm{s}

Ki=1.9225.8=0.075 s−1K_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1.92}{25.8} = 0.075\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

The Cohen–Coon settings are more aggressive than the Ziegler–Nichols settings because TiT_{\mathrm{i}} is shorter, even though KcK_{\mathrm{c}} is similar. A short TiT_{\mathrm{i}} relative to θ\theta increases the risk of oscillation and integral windup effects.

Method 3: Ultimate-gain check

The ultimate frequency is ωu\omega_{\mathrm{u}}, in radians per second (rad s−1\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}), defined as the frequency at which the phase of GpG_{\mathrm{p}} reaches −180∘-180^{\circ}. The phase condition, with angular frequency ω\omega, in rad s−1\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}, is

arctan⁡(ωτ)+ωθ=π\arctan(\omega \tau) + \omega \theta = \pi

Solving arctan⁡(45ω)+12ω=π\arctan(45\omega) + 12\omega = \pi gives ωu=0.144 rad s−1\omega_{\mathrm{u}} = 0.144\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.

The ultimate period is PuP_{\mathrm{u}}, in s\mathrm{s}, defined as Pu=2π/ωuP_{\mathrm{u}} = 2\pi / \omega_{\mathrm{u}}:

Pu=2π0.144=43.7 sP_{\mathrm{u}} = \frac{2\pi}{0.144} = 43.7\ \mathrm{s}

The ultimate gain is KuK_{\mathrm{u}}, dimensionless, defined as the proportional gain that places the loop at the stability limit:

Ku=1+(ωuτ)2Kp=1+(0.144×45)21.8=6.541.8=3.63K_{\mathrm{u}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + (\omega_{\mathrm{u}} \tau)^{2}}}{K_{\mathrm{p}}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + (0.144 \times 45)^{2}}}{1.8} = \frac{6.54}{1.8} = 3.63

The Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop PI rules, Kc=0.45KuK_{\mathrm{c}} = 0.45 K_{\mathrm{u}} and Ti=Pu/1.2T_{\mathrm{i}} = P_{\mathrm{u}} / 1.2, give

Kc=0.45×3.63=1.64,Ti=43.71.2=36.4 sK_{\mathrm{c}} = 0.45 \times 3.63 = 1.64, \qquad T_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{43.7}{1.2} = 36.4\ \mathrm{s}

consistent, within the difference expected between the two Ziegler–Nichols variants, with Method 1 (Kc=1.88K_{\mathrm{c}} = 1.88, Ti=40 sT_{\mathrm{i}} = 40\ \mathrm{s}). Any KcK_{\mathrm{c}} approaching Ku=3.63K_{\mathrm{u}} = 3.63 at short TiT_{\mathrm{i}} is unstable in practice once model error is present, which confirms that Kc≈1.6K_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 1.6–1.91.9 is already in the aggressive range (about 4545–52%52\% of KuK_{\mathrm{u}}).

Method 4: Internal Model Control / Skogestad (SIMC) rules for PI control — recommended basis

The closed-loop time constant is λ\lambda, in s\mathrm{s}, defined as the desired time constant of the closed-loop set-point response and selected by the designer. The SIMC choice λ=θ\lambda = \theta gives fast response subject to a robustness constraint that is standard for this rule. The SIMC PI rules are

Kc=1Kpτλ+θ,Ti=min⁡(τ, 4(λ+θ))K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{K_{\mathrm{p}}} \frac{\tau}{\lambda + \theta}, \qquad T_{\mathrm{i}} = \min\left( \tau,\ 4(\lambda + \theta) \right)

With λ=θ=12 s\lambda = \theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}:

Kc=11.8×4512+12=0.556×1.875=1.04K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{1.8} \times \frac{45}{12 + 12} = 0.556 \times 1.875 = 1.04

Ti=min⁡(45, 4×24)=min⁡(45, 96)=45 sT_{\mathrm{i}} = \min\left( 45,\ 4 \times 24 \right) = \min(45,\ 96) = 45\ \mathrm{s}

Ki=1.0445=0.023 s−1K_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1.04}{45} = 0.023\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

The SIMC gain is about 29%29\% of KuK_{\mathrm{u}}, which provides a substantially larger gain margin (approximately Ku/Kc=3.5K_{\mathrm{u}} / K_{\mathrm{c}} = 3.5 on proportional action alone) than the Ziegler–Nichols and Cohen–Coon settings, while Ti=τT_{\mathrm{i}} = \tau cancels the process pole in the nominal model and gives a non-oscillatory nominal response.

Recommendation

Recommended initial settings, for commissioning on the process as modelled:

Kc=1.0,Ti=45 s,Ki=0.023 s−1K_{\mathrm{c}} = 1.0, \qquad T_{\mathrm{i}} = 45\ \mathrm{s}, \qquad K_{\mathrm{i}} = 0.023\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

in the form Gc(s)=Kc(1+1/(Tis))G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) = K_{\mathrm{c}} \left( 1 + 1/(T_{\mathrm{i}} s) \right), reverse-acting for Kp>0K_{\mathrm{p}} > 0.

Rationale, stated as operating conditions:

  1. If minimum settling time for load disturbances is the priority and oscillation and overshoot are acceptable, the Ziegler–Nichols settings Kc=1.88K_{\mathrm{c}} = 1.88, Ti=40 sT_{\mathrm{i}} = 40\ \mathrm{s} may be used, with anti-windup protection fitted, because integral action at Ki=0.047 s−1K_{\mathrm{i}} = 0.047\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} with a 12 s12\ \mathrm{s} dead time accumulates error during any saturation interval.
  2. For general operation, the SIMC settings are preferred. The nominal closed-loop response has a time constant of order λ+θ=24 s\lambda + \theta = 24\ \mathrm{s}, no steady-state offset for step set-point or step load changes (a consequence of the integral term, provided the loop remains stable and unsaturated), and a gain margin adequate for the model error typical of a first-order-plus-dead-time fit.
  3. Fine-tuning in service: increase KcK_{\mathrm{c}} in steps of about 20%20\% toward 1.61.6 if the response is sluggish and remains non-oscillatory; decrease KcK_{\mathrm{c}} or increase TiT_{\mathrm{i}} if sustained oscillation with period near Pu=43.7 sP_{\mathrm{u}} = 43.7\ \mathrm{s} appears, because that period identifies the dead-time-driven stability limit.
  4. Anti-windup (clamping or back-calculation), output limits, and set-point weighting or a set-point filter should be configured before the aggressive settings in rows 1–3 of the comparison table are applied to a set-point change, because PI tuning rules of the Ziegler–Nichols and Cohen–Coon type were derived for load response and produce large set-point overshoot without them.
Final answer

For Kp=1.8K_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.8, τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}: use, as the balanced commissioning tuning, a PI controller with controller gain Kc≈1.0K_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 1.0 (dimensionless) and integral time Ti≈45 sT_{\mathrm{i}} \approx 45\ \mathrm{s} (integral gain Ki≈0.023 s−1K_{\mathrm{i}} \approx 0.023\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}). The classical aggressive alternative is Kc≈1.9K_{\mathrm{c}} \approx 1.9, Ti≈40 sT_{\mathrm{i}} \approx 40\ \mathrm{s} (Ziegler–Nichols open-loop).

Response with the skill (generic layer)

PI Tuning for a First-Order-Plus-Dead-Time Process

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. PI (proportional-integral) tuning for a FOPDT (first-order-plus-dead-time) process is not determined by the process model alone. Every published tuning rule is a fitted, empirical correlation that encodes an unstated trade-off between speed of response, overshoot, disturbance rejection, and robustness to model error. Different well-established rules applied to the same model differ by roughly a factor of 2 in controller gain and by a factor of about 4 in integral time in this case (Section 5). No rule can be verified from the model parameters alone; only a closed-loop test on the actual loop settles whether a tuning is acceptable.

Confidence rating: low to moderate. Moderate (about 60 %) that the conservative range recommended in Section 5 gives a stable, non-oscillatory loop if the stated FOPDT model is accurate to about ±20 %. Low (below 40 %) that any single pair of settings is "optimal" in any sense, because no performance objective was supplied (Section 3), and low that the FOPDT model itself represents built equipment over its full operating range (Section 8). A single-value answer with no range would overstate what the information supports.

3. Missing quantities — Prompt 2: fill the gaps first

The problem as stated supplies three numbers and nothing else. The following quantities, which the solution needs, are missing. None was taken in silence; each is either carried as an explicit assumption or solved under alternatives.

  1. Performance objective — missing. Servo (set-point tracking), regulatory (load-disturbance rejection), minimum overshoot, minimum integral error, and maximum robustness give different tunings. Treatment: results are reported for a robust / moderately conservative objective and for aggressive objectives side by side (Section 5), not merged into one value.
  2. Controller action and sign convention — missing. Direct- or reverse-acting, and the sign of KcK_c, depend on the sign convention for error and on fail-safe valve action. Treatment: magnitudes only are reported; the sign must be set so the loop is negative feedback for the actual KpK_p sign (given as positive) and valve action.
  3. Signal scaling / engineering units — missing. KpK_p is given as dimensionless, so KcK_c is dimensionless only if controller input and output are expressed on the same normalised (e.g. per-cent of span) scaling. If the transmitter span or valve span differs, KcK_c in per-cent-per-engineering-unit changes by the span ratio, with no change in loop behaviour. Treatment: all KcK_c values are on the normalised scaling implicit in the given KpK_p; conversion to instrument settings is a separate, unsupplied step.
  4. Controller form — missing. Parallel (ideal) form, series (interacting) form, integral time versus reset rate (1/Ti1/T_i, in repeats per second), and proportional band (proportional band =100/Kc= 100/K_c in per-cent, on normalised scaling) are vendor-specific. Treatment: the parallel form above is assumed. On an interacting controller the effective TiT_i differs and the settings must be converted by the vendor formula.
  5. Sampling interval and implementation — missing. A digital implementation adds about half a sampling interval of effective dead time. Treatment: continuous-time tuning is reported; Section 9 states the sampling condition under which it changes by more than 10 %.
  6. Anti-windup, output limits, and operating point — missing. Saturation and windup dominate large-signal behaviour and are not in any rule below. Treatment: noted as out of scope, Section 9.
  7. Accuracy and provenance of the model — missing. Whether KpK_p, τ\tau, θ\theta are measured, fitted from a step test, or nominal design values, and over what operating range, is not stated. Treatment: a plausible uncertainty of ±20 % on each parameter is assumed for the range calculation in Section 6; this is an assumption, not data. Data supplied by the user, plant, or vendor would supersede it.
  8. Basis items that do not apply. Composition basis, pressure basis, reference state, and per-pass versus overall conversion have no meaning for this control problem and are recorded as not applicable rather than silently omitted.

5. Results — a range, not a single value

All values below were computed in executed code (Section 7), not by hand arithmetic.

5.1 Tuning rules applied

SIMC (Skogestad internal model control) rule — fitted relation. For a FOPDT process: Kc=(1/Kp) τ/(τc+θ)K_c = (1/K_p)\,\tau/(\tau_c+\theta) and Ti=min⁡(τ,  4(τc+θ))T_i = \min(\tau,\; 4(\tau_c+\theta)). With the assumed τc=θ=12\tau_c = \theta = 12 s: Kc=(1/1.8)(45/24)=1.04K_c = (1/1.8)(45/24) = 1.04, Ti=45T_i = 45 s. Sweeping the assumed τc\tau_c from 8 s to 20 s gives KcK_c from 1.25 down to 0.78, Ti=45T_i = 45 s throughout.

IMC (internal model control, Rivera–Morari form) — fitted relation. Kc=(1/Kp) (τ+θ/2)/(λ+θ/2)K_c = (1/K_p)\,(\tau+\theta/2)/(\lambda+\theta/2) and Ti=τ+θ/2=51T_i = \tau + \theta/2 = 51 s. Sweeping the assumed λ\lambda from 10 s to 25 s gives KcK_c from 1.77 down to 0.91. At λ=20\lambda = 20 s, Kc=1.09K_c = 1.09, close to the SIMC value above.

Ultimate (closed-loop) quantities, computed from the model. Solving arctan⁡(ωuτ)+ωuθ=π\arctan(\omega_u \tau) + \omega_u \theta = \pi gives ωu=0.144\omega_u = 0.144 rad s−1^{-1}, hence Pu=2π/ωu=43.7P_u = 2\pi/\omega_u = 43.7 s and Ku=1+(ωuτ)2/Kp=3.63K_u = \sqrt{1+(\omega_u\tau)^2}/K_p = 3.63.

Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop PI rule — fitted relation. Kc=0.45 Ku=1.64K_c = 0.45\,K_u = 1.64, Ti=Pu/1.2=36.4T_i = P_u/1.2 = 36.4 s.

Ziegler–Nichols open-loop (reaction-curve) PI rule — fitted relation. Kc=0.9 τ/(Kpθ)=1.88K_c = 0.9\,\tau/(K_p\theta) = 1.88, Ti=3.33 θ=40.0T_i = 3.33\,\theta = 40.0 s.

Cohen–Coon PI rule — fitted relation. Kc=(τ/(Kpθ)) (0.9+θ/(12τ))=1.92K_c = (\tau/(K_p\theta))\,(0.9 + \theta/(12\tau)) = 1.92, Ti=θ (30+3θ/τ)/(9+20θ/τ)=25.8T_i = \theta\,(30 + 3\theta/\tau)/(9 + 20\theta/\tau) = 25.8 s.

Tyreus–Luyben PI rule — fitted relation. Kc=Ku/3.2=1.14K_c = K_u/3.2 = 1.14, Ti=2.2 Pu=96.2T_i = 2.2\,P_u = 96.2 s. This rule targets robustness for integrating and lag-dominant processes and is included as the conservative bound on TiT_i.

6. Range under parameter uncertainty

Holding the SIMC rule fixed (τc=θ\tau_c = \theta, re-set at each θ\theta) and varying the assumed ±20 % parameter ranges of Section 4 one at a time, KcK_c spans 0.83 to 1.30 and TiT_i remains 45 s (the min⁡(τ,4(τc+θ))\min(\tau, 4(\tau_c+\theta)) term is set by τ\tau except at the low-τ\tau end, where TiT_i would fall to 36 s). Combined worst-case corners move KcK_c further, by roughly the product of the individual effects. The recommended range in Section 5.2 (KcK_c 0.8 to 1.1) was checked for stability at the perturbed corners rather than re-tuned at each corner; see Section 7, check 3.

7. Independent verification — Prompt 3: check the work

Primary sources that settle the rule formulas are the original publications: Ziegler and Nichols (1942); Cohen and Coon (1953); Tyreus and Luyben (1992); Skogestad, "Simple analytic rules for model reduction and PID controller tuning" (2003); and the IMC derivation in Rivera, Morari and Skogestad (1986), as collected in Seborg, Edgar, Mellichamp and Doyle, Process Dynamics and Control. Status: unverified against those primary sources in this solution. The formulas were used in their standard textbook form; coefficient-level verification requires the originals, and any coefficient error there would propagate unchanged into Section 5. Agreement with another AI model was not used as verification, and is not verification for this problem type.

Checks performed, by routes independent of the rule formulas:

  1. Frequency-domain margins, computed in code. For each tuning, the loop transfer function Gc(s)Gp(s)G_c(s)G_p(s) was evaluated over frequency; PM and GM were read from the gain- and phase-crossover frequencies. Results: SIMC (Kc=1.04K_c=1.04, Ti=45T_i=45 s): PM 61°, GM 3.14 (9.9 dB). IMC (λ=20\lambda=20 s): PM 64°, GM 3.05. Tyreus–Luyben: PM 76°, GM 3.07. Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop: PM 40°, GM 1.94. Ziegler–Nichols open-loop: PM 36°, GM 1.72. Cohen–Coon: PM 24°, GM 1.51. Interpretation: the ordering of rules by margin matches their intended character (robust versus aggressive), and the recommended range sits at PM about 60°, GM about 3 — within the commonly used robustness band of PM 45° to 65° and GM 2 to 4. That band is itself a rule of thumb, labelled as such, not a standard invoked here.
  2. Limiting cases, known by sight. (a) As θ→0\theta \to 0, Ku→∞K_u \to \infty for a first-order lag, i.e. a lag alone cannot be driven to marginal stability by gain alone — the computed KuK_u formula has this behaviour, since ωu→∞\omega_u \to \infty. (b) As τc→∞\tau_c \to \infty in SIMC, Kc→0K_c \to 0: demanding an infinitely slow closed loop gives no control action, as required. (c) At Kc=Ku=3.63K_c = K_u = 3.63 with proportional-only control, the computed period is 43.7 s, about 3.6 θ3.6\,\theta and close to τ\tau, which is the expected scale for θ/τ=0.267\theta/\tau = 0.267. No limiting-case check failed.
  3. Robustness of the fixed recommended tuning. The single starting pair Kc=1.04K_c = 1.04, Ti=45T_i = 45 s, applied without re-tuning to perturbed plants, was re-checked in code: nominal PM 61°, GM 3.14; KpK_p +20 %: PM 56°, GM 2.62; θ\theta +20 %: PM 56°, GM 2.62; τ\tau −20 %: PM 61°, GM 2.60; combined worst corner (KpK_p +20 %, θ\theta +20 %, τ\tau −20 %, all assumed perturbations): PM 45°, GM 1.82. The loop remains stable at all corners checked, but GM at the worst corner falls below 2, so the margin claim is conditional, not absolute. This check qualifies — it does not overturn — the recommendation.
  4. Correlation valid range. SIMC and IMC in the forms used are derived for θ/τ\theta/\tau roughly between 0.1 and 1; the given ratio 0.267 is inside that range. Ziegler–Nichols open-loop and Cohen–Coon were developed for θ/τ\theta/\tau roughly 0.1 to 1 as well; also satisfied. No rule was applied outside its stated range.
  5. Balance closure. There is no material or energy balance in a tuning calculation; the analogue — that every number in Section 5.2 be reproducible from the stated formulas and given inputs — was checked by executing all formulas in code in one script. All table entries reproduced. No check failed, subject to the coefficient caveat at the head of this section.
8. Audit against built equipment — Prompt 4

Three points most likely to differ between this model-based result and a built loop, as a practising control engineer would flag them:

  1. The process is not FOPDT. Real loops carry higher-order lags (transmitter, valve actuator, additional volumes) that appear as extra apparent dead time, and gain that varies with operating point. Direction and size: effective θ\theta larger by typically 20 % to 50 % once actuator and measurement lags are lumped in, which moves the safe KcK_c down by a comparable fraction and can halve the phase margin of the aggressive tunings. Settling record: a step test (or relay test) on the actual loop at the actual operating point, with the fitted model and its residuals recorded.
  2. Valve and measurement non-idealities. Stiction, deadband, hysteresis, and a non-linear installed valve characteristic produce limit cycling that no linear tuning removes, and make the effective gain direction-dependent. Direction and size: sustained oscillation of a few per cent of span is common with stiction of 1 % to 5 % of valve travel, independent of KcK_c and TiT_i within wide limits. Settling record: valve travel versus controller output trend (a valve signature / diagnostic test) and the loop's historian record at steady operation.
  3. Dead time varies in operation. Transport delay varies inversely with flow, so θ\theta at low throughput can be roughly double its value at design flow if the delay is flow-driven. Direction and size: tuning set at design flow becomes under-margined at low flow; at θ=24\theta = 24 s the SIMC margins of Section 7 would fall to approximately PM 40° or below (estimated by the same frequency calculation, not measured). Settling record: step tests at minimum and maximum operating flow, or a throughput trend against the fitted delay.
9. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model. Non-linearity and gain scheduling; higher-order dynamics; interacting multivariable effects and disturbances entering elsewhere than at the manipulated input; measurement noise (no filtering or derivative action is considered — the controller is PI only, as asked); actuator saturation, rate limits, and integral windup; discrete sampling and computation delay; set-point weighting and bumpless transfer.

Information not available here. The vendor's exact controller algorithm and form; the transmitter and valve spans needed to convert KcK_c to instrument units; the plant's own tuning standards and the operating history of this loop, if it exists. Rule coefficients rest on textbook presentations marked unverified in Section 7.

Effects that appear only in running equipment. Stiction-induced limit cycling; fouling or catalyst change moving τ\tau and KpK_p over weeks; delay variation with throughput (Section 8, item 3).

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %. (i) Any process parameter in error by more than about 10 % moves the re-tuned KcK_c by more than about 10 % (Section 5.3). (ii) A sampling interval above about θ/4≈3\theta/4 \approx 3 s adds effective dead time above about 12 % of θ\theta and shifts the appropriate KcK_c down by a comparable amount (estimated). (iii) A change of objective from robust to aggressive changes KcK_c by 60 % to 85 % (Section 5.2) — the largest single effect. (iv) Conversion from parallel to interacting controller form, or from integral time to reset rate, changes the numbers entered into the instrument even at identical loop behaviour.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used. 1. What objective — set-point, disturbance, overshoot limit, robustness target — are these settings meant to meet? 2. Where did KpK_p, τ\tau, and θ\theta come from, at what operating point, and what were the fit residuals? 3. What are the transmitter span, valve span, controller form, and action, and has KcK_c been converted to those units? 4. What is the sampling interval, and is anti-windup fitted and enabled? 5. Has the loop been step-tested at low and high throughput, and does the fitted dead time change with flow? 6. What output movement and overshoot are acceptable on the first closed-loop test, and who is authorised to detune if the loop oscillates?

10. Answer in brief

On the given model (Kp=1.8K_p = 1.8, given; τ=45\tau = 45 s, given; θ=12\theta = 12 s, given), start at Kc=1.0K_c = 1.0 (dimensionless, normalised scaling) and Ti=45T_i = 45 s, within the robust range KcK_c 0.8 to 1.1 and TiT_i 45 s to 51 s. The full range across established rules is KcK_c 0.78 to 1.92 and TiT_i 26 s to 96 s; the spread is due to the unstated tuning objective, which must be supplied, and to model accuracy, which must be established by a test on the actual loop, before any value narrower than the range above is relied on.

Data Reconciliation of Three Flow Meters

Given data and symbols

The corresponding variances, denoted σF2\sigma_F^2, σP2\sigma_P^2 and σR2\sigma_R^2, are

σF2=9.9225,σP2=6.9696,σR2=2.1904\sigma_F^2 = 9.9225, \qquad \sigma_P^2 = 6.9696, \qquad \sigma_R^2 = 2.1904

in squared flow units.

The meters are taken to be independent, with no systematic (bias) error stated, so the standard weighted least-squares reconciliation applies. The percentages are applied to the readings, as stated in the problem, so the standard uncertainties above are fixed numbers in the calculation.

Balance constraint and measured imbalance

Steady-state mass conservation for the unit, with no accumulation and no other inlet or outlet stream, requires

F^=P^+R^.\hat{F} = \hat{P} + \hat{R}.

The measured values do not satisfy the balance. The measured imbalance, denoted ee and defined as the measured feed minus the sum of the measured product and residue, is

e=mF−mP−mR=210−132−74=4.e = m_F - m_P - m_R = 210 - 132 - 74 = 4.

The standard uncertainty of ee, denoted σe\sigma_e, follows from independence of the three meters:

σe=σF2+σP2+σR2=9.9225+6.9696+2.1904=19.0825=4.37.\sigma_e = \sqrt{\sigma_F^2 + \sigma_P^2 + \sigma_R^2} = \sqrt{9.9225 + 6.9696 + 2.1904} = \sqrt{19.0825} = 4.37.

The ratio e/σe=4/4.37=0.92e / \sigma_e = 4 / 4.37 = 0.92 is of order unity, so the imbalance is consistent with the stated random uncertainties alone. No gross error (for example a failed or grossly biased meter) is indicated, and all three measurements are retained in the reconciliation.

Weighted least-squares formulation

Let aFa_F, aPa_P and aRa_R denote the adjustments to the feed, product and residue readings, respectively, each in flow units, defined by

F^=mF+aF,P^=mP+aP,R^=mR+aR.\hat{F} = m_F + a_F, \qquad \hat{P} = m_P + a_P, \qquad \hat{R} = m_R + a_R.

The reconciled values minimise the weighted sum of squared adjustments, denoted JJ:

J=(aFσF)2+(aPσP)2+(aRσR)2,J = \left(\frac{a_F}{\sigma_F}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{a_P}{\sigma_P}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{a_R}{\sigma_R}\right)^2,

subject to the balance constraint. Substituting the definitions of aFa_F, aPa_P and aRa_R into F^=P^+R^\hat{F} = \hat{P} + \hat{R} gives the constraint in terms of the adjustments:

aF−aP−aR=−e=−4.a_F - a_P - a_R = -e = -4.

Weighting by 1/σ21/\sigma^2 for each meter means that a meter with a larger standard uncertainty receives a larger adjustment, and a meter with a smaller standard uncertainty receives a smaller adjustment.

Solution by Lagrange multiplier

Let μ\mu denote a Lagrange multiplier, with units of reciprocal flow units, for the balance constraint. Stationarity of the Lagrangian formed from JJ and twice μ\mu times the constraint gives

aF=−μ σF2,aP=+μ σP2,aR=+μ σR2.a_F = -\mu \, \sigma_F^2, \qquad a_P = +\mu \, \sigma_P^2, \qquad a_R = +\mu \, \sigma_R^2.

The minus sign for the feed and the plus signs for the product and residue come from the signs with which the three flows enter the constraint aF−aP−aR=−4a_F - a_P - a_R = -4.

Substituting these three expressions into the constraint:

−μ(σF2+σP2+σR2)=−4,-\mu\left(\sigma_F^2 + \sigma_P^2 + \sigma_R^2\right) = -4,

μ=4σF2+σP2+σR2=419.0825=0.2096.\mu = \frac{4}{\sigma_F^2 + \sigma_P^2 + \sigma_R^2} = \frac{4}{19.0825} = 0.2096.

The adjustments are then

aF=−0.2096×9.9225=−2.08,a_F = -0.2096 \times 9.9225 = -2.08, aP=+0.2096×6.9696=+1.46,a_P = +0.2096 \times 6.9696 = +1.46, aR=+0.2096×2.1904=+0.46.a_R = +0.2096 \times 2.1904 = +0.46.

The feed reading is adjusted downward and the product and residue readings are adjusted upward, which is the direction required to remove the positive imbalance e=4e = 4. Each adjustment is shared in proportion to the corresponding meter variance, not in proportion to the flow or to the relative uncertainty alone. The residue meter, having the smallest absolute standard uncertainty (σR=1.48\sigma_R = 1.48), receives the smallest adjustment.

Weakness: weighted least-squares data reconciliation is exact algebra once the error model is fixed, but the result rests entirely on an error model that the problem statement only partly specifies — the relative sizes, independence, and distribution of the meter errors, and the absence of a gross error, a leak, or accumulation. No arithmetic step is in doubt; every doubt is about those inputs.

Confidence rating: moderate for the point estimate under the stated error model (the calculation is verified by two independent routes, §6); low-to-moderate for the reconciled value as a statement about the plant, because independence, simultaneity, and the absence of a gross error are assumed, not given (§2, §7). 3. Method (Prompt 1)

Weighted least-squares reconciliation: choose xF,xP,xRx_F, x_P, x_R to minimise the sum of squared standardised adjustments, [(xF−yF)/σF]2+[(xP−yP)/σP]2+[(xR−yR)/σR]2[(x_F-y_F)/\sigma_F]^2 + [(x_P-y_P)/\sigma_P]^2 + [(x_R-y_R)/\sigma_R]^2, subject to xF−xP−xR=0x_F - x_P - x_R = 0. This is the standard linear data-reconciliation solution (primary source that settles the method: a data-reconciliation text such as Narasimhan and Jordache, Data Reconciliation and Gross Error Detection, or Crowe's reconciliation papers, and the JCGM Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement for "standard uncertainty" — unverified: not checked against those sources in this solution; the algebra itself is verified in §6, which does not depend on the citation).

7. Audit — three points most likely to differ in built equipment (Prompt 4)
  1. One meter biased, not randomly scattered (gross error). Reconciliation spreads a single meter's bias over all three readings, so a fouled, drifting, or mis-ranged product meter would pull xPx_P toward the wrong value while appearing consistent. Direction: unknown (sign of the bias); size: a bias equal to the whole 4-unit imbalance, if wholly in one meter, moves xPx_P by up to about 1.5 units (≈1 %) versus the base allocation. Settled by: the meter's calibration certificate and zero/span check records for the actual instrument, and a repeat reconciliation over several time periods (a persistent one-sided adjustment pattern indicates bias) — unverified until those records are checked.
  2. Hold-up and unsynchronised readings. A real unit with inventory between the feed and outlet meters shows a transient imbalance during rate changes that is accumulation, not error; reconciling it away misstates all three flows. Direction: product overstated here if inventory was in fact rising (part of the 4 units is stored, not missing). Size: up to the full 4 units shared across the outlets, ≈1 % on xPx_P. Settled by: time-aligned historian records for the three meters and the unit's level / inventory records over the same period — unverified until checked.
  3. Correlated errors from a shared correction. If two or three meters share a density, temperature, or flow-computer correction, their errors are correlated and the independence assumption (assumed, §2) under-weights the shared component, biasing the split of the adjustment. Direction: depends on which meters share the correction; size: bounded by the §5 re-weighting scenarios, ≲1 %. Settled by: the flow-computer configuration and the vendor uncertainty budgets for the actual meters — unverified until checked.
8. What is not covered (Prompt 5)
  • Effects not in the model: meter dynamics and damping, drift between calibrations, non-Gaussian and time-correlated noise, robust (gross-error-resistant) estimators, and any second constraint (e.g. component balances) that would add information.
  • Information not visible here: the meters' types, ranges, calibration history, and installation (straight-run, tapping) details, held in plant and vendor records; any restricted databank values behind the stated percentages.
  • Effects appearing only in running equipment: fouling, pulsation, two-phase or flashing flow at a meter, and inventory swings (§7, points 1–3).
  • Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 % (i.e. xPx_P outside roughly 120–147): re-weighting alone cannot do it (§5, maximum ≈1.2 %). It would require a different physical picture — an unmeasured stream, leak, or accumulation of order 13 flow units or more, a gross error of that size in the product meter, or readings that are not for the same period or not in common units (e.g. an uncorrected volumetric/mass mismatch).
  • Questions a reviewer should ask before use: (1) Are the three readings time-aligned averages over the same period, at steady state? (2) Do calibration records support the three stated standard uncertainties, as percent of reading, for these actual meters? (3) Are the meter errors independent, or is a correction shared? (4) Is there any leak, vent, drain, or unmeasured stream between the feed meter and the two outlet meters? (5) Is the ≈95 % range in §4 (129.3–137.6) narrow enough for the decision this number feeds, or is a repeat reconciliation over multiple periods needed?
