F3. Corrosion and Remaining Life — Second Vessel

Response without the skill

Remaining Life of a Vessel — Estimate

Symbols
  • t_measured = measured wall thickness, in millimetres (mm)
  • t_required = minimum required wall thickness, in millimetres (mm)
  • a = available metal loss, in millimetres (mm), defined as t_measured minus t_required
  • r = general corrosion rate, in millimetres per year (mm/year)
  • L = remaining life, in years (year)
Given data
  • t_measured = 15 mm
  • t_required = 9 mm
  • r = 0.22 mm/year
Method

For uniform general corrosion at a constant rate r, the wall thickness decreases by r per year. The vessel can remain in service until the wall thickness reaches t_required. The metal that can be lost before that limit is reached is a, defined above. The remaining life L is therefore a divided by r:

L = a / r, where a = t_measured − t_required.

Calculation

Available metal loss:

a = t_measured − t_required a = 15 mm − 9 mm a = 6 mm

Remaining life:

L = a / r L = 6 mm / (0.22 mm/year) L = 27.2727… year L ≈ 27.3 year

Check: 0.22 mm/year × 27.2727 year = 6.0 mm, which equals a.

Result

The estimated remaining life is approximately 27.3 years.

Assumptions and scope
  • Corrosion is general (uniform) and proceeds at the constant rate r = 0.22 mm/year over the remaining life.
  • t_required = 9 mm remains the applicable minimum required thickness, with no change in design pressure, temperature, loading, or code requirements.
  • No other damage mechanism (for example pitting, cracking, erosion, or localised thinning) governs before the general metal loss reaches a.
  • The measured value t_measured = 15 mm is representative of the thinnest governing location. In practice the next inspection interval is normally set well below L, with a suitable safety factor, rather than operating to the full calculated life.

No physical property, fitted relation, correlation, or rule of thumb other than the linear metal-loss model in Section 4 is used. No density, allowable stress, pressure, or temperature value is used, because none is required by the stated model and none was supplied.

4. Calculation and result as a range

Linear metal-loss model, valid only for uniform general corrosion at a constant rate, with no change in fluid, temperature, pressure, or mechanism, and with tmint_{\mathrm{min}} unchanged:

L=Δtr=ta−tminrL = \frac{\Delta t}{r} = \frac{t_{\mathrm{a}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}}{r}

Nominal case, using the given values:

L=6 mm0.22 mm/year=27.27 yearL = \frac{6\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 27.27\ \mathrm{year}

Result, reported as a range, not a single value. The nominal value is 27.327.3 year. Under the assumed combined uncertainty band in Section 3 (Δt\Delta t from 5.55.5 to 6.5 mm6.5\ \mathrm{mm} and rr from 0.1760.176 to 0.264 mm/year0.264\ \mathrm{mm/year}, i.e. ±20%\pm 20\% on rr):

  • Low end: 5.5/0.264=20.85.5 / 0.264 = 20.8 year
  • High end: 6.5/0.176=36.96.5 / 0.176 = 36.9 year
  • Plausible range under those assumed bands: about 2121 to 3737 year, nominal 27.327.3 year.

Wider scenario range, if the future rate differs by a factor of two from the given rate (a scenario, not a measured band):

  • r=0.44 mm/yearr = 0.44\ \mathrm{mm/year} (double, assumed scenario): L=13.6L = 13.6 year
  • r=0.11 mm/yearr = 0.11\ \mathrm{mm/year} (half, assumed scenario): L=54.5L = 54.5 year

Half of the nominal remaining life is 13.613.6 year. A half-life inspection interval is a convention associated with pressure-vessel inspection practice (American Petroleum Institute API 510). Unverified until checked against the current edition of API 510 and the owner's inspection plan; it is not used to set an interval here.

5. Missing quantities — problem not completed silently (Prompt 2)

The following quantities are needed for a decision-grade answer and were not supplied. The solution above is therefore conditional on the given tmint_{\mathrm{min}} and rr.

  1. Basis of rr. Short-term rate (between the last two inspections) or long-term rate (from original thickness)? From thickness readings, coupons, probes, or literature? Inspection practice commonly takes the greater of short-term and long-term rates. If the supplied 0.220.22 mm/year is a long-term rate and the short-term rate is higher, life is shorter in proportion (table in Section 4). Primary source that settles the point: the vessel's own inspection history with dated thickness readings at identified locations. Unverified here.
  2. Reference state for thickness. Date of the 1515 mm reading; original nominal thickness; location of the reading; whether 1515 mm is the minimum reading, a single reading, or an average. An average instead of a minimum overstates Δt\Delta t at the thinnest point and overstates LL.
  3. Pressure basis for tmint_{\mathrm{min}}. Design pressure and maximum allowable working pressure, stated as gauge or absolute; design temperature; material and its allowable stress at temperature; weld joint efficiency; corrosion allowance already included or not; code and edition (for example American Society of Mechanical Engineers ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section VIII). A change in any of these changes tmint_{\mathrm{min}}; each 11 mm change moves LL by 4.54.5 year at nominal rr. Primary source: the vessel rating calculation and data sheet / manufacturer's data report. Unverified here.
  4. Composition basis for future corrosion. Fluid composition, water content, acidity, chlorides, sulfur species, solids, and any planned process change. No composition was supplied; the constant-rate assumption stands in for it.
  5. Per-pass or overall analogue. Not applicable to wall loss directly; the corresponding distinction here is local versus overall: is rr an overall (area-averaged) rate or the rate at the controlling (thinnest, fastest-corroding) location? Life is governed by the controlling location. If rr is an average and the local maximum rate is twice the average, LL falls to about 13.613.6 year.
  6. Damage mechanism confirmation. That the mechanism is general corrosion only, with no localised corrosion, erosion, stress corrosion cracking, hydrogen damage, creep, or fatigue. Not supplied.
  7. Measurement uncertainty. Ultrasonic thickness instrument accuracy, surface condition, and reading repeatability. Not supplied; ±0.5\pm 0.5 mm was assumed in Section 4.
  8. Required decision rule. Retirement date, next inspection date, or a risk-based interval, and any owner-imposed cap on interval. Not supplied.

Two most likely alternative interpretations, solved: - (a) rr is the controlling long-term general rate and 1515 mm is the minimum reading: L=27.3L = 27.3 year nominal, range 2121–3737 year under Section 4 bands. - (b) rr is an average rate and local loss proceeds at twice rr: L=13.6L = 13.6 year nominal, and the low end under the same bands is about 1010 year (5.5/(2×0.264)5.5 / (2 \times 0.264)).

6. Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run; failures are reported and the solution was not altered to make them pass.

  1. Dimensional check — passes. mm divided by mm/year gives year.
  2. Closure check — passes. r×L=0.22×27.27=6.00r \times L = 0.22 \times 27.27 = 6.00 mm, equal to Δt\Delta t. Metal lost over the nominal life equals the available metal loss exactly; there is no other material or energy balance in this model to close.
  3. Limiting cases — pass. Δt→0\Delta t \to 0 gives L→0L \to 0 (a vessel already at tmint_{\mathrm{min}} has no remaining life). r→0r \to 0 gives L→∞L \to \infty (no corrosion, no corrosion-limited life). Both match the behaviour expected by sight.
  4. Executed code — passes. The calculation and all table values were recomputed in Python (executed for this solution): Δt=6.0\Delta t = 6.0 mm, L=27.2727L = 27.2727 year, half-life 13.6413.64 year, r=0.15r = 0.15 mm/year gives 40.0040.00 year, r=0.30r = 0.30 mm/year gives 20.0020.00 year, Δt=5.0\Delta t = 5.0 mm gives 22.7322.73 year, Δt=7.0\Delta t = 7.0 mm gives 31.8231.82 year. Code values match the hand values.
  5. Valid-range check on the model — conditional pass. The linear model has no correlation range to check; its validity condition is mechanistic (uniform general corrosion, constant environment). That condition is assumed, not demonstrated by the supplied data.
  6. Check that fails — verification of inputs. tmin=9t_{\mathrm{min}} = 9 mm and r=0.22r = 0.22 mm/year cannot be checked against any primary record from the data supplied. Both are taken as given. This check fails as a verification step and limits the confidence rating in Section 1.
7. Primary sources that settle the open points

Each claim resting on these sources is unverified until checked against the source itself.

  • Vessel inspection history: dated ultrasonic thickness readings at identified monitoring locations on this vessel — settles tat_{\mathrm{a}}, its minimum-versus-average status, and short-term and long-term rr.
  • Vessel rating calculation, data sheet, and manufacturer's data report, with the current ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section VIII, edition adopted by the jurisdiction — settles tmint_{\mathrm{min}}.
  • API 510, Pressure Vessel Inspection Code, current edition — settles inspection interval and remaining-life practice for in-service vessels.
  • API Recommended Practice 581, Risk-Based Inspection Methodology, current edition — settles damage-mechanism screening and rate treatment.
  • Corrosion data for the actual fluid–material pair: plant coupons / probes on this service, or a primary databank entry for the same material, fluid, and temperature — settles whether 0.220.22 mm/year is representative. A generic literature rate does not settle it.
8. Audit as by an experienced plant engineer (Prompt 4)

Three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. Localised loss controls, not the general rate. Pitting, corrosion under insulation, under-deposit corrosion, and inlet impingement commonly proceed at 22 to 1010 times the general rate at small areas. Direction: actual life shorter, by a factor of 22–1010 at the controlling spot (nominal LL of 27.327.3 year becomes about 2.72.7–13.613.6 year in those scenarios). Settled by: a gridded ultrasonic thickness survey or profile radiography of this vessel, and the inspection report identifying the minimum reading and its location.
  2. The future rate differs from the past rate. Temperature increase, water ingress, feed or composition change, or loss of a protective scale or coating raises rr; a +25%+25\% rise in rr cuts LL by 20%20\% (to 21.821.8 year). Direction: usually shorter life after an upset or process change; longer only if the service becomes milder. Settled by: process operating records, corrosion coupon / probe trends in this service, and comparison of short-term versus long-term rates from the inspection history.
  3. tmint_{\mathrm{min}} for the built vessel differs from the stated 99 mm. Re-rating, a pressure or temperature change, a lower joint efficiency after repair, or a different code edition moves tmint_{\mathrm{min}}. Direction: either way; each 11 mm moves LL by 4.54.5 year at nominal rr (16.7%16.7\% per mm). Settled by: the rating calculation for this vessel under the current code edition, confirmed by the authorised inspector's record.
9. What the calculation does not cover (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model: localised corrosion of all forms; erosion and erosion–corrosion; stress corrosion cracking; hydrogen damage; fatigue (pressure or thermal cycling); creep if operation is in the creep range; brittle fracture; external corrosion including corrosion under insulation as a separate external rate; microbiologically influenced corrosion; damage at nozzles, welds, and attachments where geometry and stress differ from the shell; simultaneous thinning on inner and outer surfaces (the stated model counts loss against one Δt\Delta t only).

Information not available here: the vessel's inspection history, rating calculation, drawings, and operating records (owner-held); restricted code text and primary corrosion databanks not supplied with the problem. Claims depending on them are marked unverified in Sections 5 and 7.

Effects appearing only in running equipment: rate acceleration after upsets, wet–dry cycling, scale spallation, coating failure, fouling-driven under-deposit attack, and changes after a turnaround repair or lining failure.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10%10\%: - rr changes by more than about 0.0220.022 mm/year (10%10\% of nominal) in either direction. - tat_{\mathrm{a}} or tmint_{\mathrm{min}} is in error by more than 0.60.6 mm (10%10\% of Δt\Delta t). - Loss is localised at more than 1.11.1 times the general rate at the controlling location. - A re-rating changes tmint_{\mathrm{min}}, or a process change alters temperature or fluid composition enough to move rr by the amount above. - Thinning occurs on both surfaces while rr describes only one.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used: 1. Is 1515 mm the minimum reading on this vessel, at which location, and on what date? 2. Is 0.220.22 mm/year the short-term rate, the long-term rate, or a literature value — and which is larger for this vessel? 3. What calculation, code edition, pressure basis (gauge or absolute), temperature, and joint efficiency produce tmin=9t_{\mathrm{min}} = 9 mm? 4. Has a damage-mechanism review excluded localised corrosion, cracking, and the other mechanisms in this section? 5. What inspection coverage supports the claim that no location is thinner than the reported reading? 6. Has the service, temperature, or composition changed since the rate was established, or is a change planned? 7. What decision will the number drive — retirement, next inspection, or continued operation — and what interval cap does the owner or API 510 (current edition, to be checked) impose regardless of the calculated life? 8. Who is the authorised inspector or engineer accepting this remaining-life figure?

10. Summary

At the given inputs, nominal remaining life is 27.327.3 year from 66 mm of available metal loss at 0.220.22 mm/year. Reported as a range under assumed uncertainty bands: about 2121 to 3737 year; about 13.613.6 year if the controlling local rate is twice the given rate. Confidence in the prediction is low until tat_{\mathrm{a}}, rr, and tmint_{\mathrm{min}} are checked against the vessel's inspection history and rating calculation named in Section 7.

G1. Capital Cost Estimation — Second Plant

Response without the skill

Cost Estimate by Capacity Scaling

Symbols
  • C1C_1 is the known cost of the reference unit, in million United States dollars (million USD).
  • C2C_2 is the estimated cost of the new unit, in million USD.
  • S1S_1 is the production capacity of the reference unit, in kilotonnes per year (kt/a), where 1 kt is 1,000 tonnes.
  • S2S_2 is the production capacity of the new unit, in kt/a.
  • nn is the capacity exponent, with no units.
Given values
  • S1=200 kt/aS_1 = 200\ \text{kt/a}
  • C1=26 million USDC_1 = 26\ \text{million USD}
  • S2=320 kt/aS_2 = 320\ \text{kt/a}
  • n=0.6n = 0.6
Method

For the same process, cost is estimated from a known unit by the capacity power law:

C2=C1(S2S1)nC_2 = C_1 \left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^{n}

The ratio S2/S1S_2/S_1 has no units, because both capacities are in kt/a.

Calculation

S2S1=320200=1.60\frac{S_2}{S_1} = \frac{320}{200} = 1.60

(S2S1)n=1.600.6=1.326\left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^{n} = 1.60^{0.6} = 1.326

C2=26×1.326=34.47 million USDC_2 = 26 \times 1.326 = 34.47\ \text{million USD}

Result

The estimated cost is approximately 35 million USD, or 34.5 million USD before rounding to two significant figures appropriate to this type of estimate.

Scope and limitation

The reference cost is stated to be from a different year and a different place, but no cost index for the change in year and no location factor for the change in place are given. The value above is therefore on the same year and place basis as the reference cost of 26 million USD.

A correction for year and place would require two additional quantities: a cost index ratio, defined as the cost index at the new year divided by the cost index at the reference year, with no units, and a location factor ratio, defined as the location factor at the new place divided by the location factor at the reference place, with no units. The corrected estimate would be the value above multiplied by both ratios. Without numerical values for those ratios, no corrected cost for the new year and new place can be calculated from the data given.

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Cost Estimate for a 320 kilotonne per year Unit by Capacity Scaling

Symbols, defined before first use
  • C1 (million United States dollars, USD, in the reference year and at the reference place) — capital cost of the reference unit.
  • C2 (million USD, basis stated in each result below) — capital cost of the new unit.
  • S1 (kilotonnes per year, kt/yr) — production capacity of the reference unit.
  • S2 (kt/yr) — production capacity of the new unit.
  • n (dimensionless, no units) — capacity exponent in the scaling relation.
  • F_t (dimensionless) — time correction factor, the ratio of a cost index in the target year to the same cost index in the reference year.
  • F_L (dimensionless) — location correction factor, the ratio of installed cost at the target place to installed cost at the reference place, other conditions equal.
  • F (dimensionless) — combined correction factor, F = F_t × F_L.
Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness: the problem gives a capacity scaling relation and a reference cost, but gives neither the reference year nor the target year, and neither the reference place nor the target place. The statement says the year and the place differ, so the two corrections that convert a reference cost into a target cost are exactly the corrections for which no data are supplied. The scaling arithmetic is therefore identifiable, and the actual cost of the new unit in its own year and place is not identifiable from the supplied data alone.

Confidence rating:

  • Arithmetic of the scaling step, on its stated basis: high.
  • Result as a cost in the reference year and at the reference place, for the same scope and design: low to moderate, because n is a fitted empirical exponent and the scope of C1 is not stated.
  • Result as the actual cost in the target year and at the target place: low. No defensible single value exists from the supplied data. A range under stated assumed correction factors is given instead, and that range is a scenario range, not a confidence interval.
Inputs, labelled at the point of use
  • S2 = 320 kt/yr — given.
  • S1 = 200 kt/yr — given.
  • C1 = 26 million USD — given. Its scope, year, and place are not given; see the missing-quantities list.
  • n = 0.6 — given for this problem. In general use this exponent is fitted (an empirical value fitted to cost data for similar plant), not measured on this plant. Its plausible range is treated below as an estimated range.
  • Same process, same product, and same design for both units — given in words ("a unit of the same process"), with the detailed scope left unstated.
  • F_t = 1 and F_L = 1 in the base result — assumed, for the base case only. These assumed values mean "no time correction and no location correction", i.e. the base result is expressed in the reference year and at the reference place. They are not claims about the actual target year or place.
Missing quantities (Prompt 2 — gaps filled by stated alternatives, not in silence)

No value below was taken in silence. Each missing quantity is either left as a factor in the formula or covered by the scenario alternatives in the results section.

  1. Basis of C1 — missing. Whether 26 million USD is inside-battery-limits cost, total installed cost, total module cost, engineering, procurement and construction cost, or total project cost including land, utilities and off-sites, owner's costs, start-up, working capital, taxes and duties, and contingency. This is the largest single gap: scope differences alone commonly change a plant total by tens of percent.
  2. Reference year and target year — missing. Needed to form F_t from a cost index.
  3. Identity and values of the cost index — missing. No index value is supplied for either year.
  4. Reference place and target place — missing. Needed to form F_L, and to account for labour rates, labour productivity, freight, taxes, duties, and local codes.
  5. Capacity basis — missing. Whether S1 and S2 are nameplate capacity, design capacity, or sustained operating rate, and the on-stream time (operating hours or days per year) behind "per year".
  6. Composition and specification basis — missing. Feed composition, product purity and specification, and conversion basis (per pass or overall) are not stated. For a cost-scaling estimate these matter only in so far as a change in any of them changes the design; "same process" is assumed to mean none of them change.
  7. Pressure and design basis — missing. Design pressures, temperatures, materials of construction, and the code edition and environmental and safety standards applied. A change in any of these between the two units breaks the "same design" assumption.
  8. Train configuration — missing. Whether each unit is a single train, and whether the larger unit stays within the size range of single items of equipment.
  9. Currency basis — stated only in part. Both costs are in USD (given for C1; assumed for C2). If either cost originates in another currency, the exchange rate and its date are missing.

Primary sources that settle these points, with every claim resting on them marked unverified until checked against the source itself: (a) the cost index series itself — the Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index as published by Chemical Engineering magazine, or an equivalent published index series — for F_t; (b) a published location-factor source for the two named places, or a contractor's location study, for F_L; (c) the reference plant's own cost breakdown or the vendor / engineering contractor document that produced the 26 million USD figure, for the scope of C1; (d) the AACE International recommended practice on estimate classification for the accuracy range attaching to an estimate of this class. No index value, location factor, scope definition, or accuracy range from those sources is used in the numbers below, because none was supplied and none has been checked here; any such number quoted elsewhere should be treated as unverified until checked against the source.

Relation used, its origin, and the range where it holds

Relation (fitted): C2 = C1 × (S2 / S1)^n, and with time and location corrections, C2 = C1 × (S2 / S1)^n × F_t × F_L.

Origin and status: this is the capacity-ratio ("six-tenths") rule, an empirical fitted relation for the capital cost of similar plant, in general use in process cost estimation (textbook treatments include Turton and co-authors, Analysis, Synthesis and Design of Chemical Processes, and Peters, Timmerhaus and West, Plant Design and Economics for Chemical Engineers — bibliographic details unverified here against the publisher record, and relied on only for the existence of the method, not for any number). It is a rule of thumb, not a physical law, and no property value of any material is used anywhere in this solution.

Range where it holds: similar technology, similar scope, similar design conditions, and a capacity ratio near unity. The ratio here, S2 / S1 = 1.6, is a modest extrapolation and is within the range in which the rule is normally applied. The rule degrades when the capacity ratio is large, when a size limit forces a second parallel train, when scope or standards change, and when n fitted for one class of plant is applied to another. A single exponent for a whole plant is an average over many items of equipment whose individual exponents differ.

Calculation (Prompt 1 and Prompt 3 — worked in code)

Capacity ratio: S2 / S1 = 320 / 200 = 1.6 (dimensionless).

Scaling factor at the given exponent: 1.6^0.6 = 1.3258 (dimensionless).

Base result, with F_t = 1 (assumed) and F_L = 1 (assumed):

C2 = 26 × 1.3258 = 34.47 million USD, reported as 34.5 million USD, in reference-year USD at the reference place and for the reference scope.

Executed check: the calculation was run in Python (26 * (320/200)**0.6), which returned 34.47032178033586 million USD. An independent route, the logarithmic form C2 = C1 × exp(n × ln(S2 / S1)), returned the same scaling factor, 1.325781606935995. The two routes agree to the digits shown; this is an arithmetic check only, not verification of the model.

Range from the exponent, the fitted input that carries the main model weakness

Plausible range for n: 0.5 to 0.7 — estimated, stated as a working range around the given 0.6 for whole-plant scaling, not measured or fitted for this process.

  • n = 0.5 (estimated, low end): C2 = 26 × 1.6^0.5 = 26 × 1.2649 = 32.9 million USD.
  • n = 0.6 (given): C2 = 34.5 million USD.
  • n = 0.7 (estimated, high end): C2 = 26 × 1.6^0.7 = 26 × 1.3896 = 36.1 million USD.

Scaling-only range: 32.9 to 36.1 million USD, on the reference basis (F = 1, assumed).

Sensitivity of the result to each guess, in percent, relative to 34.5 million USD:

  • n lower by 0.05, to 0.55: 33.7 million USD, a change of −2.3 percent.
  • n higher by 0.05, to 0.65: 35.3 million USD, a change of +2.4 percent.
  • n lower by 0.10, to 0.5: −4.6 percent. n higher by 0.10, to 0.7: +4.8 percent.
  • F different from 1 by any amount: the result moves by exactly that amount in percent, because F enters linearly. F = 1.2 moves the result by +20 percent; F = 0.8 moves it by −20 percent.
  • C1 read as a two-significant-figure figure, i.e. 25.5 to 26.5 million USD (assumed rounding range): the result moves by about −1.9 percent to +1.9 percent, to 33.8 to 35.1 million USD at n = 0.6.
  • Capacity figures taken as exact (given): no sensitivity assigned. If either capacity were a rounded nameplate figure, the effect would enter through the ratio 1.6 in the same way as the exponent effect, and would be smaller than the exponent effect for rounding at the level of a few percent.
Result for the target year and target place, under stated alternatives

Because F_t and F_L are both missing, the target-basis cost is reported as C2 = (scaling-only result) × F, for assumed values of F. Every F in this table is assumed for illustration of the arithmetic and the size of the effect; none is estimated from an index or a location source, and none should be used as a prediction.

Assumed F (dimensionless) C2 at n = 0.6 (million USD) C2 over n = 0.5 to 0.7 (million USD)
0.8 27.6 26.3 to 28.9
1.0 34.5 32.9 to 36.1
1.2 41.4 39.5 to 43.4
1.5 51.7 49.3 to 54.2

Scenario range, across the assumed F values 0.8 to 1.5 and the estimated exponent range 0.5 to 0.7: 26.3 to 54.2 million USD. This range is wide because the missing corrections are multiplicative and unbounded by the supplied data; a longer time gap or a larger location difference would widen it further. The correct use of this table is to read off the result once F_t and F_L have been obtained from the primary sources named above, not to adopt any row as the answer.

Final answer, stated with its basis: 34.5 million USD on the reference basis (reference year, reference place, reference scope), with a scaling-only range of 32.9 to 36.1 million USD for n from 0.5 to 0.7; the cost in the target year and at the target place is 34.5 million USD multiplied by F_t and by F_L, both of which are missing and must be supplied from a published cost index and a location source before a target-basis figure is used.

Independent checks (Prompt 3)

Checks were run as stated, and failing or inapplicable checks are reported rather than adjusted away.

  1. Limiting case, equal capacities: S2 = S1 gives a scaling factor of 1 and C2 = C1 = 26 million USD, as required. Pass.
  2. Limiting case, n = 0: cost independent of capacity, C2 = 26 million USD for any capacity. This is the known behaviour of the relation at that exponent and is not a realistic plant; it confirms the formula, not the plant. Pass as a formula check.
  3. Limiting case, n = 1: cost proportional to capacity, C2 = 26 × 1.6 = 41.6 million USD. The given exponent 0.6 gives a result below this, which is the expected direction for economies of scale. Pass.
  4. Monotonicity: the computed cost rises with n and with capacity over the range checked in code (n from 0.5 to 1.0). Pass.
  5. Material and energy balance closure: not applicable. This is a capital cost scaling with no material or energy quantities; there is no balance to close. Reported as inapplicable, not as passed.
  6. Valid-range check on the fitted relation: capacity ratio 1.6 is modest and within the range in which the rule is normally applied, provided train configuration and scope are unchanged — both of which are missing quantities, so this check is conditional, not a clean pass.
  7. Independent arithmetic route: direct power and logarithmic form agree, as reported in the calculation section. Pass, for arithmetic only.
  8. Agreement with another AI model: not used, and not treated as verification.

No check was failed by the arithmetic. The checks that do not pass cleanly are the model checks (items 5 and 6), and they do not pass because the scope, train configuration, year, and place are missing, not because of an arithmetic error.

Audit as for built equipment (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ between this estimate and built equipment, each with direction, rough size, and the record that would settle it:

  1. Train and maximum equipment size. If any item in the 320 kt/yr unit exceeds the largest size that can be fabricated, transported, or operated as a single item, that section is built as two parallel trains and its cost rises in a step rather than along the smooth scaling curve. Direction: upward. Rough size: of the order of 10 to 30 percent on the affected section, and a smaller but material amount on the plant total; the figures are estimated and unverified. Settling document: the equipment list with item sizes for both units, and vendor confirmation of maximum single-item sizes.
  2. Time and place effects larger than any assumed factor. Construction labour productivity, labour rates, freight, duties, permitting, and code requirements at the target place, and cost escalation between the two years, act multiplicatively on the whole total and are entirely absent from the supplied data. Direction: either direction; upward over a long time gap is the more common case. Rough size: a combined factor anywhere in the assumed 0.8 to 1.5 range used above is plausible, and values outside it are not excluded; estimated and unverified. Settling sources: the published cost index values for the two years, and a location-factor study or contractor quotation for the two places.
  3. Scope and standards growth between the two units. A later unit is commonly built to tighter environmental, safety, and product-specification requirements, and with more utilities, off-sites, automation, and contingency than the reference unit carried. Direction: upward. Rough size: of the order of 10 to 50 percent on total project cost if the reference figure is a battery-limits figure and the required figure is a total project figure; estimated and unverified. Settling document: the reference cost breakdown and a scope definition (battery-limits diagram and an inclusions and exclusions list) for the new unit, priced by an engineering contractor.

General accuracy expectation: an estimate made from a single reference cost and an exponent, with no scope definition, is a study-grade estimate. Published classification practice (AACE International, unverified here against the current edition) attaches ranges of the general order of −50 percent to +100 percent to the lowest class of estimate; that range is quoted only to indicate the class of the estimate and must be checked against the current recommended practice before use.

What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model:

  • Any change in technology, design conditions, materials, product specification, feed, environmental or safety standards, or automation level between the two units.
  • Train splitting and all other step changes in cost with size; the relation is smooth and real plant cost is not.
  • Utilities, off-sites, land, infrastructure, grid or feedstock connections, and owner's costs, unless they were inside the scope of C1 in the same proportion.
  • Financing cost, escalation during construction, schedule effects, market conditions at the time of contracting, contractor capacity, and currency movement.
  • Contingency, and any difference in contingency policy between the two estimates.
  • Operating cost, maintenance cost, catalyst and chemicals, and revenue: this is a capital cost estimate only.

Information not available to this calculation: the reference plant's cost breakdown, vendor quotations, contractor location studies, and the values in commercial cost databanks and in the current editions of codes and recommended practices, all of which are held by their publishers or owners and none of which has been checked here. Every statement above that rests on such a source is marked unverified.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: actual achieved capacity against nameplate capacity (which changes the effective cost per unit of real output), fouling, degradation and reliability differences that drive sparing and therefore installed cost, and site conditions found during construction. None of these is represented.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 percent:

  • F, the product of F_t and F_L, differs from 1 by more than 0.10 in either direction — a modest escalation over a few years, or a move to a higher-cost location, is sufficient.
  • The scope required is total project cost while C1 is a battery-limits cost, or the reverse.
  • A main section splits into two trains at the larger capacity.
  • Design standards, materials, or product specification change between the two units.
  • n fitted for this process differs from 0.6 by more than about 0.2 (at a capacity ratio of 1.6, a change of 0.1 in n changes the result by about 5 percent, so a change of 0.2 changes it by about 10 percent).

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. What exactly does the 26 million USD include, and is the required figure on the same scope?
  2. Which years and which places, and what are F_t and F_L from the published index and a location source, checked at source?
  3. Is n = 0.6 fitted for this process and this plant class, and over what capacity range?
  4. Are both capacities on the same basis (nameplate, design, or sustained rate, at the same on-stream time)?
  5. Is the 320 kt/yr unit a single train, within maximum single-item equipment sizes?
  6. Have codes, environmental and safety standards, materials, or product specification changed between the two units?
  7. What contingency and accuracy range does the user of the estimate require, and is a study-grade estimate sufficient for the decision it will support?
  8. Has an independent estimate (equipment-factored or vendor-based) been made for comparison, rather than a second application of the same scaling rule?

G2. Energy Integration — Second Saving

Response without the skill

Yearly Money Saving from Heat Recovery

Given data
  • The minimum approach temperature, defined as the smallest temperature difference between a hot stream and a cold stream in the heat recovery system, is 15 kelvin (K).
  • The recovered heat duty, defined as the rate of heat transfer recovered by the change, symbol QQ, is 6 megawatts (MW), where 1 megawatt (MW) is 10610^6 watts (W).
  • The unit cost of energy, symbol cc, is 28 United States dollars per megawatt hour (USD/MWh), where a megawatt hour (MWh) is the energy transferred at 1 megawatt (MW) for 1 hour (h).
  • The annual operating time, symbol tt, is 8,000 hours per year (h/yr).
Calculation

The annual recovered energy, symbol EE, in megawatt hours per year (MWh/yr), is the recovered heat duty QQ multiplied by the annual operating time tt:

E=Q×tE = Q \times t

E=6 MW×8,000 h/yr=48,000 MWh/yrE = 6\ \mathrm{MW} \times 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/yr} = 48{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/yr}

The yearly money saving, symbol SS, in United States dollars per year (USD/yr), is the annual recovered energy EE multiplied by the unit cost of energy cc:

S=E×c=Q×t×cS = E \times c = Q \times t \times c

S=48,000 MWh/yr×28 USD/MWh=1,344,000 USD/yrS = 48{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/yr} \times 28\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} = 1{,}344{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/yr}

Result

The yearly money saving is 1,344,000 United States dollars per year (USD/yr), approximately 1.34 million United States dollars per year.

This estimate assumes that the recovered heat duty QQ of 6 megawatts (MW) at the minimum approach temperature of 15 kelvin (K) is maintained over the full 8,000 hours per year (h/yr), and that each megawatt hour (MWh) recovered displaces energy that would otherwise be purchased at 28 United States dollars per megawatt hour (USD/MWh).

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Yearly Money Saving from Heat Recovery — Estimate

Symbols and units

Defined before first use:

  • SS = yearly money saving, in United States dollars per year (USD/year)
  • QrecQ_{\mathrm{rec}} = recovered heat duty, in megawatts (MW); 1 MW = 1 megawatt of thermal power
  • cEc_{E} = energy price, in United States dollars per megawatt hour (USD/MWh)
  • topt_{\mathrm{op}} = plant operating time per year, in hours per year (h/year)
  • ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} = minimum approach temperature in the heat-exchanger network, in kelvin (K)
  • η\eta = efficiency of the heater, boiler, or furnace whose fuel input is displaced, dimensionless (no unit)
  • ff = utilisation factor, the fraction of operating time at which the full recovered duty is actually realised, dimensionless
1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The arithmetic is exact. The weakness is the translation of a design recovered duty into a realised cash saving. A recovered duty obtained at a stated ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} is normally a pinch-analysis or design estimate, not a metered, year-average duty on built equipment. The calculation as stated treats every recovered megawatt hour as one purchased megawatt hour saved, at a constant price, for every operating hour. Built equipment departs from that in fouling, control, availability, displaced-utility identity, and the efficiency of the equipment whose load is displaced.

Confidence rating.

  • Arithmetic from the stated inputs: high, essentially 100 %, verified in code below.
  • SS as the realised yearly cash saving: low to moderate, about 50–60 % that the realised value lies within ±10 % of the headline figure, until the basis of cEc_{E} (delivered heat or fuel input), the displaced utility, and a measured average QrecQ_{\mathrm{rec}} are supplied. The range in §3, not the single headline value, is the defensible result.
2. Headline calculation — Prompt 1

Inputs, labelled at the point of use:

  • Qrec=6 MWQ_{\mathrm{rec}} = 6\ \mathrm{MW} — given in the problem, at ΔTmin⁡=15 K\Delta T_{\min} = 15\ \mathrm{K} (given). Its origin (pinch target, design rating, or measurement) is not stated; treated here as an estimated design value, not a measured year average.
  • cE=28 USD/MWhc_{E} = 28\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} — given. Whether it is a fuel-input price or a delivered-energy price is not stated; see §4.
  • top=8,000 h/yeart_{\mathrm{op}} = 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year} — given.

Relation used:

S=Qrec×top×cES = Q_{\mathrm{rec}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}} \times c_{E}

Substitution:

S=6 MW×8,000 h/year×28 USD/MWh=1,344,000 USD/yearS = 6\ \mathrm{MW} \times 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year} \times 28\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} = 1{,}344{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}

Headline result: S=1.34S = 1.34 million USD/year, on the delivered-energy basis, before capital, maintenance, and extra pumping costs, and before any efficiency correction.

No property value, correlation, or fitted relation is used. There is no fluid, composition, pressure, or phase in the stated problem, so no databank property enters. The only relations are the definition of energy as power multiplied by time, and the definition of cost as energy multiplied by unit price.

3. Range, not a single value

The input that carries the weakness is the effective yearly displaced energy. Two assumed factors bound it, neither supplied in the problem:

  1. η\eta, assumed in the range 0.75 to 0.90 if cEc_{E} is a fuel price. A typical industrial boiler or fired-heater efficiency range used here only as a scenario bound; it is unverified for this plant and must be settled against the plant's own heater record (see §6). If cEc_{E} is instead a delivered-heat or steam price, η=1\eta = 1 by definition of that basis and no correction applies. Effect on SS: dividing by η\eta raises SS by +11 % (η=0.90\eta = 0.90) to +33 % (η=0.75\eta = 0.75).
  2. ff, assumed in the range 0.90 to 1.00, allowing for fouling, turndown, control loss, and periods when the source or sink stream is unavailable. Effect on SS: −10 % to 0 %.

Range computed at the ends, with S=f×Qrec×top×cE/ηS = f \times Q_{\mathrm{rec}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}} \times c_{E} / \eta where the η\eta division is applied only on the fuel-price basis:

Case Basis (labelled) ff (assumed) η\eta SS (USD/year)
Low, delivered basis cEc_{E} is delivered-energy price 0.90 1.00 1,209,600
Headline, delivered basis cEc_{E} is delivered-energy price 1.00 1.00 1,344,000
Fuel basis, high η\eta cEc_{E} is fuel-input price 1.00 0.90 (assumed) 1,493,333
Fuel basis, low η\eta cEc_{E} is fuel-input price 1.00 0.75 (assumed) 1,792,000
Combined low delivered basis, low utilisation 0.90 1.00 1,209,600
Combined high fuel basis, full utilisation 1.00 0.75 (assumed) 1,792,000

Reported result: SS in the range 1.21 to 1.79 million USD/year, with 1.34 million USD/year on the stated, delivered-energy, full-utilisation basis.

Sensitivity of each guess, stated separately:

  • η\eta from 1.00 to 0.75: +0 % to +33 %.
  • ff from 1.00 to 0.90: 0 % to −10 %.
  • A ±10 % change in cEc_{E}, QrecQ_{\mathrm{rec}}, or topt_{\mathrm{op}} each moves SS by exactly ±10 %, because SS is linear in all three. No non-linear amplification is present.

Data supplied by the user supersede these assumed ranges: a plant-supplied η\eta, ff, or metered average duty replaces the corresponding scenario bound for that case.

4. Missing quantities — Prompt 2

The problem was not completed silently. The following quantities are missing. The headline value is conditional on the stated alternative in each row.

Missing quantity Why it matters Alternatives solved

5. Independent check — Prompt 3

Checks performed in executed code (Python), separate from the hand arithmetic:

  1. Direct recomputation. 6.0×8,000×28=1,344,0006.0 \times 8{,}000 \times 28 = 1{,}344{,}000 USD/year. Agrees with §2.
  2. Per-unit route. One megawatt recovered for 8,0008{,}000 h/year at 2828 USD/MWh saves 224,000224{,}000 USD/year per MW. Six megawatts: 6×224,000=1,344,0006 \times 224{,}000 = 1{,}344{,}000 USD/year. Agrees.
  3. Daily route. 6 MW×24 h×28 USD/MWh=4,0326\ \mathrm{MW} \times 24\ \mathrm{h} \times 28\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} = 4{,}032 USD per operating day. At 8,0008{,}000 h/year there are 333.3333.3 operating days per year; 4,032×333.3=1,344,0004{,}032 \times 333.3 = 1{,}344{,}000 USD/year. Agrees.
  4. Dimensional check. MW × (h/year) = MWh/year; MWh/year × USD/MWh = USD/year. Units close.
  5. Limiting cases, known by sight. Qrec=0Q_{\mathrm{rec}} = 0 gives S=0S = 0; top=0t_{\mathrm{op}} = 0 gives S=0S = 0; η=1\eta = 1 on the fuel basis recovers the delivered basis. All pass.
  6. Energy-balance closure. There is no material balance in this problem. The energy statement is an identity, recovered energy =Qrec×top=48,000= Q_{\mathrm{rec}} \times t_{\mathrm{op}} = 48{,}000 MWh/year, so closure is exact by construction; this is a statement about the arithmetic, not evidence that 48,00048{,}000 MWh/year is physically displaced in a plant. That physical closure can only be checked against metered fuel or steam use before and after the change.

No check failed. No check was adjusted to pass. Agreement with any other model or AI output is not claimed as verification; the checks above are arithmetic and dimensional only.

6. Audit against built equipment — Prompt 4

Three points most likely to differ from built-equipment behaviour:

  1. Fouling and duty decay. Direction: realised QrecQ_{\mathrm{rec}} falls below the clean or target duty, so SS falls. Rough size: 5–20 % over a run between cleanings for fouling services, captured only partly by f=0.90f = 0.90 in §3. Settling document: exchanger datasheet fouling resistances and the plant historian trend of the exchanger inlet and outlet temperatures and flows on the actual unit.
  2. Displaced load is not the design load. The recovered heat may displace steam let-down, a partially loaded boiler, or a heater operating at an efficiency different from its nameplate value, or it may at times exceed what the sink can accept and be vented or bypassed. Direction: usually lower saving, occasionally higher on a fuel basis if the displaced heater is inefficient. Rough size: ±10–30 %. Settling record: utility meter and fuel invoice data for the affected system, before and after, normalised for production rate and ambient conditions; boiler or furnace efficiency test on the actual equipment.
  3. Added pressure drop and utility interactions. New or re-piped exchangers add pressure drop, raising pumping or compression power, and may shift load to cooling water or refrigeration elsewhere. Direction: net saving lower than gross. Rough size: commonly 1–5 % of the gross saving, larger where a new pump or fan is required. Settling document: the hydraulic calculation and pump datasheets for the modified circuit, and metered cooling duty after the change.

Primary source that settles the central point: the plant's own metered utility consumption and fuel invoices, together with the data historian record for the modified exchangers, on the actual plant. The assumed ranges for η\eta and ff in §3 are unverified until checked against those records. No vendor document or databank value in this solution is presented as verified.

7. What is not covered — Prompt 5

Effects not in the model:

  • Capital cost of exchangers, piping, controls, installation, and downtime for the change, and therefore payback period and return on investment. SS is a gross operating saving, not a project return.
  • Maintenance, cleaning, inspection, and exchanger replacement over life.
  • Extra pumping or compression energy, and any increase in cooling-water, refrigeration, or effluent-treatment load.
  • Carbon dioxide emissions change and any carbon price, credit, or allowance value.
  • Price escalation, contract renegotiation, taxes, and the time value of money.
  • Operability effects: start-up, shutdown, turndown, control stability, product quality, and safety-system changes arising from tighter heat integration, including reduced flexibility at low ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} margins.
  • Degradation of QrecQ_{\mathrm{rec}} if feed composition, throughput, or stream temperatures move away from the design case used for the pinch target.

Information not available to this calculation: plant historian data, utility contracts and invoices, exchanger datasheets, and any restricted design or databank material held by the plant or its licensor. None was seen.

Effects that appear only in running equipment: fouling rates, maldistribution, bypassing, control-valve saturation, and seasonal variation in source and sink temperatures.

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %:

  • cEc_{E} is a fuel price and η<0.91\eta < 0.91 (+10 % or more).
  • Realised average duty falls more than 10 % below 6 MW, from fouling, unavailability, or sink limitation.
  • Actual operating time or full-duty utilisation falls more than 10 % below 8,0008{,}000 h/year.
  • Energy price moves more than 10 % from 28 USD/MWh.
  • Net costs (pumping, maintenance, annualised capital) exceed 10 % of the gross saving, if a net figure is required.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used:

  1. Is 28 USD/MWh a fuel-input price or a delivered-energy price, and for which utility?
  2. Is 6 MW a pinch target, a clean design duty, or a measured average, and over what period?
  3. Which heater, boiler, or steam header loses load, and what is its measured efficiency at its actual operating load?
  4. What are the added pressure drops, and what pump or fan power do they cost?
  5. What capital and maintenance costs must be set against the gross saving, and over what project life?
  6. How will the saving be verified after implementation — which meters, over what period, normalised for what production and ambient variables?
Result
  • Gross yearly energy saving on the stated basis: 1,344,000 USD/year.
  • Defensible range under the labelled assumed alternatives: 1,209,600 to 1,792,000 USD/year.
  • Confidence: high in the arithmetic; low to moderate (about 50–60 % for ±10 % accuracy) in the realised cash saving, pending the price basis, the displaced equipment efficiency, and a measured average recovered duty from the plant's own records.

G3. Carbon Intensity — Second Plant

Yearly Greenhouse Gas Emissions — Estimate

Given data and definitions

1. Carbon dioxide from fuel combustion

ECO2=Q×EFE_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = Q \times EF

Convert QQ to gigajoules per year (GJ/year):

Q=900 TJ/year×1000 GJ/TJ=900,000 GJ/yearQ = 900\ \mathrm{TJ/year} \times 1000\ \mathrm{GJ/TJ} = 900{,}000\ \mathrm{GJ/year}

Methane released unburned is not counted at its own mass alone. It is converted to carbon dioxide equivalent using GWP100GWP_{100}:

ECH4=mCH4×GWP100E_{\mathrm{CH_4}} = m_{\mathrm{CH_4}} \times GWP_{100}

ECH4=900 t/year×28=25,200 t CO2e/year≈25.2 kt CO2e/yearE_{\mathrm{CH_4}} = 900\ \mathrm{t/year} \times 28 = 25{,}200\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/year} \approx 25.2\ \mathrm{kt\ CO_2e/year}

The methane term is therefore about one third of the total, although its mass (900 t/year) is much smaller than the mass of combustion carbon dioxide. Omitting it, or adding 900 t/year directly without the GWP100GWP_{100} factor, would understate the total materially.

Etotal≈75,700 t CO2e/year≈75.7 kt CO2e/year\boxed{E_{\mathrm{total}} \approx 75{,}700\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/year} \approx 75.7\ \mathrm{kt\ CO_2e/year}}

I=EtotalPI = \frac{E_{\mathrm{total}}}{P}

Response with the skill (generic layer)

Yearly Greenhouse Gas Emissions — Estimate

1. Weakness and confidence rating

Weakness. The carbon dioxide (CO₂) part is a direct multiplication and is well determined. The total greenhouse gas (GHG) result, expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e), is not. The problem gives no:

  • global warming potential (GWP) for methane (CH₄) — the factor, in kilograms of CO₂e per kilogram of CH₄, that converts a mass of CH₄ to CO₂e over a stated time horizon;
  • time horizon for that GWP (20 years or 100 years give values differing by about a factor of 3 for CH₄);
  • assessment version or inventory convention that fixes the GWP (for example Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fourth, Fifth, or Sixth Assessment Report, hereafter AR4, AR5, and AR6);
  • statement of whether the CH₄ is fossil in origin (fossil CH₄ carries an extra CO₂ term when it oxidises in the atmosphere, so its GWP is higher).

Confidence rating: Low for a single total CO₂e value; High for the combustion CO₂ value alone.

  • Combustion CO₂: high confidence, conditional on the given emission factor and on the energy basis behind it (Section 2).
  • Total CO₂e on a 100-year horizon: moderate confidence as a range (Section 3), because the plausible GWP range is narrow.
  • Total CO₂e as a single number, and any comparison with another plant or a reporting threshold: low confidence until the GWP convention, the horizon, and the inventory scope are fixed in writing. Changing only the horizon from 100 years to 20 years moves the total by about +65 % (Section 4), which is larger than every other uncertainty in the problem combined.

No single total is therefore reported as the answer. A 100-year range is reported as the main result, and the 20-year result is reported alongside it.

2. Inputs, labelled at the point of use, and missing quantities (Prompts 1 and 2)
2.1 Given inputs
Quantity Value State
Fuel gas energy supplied, EE (terajoules per year, TJ yr⁻¹; 1 TJ = 1,000 gigajoules, GJ) 900 TJ yr⁻¹ given
Emission factor for the fuel gas, EFEF (kilograms of CO₂ per gigajoule, kg GJ⁻¹) 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹ given
CH₄ released unburned, mCH4m_{\mathrm{CH4}} (tonnes per year, t yr⁻¹; 1 t = 1,000 kg) 900 t yr⁻¹ given
Product made, PP (kilotonnes per year, kt yr⁻¹; 1 kt = 1,000 t) 60 kt yr⁻¹ = 60,000 t yr⁻¹ given

No input is stated in the problem to be measured, fitted, or estimated. In practice the 900 t yr⁻¹ CH₄ figure in a real plant is almost always an estimated inventory figure (from leak factors, component counts, or a mass balance difference), not a directly measured one; it is treated here as given for the arithmetic, and as estimated, with large uncertainty, for the audit in Section 6. That distinction must be resolved before the result is used (Section 7).

2.2 Missing quantities — not taken in silence
  1. GWP value, horizon, and source. Missing. Solved under the plausible alternatives in Section 3: AR4, AR5, and AR6 100-year values, and AR6/AR5 20-year values.
  2. Fossil or non-fossil CH₄. Missing. The plant burns fuel gas, so the escaped gas is most plausibly fossil, which selects the higher AR6 value (29.8 rather than 27.2). Both are carried in the range.
  3. Energy basis of EE and EFEF. Missing: net calorific value (NCV, also called lower heating value) or gross calorific value (GCV, also called higher heating value). The value 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹ matches the IPCC 2006 default CO₂ emission factor for natural gas, which is stated on an NCV basis — unverified until checked against that source (Section 5). If the 900 TJ yr⁻¹ was metered on a GCV basis and multiplied by an NCV factor, the combustion CO₂ is overstated by roughly the GCV/NCV ratio for natural gas, about 10 %. This one basis error alone can move the combustion term by about 10 %.
  4. Scope of the emission factor. Missing: whether EFEF covers CO₂ only, or CO₂ plus the small CH₄ and nitrous oxide (N₂O) formed in combustion. The units given (kg CO₂ per GJ, not kg CO₂e per GJ) indicate CO₂ only. Combustion CH₄ and N₂O are treated as excluded; for gas firing they are normally well under 1 % of the combustion CO₂e, but that is an assumed magnitude, not a given one.
  5. Inventory scope. Missing: whether "GHG emissions of the plant" means direct (Scope 1) emissions only — fuel combustion plus fugitive CH₄ — or also purchased electricity and heat (Scope 2) and upstream and downstream emissions (Scope 3). Only Scope 1 can be computed from the data given. The result below is a Scope 1 result and must be labelled as such wherever it is used.
  6. Reference state and pressure basis. Not needed for this calculation: no gas volume, density, or standard-cubic-metre quantity is used. If the 900 TJ yr⁻¹ was itself derived from a metered volume, its reference temperature, pressure basis (absolute or gauge, and the standard condition used), and composition basis would be needed to audit that derivation; none is supplied.
  7. Composition basis of the fuel gas and of the escaped gas. Missing: whether the escaped 900 t yr⁻¹ is pure CH₄ or total gas expressed as CH₄. Treated here as pure CH₄, as stated. If it is total hydrocarbon gas, the CH₄ part, and hence the CO₂e, is lower.
  8. Per-pass or overall conversion. Not applicable: no reactor conversion is stated or used. The fugitive figure is taken as an overall, plant-level yearly release.
  9. Product basis for any intensity figure. The product rate is given as a mass per year, so the intensity in Section 3 is per tonne of product as made, with no purity, dry, or saleable-product correction. Any such correction is missing.

Primary source that settles the central point. The GWP values and the horizon convention are settled by (a) the reporting framework the result will be submitted under (for example the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Standard, or the applicable national inventory / emissions-trading rules, current edition), which prescribes which assessment report to use, and (b) within that choice, the IPCC assessment report itself — for AR6, Working Group I, Chapter 7, Table 7.15 (GWP values for CH₄). The emission-factor basis is settled by the IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, Volume 2, Chapter 2, Table 2.2 (default CO₂ emission factor for natural gas), or by a fuel-specific factor from the fuel supplier's analysis for the actual gas burned. Every GWP value and the emission-factor identity used below rest on those sources and are marked unverified until checked against them.

3. Calculation and result as a range

All arithmetic was executed in code (Section 5); the figures below are the code output, rounded at the end.

3.1 Combustion CO₂

EE = 900 TJ yr⁻¹ (given) = 900 × 1,000 = 900,000 GJ yr⁻¹. EFEF = 56.1 kg CO₂ GJ⁻¹ (given).

Combustion CO₂ = E×EFE \times EF = 900,000 GJ yr⁻¹ × 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹ = 50,490,000 kg yr⁻¹

= 50,490 t CO₂ yr⁻¹ ≈ 50.5 kt CO₂ yr⁻¹.

This term does not depend on any GWP choice.

Uncertainty on this term from the emission factor alone: the IPCC default factor for natural gas carries a 95 % confidence range of about 54.3 to 58.3 kg GJ⁻¹ around 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹ — a fitted / tabulated range, unverified until checked against IPCC 2006, Volume 2, Table 2.2. Applied to the given energy, that range gives 48,870 to 52,470 t CO₂ yr⁻¹, i.e. about −3 % to +4 % on this term. A plant-specific factor from the actual gas analysis would supersede this range; data supplied by the user, the plant, or a vendor supersede the study ranges used here.

3.2 Fugitive CH₄, converted to CO₂e

mCH4m_{\mathrm{CH4}} = 900 t yr⁻¹ (given). GWP values below are assumed by choice of convention, not given, and are unverified until checked against the IPCC source named in Section 2.2.

Convention (all assumed, unverified) GWP (kg CO₂e per kg CH₄) CH₄ term (t CO₂e yr⁻¹)
AR4, 100-year 25 22,500
AR6, non-fossil, 100-year 27.2 24,480
AR5, 100-year 28 25,200
AR6, fossil, 100-year 29.8 26,820
AR6, fossil, 20-year 82.5 74,250
AR5, 20-year 84 75,600
3.3 Total — reported as a range, not a single value

Main result (100-year horizon, Scope 1 only):

  • Lower end (AR4 GWP = 25, assumed): 50,490 + 22,500 = 72,990 t CO₂e yr⁻¹
  • Central illustrative value (AR5 GWP = 28, assumed): 50,490 + 25,200 = 75,690 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ ≈ 75.7 kt CO₂e yr⁻¹
  • Upper end (AR6 fossil GWP = 29.8, assumed): 50,490 + 26,820 = 77,310 t CO₂e yr⁻¹

Report as: about 73,000 to 77,000 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ on a 100-year basis, widening to about 71,000 to 79,000 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ if the emission-factor range in Section 3.1 is combined with the GWP range (48,870 + 22,500 = 71,370; 52,470 + 26,820 = 79,290).

Alternative result (20-year horizon, Scope 1 only): 50,490 + 74,250 to 75,600 = about 125,000 to 126,000 t CO₂e yr⁻¹. This is not an error bound on the 100-year figure; it is the answer to a different question, and the two must never be mixed in one comparison.

Emission intensity (using PP = 60,000 t yr⁻¹, given):

  • 100-year: 72,990 / 60,000 to 77,310 / 60,000 = 1.22 to 1.29 t CO₂e per t product (central AR5 value 1.26 t t⁻¹).
  • 20-year: about 2.08 to 2.10 t CO₂e per t product.
  • Combustion CO₂ only, for reference: 50,490 / 60,000 = 0.84 t CO₂ per t product. Reporting this figure alone as "the GHG emissions" would omit about one third of the 100-year Scope 1 total and about three fifths of the 20-year total.

Composition of the 100-year central total: combustion 67 %, fugitive CH₄ 33 %. The fugitive term is not a minor correction.

Property values, rules, and relations used, with source and range of validity:

  • EFEF = 56.1 kg CO₂ GJ⁻¹: given. It coincides with the IPCC 2006 default for natural gas combustion on an NCV basis (unverified against that table). It holds for pipeline natural gas burned to completion; it does not hold for a fuel gas rich in hydrogen, carbon monoxide, or heavy hydrocarbons (for example refinery fuel gas of variable composition), where a composition-based factor is required.
  • GWP values (25, 27.2, 28, 29.8, 82.5, 84): from IPCC AR4, AR5, and AR6 respectively (unverified against AR6 Working Group I, Chapter 7, Table 7.15 and the corresponding AR4/AR5 tables). A GWP is a policy-weighted index integrated over its stated horizon for a pulse emission; it is not a physical property of CH₄, and it holds only within the horizon and assessment version stated with it.
  • Stoichiometric check factor 44/16 (molar mass of CO₂, 44 kg per kilomole, divided by molar mass of CH₄, 16 kg per kilomole): exact stoichiometry for complete combustion of pure CH₄; used only in Section 5.
  • Lower heating value of CH₄ of about 50 megajoules per kilogram (MJ kg⁻¹): a standard tabulated value, estimated for the plausibility check in Sections 5 and 6 only; not used in the main result.
5. Verification by an independent route (Prompt 3)

Checks were run in code; the code recomputed every figure in Section 3 from the given inputs. Checks that fail are reported as failing.

  1. Executed code. Python calculation of E×EFE \times EF, of each CH₄ × GWP product, of each total, and of each intensity reproduced the values in Section 3 exactly (50,490 t CO₂ yr⁻¹; totals 72,990, 74,970, 75,690, 77,310 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ at GWP 25, 27.2, 28, 29.8; 124,740 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ at GWP 82.5). Pass.
  2. Independent carbon-balance route. If the fuel were pure CH₄ with a lower heating value of about 50 MJ kg⁻¹ (estimated), the fuel mass burned would be 900,000 GJ yr⁻¹ / 50 GJ t⁻¹ = 18,000 t yr⁻¹, and complete combustion of that mass gives 18,000 × 44/16 = 49,500 t CO₂ yr⁻¹. The emission-factor route gives 50,490 t yr⁻¹, 2.0 % higher. A small excess is expected for real natural gas, which contains heavier hydrocarbons with more carbon per unit of energy than pure CH₄. Pass, within the expected few percent. This check would fail, and would expose a basis or transcription error, if the two routes differed by more than about 10 %.
  3. Limiting cases. (a) Zero fugitive CH₄: total = 50,490 t CO₂e yr⁻¹, the combustion term alone — correct by construction. (b) Zero fuel use with the stated leak retained: total = the CH₄ term alone (22,500 to 26,820 t CO₂e yr⁻¹ at 100-year GWP) — arithmetically correct, and physically a warning sign, since a plant burning no gas would have no gas to leak (Section 6). Pass arithmetically.
  4. Balance closure. No plant material or energy balance was supplied, so no balance can be closed beyond check 2. In particular the fuel-gas balance (gas in = gas burned + gas leaked) cannot be closed from the data given, because total gas supply is not stated. Check not possible — reported as not possible, not as passed.
  5. Correlation / factor valid range. EFEF is used at its tabulated natural-gas value, inside its stated fuel class, conditional on the NCV basis (Section 2.2, item 3). The GWP values are used only at their stated horizons. No fitted relation is extrapolated. Pass, conditional on the unverified source check in Section 2.2.
  6. No agreement with another AI model is used as verification anywhere in this solution. Verification rests only on the arithmetic, the stoichiometric route, and the named primary sources, which remain to be checked.
6. Audit as an experienced plant engineer (Prompt 4)

The three points most likely to differ from how built equipment behaves:

  1. The fugitive CH₄ figure, and the leak rate it implies. Direction: factor-based fugitive inventories most often understate real releases, because a small number of large, intermittent sources (relief events, compressor seal failures, open vents, incomplete flaring) dominate real totals and are absent from average factors; the reverse is also possible if the figure is a conservative design allowance. Rough size: the implied leak is about 5 % of throughput — 900 t yr⁻¹ leaked against about 16,400 to 18,800 t yr⁻¹ burned (from the check in Section 5, at a lower heating value of 48 to 55 MJ kg⁻¹, estimated) — which is far above the roughly 0.2 % to 2 % loss rates typical of a maintained gas plant. Either this plant has a major, findable loss, or the 900 t yr⁻¹ figure is wrong, is total gas rather than CH₄, or was transcribed from the coincidentally identical 900 TJ yr⁻¹ energy figure. An error here moves the total by tens of percent (Section 4). Settled by: the plant's leak detection and repair (LDAR) records, a fuel-gas metering balance (purchases and make versus metered burn) over a full year, flare and vent logs, and, if available, a direct measurement campaign (for example optical gas imaging survey records or a site-level airborne measurement) on the actual equipment.
  2. The fuel actually burned is not the fuel behind the default factor. Direction: refinery or process fuel gas richer in heavy hydrocarbons raises CO₂ per GJ above 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹; fuel gas containing substantial hydrogen or inerts lowers it. Rough size: commonly ±5 %, and ±10 % or more for a variable process fuel gas, before any GCV/NCV basis error (a further about 10 %, in one direction). Settled by: the fuel-gas analyser record (online gas chromatograph composition for the actual year) together with the supplier or plant fuel specification, from which a plant-specific carbon factor is computed; and by confirming, from the metering documentation, the calorific-value basis of the 900 TJ yr⁻¹.
  3. Combustion is treated as complete and steady; real burners, pilots, and flares are not. Direction: real operation adds emissions not in the calculation — CH₄ slip from incomplete combustion and unlit or inefficient flares, CO₂ and CH₄ from start-ups, shutdowns, and upsets, and N₂O from combustion — and all act upward. Rough size: normally under 1 % to 2 % of the total for well-run gas firing, but a single poorly performing flare handling a large gas stream can add several percent, and the fugitive/combustion split in the inventory can shift substantially even when the total moves little. Settled by: flare efficiency and pilot-monitoring records, burner and furnace operating logs, and the plant's continuous emissions monitoring records for the actual year.
7. What is not covered (Prompt 5)

Effects not in the model

  • Scope 2 emissions from purchased electricity, steam, or heat; Scope 3 emissions from feedstock production (including upstream CH₄ leakage in the gas supply chain, which for gas can be a substantial fraction of the combustion term), product transport, and product end use.
  • Combustion CH₄ and N₂O (assumed small, Section 4); carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds, which oxidise to CO₂ in the atmosphere; black carbon and other short-lived climate pollutants, which no CO₂e figure of this type represents.
  • Any CO₂ removed, captured, or exported (for example CO₂ sold or sent to storage), and any biogenic fraction of the fuel, which reporting frameworks treat separately.
  • Year-to-year variation: the result is a single-year figure at the stated rates, with no allowance for turnarounds, upsets, or a partial operating year.

Information not visible here

  • The plant's fuel analysis, metering basis, LDAR records, and flare records (plant-held).
  • The exact GWP table and factor set prescribed by the reporting framework that will receive this figure; some frameworks fix values that differ from the latest IPCC values, and those prescribed values are held in the current edition of that framework's documentation, which must be consulted directly.
  • Site-specific emission factors held in restricted databanks or in the plant's own emissions inventory system.

Effects that appear only in running equipment

  • Intermittent large releases, seal and packing degradation between surveys, flare behaviour in wind, and burner fouling (Section 6).

Conditions under which the answer changes by more than 10 %

  • Reporting on a 20-year rather than a 100-year horizon: about +65 %.
  • The true fugitive CH₄ differing from 900 t yr⁻¹ by more than about ±30 % (about ±10 % on the total).
  • A GCV/NCV basis mismatch between the energy figure and the emission factor: about ±7 % on the total, and about ±10 % combined with a modest factor error.
  • Inclusion of Scope 2 or upstream Scope 3 emissions at a plant with large imported power or a high-leakage gas supply: readily more than +10 %, potentially more than +100 %.
  • The fuel being a variable process fuel gas rather than natural gas, with a plant-specific factor differing from the default by more than about 15 %.

Questions a reviewer should ask before the answer is used

  1. Which reporting framework, assessment report, and time horizon fix the GWP for this figure, and is 100-year CO₂e the quantity the recipient expects?
  2. Is the figure Scope 1 only, and is it labelled as such everywhere it appears?
  3. How was the 900 t yr⁻¹ CH₄ figure obtained — measured, metered by difference, or factor-estimated — what is its stated uncertainty, and can the roughly 5 % implied leak rate be reconciled with the plant's metering and LDAR records?
  4. On what calorific-value basis are both the 900 TJ yr⁻¹ and the 56.1 kg GJ⁻¹ stated, and is there a plant-specific fuel factor from the year's actual gas composition?
  5. Does the escaped-gas figure denote pure CH₄ or total gas, and is the CH₄ fossil?
  6. Have flare efficiency, start-up and upset emissions, and combustion CH₄ and N₂O been assessed for this plant, rather than assumed small?
  7. Has every GWP and emission-factor value been checked against the primary sources named in Section 2.2, so that no value in the issued figure remains marked unverified?
